en: The First Chapter of the Treasury.
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!
He who has utterly destroyed all darkness in every way has lifted the world out of the mire of saṃsāra.
Having paid homage to that Teacher of reality, I shall proclaim the treatise known as the Abhidharmakośa. //1//

Desiring to compose this treatise, and for the purpose of making known the majesty of his Teacher, he begins with a salutation preceded by a description of his qualities, starting with the word "He who. Referring to the Buddha, the Blessed One, he says: "One by whom darkness has been destroyed" (*hatāndhakāraḥ*), or "one by whom [darkness] has been destroyed";

thus, one by whom darkness has been destroyed in every way and regarding everything is "one by whom darkness has been destroyed in every respect and regarding everything" (*sarvathāsarvahatāndhakāraḥ*).
Ignorance is indeed darkness because it obstructs the vision of reality as it truly is.

And that [ignorance] has been utterly destroyed in every way and regarding all objects of knowledge by the Blessed Buddha through the attainment of its antidote, such that it is of a nature never to arise again.
Therefore, he is one who has completely destroyed all darkness in every respect.
Even Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas have indeed destroyed the darkness regarding all things, due to the absolute departure of afflicted delusion;
however, this is not in every respect.
For indeed, regarding these Buddha-qualities, as well as objects extremely remote in space and time, and objects of infinite variety, there exists precisely non-afflicted ignorance.

Having thus praised the Blessed One for his perfection in the practice of his own welfare, he praises him again for his perfection in the practice of the welfare of others with the words, "He has lifted the world out from the mire of *saṃsāra*.

For *saṃsāra* is like a mire because it is a place where the world becomes stuck and because it is difficult to cross. Out of compassion for the world submerged therein and without protection, the Blessed One rescued it according to their respective capacities by extending the hand of the teaching of the True Dharma.
Thus: "Having paid homage"—that is, having prostrated with the head—to him who is thus endowed with the perfection of practice for the benefit of himself and others;
he is a "Teacher according to reality" (*yathārtha-śāstṛ*) because he teaches in accordance with reality, without error.
By this, he reveals his means for practicing for the benefit of others.

Because he is a Teacher (śāstṛ) by virtue of teaching according to reality, he has rescued the world from the mire of saṃsāra, and not through the power of supernatural feats or the granting of boons.
Having paid homage to him, [the author] states what he will do: "I shall expound the treatise" (śāstra).
It is called a *śāstra* because it instructs disciples (*śiṣya*).
"What is that treatise? he asks; [the answer is] the *Abhidharmakośa*. What is this so-called Abhidharma?
"Abhidharma is stainless wisdom together with its attendants."
In this context, wisdom (*prajñā*) is the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*). "Pure" means untainted (*anāsrava*);
"with its attendants" means together with its retinue (*saparivāra*).
Thus, it is said that the Abhidharma consists of the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-pañcaskandhaka*).
This, first of all, is the ultimate (*pāramārthika*) Abhidharma; as for the conventional (*sāṃketika*), however—
Furthermore, whatever path leads to its attainment and whatever treatise [leads to it];
and whatever contaminated wisdom (*prajñā*) consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as well as that acquired at birth, together with their attendants;
and whatever treatise is for the sake of attaining this uncontaminated wisdom—because these constitute its equipment (*saṃbhāra*), they too are called Abhidharma.
As for its etymological definition: it is called *dharma* because it maintains (*dhāraṇa*) its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, this is *Abhidharma* because it is directed toward (*abhimukha*) either the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dharma*), which is *nirvāṇa*, or the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*).
Thus, *Abhidharma* has been explained.
But how is this treatise the *Abhidharmakośa*?
Because the Abhidharma has entered into this [treatise] by way of its meaning, and because it is the basis for that [Abhidharma], it is called the *Abhidharmakośa*. (2)
For that Abhidharma, known as the "treatise" (śāstra), is contained within this [work] according to its meaning and its primary importance; thus, this treatise serves as its "sheath" (kośa).
Alternatively, that Abhidharma is the basis (āśraya) of this treatise, for it has been extracted from that very source.
Therefore, since this very [Abhidharma] is its treasury (kośa), this treatise is the *Abhidharmakośa*.
But for what purpose is the teaching of Abhidharma, and by whom was it first taught, such that the Master takes care to speak the *Abhidharmakośa*?
He said:

Since there is no means for the pacification of the afflictions other than the discernment of phenomena, and it is because of the afflictions that the world wanders here in the ocean of existence, this treatise was indeed proclaimed by the Teacher for that purpose. //3//

Since there is no means for the pacification of the afflictions without the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), and since it is the afflictions that cause the world to wander in this great ocean of *saṃsāra*,
it is for that reason— and for the sake of that discernment of phenomena— that the Abhidharma was indeed taught by the Teacher, the Buddha.
"For without the instruction of Abhidharma, a disciple is not able to discern phenomena (*dharmas*).

The Vaibhāṣikas say: "That [Abhidharma], though taught by the Blessed One in a scattered manner, was compiled and established by the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra and others, just as the Venerable Dharmatrāta composed the *Udānavarga*. Furthermore, he asks: "Which are those phenomena for the sake of whose discernment there is the instruction of Abhidharma? He says:
Dharmas are either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*).
This is the summary exposition of all dharmas.
Among these, which are the dharmas with outflows? He says:
Conditioned phenomena, excluding the path,
are with outflows.
With the exception of the truth of the path, all other conditioned phenomena are with outflows.
What is the reason?
Because the outflows (āsrava) adhere to them. //4//

Granted that outflows (āsrava) do arise even with the truths of cessation and the path as their objects, they do not adhere (anuśerate) therein; therefore, there is no consequence of those two being "with outflows" (sāsrava).
How it is that they do not adhere in those cases will be explained later, precisely in the exposition of the adherents (anuśaya).
The [factors] with outflows have been explained.
What are the untainted (anāsrava)?
The untainted are the truth of the path and the threefold unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). What is the threefold?
Space and the two kinds of cessation—
what are these two?
They are cessation through deliberation and cessation not through deliberation.
Thus, these three kinds of unconditioned phenomena—space and so forth—and the truth of the path are the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.
What is the reason?
Because the outflows (āsravas) do not adhere (anuśerate) within them.
Regarding these three kinds of unconditioned phenomena that have been indicated, among them, space is non-obstruction. //5//
Space has the nature of non-obstruction, wherein there is the movement of form.

Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is that which is dissociation; that which is dissociation from contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) is cessation through deliberation. Deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā*) is the discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) of the Noble Truths, such as suffering and so forth; it is a specific kind of wisdom (*prajñā*). Cessation attained by means of that [wisdom] is cessation through deliberation.
This is due to the elision of the middle term, as in the compound *go-ratha* (ox-cart).
But is there only one single analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) for all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena?
He says: "No."
What then? They are distinct. For as many substances as there are of conjunction, so many are there of disjunction.
Otherwise, from the direct realization of the cessation of the afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, there would follow the direct realization of the cessation of all afflictions;
and if this were so, the cultivation of the remaining antidotes would be rendered useless.
As for what was said, "Cessation has no counterpart"—what is the meaning of this?
The meaning of this statement is that it has no similar cause (sabhāga-hetu) whatsoever, nor is it the [cause] of anything; it does not mean that nothing at all is similar to it.
Thus has cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) been explained.
The other kind of cessation, which is the absolute obstruction of arising, occurs through non-analytical means. //6//
Apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha is that cessation other than disjunction which constitutes an absolute obstacle to the arising of future dharmas;
for it is not obtained through analytical discernment (pratisaṃkhyā).
What then?
Due to the deficiency of conditions (*pratyayavaikalyāt*).

For example, when the eye and mind are occupied with a single form, other forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles pass by; it is impossible for the five groups of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*) that would have those as their objects to arise again, because they are not capable of taking a past object as their objective support (*ālambana*).
Therefore, their non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha) is attained due to the deficiency of conditions. In this regard, there are four alternatives:
there are those dharmas for which only analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha) is obtained; [and so forth].

For example, there are those contaminated phenomena of the past and present that are subject to arising, for which there is only non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*). For example, there are those uncontaminated conditioned phenomena that are subject to non-arising (*anutpattidharma*).
There are those for whom both exist, namely, those [dharmas] that are with-outflows (sāsrava) and are of a nature not to arise (anutpatti-dharmin). There are those for whom neither exists.
Namely: those that are past, present, and destined to arise, and which are untainted (*anāsrava*). Thus, the threefold unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has been explained.
As for what was stated— that "conditioned phenomena, excluding the Path,
are with-outflows" (sāsrava)— what are those conditioned phenomena?
Those conditioned phenomena, moreover, are the five aggregates beginning with form (rūpa).

The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness—these are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
They are called "conditioned" because they are produced by conditions coming together and combining;
for there is nothing whatsoever that is produced by a single condition alone.
Because it belongs to that same class, there is no contradiction regarding future things, just as in the case of milk and fuel.
These very [factors] are the time-periods, the bases of discourse, those with departure, and those with a causal basis. //7//
These very conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are called "paths" (*adhvan*) because they have gone, are going, or will go; or alternatively, because they are consumed by impermanence.

"Speech" (*kathā*) means a sentence; its "subject matter" (*vastu*) is a name (*nāman*). However, because it refers to a subject matter that possesses meaning, the conditioned is called the "subject matter of speech" (*kathāvastu*).
Otherwise, the treatise (*prakaraṇagrantha*) would be contradicted:
"The bases of discourse (*kathāvastu*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
Escape (*niḥsaraṇa*) is the departure (*niḥsāra*), which is *nirvāṇa* for all that is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Because these [phenomena] possess that [nature], they are "with departure" (saniḥsāra).
Because they have causes, they are "with a basis" (savastuka).
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the word *vastu* is indeed a synonym for "cause."
These are the synonyms for conditioned phenomena.
Furthermore, those very conditioned phenomena which are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) are the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*); what is established by this?

Those which are the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) would also be aggregates; however, there are aggregates that are not aggregates of clinging, namely, the uncontaminated conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskāra*). In this context, "clinging" (*upādāna*) refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*).
They are called "appropriation aggregates" (upādāna-skandha) because they arise from that [appropriation],
like a fire from grass or chaff;
or because they are subject to it, like a king's servant.
Or, because clinging arises from them, they are called "clinging-aggregates" (*upādānaskandha*), like a tree that bears flowers and fruit.
These very same contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are also called "with strife" (*saraṇa*), for the afflictions (*kleśa*) are indeed the strifes.
They are "with strife" (saraṇa) because they afflict oneself and others, and because they are accompanied by underlying tendencies (anuśaya),
just like the "outflows" (sāsrava).
Furthermore, they are suffering, its origin, the world, the locus of views, and existence. //8//
It is suffering (*duḥkha*) because it is disagreeable to the noble ones (*ārya*).
It is the origin (*samudaya*) because suffering arises from it. It is the world (*loka*) because it is broken (*lūjyate*).
Because view persists within this through its latent tendency (*anuśayana*), it is called a "basis for views" (*dṛṣṭisthāna*).
It is called "existence" (*bhava*) because it comes into being (*bhavati*).
These are the etymological synonyms for contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*).
It has been stated that there are five aggregates, beginning with form. Among those:
form consists of the five sense faculties, the five objects, and also non-informative matter (avijñapti).
The five faculties are the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
The five objects are the respective five spheres of those very faculties, beginning with the eye, known as visible form, sound, odor, taste, and the tangible.
And [the category] is "non-informative" (avijñapti).
This much is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).

Among these, those which have been described as the five objects beginning with form—namely, the eye and so forth—are the translucent forms (rūpaprasāda) that serve as the bases for their respective consciousnesses. //6//

Those five translucent material entities (*rūpaprasāda*) which serve as the bases for the consciousnesses of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects should be understood, respectively, as the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
As the Blessed One said: "O monk, the eye is an internal sense-field (*āyatana*), a translucent materiality derived from the four great elements," and so forth. (1)
Alternatively, regarding those which have been mentioned as the eye and so forth: "the eyes and so forth are translucent forms that serve as the bases for their respective consciousnesses";
the meaning is that they are the bases for visual consciousness and the others.
And by doing so, the *Prakaraṇapāda* treatise is also followed:
"What is the eye?
It is the translucent matter that is the basis of visual consciousness," and so forth.
The five faculties have been explained;
now the five objects are to be explained.
In that regard, first:
Form is twofold: color and shape.
Among these, color is of four kinds, beginning with blue.
The others are its subdivisions. Shape is of eight kinds, beginning with long and ending with irregular.
That very same [aggregate] is further called the sense-sphere of visible form (rūpāyatana).
It is twentyfold, namely: blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, square, circular, high, low, even, uneven, cloud, smoke, dust, mist, shadow, glare, light, and darkness.
Some recite twenty-one [elements], including space as having a single color; therein, *sāta* is even placement, and *visāta* is uneven placement; *mahikā* is mist.
Heat is the radiance of the sun;
light is the radiance of the moon, stars, fire, medicinal herbs, and gems;
shadow is that wherein forms are perceived.
From the opposite, there is darkness;
the remainder is not elaborated upon because it is easy to understand.
There is the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) that exists by way of color (*varṇa*) but not by way of shape (*saṃsthāna*);
it is known as blue, yellow, red, white, shadow, glare, light, and darkness.
There is [visible form] that exists by way of shape but not by way of color.
The portion of [the category of] length and so forth that has the nature of bodily intimation exists in both ways;
the remainder is the sense-sphere of visible form.
Others maintain that "only heat and light exist as color," for "the demarcation of length and so forth is indeed seen in blue and other colors."
But how can a single substance exist in both ways?
Because both [aspects] are perceived therein.
For this verb *vid* has the sense of "knowing," not the sense of "existence."
In that case, the same consequence would apply to bodily intimation as well.
Thus, the sense-sphere of form has been explained.
Sound is of eight kinds:
it is fourfold, being caused by the primary elements (mahābhūta) that are either appropriated or non-appropriated, and being designated as either sentient or non-sentient;
this, further, becomes eightfold through the distinction between the agreeable and the disagreeable.
Among these, that which has appropriated primary elements as its cause is, for example, the sound of the hand or speech;
that which has unappropriated primary elements as its cause is, for example, the sound of wind, forest trees, or a river;
and that which is designated as a sentient being is the sound of vocal intimation.
Another [type of sound] is called non-sentient (*asattvākhya*).
Others maintain that there is also sound caused by both appropriated (*upātta*) and unappropriated (*anupātta*) primary elements (*mahābhūta*),
such as that produced by the conjunction of a hand and a drum.
But just as a single atom of color is not accepted as being derived from two sets of the four primary elements, so too it should not be accepted in this case.
Sound has been explained.
Taste is sixfold,
distinguished as sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent.
Odor is of four kinds, due to the distinction between pleasant and unpleasant odors, and between even and uneven odors;
however, in the treatise, it is said to be of three kinds.
"Fragrant, foul-smelling, and neutral-smelling"—the tangible consists of eleven types. //10//
The tangible has the nature of eleven substances:
the four great elements, smoothness, roughness, heaviness, lightness, cold, hunger, and thirst.
Among these, we shall explain the elements later.
Smoothness is softness;
roughness is harshness;
heaviness is that by which things are weighed.
Lightness is the opposite [of heaviness].
Coldness produces the desire for warmth. Hunger produces the desire for food. Thirst produces the desire for drink.
This is because the effect is metaphorically attributed to the cause; as it is said: "The arising of Buddhas is blissful; the teaching of the Dharma is blissful."
"Happiness is the concord of the Saṃgha; for those who are in harmony, austerity is happiness. In that regard, in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), hunger and thirst do not exist;
the remainder exists.
Although in that place garments do not weigh the same when individual, they do weigh the same when accumulated.
There is no harmful cold;
indeed, there is beneficial [cold].

Regarding this manifold form that has been described, visual consciousness arises at times from a single substance when there is a discernment of its specific type; it arises at other times from many substances when there is no such discernment.
This is as, for example, when one sees from a distance an array of troops with various colors and shapes, or a collection of jewels.
In the same way, the consciousnesses of the ear and so forth are to be understood.
However, some maintain that body-consciousness arises at most from five types of tangible objects:
the four great elements and one [quality] such as smoothness.
Others say that [the five consciousnesses] arise from all eleven [bases].

But if this is so, since they would have a collective object (*samastālambana*), it follows that the five groups of consciousness would have general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) as their objects, rather than particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

There is no fault here, because these are held to have particular characteristics as their objects with respect to the particular characteristic of the sense-field (*āyatana-svalakṣaṇa*), and not with respect to the particular characteristic of the substance (*dravya-svalakṣaṇa*).
This is now investigated:
when the objects of the body and tongue faculties are reached simultaneously, which consciousness arises first?
That whose object is more intense.
When the objects are encountered simultaneously, however, tongue-consciousness arises first,
because the mental continuum is inclined toward the desire to eat.
Thus have been explained the five sense-faculties and their objects, as well as the manner of their apprehension.
Now, non-informative matter (avijñapti) must be explained; it is described as follows:

that serial continuity, whether wholesome or unwholesome, which exists even for one whose mind is distracted or who is without mind, and which is derived from the great elements—this indeed is called non-informative matter. (11)
"Of one whose mind is distracted" means also of one whose mind is directed toward something else.
"Also of one who is without mind" means also of one who has entered the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
By the word "also," it is understood that this applies even to one whose mind is undistracted and well-composed.
"Continuity" (*anubandha*) refers to a stream (*pravāha*).
"Pure or impure" (*śubhāśubha*) means wholesome or unwholesome.
Since such a stream also exists for acquisitions (*prāpti*), it is stated "derived from the great elements" (*mahābhūtānyupādāya*) in order to distinguish it [from that].
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that "derived" means "having a cause," because it functions as a cause for production and so forth.
The word "for" (hi) is used to indicate the reason for applying that name, namely, that it is indeed non-informative (avijñapti).
Although it has the nature of form and action, it is called "non-informative" (*avijñapti*) because, unlike informative action (*vijñapti*), it does not inform another.
The phrase "it is said" indicates that this is the statement of the Master [Vasubandhu].
In brief, however, non-informative action is wholesome or unwholesome form produced by informative action or meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
It has been stated that [the derived forms] exist "depending upon the great elements" (*mahābhūtāny upādāya*). What are these elements?
The elements are the earth element, the water, fire, and air elements.
These four are called the "great elements" (*mahābhūtāni*) because they maintain their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and maintain derived form (*upādāyarūpa*).
Their "greatness" (mahattva) is due to their coarseness (audārikatva), as they serve as the substrata for all other forms;
or alternatively, it is because they possess a vast configuration (mahāsanniveśa) within the aggregates of earth, water, fire, and air when their activity is manifest.
Furthermore, in what function are these elements established, and what is their intrinsic nature (svabhāva)? To this he says:
The elements of earth, water, fire, and air are fully established in their respective functions of supporting, cohesion, maturation,
and expansion; furthermore, "expansion" should be understood as growth and spreading.
This is their function;
their intrinsic natures, however, are respectively solidity, moisture, heat, and motion. (12)
Hardness is the earth element;
moisture is the water element;
heat is the fire element.
The wind element is motion (*īraṇā*). It is called motion because by means of it the stream of primary elements is moved to arise in other locations, like the movement of a flame.
In the *Prakaraṇapāda* and in the Sūtra, it is stated: "What is the wind element? It is lightness and mobility."
That lightness is also described as a form derived from primary matter (*upādāyarūpa*) in the *Prakaraṇas*.
Therefore, that phenomenon whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is motion is the wind element (*vāyudhātu*); thus, its intrinsic nature is made manifest by its function (*karman*).
What, then, is the distinction between earth and so forth, and the earth element and so forth? Earth is said, according to worldly convention (*lokasaṃjñā*), to be color and shape.
For instance, when demonstrating earth, one demonstrates its color and shape;
as it is with earth, so it is with water and fire.
It is merely color and shape that are designated by the worldly convention as "wind";
however, that which is the wind-element is precisely what is called "wind" in the world.
And yet, moreover: //13//
Just as the earth is called "color" and "shape" according to worldly convention, so too is the wind [described] as "a blue whirlwind" or "a circular whirlwind.
Why, then, is this [collection], ending with the unmanifest (avijñapti), called the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha)?
Because of being affected (*rūpaṇa*).
It was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, it is affected, it is affected; therefore it is called the aggregate of clinging to form (*rūpopādānaskandha*).
By what is it affected?"
"Even when touched by the touch of a hand, it is affected," and so forth. "Is affected" means it is afflicted. For it is said thus in the *Arthavargīya*:
"If those desires of that embodied being who longs for them and is filled with longing do not come to fulfillment, he suffers as if pierced by a thorn.
But what is the affliction of form?

Others say that "form" (*rūpaṇā*) consists in transformation, production, and resistance. In that case, however, the form of an atom would not qualify as "form," because it lacks the quality of being formed.
Indeed, a single atom as a distinct entity does not exist; rather, it is only when situated in an aggregate that it possesses form. In that case, however, past and future form would not be included.
That too is matter (rūpa), like fuel, because it has been manifested, will be manifested, or belongs to that same category.
In that case, however, non-informative matter (avijñapti) would not be included;
yet even that is manifested through the manifestation of informative matter (vijñapti).
It would be like the movement of a shadow when a tree moves;
[but this is not so] because there is no such modification.

Furthermore, upon the cessation of the manifest action (vijñapti), there would have to be a cessation of the unmanifest action (avijñapti), just as there is an absence of shadow when the tree is absent.

Others say: "Because its basis is subject to transformation (*rūpaṇā*). [Objection: "In that case, it would follow that visual consciousness and the others are also *rūpa*, because their bases (the sense organs) are subject to transformation.
[Response: "This comparison is unequal.
For non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) exists depending upon the primary elements (*bhūta*), just as a shadow depends on a tree or light depends on a gem."

Visual consciousness and the others do not exist in dependence upon the eye and so forth in that manner; rather, those [faculties] serve merely as the causes for their arising. This view, however, is not that of the Vaibhāṣikas, who maintain that "shadow exists in dependence upon a tree" and "radiance exists in dependence upon a gem," because they admit that the atoms of color such as shadow each depend upon their own set of four primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Moreover, even though shadow and light are dependent on their respective bases, it is not tenable for non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) to be dependent in that same way;
for it is admitted that non-informative matter does not cease even when its bases, the great elements (*mahābhūta*), have ceased.
Therefore, this is not a valid rebuttal.
Others, however, offer this rebuttal here: the bases of visual consciousness and the others have become differentiated;
some, such as the eye and so forth, are material (rūpyate), while others, such as the mind, are not material.
But non-informative matter (avijñapti) is not like this;
therefore, the consequence is not the same. Thus, it is established that it is called "matter" (rūpa) because its basis is subject to transformation (rūpaṇā).
Those very faculties and objects that have been described as having the nature of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) are intended to be the ten bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu).
In the systematic arrangement of the bases, they constitute the ten bases.
The eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), the form-base (*rūpa-āyatana*), up to the body-base (*kāya-āyatana*) and the tangible-base (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*).

In the systematic arrangement of the elements (*dhātu-vyavasthāna*), these same [bases] are the ten elements: the eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*), the form-element (*rūpa-dhātu*), up to the body-element (*kāya-dhātu*) and the tangible-element (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*).
Thus has the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) been explained, along with its systematic arrangement as bases and elements.
Feeling and the other [aggregates] must now be explained.
Among them, feeling is experience.
The aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is a threefold experience:
pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
When further divided, it consists of the six groups of feeling: feeling born of eye-contact, up to feeling born of mind-contact.
Perception has the nature of grasping signs. // 14 //
The apprehension of signs such as blue, yellow, long, short, woman, man, friend, enemy, pleasure, pain, and so forth—this is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
When further divided, it consists of six groups of perception, just like feeling (*vedanā*).
The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), however, consists of those formations other than the four [aggregates].
That is to say, the formations other than the four—form, feeling, perception, and consciousness—are the aggregate of formations.
Yet, in the Sūtra, the Blessed One stated that there are "six groups of volition" (*ṣaṭ cetanākāyāḥ*) because of their predominance.
For that [volition] is primary in the process of conditioning because its very nature is karma;
therefore, the Blessed One said: "It conditions the conditioned; for that reason, it is called the appropriated aggregate of formations."

For otherwise, because the remaining mental factors (*caitasika*) and dissociated factors (*viprayukta*) would not be included within the aggregates (*skandha*), they would not constitute the truths of suffering and its origin; consequently, there would be neither full comprehension (*parijñā*) nor abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
And it was said by the Blessed One: "I do not say that there is an end to suffering without having directly known and fully comprehended even a single dharma.
Likewise, it was said: "[without] abandoning [it] in this way. Therefore, one must necessarily accept that these are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).

Furthermore, these three— the aggregates of feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and mental formations (saṃskāra)— are designated as the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) and the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu) in the classification of spheres and elements, together with unmanifest form (avijñapti) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). // 15 //
These seven substances are designated as the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the constituent of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Consciousness is the individual representation;
the representation, or apprehension, of each respective object is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
Furthermore, that consists of the six groups of consciousness, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness.
This very aggregate of consciousness that has been described is, in the classification of the bases (*āyatana*),
the mind-base (*manāyatana*); and in the classification of the elements (*dhātu*), it is likewise that same [element].
The elements are also considered to be seven.
Which seven?
The six consciousnesses and, moreover, the mind. (16)
The eye-consciousness element, up to the mind-consciousness element, and the mind element.
Thus, herein the five aggregates (skandhas), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the eighteen elements (dhātus) are explained.
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), excluding unmanifest form (avijñapti), constitutes ten bases and ten elements.

The three aggregates beginning with sensation (vedanā), along with unmanifest form and the unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), constitute the base of mental objects (dharmāyatana) and the element of mental objects (dharmadhātu). The aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) constitutes the mind base (manaāyatana), the six consciousness elements (vijñānadhātu), and the mind element (manodhātu).
But has it not been stated that the six groups of consciousness constitute the aggregate of consciousness?
Then what is this mind-element (manodhātu) other than them? Indeed, there is nothing else.
What then?
Among those very six [consciousnesses], the consciousness that has just passed away is the mind (manas).
Whatever consciousness has ceased in immediate succession is called the mind-element (manodhātu).
Just as that very same son becomes the father of another, so too that very same fruit becomes the seed of another.

If that is so, then in terms of substantial entities (*dravyataḥ*), there would be either seventeen elements (*dhātu*)—due to the mutual inclusion of the six consciousness-elements and the mind-element—or twelve; why, then, are eighteen established?
Even though this is the case, the elements are traditionally taught as eighteen for the purpose of establishing a basis for the sixth [consciousness]. (17)
For the five consciousness-elements, there are five supports, namely the eye-element and so forth.
For the sixth, the mind-consciousness-element, there is no other support;
therefore, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) was taught in order to establish its support.
Thus, through the establishment of these sixfold sets of basis, based [consciousness], and object, there come to be eighteen elements (dhātus).
"In that case, the final mind of an Arhat would not be the *manas*,
for there exists no [subsequent mind] of which it could be the immediately preceding past.
No.
Because that [consciousness] also exists in the form of the mental faculty (*manas*),
the subsequent consciousness does not arise due to the deficiency of other causes.
In this regard, the inclusion of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) is by means of the aggregates (*skandha*);

the inclusion of all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) is by means of the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*); and the inclusion of all phenomena (*dharma*) is by means of the bases (*āyatana*) and the elements (*dhātu*). However, it should be understood in brief as follows:
The inclusion of all [phenomena] by means of one aggregate, one base,
and one element should be understood as follows: the inclusion of all phenomena is accomplished by the aggregate of form, the mind base, and the dharma-element.
Indeed, wherever this summary is stated, it should be understood as being by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and not by way of extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*).
What is the reason? Because of the dissociation from other-nature. // 18 //
For a phenomenon is indeed dissociated from that which is other than itself;
therefore, it is not logical for it to be subsumed by that very thing from which it is dissociated.
For example, the eye-faculty is subsumed by the aggregate of form, by the sense-base and element of the eye, and by the truths of suffering and its origin.
Because it has that as its intrinsic nature,
and because it is devoid of the existence of other aggregates and so forth;

however, when the inclusion of one thing by another is spoken of— such as the inclusion of assemblies by the means of attraction— that should be understood as merely conventional, since it occurs only occasionally.
[Objection: But surely there ought to be twenty-one elements, because the eyes are two, as are the ears and the nostrils. [Response:
There need not be.
Because the genus, the object-field, and the consciousness are common, the eye and the other [faculties] constitute a single element (*dhātu*), even though they exist as pairs.
In this regard, there is a commonality of genus because both have the nature of the eye;
a commonality of domain because both have visible form as their object;
and a commonality of consciousness because both serve as the basis for the same visual consciousness.
Therefore, the eye-element is indeed one;
the same should be applied to the ear and the nose as well.
However, they arise as pairs for the sake of beauty. (16)
However, although the eye and so forth each constitute a single element (*dhātu*), they occur as pairs for the sake of the beauty of their physical basis;
for otherwise, due to the occurrence of only a single location for the eyes and ears and a single nostril cavity, there would be great ugliness.
The aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) have thus been explained.
However, this must be stated: what is the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha), "base" (āyatana), and "element" (dhātu)?
Aggregates, bases, and elements have the meanings of "heap," "gate of arrival," and "lineage," respectively.
"Whatever form there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior..."

Because of the statement in the Sūtra, "Whether it be inferior or excellent, whether far or near, all that, having been gathered together into one, receives the designation 'aggregate of form' (rūpaskandha)," it is established that the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha) is the sense of a "heap" (rāśi).
Among these, past form is that which has ceased through impermanence.
The future is that which has not yet arisen;
the present is that which has arisen but not yet ceased.
The internal is that which belongs to one's own continuum; the external is other than that, or [distinguished] by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*).
The gross is characterized by resistance, while the subtle is non-resistant; alternatively, they are relative.
If it is argued that [the distinction] is unestablished because of its relativity, we say no.
This is due to the difference in relativity:
that which is coarse in relation to something else can never be subtle in relation to that same thing, just like a father and a son.
That which is inferior is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*).
That which is sublime is undefiled;
that which is distant is the past and future;
that which is near is the present.
Thus it continues up to consciousness;
however, this is the distinction:
that which is based on the five sense-faculties is coarse, while that which is mental is subtle.
Or "according to the stages," say the Vaibhāṣikas.

The Venerable One said: "Gross form is that which is apprehended by the five sense faculties; subtle is the other. Inferior is what is unpleasant; superior is what is pleasant. Distant is that which is in an invisible location."
"Near" refers to the visible location.
Since past [time] and so forth are expressed by their own respective terms,
feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [aggregates] should be understood in the same way.
Their state of being distant or near, however, is due to the influence of their bases;
their grossness or subtlety is as previously described.

The meaning of "base" (*āyatana*) is the sense-gate through which mind and mental factors arise. As for its etymological derivation: they are called bases (*āyatanāni*) because they extend (*tanvanti*) the arrival (*āyam*) of mind and mental factors; that is to say, they cause them to expand.
The meaning of *gotra* is the meaning of *dhātu*.

Just as in a single mountain there are many *gotras*—such as iron, copper, silver, gold, and so forth—which are called *dhātus*, so too within a single basis (*āśraya*) or continuum (*saṃtāna*), there are eighteen *gotras* which are called the eighteen *dhātus*.
In this context, the word *gotra* refers to mines (*ākara*).
Of what are these— the eye and so forth— the sources? Of their own kind, because they are homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).
"In that case, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) would not be a constituent element (dhātu).
To this, others reply: "In that case, this word *dhātu* denotes the genus (*jāti*) of mind and mental factors;
the eighteen constituents are the eighteen genera or intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of the eighteen phenomena."

If the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha) were the same as the meaning of "heap" (rāśi), it would follow that the aggregates are merely conceptual existents (prajñaptisat), because they are collections of multiple substances, like a heap or a person (pudgala).
This is not so.
Because even a single substantial atom (dravya-paramāṇu) constitutes a "heap" (skandha),
it cannot be said that the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha) is the sense of a "pile";
for a single thing does not possess the nature of a pile.
Others maintain that the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) is the bearing of the burden of what is to be done, or else it has the sense of "cutting off.
For instance, speakers say: "We shall give the gift in three installments (*tribhiḥ skandhaiḥ*)."
This [interpretation] deviates from the sūtra.
For the sūtra declares that the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha) is precisely that of a "heap," stating at length: "Whatever form there is—past, future, or present," and so forth.
In that [sūtra], it is made known that each individual instance of past and other forms constitutes an aggregate.
All this, beginning with the past and so forth, is form; each individual instance is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
It is not possible to understand it in this way, because of the statement: "having condensed all that into a single unity."
Therefore, like a heap, the aggregates exist only as designations.
In that case, it follows that even the material sense-bases (āyatana) would exist only as designations,
because they consist of many atoms of the eye and so forth acting as gateways for the arrival [of objects].
No;
because the totality [of conditions] acts as the cause individually, or because the sense organ functions in cooperation with its object, the sense organ would not be a separate *āyatana*.
However, it is stated in the *Vibhāṣā*: "If an Abhidharma master takes into account the designation (*prajñapti*) of the aggregates..."
He said: "An atom is a portion of one element, of one sense-base, and of one aggregate.
Then, [if] it does not depend [on these], he said:
"A single atom is one element (dhātu), one sense-base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha).
Indeed, even with respect to a part, there is a metaphorical designation (upacāra) as if it were the whole, just as when one part of a cloth is burned, one says "the cloth is burned.
For what purpose does the Blessed One undertake this threefold teaching by way of the aggregates and so forth?
He said: Because those to be trained possess a threefold variety in terms of delusion, faculties, and inclinations, there are three teachings: the aggregates and so forth. (20)
"Threefold" means of three kinds. It is said that the delusion of sentient beings is of three types:
some are deluded regarding mental factors because they grasp at them as a unified self.
Some [belong] to form alone;
some to both form and mind.
The faculties are also of three kinds.
Because their faculties are sharp, middling, or dull,
inclination is also threefold,
due to an inclination toward concise, middling, or extensive texts.
For them, respectively, there are the three teachings on the aggregates (skandha), the bases (āyatana), and the elements (dhātu).

"What, then, is the reason that while the other mental factors (*caitasika*) are placed together within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are made into separate aggregates? To this he says:

Because they are the roots of dispute and the causes of *saṃsāra*, and for the sake of establishing a specific order, feeling and perception are established as separate aggregates from among the mental factors. (21)
There are two roots of dispute:
attachment to sensual desires and attachment to views.
Of these two, feeling and perception are, respectively, the primary causes.

For it is through the power of relishing feeling that one clings to sensual desires, and through the power of perverted perception that one clings to views; these two are thus the primary causes of saṃsāra. For one who is greedy for feeling and possesses perverted perception wanders in saṃsāra.

Furthermore, because of the reasons for the sequence of the aggregates that will be taught, one should understand that these two are established as separate aggregates from those reasons for the sequence;
this we shall demonstrate in three ways.
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are not mentioned among the aggregates because they do not accord with their meaning.
For that [unconditioned element], when discussed among the aggregates, cannot be subsumed within these very [five] because it does not correspond to their meaning;
for it is neither form, nor anything up to consciousness.
Nor can a sixth aggregate be asserted;
why?
Because it is logically untenable.
It has been stated that "the meaning of *skandha* is the meaning of 'heap' (*rāśi*).

However, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not differentiated by distinctions such as past and so forth in the same way that form (*rūpa*) and other [conditioned phenomena] are; therefore, it cannot be designated as an "unconditioned aggregate" (*asaṃskṛtaskandha*) by collecting all of it together into a single mass.

Indeed, the term "appropriation-aggregate" (*upādānaskandha*) is used for the purpose of making known the basis of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), whereas the term "aggregate" (*skandha*) is used for the purpose of making known both the bases of affliction and purification (*vyavadāna*).
Since it is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in either way, and because [the definition] would be logically inconsistent, it is not established among them.
Others maintain that just as the cessation of a jar is not the jar itself, so too the cessation of the aggregates cannot be the aggregates.
For them, this same consequence would apply to the elements (dhātu) and the bases (āyatana).
Thus has another classification of the aggregates been explained.
Furthermore, the sequence [of the aggregates] is according to their relative grossness, the order of defilement, the analogy of a vessel and so forth, and the elements of existence. (22)
For form is coarse because it possesses resistance;
among the formless [aggregates], feeling is coarse by way of its manifest activity, for people designate it thus: "I have a feeling in my hand," or "I have a feeling in my foot."

Furthermore, perception (*saṃjñā*) is coarser than two [of the other aggregates], and formations (*saṃskāra*) are coarser than consciousness (*vijñāna*); therefore, that which is coarser was mentioned first.
Alternatively, in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), men and women take delight in one another’s forms, and this is due to their craving for the taste of feeling (*vedanā*).
Craving for that [existence] arises from the perversion of perception;
that perversion arises from the afflictions, and the mind is defiled by them—thus the sequence follows the order of defilement.
Alternatively, it is according to the analogy of the vessel and so forth.
For the aggregates, beginning with form, are like the vessel, the food, the condiments, the cook, and the eater; or alternatively, from the perspective of the realms:
the desire realm is characterized by the forms that constitute the objects of sensual pleasure.
The meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are characterized by feeling;
the three formless attainments (ārūpya) are characterized by perception;
and the peak of existence (bhavāgra) is characterized by formations alone.

These very [four] are the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), and consciousness is established within them; thus, the sequence of the aggregates (*skandha*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the field and the seed.
For this very reason, there are five aggregates, neither fewer nor more.
And for this same reason of the sequential order, feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are made into separate aggregates from among the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Because these are the more gross causes for the sequence of afflictions, serving as the vessel and the condiment, and because the two realms are manifested by them.
The sequence of the six bases and elements, beginning with the eye, must be explained;
for it is precisely by virtue of that [sequence] that the sequence of their corresponding consciousnesses and objects is established.
Furthermore, regarding those same six:
First, the five [faculties] beginning with the eye were mentioned earlier because they have present objects; that is, because their objects are restricted to the present.
The mind, however, has unrestricted objects.
Some have the present as their object, and some have the three times or the non-temporal as their object. The phrase "the four [mental] groups consisting of derived matter" applies to what precedes.
Furthermore, among the five [senses], four have been previously mentioned [as having external objects],
because they have derived matter as their object;
however, the object of the body is not fixed.
Sometimes [the sense organs perceive] the primary elements (bhūta), sometimes the derivative matter (bhautika), and sometimes both;
the others function more slowly than the rest.
Furthermore, the remainder is described as being "prior" in accordance with their respective functions of acting at a distance or more rapidly.
For the eye and the ear have distant objects;
therefore, they were mentioned before the other two.
Between those two as well, the activity of the eye extends to a more distant range.
Even when seeing a river from a distance, one does not hear its sound; therefore, that [the ear] was mentioned before it.
However, the nose has no functioning at a distance, nor does the tongue.
Because these two function more rapidly, the nose is mentioned first, since it perceives the odor of food even before the tongue has reached it;
or else, the order follows their respective locations. // 23 //
Alternatively, in this body, the seat of the eye is situated at the top;
below that is the seat of the ear;
and below that is the seat of the nose.

Therefore, [the order] is according to their location: first the tongue, then the body because it occupies the greatest extent, and finally the mind, which is dependent on those very [senses] and has no fixed location. Thus would be their sequence.

What, then, is the reason that among the ten bases (āyatana) subsumed under the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), one alone is called the base of form (rūpāyatana), and among all things whose nature is phenomena (dharma), one alone is called the base of phenomena (dharmāyatana)? He says:
for the sake of distinction, because of its preeminence, and because it includes many supreme phenomena.
One base is called form, and one is called the dharma-base. // 24 //
How is it for the sake of specification?

It is so that it may be understood that each of these ten possesses the status of an *āyatana* individually, by virtue of being established as object (*viṣaya*) and subject (*viṣayin*), and not collectively.

Furthermore, since that which is not designated as "eye" and so forth—namely, form (*rūpa*)—will be known as the "form *āyatana*" once distinguished by the [terms] "eye" and so on, no other name is stated for it.
Alternatively, it is because of the predominance of the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*); for that, being characterized by resistance (*sapratighatva*),
is "formable" (*rūpyate*) when touched by the contact of hands and so forth.
And because it is visible (*sanidarśana*);
for it can be specified as "this is here" or "that is there," and in the world, too, it is recognized as being of such a nature, whereas the others are not.
Furthermore, it is precisely for the sake of distinction that only one base, the *dharmāyatana*, is mentioned and not all of them; moreover,
since many phenomena such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth are included therein,
they are designated by the general term "dharma."
And it is here that the supreme dharma of nirvāṇa is subsumed, and not in others.

Others maintain that the single sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is established as such because it is gross due to its twentyfold variety, and because it is the object of the three types of eyes: the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the noble eye of wisdom.

Other things designated as aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are also found in the sūtras. Should they be understood as being included within these [five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements] alone, or are they distinct from them?
They are included within these alone; they are not distinct.
In that regard, first:
The eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma that the Sage proclaimed—these are either speech or names; they are included within the [aggregates of] form and mental formations. (25)
For those for whom the word of the Buddha has speech as its intrinsic nature, these are subsumed within the aggregate of form;
for those for whom it has name as its intrinsic nature, they are subsumed within the aggregate of formations.
Furthermore, what is the measure of a *dharmaskandha*?
Some say it is the measure of the treatise (*śāstra*).
First, some maintain that its measure is that of this very Abhidharma treatise known as the *Dharmaskandha*.
And that consists of six thousand [verses]. Others, however, say that it is a discourse on each of the aggregates and so forth individually.

The discourse on each of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), truths (*satya*), nutriments (*āhāra*), meditations (*dhyāna*), immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), formless attainments (*ārūpya*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), and absence of strife (*araṇā*), etc., is individually called a "dharma-aggregate" (*dharmaskandha*).
However, it is described that the dharma-aggregate is actually the antidote to [specific] conduct (*caritapratipakṣa*). (Verse 26)
Thus, they describe eighty thousand types of conduct among sentient beings,
distinguished by the variations of their conduct such as passion, hatred, delusion, pride, and so forth.
As an antidote to these, the Blessed One taught eighty thousand aggregates of dharma (*dharmaskandha*).
Just as these eighty thousand aggregates of dharma (dharmaskandha) are established within these very five aggregates,

so too should other aggregates, bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) be established as appropriate within those already mentioned, after having carefully considered their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa). //27//

Furthermore, whatever other aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are mentioned in other sūtras, they too are to be subsumed within these very aggregates and so forth as already described, after having carefully determined their respective characteristics as established in this treatise.

Among them, first, of the five aggregates of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*), the aggregate of ethical discipline is included within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
The remaining [totalities] are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Of the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), eight—because their intrinsic nature is non-greed (*alobha*)—are included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

However, when accompanied by their attendants (*saparivāra*), they consist of the five aggregates and are thus included within both the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Likewise, the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are included:

the two totalities (*kṛtsna*) of infinite space and infinite consciousness, as well as the four beginning with the sphere of infinite space, have the four aggregates as their intrinsic nature and are therefore included within the spheres of mind (*manāyatana*) and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
The five spheres of liberation (*vimuktyāyatana*), having wisdom as their intrinsic nature, are included within the sphere of mental objects.
Together with their retinues, they are comprised of the spheres of sound, mind, and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Of the two [remaining] spheres, the beings without perception (*asaṃjñisattva*) consist of ten spheres, because of the absence of the spheres of odor and taste.
Those who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanopaga*) consist of the spheres of mind and mental objects.
In the same way, sixty-two elements are taught in the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*;
their inclusion within [the eighteen elements] should be understood according to their respective correspondence.

Regarding these six elements mentioned there—the earth element, water element, fire element, wind element, space element, and consciousness element—the characteristics of two of them have not been stated.
Should one understand that space itself is the space element, and that all consciousness is the consciousness element?
He says: No.
What then?
It is the aperture in the doors, windows, mouth, nose, and so forth, which is called the space element (ākāśadhātu).
What is to be understood by that which is called a "cavity"?
It is said to be light and darkness;
for no cavity is perceived apart from light and darkness.
Therefore, it is said that the space element (ākāśadhātu) should be understood as having light and darkness for its intrinsic nature, and as having night and day for its intrinsic nature;
and that very same [element] is called "matter neighboring the impenetrable" (aghasāmantaka-rūpa).
It is said that "impenetrable" (agha) refers to matter that is accumulated.
Because it is extremely destructive;
thus, it is the "neighborhood" (*sāmantaka*) of that [space].
Others say: it is "evil" (*agha*) because other matter does not encounter resistance there, and it is the "neighborhood" (*sāmantaka*) of other matter.
The consciousness element is consciousness that is with-outflows; why is it not said to be without-outflows?
Because these six elements are intended [to be with-outflows].
The bases of birth. //28//
For these [elements] serve as the common basis for everything from the mind at the moment of rebirth-linking up until the mind at the moment of death;
however, untainted (anāsrava) phenomena are not like this.

Thus, among these, four elements are included within the tangible element (spraṣṭavyadhātu), the fifth is included within the form element (rūpadhātu), and the sixth is included within the seven consciousness elements (vijñānadhātu).

Furthermore, among these eighteen elements that have been mentioned, how many are with demonstration (*sanidarśana*) and how many are without demonstration (*anidarśana*)? Here, one is with demonstration, namely form (*rūpa*), for it can be demonstrated as being "here" or "there. It follows by implication that the remaining ones are without demonstration.
How many are with resistance and how many are without resistance?
Ten are with resistance;
they are the material [elements].

Those ten elements which have been mentioned as being comprised within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) are characterized by resistance (sapratigha). "Resistance" means obstruction; and it is of three kinds: obstruction as hindrance (āvaraṇa-pratighāta), obstruction regarding the object-field (viṣaya-pratighāta), and obstruction regarding the objective support (ālambana-pratighāta).
In this context, obstruction by resistance (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*) is the prevention of another's arising in one's own location;
for example, a hand is obstructed by another hand or by a stone,
and a stone likewise [obstructs] those two.
The obstruction of the object refers to the sensory faculties, such as the eye and so forth, being obstructed by their respective objects, such as visible forms and so forth.
As it is stated in the *Prajñapti*: "There is an eye that is obstructed in water but not on land, such as that of fish."
It exists on land but not in water,
as is generally the case for humans;
it exists in both places.
For crocodiles, frogs, piśācas, fishermen, and so forth,
there is neither;
setting aside these cases.
There is an eye that is obstructed at night but not by day,
such as that of bats, owls, and the like;
[there is also one] that is obstructed by day but not at night.
Generally, for humans,
as well as for dogs, jackals, horses, leopards, cats, and so forth, [it occurs] both by night and by day.
"Not in both cases;
setting aside these modes" refers to this resistance regarding the object (*viṣayapratighāta*).
Resistance regarding the focal object (*ālambanapratighāta*) pertains to the mind and mental factors with respect to their own respective focal objects.
What, then, is the distinction between an object (*viṣaya*) and an objective support (*ālambana*)?
That in which something exercises its activity is its object;
that which is grasped by the mind and mental factors is the objective support.
But how, then, is it said that [the mind] is obstructed while operating upon its own object or focal point?
It is because it does not operate beyond that;
or rather, "obstruction" here refers to the very act of operating within its own domain.
In this context, the ten [elements] should be understood as having resistance (*sapratighatva*) by way of obstruction and impact (*āvaraṇapratighāta*), because they obstruct one another.

Regarding those factors (*dharmas*) that have resistance by way of resistance to objects (*viṣayapratighāta*), there is a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) concerning whether they also have it by way of obstruction and impact.
The first alternative consists of the seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*) and that portion of the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*) which is associated (*saṃprayukta*).
The second consists of the five objects;
the third consists of the five faculties;
and the fourth consists of a portion of the dharma-element, excluding those factors associated with consciousness.

Those dharmas which are "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) by way of resistance toward an object (*viṣaya-pratighāta*) are they also [with resistance] by way of resistance toward an objective support (*ālambana-pratighāta*)?
This is the "consequent" (*paścātpādaka*).
First, those that are with resistance by way of resistance toward an objective support are necessarily also with resistance by way of resistance toward an object.

The five sense faculties (pañcendriya) are characterized solely by resistance with respect to their objects (viṣaya-pratighāta), and not by resistance with respect to their cognitive objects (ālambana-pratighāta). As it is said: "That wherein the mind, as it is about to arise, can be resisted by others—that alone should be known as 'with resistance' (sapratigha); by contrast, the opposite is held to be 'without resistance' (apratigha)."
The Venerable Kumāralāta.
Those that are with resistance and those without resistance have been explained.
Among these eighteen elements, how many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate?
Eight are indeterminate.
Which eight?
Those ten which were stated to be with resistance (sapratigha) are the same [elements], excluding visible form and sound. // 26 //
The five sense-faculties and the elements of odor, taste, and tangibles—

these eight are indeterminate because they cannot be defined as being either wholesome or unwholesome. Others maintain that they are indeterminate because they cannot be defined in terms of their maturation (*vipāka*).
In this way, the same consequence would apply even to that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
The other ten elements are of three kinds: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
Among them, the seven mental elements are wholesome when associated with non-attachment and the other [wholesome roots].
Those associated with greed and so forth are unwholesome;
others are indeterminate.
The dharma-element is wholesome when it has as its intrinsic nature or association the absence of greed and so forth, or when it is produced [by such states], as well as analytical cessation.
That which is associated with and originated from the nature of greed and so forth is unwholesome;
others are indeterminate.
The elements of visible form and sound, when originated by wholesome or unwholesome minds, are wholesome or unwholesome, being comprised within bodily and vocal intimation.
The other two are indeterminate.
The nature of [the dharmas] as wholesome and so forth has been explained.
Among these eighteen elements, how many belong to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and how many belong to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*)?
All those obtained in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) are acquired and not dissociated; this means they are bound to the desire realm. In the form realm (rūpadhātu), there are fourteen.
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are fourteen elements (dhātu), excluding the elements of odor, taste, olfactory consciousness, and gustatory consciousness. (30)
For in that realm, odor and taste do not exist;
since these two constitute edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), and those who are free from passion for such food are reborn there,
the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses also do not exist there.
Because of the absence of an objective referent.
If that were so, it would follow that the element of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) would also be absent there,
because it consists of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
That which does not have the nature of food exists there.
This same consequence applies to odor and taste as well:
there is no enjoyment of odor and taste without ingestion;
however, there is enjoyment of the tangible through its function as the support for the sense faculties, as clothing, and as sustenance.
Therefore, for those who are free from desire for food, smell and taste are useless there, but not so the tangible.
Others, however, say: "By relying on the meditative attainments (*dhyāna-samāpatti*), forms are seen here and sounds are heard;
and the body is sustained by a specific tangible quality accompanied by pliancy (*prasrabdhi*)."
Therefore, it is only these three that are possible upon rebirth in the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), but not odor or taste.
If that were so, it would follow that the sense-faculties of the nose and tongue do not exist, because they would be purposeless.
But there is a purpose; for without those two, [the body] could not...
And there would be the following contradiction: "The beauty of the locus itself would not exist.
If this were the purpose, let there be only the locus for the sake of beauty and for the sake of articulation; let there be no sense-faculty.
However, a locus that is not a sense-faculty is impossible.
It is like the physical basis of the male organ;
its non-occurrence is logical because it serves no purpose,
whereas the physical bases of the olfactory and gustatory organs do serve a purpose.
Therefore, its arising is possible even without a sense faculty;
furthermore, the production of a sense faculty occurs even when it serves no purpose,
as in the case of those destined to die in the womb.
Granted that [the arising of the faculties] may be purposeless, it cannot be without a cause.
And what is the cause for the arising of the faculties?
It is a specific karma of one who possesses craving for the faculties.
And since one who is free from craving for an object is necessarily so regarding the sense faculty as well,
it is not possible for the olfactory and gustatory faculties to arise in those who have abandoned attachment to their respective objects.
Or rather, why would the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) not also be produced?
Because it would cause ugliness;
for what would not be beautiful in those whose private parts are concealed within a sheath?
Furthermore, their arising does not depend upon utility.
What then? By the power of causes, even that which produces ugliness would certainly arise when the cause is present. In that case, however, the Sūtra is contradicted.
Regarding the phrase "complete, with unimpaired faculties":
what contradiction is there in saying they possess unimpaired faculties by means of whatever faculties exist therein?
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the male faculty would also [be required].
However, they describe it thus:
the faculties of smell and taste do indeed exist there, but not their objects, odor and flavor;
for craving operates with respect to the six sense bases by way of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), not by way of the external objects.
But in the case of the male faculty, it is by way of the touch of sexual intercourse.
Therefore, it is established that fourteen elements belong to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
The mind-element (*manodhātu*), the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) pertain to the formless realm (*ārūpyāpta*).

Since those who are free from passion for form are born there, the ten elements whose intrinsic nature is form, as well as the five consciousness-elements that have them as their basis and objects, do not exist there.
How many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?

These three— the mental faculty element (*manodhātu*), the phenomena element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*)— which have been mentioned, are both with outflows and without outflows.
Those factors included within the truth of the path and the unconditioned are untainted (anāsrava); others are tainted (sāsrava). The remaining ones, however, are tainted. // 31 //
The remaining fifteen elements, however, are exclusively with outflows.
How many are with vitarka and with vicāra? How many are without vitarka and with vicāra only? How many are without vitarka and without vicāra?
The five consciousness-elements (vijñānadhātu) are indeed with vitarka and vicāra;
these are always associated with both vitarka and vicāra.
The word "hi" has the sense of restriction.
The last three are of three kinds;
the mind-element (manodhātu), the mental-object-element (dharmadhātu), and the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu) are the last ones,
and these three are of three types.

In that regard, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), and the associated portion of the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*)—excluding initial thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*)—are accompanied by both initial and sustained thought (*savitarkāḥ savicārāḥ*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and in the first dhyāna.
In the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), they are without initial thought and possess only sustained thought (*avitarkā vicāramātrāḥ*).
From the second dhyāna up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), they are without both initial and sustained thought (*avitarkā avicārāḥ*).
The entire unassociated dharmadhātu and vicāra in the intermediate dhyāna [are without vitarka].
Vitarka, however, is always without vitarka and consists of vicāra alone, because of the absence of a second vitarka and because of its association with vicāra.
Vicāra in the desire realm and in the first dhyāna is not included within these three categories.
How should it be described?

It is "without investigation and with only initial mental application" (avitarko vicāramātraḥ), because of the absence of a second investigation and because of its association with initial mental application.
Therefore it is said: "In the stage that is with applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savichāra*), there are four types of phenomena (*dharma*):
those associated [with mind] which possess both applied and sustained thought, excluding [the factors of] sustained thought and applied thought themselves;
applied thought, which is without applied thought but possesses only sustained thought; [and the remaining two]."
"Without applied thought and without sustained thought, they are unassociated;
[the second dhyāna] is without sustained thought and consists of applied thought only; [the third dhyāna] is sustained thought."
The remaining [dharmas] are devoid of both. //32//
The ten material elements and the remaining [elements] are always without vitarka and without vicāra, because they lack application.
If the five groups of consciousness possess both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), how can they be said to be non-conceptual?
They are non-conceptual with respect to the conceptualization of investigation (*nirūpaṇa-vikalpa*) and the conceptualization of recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*).
It is said that there are three kinds of conceptualization.
There are the conceptualizations of intrinsic nature, investigation, and recollection;
among these, they possess the conceptualization of intrinsic nature, but not the other two.
Therefore, they are called "non-conceptual.
This is just as a one-legged horse is called "legless.
In that context, conceptualization by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavikalpa*) is discursive thought (*vitarka*).
That will be explained later among the mental factors (*caitta*).
As for the other two, however, what is their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?
[They are] respectively:
Those two are distracted mental wisdom; all memory whatsoever is mental.
Wisdom associated with the mental consciousness is called "mental";
when not in a state of meditative concentration, it is called "distracted.
For that is the conceptualization of investigation (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*).
All mindfulness, whether concentrated or unconcentrated, is indeed mental; it is the conceptualization of recollection.
How many have an object (sālambana) and how many are without an object (anālambana)? Seven consciousness-elements (cittadhātu) have an object:

the visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, mental-consciousness elements, and the mind-element. These seven consciousness-elements have an object because they grasp their respective domains.
And half [of the dharma-element] is by its very nature;
that which has an object is of the nature of mental factors.
It is established that the remaining ten material elements and the portion of the dharma-element that is dissociated [from mind] are without objects.
How many are appropriated and how many are non-appropriated?
Nine are non-appropriated;
which nine?
Those seven which were said to have objects of cognition, together with half of the eighth—
these eight, along with sound,
these nine are non-appropriated.
The seven mind-elements, the dharma-element, and the sound-element [are exclusively internal];
the other nine are of two kinds. (34)
They are both appropriated and non-appropriated.
Among them, the present eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body are appropriated;
those of the past and future are non-appropriated.
The present elements of visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility that are inseparable from the sense faculties are appropriated (*upātta*).

Others are non-appropriated (*anupātta*), such as those found in hair, body hair, nails, and teeth—excluding their roots—as well as in feces, urine, saliva, nasal mucus, blood, and so forth, and in earth, water, and the like.
What is the meaning of "appropriated"?

That which is appropriated by the mind and mental factors as their basis, because they conform to one another through benefit and injury, is what is called "sentient" in the world. How many elements have the nature of primary matter (*bhūta*), and how many are derived from primary matter (*bhautika*)?
Tangible objects are of two kinds: the primary elements and the derivative matter. Among these, the primary elements are four.
The derivative [matter] consists of seven types, such as smoothness and so forth,
because it exists within the primary elements.
The remaining nine material [dharmas] are derivative.
The five sense-faculty elements and the four objects—
these nine elements are exclusively derived matter,
as is one portion of the dharma-element.
That which is designated as non-informative (avijñapti) is derived from the primary elements;
the remaining seven mental elements (cittadhātu) and the dharma-element (dharmadhātu), excluding non-informative matter, are neither of the two [types].
The Venerable Buddhadeva maintains that the ten bases consist of the primary elements alone;
however, this is not so, because the Sūtra determines that the primary elements are fourfold, characterized by solidity and so forth, and because they are of the nature of the tangible.
For hardness and the other [tangible qualities] are not grasped by the eye and the other [faculties], nor are color and the other [visible qualities] grasped by the body-faculty.
And it is said in the Sūtra: "O Bhikṣu, the eye is an internal sense-field, derived from the four great elements, a translucent form, invisible and possessing resistance; and so on up to the body.
O Bhikṣu, visible forms are an external sense-field, derived from the four great elements, possessing form, visible and possessing resistance."
"Sound, O monk, is an external sense-field; it is derived from the four great elements, is material, invisible, and offers resistance.
The same applies to odors and tastes.
Tangibles, O monk, are an external sense-field; they consist of the four great elements and are derived from the four great elements, are material, invisible, and offer resistance."

Since the primary elements (*bhūta*) are included only within a portion of the sense-field of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), it is clearly demonstrated that the remainder are not primary elements.
