As for what was stated in the Sūtra— "that which is hard and possesses hardness in the lump of flesh in the eye"—
this is a teaching concerning the lump of flesh which exists inseparably [from those elements].
The statement in the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*, "O monk, this person consists of six elements," is for the purpose of demonstrating the fundamental substance of a sentient being;
furthermore, because of the subsequent mention of the six bases of contact (*sparśāyatana*), there would otherwise follow the absurd consequence that mental factors (*caitta*) do not exist.
Moreover, it is not tenable to maintain that the mind itself is the mental factors.
Because of the statement in the Sūtra, "Perception and feeling are mental factors; this phenomenon is dependent upon the mind," and because of the mention of "the mind with passion" and so forth,
the elements and their derivatives possess the nature of being primary elements and derivative matter, as previously stated.
How many are accumulated and how many are non-accumulated? Ten material [elements] are accumulated. (35)
The five sense-faculty elements and the five objects are aggregated,
because they consist of a collection of atoms.

Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), who cuts and who is cut? Who burns and who is burned? Who weighs and who is weighed? Only the four external elements—designated as form, odor, taste, and the tangible, and known as the axe, the wood, and so forth—both cut and are cut.
What is this phenomenon called "cutting"?
It is the production of a division in a stream of composite matter that arises in connection [with its parts].
The body-faculty and so forth are not cut.
Because even when the limbs are severed without remainder, there is no bifurcation of those [faculties];
for the sense-faculties do not become twofold,
since a severed limb is devoid of sense-faculties.
Nor do they cut [it],
because it is as clear as the luster of a jewel.
Just as the four external elements cut and are cut, burn and weigh, so too do they burn and weigh themselves;
but the sense faculties do not, because of their transparency, like the luster of a gem.
Sound is not [the self], because it is subject to cessation.
There is a dispute regarding the two [qualities] of burning and being equal. // 36 //
Some say that those same four elements are both the burner and the weighed; others say that the fire element alone is the burner, while heaviness alone is what is weighed.

[How many elements are born of maturation (*vipākaja*), how many are accumulative (*aupacayika*), how many are outflowing (*naiḥṣyandika*), how many are substantial (*dravyayukta*), and how many are momentary (*kṣaṇika*)?
He said:
Five internal [elements] are born of maturation and are accumulative.]
First, regarding the internal [elements], the five elements beginning with the eye are born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and accumulative (*aupacayika*);
they are not outflowing (*naiḥṣyandika*),
because there is no outflow distinct from those two.
In this context, those things born from a ripening cause (*vipākahetu*) are called "born of ripening" (*vipākaja*),
by the elision of the middle term, as in the word "ox-cart" (*goratha*). Alternatively, karma that has reached the time of its fruition is itself called "ripening."
Because it is that which ripens;
therefore, those things born from it are "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
But since maturation itself is the fruit, it is called "maturation" (*vipāka*).
Or let there be a metaphorical designation of the fruit for the cause, just as there is a metaphorical designation of the cause for the fruit—as in:
"These six spheres of contact are to be understood as past karma."
Those produced by accumulation (*aupacayika*) are those nourished by specific types of food, refinement, sleep, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
some say they are also nourished by celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
However, by that [celibacy] there would be merely a lack of impairment, not actual accumulation.
The stream of accumulation acts as a protection for the stream of maturation, like an outer wall.
Sound is both accumulative and outflowing;
sound is not born of maturation.
What is the reason? Because activity proceeds from volitional effort (*īhā*).

As for what is stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*: "Because of the thorough cultivation of abstaining from harsh speech, the mark of a Great Man consisting of a Brahma-like voice (*brahmasvaratā*) is produced."
Some say this is a threefold sequence:
"for from actions come the elements, and from the elements comes sound.
Others say it is a fivefold sequence.
For from karma arise the great elements born of maturation (*vipākaja*); from those, the accumulative (*aupacayika*) ones; from those, the outflowing (*naiḥṣyandika*) ones; and from those, sound.
If that were so, then even bodily sensation would not be considered maturation, because it arises from great elements produced by karma—unless, like sound, there were a contradiction with reason.
The eight non-obstructive [elements] are both outflowing and born of maturation. // 37 //
Which eight?
The seven mind-elements and the dharma-element.

Those that are outflowing (*naiḥṣyandika*) are produced by the similar-cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive-cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*). Those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) are produced by the maturation-cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
There are no accumulative [forms] among those that are non-resistant, because there is an absence of accumulation.
The others are of three kinds;
the remaining four— the elements of visible form, taste, odor, and tangibility—
are born of maturation (*vipākaja*), accumulative (*aupacayika*), and outflowing (*naiḥṣyandika*).
One is substantial:
for the unconditioned is a substance because of its essentiality;
and since that exists within the dharma-element, the dharma-element alone is endowed with substantiality.

The last three are momentary: the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mental-object-element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*). These are the "last" according to the order of recitation.

They are called "momentary" because, for a single moment, they are non-outflow (*anaḥsyandika*) within the first untainted complex of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣāntikalāpa*). Thus, they are said to be momentary.
There is no conditioned phenomenon produced by anything other than [its own causes] that is not of the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*).

In that regard, the mind associated with the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) is the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); the remaining co-existent factors are the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*).
This is investigated:
Is one who acquires possession of the eye-element (cakṣurdhātu) also [simultaneously] acquiring possession of the eye-consciousness-element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu),
or is one who [acquires] the eye-consciousness-element also [simultaneously] acquiring possession of the eye-element?
He said:
There may be the acquisition of the eye and the visual consciousness element either separately or together. (38)
First, there may be one who possesses the eye-element but not the eye-consciousness-element:
namely, one in the desire realm gradually obtaining the eye-faculty,
or one passing away from the formless realm and being reborn in the second or higher meditative absorptions.
There may be one who possesses the eye-consciousness element but not the eye element:
namely, one born in the second or higher dhyānas who brings eye-consciousness into manifestation, or one who has passed away from there and is being reborn in a lower realm.
There may also be one who simultaneously acquires possession of both.
One who has passed away from the formless realm and is being reborn in the desire realm or the Brahma-world;
and neither [of these],
excluding these cases.
One who is endowed with the eye-element (cakṣurdhātu) is also endowed with the eye-consciousness-element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu)?
This is a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika).
The first alternative is one born in the second or higher dhyānas who does not bring eye-consciousness into manifestation.
The second [category] consists of one who has not obtained or has lost the eye in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The third consists of one who has obtained and not lost the eye in the desire realm, or one born in the first dhyāna, or one born in the second dhyāna or above, while seeing.
The fourth consists of those who exclude these aforementioned modes.

In this way, the acquisition (*pratilambha*) and possession (*samanvāgama*) of the eye-element and the form-element, as well as of the eye-consciousness-element and the form-element, are to be inferred accordingly.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate this discussion, as in the phrase "even together with. How many elements are internal (*ādhyātmika*) and how many are external (*bāhya*)?
Twelve are internal.
Which twelve? Excluding the six consciousnesses such as form and so forth, the six bases are these twelve internal elements.
The six objective spheres, beginning with form, are external.
Since a self does not exist, how can there be anything internal or external?
Because it is the basis for the conceit of "I," the mind is metaphorically designated as the "self."
It has been said: "By means of a well-tamed self, the wise person attains heaven";
and elsewhere, the Blessed One spoke of the taming of the mind.
“The taming of the mind is good; a tamed mind brings happiness.

Therefore, because the eyes and other [faculties] are proximate by virtue of being the support for the mind—which has become the self—they are internal; whereas form and other [objects], by virtue of being objects, are external.
If that were so, then the six consciousness-elements would not qualify as internal;
for these do not become the support of the mind until they have attained the state of the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
At whatever time [they become the support], they remain those very same things and do not transcend their defining characteristic.
Otherwise, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) would exist only in the past, not in the future or the present;
yet the eighteen elements are accepted as belonging to all three time periods.
Furthermore, if future and present consciousness did not possess the characteristic of the mind-element, the mind-element could not be established even in the past time.
For there is no deviation of the characteristic from the time-periods.
How many elements (dhātu) are homogeneous (sabhāga), and how many are partially homogeneous (tatsabhāga)?
First, that which is designated as the "dharma" element is exclusively [homogeneous].

The "homogeneous" (sabhāga) is that object which is fixed for a particular consciousness; if that consciousness has arisen with respect to it, or is destined to arise, that object is called homogeneous.
And there is no part of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) where infinite mental consciousness has not already arisen or will not arise.
For indeed, this thought necessarily arises in all noble persons (āryapudgala): "All phenomena (dharmas) are without self.
And for that [thought], all phenomena—being free from its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and its co-existent factors—are the object (ālambana).
Furthermore, since that moment of consciousness is itself the object of another moment of consciousness, all phenomena indeed become the object across two moments.
Therefore, the dharma-element is always homogeneous;
the remaining [elements] are both "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga) and "homogeneous" (sabhāga), which is why the word "and" (ca) is used.
What is this so-called "homogeneous" (tatsabhāga)? It is that which does not perform its own function. (36)
What is meant is this: that which performs its own function is "homogeneous" (sabhāga).
In this context, that eye by which one has seen, sees, or will see forms is called "functioning" (sabhāga) vision.
The same should be stated for the others up to the mind, according to their own activity regarding their respective objects.
According to the Kaśmīris, that functioning eye is of four kinds:
That which has ceased without having seen forms, that which is ceasing, that which will cease, and that which is of a nature not to arise—these constitute the fivefold category for those of the West.
Furthermore, that very same category of what is of a nature not to arise is divided into two: that which is associated with consciousness and that which is dissociated from consciousness.
In this same way, it should be understood up to the body;
however, the mind is exclusively "of the same class" (tatsabhāga) as that which is subject to non-arising.
Those forms which one has seen, sees, or will see with the eye are "homogeneous" (sabhāga).
Those that are "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga) are of four kinds:
those which have ceased, are ceasing, or will cease without ever having been seen, and those whose nature is not to arise at all.
In this manner, up to the tangible objects,
they should be understood as being "homogeneous" (sabhāga) or "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga) according to the functioning of their respective sense faculties.
When the eye of one person is "functioning" (sabhāga), it is so for all;
likewise for that which is "non-functioning" (tatsabhāga).
This applies similarly up to the mind.
As for visible form (*rūpa*), that which one person sees is "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) for them; for one who does not see it, it is "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*).
What is the reason?
For there is the possibility that a visible form which one person sees may also be seen by many, as in the case of viewing the moon, a dancer, or a wrestler.
However, it is impossible for two people to see with a single eye;
therefore, because this [eye] is not common [to both], its establishment is by virtue of a single continuum.
But because visible form is common, its establishment is by virtue of multiple continua.
Just as it is with the element of visible form, so too should the elements of sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects be understood.
"Let it be so for sound.

However, as for odors and the rest, those which are perceived by one person are not perceived by another, because they are apprehended through contact; thus, due to their specific nature, it is logical to extend the same rule to them as to the eye and the other sense organs.
This is indeed so, yet even these possess commonality with respect to their occurrence."
For there is this possibility: those very same odors and so forth that produce olfactory consciousness and the rest for one person may also produce them for others;
but it is not so with the eyes and other sense organs.
Therefore, these [organs] are treated by analogy with visible forms and the other objects.

The visual consciousnesses and so forth possess the state of being homogeneous or partially homogeneous, depending on whether they are subject to arising or non-arising, just as in the case of the mind-element.
What is the meaning of "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*)?

"Part" (*bhāga*) refers to the mutual sharing among the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness, or the sharing of their functional activity (*kāritra*). That which possesses this [part] is "homogeneous."
Or, it is because they have the same effect as contact (*sparśa*).

Furthermore, those which are non-homogeneous (*asabhāga*) are called "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*) because they share the state of being homogeneous with those [factors] that are homogeneous by virtue of their commonality of genus (*jātisāmānya*).
How many elements are to be abandoned by seeing, how many are to be abandoned by cultivation, and how many are not to be abandoned?
First, the ten material elements are to be abandoned by cultivation, as are five others.
The elements of consciousness:
the last three are of three kinds—
the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.

These three elements, according to the order of their enumeration, are of three types. The eighty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), along with their co-existent factors, their acquisitions (*prāpti*), and their attendants, are to be abandoned by vision (*darśanaheya*).
The remaining contaminated (*sāsrava*) factors are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).
The uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) factors are not to be abandoned.

But is it not the case that there are other things to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), such as the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) and the bodily and vocal actions leading to the miserable destinies (*āpāyika*), because they are in opposition to the Noble Path?
It is not the case that these are to be abandoned by vision;
for this is the summary [of the matter].
That which is non-afflicted is not to be abandoned by vision, nor is form;
there is nothing whatsoever that is non-afflicted and to be abandoned by vision, nor is form such.
Furthermore, the state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) is non-afflicted and neutral.
Because even those whose roots of merit are severed and those who are free from passion possess that [form], form consists of bodily and vocal action;
therefore, it is not to be abandoned by seeing.

Furthermore, because there is no misconception regarding the truths, and because it would follow that one would still be an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) during the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
Nor is it produced from that which is not the sixth. //40//
The sixth is said to be the sense-base of the mind (*manāyatana*).

Therefore, that which is born from elsewhere—namely, that which is not born from the sixth and that which is born from the five [physical] faculties—is also not to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaprahātavya*).
Among the eighteen elements (dhātu), how many are views (dṛṣṭi) and how many are not views?
The eye and a portion of the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu) are views. As to which that portion is, he says:
It is eightfold:

the five views beginning with the view that the effect exists in the cause (*satkāryadṛṣṭi*), worldly right view, the view of one in training (*śaikṣī dṛṣṭi*), and the view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣī dṛṣṭi*). This eightfold *dharmadhātu* is "view"; the remainder is not view.
Among these, the explanation of the view that the effect exists in the cause and the others will occur at the appropriate time during the exposition of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Furthermore, mundane right view (*laukikī samyagdṛṣṭi*) is wholesome, contaminated wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The uncontaminated view of one in training (*śaikṣa*) is "view of one in training" (*śaikṣī*), and that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is "view of one beyond training" (*aśaikṣī*).

The vision of phenomena (*dharmadarśana*) by means of these views—mundane afflicted and unafflicted, as well as those of one in training and one beyond training—is like seeing forms at night and during the day, whether under cloudy or cloudless skies.

Now, why is it said that mundane right view is associated exclusively with mental consciousness? Because wisdom arising simultaneously with the five [sensory] consciousnesses is not "view," due to its lack of investigative judgment. (41)
For a view (*dṛṣṭi*) is investigative because it functions through close examination;
however, the wisdom (*prajñā*) co-arising with the five sensory consciousnesses is not like that, and thus it is not a view.
For this very reason, other wisdom as well—whether afflicted or unafflicted—is not a view.
Now, if the eye does not possess the capacity for investigation (*asamtīraka*), how can it be "seeing"?
It is so called in the sense of the observation of form (*rūpālocana*).
For:
The eye sees forms;
if it were the eye that saw, then even one who is possessed of another consciousness would see.
It is certainly not the case that every eye sees.
Rather,
it sees when it is "homogeneous" (sabhāga) and possessed of consciousness; at other times, it does not.
If that is the case, then let it be that the very consciousness supported by the eye sees;
it is not the consciousness supported by [the other sense organs] that sees.
It can be determined that [the eye] sees.
What is the reason?
Because a form that is not obstructed is indeed seen. //42//
For it is said that a form obstructed by walls and the like is not seen.
If consciousness were the seer, then because it is non-obstructive, there would be no resistance against walls and such; thus, one should see even a concealed form.
However, visual consciousness does not arise with respect to what is concealed; how then can that which has not arisen see?
What indeed does not arise?

For one who holds that the eye sees, because the eye possesses resistance (*sapratighatva*), there is an absence of activity with respect to what is obstructed; thus, the non-arising of consciousness is logical, since it functions upon the same object as its basis (*āśraya*).
But is the eye actually one that reaches its object (*prāptaviṣaya*), like the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), such that it would not see what is covered?
Because it possesses resistance (*sapratighatva*),
how is it that an object obstructed by glass, a film of clouds, crystal, or water is still seen?
Therefore, it is not because of the eye's possession of resistance that an obstructed form remains unseen.
What then?

Where there is no obstruction to light, even when a form is concealed, visual consciousness certainly arises there. But where there is an obstruction, it does not arise; because it has not arisen, one does not see what is concealed.

[As for what was said in the Sūtra, "having seen forms with the eye," the intended meaning here is "by means of that basis," just as it says, "having cognized phenomena with the mind," yet the mind does not cognize phenomena.]
Because it has passed away;
what then?
It is the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
Alternatively, the action of that which is supported is metaphorically attributed to its support,
as in the expression "the beds cry out," and as it is said in the Sūtra: "forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable and lovely."
And those [forms] are not cognized by the eye.

It is said in the Sūtra: "The eye, O Brahmin, is merely a gateway for the seeing of forms. From this it is understood that consciousness sees through the gateway of the eye; in the act of seeing, the term "gateway" is applied there.
This is not tenable:
that "the eye is the seeing for the purpose of seeing forms. If consciousness sees, then what is it that cognizes? And what is the distinction between these two?
For that which is the cognition of form is itself its seeing.
Just as a certain kind of wisdom is said both to "see" and to "understand," so too a certain kind of consciousness is said both to "see" and to "cognize."
Others, however, say: "If the eye sees, one must explain what other act of seeing there is for the eye, which has become the agent.
This objection is not to be raised.
For if it is maintained that consciousness cognizes, yet there is no distinction between agent and action in that case,
the same applies here as well.
Others, however, say: "Visual consciousness is the seeing; because it is the basis for that [seeing], the eye is said to see, just as a bell is said to ring because it is the basis for the sound."
But if this is so, does it not follow that because the eye is the basis of consciousness, "the eye cognizes"?
It does not so follow;
for in common worldly usage, it is that consciousness which is conventionally established as "seeing."
For when that [eye-consciousness] has arisen, it is said that "form is seen," not that it is "cognized.
It is also stated in the *Vibhāṣā*: "That which is reached by the eye and experienced by eye-consciousness is called 'seen'.
Therefore, it is simply said that "the eye sees," not that it "cognizes."
Consciousness, however, is said to cognize form by its mere presence, just as the sun is called the "maker of the day."
On this point, the Sautrāntikas say:
"Why is this space being gnawed at?
For it is in dependence upon the eye and visible forms that visual consciousness arises."
In that regard, who sees or what is seen?
For this is devoid of activity, being merely phenomena and merely cause and effect.
In this context, conventional designations are applied at will for the sake of worldly discourse.

One should not become attached to the idea that "the eye sees" or "consciousness cognizes," for the Blessed One has said: "One should not adhere to local dialects, nor should one pursue the common designations of the world."
This, however, is the established tenet (*siddhānta*) of the Vaibhāṣikas of Kaśmīra:
"The eye sees, the ear hears, the nose smells, the tongue tastes, the body touches, and the mind cognizes.
Now, if it is the eye that sees, does it see forms with one eye or with both?
There is no fixed rule here;
one sees with both eyes because of the clarity of vision.
The Abhidharmikas maintain that one sees with both eyes.
For instance, when both eyes are open, the vision is much clearer; however, when one eye is opened and the second is half-closed, there occurs the perception of two moons and so forth,
not because of any alteration in one of the eyes.
Nor does it follow that consciousness would be subject to interruption due to the separation of its basis, because—unlike material form—it is not localized in space.

[If it is the case that the eye sees, the ear hears, and so on up to the mind cognizes, do these [faculties] have an object that is reached (*prāpta*) or one that is not reached (*aprāpta*)? The eye, ear, and mind have objects that are not reached;
for instance, one sees a form from afar, yet one does not see the collyrium applied to the eye.]
One hears sound from a distance;
and if these faculties were restricted to reaching their objects, then the divine eye and ear would not arise here for those practicing meditation,
just like the nose and the other [senses].

If the eye does not reach its object, why does it not see everything that is not reached, such as distant things or those obstructed by barriers? In the first place, why does a magnet not attract all iron that is not in contact with it?
This same objection applies even if the eye were to have an object that it reaches.
Why does it not see everything with which it comes into contact, such as collyrium or an applicator stick?

And just as for the nose and other [senses], the object is one with which there is contact, yet not everything [is perceived], because they do not apprehend the odor and so forth that coexist [with the object].
In this way, the eye also does not reach its object, yet it does not [perceive] everything.
The mind, however, because it is formless, is incapable of reaching [an object] at all.
Some, moreover, consider the ear to have both reached and unreached objects as its domain.
Because sound is heard even within the interior of the ear.
The remaining three, known as the nose, tongue, and body, are otherwise. (43)
The meaning is "having reached its object.
How is the sense of smell one that has reached its object? Because odor is not perceived by one who is breathless.
What is this so-called "attainment"?
It is uninterrupted arising.
Furthermore, do atoms touch one another or not?
The Kashmiris maintain that they do not touch.
What is the reason?
If they were to touch with their entire being, the substances would become commingled; if they were to touch by way of a single part, it would follow that they possess parts,
yet atoms are partless.
How, then, does the production of sound occur?
Precisely for this reason: if they were to touch, a hand struck by a hand would stick to it, and a stone [struck] by a stone [would stick].
Why, then, does a mass [of atoms], when struck, not shatter apart?
Because it is sustained by the wind element:

some wind elements function for the purpose of dispersal, as during the period of destruction (*saṃvartanī*), while others function for the purpose of sustaining, as during the period of evolution (*vivartanī*).
How, then, is it said that the triad [of sense organs] has reached its object through uninterrupted contact?
Their very state of being "uninterrupted" is simply that there is nothing at all between them.
Furthermore, since aggregates possess parts, they do indeed touch; thus, there is no fault.
And by taking it in this way, this passage in the *Vibhāṣā* also becomes logical.

After posing the question, "Does that which is touched arise from a cause that is touched, or rather from a cause that is not touched? it says: "It depends on the cause. Sometimes that which is not touched arises from a cause that is touched, as when [an object] disintegrates."

"Sometimes that which is touched has a cause that is not touched, as when it undergoes accumulation; sometimes that which is touched has a cause that is touched, as when there is an accumulation of things that have already accumulated; and sometimes that which is not touched has a cause that is not touched, as in the case of dust in a window-beam.
The Venerable Vasumitra says: "If atoms were to touch one another, they would persist into the subsequent moment."
"But they do not touch [one another] even when there is no interval; however, the designation 'touched' is used," says the Bhadanta.
And the opinion of the Bhadanta is to be accepted.
For otherwise, what would obstruct the movement of atoms that have intervals between them through those empty spaces,
given that they are held to be resistant?
Moreover, aggregates are not something other than the atoms themselves.
It is those very aggregates that are touched, just as they are perceived through their resistance.
Furthermore, if a distinction of spatial parts is imagined for an atom, then whether it is touched or untouched, the consequence follows that it must possess constituent parts;
if not, then even the case of being touched does not entail such a consequence.

Furthermore, do these [senses], beginning with the eye, grasp an object equal in size to themselves— such that mountains and the like appear as a circle of fire due to rapid movement— or do they grasp objects both equal and unequal?
Regarding those which were stated to reach their objects, it is held that by these three, beginning with the nose, there is the grasping of an object equal in size.
For as many atoms as there are in the sense organ, so many atoms of the object come together to produce consciousness.
However, in the case of the eye and the ear, there is no fixed rule;
sometimes they are fewer, as when one sees the tip of a hair.
Sometimes they are equal when one sees a grape fruit;
sometimes they are greater when one sees a massive mountain with the mere opening of the eyes.
The same should be applied to the hearing of sounds such as mosquitoes or thunderclouds by means of the ear.
Since the mind is indeed formless, its measurement or spatial limitation is not determined.
Furthermore, what is the arrangement of these atoms of the sense-faculties, such as the eye?
To begin with, the atoms of the visual faculty are situated in the pupil of the eye like cumin flowers;
however, being covered by a transparent membrane, they do not scatter.
Others maintain that they are situated like a cluster of balls, arranged one above the other;
yet they do not obstruct one another because they are as transparent as crystal.
The atoms of the auditory faculty are situated within the interior of the ear-cavity.
The atoms of the olfactory faculty are situated inside the nose like a probe;
the first three faculties are arranged like a garland;
and the atoms of the gustatory faculty are shaped like a half-moon.
It is said that [the faculty] on the middle of the tongue is the size of a hair-tip, not pervaded by the atoms of the tongue-faculty.
The atoms of the body-faculty are situated like the body itself.
The atoms of the female faculty are like the hollow of a drum.
The atoms of the male faculty are like a thumb.
In that regard, the atoms of the eye-faculty are sometimes all functioning (sabhāga),
sometimes all non-functioning (tatsabhāga), and sometimes some are functioning while others are non-functioning;
this remains the case up to the atoms of the tongue-faculty.
However, not all atoms of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) are "functioning" (*sabhāga*).
For even among those beings confined within the blazing hells, immeasurable atoms of the body-faculty are "non-functioning" (*tatsabhāga*).
It is said that if consciousness were to arise through all [atoms] simultaneously, the physical basis (*āśraya*) would disintegrate.
Furthermore, neither a single sensory atom nor a single object atom produces consciousness,
because the five groups of consciousness have accumulated bases and objects as their conditions.
For this very reason, an atom is non-demonstrable, since it is invisible.

Regarding these six consciousness-elements that have been mentioned—ranging from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—is their support (āśraya) the same as their object? For the five [consciousnesses], the object is present, whereas for the last one, it belongs to all three times.
He says: "No. What then?
The support of the last [consciousness] is past;
for the mental consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), the mind that has just ceased is the support.
For the five [sensory consciousnesses], it is also simultaneous with them. //44//
The word "and" (ca) implies "also past.
In this regard, the eye is the simultaneous support (*sahaja-āśraya*) of eye-consciousness, and so on, up to the body being the support of body-consciousness.
Furthermore, the mind (*manas*) is their past support; thus, these five groups of consciousness have two types of faculties as their supports.
Therefore it is said: "That which serves as the basis for visual consciousness also serves as its immediately preceding condition. This involves four alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).
The first alternative is the eye.
The second [category] is the mental factors (caitasika) of the dharma-sphere that have just passed away; the third is the mind (manas) that has just passed away;
the fourth alternative consists of those phenomena (dharmas) excluded from what has been mentioned.
In this manner, it should be stated up to the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) that its own respective faculty is its basis.
For mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the preceding term applies:
that which serves as its basis also serves as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

It may be that [the mental factors] exist by way of being the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), but not by way of being the basis (*āśraya*). For the mental factors that have just passed away constitute the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

Furthermore, what is the reason that, although the arising of consciousness depends upon both [the sense organ and the object], only the eyes and so forth are called the bases, and not visible forms and so forth?
Because they undergo change according to the changes in those [bases], the eyes and so forth are the supports;
this is the governing rule for the term "elements" (*dhātu*).

For when there is a change in the eyes and so forth, there is a corresponding change in their respective consciousnesses, because [the consciousnesses] conform to the benefit, injury, acuity, or dullness [of the senses]; however, such a change does not occur in them due to a change in visible forms (*rūpa*) and so forth.

Therefore, because they are dependent upon them, those [faculties] alone are the bases (*āśraya*), and not form and the other objects. What, then, is the reason that while form and the others are cognized by them, it is called "eye-consciousness" up to "mind-consciousness," and not "form-consciousness" up to "dharma-consciousness"?
Since these bases, such as the eye and so forth, are their uncommon [causes], consciousness is designated by them. //45//
In what sense is it unique?
For the eye is not capable of serving as the support for any other consciousness;
whereas visible form serves as the object of mental consciousness as well as of the visual consciousness of another person.
In this way, it should be understood up to the body.

Therefore, because of its status as the basis and because of its uniqueness, consciousness is designated by those [faculties] alone and not by form and so forth, just as one says "the sound of a drum" or "a barley sprout. Now, when one situated in a certain body sees forms with the eye, do that body, eye, form, and consciousness belong to the same level (*bhūmi*), or rather to different levels?
He said:
There is a distinction among all of them.
For one born in the desire realm who sees their own forms with their own eye, everything belongs to their own level.

When one sees one's own forms with the eye of the first dhyāna, the body and the forms belong to one's own level (the desire realm), while the consciousness and the eye belong to that level (the first dhyāna). When seeing forms belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, all three belong to that level.

When seeing one's own forms with the eye of the second dhyāna, the body and the forms belong to one's own level, the eye belongs to that level (the second dhyāna), and the consciousness belongs to the level of the first dhyāna.

When seeing forms belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, the consciousness and the forms belong to that level, the body belongs to the desire realm, and the eye belongs to the level of the second dhyāna.

For one seeing forms belonging to the level of the second dhyāna with eyes belonging to that same level, the body belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) and the consciousness belongs to the level of the first dhyāna.
In the same way, this should be applied to one seeing forms belonging to their own level or to lower levels with eyes belonging to the third or fourth dhyāna.

For one born in the first dhyāna who sees his own forms with his own eyes, everything belongs to his own level; for one seeing lower forms, three [elements—body, eye, and consciousness] belong to his own level.
When one sees one's own forms with the eye of the second dhyāna, three factors belong to one’s own level (svabhūmika) and the eye belongs to that [second] level.
When seeing forms belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara), the body and consciousness belong to one’s own level and the forms belong to a lower level, while the eye belongs to that [second] level.
When seeing forms belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, the eye and the forms belong to that level, while the rest belong to one’s own level.
In this same way, it should be applied to the eye of the third dhyāna.
For one born in the second or higher dhyānas who sees forms belonging to their own or other levels with the eyes of their own or other levels, it should be applied accordingly as appropriate.
However, this is the fixed rule:
The eye does not belong to a lower level than the body;
for the body, the eye, and visible forms belong to five levels, ranging from the desire realm up to the level of the fourth dhyāna.
Visual consciousness belongs to two levels: the desire realm and the level of the first dhyāna.
In this regard, the eye belongs to the same level as the body, or it belongs to a higher level, but never to a lower level.
Visual form that serves as the object belongs to the same level as the eye, or to a lower level;
however, visual form of a higher level is not the object of the eye.

For form belonging to a higher level can never be seen by an eye belonging to a lower level; and consciousness does not exist above the eye in the same way that form does. However, its [the eye's] object is form, while both [eye and consciousness] are present everywhere relative to the body. (46)
"Of this"—that is, of the visual consciousness just mentioned—form is the object from all sides: above, below, and on its own level.
For the body, both form and consciousness exist from all sides.
And just as this has been stated regarding the eye, so it should be understood in detail.
Likewise, regarding the ear: "The ear is not lower than the body; sound is not higher than the ear;
its consciousness [is not higher than the ear]; but sound and both [the ear and its consciousness] are [in relation to] the body in all ways."
This should be applied in detail.

However, for the three [elements]—the nose, tongue, and body—the entire [set] belongs to their own level; that is, the body, its own object, and the consciousnesses of these three elements belong exclusively to their own level.
Having established this by way of a general rule, an exception is now introduced for the sake of further specification:
body-consciousness always belongs to its own level or to a lower level; the body, the body-element, and the tangible object always belong exclusively to its own level.

However, for some, body-consciousness belongs to its own level, as in the case of those born in the desire realm or the first dhyāna; for others, it belongs to a lower level, as in the case of those born in the second dhyāna and above.
The mind, however, is not fixed [to a specific level]. (47)
Sometimes the mind belongs to the same level as the body, the mental consciousness, and mental phenomena; sometimes it belongs to a higher or lower level.

For even when the body belongs to five levels, the mind and so forth can belong to all levels at the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) or rebirth (*upapatti*), according to the circumstances. This has been explained in detail in the section on meditative attainments in this treatise (*kośasthāna*).
However, for the sake of avoiding an excessive burden of text, it is not explained again here.
"The purpose is small and the effort is great"—with this, the incidental discussion is concluded.
Now, the following is investigated:
among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), which is cognizable by which?
He said: "The five external [elements] are cognizable by two [consciousnesses].

The elements of form, sound, odor, taste, and tangibles, having been experienced respectively by the visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses, are then cognized by the mental consciousness."
Thus, each of these is to be cognized by two types of consciousness.

It is explained that the remaining thirteen elements (dhātus), because they are not the objects of the five groups of sensory consciousness, are to be cognized by the mental consciousness alone. Among these eighteen elements, how many are permanent and how many are impermanent?
Not a single element in its entirety is permanent; rather—
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are eternal;
therefore, one portion of the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*) is eternal, while the remainder are impermanent.
How many are faculties (*indriya*), and how many are not faculties?
Half of the dharmas are faculties, as are those twelve which are known as internal. //48//
Twenty-two faculties are taught in the Sūtra:

the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty, the mind faculty, the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty, the pleasure faculty, the pain faculty, and the mental joy faculty.

The faculty of mental displeasure (*daurmanasyendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*),

the faculty "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of one who has known (*ājñātāvīndriya*). However, the Abhidharmikas, disregarding the established order of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), recite the faculty of mind (*manaindriya*) immediately after the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Because they possess an object (*sālambanatva*).

Among those, half of the *dharmas*—namely, the eleven faculties beginning with the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and a portion of three others—are included because they belong to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*).
Of the twelve internal [faculties], the five beginning with the eye are designated by their own names.
The seven mental elements (*cittadhātu*) constitute the mind-faculty (*manaindriya*). It will be explained later that the female and male faculties are portions of the body-element (*kāyadhātu*).
It is established that the remaining five elements and a portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) are not faculties.
The first treasury-location (kośasthāna), titled "Exposition of the Elements" (dhātunirdeśa), in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, is completed. — :::—
Those phenomena that arise from causes, their cause the Tathāgata has indeed explained...
And that which is the cessation of these—such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.
This was caused to be written by the illustrious Lāmāvāka. The second treasury-location (kośasthāna).
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!
The faculties (indriya) have been explained.
What, then, is the meaning of "faculty" (indriya)? [The root] *idi* means "supreme sovereignty. Those which exercise that sovereignty are the faculties (*indriyāṇi*).
Therefore, the meaning of "faculty" (indriya) is the sense of sovereignty (ādhipatya). And what is the sovereignty of these [faculties] over what?
Five [faculties] have sovereignty over four matters.
First, the eye and the ear each possess sovereignty with respect to four objects:
with regard to the beauty of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), because those who are blind or deaf lack an attractive form;
and with regard to the maintenance of the personal existence, because by seeing and hearing, one avoids dangerous places.
In the arising of the visual and auditory consciousnesses along with their associated mental factors;
in being the uncommon causes for the seeing of forms and the hearing of sounds;
and in the beauty of the personal existence of the nose, tongue, and body—as in the previous case.
Regarding the maintenance of the physical body through the consumption of solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*),
and regarding the arising of the olfactory and other consciousnesses along with their associated mental factors,
[the nose and so forth] serve as the specific causes for the smelling of odors, the tasting of flavors, and the touching of tangibles.
It is said that [it arises] from two;
[namely,] from four: the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty, and the mind faculty.

Each of the two [faculties] exercises sovereignty over two matters. First, regarding the female and male faculties, they exercise sovereignty over the differentiation and the conceptualization of sentient beings.
In this context, the "differentiation of sentient beings" refers to [the distinction between] "female" and "male."
The discrimination of sentient beings (*sattva-vikalpa*) refers to the differences in physical form, voice, and conduct, such as those of women and so forth;
others say it refers to the distinction between affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*).

For indeed, among those who lack such discrimination—namely, eunuchs, impotent men, and those with both sexual organs—there is no non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), no immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), and no severance of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla-samuccheda*); nor do they possess restraint (*saṃvara*), the attainment of fruits, or detachment (*vairāgya*).
And [the function] of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is the connection with and the maintenance of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*);
whereas that of the mind-faculty (*manaindriya*) is the connection to renewed existence and the conformity to mastery over it.

Furthermore, regarding the connection to renewed existence, it has been said: "At that time, for the gandharva, one or the other of two types of consciousness becomes manifest—either accompanied by attachment or accompanied by aversion.
Regarding the conformity to mastery, it has been said: "By the mind this world is led," and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the five faculties beginning with pleasure and the eight beginning with faith—of these five and eight [faculties], [the sovereignty] pertains to defilement and purification. (1)
Dominance belongs, respectively, to the five [faculties] beginning with pleasure in regard to defilement,
because passion and the others adhere to them;
and to faith and the others in regard to purification.
Others maintain that it is purified by them, and that even in purification, pleasure and the other [feelings] have sovereignty,
because "the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated."
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that joy and the other [mental factors] have suffering as their proximate cause, faith as their basis, and renunciation as their support.
Others, however, say:
the drawing forth of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) does not occur by means of the eye and ear through the cognition [of objects], because one avoids dangers;
rather, the sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) over those two belongs to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Nor is there any seeing of form or hearing of sound other than consciousness;
for it would only be logical to grant them separate predominance if they were the uncommon causes of those two.
Therefore, their status as faculties is not established in this way.
How, then, is it so?
Because of their sovereignty over the apprehension of their respective objects, all six are sense-faculties (*indriya*).
The five beginning with the eye possess sovereignty over the apprehension of each of their own respective objects.
Furthermore, the mind has sovereignty over the apprehension of all objects;
therefore, these six are each individually an *indriya*.
[But is it not the case that objects also have sovereignty here?]
It does not possess sovereignty;
for sovereignty is superior power,
and the eye has superior mastery over the perception of visible forms.
Because it is the common cause for the perception of all forms, and because perception conforms to its own intensity, dullness, and so forth;
it is not [the cause] of form,
as the opposite is the case.
In this same manner, [the application] should be extended up to the mind with respect to mental objects.
However, the female and male faculties arise from the body due to their predominance over femininity and masculinity. (2)
The female and male faculties are established as distinct from the body faculty itself; they are not separate entities.
Rather, there is a certain portion of the body faculty located in the region of the genitals which receives the designation of the female and male faculties.
This is because they exercise sovereignty over femininity and masculinity respectively.
In this context, the female state consists of the female form, voice, gestures, and intentions;
for these indeed constitute the femininity of a woman.
Masculinity consists of the male form, voice, gestures, and intentions;
for this indeed is the masculinity of a man.
[It is established] by virtue of its sovereignty over the stability of the group, defilement, and purification.
The five feelings of life and faith and the others are considered faculties (indriyas). //3//
The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) has sovereignty over the persistence within a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*). The sensations (*vedanā*) have sovereignty over defilement (*saṃkleśa*);

for it is said in the Sūtra that passion (*rāga*) underlies pleasant sensation, aversion (*pratigha*) underlies painful sensation, and ignorance (*avidyā*) underlies neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation.
Faith (*śraddhā*) and the other four faculties have sovereignty over purification (*vyavadāna*).
For in this way, by means of them, the afflictions are suppressed and the Path is brought forth;

therefore, these too are each accepted as faculties. Likewise, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known" [are faculties] because they exercise sovereignty over the successive attainment of higher stages and Nirvana, etc. (4).
The word "likewise" (*tathā*) is used for the purpose of showing that each [faculty] is individually [dominant].
Among them, the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) has sovereignty in the attainment of the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*);
the faculty of "knowing" has sovereignty in the attainment of the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*); and the faculty of "one who has known" has sovereignty in *parinirvāṇa*.
For there is no final nirvāṇa for one whose mind is not liberated.
The word "etcetera" (ādi) is intended to indicate other synonymous expressions. What is this other expression?
The faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) has sovereignty with respect to the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing;
the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*) has sovereignty with respect to the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation;
and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) has sovereignty with respect to dwelling in happiness in the present life.
Because of the experience of the joy and bliss of liberation.
If being a faculty (*indriya*) consists in exercising sovereignty (*ādhipatya*), then ignorance (*avidyā*) and the others must also be included among the faculties;
for ignorance and the rest likewise exercise sovereignty over the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth, and therefore their status as faculties must also be added.
This applies to speech and the other [faculties] as well.

The status of speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals as faculties (*indriya*) should also be added [to the list], because they exercise sovereignty over speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and sexual pleasure. However, they should certainly not be added.
Because here [in this system], the basis of the mind, its differentiation, its duration, as well as affliction, the equipment, and purification— whatever these may be— are the faculties. (5)

In this context, the basis of the mind consists of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*). These six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) constitute the fundamental substance of a sentient being. Its differentiation as female or male is by means of the female and male faculties (*strīpuruṣendriya*); its persistence is by means of the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*); and its defilement is by means of the [five] feelings (*vedanā*).
The equipment for purification is by means of five [faculties], while purification itself is by means of three;
therefore, ignorance and the others are not accepted as faculties.
This is because [the faculties] function through being the basis for the process of existence, its arising, its maintenance, and its experience.
Likewise, there are fourteen other faculties pertaining to cessation.
The word "or" (vā) has the sense of an alternative opinion;
others, however, say:
the basis of active engagement (*pravṛtti*) is the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*).
Arising consists in the female and male faculties, because they arise from those;
maintenance consists in the life-faculty.
Because of that state,
there is experience by means of the feelings;
therefore, these are the fourteen faculties.
In that same manner, the others are for the sake of cessation (*nivṛtti*).
For faith and the other [faculties] are the basis of cessation;

the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is its origination; the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*) is its stability; and enjoyment occurs through the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*). Therefore, there are exactly these many faculties.
For this very reason, their sequence is as follows:
speech does not constitute a sense-faculty (*indriya*) because its function of speaking depends upon specialized training;
and the hands and feet do not [constitute separate faculties] because they are not distinct from the acts of grasping and moving.
For that very same [action] is called "taking up" when it arises in one place and "moving about" when it arises elsewhere.
Furthermore, taking up and moving about occur even for snakes and the like without hands or feet.
Nor does the anus possess the status of a sense faculty with respect to excretion, because heavy objects fall everywhere in space [due to gravity].
Furthermore, because it is impelled by the wind (*vāyu*), the sexual organ (*upastha*) also lacks the status of a faculty (*indriya*); for that pleasure is produced by the male and female faculties.

Moreover, it would follow that the throat, teeth, eyelids, and joints would also possess the status of faculties with respect to the actions of swallowing, chewing, opening and closing the eyes, and contracting and expanding [the limbs], or that everything which serves as a cause for its own specific action would be a faculty; thus, it is incorrect to claim that speech and the others are faculties.

Among those, the exposition of the faculties beginning with the eye and ending with the male faculty has already been made. Since the life-faculty is a dissociated factor, its exposition will be given among the dissociated factors themselves. The exposition of faith and the others will be given among the mental factors (caitta).
The [definition] of pleasure and the other [feelings], as well as the faculty of "I shall come to know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) and the others, must be stated;
this is now being provided:
the faculty of suffering is that bodily sensation which is unpleasant.
"Unpleasant" (aśātā) means that which is harmful; it means suffering (duḥkha). "Pleasant" (sukha) is that which is agreeable (śātā).
The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is a pleasant bodily sensation (*kāyikī śātā vedanā*).
"Pleasant" (*śātā*) means beneficial, which is to say, "pleasure" (*sukha*).
However, in the third dhyāna, that same [pleasant sensation], when it is mental (*caitasī*), is the faculty of pleasure. (7)
In the third dhyāna, however, that same pleasant mental sensation is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*);
for there is no bodily sensation there,
due to the absence of the five groups of sensory consciousness.
Elsewhere— that is, apart from the third dhyāna, in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and in the first and second dhyānas— that mental feeling of pleasure is the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya).
However, in the third dhyāna, because of the absence of passion for rapture (prīti), it is exclusively the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) and not the faculty of joy.
For joy (*prīti*) is mental ease (*saumanasya*);
furthermore, that which is unpleasant to the mind is mental distress (*daurmanasya*); but equanimity (*upekṣā*) is that which is intermediate.
Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, which is neither agreeable nor disagreeable, is called "the intermediate. It is the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Is it bodily or mental? He says: [it is both].
It is both; what, then, is the reason that these two are combined and made into a single faculty? Because it is free from conceptual construction (avikalpanāt). //8//
For mental pleasure and pain generally arise from conceptual construction, whereas physical pleasure and pain do not;
since they arise even in Arhats by the power of external objects,
there is a distinction between the two on account of their being faculties (*indriya*).
Equanimity (*upekṣā*), however, arises by its own nature without conceptualization, whether it is physical or mental; thus, it is established as a single faculty.
Furthermore, it benefits physical pleasure in one way and mental pleasure in another;
likewise, it harms physical pain in one way and mental pain in another.
However, this distinction does not exist in the case of equanimity (*upekṣā*); therefore, there is no differentiation with respect to the act of equanimity because it is non-conceptual.
On the paths of seeing (*darśana*), cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), there are nine [faculties]:
the mind, pleasure (*sukha*), mental joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
These nine faculties are called three faculties within the three paths:

on the path of seeing, it is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*); on the path of cultivation, it is the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*); and on the path of no-more-learning, it is the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
What is the reason for this?

For on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one has set out to know what was not yet known (*anājñātamājñātuṃ pravṛtta*). On the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is nothing previously unknown to be known; rather, one knows that very same [truth] for the sake of abandoning the remaining latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
On the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), however, the realization that "it is known" (*ājñātam*) is the state of having known (*ājñātāva*).
One who possesses this is called *ājñātāvī*;
or rather, one whose nature it is to protect what has been known (*ājñāta*),
because of having attained the knowledge of destruction and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*).
"The suffering has been fully known by me; it is not to be fully known again"—the faculty of one who has become thus is the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

Having provided this explanation of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the classification of its types must now be stated: how many faculties are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*), and so forth.
In that regard, first, as for these [faculties] just mentioned, beginning with the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*):
The triad is stainless; that is to say, it is untainted (*anāsrava*),
because "stains" (*mala*) is a synonym for "taints" (*āsrava*).
The seven material faculties, the life-faculty, and the two faculties of suffering and mental distress are exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*). Furthermore,
the seven material [faculties]...
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, female, and male faculties are included within the aggregate of form; thus, nine [faculties] are of two kinds. (6)

The mental faculty (*manas*), pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*)—these nine faculties are both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*).
Some maintain that the [five] beginning with faith are exclusively without-outflows.

For it was said by the Blessed One: "In whomsoever these five faculties are entirely and in every way absent, him I call an outsider, one who stands on the side of the ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*)."
This is not a proof, because the statement was made with reference to those [dharmas] that are without outflows (*anāsrava*).
For, having established the classification of noble persons (*āryapudgala*), he said, "one for whom these [exist]";
whereas ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are of two kinds: the internal one whose roots of merit are not severed, and the external one whose roots of merit are severed.
Referring to this, he says: "I declare that [the person] stands on the side of the worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

And it is said in the Sūtra, even before the Wheel of Dharma had been set in motion: "There are beings born in the world and grown up in the world who possess sharp faculties, middling faculties, and even dull faculties.
Therefore, the defiled (*sāsrava*) faculties such as faith and the rest certainly exist.

Furthermore, it is said: "As long as I did not understand, as they really are, the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these five faculties, for that long I did not [claim to have awakened] from this world with its gods," and so forth in detail.
And this mode of examination does not apply to untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena.
How many faculties are fruition (*vipāka*), and how many are not fruition? First of all, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is exclusively fruition.
Now, as for the fact that an Arhat monk sustains the life-formations (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*), of what is that life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) the maturation?
It is stated in the Śāstra: "How does he sustain the life-formations?

An Arhat monk, possessing supernormal powers (*ṛddhimat*) and having attained mastery over the mind, [sustains them] for the sake of the Saṅgha or for an individual, [giving away] his bowl or his robe..."
Having given either one or another of the requisites for the life of a recluse, he enters the fourth dhyāna of the ultimate limit, having made that his vow.
Emerging from that, he generates the thought and utters the words: "May whatever is my maturation of wealth become a maturation of longevity."
Whatever was its maturation as experience becomes its maturation as lifespan.
However, those who hold the view that "the remainder of maturation matures" say: it is the remainder of maturation from karma performed in a previous birth.
"By the power of cultivation, he draws it forth and experiences it.
How does he relinquish the life-formations?
In that same manner, having given a gift and made a vow, he enters the fourth dhyāna of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika*).
"May that which was the ripening of my lifespan become the ripening of my enjoyments. For him, it becomes so.
But the Venerable Ghoṣaka says:

"In that very same basis, one brings into manifestation through the power of meditative concentration (dhyāna) the great elements belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara), which are either conducive to or contrary to life.
In this way, one sustains the formations of life (āyuḥ-saṃskāra); in this way, one relinquishes them."
But it must be understood in this way:

such is the power of their meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that they cause the momentum of the sense-faculties and primary elements (*mahābhūta*) born of prior karma—which determines the duration of their stay—to cease, and they project a new momentum born of concentration.
Therefore, that life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*); other than that, however, it is a result of maturation.
From one question, another arises:
for what purpose do they sustain the life-formations? Is it for the sake of the welfare of others, or for the sake of the endurance of the Teaching?
For they perceive their own lifespan to be exhausted, and they see no one else there who is capable [of saving them].
Now, for what purpose do they renounce? They perceive that the benefit to others in this life is slight, and that their own physical existence is overcome by disease.
As it has been said:
"When this holy life has been well-practiced and this path has been well-cultivated..."
“He becomes content with the exhaustion of his lifespan, just as one is upon the departure of a disease.
Thus it is said.
Now, where and for whom should this relinquishing or the stabilization of the life-force formations (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) be understood?

It occurs only among humans in the three continents, for a male or female Arhat who is liberated at all times (*asamayavimukta*) and has attained the meditative absorption of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*).
For such a person possesses mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
And the continuum is not supported by the afflictions.
The Sūtra states: "The Blessed One, having sustained the formative forces of vitality (*jīvita-saṃskāra*), relinquished the formative forces of life-span (*āyus-saṃskāra*).
What is the distinction between them?
Some say there is none at all.
For it has been said: "What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)? It is the vitality (*āyus*) belonging to the three realms.
Others say: "The formations of vitality (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) are the fruit of past karma, while the formations of life (*jīvita-saṃskāra*) are the fruit of present karma."
Alternatively, those by which one remains in a homogeneous class of beings are the formative forces of lifespan (āyuḥ-saṃskāra);
whereas those by which one lives for a certain period of time are the formative forces of vitality (jīvita-saṃskāra).
The plural form is used because of the relinquishing and sustaining of many moments of the life-force (*āyus*) and the formations of vitality (*jīvita-saṃskāra*);
for there is no relinquishing or sustaining of a single moment.
Some say it is for the purpose of indicating that life is not a single, enduring substance that persists over time.

Others maintain that the designation "life-span" (āyus) applies only to the conditioned factors (saṃskāras) collectively; there is no single, substantial entity called life-span. Otherwise, they argue, [the Buddha] would not have used the term "conditioned factors."
For what purpose, then, did the Blessed One relinquish and then sustain the life-formations?
He relinquished them to demonstrate mastery over death, and he sustained them to demonstrate mastery over life.
Why only for three months and no longer? Because there was no further work to be done for those to be trained.

Furthermore, it is for the sake of fulfilling that which was promised: "When these four bases of psychic power have been cultivated in this way, should I so desire, I could remain for an eon, or even for the remainder of an eon.
According to the Vaibhāṣikas, it is also for the sake of conquering the Māra of the aggregates and the Māra of death.
At the foot of the Bodhi tree, the Māras of the afflictions and the son-of-a-god were conquered.
The incidental discussion is concluded.
The subject at hand is now commenced:
the twelve are twofold.
Which are the twelve?
Except for the last eight and mental distress;
that is, excluding the last eight— namely faith and the others— and mental distress.
The twelve faculties other than the life-faculty are of two kinds: both fruition (*vipāka*) and non-fruition (*avipāka*).
Among them, the seven beginning with the eye-faculty are accumulative (*aupacayika*) and thus non-fruition;
the remaining ones are fruition.

The faculties of mental suffering, pleasure, joy, and equanimity, when they are wholesome or afflicted, are not fruition; as are those pertaining to deportment, those pertaining to concentration, and those pertaining to emanation, according to the case.
The remaining ones are fruition.
It is established that, with the exception of the life-faculty and the twelve beginning with the eye-faculty, the remaining [faculties] are non-retribution (avipāka).

If the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*) is not a maturation (*vipāka*), how is the Sūtra to be interpreted when it says: "There are three types of actions: action to be experienced as pleasure, action to be experienced as mental distress, and action to be experienced as equanimity"? This was stated with reference to being experienced through association (*saṃprayoga-vedanīyatā*). Action associated with mental distress is "action to be experienced as mental distress."
Just as contact associated with pleasure is "to be experienced as pleasure," so too will karma associated with mental joy (*saumanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) be likewise.
Let it be as you wish.

There is no fault even in its association [with other factors], nor is there any fault in its being a ripening (*vipāka*). For, having no other recourse, one must understand it in this way. But what is the reasoning here that mental distress (*daurmanasya*) is not a ripening?
For mental distress (*daurmanasya*) is produced and pacified by specific conceptual constructions (*parikalpa*),
whereas maturation (*vipāka*) is not like this.
[In that case,] mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) would likewise not be maturation.

If, then, mental distress (*daurmanasya*) were a maturation (*vipāka*), then for those who have committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*), that karma would be matured because mental distress arises on account of it.
Likewise, if mental joy (*saumanasya*) were a maturation, then for those who have performed meritorious deeds, that karma would be matured because mental joy arises on account of it.
In that case, since mental distress is impossible for those free from passion (*vītarāga*),
it cannot be a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
Likewise, what kind of maturation could their neutral mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) be?

"Let it be as it may; however, when there is the possibility of mental joy (*saumanasya*), there is room for its maturation (*vipāka*), but not for mental grief (*daurmanasya*), because the latter never occurs [as a result of karma]. Thus, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that mental grief is never a maturation."

In that regard, the eight faculties beginning with the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) are the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome karma in a happy rebirth (*sugati*), and of unwholesome karma in a miserable rebirth (*durgati*). The mind-faculty (*manaindriya*) is the maturation of both types of karma in both types of rebirth.
The faculties of pleasure, mental joy, and equanimity are the maturation of wholesome karma.
The faculty of suffering belongs to the unwholesome;
for one possessing both sexual organs in a happy rebirth, there is the acquisition of that state through the unwholesome,
but not the acquisition of the faculty itself, because it is projected by the wholesome.
This has been explained.
This must now be stated:
how many faculties have maturation (savipāka), and how many are without maturation (avipāka)? Regarding that faculty of mental distress (daurmanasya) which was just mentioned:
In reality, that one [karma] possesses fruition;
that very one indeed possesses fruition.
It should be understood that the word "tu" (but/indeed) has the sense of "eva" (indeed/exclusively) and its position is displaced.
For that [mental dissatisfaction] is neither neutral (*avyākṛta*) nor untainted (*anāsrava*), because it is not in a state of meditative concentration (*asamāhita*).
Therefore, there is no mental dissatisfaction that is without karmic ripening (*avipāka*).
Ten [factors] are of two kinds. (10)
They are both with fruition (*savipāka*) and without fruition (*avipāka*).
Which are the ten? They are the mind (*manas*), the other feelings (*anyavitti*), and faith (*śraddhā*) and the others.
By the inclusion of "other feelings," a feeling other than mental distress (*daurmanasya*) is understood.
Faith and the others are faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Among them, the mind, pleasure, mental joy, and equanimity—whether unwholesome or wholesome and with outflows—are subject to maturation;
those that are without outflows or indeterminate are not subject to maturation.

The faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) is both wholesome and unwholesome when it has maturation (savipāka), and it is neutral when it lacks maturation (avipāka). The faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā) have maturation when they are with outflows (sāsrava), and lack maturation when they are without outflows (anāsrava).
It is established that all others lack maturation.
How many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate?
First of all, eight are exclusively wholesome.
The five beginning with faith and the three beginning with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" are of two kinds; as is the faculty of mental dissatisfaction.
The wholesome and the unwholesome;
and the mind and the other sensations are of three kinds: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
The other is of one kind. // 11 //
There is another [category]:
the eye and so forth, with life as the eighth;
this is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Which faculty belongs to which realm among these faculties?
First, it should be understood that, excluding the stainless (anāsrava) ones, all faculties are associated with the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).

Excluding the three faculties beginning with *ājñāsyāmīndriya*, which are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), [the remaining faculties] belong to the realm of form (*rūpāpta*). Among these, the female and male faculties are excluded. This is because those [three] are not bound to any realm (*apratisaṃyukta*) at all.
"And having abandoned [the faculties] in relation to suffering,
and the stainless one as well"— this is how it continues.
"In relation to suffering" means in relation to physical pain (*duḥkha*) and mental distress (*daurmanasya*).
In that regard, because of their detachment from the practice of sexual intercourse and because it would be unseemly, the female and male faculties do not exist in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
How then are they called "men" now? Where are they so called?
In the Sūtra it is said:
"It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a woman should exercise the role of a Brahmā;
this is not possible."
"It is possible that there is such a person"— this refers to another state of being male which exists among males in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). There,
the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) does not exist, because the physical basis is translucent and because unwholesome states are absent.

The faculty of mental grief does not exist [there], because the mental continuum is moistened by tranquility (*śamatha*) and because there is an absence of objects of malice. Furthermore, having excluded the two types of pleasure and all that is material, [the faculties] pertain to the formless realm (*ārūpyāpta*). (12)
The phrase "excluding the female and male faculties, the two [faculties] of suffering, and the pure [faculties]" continues to apply here.
What remains?
The mental faculty, the life faculty, the equanimity faculty, and the five beginning with faith.
These are associated with the formless realm; there are no others.

How many faculties are to be abandoned by seeing? How many are to be abandoned by cultivation? How many are not to be abandoned? The mind and the three sensations are of three kinds; which are the three sensations?
Pleasure, mental joy, and equanimity [are abandoned by cultivation]; mental distress is to be abandoned by both;
mental distress is to be abandoned by both [vision and cultivation].
The section concerning those things to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) is as follows:
the eye and the other [faculties], with the life-faculty as the eighth, as well as the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), are exclusively to be abandoned by cultivation.
The five beginning with faith are both to be abandoned by cultivation and not to be abandoned,
because they are both contaminated and uncontaminated.
Not the triad. //13//
The triad beginning with the faculty of "I shall come to know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) is not to be abandoned at all, because it is untainted (anāsrava);
for that which is faultless does not deserve abandonment.
The classification by way of type has been explained.
The acquisition [of faculties] must now be explained.
How many faculties are acquired as maturation (*vipāka*) for the first time in which realm? In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), two faculties are acquired as maturation at the outset.
The body faculty and the life faculty;
moreover,
these two are not [possessed] by those born spontaneously.
