Because of the exclusion of the spontaneously born (*upapāduka*), it should be understood that [the intermediate state] consists of the egg-born, the womb-born, and the moisture-born.
Why are the mind-faculty (*manas*) and the equanimity-faculty (*upekṣendriya*) not included?
Because at the time of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*), those two are necessarily defiled (*kliṣṭa*).
Now, how many are acquired by those of miraculous birth?
They acquire six,
if they are without sexual organs.
As with those of the first eon.
Which six?
The faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and life. Or seven.
If they possess only one gender organ,
as among the gods and so forth,
or if they possess eight organs.
If they possess both sexual organs,
do those with both organs also arise through spontaneous birth?
They do so in the miserable realms.
Thus far regarding the desire realm; now, as to how it is in the form realm and the formless realm, he says:
"In the form [realms], six."
Because desire is predominant, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is designated as "desires" (*kāmāḥ*);
because form is predominant, the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is designated as "forms" (*rūpāṇi*).
It is also said in the Sūtra: "O monks, those peaceful liberations which, having transcended forms, are formless (*ārūpya*)."

In that realm of form (rūpadhātu), six faculties are first obtained as maturation (vipāka)—the same as those obtained by spontaneously born beings (upapāduka) without sexual organs in the realm of desire (kāmadhātu). In the higher [realm], there is one more. (14)
The formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is superior to the form realm (rūpadhātu),
both because it is higher in terms of meditative attainment (samāpatti) and because it is more preeminent in terms of rebirth (upapatti).
In that [realm], only the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is initially obtained as fruition (vipāka), and no other.
The acquisition [of faculties] has been explained;
now the relinquishment must be discussed:
in which realm does one dying cease how many faculties?
In the formless realm (ārūpya), one ceases vitality, mind, and equanimity through death; in the form realm (rūpa), eight [faculties] are ceased.
Dying in the form realm, one ceases eight [faculties].
And those three, beginning with the eye, become five;
for all those born by apparitional birth (upapāduka) are born and die with their sense-faculties complete.
In the desire realm, there are ten, nine, or eight. (15)
One who dies in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) with both sexual organs ceases ten faculties:
those eight [already mentioned] plus the female and male faculties.
One with a single sexual organ ceases nine.
One without sexual organs has eight [faculties]. This rule applies to simultaneous death; however, in the case of gradual death, there are four.
One who dies gradually, however, ceases four faculties:
the faculties of body, life, mind, and equanimity;
for these do not cease separately.
And this principle is to be understood as applying to death with a defiled or neutral mind.
But when one dies while abiding in a wholesome state of mind, then in all cases five [faculties] are present in the wholesome.
One dying with a wholesome mind ceases the faculties as previously described in every case,
with the addition of the five beginning with faith.
These [factors] necessarily exist within a wholesome mind.
In the same way, one should calculate in detail that in the formless realms one ceases eight [faculties], while in the realm of form one ceases thirteen.
In this section on the faculties (*indriya-prakaraṇa*), all the characteristics of the faculties are investigated.
Now, which fruit of asceticism is attained by how many faculties?
The attainment of the two final fruits is by nine faculties; the attainment of the two final fruits is by nine faculties.
Which, then, are the last? The fruit of stream-entry and arhatship. Which are the middle ones?
The fruit of once-returning and the fruit of non-returning.
Among these, the fruit of stream-entry is attained by nine faculties: the [five] beginning with faith, excluding the faculty of one who has already known; and the faculties of mind and equanimity.

The faculty of "I shall come to know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) is to be understood as being in the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantaryamārga), and the faculty of knowing (ājñendriya) is in the path of liberation (vimuktimārga).
For its attainment is through both [the faculties], because they respectively serve as the bringer-about and the support for the attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*).

Furthermore, his state of Arhatship is attained through nine: by means of the seven beginning with faith (excluding the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"), the mind-faculty (*manas*), and any one of the faculties of pleasure, mental joy, or equanimity.
[The verse states: "By seven, eight, or nine, in two cases. (16)
The attainment of the fruits of once-returner and non-returner occurs respectively through seven, eight, or nine faculties. How so?
First, regarding the fruit of once-returner: if one who follows the gradual path attains it by means of the worldly path, its attainment is by means of seven faculties.
It is attained by means of the five beginning with faith, together with the faculties of equanimity and mind;
furthermore, when attained by means of the supramundane path, it is attained by means of eight faculties,
with the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*) as the eighth.
Now, if one who is further detached from passion attains [the fruit of non-returning], it is by means of nine faculties, just as in the case of the fruit of stream-entry.
If he attains the fruit of non-returning through the gradual path and by means of the worldly path, its attainment is by seven faculties,
just as in the case of the fruit of once-returning.
Now, if one attains it by means of the supramundane path, it is likewise through eight;
or if one who is already free from passion attains it, it is through nine,
just as in the case of the fruit of stream-entry.
However, this is the distinction:
there is one or another of the faculties of pleasure, mental joy, or equanimity,
due to the difference in the basis.

Even when one who follows the gradual path enters dhyāna by means of the worldly path during the ninth path of liberation because of having sharp faculties, he still attains the fruit of non-returning through eight faculties.

For in that case, the faculty of mental happiness (*saumanasyendriya*) is the eighth in the ninth path of liberation, whereas in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), there is always only the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); and its attainment occurs through both of these.
Now, if one enters by means of the supramundane [path], his attainment is by means of nine faculties;
the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*) is the ninth.
As for what was stated in the Abhidharma—"By how many faculties does one attain arhatship? It says: by eleven"—[how is this to be understood?]
How then is it said that [the fruit of non-returning] is attained by nine? It is indeed attained by nine alone.
However, the attainment of arhatship is said to be by eleven because it is possible for a single person [to attain it through all eleven].

There is the possibility that a single person (pudgala), falling away again and again, might attain arhatship through pleasure, mental joy, and equanimity; therefore, it was stated [that one attains it] by means of eleven [faculties].
However, there is certainly no possibility for pleasure and the others to exist at one and the same time.
Why, then, does this same consequence not apply to the non-returner (anāgāmin) as well?
For one who has fallen away from it never attains it again by means of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), nor does one who was previously free from passion fall away [from that state],
because that detachment is attained through both paths.
This is now investigated.
With which faculty is one endowed, and with how many is one necessarily endowed?
In that regard:
one who is possessed of equanimity, life, and mind is necessarily endowed with three. (17)

Whoever is endowed with any one of these, such as equanimity (upekṣā) and the rest, is necessarily endowed with these very three faculties; for there is no possession of them without their mutual presence. However, regarding the remaining faculties, there is no fixed rule.
One may be possessed [of them], or one may not be possessed [of them].
In that regard, first, one born in the formless realm (ārūpya) is not possessed of the faculties of eye, ear, nose, and tongue;
nor is one in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) possessed of those which have not been acquired or have been lost.

One born in the formless realm is not endowed with the body-faculty. One born in the realm of form or the formless realm is not endowed with the female faculty. In the desire realm, one is not endowed with it if it has not been acquired or has been lost.
Likewise, an ordinary person born in the fourth dhyāna or the formless realms is not endowed with the male faculty or the pleasure faculty.
An ordinary person born in the third or fourth dhyāna or the formless realms is likewise not endowed with the mental joy faculty.
One born in the form or formless realms lacks the faculty of suffering; one who is free from passion for the desire realm lacks the faculty of mental grief;
and one whose roots of merit are severed lacks faith and the other [faculties].
Ordinary persons and those established in the fruits [of the path] are not endowed with the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
Ordinary persons, those on the path of seeing, and those on the path of no-more-learning are not endowed with the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*).
Ordinary persons and those in training (*śaikṣa*) are not endowed with the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
In states that are not prohibited, one should be understood as being endowed with [the faculties] as previously described.

One who is endowed with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) by means of four [faculties]— namely, those three beginning with equanimity (*upekṣā*) and the faculty of pleasure— is necessarily endowed with those four faculties.

One who possesses the body-faculty (kāyendriya) also possesses four: those three [previously mentioned] and the body-faculty itself. One who possesses the eye-faculty (cakṣurindriya) and so forth possesses five.
One who possesses the eye-faculty necessarily possesses five: the faculties of equanimity (upekṣā), life (jīvita), mind (manas), and body (kāya), as well as that [eye-faculty] itself.
It should be understood in the same way for the ear, nose, and tongue faculties.

And one who possesses the faculty of mental joy (*saumanasyendriya*) necessarily possesses five: equanimity (*upekṣā*), life-force (*jīvita*), mind (*manas*), pleasure (*sukha*), and mental joy (*saumanasya*).
With which faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is one born in the second dhyāna but not yet having attained the third dhyāna endowed?

By means of the afflicted [mind] belonging to the level of the third dhyāna. However, one who possesses the faculty of suffering necessarily possesses seven: the body, life, mind, and the four faculties of sensation.
One who possesses the female faculty and so forth. //18//
Whoever is endowed with the eight [faculties] together with the female faculty (strīndriya) necessarily possesses those seven [faculties] along with the female faculty.
By the word "etc. (ādi), there is an inclusion of the male faculty (puruṣendriya), the faculty of mental distress (daurmanasya), faith (śraddhā), and so forth.
One who possesses that [state] is also endowed with each of eight faculties:
namely, those seven and the eighth, which is the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*);
likewise with the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*).
One who possesses [the faculties] beginning with faith has them along with those five, as well as equanimity, life, and mind—thus eleven.
However, one endowed with the faculty of "having known" (ājñātendriya) possesses eleven;
the faculty of one who has known is the faculty of having known (ājñātendriya).

One who is endowed with the faculty of "one who has known" (ājñātendriya) is necessarily endowed with eleven: pleasure, mental joy, equanimity, life, mind, faith, and so forth, as well as the faculty of "one who has known. The same applies to the faculty of "one who has fully known" (ājñātāvīndriya); one is endowed with those same ten plus the faculty of "one who has fully known."
One who possesses the faculty of "I shall come to know" is endowed with thirteen [faculties]. //19//
By which thirteen?
By the faculties of mind, life, and body; by the four feelings; by faith and the others; and by the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
Now, as for one who is endowed with the minimum number [of faculties], with how many faculties is he endowed?
One who is devoid of all merit is endowed with the minimum of eight: the [five] sensations, mind, body, and life.
One whose roots of merit are severed and who is devoid of wholesomeness is endowed with at least eight faculties:
the five beginning with sensation (feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness), as well as the body, mind, and life-faculties.
For feeling (*vedanā*) is "feeling" (*vit*), in the sense that it feels;
or "feeling" (*vedana*) is "feeling" (*vit*), just as "attainment" (*saṃpadana*) is "attainment" (*saṃpat*).
And just as one devoid of the wholesome is endowed with at least eight faculties,
so too is a fool in the formless realm;
"fool" (bāla) is a designation for an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
By which eight? By equanimity, life-force, mind, and the wholesome [faculties]. // 20 //
[They are] with equanimity, life-faculty, mind-faculty, and faith and the others.
Because they are exclusively wholesome, faith and the others are included by the term "wholesome" (*śubha*).
[Objection: There would then be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the others are also included.
No;
because of the context of the eight [liberations] and because of the context of the foolish.
Now, as for one who is endowed with the maximum number of faculties, with how many is he endowed?
One endowed with the maximum is possessed of nineteen, excluding the stainless ones;
that is, excluding the three untainted (anāsrava) faculties.
Furthermore,
he who possesses both genders and both sexual characteristics, having all his faculties complete, is endowed with nineteen [faculties].
And who else?
A noble one who possesses attachment—
a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has not yet abandoned attachment— is endowed with all the maximum, namely, nineteen [faculties].
By those who are free from the two impurities of the single liṅga. // 21 //
Excluding one faculty and two untainted faculties—
the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya) and either of the other two [untainted faculties]—
the detailed classification of the faculties that were introduced in the context of the analysis of the elements (dhātu) has now been explained.
Now this is investigated:
Are these conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) such that they arise separately just as they have distinct characteristics, or are there some that necessarily arise together?
He says: "There are."
All these phenomena are fivefold:
matter, mind, mental factors, formations dissociated from mind, and the unconditioned.
Among these, the unconditioned never arises.
However, this is the rule regarding material phenomena (*rūpin*):
in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), an atom (*paramāṇu*) that is devoid of sound and lacks sense-faculties consists of eight substances.
For the most subtle aggregation of matter is called an "atom."
Since neither of the two [other types] would be cognized, that [soundless and non-facultied atom] arises in the desire realm consisting of eight substances, lacking none of them.
The eight substances are the four great elements and the four derived forms: visible form, odor, taste, and the tangible.
A single atom possessing a sense-faculty, being devoid of sound, arises as consisting of nine substances or ten substances.
Among these, first, that which possesses the body-faculty consists of nine substances.
One who possesses the body-faculty is called "possessing the body-faculty" (kāyendriyī).
In that case, there are nine substances:
those eight [previously mentioned] and the body-faculty itself.
The other sense organ consists of ten substances. // 22 //
In whichever atom there is another faculty, there are ten substances:
those same nine plus any one of the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, or tongue.
Furthermore, when these atoms arise accompanied by sound, they arise as nine, ten, or eleven substances respectively.
For there is also sound that is inseparable from the sense faculties, which has as its cause the appropriated primary elements.
How is it that here, among the elements which are inseparable, only a certain aggregate arises as solid, while another arises as liquid, hot, or mobile?
That which is most intensely manifested there by its power is what is perceived therein,
just like the touch of a bundle of needles and grass, or like the taste of a powder of flour and salt.
Furthermore, how is the existence of the remaining [elements] within those [others] understood?
It is known through their functions: cohesion, support, ripening, and expansion;

and because, when the appropriate conditions are met, solid substances and the like undergo states such as liquefaction. Others maintain that in water, heat is inferred from the extreme intensity of its coldness.
However, even when there is no differentiation, there may be an excellence of coolness,
just as there is an excellence of sound or sensation;
others hold that their existence within those [atoms] is due to their seeds, not due to their own essential nature.

Because of the statement, "There are various elements within this block of wood," how can there be the existence of color in wind? This matter is to be accepted through faith; it is not to be established by inference.

Because odor is perceived through contact and because its color does not deviate [from that contact], it has been stated that odor and taste are absent in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). Therefore, since the atoms existing there consist of six, seven, or eight substances (*dravya*) as previously described, they are not mentioned again here.
Furthermore, in this context, is "substance" (*dravya*) understood as a substantial entity itself, or rather as a sense-base (*āyatana*)?
What follows from this?
If "substance" is taken to mean only a primary substance (*dravya*), then it is far too little to say that [the body] consists of eight, nine, or ten substances;
for it must necessarily also consist of the substances that constitute its shape (*saṃsthāna*).
Because that too is an accumulation of atoms;
and because it possesses either heaviness or lightness, smoothness or roughness,
and sometimes also cold, hunger, and thirst.
Moreover, if the substance of the sense-base (*āyatana*) is taken [as the referent], then it is said that "this consists of eight substances," which is an overstatement;
for it should rather be said to consist of four substances, since the primary elements (*bhūta*) are also the sense-base of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).

In this context, some "substance" refers to the substance that serves as the basis (*āśrayabhūta*), while some "substance of the sense-base" refers to the substance that is based upon it (*āśritabhūta*).

Even so, there would be many elemental substances (*bhūtadravya*), because each of the derived forms (*upādāyarūpa*) is supported by its own set of four primary elements. Here, however, the substance as a genus (*jātidravya*) is intended, because other sets of four primary elements do not transcend their own genus. But who is it that speaks thus with such a distinction?
For the production of words occurs according to one's will, but their meaning must be examined.
The rule regarding the simultaneous arising of material phenomena has been stated; now, that which pertains to the remaining [phenomena] must be explained. In that regard:
Mind and mental factors necessarily arise together, for they are not capable of existing without one another;
likewise, everything arises together with the characteristics of conditioned phenomena.
The word "necessarily" (avaśyam) carries over [from the previous context].

Whatever arises— whether it be matter (rūpa), mind (citta), mental factors (caitasika), or dissociated phenomena (viprayukta)— all arise together with the characteristics of the conditioned (saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa) or with possession (prāpti).
The word "or" (vā) has the sense of a distinction, meaning that [the mind] arises together with its acquisition (prāpti) as something designated as a sentient being (sattvākhya), and not otherwise.
They are called mental factors (caitta).
What are these mental factors?
Mental factors (caitta) are fivefold, according to the divisions of the great ground and so forth.

There are five types of mental factors: those of the great ground (mahābhūmika), those of the great wholesome ground (kuśalamahābhūmika), those of the great afflictive ground (kleśamahābhūmika), those of the great unwholesome ground (akuśalamahābhūmika), and those of the limited afflictive ground (parīttakleśamahābhūmika).
"Ground" (bhūmi) refers to a sphere of occurrence.
For that which is the sphere of movement for something is called its "ground" (bhūmi).
In this context, they are called "great-grounded" (*mahābhūmikā*) because this ground is great for them—that is, those which exist in every state of mind.
Which ones, then, exist in every state of mind?

Feeling (*vedanā*), volition (*cetanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), desire-to-act (*chanda*), contact (*sparśa*), discernment (*mati*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), [attention (*manaskāra*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), and concentration (*samādhi*)].
Attention, resolve, and concentration are present in every state of consciousness. (24)
It is said that these ten factors are present in their entirety in every moment of consciousness.
Among them, feeling (*vedanā*) is a threefold experience:
pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

Volition (*cetanā*) is the mental formation that conditions the mind; it is mental action (*manaskarma*). Perception (*saṃjñā*) is the act of perceiving; it is the grasping of the signs of objects. Desire (*chanda*) is the wish to act.
Contact (*sparśa*) is the state of touching born from the coming together of the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness.
Intellect (*mati*) is wisdom (*prajñā*), the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the non-forgetting of the focal object.
Attention is the mental engagement of the mind;
resolve is conviction;
concentration is one-pointedness of the mind.
For the distinction between mental states and their concomitants is subtle;
it is difficult to discern even within continuous streams, let alone within single moments.

Even in the case of material medicinal plants with many flavors, certain specific tastes perceivable by the senses are hard to determine; how much more so for those phenomena that are formless and perceivable only by the intellect?
This is their "great wholesome ground" (kuśalamahābhūmi); thus, those which always exist in a wholesome mind are called the "great wholesome mental factors" (kuśalamahābhūmika).
What, then, are they? They are: faith (śraddhā), heedfulness (apramāda), pliancy (praśrabdhi), equanimity (upekṣā), moral shame (hrī), and dread of blame (apatrapā).
The two roots, non-violence, and vigor are always present in the wholesome. (25)
These ten factors are always present in a wholesome mind.
Among them, faith is the clarity of the mind;
others say it is conviction in the truths, the jewels, and the results of karma.
Heedfulness is the cultivation of wholesome states.
What, then, is this cultivation other than those states?
It is the state of being attentive toward them.
"Guarding of the mind"—thus do those belonging to other schools recite in their sūtras.
Pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is the serviceability of the mind.
[Is it not the case that pliancy of the body is also mentioned in the Sūtra?
Indeed, it is not that it was not mentioned.]
That, however, should be understood as being like bodily sensation.
[How then can it be included among the factors of enlightenment?
In that case, bodily pliancy should be understood as simply the serviceability of the body.
How is it called a limb of enlightenment? Because it is conducive to the limbs of enlightenment; for that pliancy of body and pliancy of mind brings about the limbs of enlightenment.
Furthermore, is this seen elsewhere as well? He replied: "It is.
For example, the Blessed One has stated that joy (*prīti*) and the factors conducive to joy are the factor of enlightenment consisting of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*).
Hostility and the cause of hostility are called the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*).
Right view, right resolve, and right effort are said to be the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*).
However, resolve and effort do not have wisdom as their intrinsic nature; rather, they receive that designation because they are conducive to it.
In the same way, bodily pliancy also receives the designation "factor of enlightenment" because it is conducive to the factors of enlightenment.

Equanimity is the evenness of mind and the state of non-exertion of the mind. How, then, can this be consistent with the statement: "In that very same mind, there is both attention, which consists of exertion, and equanimity, which consists of non-exertion"?
But was it not said that "the distinction between these is difficult to understand"?
Indeed, even that which is difficult to understand is understood;
however, this is truly exceedingly difficult to understand—that there is no contradiction even where there is contradiction.
What contradiction is there in [the mind] having application toward one object and non-application toward another?
If that is the case, then it follows that not all associated mental factors would have the same object at once.
Whatever principle applies to other matters of this kind that may arise here should also be understood to apply to this case.
Moral shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) will be explained later.
The two roots are the two wholesome roots, namely non-greed (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adveṣa*).
Non-delusion (*amoha*) also exists, but it has the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*).
And since wisdom (*prajñā*) is a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*), it is not mentioned here as being exclusively among the wholesome universal factors.
Non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) is non-injury (*aviheṭhanā*).
Vigor (*vīrya*) is the enthusiasm of the mind. Thus have been explained the wholesome universal factors.

"Great ground" (*mahābhūmi*) means a vast ground. Those afflictions for which this is the great ground are the "great-ground afflictions" (*kleśamahābhūmika*); these are the factors that always exist in an afflicted mind.
Which, then, are those that always exist in an afflicted mind?
Delusion, negligence, laziness, lack of faith, lethargy, and restlessness are always present in the defiled [mind].
Among these, "delusion" refers to ignorance, which is a lack of knowledge and a failure to perceive clearly.

Heedlessness (*pramāda*) is the non-cultivation of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*); it is the mental state that is the opposite of heedfulness (*apramāda*). Laziness (*kauśīdya*) is the lack of enthusiasm in the mind; it is the opposite of vigor (*vīrya*). Lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) is the absence of clarity in the mind; it is the opposite of faith (*śraddhā*).
What is *styāna*?
It is heaviness of the body, heaviness of the mind, unfitness of the body for action, and unfitness of the mind for action.
In the Abhidharma, it is stated that there is physical *styāna* and mental *styāna*.
How can a mental factor be called bodily?
It is just as [bodily] sensation is.
Furthermore, restlessness is the lack of tranquility of the mind.
Thus, these are the six universal mental factors of affliction (*kleśamahābhūmika*).
But are not ten universal factors of affliction taught in the Abhidharma?

Namely: lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kauśīdya*), forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*), distraction of mind (*cetaso vikṣepaḥ*), ignorance (*avidyā*), lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*), improper attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*), wrong resolve (*mithyādhimokṣa*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and heedlessness (*pramāda*).
The "Beloved of the Gods" (the King) knows what has been attained, but he does not know what is intended.
What, then, is intended here?

Forgetfulness, distraction, lack of clear comprehension, improper mental attention, and false resolve are not restricted solely to the great ground of afflictions, because they belong to the great ground [of all mental states].
Just as non-delusion (amoha), being of the nature of wisdom (prajñā), is not separately established as a great wholesome ground-factor,
so too afflicted mindfulness is simply forgetfulness (muṣitasmṛtitā),
and afflicted concentration is simply distraction (vikṣepa), and so forth.
Therefore it is said: "Those which are universal mental factors (mahābhūmika) are also universal afflictive factors (kleśamahābhūmika).
This constitutes a fourfold logical alternative (catuṣkoṭika).
The first alternative consists of feeling (vedanā), volition (cetanā), perception (saṃjñā), desire (chanda), and contact (sparśa).
The second [category] consists of lack of faith, indolence, ignorance, restlessness, and negligence.
The third consists of the five defiled factors beginning with forgetfulness, as previously described.
The fourth is defined as "excluding these aforementioned modes."
However, some maintain that distraction is a state of mind other than false concentration (*mithyāsamādhi*).
For them, the fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭika*) is formulated differently.

Furthermore, since torpor (*styāna*) is held to be associated with all afflictions (*kleśa*), whose fault is it that it is not recited among the universal mental factors of affliction (*kleśamahābhūmika*)?

Thus they say: it ought to have been recited there, but it was not recited because it is concordant with meditative concentration (*samādhi*). It is said that one whose temperament is characterized by lethargy (*styāna*) would more quickly produce concentration than one whose temperament is characterized by restlessness (*auddhatya*). But who is the one characterized by lethargy who is not characterized by restlessness, or who is the one characterized by restlessness who is not characterized by lethargy?
For these two never abandon their state of coexistence;
nevertheless, whichever of them is predominant in a person, that person should be known as being characterized by that [corresponding] conduct.
Therefore, it is established that there are exactly six universal ground-factors of affliction (*kleśamahābhūmika*).
For these two always exist only in a defiled mind and nowhere else; however, lack of shame (āhrīkya) and lack of dread (anapatrāpya) exist in unwholesome [minds]. (26)

In an unwholesome mind, however, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) are always present; thus these two factors are called the "great ground of the unwholesome" (*akuśalamahābhūmika*). Their definitions will be explained later.
Anger (*krodha*), enmity (*upanāha*), guile (*śāṭhya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), malice (*pradāsa*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), and avarice (*matsara*);
Deceit, intoxication, and harmfulness are the limited universal mental factors of affliction. // 27 //

The ground of these [factors] consists of limited defilements; thus, they are called "belonging to the ground of limited defilements" (*parīttakleśabhūmika*) because they are associated solely with ignorance that is to be abandoned by cultivation and belongs exclusively to the mental level (*manobhūmika*).
Their detailed exposition, however, will be given among the secondary defilements (*upakleśa*).
These five types of mental factors (*caitta*) have been explained.
There are also other indeterminate factors, such as applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), torpor (*middha*), and so forth.
In this regard, it must be stated how many mental factors necessarily arise in which state of mind.
First, the mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is of five kinds.
There is the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Among these, the unwholesome is of two kinds: that which is unique and that which is associated with other afflictions.
The indeterminate is of two kinds: the obscured-indeterminate and the unobscured-indeterminate.
In that regard, first of all, a mind belonging to the desire realm is necessarily accompanied by vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought);
therefore, because it possesses vitarka and vicāra, [the following applies] to a wholesome mind of the desire realm.
Twenty-two mental factors are necessarily present:
the ten universal factors (*mahābhūmika*), the ten virtuous universal factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), and applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
In some cases, there is additionally remorse. // 28 //
For remorse does not exist in every wholesome state of mind;
however, where it does exist, by adding that very factor, there are twenty-three mental concomitants.
What is this so-called remorse?
The state of having done what is bad is *kaukṛtya*. However, in this context, the mental factor that has remorse (*kaukṛtya*) as its object is called *kaukṛtya*; it is the regret of the mind.
For example, the door of liberation that has emptiness as its object is called "emptiness," and non-attachment that has the foul as its object is called "the foul."
Moreover, in common worldly usage, we see the designation of the occupant by means of the location, as in "the whole village has arrived" or "the whole country has arrived.
And remorse (*kaukṛtya*) serves as the locus for regret (*vipratisāra*);
or rather, this is a metaphorical application of the cause to the effect.
As it has been said: "These six spheres of contact (sparśāyatana) are to be understood as past karma.
How, then, can that which has an unperformed object be remorse (kaukṛtya)?
Even regarding what has not been done, there occurs the designation of "done," as in: "It was not well done by me that I did not do it."
What is wholesome remorse? It is that which one feels regret for having failed to perform a wholesome deed and for having performed an unwholesome one.
By contrast, unwholesome remorse is the opposite.
Thus, both of these [categories] have both as their basis.
However, in the case of unwholesome [minds] that are unique (*āveṇika*) and those associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*), there are twenty [mental factors].
In that unwholesome mind which is unique, there are twenty mental factors (*caitta*).

There are ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), six universal defiled factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*), two universal unwholesome factors (*akuśalamahābhūmika*), as well as initial thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
A "solitary" (*āveṇika*) mind is one in which ignorance alone is present and no other affliction such as attachment exists.
Even in an unwholesome state associated with views, there are twenty factors, which are the same as those in the solitary mind.
But is it not the case that there are twenty-one [mental factors] because of the addition of *dṛṣṭi* (view)?
No, they are not.
For a certain specific kind of wisdom (*prajñā*) among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) is what is called "view."

Among those, unwholesome [citta] associated with views consists of that in which there is either false view (mithyādṛṣṭi), adherence to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), or adherence to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
With the four afflictions [beginning with greed], along with anger and so forth, and with remorse (kaukṛtya), there are twenty-one [factors]. (26)

Furthermore, when an unwholesome mind is associated with any of the four afflictions—whether with attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), or doubt (*vicikitsā*)—there are twenty-one [mental factors] present:
that specific affliction and the twenty mentioned as being unique (*āveṇika*).

When the mind is associated with the aforementioned secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth, there are likewise twenty-one: those same twenty and that specific secondary affliction.
With remorse as well, there are twenty-one;
that same remorse becomes the twenty-first. In brief, there are twenty factors in an unwholesome mind that is either independent (*āveṇika*) or associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*).
However, when associated with other primary or secondary afflictions, there are twenty-one [mental factors].

In the desire realm, a mind associated with the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) or the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) is "obstructed-neutral" (nivṛtāvyākṛta), and in that case, there are eighteen [factors].
In that regard, there are eighteen mental factors (*caitta*):
ten universal factors (*mahābhūmika*), six universal factors of defilement (*kleśamahābhūmika*), and both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
As before, *dṛṣṭi* (view) is not additional.
Elsewhere, twelve [mental factors] are considered to be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Apart from the obscured (*nivṛta*), the indeterminate is the unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*);
therein, twelve mental factors are held to exist.
There are ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), as well as applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
The masters of the outer regions (*bahirdeśaka*) maintain that remorse (*kaukṛtya*) can also be neutral (*avyākṛta*);
for them, when that [neutral remorse] is associated with the mind, there are thirteen [mental factors].
Because drowsiness is not in conflict with any [of the hindrances], wherever it may be present, it is indeed additional.
Drowsiness (*middha*) is not incompatible with all these aforementioned mental factors (*caitta*), because it may be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.
Therefore, wherever that [drowsiness] occurs, it should be understood as an addition:
where there are twenty-two, there are twenty-three; where there are twenty-three, there are twenty-four, and so forth.
The same restriction regarding mental factors (*caitta*) that was stated for the desire realm applies here as well:
remorse (*kaukṛtya*), torpor (*middha*), and unwholesome states do not exist in the first dhyāna.
Therefore, according to what has been said, remorse and torpor—and whatever is unwholesome—are entirely absent in the first dhyāna.
Hostility, along with anger and the other [secondary afflictions] excluding guile, pride, and deceit, as well as lack of shame and lack of dread, [are absent].
Everything else is exactly the same; those very [afflictions] that do not exist in the first dhyāna [are likewise absent here].
In the intermediate dhyāna, applied thought (vitarka) is also absent;
the rest is exactly as before.
And beyond that, there is also *vicāra*. // 31 //
Beyond the intermediate dhyāna, in the second and subsequent dhyānas as well as in the formless attainments (ārūpyas), there is no investigation (vicāra), except as previously prohibited;
by the word "also" (api), it is implied that deceit (māyā) and guile (śāṭhya) are likewise absent.
The remainder is exactly as before.
For it is taught that Brahmā possesses guile only up to the extent of his own assembly, but not beyond it. Thus,
when he was asked a question by a monk who had defeated him in his own assembly— namely, "Brahmā, where do these four great elements cease without remainder?"—
he, being unable to answer, made a evasive remark.
“I am Brahmā, the Lord, the agent, the fashioner, the creator, the progenitor, the father of all beings.
This has been stated regarding which stage [of existence], in which mind, and how many mental factors (caitta) are present.
Now, the various distinctions among certain mental factors (caitta) as established in the treatise will be explained.
What is the distinction between lack of shame (āhrīkya) and lack of dread (anapatrāpya)? Lack of shame is a lack of respect (agurutā).

Lack of respect and lack of deference toward virtues and those possessed of virtue, characterized by fearlessness and lack of subordination, is *āhrīkya* (shamelessness); it is a mental state that stands in opposition to reverence (*gaurava*).
Lack of shame (*anapatrāpya*) is the failure to perceive fear in what is blameworthy. "Blameworthy" refers to that which is censured by the virtuous;
the failure to perceive fear regarding that is lack of shame.
"Fear" here refers to an undesirable result, for one fears it.
How is this to be understood: is "seeing fearlessness" (*abhayadarśitā*) the perception of fearlessness, or rather the non-perception of fear?
And what follows from this?
If the non-perception of fear is understood, it will be recognized as wisdom (*prajñā*); if the perception of fear is understood, it will be recognized as ignorance (*avidyā*).
For indeed, perception itself is not the perceiver, nor is non-perception the non-perceiver.
What then?
That which is the cause of those two [shamelessness and lack of dread] is the secondary affliction called *anapatrāpya* (lack of dread).
Others, however, say:
"Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) is the absence of embarrassment regarding one's faults with respect to oneself; lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) is the same with respect to others."
Even so, how could these two dependencies be established simultaneously?
Indeed, it is not said that one depends on both self and other at once; rather, there is a certain lack of shame which occurs even when one is depending on oneself—that is *āhrīkya* (shamelessness).
There is another which occurs when one is depending on others—that is *anapatrāpya* (lack of dread of blame).

Shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) should be understood as the opposite. According to the first interpretation, shame is having reverence and respect, rather than acting out of fear; dread of blame is the failure to see danger in what is blameworthy.
According to the second interpretation, regarding the two types of shame (*hrī*) based on consideration for oneself and others,
what is the difference between affection (*preman*) and reverence (*gaurava*)?
Affection is faith (*śraddhā*).
For affection is of two kinds: afflicted and unafflicted.
Among these, the afflicted is craving, such as that toward one's children, wife, and so forth;
the unafflicted is faith, such as that toward the Teacher, gurus, and those endowed with virtuous qualities.
There may be faith that is not love:
faith that has suffering and its origin as its object.
There may be love that is not faith.
Afflicted affection is one;
faith that takes cessation and the path as its object is both;
and, setting aside these modes, there is that which is neither.
Regarding persons, there is affection (*prema*) but not reverence (*gaurava*) toward one's children, wife, co-residents, and disciples;
there is reverence but not affection toward other teachers;
and both exist toward one's own teachers.
Setting aside these two modes,
faith is indeed the estimation of qualities;
and affection preceded by that [faith] is love.
Therefore, others maintain that it is not affection itself;
for shame (*hrī*) is gravity (*gurutva*),
and gravity indeed means a sense of reverence.
And that [reverence] preceded by it is *hrī* (moral shame).
Therefore, others maintain that *hrī* is not merely reverence.
Furthermore, those two exist in the realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and form (*rūpadhātu*). (32)
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), affection (*prema*) and respect (*gaurava*) do not exist.
But is it not the case that faith (*śraddhā*) and shame (*hrī*) are present there as well, since they belong to the great ground of wholesome factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*)?
For faith is of two kinds: [faith] in phenomena (*dharma*) and [faith] in persons (*pudgala*).

The same applies to reverence (*sapratīśatā*). In that context, those [qualities] which are faith (*śraddhā*) and shame (*hrī*) directed toward a person do not exist there; rather, it is love (*prema*) and respect (*gaurava*) that are intended here.
What is the difference between applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*)? Applied thought and sustained thought are grossness and subtlety; of what? Of the mind.
He will explain "of the mind" later on:
grossness of mind is *vitarka*;
subtlety of mind is *vicāra*.
But how, then, is there a conjunction of these two in a single moment of consciousness?
Some say:
it is like clarified butter dropped into water that, when touched from above by the rays of the sun, neither solidifies too much nor melts away too much.
Thus, through the conjunction with applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), the mind becomes neither too subtle nor too gross; therefore, both have an operation therein.

If that is so, then applied thought and sustained thought would be the causes of grossness and subtlety, respectively—just as water and heat are the causes of the solidification and melting of ghee—but they would not themselves possess those intrinsic natures.

Furthermore, since grossness and subtlety are relative according to the distinctions between stages (*bhūmi*) and types, it would follow that applied thought and sustained thought would exist all the way up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Nor is a distinction between types justified on the basis of coarseness and subtlety.
Others, however, say:
"Initial inquiry (vitarka) and sustained investigation (vicāra) are stated in the Sūtra to be the formative forces of speech:
'Having inquired and having investigated, one utters speech; not without having inquired and investigated.'"
In that regard, those which are gross are *vitarka* (applied thought), and those which are subtle are *vicāra* (sustained thought).
If, within a single moment of consciousness, one factor is gross and another is subtle, what contradiction is there?
There would be no contradiction if there were a difference in their genus (*jāti*), as is the case with feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).
Within a single category, the states of weak and intense cannot exist simultaneously;
furthermore, there is a distinction between categories.
Therefore, that [distinction] must be explained.
For this [defect] is difficult to express; therefore, it is manifested through its mildness and intensity.
It is not manifested in this way [by the whole], because each individual genus possesses both mildness and intensity.
For others [hold] that vitarka and vicāra do not indeed exist together in a single moment of mind.
How, then, is the first dhyāna endowed with five factors?
It is endowed with five factors by way of its stage (bhūmi), not by way of each individual moment.
What is the difference between pride (*māna*) and arrogance (*mada*)? Pride is haughtiness; arrogance, however, is the total absorption of the mind of one who is attached to his own qualities. //33//
Pride (*māna*) is the inflation of the mind due to any conceptualization of superiority over others. Intoxication (*mada*), however, is the total absorption of the mind in one's own qualities alone;
just as it arises from liquor, so too does it arise from passion (*rāga*).
Others maintain that *mada* (intoxication) is a specific kind of exhilaration (*saṃpraharṣaṇa*).

Thus have the mental factors (*caitta*) been explained along with the mind; furthermore, these technical designations for them are now defined, because by means of these terms, correct linguistic usage (*sadvyavahāra*) occurs within the teaching (*pravacana*).
Citta, manas, and vijñāna have the same meaning: it is called *citta* because it accumulates (*cinoti*);
it is called *manas* because it cognizes (*manute*).
It is called consciousness because it cognizes.
It is called "citta" because it is accumulated by pure and impure elements;
that same [entity], when serving as the basis, is "manas," while others maintain that when it serves as the supported, it is "vijñāna."
Just as *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* have one and the same meaning,
so too do *citta* and the *caittas*.
Having a basis, an object, and an aspect, as well as being associated— these constitute a single meaning.
For it is those very same minds and mental factors that are called "having a basis," because they depend upon the sense faculties.
They have an object (*sālambana*) because they grasp an objective field; they possess an aspect (*sākāra*) because they represent that very object according to its specific mode;
they are associated (*saṃprayukta*) because they are conjoined equally.
In what manner are they applied equally? He says:
"in five ways" (34).
By five kinds of equality: equality of basis, object, aspect, time, and substance.
What is this equality?
For just as the mind is one, so too each mental factor (*caitta*) is one.
The mind and mental factors have been explained with their detailed classifications.
The formations dissociated from mind are: acquisition, non-acquisition, homogeneity, the state of non-ideation, the two attainments, vitality, and the characteristics. (35)
The name-aggregates and so forth—these formations are neither associated with the mind nor do they have the nature of matter; therefore, they are called "dissociated from the mind."
In this context, "attainment" (prāpti) means acquisition (lābha) and possession (samanvaya).
For attainment is twofold: the acquisition of what was previously unobtained or lost, and the possession of what has already been acquired.
It is established that non-attainment is the opposite of this.
Furthermore, to whom do these possession (*prāpti*) and non-possession (*aprāpti*) belong?
Possession and non-possession belong to those factors that fall within one's own continuum (*svasaṃtāna*), not to those that fall within the continua of others (*parasaṃtāna*).
No one is possessed of [dharmas] belonging to another, nor of those that do not fall within a [personal] continuum;
for no one is possessed of those reckoned as non-sentient.
This, first of all, is the rule regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, regarding the unconditioned, possession and non-possession pertain to the two types of cessation. (36)
All sentient beings are endowed with analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
For this very reason, it is said in the Abhidharma: "Who is endowed with untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*)?
It is replied:"
Regarding "all sentient beings":

by means of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), all noble ones (*ārya*)—with the exception of those abiding in the first moment [of the path] who are still bound by all fetters—and some ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) are possessed of it.
However, no one is possessed of space (*ākāśa*).
Therefore, this [non-acquisition] has no acquisition;
and it is an established tenet that for whatever has no acquisition, there is likewise no non-acquisition.
[Is it the case that] "acquisition" (*prāpti*) is some distinct entity?
From what is this known?
It is said: from the Sūtra.

For it is stated in the Sūtra: "By the arising, the acquisition, and the possession of these ten qualities of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), one becomes a noble one who has abandoned five factors," and so forth.
If that is so, then it would follow that there is possession even of those things designated as non-sentient, and even of other sentient beings.
What is the reason?
From the statement in the Sūtra: "O monks, a wheel-turning monarch is endowed with seven jewels," and so forth;
here, the word "endowment" (*samanvāgama*) refers to mastery (*vaśitva*).
"He has mastery over those jewels, acting according to his will.

In this context, "mastery" (*vaśitva*) means possession (*samanvāgama*); otherwise, it would be a separate substantial entity (*dravyāntara*). Why is this so? What, then, is the inconsistency in such a [substantialist] view?

This is untenable: for its intrinsic nature is not perceived, unlike that of form, sound, and so forth, nor like that of passion, hatred, and so forth; nor does it have a function, like the eye, the ear, and so forth.
Therefore, because a substantial entity (dravyadharma) is impossible, [the theory] is untenable.
If it is argued that acquisition (*prāpti*) is the cause for the arising of dharmas—
It would not exist for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, how could there be the arising of those dharmas which have not yet been attained, or those which have been abandoned through changing levels (*bhūmi*) or through detachment (*vairāgya*)?
If it is argued that they arise with innate possession (*sahajā prāptiḥ*) as their cause, [then...]
Now, would birth (*jāti*) or the "birth of birth" (*jātijāti*) be its servant?

Furthermore, there would be no distinction in the arising of weak, medium, or intense afflictions (*kleśa*) among those bound by all fetters, because there would be no distinction in what is attained.
Or rather, let that very [distinction] from which such a difference arises be the cause of their production.
Therefore, acquisition is not a cause of arising.
And who says that acquisition is the cause of arising? Rather,
it is the cause of differentiation.

For if possession (*prāpti*) did not exist, there would be no distinction between noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) regarding those who possess mundane mental states; one could not establish that "these are noble ones" and "these are ordinary persons.
This distinction must arise from the difference between having abandoned or not having abandoned the afflictions (*kleśa*).
But how will this [distinction] be established—that for these people the afflictions have been abandoned, while for those they have not?
This is established when attainment occurs, due to the departure or non-departure of that [attainment].
This is established through a specific transformation of the basis (*āśraya-viśeṣa*).

For the basis of the noble ones is transformed by the power of the paths of seeing and cultivation in such a way that it is no longer capable of the regrowth of those afflictions (*kleśa*) which were to be abandoned by them.
Therefore, when the basis has become seedless regarding the afflictions—like rice grains burnt by fire—one is said to have abandoned the afflictions;
or [when they are abandoned] by the mundane path through the impairment of their seed-state.
By the opposite of this, one has not abandoned the afflictions.
It is designated that one who has not abandoned [a defilement] is possessed of it, and one who has abandoned it is not possessed of it.

Wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*) are also of two kinds: those that arise without effort and those that arise with effort; these are called "acquired at birth" (*utpatti-pratilambhika*) and "acquired through application" (*prāyogika*).

Among these, one is said to be "endowed" (*samanvāgata*) with those arising without effort because the state of their seeds within the basis (*āśraya*) has not been impaired; conversely, due to impairment, one is said to be "not endowed," as in the case of one whose wholesome roots are severed (*samucchinna-kuśalamūla*).
That impairment, however, should be understood as occurring through wrong view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).

However, there is certainly no absolute eradication of the seed-nature of wholesome dharmas within the continuum. Furthermore, regarding those [wholesome dharmas] that arise through effort, once they have arisen, one is said to be "endowed" with them because the mastery over their arising is unimpeded within the continuum.

Therefore, it is the seed itself—when it has not been uprooted, not impaired, and cultivated—which receives the designation of "endowment" at the time of mastery; it is not some other distinct substance.
What, then, is this so-called "seed"?
It is that name-and-form which is capable of producing a fruit, either directly or through a succession [of causes], by means of a specific transformation of the continuum.
What is this so-called transformation? It is the alteration of the continuum. And what is this continuum?
The conditioned phenomena belonging to the three time periods, which exist as cause and fruit.
As for what was said— that one who is possessed of greed (*lobha*) is incapable of cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)—
in that context, "possession" (*samanvāgama*) refers either to the tolerating or the non-dispelling of greed.
For as long as one remains a tolerator and does not dispel it, one is incapable of cultivating them.
Thus, this possession (*samanvāgama*) is in every respect a nominal phenomenon (*prajñaptidharma*) and not a substantial phenomenon (*dravyadharma*);
and its negation is non-possession (*asamanvāgama*).
The Vaibhāṣikas, however, describe both as being substantial entities (dravya).
For what reason?
Because this is our established tenet (siddhānta).

This acquisition (*prāpti*) of factors belonging to the three time periods is of three kinds: for past factors, there is an acquisition that is past, as well as one that is future, and also one that is present.
In this way, for each of the future and present [dharmas], there are three kinds.

The acquisition (prāpti) of wholesome and so forth is wholesome and so forth; that is, the acquisition of the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral [dharmas] is respectively wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.
For those [dharmas] belonging to a particular realm, the acquisition belongs to that same realm.
For those dharmas that belong to a particular realm, their acquisition (prāpti) belongs to that same realm;

for dharmas belonging to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, the acquisition belongs respectively to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness. For dharmas not belonging to any realm, the acquisition is of four kinds. // 37 //
The acquisition (*prāpti*) of untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena is fourfold:
in brief, it belongs to the three realms and it is untainted.

Among these, the acquisition of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) belongs to the three realms; the acquisition of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) belongs to the form and formless realms and is also untainted.
The acquisition of the truth of the path is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
Thus, taken collectively, it is of four kinds:

the acquisition of the factors of those in training (*śaikṣa*) is itself of the nature of training; that of the factors of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is itself of the nature of beyond-training; but for those factors that are neither of training nor beyond-training, there is a distinction.
It is explained as being threefold: [the attainment] of those who are neither-learner-nor-non-learner refers to contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Their attainment is of three types according to the distinction of learner (*śaikṣa*) and so forth.
First, for contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*), the acquisition (*prāpti*) is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣānāśaikṣī*).
This also applies to non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) when it is acquired by a non-noble person.

For that same analytical cessation, when it is acquired by the learner’s path (*śaikṣamārga*), the acquisition is learner (*śaikṣī*); when acquired by the non-learner’s path (*aśaikṣamārga*), it is non-learner (*aśaikṣī*).

The acquisition (*prāpti*) of those [dharmas] to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) is, respectively, only to be abandoned by seeing and only to be abandoned by cultivation. However, there is a distinction regarding those that are not to be abandoned (*aheya*); that is now explained:
Those [dharmas] not to be abandoned are considered to be of two kinds; the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas are not to be abandoned.

Among them, the acquisition (prāpti) of analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha) is to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya), as is the acquisition of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha) when it has been acquired by one who is not an Ārya.
And [it is the possession] of that very [path] which has been attained through the noble path, as well as of the untainted truth of the path, which is not to be abandoned.
Regarding what was stated—"for those belonging to the three time periods, [the acquisition] is of three kinds"—this is the exception to that general rule:
the acquisition of the neutral (*avyākṛta*) is simultaneous;
for non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) states, the acquisition is only simultaneous, neither preceding nor following in time.
Because of their weakness;
therefore, for those [dharmas] that are past, [the possession] is only past, and so on up to those that are present, it is only present.
[Is this true] for all that is non-obscured and neutral?
Not for all;
excluding the supernormal powers and those produced by magical transformation. (38)

Excluding the two neutral supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*), for these possess strength because they are accomplished through a specific application; therefore, their acquisition (*prāpti*) occurs before, after, and simultaneously [with the dharma]. Some also maintain that this applies to certain states of deportment (*īryāpathika*) that have been intensely practiced, such as those belonging to the stage of "standing firm like a mountain" (*śailasthānika*).
[He asks: Is the co-nascent acquisition (*sahajā prāpti*) only for that which is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*)? He replies:
It is also for obscured form (*nivṛtasya ca rūpasya*).

Even for informative form (*vijñaptirūpa*) that is obscured-unspecified, the acquisition is only co-nascent; for it is established that it is weak because it does not give rise to non-informative form (*avijñapti*), even when it is intense.

"Just as there is this distinction in the acquisition (*prāpti*) of neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas, is there likewise some distinction in the acquisition of wholesome (*kuśala*) and unwholesome (*akuśala*) ones? He says: 'There is; however, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the acquisition of a form-dharma (*rūpa*) does not arise prior [to the dharma itself]. "
For the form of informative and non-informative matter belonging to the desire realm, there is no acquisition (*prāpti*) that arises prior to it in any way;
however, there is acquisition that arises simultaneously with it and that which arises at a later time.
Is there also a distinction in its modes, as there is for acquisition (*prāpti*)?
He says: no.
What then? Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is undefiled and neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*).
All non-attainment is exclusively unobscured-neutral.
Furthermore, according to the distinction of time periods,
that [non-arising] is threefold in the cases of the past and the unborn.
For that which is present, there is no non-acquisition that is itself present; however, for the past and the future, non-acquisition belongs to all three time periods.
The phrase "is of three kinds" applies to those obtained in the desire realm and so forth, as well as to the immaculate ones.
For those obtained in the desire realm, [the acquisition] belongs to the desire, form, and formless realms.
The same applies to those factors pertaining to the form and formless realms, as well as to the untainted (anāsrava) factors. There is no such thing as an untainted non-acquisition (aprāpti);
for it is held that there is no non-acquisition of the Path.
Regarding the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*):
"What is the state of being an ordinary person? It is the non-attainment of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*)," so says the text of the treatise.
Non-acquisition (*alābha*) is indeed non-attainment (*aprāpti*). Furthermore, the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) cannot possibly be untainted (*anāsrava*).
[Of which noble dharmas (*āryadharma*) is there non-acquisition?]
Because it is stated without distinction for all [beings]. However, that "non-possession" (alābha) refers to the absence of acquisition;
otherwise, even a Buddha would be a non-noble one (anārya), since he would lack the possession of the lineages (gotra) of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
"In that case, the word *eva* should be recited. "It need not be recited;
for even single words can function as exclusives (*avadhāraṇa*)."
For example, it is like saying "one who eats water" or "one who eats air."
Others say that it is the non-acquisition of the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and its co-arising factors.
Nor does this entail the consequence of being a non-noble person (*anāryatva*) due to the possession of that [non-acquisition], because that non-acquisition has been utterly destroyed.
In that case, they belong to the three lineages (*trigotra*); of which [lineages] is there non-attainment?
Of all of them.
If that is so, then the same fault remains.
Furthermore, that same refutation applies:
in that case, effort would be useless;
rather, it is correct as the Sautrāntikas maintain.
And how is it for the Sautrāntikas? "The state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) is the continuity [of a stream] in which the noble dharmas have not yet arisen."
Now, how is this non-acquisition (aprāpti) abandoned?

When there is the acquisition of a particular dharma for someone, that [non-acquisition] is abandoned through the acquisition of that [dharma], through death, or through the transition to another stage (bhūmi). //40//

Just as the non-attainment of the noble path constitutes the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), which is abandoned through the attainment of that path and through the transition to another stage (*bhūmi*), so it should be applied to other cases as well.
Regarding the term "is abandoned": the non-attainment of that [non-attainment] arises, and its possession (*prāpti*) is severed.
Furthermore, do acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) themselves have acquisition and non-acquisition?
They say that both possess both.
[But would this not then lead to the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding acquisitions?]
There is no consequence of infinite regress,
because they arise in mutual association;
for a phenomenon arises with itself as the third.
That dharma, its acquisition (prāpti), and the acquisition of the acquisition (prāptiprāpti) constitute it.

In this regard, through the arising of the acquisition, one becomes possessed of that dharma and with the acquisition; and through the arising of the acquisition of the acquisition, one again becomes possessed of the acquisition itself. Therefore, there is no infinite regress.
And having established it thus, for a third dharma—whether wholesome or afflicted—three acquisitions (*prāpti*) arise in the second moment;
and for those [three], there are again three subsequent acquisitions (*anuprāpti*), so that there are six.
In the third moment, there are nine acquisitions of the entities produced in the first and second moments, together with their subsequent acquisitions, making eighteen.

If this were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of an infinite progression; for these acquisitions (*prāpti*), spreading forth, would arise moment by moment in an individual being as infinite entities—since they would belong to all past and future moments of primary and secondary afflictions, as well as to innate wholesome moments, along with their associated and co-existent factors included within the beginningless and endless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
Thus, the moments of personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) within each continuum would consist of infinite substances.
They exist for sentient beings;
indeed, this great festival of acquisitions is taking place.
However, they are solely non-obstructive, since they find space within space.
Otherwise, indeed, there would be no room even in space for a second living being.
Now, what is this "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā)? Homogeneity is the similarity among sentient beings; it is a real entity (dravya) called homogeneity.
The similarity among sentient beings is designated in the treatise as "homogeneity" (*nikāyasabhāga*). This, moreover, is both undifferentiated and differentiated.
The undifferentiated is the homogeneity of sentient beings (*sattvasabhāgatā*) common to all sentient beings.

It exists in all [beings] with respect to each individual being (*pratisattvam*). However, they are distinct (*bhinnā*) as they are specifically determined (*pratiniyatā*) by the differences among those very beings—such as realm (*dhātu*), stage (*bhūmi*), destiny (*gati*), mode of birth (*yoni*), caste (*jāti*), female, male, lay follower (*upāsaka*), monk (*bhikṣu*), learner (*śaikṣa*), and non-learner (*aśaikṣya*). Furthermore, the homogeneity of phenomena (*dharma-sabhāgatā*) is based on the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). If the homogeneity of beings (*sattva-sabhāgatā*) were not a distinct substance (*dravya*), there would be no undifferentiated cognition (*buddhi*) of "being, being" with respect to beings who are otherwise distinguished by their mutual differences.
And there is designation (*prajñapti*).
In this same way, the cognitions and designations of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are also to be applied.
Could it be that one would die and be reborn, yet neither abandon nor acquire the homogeneity of sentient beings? There are four alternatives.
The first alternative is: dying from a certain place and being reborn in that very same place.
The second [case] is one who enters into the determination of correctness (*niyāma*);
for he abandons the homogeneity of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana-sabhāgatā*) and acquires the homogeneity of a noble one (*ārya-sabhāgatā*).
The third is due to the transition between realms of existence (*gati*).
The fourth alternative is excluding these aforementioned cases.
If there were a substantial entity called "ordinary-person homogeneity" (*pṛthagjana-sabhāgatā*), what further purpose would there be for "ordinary-personhood" (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
For one does not postulate "humanity" (*manuṣyatva*) as something distinct from "human homogeneity" (*manuṣya-sabhāgatā*).

Furthermore, the world does not perceive *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) because it is formless (*arūpin*), nor does one discern it through wisdom; yet, one still recognizes the lack of difference in the births of sentient beings. Thus, even if *sabhāgatā* exists, how could it have any functional activity (*vyāpāra*) in that regard? Moreover, why is the homogeneity of non-sentient things (*asattvasabhāgatā*) not also accepted?

[This is so] because rice, barley, mung beans, black gram, iron, copper, gold, and so forth, possess similarity within their own respective classes. And how can a designation of "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) be made without distinction for those various homogeneities which are mutually distinct? In this way, the Vaiśeṣikas are also [implicitly] illuminated; for they too hold this established tenet: [The Vaiśeṣika Sūtra states: "Generality (*sāmānya*) is that which, being one, resides in many. There exists a category called "generality" (sāmānya), from which the arising of a common cognition occurs even with respect to things of dissimilar types.
However, this is its distinction [from other categories]:
although it is one, it subsists in many. Whether it is explicitly expressed or not expressed, [it remains so].
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that this "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) exists because it is mentioned in the Sūtra.

For the Blessed One said: "If he comes to such a state, [he attains] the homogeneity of humans. This has indeed been stated, but it has not been stated that it is a separate substantial entity (dravyāntara).
What, then, is that?

It is simply those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) existing in such a way that the designation "human" and so forth is applied to them, just as the homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*) is applied to rice and other grains.
However, they do not describe it in this manner.
Now, what is this so-called "state of non-perception"? The state of non-perception exists among those who are non-percipient;
it is the cessation of mind and mental factors.

For those reborn among the gods who are non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), that cessation of mind and mental factors is a substantial entity called "non-perception" (*āsaṃjñika*). By means of this, mind and mental factors are completely suppressed for a certain period in the future time and do not obtain the opportunity to arise, just like the damming of river water.
Furthermore, that which is exclusively maturation— of what is it the maturation?
Regarding the attainment of non-perception:
who are those beings among whom are the non-percipient beings?
They are the Bṛhatphala [gods]. //41//
There are gods named Bṛhatphala, some of whom are non-percipient beings (asaṃjñisattva) in a certain region, like those in the intermediate dhyāna. But do they ever possess perception?
They do, at the time of birth and at the time of death.
The reading in the Sūtra is: "Even after remaining for an extremely long time, when perception arises, those beings undergo a fall from that place.
Having fallen from there like those who have awakened from a long sleep, they are reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and nowhere else;

because their previous formative forces (*saṃskāra*) from meditative attainment are exhausted and no new ones are accumulated, they fall to the earth like arrows shot [into the air] whose momentum has been spent.
Furthermore, for one who is to be reborn there, there must necessarily be karma belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*),
just as the case of the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, whose karma is to be experienced upon rebirth in the heavens. Now,
regarding what was said concerning "the two attainments" (*samāpatti*), which are those two attainments?
The attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). What is this attainment of non-perception?
Just as it was stated regarding the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*) that "it is the cessation of mind and mental factors," so too is the attainment of non-perception.
The attainment of non-perception, or non-perception itself, is the "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
It, too, is the cessation of mind and mental factors.
This much is drawn forward by the word "likewise" (*tathā*).
That attainment, however, occurs in the final dhyāna;
the final dhyāna is the fourth, and it is included within that [dhyāna], not belonging to any other stage.
For what purpose do they enter this meditative attainment?
Out of a desire for liberation;
they consider this to be liberation.
Therefore, out of a desire for liberation, they enter into meditative absorption.
It is established that the state of non-perception (āsaṃjñika) is neutral because it is a result of maturation;
however, this [state] is wholesome.
The attainment of non-perception is exclusively wholesome;
its maturation consists of the five aggregates among the non-percipient beings.
Being wholesome,
it is exclusively to be experienced upon rebirth;
that is, it is necessarily to be experienced in the next life.
It is neither to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-paryāya-vedanīya*) nor is it indeterminate (*aniyata*).
Even one who, having produced it, falls away from it, is said to necessarily produce it again and be reborn among the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñi-sattva*).
For this very reason, one who has attained it does not enter the path of certainty (*niyāma*).
This [attainment] is held to belong only to ordinary persons (pṛthagjana), not to noble ones (ārya);
for noble ones do not enter the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), viewing it as if it were a place of downfall.
For they enter that attainment perceiving it as a means of escape.
Now, do the Noble Ones, upon attaining the fourth dhyāna, acquire [the knowledge of] the past and future just as they do the dhyāna itself?
Even others do not acquire it;
what is the reason?
For although this [attainment] is indeed appropriate, it is [not considered "proper"] because it must be accomplished through great effort and because it is devoid of mental activity.
It is acquired as belonging to a single time period. // 42 //
The meaning is "belonging to a single time";
it is obtained as pertaining only to the present time,
just like the Prātimokṣa restraint.
Once it has been attained, however, one remains possessed of it even in the past state during the second and subsequent moments, as long as one does not abandon it.
Because there is no mind [in that state], the future [state] is not cultivated.
Now, what is the attainment of cessation? It is called "cessation" and is exactly like this [attainment of non-conception].
By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), what aspect is being grasped?
It is the phrase: "the cessation of mind and mental factors."
But this is its distinction:
it is for the purpose of dwelling.
They enter this [attainment] by means of mental attention preceded by the perception of peaceful dwelling;
however, they enter that [other attainment] by means of mental attention preceded by the perception of deliverance.
That indeed belongs to the level of the fourth dhyāna,
whereas this one is born from the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
It belongs exclusively to the level of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
And this [state] is auspicious and indeed wholesome; it is neither afflicted nor neutral.
Being wholesome, it is of two types of experience and indefinite;
it is to be experienced at two times: either to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) or to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).

And it is indefinite with respect to its maturation, for it may sometimes not mature at all if one were to attain parinirvāṇa here [in this life]. For its maturation consists of the four aggregates at the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
And this [attainment] belongs exclusively to the noble one;

for ordinary persons are unable to produce the attainment of cessation because they fear annihilation, whereas it is produced by the power of the noble path, and thus there is an inclination toward it as being nirvana in the present life.
And this [knowledge] of the noble one is not obtained through detachment;
what then?
It is obtained through application. //43//
This is obtainable only through application;
it is not obtained as something past, nor is it cultivated as something future,
because its cultivation occurs through the power of the mind.
Is the [knowledge] of the Blessed One also acquired through application?
No; he says:
for the Sage, it is obtained through enlightenment.
