One consisting of four aggregates has a single fruit: wholesome or unwholesome mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) together with their birth-characteristics and so forth.

In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), a ripening cause (vipākahetu) consisting of a single aggregate has a single fruit: acquisition (prāpti) and the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñisamāpatti), together with their [characteristics] such as birth. A ripening cause consisting of two aggregates has a single fruit: informative action (vijñapti) in the first dhyāna, together with its [characteristics] such as birth.
A ripening cause consisting of four aggregates has a single fruit: when there is a wholesome mind that is not in meditative absorption.
The five aggregates have a single fruit when in a state of meditative concentration.

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), a ripening cause (*vipākahetu*) consisting of a single aggregate (*skandha*) has a single fruit: namely, acquisition (*prāpti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), together with their [characteristics] such as birth (*jāti*).
A ripening cause consisting of four aggregates consists of wholesome mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) and their [characteristics] such as birth.
There is karma whose ripening matures as only a single sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), namely, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
For one who possesses the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*), there are two [bases]: the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).

Likewise, for one who possesses the sense-base of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) or the sense-base of the body (*kāyāyatana*), there are three: the sense-bases of body, the tangible, and phenomena.
The same applies to one who possesses the sense-bases of visible form, odor, or taste.
For one who possesses the sense-base of the eye, there are four [bases]: the eye, body, tangible objects, and mental phenomena bases.
Likewise for one who possesses the sense-bases of the ear, nose, or tongue.
There is such karma for which five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, or eleven sense-bases ripen as its maturation.
Because karma has both variegated and non-variegated fruits, just like external seeds.
For example, some external seeds have variegated fruits, such as those of the lotus, pomegranate, and banyan tree.
Some have unvariegated fruits, such as those of barley, wheat, and so forth.

The maturation of a karma belonging to a single time-period ripens as something belonging to all three time-periods; however, even for a karma belonging to two time-periods, it does not ripen as something belonging to only one time-period, lest the fruit be less than its cause. Likewise, the maturation of a karma of a single moment is of many moments, but not the reverse.

Furthermore, the maturation does not ripen simultaneously with the karma, nor does it ripen immediately after it, because the immediately succeeding moment is drawn forth by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
For the cause of maturation depends upon a continuum.
Now, what is the temporal restriction for these causes?
The restriction regarding their time periods has been explained by implication, but it has not yet been formulated as a formal aphorism (sūtra); therefore, it is now set forth:
"The omnipresent (sarvatraga) and the similar (sabhāga) [causes] belong to two time periods; they exist only in the past and the present, and do not exist in the future."
And the reason for this has been stated: "The three [causes] belong to the three time periods;
the co-existent, associated, and retributive causes belong to all three times."
The efficient cause (kāraṇahetu), however, should be understood as belonging to all time periods and as being dissociated from time, because no restriction of time is demonstrated for it.
The causes have been explained.
What, then, is that fruit of which these are the causes? It is the conditioned, together with the fruit of dissociation.
Which phenomena are the fruits?

"Conditioned phenomena and analytical cessation," so says the treatise. If that is the case, then because the unconditioned is a fruit, it must have a cause of which it is the fruit; and because it is a cause, it must have a fruit of which it is the cause.
It is only for conditioned phenomena that cause and fruit exist.
For you, there is no [arising] of the unconditioned. // 55 //
What is the reason?
Because the six kinds of causes are impossible and the five kinds of fruits are impossible.
Why, then, is the path not accepted as the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*)?
Because it is established as being non-obstructive to arising, and the unconditioned does not possess the quality of arising;
of what, then, is this the fruit, or how is it the fruit of the Path? It is the fruit because it is attained through the power of that [Path].
In that case, it follows that attainment alone is the fruit of the path,
because the path has efficacy with respect to that [attainment] and not with respect to dissociation;
for its efficacy regarding attainment is of one kind, while its efficacy regarding dissociation is of another.
How does it have the capacity for its attainment?
By way of producing it.
How [does it have the capacity] for dissociation?
Because it is that which is attained;
therefore, its path is in no way its cause.
And its fruit is dissociation (*visaṃyoga*).
Now, if there is no dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), how can the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) be a causal condition (*kāraṇahetu*)?
It is a causal condition by virtue of being a non-obstruction to arising.
Furthermore, it has no fruit, because that which is liberated from the [three] time periods is incapable of either receiving or giving a fruit.
For the Blessed One has never stated anywhere that the unconditioned is a cause;
however, the Sautrāntikas maintain that it is stated to be a cause by way of a particular formulation (paryāya).
How was this stated?
"The causes and conditions for the arising of form are themselves impermanent.
Since form has arisen in dependence upon causes and conditions that are indeed impermanent, how could it be permanent?
This applies in the same way up to consciousness.
If that is the case, then the unconditioned would not even qualify as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for consciousness; however,
it does so qualify because of the restriction [in the definition] "for the sake of arising."
It was stated: "Those causes and those conditions for the arising of consciousness are also impermanent," but it was not stated: "Those which are conditions for consciousness are also impermanent.

However, since it is said that only those causes which [bring about] arising are impermanent, this does not preclude the unconditioned from being a causal condition (*kāraṇahetu*) by virtue of its mere state of non-obstruction.

The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) has been mentioned in the Sūtra, but it is not stated there that it is a non-obstructing cause; therefore, the causal status of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not established by the Sūtra.
Even if it was not explicitly mentioned, it was certainly not prohibited.
Furthermore, since many Sūtras have disappeared, how can it be determined with certainty that it was not mentioned?

Now, what is this so-called "disjunction" (visaṃyoga)? Was it not already stated previously that it is "cessation through deliberation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha)? At that time, it was asked, "What is cessation through deliberation? It is disjunction," whereas now it is stated, "Disjunction is cessation through deliberation."
This circular explanation is incapable of illuminating its intrinsic nature;
therefore, its intrinsic nature must be stated otherwise.
[That intrinsic nature is to be personally realized by the Noble Ones alone.]
This much, however, can be said: there exists a distinct entity that is eternal and wholesome;
its dissociation is called cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The Sautrāntikas, however, maintain that all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are non-substantial (*adravya*).
For it is not a separate entity like form, feeling, and so forth;
what then? Space is merely the absence of the tangible.
For example, just as people say "space" when they find no resistance in the darkness;

so too, the cessation of arisen latent dispositions and their manifestations through the power of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*), such that others do not arise, is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
That which is non-arising due to the deficiency of conditions, even without analytical discernment, is [non-analytical cessation].
That is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
For example, it occurs when there is death midway while a portion of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) remains.
However, those belonging to other schools say:
The capacity of wisdom (*prajñā*) lies in the arising of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*); therefore, this is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

On the other hand, that which is the non-arising of suffering occurs simply due to the deficiency of the latent dispositions—the causes of arising—and thus wisdom has no capacity regarding it; therefore, this is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Nevertheless, since even that is not established without analysis (*pratisaṃkhyā*), it is indeed analytical cessation.

"Others maintain that non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is precisely that absence which occurs after something has arisen, due to its cessation by its own inherent nature (*svarasa-nirodha*).
However, according to this conception, non-analytical cessation would result in being impermanent, because it does not exist as long as [the entity] has not yet perished.
But would it not follow, then, that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is also impermanent?"
Because it is preceded by analytical discernment (pratisaṃkhyā).

Indeed, that [non-arising] is not preceded by analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*), for it is not the case that discernment comes first and subsequently there is the non-arising of those things that have not yet arisen.
What then?
That non-arising of theirs exists from the very beginning.
However, those phenomena which would have arisen in the absence of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) do not arise again once that discernment has arisen;
this is the efficacy of analytical discernment here, namely, its state of being an obstruction to the arising of those things whose arising was previously unobstructed.

If, then, non-arising alone is nirvāṇa, how is this scriptural passage to be interpreted: "These five faculties, when cultivated, developed, and practiced extensively, lead to the abandonment of suffering past, future, and present"?
For abandonment is nirvāṇa, and non-arising pertains only to the future, not to the past or the present.
This is indeed so;

however, it was stated by the Blessed One that the abandonment of suffering results from the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that take those [aggregates] as their object: "Whatever desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) there is for form, abandon it.
When desire and lust are abandoned, in this way that form will be abandoned and fully understood," and so on in detail up to consciousness.
In this way, the abandonment of suffering belonging to the three time periods is also logical.
Furthermore, even if it were said that [the path] is for the sake of abandoning past, future, and present afflictions,
this same principle applies here as well.
Alternatively, this may be the intended meaning: past affliction refers to that belonging to a previous birth, while present affliction refers to that belonging to the current birth.

For example, regarding the eighteen modes of craving (*tṛṣṇā-vicarita*), it is said that "the eighteen modes of craving based on the past time" refer specifically to a past birth, and so on up to the present.
And by those two types of afflictions, the state of a seed has been deposited in this continuum for the sake of the arising of future [afflictions].
Through their abandonment, that [continuum] also becomes abandoned,
just as karma is exhausted through the exhaustion of its maturation (*vipāka*).
Furthermore, abandonment is the absolute non-arising of future suffering or affliction due to the absence of their seeds;
for otherwise, what would there be to abandon regarding the past or the present?
Indeed, effort is not purposeful toward that which has already ceased or is in the process of ceasing.

If the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) does not exist at all, then how could that which was said by the Blessed One—“Of whatever dharmas there are, whether conditioned or unconditioned, detachment (*virāga*) is declared to be the foremost among them”—be possible? For how could that which is non-existent be the foremost among things that are non-existent? We do not say, however, that the unconditioned simply does not exist.
This matter is exactly as we have stated:
for instance, it is said that there is the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of a sound and there is its posterior non-existence (paścādabhāva);
and yet, moreover, non-existence does not establish itself as a positive entity (bhāva).
In this way, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) should also be viewed.

Furthermore, even a certain kind of non-existence (*abhāva*) can be most praiseworthy— namely, the absolute non-existence of all affliction— and thus it deserves to receive praise as "the foremost" among other things,
for the purpose of enticing those to be trained (*vineya*) toward it.
Even if the unconditioned were a mere non-existence, cessation would not be a Noble Truth; for it would not exist as anything at all. What, then, is the meaning of "truth" (satya)?
But is it not the case that its meaning is non-erroneous?

Both of these are seen as non-erroneous by the Noble Ones: namely, that suffering is indeed suffering, and the absence of suffering is indeed an absence. What contradiction is there in this being a Noble Truth? How, moreover, can an absence be called the third Noble Truth?
The Noble Truths have been explained as they were taught; since the second was both seen and pointed out immediately following [the first], it becomes the third.

If the unconditioned were merely a non-entity, then consciousness having space and nirvana as its objects would have a non-existent object. We shall consider this further when examining the existence of the past and the future.
Furthermore, if the unconditioned were intended to be a substantial entity, what would follow?
Furthermore, what would happen? The Vaibhāṣika position would be protected,
provided that the deity considers it worthy of protection and shall protect it.
But it would be an unreal conceptual construction.
For what reason?
Because its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not perceived, as is the case with form, sensation, and so forth, nor is its function (karma) perceived, as is the case with the eye and so forth.
Furthermore, how can the grammatical construction of the genitive case—expressing "this is the cessation of that entity"—be established?
For there is no relationship whatsoever between the two, since a causal relationship or any similar connection is impossible.
What is appropriate, however, is a mere negation, such as "the non-existence of that."
Even though it is a distinct entity, that cessation which is attained through the severance of the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a particular affliction is designated as "belonging to" that affliction.
What, then, is the cause for the restriction of its acquisition?
It is said in the Sūtra: "A monk has attained Nirvāṇa in this very life."
In that case, how could there be the attainment of a non-existence?
It is said that Nirvana is attained because, through the acquisition of the antidote, one acquires a basis that is absolutely opposed to the arising of afflictions and further existence;
moreover, scripture also indicates that it is a mere non-existence.
For thus it is said:

"That which is the complete abandonment, relinquishment, exhaustion, destruction, fading away, cessation, pacification, and disappearance of even this small amount of suffering, and the non-linking, non-arising, and non-manifestation of further suffering—this is lovely, this is sublime; namely, the relinquishing of all acquisitions (*upadhi*), the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and Nirvana."
"Why is it not accepted that 'aprādurbhāva' (non-manifestation) means 'it does not manifest in this'?
We see this locative case (*saptamī*) as being semantically untenable.
What, then, is being asserted?"
If [the phrase] "it does not appear in this" is connected with the word "existing," then it follows that non-appearance would be eternal, because Nirvana is eternal.

If, on the other hand, it is connected with the word "attained," then one must accept that the non-appearance of suffering occurs precisely when that [Nirvana] is either being realized or has been attained—since it is only from that [realization or attainment] that its acquisition is postulated. And in this way, the illustration is well-applied.
"The liberation of his mind is like the extinguishing of a lamp.
Just as the extinguishing of a lamp is non-existence, so too is the liberation of the Blessed One's mind.
It is also said in the Abhidharma: "Which are the phenomena that lack a real basis?"
"Unconditioned phenomena" means that they are said to be without a basis,
without a body, and without intrinsic nature.
This is not its meaning; what then? It refers to the fivefold category of objects.
The entity as intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavastu*), as it is said: "Whatever entity has been acquired, one is endowed with that entity.
The entity as object (*ālambanavastu*), as it is said: "All phenomena to be known are known by knowledge according to their actual state (*yathāvastu*)."

The object of conjunction (*saṃyogavastu*), as it has been said: "In whatever object attachment is associated with the fetter of attraction (*anunayasaṃyojana*), in that very same [object] it is also [associated] with the fetter of aversion (*pratighasaṃyojana*).
The causal object (*hetuvastu*), as it has been said: "Which are the phenomena that possess a basis (*savastukā dharmāḥ*)?"
"Conditioned phenomena" refers to the objects of appropriation,
as it is said: "the object of a field, the object of a house," and so forth.
In this context, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the word "entity" (vastu) refers to a cause; therefore, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) certainly exists as a substantial entity (dravyataḥ).
However, it possesses neither cause nor fruit. This much has been established.
Now, among these fruits, which fruit belongs to which cause?
The fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) belongs to the last [cause], because the cause of maturation (*vipākahetu*) is stated to be the last; thus, it is the "last" one.
This is its fruit of maturation.
The fruit of the first is the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
The efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) is "the first" because it was mentioned first;
its fruit is that which is born of sovereignty (*adhipaja*).
What is the predominance (*ādhipatya*) of that which exists merely as a state of non-obstruction?

It is precisely this. Furthermore, the causal condition (*kāraṇahetu*) also possesses the status of being a constituent factor (*aṅgībhāva*), as for example: the ten bases (*āyatana*) in relation to the five groups of consciousness, and karmic actions in relation to the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
Even the ear and other [senses] possess a predominance in the arising of visual consciousness by way of succession.
"Having heard [it], the desire to see arises"—thus the sequence beginning with these words is to be applied.

The outflow [result] belongs to the homogeneous and the pervasive [causes], because these two have similar results; thus, their result is the outflow-result (niṣyandaphala). The virile result (pauruṣaphala) belongs to the other two [causes]. (56)
The fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) belongs to the co-existent cause (sahabhūhetu) and the associated cause (saṃprayuktakahetu).
Since "human effort" (puruṣakāra) is not distinct from the state of being a person (puruṣabhāva), "human effort" is simply the person himself; its fruit is the "fruit of human effort" (pauruṣa).
What is this so-called "human effort" (puruṣakāra)?
It is the activity (kāritra) of a given dharma;
for human effort is so called because it is like the effort of a person.
For example, as with the *kākajaṅghā* herb or a person who is "drunk-handed" (*mattahasta*).
[Question: Does the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) belong only to these two, or does it also belong to others? [Answer:
It belongs to others as well, except for the ripening cause (*vipākahetu*).
Because the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) is either co-arisen or immediately arisen,
whereas the ripened fruit (vipāka) is not;
yet even for that [ripened fruit], there exists a remote fruit of human effort.
Others say it is like the crop of farmers.
Furthermore, what is this so-called "fruition of maturation" (*vipākaphala*), and so on up to the "dominant fruit" (*adhipatiphala*)?
Maturation is an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomenon;
for it is an unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomenon that constitutes maturation.
It might also be called "non-sentient"; therefore he says:
it is called "sentient.
It might also be "accumulative" (aupacayika) or "resultant" (naiḥṣyandika); therefore he says: [it is accumulative].
It arises from the "determined" (*vyākṛta*).
For that which is wholesome or unwholesome is called "determined" because it is determined with respect to its maturation (*vipāka*).
And from that, [the result] arises at a later time—not simultaneously and not immediately after; that is maturation.
This is the characteristic of maturation (*vipāka*). Why is an object not designated as a sentient being, though born of karma, not considered maturation?
Because it is common to all.
For indeed, anyone else would also be capable of enjoying that very same thing;
however, the ripening [of karma] is not shared.
One person does not experience the ripening of karma performed by another.
Why does one experience the dominant fruit?
Because it arises from collective karma.
The outflow is that which resembles its cause;
whatever dharma is similar to its cause is the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*),
as is the case with the homogeneous and pervasive causes.
If the fruit of the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*) is also the same [as that of the similar cause], why is it not accepted as being merely a similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*)?
Because its similarity [to its fruit] is based on its level (*bhūmi*) and its defiled nature (*kliṣṭatā*), but not on its specific type (*prakāra*).
However, that which possesses similarity even by way of its specific type is indeed accepted as a similar cause.

For this very reason, a fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭika*) is established regarding whether that which is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for something is also its pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*):
the first alternative is a homogeneous cause that is not pervasive;
the second is a pervasive cause belonging to a different category (*anya-naikāyika*).
The third [category] consists of those belonging to a single homogeneous class that are universal causes (*sarvatragahetu*).
The fourth [category] is "excluding these aforementioned modes. Disjunction (*visaṃyoga*) is destruction by means of wisdom (*dhiyā*). (57)
"Kṣaya" means cessation (nirodha).
"Dhī" means wisdom (prajñā).
By this, it is stated that analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is the fruit of dissociation (visaṃyoga-phala).
That which arises by the power of something else is a fruit born of human effort (*puruṣakāraja*).

For example: the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of a higher stage arising from the preparatory mind (*prayogacitta*) of a lower stage; the untainted (*anāsrava*) arising from the tainted (*sāsrava*); the emanation-mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) arising from a dhyāna-mind, and so forth.
However, regarding analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), it must be stated that it is attained by the power of something else.
That which is unprecedented (apūrva) is the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala) of only that which is conditioned (saṃskṛta). // 58 //
A conditioned dharma other than one that has previously arisen is the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*) of every conditioned phenomenon.
What is the distinction between the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the sovereign fruit?
The fruit of human effort belongs to the agent.
Even for one who is not the agent, there is the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
For example, in the case of an artisan, the craft is both the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit;
for others, it is solely the sovereign fruit.
Now, among these causes, which cause grasps or gives its fruit at what time?
The five present causes grasp their fruit; past causes do not, because they have already been grasped, nor do future causes, because they lack human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
The efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) is also like this; however, it is not mentioned [in the same context] because it does not necessarily possess a fruit. Two [causes] bestow [their fruit].
The co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*) bestow their fruit while they are present;
for the giving and receiving of the fruit by these two occurs at exactly the same time. The other two [causes] bestow their fruit when they are present and past.
It is indeed logical that the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) bestow their fruit when they are past;
but how do these two bestow their outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) while they are present?
Because they turn back immediately;
however, once the fruit has been realized, those two [causes] have passed away, and the fruit has already been given— it is not given again.
Is there a wholesome homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) that receives a fruit but does not give one? There are four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*).

The first alternative consists of those acquisitions (*prāpti*) which one abandons last of all when severing the roots of wholesomeness (*kuśalamūla*). The second consists of those [acquisitions] which one acquires first of all when reconnecting the roots of wholesomeness.
It should rather be stated as follows:
the first [alternative] would apply to those very states of reconnection; the third applies to one whose roots of merit are not severed during the remaining states;
and the fourth applies to all cases except for these aforementioned modes.
But for the unwholesome, the first alternative is as follows:

when one attains detachment from the desire realm, those acquisitions (*prāpti*) which one abandons last of all; the second is when one falls away from detachment from the desire realm, those [acquisitions] which one acquires first of all.
However, it should be stated in this way:
The first would belong to one who is falling away from those [attainments].
The third belongs to one who is not yet free from passion for the desire realm during the remaining states.
The fourth is excluding these aforementioned modes.
In the same way, for the obscured-unspecified [mind], it should be applied accordingly based on the attainment or loss of arhatship.
For the unobscured-unspecified [mind], there is a "consequent" [condition]:
whatever [karma] one gives, that one also receives.
It may be that [the cause] receives but does not give, as in the case of the final aggregates of an Arhat;
however, this is according to the restriction of having an object (sālambana), moment by moment.
Thus, a wholesome homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) receives its fruit but does not give it.
There are four alternatives.
The first alternative is that immediately after a wholesome mind, one brings forth either a defiled or an indeterminate mind.
The second is the reverse.
The third [alternative] is when a wholesome state follows immediately after a wholesome state;
the fourth is excluding these aforementioned modes.
In the same way, unwholesome states and so forth should also be applied accordingly.
How, then, is the fruit received? Because it has attained the state of being its seed. One [cause], when past, bestows it. (56)
The ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) bestows its fruit only when it is past,
because the ripening effect does not exist either simultaneously with or immediately after [the cause].
Furthermore, others speak of four kinds of fruits.
The fruit of establishment (*pratiṣṭhā-phala*):
as the water mandala is [the support] for the wind mandala, up to grass and so forth for the earth.
The fruit of application (*prayoga-phala*).
Just as, for example, the knowledge of non-arising resulting from [the cultivation of] the foul is the fruit of the causal complex (*sāmagrīphala*),
so too are the visual consciousnesses and so forth the fruits of the eye and other [faculties].
The fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanāphala*) is,
for example, the emanation (*nirmāṇa*) of a mind belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*).
This, however, is included within the fruits of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and sovereign dominance (*adhipatiphala*).
The causes and the fruits have been explained.

In that regard, which phenomena arise from how many causes? He says: in brief, these phenomena are of four kinds, namely: afflicted phenomena, those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), the first untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena, and the remainder besides these.
But what, then, are the "remainder"?

Excluding those that are results of maturation (*vipāka*), the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) factors, and excluding the first moment of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state, the wholesome (*kuśala*) factors— these four kinds of phenomena—
are, respectively, afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), born of maturation (*vipākaja*), the remaining [neutral] ones, and the first noble (*ārya*) ones.
Excluding the resultants, the universal [factors], and those two [wholesome and unwholesome] factors that are similar, the remaining [factors] arise from them. // 60 //
Defiled (*kliṣṭa*) phenomena arise from the remaining five causes, excluding the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Phenomena born of ripening (*vipākaja*) arise from exactly the remaining five causes, excluding the omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
All other phenomena arise from the remaining four causes, excluding those two—the ripening cause and the omnipresent cause.

Those two [types of] first [momentary] untainted phenomena arise from the remaining three causes, excluding the fruition cause (*vipāka-hetu*), the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
He asks: "Which are these four kinds of phenomena that have been taught? and replies:
"They are mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*)."
Now, as for those factors that are dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*) and those that are material (*rūpin*), he asks: "How are they? He says:

"Likewise, others also, excluding the associated cause. Other factors as well—such as the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and so forth—arise in the same manner as in that case, being excluded by only the single associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*).
Defiled dharmas arise from four causes, as do those born of maturation;
the remaining ones arise from three; the first pure dharmas arise from two.
There is no dharma that arises from a single cause.
The detailed exposition of causes is concluded! What are the conditions?
Four conditions have been taught.
It is stated in the Sūtra:
"There are four conditions."
"Causal conditionality, immediate conditionality, objective conditionality, and dominant conditionality"—
this class of conditions is what is meant by "conditionality."
Among those, that which is called "cause" consists of five causes. // 61 //
With the exception of the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*), the five causes constitute the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*).
Minds and mental factors that have arisen, excluding the final ones [of an Arhat], are the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Excluding the last minds and mental factors of an Arhat, those that have arisen are the immediately preceding condition.
It is called the "immediately preceding condition" because it is both equal (*sama*) and immediate (*anantara*) as a condition.

For this very reason, form (*rūpa*) is not an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), because its arising is irregular. To explain: immediately after a form belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there sometimes arises an unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) belonging both to the desire realm and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and sometimes one belonging both to the desire realm and the untainted (*anāsrava*) realm; thus, the manifestation of form is disordered. An immediately preceding condition, however, is not disordered, as it arises only when a single stream of accumulated form (*aupacayika-rūpa*) has not yet ceased, according to the Venerable Vasumitra.
The Venerable [Vasumitra] says it is because of the arising of the smaller from the larger;
for sometimes a small amount arises from a large form, such as ashes from a heap of straw.
Sometimes many arise from few, as for example, from a single banyan seed (*vaṭanikā*) there gradually arises a banyan tree (*nyagrodha*) with many branches and aerial roots.
But is it not the case that among mental factors (*caitta*) as well, there is an arising of more from less?
In wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral minds, as well as in the three types of concentration beginning with that characterized by applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*),
there is [a predominance] in relation to a different category (*jātyantara*), but not in relation to its own category.
For never does feeling (*vedanā*) arise in greater measure, nor do perception (*saṃjñā*) and the other [mental factors].
But is it the case that only [factors] of the same category serve as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
This is not so.

Rather, an entire complex (*kalāpa*) is the immediately preceding condition for another entire complex; what is stated here is merely that a copious substance of feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth does not arise from a small substance of feeling and so forth.
However, the Santānasabhāgikas maintain that "the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) belongs only to its own kind;
for example, mind [is the condition] for mind alone, and feeling for feeling alone," and so forth.

But when a defiled state arises after an interval of non-defiled states, the previously ceased defilement is the immediately preceding condition for that defilement—just as, for example, the mind at the moment of entering the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is the condition for the mind upon emerging from it.

This cannot be accepted, because it would entail the consequence that the first untainted (*anāsrava*) mind could never arise. Furthermore, even those formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*) are not "immediately preceding conditions" (*samanantara-pratyaya*) precisely because they appear in a disordered manner; for those belonging to the three realms and those that are unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*) can manifest simultaneously.
Why is the future not accepted as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
Because the future time period is disordered, lacking the distinction of prior and subsequent.
[How then does the Blessed One know that "immediately after this specific future [moment], this other future [moment] will arise"?]
Because of inference from the past and the present:
the Blessed One indeed perceives the past path, seeing that from such a kind of action, such a kind of maturation arose— whether it was non-dharma or dharma—
and he sees that this present action is also of such a kind.
Therefore, he knows that from this [cause], a result of such a kind will arise—whether it be non-dharma from non-dharma or dharma from dharma.
And this knowledge is not merely inferential;

for by means of an inference based on the past and the present, the Blessed One perceives directly those future entities scattered about and knows: "By this person performing such an action, this specific future [result] will come to pass."
"The fruit has been grasped.
If that were so, then the Blessed One would not know the future limit (aparānta) without having seen the past limit (pūrvānta).
Others, however, say:

There exists a specific conditioning factor (*saṃskāraviśeṣa*), dissociated from thought (*cittaviprayukta*), within the continuum of sentient beings that serves as a sign of their future results; by observing this, the Blessed One knows the future even without bringing meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) or supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) into the present.
If this were the case, the Blessed One would merely be a "reader of signs" (*naimittika*), and not one who possesses direct realization (*sākṣātkārī*).
Therefore, the Sautrāntikas maintain that the Blessed One knows everything by mere intention;
for it was said by the Blessed One: "The range of the Buddhas' cognition is indeed inconceivable."

Now, if the future does not exist with a fixed order of succession, why is it that immediately after the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*agradharma*), only the Receptivity to the Knowledge of Dharma regarding Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises and no other dharma?
And likewise, up until the point where immediately after the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama*), only the Knowledge of Destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) arises and no other dharma?
That whose arising is dependent upon another arises immediately after that [other].
For example, sprouts and so forth arise from seeds and so forth even without an immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya).
Why are the final mind and mental factors of an Arhat not a *samanantara-pratyaya* (immediately preceding condition)?
Because they are not connected to any subsequent mind.

But if that is so, since it is said that "the mind that has just ceased becomes the *manas*," then because there is no subsequent consciousness, the final mind would also fail to qualify as the *manas*.
The mind (*manas*) is manifested by way of its state as a support (*āśraya-bhāva*), not manifested by way of its activity (*kāritra*); thus, the state of being a support certainly exists.
However, because of the deficiency of other causes, another consciousness does not arise.

But as for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), which is manifested by way of its activity, no phenomenon whatsoever—neither by all phenomena nor by all living beings—is able to obstruct that dharma which has been grasped as a fruit by it.
Just as it does not arise.
Are those phenomena which have the mind as their immediate antecedent also without interval from the mind? There are four alternatives.
The first alternative consists of the mind emerging from a mindless attainment and the second and subsequent moments of that attainment.
The second alternative consists of the birth and other characteristics of the first moment of attainment and of the state accompanied by mind.
The third alternative consists of the first moment of attainment and the state accompanied by mind.
The fourth alternative consists of the birth and other characteristics of the second and subsequent moments of attainment, as well as those of the mind of emergence.
[Are those dharmas which have the mind as their immediate antecedent also those that are immediately preceded by the meditative attainments?
This is a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika).
Those that are the third and fourth [alternatives] should be made the first and second; those that are the first and second should be made the third and fourth.

[Question: How can it be said that the mind of emergence, which is separated by a vast interval, is the immediate antecedent (samanantara) to the mind of meditative attainment? [Answer: Because it is not intervened by another mind.
The immediately preceding condition has been explained.

The objects of focus are all phenomena (*sarvadharma*); specifically, according to their respective applications, they are visible form for visual consciousness together with its associated mental factors,
and sound for auditory consciousness.
Odor is the object of olfactory consciousness; taste is the object of gustatory consciousness;
and the tangible is the object of tactile consciousness.
The objects of mental consciousness are all phenomena.
Whatever dharma is the object of another dharma, that dharma is never not the object of that [other] dharma;
for even when it is not being apprehended as an object, it possesses that same characteristic.
Just as wood and the like are called "fuel" even when they are not being burned, because they possess that same characteristic.
These very phenomena—the mind and mental factors—are fixed upon their respective objects by way of the determination of their bases, substances, and characteristics.
Are they also fixed by way of the determination of their supports? He replied: "Yes."
Those that have arisen are conjoined with their basis; those that have not yet arisen and those that are past are dissociated from their basis.
Others, however, maintain that even past [dharmas] are conjoined with their basis.
The object-condition has been explained.
That which is called the cause is known as the dominant condition. // 62 //
That which is the causal cause (kāraṇahetu) is itself the sovereign condition (adhipatipratyaya).
This condition is called the "dominant condition" (*adhipati-pratyaya*) because it is superior.
[Objection: Since all phenomena (*sarva-dharmāḥ*) are both objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and dominant conditions, what is its superiority? [Response:
Co-existent phenomena never become an objective condition.
But they become dominant conditions; this alone is their distinction.
Alternatively, every condition is the condition for everything that is conditioned, excluding its own intrinsic nature.

There may be a phenomenon that is not a condition for another phenomenon even by way of all four conditions. This may be the case with respect to self-nature being a condition for self-nature. Furthermore, other-nature may also be a condition:
conditioned phenomena for unconditioned phenomena, and unconditioned phenomena for unconditioned phenomena.
Now, while these conditions are performing their activity (*kāritra*), in what state of the dharma do they perform it?
First, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) has been stated to be of five kinds;
therein—
Two causes exercise their activity upon that which is ceasing;
"ceasing" means being present,
because it is facing toward cessation.

In that regard, the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) and the associated cause (*saṃprayuktakahetu*) exercise their activity; their operation pertains even to a fruit that has arisen simultaneously with them. There are three [types of causes].
Regarding "at the time of arising": that which is called "arising" is the future [dharma] facing toward production.
In that state, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) exercise their activity (*kāritra*).
Thus, first, is the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya); the other two conditions, however, are the reverse of that. //63//

By the same principle of activity (*kāritra*) by which the cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) were explained as being twofold, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) should be understood through their respective opposites.
The immediately preceding condition performs its activity while [the mental state] is arising, by providing an opportunity;
the object-condition performs its activity while [the mental state] is ceasing.
Because it grasps [objects] by means of present mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*),
and because the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) exists in every state by way of non-obstruction— this alone is its functional activity (*kāritra*).
The conditions, together with their functions, have been explained.
Now, which phenomenon arises from how many conditions? Mental states and mental factors arise from four;
therein, the causal condition for these consists of all five causes.
The immediately preceding condition consists of preceding mind and mental factors that are not separated by others.
The object-condition consists of the five sense objects and all phenomena, as appropriate.
The dominant condition consists of all phenomena, excluding its own self-nature.
The two attainments [of cessation and non-perception] are [conditioned] by three [conditions].
For the attainment of cessation and the attainment of non-perception, there is no object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*),
because they do not have an object.
As for their causes and conditions, there are two kinds of cause:

the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*), which consists of [the factors] such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth; and the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), which consists of previously arisen wholesome phenomena belonging to the same level.
The immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is the mind of meditative attainment (*samāpatticitta*) together with its associated mental factors (*saṃprayoga*).
The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as before.
Because these two attainments (*samāpatti*) are born from the mental formation (*cittābhisaṃskāra*), they are "immediately preceding" (*samanantara*) to the mind;
however, because they obstruct the arising of the mind, they are not the "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Others, however, arise from two [conditions];

others, moreover, such as the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*) and material phenomena (*rūpin*), arise from the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), exactly as prescribed. But it has been said that entities arise from conditions, and not that God (*īśvara*), the Primordial Spirit (*puruṣa*), Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*), or the like, is the cause of the entire world.
What is the reason for this?

If you indeed believe that establishment is produced by a cause, then does it not follow that this very doctrine is refuted, namely, that a single cause such as Īśvara and so forth is the cause of everything?
Furthermore, [the world] does not arise from a creator god (īśvara) and so forth, because of [the observed] succession and other such characteristics. //64//
For if God, or any other single cause, were the sole cause, the entire world would have to come into being simultaneously;
yet we observe that the arising of entities occurs in a sequence.
In that case, it must be by the power of God's will that [the sequence occurs], such that: "Let this arise now, let this cease, and let this arise later."
In that case, it would follow that there are multiple causes due to the diversity of desires;
yet that [diversity] could not exist because its cause, Īśvara, is non-differentiated.
Alternatively, if he were to depend on a difference in other causes, then Īśvara alone would not be the cause.

Furthermore, if these [effects] were to arise sequentially, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress because they would depend on a distinction among other causes; thus, by accepting that this beginningless succession of causes possesses infinite diversity, this proponent of God as the cause would not have transcended the very same logic previously held by the Śākyas. Even if [the desires of] God were simultaneous, the world would not be simultaneous.
If it is argued that [this is so] because they are produced according to one's desire,
we say no;
for there is no subsequent distinction among them.
Furthermore, what possible purpose could there be for the Lord in such an effort toward creation?

If it is pleasure [that he seeks], then since he is unable to produce that pleasure without a means, he would not be the Lord with respect to that pleasure, nor likewise with respect to anything else. And if the Lord, having created beings afflicted by many calamities in the hells and other realms, takes pleasure therein—homage be to such a Lord!
And regarding this, there is a well-known verse:
"Because he burns, because he is sharp, because he is fierce, because he is majestic, and because he consumes flesh, blood, and marrow, he is therefore called Rudra."
Furthermore, by accepting a single cause for the world, the directly perceived human effort regarding other things would be denied.
Moreover, one who postulates God as the agent even alongside other causes would be engaging in mere devotional rhetoric;
for apart from those causes, no further operation of Him is observed in their production.
Furthermore, if there were other auxiliary causes, God would not be the sole sovereign (*īśvara*). If, on the other hand, the initial creation were caused by God,
then because that [initial creation] too would be independent of anything else, it would follow that it is beginningless, just like God himself.
The same should be stated, as appropriate, regarding the *pradhāna* as well.
Therefore, there is no single cause for the world;
rather, it is their own respective karmas that produce them in this or that particular birth.

But those wretched ones of unrefined intellect, while experiencing their own respective fruits of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and fruits of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*), falsely imagine another, namely Īśvara.
This concludes what was said regarding the statement, "Others, however, are born from two.
Now, how are the primary elements (*bhūta*) the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*) for the primary elements?
The primary elements are its cause in two ways; that is to say,
they are its cause as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) and co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).
But for the derivative [matter], it is fivefold.
For derivative matter, the primary elements are a cause in five ways.
How so?
“By way of producing, supporting, abiding, sustaining, and nourishing”—
this very *kāraṇahetu* (efficient cause) is further divided into five types:
the producing cause (*jananahetu*), because [the effect] arises from them.

The supporting cause (*niśraya-hetu*) is so called because that which has arisen conforms to the primary elements (*bhūta*), like a disciple’s reliance on a teacher and others; it is the cause of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).

The foundational cause (*pratiṣṭhā-hetu*) is so called because it serves as a basis, like a painting. The sustaining cause (*upastambha-hetu*) is so called because it is the cause of non-interruption.
Thus, it has been explained that these [elements] serve as the cause for the birth, transformation, support, maintenance, and growth [of derived matter].
Derived matter acts as a cause for other derived matter in three ways:

by way of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*). The efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is not always enumerated because it functions without distinction [from all other phenomena].
In that regard, co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) consists of bodily and vocal action that follows the mind, mutually [with one another], but not other derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
Similar-type cause (*sabhāgahetu*) consists of everything previously arisen for that which is of a similar type.
The ripening cause is that vocal karma of which the eyes and so forth are the ripening result.
That [state] of all beings is indeed one and the same. // 65 //

However, that derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) of the primary elements (*bhūta*) is exclusively a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), for the primary elements are the ripening of that bodily and vocal action.

While mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) have been described generally as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), no specific restriction has been stated as to which mental state arises immediately after which one;
that must now be explained.
In that regard, first of all, there are briefly twelve states of mind.
To the question "For what purpose?", he says:
"The wholesome and unwholesome, and the obscured and unobscured mind, exist in the realm of desire."
In the desire realm, there are four types of consciousness:
wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, and unobscured-unspecified.
In the form and formless realms, there is no unwholesome consciousness; there are only the others.
In the form realm (rūpadhātu), there is no unwholesome [state];
three exist.
Likewise in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Thus, these constitute the ten types of consciousness with outflows (*sāsrava*);
the untainted (*anāsrava*) is of two kinds. (66)
[The mind] of one in training and that of one beyond training;
thus, there are these twelve types of mind therein.
Regarding the statement that "in the realm of desire (kāma), these [nine] arise immediately after a wholesome mind," it will be explained later:
from whatever wholesome mind exists in the desire realm, nine minds arise immediately thereafter.
There are four [minds] belonging to its own level;
two belong to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*):
at the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), it is wholesome (*kuśala*), and at the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*), it is obscured-unwholesome (*nivṛta*).
At the time of rebirth-linking, only the obscured [neutral] mind of the formless realm occurs;
the wholesome mind does not, because it is too remote.
For the formless realms are distant from the desire realm by way of four kinds of remoteness.
Through distance in terms of basis, aspect, object, and antidote,
as well as that which pertains to those in training and those beyond training—
it arises from exactly eight [causes].
Furthermore, in that regard, a wholesome mind of the desire realm arises immediately after eight [minds]:
from the four belonging to its own level, from two of the form realm,
and from the wholesome [mind] at the time of emergence from meditative absorption.
From the obscured [neutral], because one who is oppressed by an afflicted attainment (kliṣṭa-samāpatti) resorts to the wholesome stages that serve as its support;

and from the states of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), at the time of emergence. Unwholesome [mind] arises from ten [minds], excluding the states of those in training and those beyond training. For in the desire realm, at the moment of rebirth-linking (pratisandhi), an unwholesome mind arises immediately after all minds of the form and formless realms.
Therefore, there are four;
from an unwholesome mind, minds of its own level alone arise immediately thereafter.
Just as the unwholesome has been described in the desire realm, so it is here.
And likewise, that which is obscured. // 67 //
Immediately after the ten [minds], only four [minds] arise; and from those four, again only four arise;
from the five [minds], the unobscured-unspecified arises.
The term "desire realm" (kāma) continues to apply here.
A non-obscured neutral mind arises immediately after five [minds]:
from the four minds of its own level and from the wholesome mind of the form realm that is a mind of transformation (nirmāṇacitta).
Therefore, seven minds arise immediately after [an] unobscured-neutral mind of the desire realm: four belonging to its own level,
and two belonging to the form realm.
A wholesome [mind] arises immediately after a mind of transformation;
a defiled [mind] arises at the time of rebirth-linking;
and a defiled mind belonging to the formless realm arises only at the time of rebirth-linking.
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), eleven [minds] arise from a wholesome mind;
from whatever wholesome mind exists in the realm of form, immediately thereafter eleven minds arise,
excluding the non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*).
Immediately after that, from the nine [factors]. // 68 //
However, a wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) arises immediately after nine [minds]:
excluding the two defiled minds of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) and the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*).
An obscured [neutral] mind arises from eight [minds].
The obscured-unspecified mind of the form realm arises from eight [minds]:
excluding the two afflicted minds of the desire realm and the minds of those in training and those beyond training.
From that [obscured-unspecified mind], six [minds] arise.
Immediately after the unobscured-neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) mind of the form realm, six [minds] arise:
the three belonging to its own level and the unobscured-neutral minds of the desire realm, excluding the obscured-unspecified.
Furthermore, from three [minds], the unobscured-neutral arises again.
The non-obscured-neutral mind of the form realm arises from only the three minds of its own level;
from it arise six minds of its own level and three defiled minds of the desire realm.
And that which belongs to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*).
Just as the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) was explained in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), such is the principle for it in the formless realm.
Therefore, that [mind] which is non-obscured-neutral also arises from only three [minds], namely those belonging to its own level.
And from that [non-obscured-neutral mind], exactly six arise:
the three belonging to its own level and the defiled minds of the lower realms.
Furthermore, from the wholesome [state]. //66//
There are nine minds:
from a wholesome mind of the formless realm, nine minds arise—
excluding the wholesome mind of the desire realm and the unobscured-neutral minds of the desire and form realms.

That [unobscured-neutral mind] arises from six: the wholesome mind of the formless realm arises from its own three [minds], from the wholesome mind of the form realm, and from the minds of those in training and those beyond training.
The obscured-neutral [mind] arises from seven.

From the obscured-unspecified (nivṛta) mind of the formless realm, there arise three minds of its own level, the wholesome and the obscured minds of the form realm, and the two afflicted minds of the desire realm.
It is likewise;
that [resultant mind] also arises from exactly seven.
Excluding the afflicted states of the desire and form realms, as well as the states of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa);
the state of one in training arises from four: from the wholesome states of the three realms and from the state of one in training.
From this [uncontaminated mind], however, those same five arise, as well as the fourth [contaminated mind] and the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
From the mind of one beyond training, however, the five [minds of one beyond training] arise. //70//

For this very reason— that is, from what was just mentioned— four types of minds arise immediately after that mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa). Thus, four minds arise in immediate succession from that mind of one beyond training.
The wholesome states of the three realms and those of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The twelve minds are completed.
Furthermore, these twelve become twenty.
How so?
By dividing the wholesome [states] acquired through application and those acquired at birth into two types within each of the three realms. (71)
In the three realms, the wholesome mind is divided into two types:
that which is acquired through application (*prāyogika*) and that which is acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*).

[The latter is further divided into: that born of maturation (*vipākaja*), that pertaining to the path of daily conduct (*airyāpathika*), that pertaining to arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*), and that which is emanated (*nairmāṇika*).
The phrase "divided fourfold in the desire realm" carries over [from the previous context]. The unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) belonging to the desire realm is divided into four types.
The mind born of maturation, the mind pertaining to postures, the mind pertaining to craftsmanship, and the mind of transformation;
in the realm of form, these are excluded from the [mind] of craftsmanship. //72//
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), it is divided into three types, excluding that which pertains to the stage of ascetic discipline (*śailpasthānika*), because of the absence of craftsmanship there.
Thus, these twelve states of mind further become twenty.
The wholesome is sixfold, and the non-obscured-unspecified is sevenfold; thus they are divided.
The minds such as those pertaining to deportment (*airyāpathika*) do not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) because of the absence of deportment and so forth.
Form, odor, taste, and tangibles are the objects of these [minds].
But for one in the state of deportment or artistic skill, even sound [is present];
these are exclusively mental consciousnesses.
However, the five groups of sensory consciousness are preparatory for both the states of deportment and artistic skill.
Others maintain that there exists a mental consciousness produced by the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) which has the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) as its object.
Furthermore, regarding these twenty types of mind, which [mind] arises immediately after which?
First, immediately after the eight minds of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), ten minds arise.
Seven [minds] of its own level, excluding the fruit of superknowledge;
the preparatory mind of the form realm; and the minds of those in training and those beyond training. That [fruit of superknowledge], moreover, arises immediately after eight minds.

From its own [level], it arises after the wholesome and the afflicted; from the two belonging to the realm of form—the preparatory and the afflicted; and from the states of one in training and one beyond training.
Immediately after the innate [attainment], nine [minds] arise:
the seven belonging to its own level—excluding the fruit of supernormal knowledge—and the two afflicted minds of the realms of form and formlessness.
Furthermore, that [unwholesome mind] arises immediately after eleven:
from its own seven as previously stated, from the two of the form realm—the preparatory and the afflicted—and from the minds of those in training and those beyond training.
Immediately after the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified minds, seven arise.
Their own [minds] are as before.
Furthermore, these arise immediately after fourteen minds:
from their own seven, and from four of the form realm, excluding the preparatory and the fruit of supernormal knowledge.
From the three [minds] belonging to the formless realm— excluding the preparatory mind—
eight [minds] arise immediately after the functional, the resultant, and the other [neutral] minds.
These are the six belonging to its own level (excluding the preparatory mind and the fruit of supernormal knowledge) and the two defiled minds belonging to the form and formless realms.

Furthermore, those [seven] arise immediately after seven minds, from their own [category] alone, as previously stated. Immediately after the minds belonging to the stage of effortlessness (*śailpasthānika*), six arise:
from their own [category] alone, excluding the preparatory (*prāyogika*) and the fruit of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñāphala*).

Furthermore, immediately after that [unshakable dhyāna], seven [minds] arise: from among its own [category], excluding only the fruit of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñāphala*); immediately after the fruit of supernormal knowledge, two arise:
its own fruit of supernormal knowledge and the preparatory mind (*prāyogika*) belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*).
That too arises from this very pair.
Now we shall explain the six [minds] belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara).
Following a preparatory mind (prāyogika), twelve [minds] arise:

two wholesome minds of the desire realm, the fruit of supernormal knowledge (abhijñā-phala), its own six [minds], the preparatory mind of the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara), and the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Furthermore, that [thought] arises immediately after ten thoughts: from the two of the desire realm—the preparatory and the fruit of superknowledge; from four of its own [realm], excluding the thoughts of deportment and those born of maturation; from the two of the formless realm—the preparatory and the afflicted; and from the thoughts of those in training and those beyond training.
Immediately after the mind acquired at birth, eight [minds] arise:
the two defiled minds of the desire realm, its own five [minds]—excluding the fruit of superknowledge—and the defiled mind of the formless realm.
That [defiled mind of the formless realm], in turn, arises from five [minds]: its own [five], excluding the fruit of superknowledge.
Immediately after a defiled [mind], nine [minds] arise:
the four wholesome and defiled minds of the desire realm, and its own five [minds], excluding the fruit of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā-phala*).
That [defiled mind], in turn, arises immediately after eleven minds.

From the states belonging to the desire realm—namely, those acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*), those pertaining to deportment (*airyāpathika*), and those born of maturation (*vipākaja*)—and from its own five [mental states], excluding the fruit of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā-phala*); and from the three states belonging to the formless realm, excluding the state produced by application (*prāyogika*).
Immediately after the state pertaining to deportment, seven [states] arise:

two from the desire realm (the defiled ones), four from its own [realm] (excluding the state produced by application and the fruit of supernormal knowledge), and one from the formless realm (the defiled one).
Furthermore, immediately after those [five], there arise only from their own [category], with the exception of the fruit of superknowledge (*abhijñā-phala*).
In this same way, that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) should be stated.
Immediately after the fruit of superknowledge, two [minds] arise.
Only in one's own [realm], namely in the results of the preparatory effort and the supernormal powers;
that too is by means of these two alone.
Now we shall speak of the four [minds] belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*).
Following a preparatory mind (*prāyogika*), seven [minds] arise:
a preparatory mind of the form realm, its own four [formless minds], and the minds of one in training (*śaikṣa*) and one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Furthermore, that [mind] arises immediately after six minds: from the preparatory mind of the form realm (*rūpāvacara-prāyogika*), from its own three [minds]—excluding the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*)—and from the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Immediately after the mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-prātilambhika*), seven [minds] arise.
[The mind] arises from its own four [minds] and the afflicted minds of the lower stages;
furthermore, that [afflicted mind] arises from its own four [minds] alone.
Immediately after an afflicted [mind], eight [minds arise].
Its own four [minds]—the preparatory and the afflicted of the form realm—and the afflicted of the desire realm [arise].
That, moreover, arises immediately after ten:
from its own four, and from the desire and form realms' minds acquired at birth, those of deportment, and those born of maturation.
Immediately after that which is born of maturation (vipākaja), six [minds] arise:
its own three, excluding the preparatory (prāyogika), and the three defiled (kliṣṭa) minds of the lower stages.
That [matured mind], in turn, arises from four: only from its own [three].
Immediately after the state of one in training (śaikṣa), six [minds] arise:

the preparatory minds (prāyogika) of the three realms, the innate mind of the desire realm (kāmāvacara-upapattipratilambhika), the mind of one in training, and the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
That [mind of one in training], moreover, arises from four [minds].
[The mind arises] from the three preparatory minds and from the learner's mind.
Immediately after the non-learner's mind, five [minds arise],
just as immediately after the learner's mind [five arise], excluding one— the learner's mind itself.
Furthermore, that [resultant mind] arises from five:

from the three preparatory minds (*prāyogika*), and from the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). What, then, is the reason that minds born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those pertaining to postures (*airyāpathika*), and those pertaining to crafts (*śailpasthānika*) arise immediately after a preparatory mind, but a preparatory mind does not arise after these?

Because they are engaged in the performance of postures and crafts, and because they are weak and proceed without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), these mental states are not conducive to the preparatory mind.

However, since the mind of renunciation proceeds without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāravāhin*), its arising immediately after a preparatory mind (*prāyogikacitta*) is logical. If that is so, then a preparatory mind would likewise not arise even from afflicted minds,
because they are discordant.
Nevertheless, for one who is weary of the active manifestation of the afflictions, the manifestation of the preparatory application is appropriate for the sake of thoroughly understanding them.

The innate [mind] of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara-upapatti-pratilambhika*), because of its acuity, arises immediately after the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as the preparatory mind of the form realm (*rūpāvacara-prāyogika*).
Because it proceeds without effort (*anabhisaṃskāra-vāhitva*), these [other minds] do not arise from it.
Immediately after a defiled mind of the form realm, the innate mind of the desire realm arises.
Because of its sharpness;
however, immediately after a defiled [mind] belonging to the formless realm, a mind acquired at birth belonging to the form realm does not arise, because it is not sharp.
There are three types of mental attention (*manaskāra*):
mental attention to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-manaskāra*),
such as, for example, "form has the characteristic of being transformed (*rūpaṇā*)," and so forth.
Mental attention to general characteristics;
mental attention associated with the sixteen aspects; and mental attention consisting of resolute belief.

In the case of the [meditations on] the foul, the immeasurables, the formless liberations, the bases of mastery, the bases of totality, and so forth, one brings the Noble Path into manifestation immediately after three kinds of mental attention; from that [Path] as well, there are likewise three kinds of mental attention. This being so, it is logical that it is said: "one cultivates the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness accompanied by the foul."
Others maintain that one brings the Noble Path into manifestation immediately after general mental attention; however, it is of three kinds [according to others].
Having first tamed the mind through the meditation on the foul, one brings the Path into manifestation immediately after general mental attention.
Therefore, with reference to the traditional lineage, it was said: "One cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga) accompanied by the contemplation of the foul.
Others maintain that even immediately after the Noble Path (āryamārga), it is indeed the general mental attention (sāmānyamanaskāra).

It may well be that when one enters the path of certainty (niyāmāvakrānti) by relying on the three stages beginning with the threshold concentration (anāgamya), one would bring into manifestation that general mental attention belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) immediately after that [Noble] Path.
Now, how is it when one enters the path of certainty (*niyāmāvakrānti*) by relying on the second dhyāna and so forth?
For a [path] belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) cannot be relied upon because it is too remote;
nor has a [path] belonging to those higher stages been previously acquired, except for the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Furthermore, the noble one does not again bring the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) into manifestation;

for it is not logical that one who has already attained the fruit should manifest its preparatory application (*prayoga*). However, another mental attention of a similar kind belonging to the general category (*sāmānyamanaskāra*) undergoes cultivation—namely, "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all dharmas are selfless, and nirvana is peace"—and he will bring that into manifestation.
They do not describe it in this way:
for one attaining arhatship by relying on the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage], the emerging mind belongs either to that level or to the desire realm;
or, by relying on the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), it belongs either to that level or to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
In the remaining [stages], it is exclusively of its own level.

In the desire realm (kāmadhātu), there are three types of mental attention (manaskāra): those consisting of hearing (śrutamaya), those consisting of reflection (cintāmaya), and those acquired at birth (upapattipratilambhika);
there is none consisting of cultivation (bhāvanāmaya).
In the form realm (rūpadhātu), there are three: those consisting of hearing, those consisting of cultivation, and those acquired at birth.
There is no [wisdom] consisting of reflection;
for when they begin to reflect, only meditative concentration (samādhi) arises for them.
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is [wisdom] consisting of cultivation and that acquired at birth.
In that regard, the manifestation of the noble path occurs immediately after five types of mental attention, with the exception of those acquired at birth,
because it is dependent upon preparatory effort.
However, immediately after the noble path, even the desire-realm [mental states] acquired at birth may manifest.
Because of its sharpness.
Regarding the twelve types of consciousness that have been mentioned, in which consciousness is there the acquisition of how many?
In a defiled consciousness of the three realms, there is the acquisition of six, six, and two respectively.
When a defiled consciousness belonging to the desire realm has become manifest, there is the acquisition of six types of consciousness.

For one who is not endowed with those [defilements]: [the acquisition] of wholesome states belonging to the desire realm occurs through the reconnection of the roots of goodness by means of doubt, and through returning to a [lower] realm; of the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified states, through returning to a [lower] realm and through falling away; of the afflicted states belonging to the form realm, through falling away;
and of the afflicted states belonging to the formless realm, through falling away; and of the state of a learner (śaikṣa).
In the case of a defiled mind of the form realm as well, there is the acquisition of six minds:
of the three belonging to the form realm, of the non-obscured-unspecified mind of the desire realm due to returning to that realm,
of the defiled mind of the formless realm, and of the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) due to falling away.
In the case of a defiled [mind] belonging to the formless realm, however, there is the acquisition of two:
of that very same defiled [mind] through falling away, and of the mind of one in training (śaikṣa). In the case of a wholesome [mind]:

In the case of the three [minds] born of form, when a wholesome mind of the form realm arises, there is the acquisition of three minds: that very wholesome mind itself, and the non-obscured-unspecified minds of the desire and form realms.
In the case of the learner's mind (*śaikṣa*), there is the acquisition of four.

Of that very same person in training (śaikṣa), and of the non-obscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) [dharmas] belonging to the desire and form realms, as well as the wholesome (kuśala) [dharmas] belonging to the formless realm;
[this occurs] upon detachment from the desire and form realms by means of the Noble Path (āryamārga); and of the remainder of that [person]. 73.
The remainder has been completed; that which was left over [is as follows]:
where the acquisition (*lābha*) of a mind has not been explained, there it should be understood that only that [mind] is acquired, and no other.
Others, however, speak by way of distinction.
"For when the mind is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), the acquisition of nine [dharmas] is indeed taught by the wise;
but when the mind is wholesome (*kuśala*), there is the acquisition of six, and certainly of that very same [mind] when it is neutral (*avyākṛta*).
In this regard, it should be stated that there is the acquisition of seven when the mind is wholesome.

[The acquisition of] wholesome [states] belonging to the desire realm occurs through the reconnection of the roots of merit by means of right view; [the acquisition of] the non-obscured-unspecified states belonging to the desire and form realms through the attainment of dispassion; [the acquisition of] the wholesome states belonging to the form and formless realms through the attainment of their respective meditative concentrations; and [the acquisition of] the states of one in training (*śaikṣa*) and one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) through entering the path of certainty (*niyāma*) and attaining arhatship, respectively. The remainder should be understood from this very explanation. There is a summary verse: *Summary Verse:* The wholesome [is acquired] through right view, Through the reconnection of the roots of merit; The non-obscured-unspecified through dispassion, And the wholesome of the two higher realms through concentration; The *śaikṣa* and *aśaikṣa* through entering certainty And the state of arhatship, respectively. "For one who does not possess it, the acquisition of the mind occurs at birth, at meditative attainment, at detachment, at falling away, and at the reconnection of wholesome roots."
Thus.
The discussion on conditions is concluded.
The second chapter of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, titled "Exposition of the Faculties," is completed.
The third treasury-location (kośasthāna) of the venerable Lāmāvāka.
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!
This must now be explained.
The exposition of the mind and so forth has been made according to the restriction of the desire, form, and formless realms.
In that regard, what are those desire, form, and formless realms?
It is said: hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and the six classes of celestial beings.
