The desire realm consists of the four destinies and the six classes of gods, namely: the Cāturmahārājakāyikas, the Trāyastriṃśas, the Yāmas, the Tuṣitas, the Nirmāṇaratis, and the Paranirmitavaśavartins; this is the desire realm together with the receptacle world.
Regarding how many locations this consists of, he says:
"It is twenty, by way of the divisions of hells and continents. (1)
The phrase "places" is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the sentence].
There are eight great hells:
Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and Avīci.
There are four continents:
Jambūdvīpa, Pūrvavideha, Avaragodānīya, and Uttarakuru.
Together with the six classes of gods mentioned immediately above, as well as animals and hungry ghosts, there are twenty locations.
The desire realm (kāmadhātu) extends from the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods down to the Avīci hell; however, including the receptacle world (sabhājana), it extends as far as the wind-mandala.
And above this realm of desire (kāmadhātu), how is it that the realm of form (rūpadhātu) consists of seventeen locations? He says:
Separately:
therein, meditation consists of three stages;
that is, the first, second, and third meditations each consist of three stages.
But the fourth [dhyāna] consists of eight stages. //2//
Therein, the first dhyāna consists of the Brahmakāyikas, the Brahmapurohitas, and the Mahābrahmans;
the second consists of the Parīttābhas, the Apramāṇābhas, and the Ābhāsvaras;
the third consists of the Parīttaśubhas, the Apramāṇaśubhas, and the Śubhakṛtsnas.

The fourth [dhyāna] consists of the Anabhrakas, Puṇyaprasavas, Bṛhatphalas, Abṛhas, Atapas, Sudṛśas, Sudarśanas, and Akaniṣṭhas; these seventeen locations constitute the realm of form (rūpadhātu), together with the sentient beings who dwell therein. According to the Kaśmīris, there are sixteen, for they maintain that among the Brahmapurohitas there is a superior location belonging to Mahābrahmā—a single-leadered place established like a council hall—but not a separate level. The formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is without location.
For there is no location for formless things;
indeed, it is a fixed rule that past, future, and non-informative (avijñapti) formless dharmas do not occupy a spatial location.
However, that...
It is fourfold by way of rebirth;
the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is fourfold according to the distinction of rebirth, namely:

the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana), the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana), the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
However, no distinction of superiority or inferiority based on location exists among them;
for in whichever place those who have attained that meditative absorption pass away, they are reborn in that very same place.
Furthermore, when passing away from there, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is produced in that very same location.

Just as the continuum of consciousness proceeds for sentient beings possessing form by depending upon form, so too, in the formless realms, what does it depend upon? Here, the continuum of consciousness depends upon the group-homogeneity (nikāyasabhāga) and the life-faculty (jīvitendriya). // 3 //
The Abhidharmikas maintain that [the mental continuum] proceeds in dependence upon the group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
If that is so, why does the mental continuum of even material beings not proceed in dependence upon those same two?
Because they are weak.
By what is its strength established?
Because it is born from a specific meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
For that attainment is one in which the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) has been transcended.
In that case, since it possesses such strength, it will proceed by itself; what then is the use of a support?
Furthermore, this must also be explained:

just as for material beings the group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) proceed depending upon form (*rūpa*), so too for immaterial beings, depending upon what do they proceed?
Those two [factors] themselves are mutually [dependent].
If that is so, then for what reason are those same two [factors] not mutually [dependent] even in the case of material phenomena?
Because those two are weak.
In that case, by what means does it possess strength?
Because it is born from a specific meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
This applies equally to the continuum of consciousness, or to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Therefore, the Sautrāntikas maintain that for formless beings, there is no support for the mental continuum other than itself.

Rather, when the cause that projects a mental continuum has become free from craving for form, that continuum arises together with form and thus proceeds depending upon form; however, when its cause has become free from craving for form, it proceeds without depending upon form.
"Because the cause is turned away from that.
Now, why are these called the desire, form, and formless realms (*kāma-rūpa-ārūpya-dhātavaḥ*)?
A realm (*dhātu*) is so called because it maintains its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

The realm associated with desire is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The realm associated with form is the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), due to the elision of the middle term, as in the cases of "diamond-studded hair" (*vajravālaka*) or "pepper drink" (*maricapānaka*).
Because there is no form (*rūpa*) here, it is "formless" (*arūpa*);
the state of being formless is "formlessness" (*ārūpya*).
That which is subject to transformation is "rūpya";
that which is not subject to transformation is "arūpya," and its state is "ārūpya.
The realm associated with that is the "ārūpyadhātu" (formless realm).
The realm of desires is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), which is that which holds (*dadhāti*) desires.
The form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*) are to be understood in the same way.
What, then, is this so-called "desire"?
In brief, it is attachment associated with physical food and sexual intercourse.

"Those variegated things in the world are not desires; rather, a person's desire is the passion of conceptualization (*saṃkalpa-rāga*). The variegated things remain just as they are in the world, yet the wise subdue [attachment] therein."
"So be it," he said.
Because of this statement in verse, the Ajīvaka replied to the noble Śāriputra:
"Those various beautiful things in the world are not desires; you say that desire here is the passion of conceptual construction."
Even a monk may become a consumer of sensual pleasures by entertaining unwholesome thoughts.
The noble Śāriputra said: "If those various things in the world are not desires for you, and if it is conceptual passion that is not desire for you,
then even your Teacher would be an enjoyer of desires upon merely seeing beautiful forms."
Furthermore, are all those phenomena whatsoever that manifest in the desire, form, and formless realms necessarily bound to the desire, form, and formless realms?
He said: No. What then?
In which [factors] do the attachments to desire, form, and formlessness lie latent? What, then, are these attachments to desire, form, and formlessness?
They are those which lie latent within the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
Now this is like the case of the horse-keeper:
"Whose is this horse-keeper? He belongs to him who owns this horse.
Whose is this horse?"
"Whose horse-tether is this?"—
thus neither [the owner] nor [the tether] is known;
this is not the property of a horse-tetherer.

For the locations within the desire realm have already been explained; the attachment of one who is not free from passion toward those locations is "desire-attachment" (*kāmarāga*). Whatever phenomenon (*dharma*) that [attachment] underlies (*anuśete*) is also associated with the desire realm (*kāmapratisaṃyukta*).
In this way, the attachment to the form and formless realms should be understood as applying respectively to one who is free from passion for the lower realms;
alternatively, attachment belonging to the non-concentrated stage is sensual attachment,
while attachment to the meditative absorptions (dhyānas) and the formless realms is attachment to the form and formless realms.

How can there be sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) in a mind of emanation (*nirmāṇacitta*)? It arises from relishing [the emanation] after having heard of it or experienced its decline; or else, by the power of the emanation, even the mind of the emanator possesses desire.
Alternatively,
its belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacaratva*) is due to the creation of odors and tastes;
for these two are not created by [beings] belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*).
Furthermore, is the triple world only one?
There is no end to the triple worlds;
as far as space extends, so do the realms extend.

For this very reason, there is no manifestation of previously non-existent sentient beings; and although incalculable numbers of sentient beings attain final nirvana with the arising of each Buddha, there is no exhaustion of sentient beings, just like space.
How, then, do the world-systems endure?

It is stated in the *Tiryaksūtra*: "Just as when it rains with a steady stream from the sky, there is no gap or interval between the falling torrents of water, so too in the eastern direction there is no gap or interval between world-systems undergoing dissolution and evolution.
As it is in the eastern direction, so it is in the southern, western, and northern directions."
However, it was not stated [in the root text] that [the world-system] extends above and below. Others maintain that it extends both above and below,
based on the reading in another school (nikāyāntara),
which states that above Akaniṣṭha there is once again the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Furthermore, below the desire realm (kāmadhātu) are the Akaniṣṭha heavens.
One who is free from passion (vītarāga) with respect to one desire realm is so with respect to all [desire realms];
likewise for the form and formless realms.

And whoever generates [the mind of enlightenment] by relying upon the first dhyāna goes only to the Brahma-world belonging to that very world-system in which they were born when they generated it, and not to any other.
Regarding these three realms that have been mentioned,
there are five destinies (gati) designated by their own names, beginning with hell; among them are the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, gods, and humans.
By their own names, five destinies (gati) have been declared among them:
four destinies in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), and a portion of the fifth;
and a portion of one destiny, that of the gods (devagati), in the form and formless realms (rūpārūpyadhātu).
Furthermore, are there realms that are free from the [five] destinies, such that these [realms] are said to exist "within the realms"?
There are indeed realms whose intrinsic nature consists of the wholesome, the afflicted, the receptacle world, and the intermediate state.
As for the five destinies, however—
These are exclusively non-defiled and neutral, designated as sentient beings, and do not include the intermediate state (antarābhava). //4//
The destinies (*gati*) are exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*);
otherwise, there would be a confusion of the destinies.
They are designated as "sentient beings" (*sattvākhya*) alone, and they do not have the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as their nature.
The *Prajñapti* states: "The five destinies (*gati*) are subsumed by the four modes of birth (*yoni*), but the four modes of birth are not subsumed by the five destinies.
What is not subsumed?
The intermediate state (*antarābhava*)."
It is also stated in the *Dharmaskandha*: "What is the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*)?

It is the translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) derived from the four great elements, which is the eye, the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), the eye-base (*cakṣurāyatana*), and the eye-element; [it exists] as that of hell-beings, of animals, of the realm of the ancestors, of gods, of humans, as that produced by meditation (*bhāvanāmaya*), and as that of the intermediate state (*antarābhavika*)."
Moreover, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is excluded from the destinies (*gati*) even in the Sūtras.
In which Sūtra?

In the one that says: "There are seven states of existence (*bhava*): the state of hell-beings, the state of animals, the state of hungry ghosts, the state of gods, the state of humans, the state of karma, and the intermediate state."
For here, the five destinies are described along with their causes and their modes of arrival;
it is for this very reason that they are established as unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*),
because their cause— karmic existence (*karmabhava*)— is excluded from them.
The Kashmiris also recite this Sūtra:
"It was said by the Elder Śāriputra: 'Venerable sir, it is through the manifestation of the outflows (*āsrava*) that one performs and accumulates karma to be experienced in the hells.

Venerable sir, for those who possess crookedness of body, speech, and mind, and who possess the defects and impurities of body, speech, and mind, it is in the hells that the ripening (*vipāka*)—consisting of form, perception, feeling, mental formations, and consciousness—ripens.'"
"When the maturation has come to fruition, it receives the designation 'hell-being.
In that regard, O Venerable One, no hell-being is apprehended apart from those dharmas.
For this reason as well, the destinies are exclusively non-obscured and neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta).
In that case, the *Prakaraṇa* treatise must be reconciled, which states: "All latent dispositions (anuśaya) adhere within the destinies (gati).

Since the minds of rebirth-linking (pratisaṃdhi-citta) for the destinies are of five types, there is no fault at all, because the term "destinies" includes the entry [into them], just as the mention of a village includes the vicinity of the village.
Others say that wholesome and afflicted [states] are also [included].
As for what was said— "because karma-existence (karmabhava) is excluded from those two"—
one is not necessarily excluded simply because of a separate mention.
For example, among the five corruptions (kaṣāya), the corruptions of afflictions (kleśakaṣāya) and views (dṣṭikaṣāya) are mentioned separately;
yet views are neither non-afflictions nor [separate from] afflictions.
In the same way, the existence of karma (karmabhava) may also be the destiny (gati).
Furthermore, its separate mention would be for the purpose of making known the cause of the destination;
however, this same consequence would apply to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as well, which it is not.
This is because [the intermediate state] is not applicable [in that context].
They go to it, thus it is a "destination" (gati). Furthermore, the intermediate state (antarābhava) cannot be a destination, because it arises at the very place of death.
Moreover, the formless realms (ārūpya) would also not be destinations.
Because it arises in the very place where death occurs.
If that is so, then it is called an "intermediate state" (*antarābhava*) precisely because it is intermediate; it is not a "destination" (*gati*), for it exists in the interval between destinations.
For if it were a destination, it would not be called an "intermediate state" at all.
As for what was said by the Elder Śāriputra, "When the maturation has been completed, one comes to be designated as a hell-being":
it was stated that the maturation has been completed, but not that the maturation itself [is the hell-being].
Furthermore, as for what was said, "In that case, O Venerable One, no hell-being is perceived other than those phenomena": [this is the meaning].
He negates a substantial person (pudgala-dravya) that goes to a state of existence, stating that "a hell-being is not perceived apart from the aggregates," but he does not negate other aggregates.
The Vaibhāṣikas, however, describe the destinies as being exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Regarding these, some maintain that they have the nature of maturation (*vipāka*) alone,
while others hold that they also have the nature of accumulation (*aupacayika*).

In this very context of the three realms and five destinies, they should be understood in their respective order as follows: those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions; those with diverse bodies and a single perception; the opposite of these (those with a single body and diverse perceptions); and those with a single body and a single perception; and the three formless ones. (Verse 5)
There are seven stations of consciousness, as stated in the Sūtra: "There are material beings who are diverse in body and diverse in perception, such as human beings and certain gods;
this is the first station of consciousness."

Who, then, are those certain gods? They are the gods belonging to the realm of desire and those belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, excluding those who have been reborn there for the very first time. They are called "diverse in body" (nānātvakāya) because their bodies are diverse.

Because they possess various colors, marks, and shapes, there is a diversity of perceptions; this is "diverse perception. Those who possess this are "those with diverse perceptions" (nānātvasaṃjñinaḥ).
Because they possess the perception of pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure,
there are those with form who have diversity of body but unity of perception, namely, the gods of the Brahma-realm who were first produced there.
This is the second station of consciousness.

For those who were first produced all have the notion that they are each individually created by this Brahmā, thinking, "We were created by this Brahmā. And it occurs to Brahmā as well, "These were created by me"; thus, because their notions of the mode of creation are identical, they possess the notion of oneness. However, since the height, girth, shape, body, speech, and manner of wearing robes of Mahābrahmā are of one kind, while those of his retinue are of another kind, they are said to have diversity of body (*nānātva-kāya*).
As it is said in the Sūtra: "It occurs to them: 'We have seen this being who was long-lived and remained for a long duration; oh, would that other beings also might be reborn here in our company!
And while this being had such a mental aspiration, we were reborn here.'"

How did they see him? Some say they were staying in the Ābhāsvara heaven, for they had fallen away from there. How then, having not yet attained the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of the second dhyāna, could they recollect their former existence belonging to that level; or, if they had attained it, how could they have recollected [a life] having Mahābrahmā as its object?
Others say that those who were settled in the view of clinging to mere rules and rituals saw [the Buddha] while staying in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Even in that case, it is not possible for them to remain there for a long duration, because there is no obstacle [to their passing away].

How did it occur to them that, "We saw this being as long-lived, remaining for a long duration"? It was because, while staying right there, they had recollected his past history and thus perceived him as remaining for a long duration; having seen him in that way, the thought subsequently arose in them, "We have seen him."
There are material beings who are uniform in body but diverse in perception, such as the Ābhāsvara gods;
this is the third station of consciousness.
Furthermore, by mentioning the limit here, it should be understood that the entirety of the second dhyāna is included.
Otherwise, in which station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) would the Parīttābhas and Apramāṇābhas be established?
In that case, because their color, gender-mark, and shape are undifferentiated, they possess a single body (*ekatvakāya*);
yet, because they possess the perception of pleasure and the perception of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, they possess diverse perceptions (*nānātvasaṃjñin*).

It is said that those who have become weary of the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*) on the fundamental stage (*maulyā bhūmau*) bring forth the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) from the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*); and being weary of the faculty of equanimity in the preparatory stage, they again bring forth the faculty of mental pleasure from the fundamental stage.
This is just as lords, when weary of sensual pleasures, experience the joy of the Dharma, and when weary of the joy of the Dharma, experience sensual pleasures.
But would this same consequence not also apply to the Śubhakṛtsna deities? No, for they do not experience weariness with that bliss.
What is the reason?

"That bliss is indeed calm, whereas mental joy (*saumanasya*) is uncalm because it causes the mind to leap up," so the Sautrāntikas explain. It is said in the Sūtra: "Just as those [beings] possess diverse perceptions:

there, those beings who have recently been reborn in the Ābhāsvara host of gods, being neither skilled in the dissolution nor skilled in the evolution of this world, become terrified upon seeing that flame."
The peaceful ones become agitated and fall into a state of trepidation, thinking:
"This flame, having burned the empty Brahmā-palace, will surely come back this way.
Then those beings who have long been reborn in the Ābhāsvara host of gods, who are skilled in the process of the world's dissolution and skilled in its re-evolution, reassure those frightened beings.
"Do not fear, worthy sirs! Do not fear, worthy sirs!

Previously, this flame also, having burned the empty Brahmā-palace, vanished right here. Because they perceive the arrival and departure of that flame, and because they perceive themselves as having been afraid, they possess diverse perceptions; it is not because they possess the perception of pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain.
There are material beings who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the Śubhakṛtsna gods;
this is the fourth station of consciousness.
In that state, they are uniform in body because their color, shape, and characteristics are undifferentiated.
They possess the perception of unity because they possess the perception of pleasure.
In that regard, in the first dhyāna, they possess the perception of unity through an afflicted perception;
in the second, they possess the perception of diversity through a wholesome perception; and in the third, they possess the perception of unity through a perception born of maturation.
The three formless [realms] are as described in the Sūtra; these are the seven stations of consciousness.
What here is the station of consciousness? It consists of the five aggregates associated with it, or four [aggregates], as appropriate.
Why are the remaining [states] not considered stations of consciousness?
Because the remaining ones possess that which causes their destruction.
What, then, remains?
The miserable realms (*durgati*), the fourth dhyāna, and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
For in these places, there are disruptions of consciousness; therefore, they are not stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
What, then, is the impairment by which consciousness is impaired?
In that regard, in the miserable states (apāya), painful feeling is the impairment because it is injurious;
in the fourth dhyāna, it is the state of non-perception (āsaṃjñika) and the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).
At the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), there is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) because of the interruption of the continuity of mind.

Furthermore, it is said that where those staying here have the desire to go, and those staying there have the desire not to depart— that is declared to be a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
In the miserable realms (apāya), both [conditions] are absent.

In the fourth dhyāna, the minds of beings are detached: ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) desire to enter the state of non-perception (āsaṃjñika), while noble ones (ārya) desire to enter the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa). Because its mental activity is not sharp, the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is not considered a station of consciousness (vijñānasthiti).
These seven stations of consciousness have been explained as they are; together with the peak of existence and the non-percipient beings, they are known as the nine abodes of beings. (6)
For it is in these that beings dwell by their own choice; others do not dwell there because they lack such desire.
Who, then, are these others?
The miserable realms (apāya).
For in them, sentient beings are made to dwell by the rākṣasas of karma against their will;
they do not dwell there by choice.
Therefore, by that [reasoning], the abodes of sentient beings are like places of confinement.
In another sutra, seven stations of consciousness are taught;
in yet another, four stations are taught again.
Which are the four?

"The stations of consciousness (vijñānasthiti) are those approaching form (rūpopagā), those approaching feeling (vedanopagā), those approaching perception (saṃjñopagā), and those approaching mental formations (saṃskāropagā).
What is their intrinsic nature (svabhāva)? They are, respectively:
The four contaminated aggregates; furthermore, these belong only to their own respective levels.
Not on any other ground.
For what reason?
Because stability is indeed a firm foundation.
Furthermore, consciousness does not abide within the aggregates belonging to a different level (visabhāgabhūmika) by the power of craving.

Why, then, is consciousness itself not called a "station of consciousness" (vijñānasthiti), as the five aggregates are among the seven stations of consciousness? Because a station is established by excluding the one who stands; for that which stands is not itself called the station.

Just as it is not said that "the king himself is the royal throne," so too, those factors upon which consciousness mounts and proceeds—according to the analogy of a boat and its helmsman—are called the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). However, consciousness does not mount and proceed by means of consciousness itself; therefore, it is not so stated, according to the Vaibhāṣikas.
If that is so, how is one to understand the statement in the Sūtra: "In the nutriment of consciousness, there is delight and there is passion;
wherever there is delight and there is passion, there consciousness becomes established and takes root"?
How is this to be explained?
“And the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) are comprised within the five aggregates (*skandha*); how is that so?

If that is the case, then, when consciousness proceeds with attachment toward the aggregates comprised within the spheres of rebirth (*upapattyāyatana*) without differentiation, consciousness itself is a station of consciousness.
However, individually, just as form and the other [aggregates] serve to defile consciousness, [so too does consciousness].
Therefore, it exists solely within the four stations of consciousness. //7//
Consciousness was not declared by the Blessed One to be a station;

furthermore, the four stations of consciousness were taught by the Blessed One as being in the nature of a field (*kṣetra*), while consciousness accompanied by grasping (*sopādāna-vijñāna*) is entirely in the nature of a seed (*bīja*). Thus, he conceived the intention that a seed is not established as a field for another seed.
Those factors that arise simultaneously with consciousness are more effective as its field; therefore, they alone are called its "stations."
Now, how are the four stations of consciousness (vijñānasthiti) subsumed within the seven stations of consciousness, or the seven within the four?
Indeed, the four are not subsumed by the seven, nor are the seven by the four;
rather, their mutual inclusion is established through a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭi).
When considering their inclusion, a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika) should be understood:
there may be that which is included by the seven but not by the four, and so forth.
The first alternative is whatever consciousness is among the seven.
The second [category] consists of the aggregates, excluding consciousness, in the miserable realms, in the fourth dhyāna, and at the peak of existence (bhavāgra).

The third consists of the four aggregates in the seven [realms]. The fourth is established by setting aside these aforementioned modes. Furthermore, it should be understood that this triple world, which has been described as divided by distinctions such as the realms of rebirth (gati) and so forth, is to be known [in these terms].
Therein, there are four modes of birth for sentient beings, beginning with those born from eggs. // 8 //
The egg-born birth, the womb-born birth, the moisture-born birth, and the spontaneously born birth.
"Birth" (yoni) means genus;
it is called "birth" because in it sentient beings are joined together and become mixed due to the commonality of their procreation.
What is the egg-born womb?
It consists of those sentient beings who are born from eggs,
such as geese, cranes, ruddy geese, peacocks, parrots, mynas, and so forth.
What is the womb-born birth?
It refers to those sentient beings who are born from a placenta,
such as elephants, horses, cattle, buffaloes, donkeys, pigs, and so forth.
What is the moisture-born mode of birth?
It refers to those sentient beings who are born from the moisture of the elements,
such as worms, insects, moths, mosquitoes, and so forth.

What is the mode of birth by transformation (*upapādukā yoni*)? It refers to those beings who are born all at once, being complete, with unimpaired faculties, and endowed with all major and minor limbs.
Precisely because they perform [their birth] well in the state of arising, they are called "beings of transformation" (*upapādukā*).
For example, those such as gods, hell-beings, and intermediate state beings (*antarābhava*).
Now, he explains how many modes of birth (*yoni*) exist within each realm of existence (*gati*):
humans and animals are of four kinds.
Humans are of four kinds.
First, those born from eggs, such as the two elders Śaila and Upaśaila who emerged from a crane, the thirty-two sons of Mṛgāra’s mother, and the five hundred sons of the King of Pañcāla.
Second, those born from a womb, such as those at present.
Those born from moisture are, for example, Māndhātṛ, Cāru, Upacāru, Kapotamālinī, Āmrapālī, and others.
Those who are spontaneously born are, moreover, the beings of the first eon.
In this way, animals also are of four kinds.
Three kinds are indeed seen;
however, those born by transformation include the nāgas, suparṇis, and so forth.
Hell-beings,
intermediate state beings, and gods are all of miraculous birth; indeed, all hell-beings, intermediate state beings, and gods are exclusively of miraculous birth.
Pretas are also born from a womb.
From the word "also" (api), it follows that there are also those born spontaneously (upapāduka).
A female ghost (pretī) informs the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"By night I have five sons, and likewise by day another five."
"Having produced them, I devour them, yet even so, there is no satisfaction for me.
Which mode of birth is the most excellent?
The apparitional (upapāduka).
Now, for what purpose does a Bodhisattva in his final existence resort to the womb-born mode of birth (*jarāyuja-yoni*), even though he has attained mastery over rebirth?
By acting in this way, he perceives a great purpose:
through the connection of kinship, he intends to lead the great Śākya clan into the Dharma, thinking, "This one belongs to the lineage of a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*)."
Furthermore, it is for the sake of inspiring respect and devotion in others, and to encourage those to be trained by showing that even those who have become human beings attain this accomplishment;

otherwise, they might imagine, "Who is this? He is some illusory person whose family and lineage are unknown," or "He is a god" or "a *piśāca*," just as other non-Buddhist sectarians falsely claim that such an illusionist appears in the world only after the passing of a hundred eons.
"Having appeared through his illusory power (*māyā*), he devours the world.
Others, however, say:
"For the purpose of establishing the relics of his body, so that humans and others, having gained understanding, may go by the thousands to heaven."
And [the statement] "and they have attained liberation" refers to spontaneously born beings (*upapāduka*), for since they lack external seeds, when they die their bodies do not remain;
they vanish like an oil lamp at the end of the night.
For those who maintain that the Blessed One possesses the power of sustained miraculous manifestation (*ādhiṣṭhānikī ṛddhi*), this rebuttal is not tenable.
From one question, another arises:

although the destruction of the body of spontaneously born beings (*upapāduka*) is not perceived, how is it stated in the Sūtra that "a spontaneously born Suparṇin seizes a spontaneously born Nāga for the purpose of eating"? It is not said that he actually eats him; rather, he seizes him for the purpose of eating out of ignorance. Thus, there is no fault.
Or it devours [the being] as long as it has not yet died; however, once it is dead, it does not satisfy [the eater].
Which birth is the most numerous?
Only the apparitional (upapāduka).
For it consists of two destinies, a portion of three [other] destinies, and all those belonging to the intermediate state.
What is this so-called intermediate state (*antarābhava*)? It is that which exists here between the state of death (*mṛtyubhava*) and the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*).
That personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) which is produced between the state of death and the state of rebirth for the purpose of reaching birth in another location is called the intermediate state.
Because it exists in the interval between states of existence.
[How is it that this is called "born" yet not "reborn"?
Because it has not reached the destination to be gone to, the intermediate state (antarābhava) is not "reborn. //10//

For one who has reached birth is said to be "born" (*upapanna*), because the root *pad* has the sense of "going. However, this intermediate state (*antarābhava*) has not yet reached the destination to which it is going; therefore, it is not "born."
But what is that place to be gone to?
It is where the projected maturation is manifested and brought to completion.
Those belonging to other schools maintain that the existence at birth arises from the existence at death as something entirely severed;
this is not accepted.
What is the reason?
Both through reasoning and through scripture.
In this regard, first, it is stated by relying on reasoning:
"The arising of existence occurs without interruption, due to its similarity to the continuity of rice.
For it is observed that the phenomena existing within a continuum appear in other locations without interruption, just as in the case of the continuity of rice.
Therefore, it is possible for this continuum of a sentient being to manifest in other locations without interruption.
Even when interrupted, manifestation is observed—just as a reflection arises from an object in mirrors and the like;
in the same way, the state of rebirth may arise from the state of death.
A reflection is not a valid example because it is unestablished [in the subject] and because of its dissimilarity. //11//

It is unestablished that what is called a reflection is the arising of something else, a distinct entity (*dharmāntara*). Even if it were established, it would not serve as a valid illustration because of its dissimilarity.
How, then, is this established?
Because two things cannot exist together in one place;
for in that very same location, both the form of the mirror and the reflection are seen.
Yet, there can be no coexistence of two forms in a single location, because their respective substrates are distinct.

Likewise, when situated in different directions, the mutual reflection of forms is perceived in a single location within a body of water by those standing in places facing one another. However, since it is not the case that two observers looking at a single form do not see it simultaneously,
it is not logical to assume the production of a second form there.
Furthermore, the simultaneous existence of both shadow and sunlight in one place has never been observed.
Yet, a reflection of the sun is perceived in a mirror situated in the shade; therefore, its manifestation there is not logical.
Alternatively, regarding the phrase "because two things do not exist together in one place," which two things are meant?
Regarding the surface of the mirror and the reflection of the moon:
the surface of the mirror exists in one place indeed, while the reflection of the moon is seen as if internal, in quite another place, like water in a well.
And that reflection, being produced there, is not perceived elsewhere.
Therefore, that [object] does not exist at all; rather,
it is due to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that such an appearance occurs,
for the differentiation of the powers of phenomena (*dharmas*) is indeed inconceivable.
Thus, first of all, [the reason] is unestablished (asiddha).
How is it that [the reflection] is not an illustration due to dissimilarity?
Because there is no continuity;
for the reflection is not part of the same continuum as the original object, since it is connected to the continuum of the mirror and because it exists simultaneously with it.

Just as the existence at birth (upapattibhava) is cited as the manifestation in other locations through the non-interruption of a continuum, and not as something that lacks a continuum—therefore, the example [of the reflection] is dissimilar; and this applies to the reflection as well.
Because of the arising from two [causes].
For the arising of a reflection occurs due to two causes:
from the object and from the mirror. It arises depending upon whichever is the primary cause.

Nor is it the case that the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) likewise arises from two causes—one from the existence at death (*maraṇabhava*) and another from some other predominant factor; therefore, this example remains unequal.
Furthermore, it is not logical to say that external semen and blood alone are the predominant cause of the sentient being.
And in those cases where beings of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*) appear even in total darkness, what [external cause] could possibly be postulated there?
Thus, by way of reasoning,
it is not accepted that the manifestation of the existence at birth occurs as something severed from the existence at death;
therefore, the intermediate state (antarābhava) certainly exists.
Moreover, it exists because it is explicitly stated in a Sūtra: "There are seven existences:
existence as a hell-being, existence as an animal, existence as a hungry ghost, existence as a god, existence as a human, existence through karma, and intermediate existence."
This sūtra is not recited by them; for this reason, however, [it is established] from the Gandharva.
The descent of the embryo into the mother’s womb occurs through the presence of three conditions:
the mother is healthy and in her fertile period;
the parents are in love and have come together; and [the being to be reborn] is present.
"And the gandharva is present.
Apart from the intermediate state (antarābhava), what else could the gandharva be? Furthermore, this [gandharva] is not even recorded by them [the Sāṃkhyas].
How, then, [is it]? [It is said: "The dissolution of the aggregates has presented itself.
If this is so, how is the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra* to be interpreted?
"You know, sirs, whether this gandharva who has appeared is a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, a vaiśya, or a śūdra;
and whether he has come from the eastern direction, or from the southern, the western, or the northern."
For it is not logical that there is an arrival of the destruction of the aggregates.
If even this is not recited, then from this [it follows]:
Because of the statement regarding the five, the Blessed One said: "There are five non-returners":

one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion, one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion, and one who flows upwards.
If there were no intermediate state (*antarābhava*), how could there be one called "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the interval" (*antarāparinirvāyī*)?
Some say that there are gods named "the interval" (*antarā*);
but if that were so, it would follow that those such as "one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" (*upapadyaparinirvāyī*) would also be gods by name.
Therefore, this conceptualization is not sound.
For this reason as well—from the *Gatisūtra* (Sūtra on Destinies): // 12 //
In this sūtra, "The seven destinations of the noble persons," three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state are mentioned,
distinguished by differences in time, place, and degree of progress.
Just as a small spark of fire might go out even as it is being produced, so is the first;
just as a spark from iron might go out even as it flies up, so is the second;
just as a spark from iron might fly up and go out before even falling to the ground, so is the third.

And it is not the case that there are such gods called "Antarā" (Intermediate) who are divided into three types according to differences in time, place, and degree; therefore, this is merely a conceptual construction.

Others, however, say: one who abandons the defilements either during the interval of the lifespan or during the interval near the gods is an "attainer of nirvana in the intermediate state" (antarāparinirvāyin).
Furthermore, he attains nirvana while having reached the realm (dhātu), or while having reached perception (saṃjñā), or while having reached discursive thought (vitarka).
Thus, there are three types:
the first attains parinirvāṇa after having taken up a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*) in the form realm;
the second does so after having experienced the prosperity of the gods.

The third [type of non-returner], having entered the Dharma-assembly of the gods, attains parinirvāṇa after entering an assembly characterized by prolonged duration; or, having largely exhausted his lifespan, he attains it rather than immediately upon being reborn. None of these are connected with the analogies of the sparks and so forth.
Because there is no distinction in the destination of the place [of rebirth].

Furthermore, one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) would also have to be mentioned among the formless realms (ārūpya), since they attain parinirvāṇa within the interval of the lifespan;
yet he is not so mentioned.

"In the verse concerning the granting of life-span: 'By means of the dhyānas there are four sets of ten; by means of the formless [attainments] three sets of seven; having formed a set of six by means of perception, the group is thus complete. Thus it is said in this verse.
Therefore, all of this as well is merely conceptual construction.
Now, these sūtras are not even recited by them;

what can we do now, since the Teacher has entered parinirvāṇa and this teaching is leaderless, split into many factions, and continues to be divided even today according to whim both in letter and in meaning?
However, for those for whom this scripture is an authority, the intermediate state (antarābhava) is established even from the perspective of their own tradition.
As for what was stated in the Sūtra, "Then furthermore, Māra Dūṣī fell with his own body into the great Avīci hell," how is that so?
For he was embraced by the flames of the hell-beings even while still alive.
The intended meaning here is that after passing away, he reached Avīci by means of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
For karmas that are extremely intense and fully matured do not wait for the casting off of the body;
therefore, his karma to be experienced in the present life ripened first, and the karma to be experienced upon rebirth ripened afterwards.
Now, how is this [scriptural passage] to be interpreted: "Having committed and accumulated the five actions of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), one is reborn in the hells immediately thereafter"?
The intention is that [one is reborn] without having gone to another realm of existence (*gati*).
In that context, it is the quality of being experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīyatva*) that is illuminated regarding that action.
Now, if it were interpreted according to the literal expression, it would follow that one must perform exactly five [offerings] and not just one,
as well as [the offerings] immediately following the action.
It does not survive for another period of time. Or rather, who would not accept that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is "being born" (*upapadyamāna*)?
For it is by means of the intermediate state itself that one is born in the hells immediately after death, because it is oriented toward that destination.
And we do not say that he has been reborn.
How, then, is this verse to be interpreted:
"O twice-born one, brought here by the force of destiny, you have indeed arrived in my presence, afflicted by old age"?
"For you have no clothing even for the interval, nor is there any provisions for the journey."

The intention here is that there is no intermediate dwelling even among humans; or else, even in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there is no dwelling for him because he is intent upon proceeding toward and reaching the place of rebirth. How can one determine whether this is the intended meaning here and not that other meaning?
This same objection applies to you as well;
therefore, since there is no contradiction with the aforementioned sūtra in either case, this does not serve as a proof for the non-existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
For indeed, a "proof" is merely a resort when no other way is possible.
Now, what kind of form does the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) assume for one who is about to go to a particular destiny?
Because it is projected by the same [karma], it has the form of the future "prior-time existence" (*pūrvakālabhava*).
By the very same karma that projects the destiny, the intermediate state is also projected for the purpose of reaching it.
Therefore, whatever destiny one is destined to go to, one's form in that destiny is identical to the form of the *pūrvakālabhava* (the existence prior to death) that is about to arrive.

[If this were so,] then since an intermediate being (*antarābhava*) belonging to all five destinies would be produced within the womb of a female dog and so forth, a hellish intermediate being would burn the womb.
Even in the case of the *pūrvakālabhava*, hell-beings are not constantly blazing while wandering through the secondary hells (*utsada*), so how much less so those belonging to the intermediate state?

Or, let it be that [the intermediate being] is ablaze; nevertheless, just as it cannot be seen, so too it cannot be touched because of the translucence (*acchatva*) of its personal existence (*ātmabhāva*). Thus, this is not a point for objection.
Furthermore, because intermediate beings do not come into physical contact with one another within the womb, and because of the obstruction of karma (*karmapratibandha*), there is no burning.

As for his size, it is like that of a five- or six-year-old child; however, he possesses fully developed faculties. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva is like a full-grown youth, endowed with the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*).
For this very reason, while entering his mother’s womb in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), he illuminated a billion four-continent world systems.
As for why the Bodhisattva’s mother saw in a dream a white elephant calf entering her womb—
That is merely a sign, because he has long since turned away from rebirth as an animal.
It is just as King Kṛkin saw ten dreams:
"An elephant, a well, flour, sandalwood, a grove of young elephants, and likewise the consecration of a monkey."
"A filthy monkey, a cloth, and a quarrel—these ten dreams were seen by King Kṛkin."
Furthermore, the intermediate state being does not enter the womb by piercing it, but rather through the mother’s birth canal.
For this very reason, between twins, the one who is born later is called the elder (*jyāyān*), and the one who is born first is called the younger (*kanīyān*).
[How is the *Dharmasūtra-vibhāṣya* to be interpreted when it says: "Like an elephant..."?

Having approached that white elephant, beautiful with six tusks and four well-proportioned feet, you entered the bed of your mother’s womb with full and specific awareness, like a seer entering a hermitage.
This need not necessarily be accepted;
for this is neither Sūtra, nor Vinaya, nor Abhidharma—
it is poetry.
And when poets compose their poetry, certain ideas are introduced through superimposition;
or rather, they must simply be conveyed.
Just as his mother saw him entering [her womb] in a dream, so too did he compose this verse.
The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*) also appears with its full proportions and clothed, because of the predominance of a sense of shame (*apatrāpya*).
The Bodhisattva appears clothed, and the nun Śuklā also appears clothed by the power of her vow; she was born fully enveloped in robes and was cremated in that very state.
Another is naked, because in the realm of desire, a lack of moral dread (anapatrāpya) is predominant.
Now, what is this so-called "existence prior to death" (pūrvakālabhava)? It is that which occurs after death and before the moment of rebirth. (13)
Existence (*bhava*), indeed, refers generally to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*);
it is divided into four types,
including the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) as previously described.
The existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) is the moment of linking (*pratisandhi*) within the realms of rebirth (*gati*).
Beyond that, excluding the final moment of death, all other existence is the "existence of the preceding period" (*pūrvakālabhava*).
The final moment is the "existence at death" (*maraṇabhava*), after which, if one is to be reborn among beings possessing form (*rūpin*), the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) occurs.

Moreover, this intermediate state (antarābhava) is visible to those of its own kind and to those with pure divine eyes; it is seen only by other beings belonging to the intermediate state who are of the same class.
And those who possess the divine eye, which is perfectly pure and consists of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), see it;
however, it is not seen with the eye of rebirth (*upapatti-cakṣus*), because it is transparent by nature.
A being in the intermediate state of a god sees all; others say that those in the intermediate states of humans, hungry ghosts, animals, and hell-beings see all except those preceding them.
"Endowed with the speed of the supernormal power of action":
supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) is the ability to travel through space;
supernormal power resulting from action is "karmic supernormal power" (*karmarddhi*).
Its "impetus" (vega) is the impetus of the supernormal power of karma (karmarddhivega), meaning its swiftness; one who possesses this is "possessed of the impetus of the supernormal power of karma.
Because of this, he cannot be obstructed even by the Buddhas.
Because this karma is more powerful.
"Sakalākṣaḥ" means possessing all five sense faculties in their entirety.
"Non-obstructive": *pratighāta* means obstruction; that which possesses this is "obstructive. [The opposite is] non-obstructive.
It is neither possessed of resistance nor devoid of resistance,
because it cannot be obstructed even by diamonds and the like.
For instance, it is reported that when a glowing iron ball was split open, a worm was found produced within its core.
Furthermore, he is in no way capable of turning back from whichever realm of existence he is about to be born into;
for a human intermediate state never disappears to become a divine intermediate state or any other.
It is certain that this intermediate state being must be reborn in whichever destiny (gati) it was directed toward at the time of its manifestation, and not in any other.
Furthermore, does even the intermediate state belonging to the desire realm consume solid food (kavaḍīkārāhāra)? He replies: "Yes."
But it is not coarse;
rather, he is a consumer of fragrance. // 14 //
For this very reason, he is called a *gandharva*;
since verbal roots have multiple meanings,
the shortening of the vowel occurs as in the words *śakandhu* and *karkandhu*.
One known as "of little power" has a foul-smelling diet, whereas one known as "of great power" has a fragrant diet.
For how long does it remain?
The Venerable One says: "There is no fixed rule," as long as it has not obtained the conditions for rebirth; for there is no separate projection of that life-span.
Because they belong to the same homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Otherwise, death-existence (*maraṇabhava*) would result from the exhaustion of that very life-span.
If there were a mass of flesh as large as Mount Sumeru, it would all be filled with worms during the rainy season.

Should it now be said that their intermediate states (antarābhava) were merely waiting for that [rebirth], or from where did they come to them at that time? This has not been stated in either the Sūtra or the Śāstra.
However, this is logical:

There is no end to those short-lived creatures who are greedy for odors and tastes; having smelled that odor and being greedy for odors and tastes, they die and awaken karma conducive to the state of a worm, and through that craving, they are reborn among worms.

Alternatively, it is surely only at a time when the conditions for that [rebirth] are abundant that the karmas conducive to such a state find the opportunity to produce their maturation, and not otherwise.

For instance, regarding the karma conducive to the arising of a universal monarch (cakravartin), universal monarchs are born when the lifespan of beings is eighty thousand years or even longer, but not at any other time.
It is for this very reason that the Blessed One said, "The ripening of the karma of sentient beings is inconceivable."
"It remains for seven days," says the Venerable Vasumitra;
"if it does not obtain the necessary conditions within that time, it dies and is reborn right there again.
Others say it remains for seven weeks.

The Vaibhāṣikas say it is for a short time; for he, having sought rebirth and having run toward it, forms the connection (saṃdhi). This is because the conditions are not yet fully assembled, and it is certain that he must be born in that place and in that species.
In that case, it is karma itself that brings about the collection of conditions for those [beings].
Alternatively, if it is indeterminate, then they are born in a similar birth in another location; so say others.
For example, mating is prevalent among cows in the heat of summer, among dogs in autumn, among bears in winter, and among horses in spring.

Furthermore, for the *gavaya*, jackal, donkey, and hyena, there is no fixed time; thus, one who is destined to be reborn among cows at another time may instead be reborn among *gavayas*, one destined for dogs among jackals, one for horses among donkeys, and one for bears among hyenas.

However, it must be stated that his intermediate state (*antarābhava*) belonging to a different group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*) cannot arise in a group-homogeneity other than its own, because it is projected by a single [karmic] impulse.
Indeed, this intermediate state (*antarābhava*), having manifested for the purpose of reaching the destination of its rebirth,
proceeds with a perverted mind toward that destination out of a desire for pleasure.
For, by means of an eye produced through the power of karma, it perceives its own place of birth even though it is situated at a great distance.
There, seeing that misconduct of his parents, since he is a male, a male passion arises toward the father;
conversely, aversion arises [toward the mother].
Thus it is recited in the *Prajñapti*: "At that time, one or the other of two states of mind becomes manifest for the gandharva—either that accompanied by attachment or that accompanied by aversion."
Thus,
being deluded by those two, out of a desire for sexual pleasure, he embraces that place and resolves upon that state as being within himself.
And when that impurity has reached the location of the womb, he becomes joyful and becomes attached to it.
Then his aggregates become solidified and the aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) disappear; thus he is said to be "reborn.

If he is to be male, he takes hold of the mother’s right flank, sits with his back toward her and his legs tucked under him; if he is female, he takes hold of the left flank and faces her belly; if he is now a neuter (*napuṃsaka*), he remains in whatever manner he was embraced by passion. Furthermore, the intermediate state being is not "without limbs," because its sense-faculties are complete.
Therefore, having entered as either a female or a male, it remains in its respective place; subsequently, as the embryo develops, it becomes a neuter.
This is now investigated:

do the very primary elements (mahābhūta) of the semen and blood themselves come to serve as the basis for the sense-faculties through the power of karma, or rather, are other primary elements produced by karmas which arise in dependence upon them?

Some say it is those very same [elements]. For the semen and blood, devoid of sense-faculties, cease together with the intermediate state (antarābhava), and that which is called the *kalala* arises endowed with sense-faculties, according to the principle of the cessation of a seed and the arising of a sprout.
And by taking it thus, this scriptural passage in the Sūtra is well-expounded: "of one produced from the impurity of the kalala of mother and father.
Likewise: "For a long time, O monks, you have increased a cemetery; a drop of blood has been taken up by you.
Others, however, say that these are indeed other primary elements (*bhūtāntara*).
It is just as in the case of a leaf-insect;
however, because the statement regarding the *kalala* refers to its arising in dependence upon impurity, there is no contradiction with the Sūtra.
Thus, first of all, one enters the egg-born and womb-born modes of birth;
however, they say that in other cases it should be explained according to what is appropriate. And in this regard, the following application is observed:
Another, desiring a particular place for its odor, enters the moisture-born womb; having gone to the place of rebirth, it proceeds out of longing toward what is impure or pure, respectively.
But one entering the apparitional womb proceeds out of a longing for the location itself.
How can there be a longing for places in the hells? Because of his perverted cognition;
for he perceives himself as being afflicted by cold winds and the drenching of rain, while seeing fire blazing within the hells.
In that regard, one runs because of a desire for warmth;
furthermore, perceiving oneself being afflicted by the heat of hot winds, sunlight, and fire, and seeing coldness in the hells, one runs because of a desire for coolness.
The former masters maintain that one runs while perceiving oneself and those beings in the state corresponding to the circumstances under which one performed the karma conducive to rebirth there.
Furthermore, among these, the intermediate state of gods moves upward, like one rising from a seat; that of humans, animals, and hungry ghosts is like that of humans and so forth;
but that of hell-beings has its feet upward. //15//
For it is stated in a verse: "Those who revile the sages— who are self-restrained and ascetic— fall into hell with their feet upwards and their faces downwards."
Regarding what was said—that one enters with a perverted mind—is it necessarily the case that every intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) enters the mother's womb in such a manner?
He says: No.
What then?

Four modes of entry into the womb are taught in the Sūtra. Which four? One enters with full awareness; [one stays with full awareness; one departs with full awareness; and one enters, stays, and departs without full awareness].
She stands and emerges with full awareness;
another also stands with full awareness— thus it continues.
Because of the word "also" [in the phrase] "he also enters," it follows that he also exits.
One enters and remains with full awareness;
another is deluded in all respects; yet another performs all of them without awareness—entering, remaining, and even departing without awareness.
These four modes of entry into the womb have been taught in reverse order for the sake of conforming to the structure of the verse. The egg-born [being] is always [the first]. (16)
A being born from an egg always acts while entirely deluded.
How can one born from an egg enter a womb?
Even one who is yet to be born is likewise born from an egg.
Alternatively, designations are made even by means of a future name, as in the Sūtra: "one conditions the conditioned," or in common usage: "he cooks rice," or "he grinds flour.
Therefore, this is not a fault.
Furthermore, how does one enter the mother’s womb without clear comprehension (*asaṃprajānan*), up until the time of emerging, and how does one do so with clear comprehension (*saṃprajānan*)?
First, for a being of little power (*alpeśākhya*), as he enters the mother’s womb, such inverted perceptions (*viparīta-saṃjñā*) and resolute convictions (*adhimokṣa*) arise:
"The wind is blowing; the rain is falling."
"Cold, bad weather, or the clamor of a great crowd of people— alas, I shall enter a thicket of grass, or a forest thicket, or crawl into a grass hut, or a leaf hut, or to the foot of a tree,
or to the root of a wall. While staying in these, he thinks, "I am staying," and while departing from them, he thinks, "I am departing."
But for a being of great majesty, [the thought occurs]: "I am entering a grove or a garden, or I am ascending a palace, or a gabled chamber, or a couch";
likewise, "I am standing" or "I am departing.
In this way, one enters without clear comprehension all the way until one departs.
But one who is fully conscious understands correctly: "I am entering the mother's womb; I am staying right here; I am emerging from this very place.
No inverted perceptions or convictions arise in him.
Regarding this, it is further stated:
There are three types of descents into the womb for the wheel-turning kings and the self-arisen ones— namely,
for the wheel-turning kings, for the two kinds of self-arisen ones (the pratyekabuddhas and the perfectly enlightened buddhas)—
as he will state in due order at the end.
Among these, the first belongs to a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*);
for he enters [the womb] with full awareness, but does not remain there nor depart with full awareness.
A solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha*) also remains there with full awareness.
The Buddha also emerges [from the womb];
here too, the designation is made by means of a future name. Alternatively, it is according to the sequence because of the clarity of action, knowledge, or both. (17)
The first belongs to those of pure deeds who perform noble meritorious actions;
the second belongs to those of clear knowledge who have cultivated discernment through extensive learning;
the third belongs to those of pure meritorious deeds and knowledge.
However, it is logical that these very individuals—the universal monarchs and so forth—are of such a nature respectively;
thus, it is established that for the remaining cases, the fourth [alternative] applies.
Now, at this point, the outsiders (bāhyaka) arise, upholding the doctrine of a self (ātmavāda), asserting:
"If it is proposed that a sentient being (sattva) transmigrates to another world, then the self is established.
This very [position] is now refuted:
There is no self;
what kind of self? That which is imagined as the one who casts off these [present] aggregates and reconnects with other aggregates—such an internal agent does not exist.

Thus it was said by the Blessed One: "Karma exists, its maturation exists, but no agent is found who casts off these aggregates and reconnects with other aggregates, except for the conventional designation of phenomena (*dharmasaṃketa*).
In this regard, this is the conventional designation of phenomena: namely, 'when this exists, that comes to be,' and so forth, in detail, [referring to] dependent origination.
What kind of self, then, is not denied?
As for "merely the aggregates": if it is merely the aggregates that are metaphorically designated as the self, then that [designation] is not refuted.
If that is the case, it follows that the aggregates themselves migrate to another world; yet, it is not the case that "merely the aggregates" migrate here.
Conditioned by afflictions and karma, it enters the womb through the continuity of the intermediate state, like a lamp. //18//
For the aggregates (*skandha*) are momentary; they lack the power to migrate.
However, that which is permeated by afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma enters the mother’s womb as a mere continuity of affliction designated as the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Just as a lamp, though momentary, reaches another location through its continuity, there is no such fault [in our position].
Therefore, it is established that even in the absence of a self, the continuum of the aggregates, conditioned by afflictions and karma, enters the mother’s womb; furthermore, that continuum,
having grown gradually according to its projection, [is driven] by afflictions and karma.
Furthermore, one goes to the next world;
for the projection of the entire continuum of aggregates (skandhasantāna) is not uniform due to the diversity of the karma that determines lifespan.
Therefore, for whichever [being] there is a certain amount of projection, for that much does the growth occur gradually.
By what sequence? "First the *kalala* flows; from the *kalala* the *arbuda* is born;
from the *arbuda* the *peśī* is born; from the *peśī* the *ghana* is born."
From the ghana, the secondary branches arise: the hair of the head, body hair, nails, and so forth;
as well as the material sense faculties and the minor marks, in due succession.
Thus say the Noble Ones.
These are the five stages of the embryo: the stages of *kalala*, *arbuda*, *peśī*, *ghana*, and *praśākhā*.
Then, after some time, when that thorn of an embryo has reached full maturity, [the following] arises within the mother’s womb through the ripening of karma:
The winds blow which, having turned that fetus-shaft, position it facing the opening of the mother’s body.
Having fallen from its place like an excessively cruel mass of excrement, it is turned with extreme suffering.
Furthermore, if at some time—due to the mother’s improper conduct regarding food and movement, or due to the fault of past karma—it [perishes] while still in the womb...
He experiences distress; then, women skilled in that matter or nurses for infants, having anointed their hands with lukewarm ghee, oil,
or well-ground *śālmalī* paste or another substance, and having fixed a sharp, thin blade thereon, enter him—
[that place] which is like a cesspool, a foul-smelling, dark, and filthy pond, an abode for many thousands of swarms of worms.

Into this great wound of the channel of desire— constantly discharging, requiring perpetual treatment, drenched and decomposed by semen, blood, lymph, and impurities, boiled and slimy, most loathsome to behold, covered by a thin skin with holes, and born from the ripening of past karma— they thrust their hands and, having cut away limb after limb, extract [the fetus].
And he too is led to some state of existence by previous karma to be experienced in a subsequent life.
Then, when he is born safely, his mother, longing for a son, or the women attending her, take hold of the newborn—
whose body is like a fresh wound— with hands whose touch is like knives or caustic acid, and bathe him.
They nourish him with breast milk or clarified butter, and gradually accustom him to taking solid food.
As he grows, through the maturation of his faculties, the afflictions (kleśas) arise once again and karma begins to accumulate.
Following the dissolution of that body, he goes once more to the next world by means of the continuity of the intermediate state (antarābhava), just as before.
Thus is the beginningless wheel of existence. //19//

In this manner, birth has its cause in afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma; afflictions and karma, in turn, have that [birth] as their cause; and from them, again, there is birth. Thus, the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) should be understood as being without beginning. For if a beginning were postulated, the fault of causelessness would attach to these [phenomena]; and if causelessness existed, all of this would manifest without any cause.

However, the efficacy of seeds and so forth in producing sprouts and so on is observed through the specific determination of place and time, as is the case with fire and so forth in relation to cooked food and the like; therefore, there is no manifestation that is without a cause.
Furthermore, the doctrine of the existence of an eternal cause has already been refuted.
Therefore, there is indeed no beginning to saṃsāra;
however, its end is logical, as it follows from the exhaustion of its causes.
Because birth is dependent upon causes, just as a sprout [depends] on the exhaustion of the seed;
this very continuum of aggregates (skandhasantāna) taught as existing in three states of birth is dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), consisting of twelve factors and three sections.

In this context, the twelve factors are ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age and death.
There are three sections: the prior limit, the subsequent limit, and the middle—that is, past, future, and present births.
How are the twelve factors established within these three sections?
There are two links each for the prior and posterior limits, eight in the middle; namely, ignorance and formations belong to the prior limit, birth and old age and death to the posterior limit,
and the remaining eight are in the middle.
Furthermore, do these eight factors exist in every birth?
He says: "No.
Then in whom do they exist?
[The qualities] of one who is fully perfected. //20//

"Paripūrī" means one who possesses completion (*paripūra*). Here, the person (*pudgala*) intended is one who touches all these various stages; it does not refer to one who dies in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), nor to one belonging to the realms of form or formlessness (*rūpārūpyāvacara*).
For instance, in the *Mahānidānaparyāya*, only a person belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*) is specified.
Because of the statement: "Ānanda, if consciousness were not to descend into the mother's womb..."

When, however, dependent origination is said to be twofold—namely, pertaining to the prior limit (*paurvāntika*) and pertaining to the posterior limit (*aparāntika*)—then seven members constitute that pertaining to the prior limit, ending with sensation (*vedanā*), while five constitute that pertaining to the posterior limit;
this is because of the inclusion of the prior and posterior limits together with their causes and fruits.
Now, what are these [factors] beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*)?
Ignorance is the state of the previous afflictions;
that which was the state of the afflictions in a previous birth is here called "ignorance."
This is due to their association, because they are under its influence, and because of their simultaneous manifestation;
just as when it is said that "the king is coming," it is established that his retinue is also coming.

The formative forces (*saṃskārāḥ*) are [the result] of prior karma; "ten" is understood [to follow]. That state of meritorious and other types of karma which existed precisely in a previous birth is here called "formative forces"—that is, the karma whose maturation (*vipāka*) occurs here [in this life].
Consciousness, however, consists of the aggregates at the moment of rebirth-linking;
at the instant of linking in the mother's womb, the five aggregates are consciousness. Name-and-form follows after that. (21)

Prior to the arising of the six sense bases—that is, from after the moment of rebirth-linking (*saṃdhicitta*) until the six sense bases have not yet arisen—that stage is "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). It is called "the six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as long as [they remain unarisen].
Although it should have been stated as "prior to the arising of the four sense bases," the expression "six sense bases" is used because at that time they are established as such.

That period prior to the coming together of the triad [of sense-faculty, object, and consciousness]—the stage that occurs once the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have arisen, lasting until the conjunction of the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness—is called the "six sense-bases.
Contact (*sparśa*) exists prior to the capacity to discern the causes of pleasure, pain, and so forth. (22)
From the coming together of the three, contact arises.
That stage during which it is capable of discerning the causes of the three types of feeling is called contact. When this capacity for discernment exists, [contact is present].
Experience (*vitti*) is the stage of sensation prior to sexual intercourse, as long as sexual desire has not yet become manifest;
craving (*tṛṣṇā*) belongs to one who craves for enjoyments and sexual intercourse.

The state in which there is the active manifestation of passion for the qualities of sensual pleasure and sexual union, so long as one has not yet begun to seek out those objects, is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Appropriation (*upādāna*), however, belongs to one who is running about in pursuit of the acquisition of enjoyments. (23)
The state in which one, having entered upon a quest to obtain objects, runs about in every direction, is called *upādāna* (clinging).
And while thus running about, he performs the karma that produces the fruit of future existence; that is *bhava* (becoming).
Running about for the sake of attaining sense objects, he accumulates karma leading to renewed existence; that is his *bhava*.
For by means of that karma, there occurs a reconnection (*pratisaṃdhi*) in the future for one who has passed away from this state.
That which is...
Rebirth-linking (pratisaṃdhi) is birth again;
that which is the member of consciousness (vijñāna-aṅga) in this life is itself birth (jāti) for him in another existence.
Thereafter—
From birth until old age and death. // 24 //
From birth onwards, up to the stage of feeling, is old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

Those very four members that are here—namely name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*)—are themselves called "old age and death" elsewhere. These are the twelve members.
And this very dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is said to be fourfold: momentary (kṣaṇika), prolonged (prākarṣika), relational (sāṃbandhika), and situational (āvasthika).
How is it momentary?
Indeed, even within a single moment, there are twelve factors.
For example, one might deprive a living being of life through the power of greed;
that which is delusion is ignorance (*avidyā*),
and that which is volition (*cetanā*) are the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
The discernment of objects is consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The four aggregates co-arising with consciousness are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
The sense faculties established within name-and-form are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Contact is the coming together of the six sense bases;
feeling is the experiencing of contact;
that which is greed is craving.
The secondary afflictions associated with those [three roots] are clinging (*upādāna*);
the bodily and vocal actions arising from them are becoming (*bhava*).
The relinquishing of those phenomena is birth (*jāti*); their maturation is aging (*jarā*); and their dissolution is death (*maraṇa*).
Furthermore, they say that it is both momentary and relational, as stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*: "What is dependent origination?
It is all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)."

The situational [dependent origination] consists of twelve states, each comprising the five aggregates, connected across three consecutive births; this is precisely what is called the protracted [dependent origination]. Among these, which one was intended by the Blessed One?
This [dependent origination] is indeed intended to be situational (*āvasthika*).
[If every member consists of the five aggregates, for what reason did [the Buddha] proclaim only the factors such as ignorance and so forth?
It is because of their predominance that the members are proclaimed.

There is no fault in stating that the state in which ignorance (*avidyā*) predominates is called "ignorance," while those in which formative forces (*saṃskāra*) predominate are called "formative forces," and so on up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

But what is the reason that in the Sūtra the twelve members are taught, whereas in the *Prakaraṇas* it is stated otherwise: "What is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)? It is all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*")?
In the Sūtra, [the teaching] is intentional (*abhiprāyika*), whereas in the Abhidharma it is definitive (*lākṣaṇika*).

Furthermore, there is a distinction [in the Abhidharma] based on whether it is situational (*avasthika*), momentary (*kṣaṇika*), protracted (*prākarṣika*), relational (*sāṃbandhika*), pertaining to sentient beings (*sattvākhya*), or not pertaining to sentient beings (*asattvākhya*).
Why, then, is it only that which pertains to sentient beings [taught] in the Sūtra?
For the sake of dispelling delusion regarding the past, the future, and the middle. // 25 //
For this very reason, it consists of three sections.
Among these, confusion regarding the past is that from which arises this doubt: "Did I indeed exist in the past, or did I not exist? Who indeed was I? How indeed was I?
Confusion regarding the future is that from which arises this doubt: "Shall I indeed exist in the future time? and so forth.
There is delusion regarding the middle [existence], from which arises this doubt: "What is this? Who are we? What shall we become?

For the purpose of dispelling these three kinds of delusion, it is taught in the Sūtra that dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), consisting of exactly three sections and designated as "sentient beings" (sattva), is presented in sequence: ignorance (avidyā) and the formative forces (saṃskāra); birth (jāti) and old age and death (jarāmaraṇa); and consciousness (vijñāna) up to existence (bhava).

For it is said in the Sūtra itself: "And because, monks, when a monk has seen dependent origination and dependently originated phenomena thus as they really are with correct wisdom, he does not resort to the past, thinking, 'Did I indeed exist in past time? and so forth.
