Others maintain that craving, grasping, and becoming are also taught for the purpose of dispelling delusion regarding the future limit (*aparānta*).
For these are indeed the causes of that very [suffering]. Furthermore, this twelve-linked dependent origination should be understood as having three natures:
afflictions, karma, and bases. Among these:
The afflictions are three;
three members—ignorance, craving, and grasping—are of the nature of affliction.
Two are karma.
Two members have the nature of karma: formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*). Seven are entities:

seven members have the nature of entities—consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Because it is the basis for afflictions and karma;
and just as the entity consists of seven members,
so too does the fruit.
Only seven members are of the nature of the fruit;
the remaining five are of the nature of causes,
because they consist of the essence of karma and afflictions.
But what is the reason that the fruit and the cause are expanded in the middle?
Because the entity (vastu) has fivefold divisions,
while the affliction (kleśa) has two.
In the future time, the fruit is summarized because it is divided into two types; in the past time, the cause is summarized because the afflictions are taught under a single heading.
Thus, there is a condensation of both fruit and cause for the two [extremes] by means of inference from the middle. // 26 //

Indeed, by means of the middle [links] alone, the detailed exposition of cause and effect for both the prior limit (*pūrvānta*) and the subsequent limit (*aparānta*) can be inferred; thus, they were not explicitly stated, so that one might not exert further effort. Furthermore, if dependent origination consisted only of twelve links, then because ignorance would have no taught cause, *saṃsāra* would be subject to a beginning, and because old age and death would have no taught fruit, it would be subject to an end.
Or else, another factor would have to be added, and for that too yet another from something else; thus there would be the consequence of an infinite regress.
It need not be added, because the Blessed One has demonstrated it here:

From affliction arises both further affliction and action; from that, the objective basis; and from that again, the objective basis and afflictions arise. This is the method of the members of existence (bhavāṅga). // 27 //
From affliction arises affliction: from craving arises grasping; from affliction arises karma;
from grasping arises existence, as well as ignorance and the formative forces.
From the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of the basis of karma comes consciousness (*vijñāna*); from existence (*bhava*) comes birth (*jāti*).

From the basis of the object, through the consciousness of the object, comes name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), up to feeling (*vedanā*) from contact (*sparśa*); and from birth come aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
From the basis of the object comes affliction (*kleśa*); from feeling comes craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Since this principle is established for the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*), it is thereby made known that ignorance (*avidyā*) also has the nature of an affliction (*kleśa*), arising either from a [prior] affliction or from a [prior] entity.

Furthermore, because of the influence of feeling (*vedanā*), an affliction will arise again from the entity of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*); thus, nothing further needs to be added here, as it is stated:
"In this way, there is the origination of this entire great mass of suffering."
For otherwise, what would its functional capacity be?
In another sutra, it is stated that ignorance has improper mental attention as its cause,
and improper mental attention has ignorance as its cause.
Others maintain that this [unwise attention] is also mentioned here because it is included within *upādāna* (clinging).
How is unwise attention included within clinging?
If it is by way of association (*saṃprayoga*).
It would follow that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) must also be included therein.
Even if they were included, how could it be made known here that ignorance has improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) as its cause?

If, then, the relationship of cause and effect is understood solely through inclusion, then since craving and ignorance would also be included there, it would be possible not to treat them as separate members [of the dependent origination].
Another, however, says:
"In another sutra, improper mental attention (ayoniśo-manaskāra) is stated to be the cause of ignorance (avidyā),
and that too is specified as occurring at the time of contact (sparśa)."
"Dependent upon the eye and forms, there arises a turbid mental attention born of delusion.
Furthermore, at the time of feeling, ignorance must necessarily be present, according to another sutra which states: "Dependent upon feeling born of contact with ignorance, craving arises."

Therefore, improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) occurring at the time of contact is established as the condition for the ignorance (*avidyā*) that co-exists with feeling (*vedanā*). Thus, ignorance is not without a cause, nor is it necessary to add another member [to the dependent origination formula]. Furthermore, there is no consequence of infinite regress, because that very improper mental attention is said to be "born of delusion" (*mohaja*), and turbid mental attention is likewise born of delusion.
In that case, should this which was stated elsewhere not be stated here again?
It need not be stated. How is it understood even when it is not being spoken?
By way of reasoning.
By what reasoning?
For a faultless sensation does not become a condition for craving in Arhats, nor does a non-perverted contact [become a condition] for an afflicted sensation.
Furthermore, by this reasoning— that the contact of an Arhat, who is free from fault, is not perverted—
an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) would result: namely,
that whatever is possible by way of reasoning is understood even if it has not been explicitly stated.
Therefore, this is not a valid rebuttal;

rather, this objection is itself untenable. Since no other members [of dependent origination] are mentioned beyond ignorance and old age-and-death, it would follow that saṃsāra has a beginning and an end.
Nor is this exposition incomplete.
What is the reason?

Because for those disciples who are confused regarding the process of cyclic existence, the intended meaning here is simply this much: how one is connected from the next world to this world, and from this world back again to the next world.

And because this has already been stated previously: "For the sake of dispelling delusion regarding the prior, posterior, and middle [limits]," the Blessed One said, "Monks, I shall teach you dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and dependently originated phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharmas*). Now, what is the distinction between these two?
According to the treatise (*śāstra*), there is none whatsoever.
For indeed, all conditioned phenomena (saṃsk�ta-dharma) possess both [characteristics].
[How then can future things, which are as yet unarisen, be said to be "dependently originated" (pratītyasamutpanna)?
Furthermore, how can future things, being as yet uncreated, be called "conditioned" (saṃskṛta)?]
Because they are willed by volition that is productive of conditioned phenomena, one might ask:
how can the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas be so?
They too are willed by wholesome volition with respect to their acquisition (prāpti).
The same consequence would apply even to *nirvāṇa*.

Since it belongs to that same class, the extension (*atideśa*) applies to it alone; just as there is no fault in saying that something is not yet "form" (*rūpa*) because it does not belong to that class, so too here there is no fault. However, this is stated as the intended meaning (*abhiprāya*) of the Sūtra.
In this context, "arising" (samutpāda) is considered the cause, and "arisen" (samutpanna) is considered the fruit.

A member [of the series] that functions as a cause is "dependent arising" (pratītyasamutpāda), because [the fruit] arises from it; a member that functions as a fruit is "dependently arisen" (pratītyasamutpanna).
In this way, all members are established in both ways.
Because of the existence of cause and fruit,
and because there is no lack of established order despite this being so due to the difference in relativity:

that in relation to which there is dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is not the very same thing in relation to which there is the dependently originated (pratītyasamutpanna), just as in the case of cause and fruit, or father and son.

The Elder Pūrṇāśa, it is said, maintained that there may be dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) that is not dependently originated (pratītyasamutpanna) phenomena; this constitutes a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika). The first alternative consists of future phenomena (anāgatā dharmāḥ).
The second [category] consists of the final moments of an Arhat;
the third consists of other past and present conditioned phenomena;
and the fourth consists of unconditioned phenomena.
On this point, however, the Sautrāntikas raise an objection: "Are these indeed mere assertions made by whoever wishes to assert them, or are they the actual meaning of the Sūtra?
They reply: "They are the meaning of the Sūtra."
If this is not the meaning of the Sūtra, then it is not the meaning of the Sūtra. How so?

First of all, as for what was said—that this dependent origination is situational (*āvasthika*), consisting of twelve states each comprising the five aggregates, and that these twelve states are the twelve factors—this contradicts the Sūtra.
Because it is explained otherwise in the Sūtra:
"What is ignorance?
It is that which is non-knowledge regarding the past," and so forth in detail.
And as for the statement that "whatever is of definitive meaning (nītārtha) does not need to be further interpreted," this is not the intended meaning of the Sūtra.
Indeed, not everything is of definitive meaning merely by virtue of its exposition;
furthermore, expositions are made according to what is primary.
For example, in the *Hastipadopama-sūtra*, with reference to the question "What is the earth element?", it says, "Hair,
body hair," even though other things such as visible form (*rūpa*) and so forth are also present there.
Likewise, in this case as well, the explanation would be given according to what is predominant.
This is not a non-application [of the definition].
For in that case, hair and so forth are not indicated by means of the earth element such that the indication would be incomplete;
rather, it is the earth element itself that is indicated there by means of hair and so forth.
And since the earth element does not exist apart from the hair and so forth, this definition of it is indeed complete.
Likewise here, the definition of ignorance and the other factors is also entirely complete and not incomplete.
[Objection: But surely the earth element exists even beyond the hair and so forth, in such things as tears, saliva, and mucus?
That too has indeed been specified;

or rather, because of the statement: "Furthermore, there is also something else in this body that is hard and of a solid nature. Or let it be that ignorance remains as a residue if it can be demonstrated [in that way].
But as for a different category [of dharma], on what basis is its inclusion in ignorance made?
And although the five aggregates exist in those states, it is that for which there is a rule of presence and absence based on the presence and absence of another that is established as a "limb.
Furthermore, even though the Arhat possesses the five aggregates, his formative forces (*saṃskāra*) do not arise with the five aggregates as their cause; what then? [They arise from ignorance.]
They have ignorance alone as their cause;
likewise, consciousness that leads to merit, demerit, or imperturbability, as well as craving and the rest, are so.
Such is the meaning of the Sūtra exactly as it has been explained.
As for what was also said— "In this context, 'arising' (samutpāda) is the cause and 'arisen' (samutpanna) is the fruit," up to the fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika)—
this too contradicts the sūtra,
because it is taught otherwise in the sūtra.

“What is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)? It is that which has been explained in detail as ‘when this exists, that comes to be. That which here is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), and so on up to non-perversion—this is called dependent origination. And what is called “the nature of phenomena” is the genus of phenomena, the inherent character (*śaili*) of phenomena.
Therefore, this which is the nature of things (dharmatā), this which is the fixed rule—
that formations (saṃskāra) arise only when ignorance (avidyā) exists and not otherwise—
this is dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), and it is not merely a cause.

Furthermore, regarding the fourfold alternative that was stated: if future phenomena were not dependently originated, it would contradict the Sūtra which asks, "Which are the dependently originated phenomena?
They are ignorance, up to birth, and old age and death."
Since it must be admitted that there is no establishment of those two in the future time, the three-part division [of the path] is undermined.
“Dependent origination is unconditioned,” so say those of other schools, on the basis of the statement: “Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this true nature of phenomena remains constant.
This [statement] is both thus and not thus, depending on the intended meaning.
How, then, is it thus, or how is it not thus?

If the intention is that— whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise— formations (saṃskāra) and so forth always arise in dependence upon ignorance (avidyā) and so forth, and never arise without such dependence or in dependence upon something else, and therefore they are permanent, then this should be accepted as being so.
Now, if the intention is that there exists some other entity called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) which is permanent,
this must be refuted as being not so.
What is the reason?
Because arising is a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*),
it is not logical for a permanent, separate entity to be the characteristic of that which is impermanent.

Furthermore, since what is called "arising" belongs to the one who arises, what connection does it have with ignorance and the other factors, such that they could be said to be "dependent origination"?
And the meaning of the term becomes untenable, for it would imply that dependent origination is both eternal and a [conditioned] entity. Now, what is the meaning of the term *pratītyasamutpāda*?
The prefix *prati* has the sense of "attaining" (*prāpti*), and the root *i* has the sense of "going" (*gati*).
Because the meaning of a verbal root is modified by its prefix, the meaning of "having attained" (*prāpya*) is the meaning of *pratītya*.
The root *pad* has the sense of "existence," while preceded by *sam-ut*, it has the sense of "manifestation.
Therefore, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) would mean "arising after having reached conditions.
This meaning of the term is not tenable.
What is the reason?

For the rule for the suffix *ktvā* applies when there are two actions performed by a single agent, [provided] the action occurring at the earlier time is expressed; as in the example: "having bathed, he eats" (*snātvā bhuṅkte*).
And there is nothing whatsoever that exists prior to its arising which, having first depended [on conditions], arises at a later time;
nor is there an action without an agent. And regarding this, it has been said:
If it is argued that [the action] "having understood" (*pratyeti*) is not tenable because it does not exist prior to arising,
and that if it were simultaneous [with the understanding], the suffix *-ktvā* would not be established here since it prescribes a prior time—
this is not a fault.
First, this grammarian should be asked:
in what state does a dharma arise—does it arise as present, or rather as future?
And what follows from this?
If that which is present arises, how can it be present if it has not arisen? Furthermore,
if that which has already arisen were to arise again, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress.
Now, if that which is future arises, how can agency be established for what is non-existent, or how can there be an action without an agent?
Therefore, in whatever state it arises, in that very same state it passes away.
In what state, then, does it arise?
The future [dharma] is that which is oriented toward arising;
it is said that while remaining in that very state, it "proceeds toward conditions" (*pratyayaṃ pratyeti*).
Furthermore, this grammatical arrangement of agent and action is not established: namely, that "it exists" (*bhavati*) is the agent and "arising" (*bhūti*) is the action.
And here we do not perceive any action of becoming other than the entity that becomes;
therefore, there is no deception in common usage.
This, however, is the meaning of the sentence.
The meaning of "when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises" is the meaning of *pratītyasamutpāda*.
Regarding this, it is said: "Just as that which is non-existent arises, so too does that which is existent [arise] through reaching [conditions]."
If one says "the arisen arises," there is the undesirable consequence that it either does not exist previously or has already arisen.
"Moreover, the suffix -ktvā occurs even when there is simultaneity: 'Having reached the lamp, the darkness departed';
and 'He sleeps with his mouth open. If [the action] were posterior, why would it not be said that he sleeps after having closed it? Others, however, conceive of another solution for this objection.

*Prati* has the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*). *Itya* means "suitable for going" (*iti*), thus referring to things that are non-abiding (*anavasthāyin*). The root *pad* preceded by the prefix *ut* has the meaning of manifestation (*prādurbhāva*).
The arising of things through the conjunction [of conditions] directed toward their respective collections of causes is *pratītyasamutpāda*.
However, this conceptualization is applicable only in that context;
how would it apply here in the case of: "Dependent upon the eye and forms, visual consciousness arises"?
For what purpose, then, did the Blessed One state the two formulations: "When this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises"?
It is for the sake of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). As he stated elsewhere: "When ignorance exists, the formative forces come to be; the formative forces do not exist apart from ignorance."
Or, it is to demonstrate the succession of factors, showing that when this factor exists, that arises, and from the arising of this factor, that arises;
[and likewise] the succession of births.
"When the prior limit exists, the middle limit comes to be; from the arising of the middle limit, the subsequent limit arises.
This demonstrates the state of being a condition both directly and indirectly;
for sometimes the formative forces arise immediately after ignorance, and sometimes they arise through an indirect succession.
Others say it is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of causelessness (*ahetu*) and eternal causes (*nityahetu*);
[namely,] that an entity does not come into being in the absence of a cause, nor is anything produced from an unoriginated, eternal principle such as *prakṛti* or *puruṣa*.
However, under this interpretation, the inclusion of the preceding word [“non-arising”] would become redundant.
Since the refutation of both positions is established by the very statement, "From the arising of this, that arises," [there is no need for further argument].

There are, however, some who imagine that when a self exists as a supporting basis, the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) and so forth come into being, and that through the arising of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest, those [factors] arise.

Therefore, in order to refute that imagination, he established this determination: "From the arising of which very thing, that which arises comes into being only when that very thing exists, and not when something else exists.
Namely: "Conditioned by ignorance are the formations," and so on, up to "thus there is the origination of this entire great mass of suffering."
The teachers maintain that this is for the purpose of making known non-abandonment and arising:
when ignorance is not abandoned, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are not abandoned; it is precisely through the arising of that [ignorance] that they arise, and so forth in detail.
Others say it is for the purpose of demonstrating duration and arising:
as long as there is a stream of causes, there is a stream of effects;
and it is precisely from the arising of the cause that the effect arises.

But when arising (*utpāda*) is the subject under discussion, what occasion is there for a statement regarding duration (*sthiti*)? And for what purpose would the Blessed One speak out of order, mentioning duration first and arising later?
Furthermore, he said: "When this exists, that comes to be," meaning "When the effect exists, the destruction of the cause occurs.
It might be thought that the effect then arises without a cause; therefore, he says: "It is not without a cause."
Because [the principle is] "from the arising of this, that arises.
If this were the meaning of the Sūtra, they would have stated it as "when this exists, that does not exist";
and they would have first explained the arising of the effect, and only afterwards stated, "when this exists, that does not exist."
For such is the proper sequence;
otherwise, what would be the occasion for speaking of destruction in response to the question, "What is dependent origination? and so forth?
Therefore, this is not the meaning of the Sūtra.
How, then, is it that "conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces," up to "conditioned by birth are old age and death"?
We shall demonstrate this merely as a connection.
For the fool, not understanding that this is merely formative forces arisen through dependent origination, remains deeply attached to the view of self and the conceit "I am."

For the sake of one's own happiness or for the sake of freedom from suffering, one initiates three kinds of karma through the body and so forth: meritorious karma for the sake of future happiness; imperturbable karma for the sake of happiness that is neither painful nor pleasant; and non-meritorious karma for the sake of worldly happiness. Of this, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) have ignorance as their condition. And by the power of the projection of karma, the continuum of consciousness goes to various states of existence (*gati*), due to its connection with the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) in the manner of the movement of a flame.
Consciousness has those other formative forces as its condition.
And by establishing it thus, the definition of the limb of consciousness becomes appropriate: "What is consciousness?
It is the six groups of consciousness."
Furthermore, preceded by consciousness, name-and-form—consisting of the five aggregates and encompassing the entire birth—is produced in each respective realm of existence.
This is because it is so explained in the *Vibhaṅga* and in the *Mahānidāna-paryāya*:
"Likewise, from the maturation of name-and-form, the six sense bases arise in due order."
Then, when there is the attainment of the object, consciousness arises; thus, the conjunction of these three is contact (*sparśa*), which is to be experienced as pleasure and so forth.
From that, the threefold feeling (*vedanā*) arises.
From that arises craving:
for one oppressed by suffering, there is craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmatṛṣṇā*) toward pleasant feeling;
toward pleasant and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, there is craving for form (*rūpatṛṣṇā*).
In the state that is neither painful nor pleasant, there is craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyatṛṣṇā*).
From that craving for desirable feeling, the arising of sensual desires (*kāma*) and so forth occurs.
In this context, "sensual desires" refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇāḥ*).
The sixty-two views are as described in the *Brahmajālasūtra*.
Morality (*śīla*) is the abstention from immorality.
Vows (*vrata*) are such things as the dog-vow, the cow-vow, and so forth.
And as it is said in detail: "The Nirgranthas and others are naked and unclothed," and so forth;
and for the Brāhmaṇas, Pāśupatas, Parivrājakas, and others, there is the undertaking of the staff, the deerskin, ashes, matted hair, the triple staff, tonsure, and so on.
Furthermore, the doctrine of self (*ātmavāda*) refers to the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
The term "self-doctrine" (*ātmavāda*) refers to that which is expressed as "this is the self.
Others say it arises from the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*).
How is it that these two constitute a self-doctrine?
Because of the statement, "The self [is derived] from these two.
For since the self does not exist, it is called the "clinging to the doctrine of self," because one clings to that which is a mere designation.
As it has been said: "O monks, the foolish, unlearned worldling, following after mere designations, thinks 'self, self,' yet herein there is neither a self nor anything belonging to a self.
Appropriation (*upādāna*) for them is the desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) directed toward those [aggregates].
For thus has it been declared by the Blessed One everywhere: "What is appropriation?"
"That which is desire and lust herein"—
furthermore, conditioned by grasping (*upādāna*), karma leading to renewed existence is accumulated; that is "becoming" (*bhava*).
Furthermore, from the Sūtra: "Ānanda, that karma which brings about renewed existence in the future is 'existence' (bhava) in this context.
And with existence as a condition, through the process of the descent of consciousness, there is future birth (*jāti*), which consists of the five aggregates.
When birth exists, old age and death occur, as specified in the Sūtra:
"In this way there is the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
The word "entire" (kevala) means devoid of anything belonging to a self (ātmīya).
"Of the great mass of suffering" means of the aggregate of suffering that is without beginning or end;
"its origin occurs" means its manifestation.
But that very principle of the Vaibhāṣikas is what was stated previously. Now, what is the meaning of "ignorance" (avidyā)? It is that which is not knowledge (vidyā).
The same consequence would apply to the eyes and other [senses].
In that case, it would be the absence of knowledge;
if that were so, nothing at all would exist.
And this is not logical;
therefore, ignorance (avidyā) is a distinct factor that is the opposite of knowledge (vidyā), just like an enemy, falsehood, and so forth. // 28 //
Just as an enemy (*amitra*) is someone who stands in opposition to a friend (*mitra*) by being its contrary, and not merely anyone other than a friend nor the mere absence of a friend; so too,
"truth" (*ṛtam*) is said to be the real (*satyam*), and a statement that stands in opposition to it is "untruth" (*anṛtam*).
Furthermore, non-dharma (*adharma*), misfortune (*anartha*), what ought not to be done (*akārya*), and so forth, are the opposites of dharma and the like;
in the same way, ignorance (*avidyā*) should also be understood as a distinct entity that is the opposite of knowledge (*vidyā*).
Why is this so?
Because it is taught as being a condition (*pratyaya*),
and furthermore,
because of the mention of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth.
In the sūtras, ignorance is described as a fetter (*saṃyojana*), a bond (*bandhana*), a latent tendency (*anuśaya*), a flood (*ogha*), and a yoke (*yoga*);
yet it cannot be a mere non-existence,
nor can it be the eye and so forth.
Therefore, ignorance is indeed a distinct entity (dharmāntara).
Just as, for example, a bad wife is called "no wife" and a bad son is called "no son," so too let ignorance be [understood].
If it is argued that it is "bad wisdom" (*kuprajñā*), it is not so, because [bad wisdom] is a view (*darśana*).
For bad wisdom is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*);
and since that has the nature of a view, it is not logical for it to be ignorance (*avidyā*).
"In that case, it will be that which is not a view.
That too cannot be so.
What is the reason?
If ignorance were wisdom, then since it is associated with views regarding what is seen, views would not be associated with it;
for two distinct substances of wisdom cannot be associated.
And for this reason as well:
because of the teaching that wisdom is an affliction (upakleśa). // 26 //
It is stated in the Sūtra: "A mind defiled by passion is not liberated; wisdom defiled by ignorance does not become pure.
And it is not logical that this very same wisdom should be the defilement of that very same wisdom.
Just as passion is a defilement of the mind that is distinct from it and of a different nature, so too is ignorance [the defilement] of wisdom.
Why, then, is it not accepted in this way:
that wholesome wisdom, being intermingled with afflicted wisdom, does not become purified; therefore, the latter is an affliction (upakleśa) of the former?
Alternatively, even when the mind is defiled by passion (*rāga*) and is not liberated, does it necessarily mean that it is currently overwhelmed (*paryavasthita*) by passion?
Rather, it is simply impaired by passion in such a way that it is not liberated.
Furthermore, one who turns away from that cultivation is liberated.
Thus, we conceive that wisdom defiled by ignorance is not purified;
for who can prevent one from conceiving such a thing?
However, they describe ignorance as being a distinct category altogether.
Even for one who thinks that "all afflictions are ignorance," their view is refuted by this very point:
if ignorance were of the nature of all afflictions, it would not be mentioned separately among the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth, nor would it be associated with [wrong] views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Alternatively, because views and the other [afflictions] do not associate with one another in succession, it would follow that the mind is said to be defiled by ignorance alone.
If it is thought that it was stated thus for the sake of specification,
then a specification of ignorance must also be made regarding wisdom (*prajñā*).
Let ignorance be a distinct dharma; but what is its intrinsic nature?
It is the non-apprehension of the truths, of karma, and of its fruits.
Yet this very point remains unknown: what indeed is this so-called "non-apprehension"?

If it is the absence of clear cognition (*saṃprakhyāna*), then even in the case of that mere absence, the same fault applies as in the case of ignorance (*avidyā*). Alternatively, if it is a distinct entity (*dharmāntara*) that stands as the opposite of clear cognition, then this too remains unknown in the same way— namely, what that entity actually is.
There are also explanations of phenomena (dharma) of this kind, such as:
"What is the eye?
It is the translucent matter (rūpaprasāda) that is the basis of visual consciousness."
The Venerable Dharmatrāta maintains that the notion "I am" (*asmi*) is the *mayatā* (the state of being) of sentient beings, which is ignorance (*avidyā*).
But what is this *mayatā* other than the pride of "I am" (*asmimāna*)?
It is that which is spoken of in the Sūtra: "Having known thus and having seen thus, [one abandons] all cravings and all views..."

"Because of the abandonment and thorough understanding of all forms of *mayatā*, of all instances of the notions of 'I' (*ahaṃkāra*), 'mine' (*mamakāra*), the conceit 'I am' (*asmimāna*), and the underlying tendencies of clinging (*abhiniveśānuśaya*), one is extinguished and free from shadow. [But] how is it known that this *mayatā* exists, and that it is indeed this very ignorance (*avidyā*)?
Since this cannot be said to be any other affliction,
might it not simply be another form of pride (*māna*)?
However, if this matter were to be further investigated, much would have to be said.
Therefore, let this rest.
Now, what is the meaning of "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa)?
As for "form" (rūpa), it has been explained in detail as previously stated.
Why are the aggregates (skandhas) called "name" (nāma), even though they are formless?
They are called "name" because they bend toward objects by the power of the name, the sense faculties, and the objects themselves.
By the power of which name?
That is to say, that which is well-known in the world as the indicator of various objects, such as "cow," "horse," "form," "taste," and so forth.
Furthermore, by what is its status as a "name" established?
Others say that because that name bends toward its respective objects,
and because it bends toward another birth when the body has been cast off here, the formative aggregates (skandhas) are called "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa).
The six sense bases have been explained; contact must now be discussed. There are six types of contact.
From eye-contact up to mind-contact; these, moreover, are born from conjunction—that is, they arise from the conjunction of the three:
the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness.
It is indeed logical that there is a coming together (*saṃnipāta*) of the five sense-faculties with their respective objects and consciousnesses, because they arise simultaneously.
But how can there be a coming together of the mental faculty (*manaindriya*), which has already ceased, with future and present phenomena (*dharma*) and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)?

This very causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) among them is what constitutes their "coming together" (*saṃnipāta*); or rather, the meaning of "coming together" is the sense of having a single effect. And all three of them become conducive to the arising of contact (*sparśa*).
In this matter, however, the opinions of the teachers have diverged.

For some explain that contact (*sparśa*) is simply the simultaneous occurrence (*saṃnipāta*) [of the three]; they cite a Sūtra as proof for this: "Thus, the meeting (*saṃgati*), the simultaneous occurrence (*saṃnipāta*), and the conjunction (*samavāya*) of these three factors—that is contact."

Others, however, explain that contact (*sparśa*) is indeed a distinct factor (*dharmāntara*) associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*), and they cite a Sūtra as proof for this: "What is the Dharma-discourse of the Six Sixes? It consists of the six internal sense-bases (*āyatana*), the six external sense-bases," and so forth.
The six groups of consciousness,
the six groups of contact,
and the six groups of feeling.
Regarding the statement, “There are six groups of craving,” here the groups of contact (*sparśakāya*) are taught separately from the sense faculties, objects, and consciousnesses.
In that regard, those who maintain that contact is merely the coming together [of the three] offer this rebuttal:
It is not the case that a separate existence follows from a separate designation;

otherwise, there would be no separate existence for feeling (*vedanā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) apart from the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). This is not a fault, because the sphere of mental objects exists even as something distinct from those two.
Furthermore, there is no other triad apart from the three that constitute contact (*sparśa*) which could be the "remainder" intended for inclusion here.
For even if the sense faculty (*indriya*) and the object (*artha*) were to exist without consciousness (*vijñāna*), consciousness cannot exist without a sense faculty and an object.
Therefore, since these three have already been specified, the separate mention of contact would be redundant.
Indeed, not all eyes and visible forms are the cause of every visual consciousness, nor is every visual consciousness the effect of every eye and visible form.
Therefore, some maintain that those [factors] which stand in a relationship of cause and effect are established as being in the state of contact (*sparśa*).

However, as for those who assert that contact is something other than the mere coming together (*saṃnipāta*), how do they reconcile this sūtra: "That which is the meeting, the coming together, the conjunction of these three, that is contact"?
Or rather, they do not read it in this way;
what then?
They read it as "from conjunction," "from meeting," or "from combination," or they say that this is a metaphorical designation of the effect for the cause.
But this discussion has become excessively prolix; enough of this digression.
The Abhidharmikas describe contact as something entirely different.
Furthermore, among those six types of contact, five are contacts involving resistance (pratigha-saṃsparśa), while the sixth is called "designation-contact" (adhivacana-saṃsparśa). //30//
The five contacts of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body are called "contacts with resistance" (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*),
because they have as their basis the sense faculties that possess resistance (*sapratigha*).
The sixth, the contact of the mind (*manaḥ-saṃsparśa*), is called "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*).

What is the reason? "Designation" (*adhivacana*) is said to be the name (*nāman*). Since that [name] is its predominant object (*ālambana*), it is therefore called "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*).
As it has been said: "By means of visual consciousness one cognizes blue, but not 'it is blue'; by means of mental consciousness one cognizes blue, and one also cognizes 'it is blue'."
The first is characterized by its basis (*āśraya*), while the second is characterized by its object (*ālambana*).
Others, however, say:
"The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) operates with respect to objects by virtue of speech, whereas the five [sensory consciousnesses] do not."

Therefore, that alone is the designation. Contact associated with that [designation] is "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*). Thus, one is characterized by its basis (*āśraya*), while the second is characterized by its association (*saṃprayoga*).
Furthermore, those same six contacts become three:
the contacts of knowledge, ignorance, and that which is other than both— namely, the contact associated with knowledge and the contact associated with ignorance.
And distinct from these two is the contact of neither-knowledge-nor-ignorance;
furthermore, these should be understood respectively as being stainless, afflicted, and the remainder.

Untainted contact (*anāsrava-sparśa*) is "contact associated with knowledge" (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*); afflicted contact (*kliṣṭa-sparśa*) is "contact associated with ignorance" (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*), because it is associated with both knowledge and ignorance. The remainder is "contact associated with neither knowledge nor ignorance," because it is associated with neither of the two.
What, then, is the remainder?
[The first] is wholesome-with-outflows (*kuśala-sāsrava*) and the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Furthermore, because a portion of the contact of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*) that frequently manifests is grasped, there are two contacts:
the contact of aversion (*vyāpāda-saṃsparśa*) and the contact of attachment (*anunaya-saṃsparśa*).

Because they are associated with ill-will and attachment; furthermore, by way of a comprehensive summary, there are three [types of feeling], beginning with that to be experienced as pleasure. // 31 //
Contact is [classified as] to-be-experienced-as-pleasant, to-be-experienced-as-painful, and to-be-experienced-as-neither-painful-nor-pleasant,
because it is conducive to pleasant feeling and so forth. Alternatively, "to-be-experienced" (vedanīya) means that which is experienced, or that which is capable of being experienced.
What is that? It is feeling. "Pleasant-to-be-felt" (sukhavedanīya) contact is that in which there is a pleasant feeling to be experienced.
In the same way, those [contacts] to be experienced as painful and as neither-painful-nor-pleasant should also be applied.
Thus, these constitute the sixteen contacts.
Contact has been explained.
Feeling (vedanā) is to be explained:
therein, the six kinds of feeling arise from the sixfold contact (sparśa) previously mentioned.
There is feeling born of eye-contact, and feelings born of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact.
Furthermore, among these, five are bodily and the other is mental.
The five feelings born of contact with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body are called bodily feeling.
Because it relies upon the physical sense faculties, [feeling born of eye-contact and so forth] is called bodily;
however, feeling born of mental contact is called mental,
because it relies upon the mind alone.
Now, does feeling arise after contact, or at the same time?
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that it is simultaneous,
because they are mutually co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*).
How can the relationship of producer and produced be established between two things that arise simultaneously?
And why is it not established? Because of a lack of capacity.
Once a phenomenon has arisen, one phenomenon lacks capacity toward another; this is no different from the original thesis.

For that very reason—namely, that there is no relationship of producer and produced between two things that arise simultaneously—is precisely why there is no [causal relation] of one dharma toward another dharma once it has already arisen.
[Objection: In that case, it would follow that they are mutual producers. [Response: This is not a fault, because such a consequence is accepted.
For it is indeed accepted that simultaneous causes (sahabhūhetu) have mutual results.
[This is accepted; however, in the Sūtra, it is not accepted that contact (sparśa) and sensation (vedanā) have mutual results, because of the statement:
"Dependent on eye-contact, feeling born of eye-contact arises; but dependent on feeling born of eye-contact, eye-contact does not arise. ]
Furthermore, it is illogical because it would violate the principle of causality (*janakadharma*).
For whatever phenomenon is established as the producer of another phenomenon is established as being at a different time from it;
for example, first the seed and later the sprout, first the milk and later the curd, first the impact and later the sound, first the mind and later the mental consciousness, and so forth.
Otherwise, because cause and effect are mutually dependent, either everything would arise simultaneously or nothing would ever arise, since there would be no subsequent distinction.
For it is not that the temporal sequence of cause and effect is unestablished;
rather, their coexistence is also established.

For example, as in the case of visual consciousness and so forth with respect to the eye and visible forms, which are both primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*bhautika*), even there the sense faculty and the object precede, and consciousness follows.
If it is accepted that a subsequent [moment] arises from a preceding collection of primary elements and derived matter, what is the objection?
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the relationship between contact and sensation is just like that between a shadow and a sprout.
"Others maintain that feeling occurs at a time subsequent to contact.

For the sense faculty and the object constitute the prior limit, while consciousness is the meeting of these three; this meeting is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises in the third moment."
"If that is so, then it follows that feeling does not occur in every consciousness, nor is every consciousness contact.
This is not a fault.
For feeling arises in a subsequent contact caused by a preceding contact; all contacts possess feeling, and all consciousness is contact.
This is untenable.
What here is untenable?
Namely, that even when two contacts have different objects, the subsequent feeling is caused by the preceding contact.

How indeed could a feeling produced by contact with an object of a different kind have that other thing as its object, such that it would have an object distinct from the mind with which it is associated?
Alternatively, let it be that at that time the consciousness constituting the contact is devoid of feeling;
and therefore, that previous consciousness which possessed feeling was not contact.
If it is the case that [the mind does not arise] due to the deficiency of conditions, what fault is there?
The rule regarding the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) would be violated, namely: "In every state of mind, there are ten universal mental factors."
And where is this restriction established?
In the treatise.
We take the sūtras as our authority, not the treatises.
For it was said by the Blessed One: "One should rely upon the sūtras.

Furthermore, this is not the meaning of "universal mental factors" (mahābhūmika): that ten universal mental factors arise in every state of consciousness. What, then, is the meaning of "universal mental factors"?
There are three levels:

the level with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarkā savicārā bhūmi*), the level without applied thought and with sustained thought only (*avitarkā vicāramātrā*), and the level without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitarkā'vicārā bhūmi*).
Furthermore, there are three others: the wholesome level (*kuśalā bhūmi*), the unwholesome level (*akuśalā bhūmi*), and the indeterminate level (*avyākṛtā bhūmi*).
Furthermore, there are three [levels]:
the level of those in training (śaikṣī bhūmi), the level of those beyond training (aśaikṣī bhūmi), and the level of neither-training-nor-beyond-training (naivaśaikṣī bhūmi).
Those factors that exist throughout all these levels are called the universal mental factors (mahābhūmikāḥ).
Those that exist only in a wholesome [state] are the great wholesome ground factors;
those that exist only in an afflicted [state] are the great afflictive ground factors.
Furthermore, others maintain that these occur alternately according to circumstances, and not all of them simultaneously.
The great unwholesome mental factors (*akuśalamahābhūmika*) were not included in the recitation;
they were not previously recited.

If, then, feeling (*vedanā*) occurs at a time subsequent to contact (*sparśa*), the Sūtra must be reconciled: "Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact, which is co-nascent."
"Feeling, perception, and volition"—here it is said they are "co-arisen," not "arisen together with contact. What is there to be refuted here?

Furthermore, this word "together" (saha) is seen even in the sense of "immediately following" (*samanantara*), as in: "He cultivates the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness accompanied by loving-kindness" (*maitrīsahagataṃ smṛtisaṃbodhyaṅgaṃ bhāvayati*). Therefore, this [example] is not a proof.

As for what is stated in the Sūtra: "That which is feeling, that which is perception, that which is volition, and that which is consciousness—these factors are conjoined, not unconjoined"—it follows from this that there is no consciousness unjoined with feelings.
First, however, one must carefully consider what the meaning of "conjoined" (saṃsṛṣṭa) is in this context.
For in that very Sūtra it is said: "What one feels, that one intends; what one intends, that one discerns; what one discerns, that one cognizes.
It is not understood whether this statement refers to a restriction regarding their object (*ālambana*) or a restriction regarding their moment (*kṣaṇa*).
Since the coexistence of vitality and heat is established by the statement that they are "conjoined" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*), the restriction regarding the moment is proven.
Furthermore, as it is stated in the Sūtra: "The coming together of the three is contact.
How could consciousness exist without the coming together of the three and without contact?
Therefore, one must necessarily admit that in every instance of consciousness there is contact, and that feeling is co-nascent with contact.
Enough with this overly prolix discourse; let us proceed with the subject at hand.
The mental feeling has thus been explained in brief.
Furthermore, it is of eighteen kinds by way of the mental applications (manopavicāra). // 32 //
Furthermore, mental feeling is divided into eighteen types based on the classification of the eighteen mental explorations (*manopavicāra*).
Moreover, a connection (*saṃdhikaraṇa*) should be observed here.
What are the eighteen mental explorations?
There are six applications of mental joy, six applications of mental grief, and six applications of equanimity. How are these established?
If by way of intrinsic nature, [then...]
There will be three:
the investigations of mental joy, mental grief, and equanimity.
Now, from the perspective of association:
It will be one,
because it is associated with the mind of all;
or, from the perspective of its object, [it is one].
There will be six [types],
because they have the six objects, beginning with form, as their objective supports.
There is also establishment by means of three.

Among these, fifteen mental applications (*manopavicāra*)—those directed toward visible forms and so forth—have unmixed objects (*asaṃbhinnālambana*), because they have specifically determined objects such as visible forms.
The three mental applications directed toward mental phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*) are of both types. [What is the meaning of "mental applications"?]
It is said that these [mental factors], such as mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) and so forth, depend upon the mind (*manas*) and range over objects;
or, according to others, they cause the mind to range over objects,
because by the power of feeling (*vedanā*), the mind ranges repeatedly over objects.
[Why is bodily feeling not a mental application (*manopavicāra*)?
For it does not rely on the mind alone, nor is it an application because it is non-conceptual; thus, it is inappropriate [to classify it as such].
Why is the pleasure of the third dhyāna not included among the mental applications?

It is said that from the very beginning, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because the faculty of pleasure belonging to the mental level (*manobhūmika*) is absent, there is likewise an absence of the mental applications (*upavicāra*) of suffering as its opposite.

If these [mental applications] belong exclusively to the mental level, then what about that which is stated in the Sūtra: "Having seen forms with the eye, one mentally applies oneself to forms that are a basis for joy," and so forth?
How so?
This was said with reference to their being produced by the five groups of consciousness: "For these belong to the mental level (*manobhūmikā*);
for example, the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) is produced by visual consciousness and yet belongs to the mental level."
However, because of the statement, "having seen... up to having touched," this is not at all a point for objection;
even those who attend to objects without seeing them, up to without touching them, these too are mental attendances (*manopavicāra*).

Otherwise, there would be no mental explorations (*upavicāra*) of visible forms and so forth in the desire realm that have the form realm as their object, nor would there be mental explorations of odors, tastes, and tangibles in the form realm that have the desire realm as their object.
However, it was stated in a more manifest manner; for even one who, having seen visible forms, mentally explores sounds—that too is a mental exploration.
Yet it was stated in a way that is not confused, by way of the distinction between the sense faculty and its respective object.
Is there any form that would be exclusively a basis for mental pleasure, up to and including a basis for equanimity?
There is, provided one restricts it to a particular continuum (*saṃtāna*), but not with respect to the object (*ālambana*).

Now, among these mental explorations (*manopavicāra*), how many are associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)? And of those, how many have what as their object (*ālambana*)? In this manner, it should be stated up to those associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
He replied:
"In the desire realm, all have themselves as their objects."
In the desire realm (kāmadhātu), all eighteen [mental applications] exist, and it is the object (ālambana) of them all.
Of those very same [applications], twelve have the form realm (rūpadhātu) as their range (gocara);
the form realm is the object of twelve, excluding the six mental applications regarding odor and taste.
Because those two do not exist there;
it follows that the latter [object] is the range of the three.
The formless realm is the object of three mental applications regarding phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*),
because of the absence of visible forms and so forth therein.
Those associated with the desire realm have been explained;
those associated with the form realm must now be discussed.
Regarding that, first:
In the first two dhyānas, excluding the twelve mental applications of dissatisfaction (*daurmanasyopavicāra*),
there are those same twelve.
Those who go toward sense-pleasures. // 33 //
They go toward desires, thus they are "desire-goers" (*kāmagā*);
the meaning is that they take the desire realm as their object (*ālambante*).
For the use of the verb *gam* (to go) is seen in the sense of grasping objects.
How is this understood?
It is understood thus:
its own object of perception consists of eight [factors].
That very same form realm (rūpadhātu) is their own [realm];
it is the object of eight mental explorations (manopavicāra), excluding the four explorations of odor and taste.
The formless realm is the object of two mental applications regarding phenomena;
however, in the first two dhyānas, there are six.
In the third and fourth dhyānas, there are only the six applications of equanimity and no others;
furthermore, the objects of those six are the sense-pleasures.
The desire realm is the object of all six [consciousnesses]. One’s own [realm] is the object of four; the form realm is the object of four there, because of the absence of odor and taste.
The object of one is the other. (34)
The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is the object of only one mental application (*dharmopavicāra*).
Those associated with the form realm (*rūpapratisaṃyukta*) have been explained; now those associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyapratisaṃyukta*) are being discussed.
There are four [mental applications] in the preliminary stage of the formless realm (*ārūpisāmanta*).
The preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space is here the "preparatory stage of the formless" (*arūpisāmantaka*).
In that [stage], there are four applications of attention (*upavicāra*) regarding visible forms, sounds, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharma*);
and these...
For those belonging to the realm of form (*rūpagāḥ*), the fourth dhyāna is indeed their object (*ālambana*).

Among them, for those whose object is differentiated (*vyavacchinnālambana*), there are [separate mental applications]; however, for those whose object is a unified whole (*paripiṇḍitālambana*), there is in that case only one mental application to phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*) with a mixed object (*saṃbhinnālambana*).
One is directed upward;
only one mental application regarding phenomena has the formless realm as its object; and one pertains to the fundamental [dhyāna].
Furthermore, in the fundamental formless realm, there is only the mental application (*upavicāra*) toward phenomena (*dharma*), and no other;
and that too has its own [formless] objects as its domain.
It has only the formless realm as its object;
for we shall explain later that the lower realm is not the object of the fundamental formless attainments.
And all these eighteen mental explorations (manopavicāra) are with outflows (sāsrava). // 35 //
There is nothing whatsoever that is untainted.
[Who is endowed with how many?

One born in the desire realm who has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm is endowed with all those belonging to the desire realm; with eight belonging to the levels of the first and second dhyānas;
with four afflicted ones belonging to the levels of the third and fourth dhyānas—excluding those having odor and taste as their objects—and with one belonging to the formless realm.]

One who has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm and is not free from passion for the desire realm possesses all ten [mental applications] belonging to the desire realm and the first dhyāna level.

Among these, one possesses four afflicted mental applications of joy (*saumanasyopavicāra*), excluding those having odor and taste as their objects; and one possesses six mental applications of equanimity (*upekṣopavicāra*) belonging to the stage of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
With eight [factors] belonging to the level of the second dhyāna;
with those belonging to the levels of the third and fourth dhyānas and the formless realms (ārūpya), as previously stated.
Following this method, the remainder is to be understood.

However, one who has been reborn in the dhyānas should be understood as being endowed with one mental application of equanimity pertaining to the desire realm, which is associated with the mind of emanation (*nirmāṇacitta*).
Another says:
"The Vaibhāṣika interpretation of the mental applications is indeed correct."
The meaning of the sūtra, however, appears otherwise;
for it is not logical that one who is free from passion toward something would still mentally explore that as an object.
Therefore, even among those associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), not all instances of mental joy (*saumanasya*) and so forth constitute mental explorations (*manopavicāra*).
What then?
They are the defiled [mental factors] by which the mind ranges over objects. And how does it range over them?
One is attracted, one is repelled, and one remains indifferent without discernment; as the antidote to these, there are the six constant abidings:

having seen forms with the eye, one is neither glad nor sad, but abides in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending; and so it continues up to "having cognized mental phenomena with the mind. For it is not that an Arhat lacks mundane wholesome joy based on mental objects; rather, what is prohibited is specifically that defiled joy which constitutes the mental applications (*manopavicāra*). Thus, the prohibition is understood to apply only to that.
Furthermore, those same mental factors, such as joy (*saumanasya*) and so forth, constitute thirty-six "Teacher's Words" (*śāstṛpada*),
distinguished by whether they are based on worldly attachment (*gardha*) or on renunciation (*naiṣkramya*),
since this distinction was established by the Teacher.
In that regard, those based on attachment are afflicted, while those based on renunciation are wholesome.
Thus, this limb of existence called "feeling" should be understood as having many varieties of distinctions.
The remaining factors are not mentioned again.
For what reason? Because:
It has been stated, and some other [factors] will be stated; here, some members have already been mentioned, while others will be explained later.
Among those, consciousness (vijñāna) has first been mentioned.
"Consciousness is the specific representation [of objects], and it is also the sense-base of mind. Thus the six sense-bases have been explained.
Furthermore, the [five] sense-faculties have been described as "the translucent forms that serve as the supports for those consciousnesses, beginning with the eye."

Formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) will be explained in the section on the Treasury of Karma; craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) will be explained in the section on the Treasury of Afflictions (*kleśa*).
And this very dependent origination has been previously explained in brief as consisting of afflictions, karma, and bases;
here, however, the affliction is intended [to be illustrated] by way of being like a seed, like a nāga, like a root, like a tree, and likewise like a husk. (36)
What is its similarity to seeds and so forth?
Just as from a seed there arises the production of sprouts, stalks, leaves, and so on, even so from affliction arise further afflictions, karma, and their bases.

Just as a lake presided over by a nāga does not dry up, and just as trees whose roots have not been pulled out grow again and again even though they are cut down, even so the realms of existence (gatis) persist when the root of the afflictions has not been pulled out.
Just as trees produce flowers and fruits from time to time, so too the afflictions (*kleśa*) repeatedly become the cause of afflictions, karma, and the bases of existence.

And just as rice grains covered by husks are capable of sprouting, but not when they are alone, so too karma covered by the husks of the acquisition of afflictions is capable of producing another birth, but not when it is alone; in this way, the affliction should be understood as being like a seed and so forth.
Karma is like rice with its husk, and likewise like medicinal herbs and flowers.
That which has a husk is called *tuṣī*; thus, the affliction (*kleśa*) is said to occupy the place of the husk.
Now, karma, which corresponds to rice in the husk, is being explained.
Just as there are medicinal herbs that, once their fruit has ripened, do not produce further ripening, so too do karmas cease after they have ripened and no longer bring about further results.
Furthermore, just as a flower is the proximate cause for the production of fruit, so should karmas be understood to be in relation to the production of their ripening.
An entity is like prepared food and drink;
just as prepared food and drink are intended solely for consumption and not for further growth, so too is the entity known as maturation (*vipāka*).
For from one maturation, another maturation does not arise in subsequent births.
For if it were to increase, liberation would not exist.
Indeed, this very continuum of birth, arising through dependent origination in this manner, does not transcend the four states of existence;
namely, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*), the state of prior time (*pūrvakālabhava*), and the state of death (*maraṇabhava*).
And these have been explained in that fourfold existence. //37//
The existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) is exclusively afflicted (*kliṣṭa*).
By which affliction?
By all the afflictions belonging to its own level:

whatever level the existence at rebirth (upapattibhava) belongs to, it is by all the afflictions belonging to that very level [that it is bound]. For there is no affliction by which the connection of rebirth (pratisaṃdhibandha) is not obstructed; thus say the Abhidharmikas.
It is indeed by the afflictions (*kleśa*), and not by independent outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
Even though that state is dull, whichever affliction one has frequently practiced and remained close to, that very same affliction arises at that time due to prior habituation.
The linking of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) should also be understood as necessarily afflicted (*kliṣṭa*).
The others are of three kinds;

the other three existences—the intermediate existence and so forth—are of three types: wholesome, afflicted, and neutral (*avyākṛta*). Now, among these existences, which one is associated with which realm?
In the three formless realms, the intermediate state is excluded;
for the formless realm is not delimited by a distinct location for the sake of reaching which an intermediate state would be produced.
Since the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) have not been specifically excluded, it is thereby admitted that all four states of existence (*bhava*) exist.
The dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of sentient beings has thus been explained in detail.
Now, as to how the persistence of sentient beings occurs, he says:
The world subsists on nutriment. //38//
"One dharma has been declared by the Blessed One, having realized it for himself through direct knowledge: namely, that all sentient beings subsist on nutriment"—this is the scriptural passage.
What, then, are the nutriments?
There are four nutriments.
The first is edible food (kavaḍīkārāhāra),
which is both gross and subtle;
it is subtle because those in the intermediate state (antarābhava) have fragrance as their food.
Because there is an absence of outflow (*niḥṣyanda*) among the gods and those of the first eon;
because it does not penetrate into the limbs as oil does into sand;
or because it is subtle, like the minute sweat-born insects found on a child.
Contact is the second;
mental volition is the third;
and consciousness is the fourth nutriment.
Furthermore, among those,
edible food exists in the desire realm, but not in the form or formless realms, because one who is free from passion for it is reborn there.
And that consists of three bases:
all the bases of odor, taste, and tangibles belonging to the desire realm are exclusively material food.
Because they are consumed by being made into mouthfuls,
and because they are partitioned into morsels for the mouth and nose;
[how then can shadow, heat, flame, and light be considered food?]
This explanation is generally stated;
however, even those things which are not ingested but maintain one's existence are also subtle food,
just like bathing and anointing with oil.
Why is the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) not considered nutriment? For even that is swallowed after being made into morsels. [The answer is:
It is not the sphere of visible form, because it does not benefit its own sense organ nor those who are liberated. (36)
For that which is called "nutriment" is what conduces to the benefit of the sense faculties and the great elements.
At the time of ingestion, the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) does not benefit its own faculty or those great elements;

how much less so other [faculties], since it has a different object? Furthermore, even when it produces pleasure and mental ease while being seen, at that time it is the contact (*sparśa*) to be experienced as pleasant—which has that [visible form] as its objective support—that constitutes the nutriment, not the visible form itself.
For those who are liberated—non-returners and arhats—there is an absence of nutriment even when they see food that is very agreeable.
The nutriments of contact, volition, and consciousness are contaminated (*sāsrava*) in the three realms.
Contact is born from the coming together of the triad.
Volition (*cetanā*), mental action (*manaskarma*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—only those that are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) are nutriments; they are found in all three realms.
For what reason are those without-outflows (*anāsrava*) not included?
Because the purpose of nutriment is for the sake of nourishing existence (*bhava*).
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that these [nutriments] have arisen for the sake of the exhaustion of existence (*bhava*).
However, it is stated in the Sūtra: "These four nutriments are for the stability and maintenance of beings who have come to be, and for the assistance of those seeking rebirth.
Since uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena are not like this, they are not nutriments.
For beings who have already been born are indeed known as "beings" (*sattva*). Now, who are those seeking rebirth?
They are the mind-made (*manomaya*), the seeker of existence (*saṃbhavaiṣin*), the gandharva, and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). (40)
The Blessed One has described the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) by these designations as "arising" (*nirvṛtti*);
it is called "mind-made" (*manomaya*) because it is produced from the mind alone.
Because it exists without depending on any external factors such as semen and blood,
it is called *saṃbhavaiṣī* (seeking rebirth) due to its nature of seeking existence. It is called *gandharva* because of its smelling (*gandharvaṇāt*).
It is called "arising" (*abhinirvṛtti*) because it is oriented toward rebirth;
this is known from the scriptural passage: "Having brought about an unafflicted personal existence, one is reborn in a world that is afflicted.
Furthermore, it is established by the fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) in the Sūtra: "There is a person for whom the fetter of arising has been abandoned, but not the fetter of rebirth."
The first category consists of non-returners who have attained freedom from passion regarding the two realms and are of the "upward-streaming" type;
the second consists of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state;
the third consists of arhats.
The fourth [category] consists of those who, setting aside these aforementioned modes, are real Arhats; as well as those seeking rebirth who possess craving.
Now, how many nutriments are for the maintenance of beings, and how many are for the benefit of those seeking rebirth?
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that all [nutriments] function in both ways;
for even the nutriment of physical food leads to renewed existence for those who possess craving for it.
For it has been said:

The Blessed One said: "These four nutriments are the root of disease, of the boil, of the thorn, and the condition for old age and death. Yet, here mental volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanā*) is also seen as being for the sake of maintenance. For they relate this story: it is said that during a famine, a father, having filled a leather bag with ashes under the pretext of "flour," hung it on a peg to reassure his two sons.
And those two, imagining her to be there, remained for a long time; when she was revealed by someone to be nothing but ashes, they fell into despair and perished.
Furthermore, men whose ship was wrecked in the great ocean rushed toward a large mass of foam, thinking it to be land; having touched it, they despaired and perished.

And it is said in the *Saṃgītiparyāya*: "From the great ocean, coarse creatures emerge from the water onto the land, lay their eggs on a sandy shore, cover them with sand, and then descend back into the great ocean."
In this regard, those mothers whose mindfulness is not lost concerning their eggs—those eggs do not rot; however, for those whose mindfulness is lost, those eggs do rot.
The Sautrāntikas do not describe it in this way, lest [it be thought that] there is nutriment through the nutriment of another.
They describe it thus:
those eggs for which mindfulness toward the mother is not lost do not become putrid;
however, those for which it is lost do become putrid.
They remember that state of contact.
Now, why are there exactly four nutriments?
Is it not the case that all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) nourish the states of existence?
Even though this is so, it has nevertheless been stated according to their predominance:
here, for the sake of nourishment, there are two [causes] for the support and the supported;
and two [causes] are for the projection and the cessation of another existence, respectively. (41)
For the basis is the body endowed with sense faculties;
edible food (kavaḍīkārāhāra) serves for its nourishment.
The supported are the mind and mental factors; contact (sparśa) serves for their nourishment.
Of these two, the former has primacy in nourishing existence (*bhava*) once it has arisen here;

the volitional intention of the mind (*manaḥsaṃcetana*), however, projects a future rebirth. Furthermore, the actualization of that projected [existence] occurs from the seed of consciousness (*vijñāna*) permeated by karma. Thus, these two have primacy in the non-production of existence that has not yet arisen.
Therefore, four [nutriments] have been taught.

For the two preceding [causes] stand in the place of nurses, because they nourish that which has not yet been born; the two subsequent [causes] stand in the place of mothers, because they give birth to it.
Regarding the statement "whatever is edible, all that would be food," there is a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika) concerning whether something is edible but not food.
The first alternative is that edible substance in dependence upon which there is a diminution of the sense faculties and a disintegration of the primary elements (mahābhūta).

The second alternative consists of the other three nutriments. The third is that edible food in dependence upon which there is the nourishment of the sense faculties and the growth of the great elements. The fourth is setting aside these aforementioned modes.
In the same way, fourfold alternatives (catuṣkoṭika) should also be formulated for contact and the other [bases], as appropriate.
It may be that, depending on contact and so forth, there is an accumulation of the sense faculties and an increase of the great elements, yet these would not be nutriments,
as they belong to other planes or are untainted (*anāsrava*).

For even that which, when consumed, brings affliction to the consumer is indeed nutriment, because it provides benefit at the moment of intake. The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that nutriment performs the function of nutriment during two periods: while it is being consumed and while it is being digested.
[Now, in which destiny (gati) are there how many nutriments?
In all of them, all [four] exist.
Likewise, even in the modes of birth (yoni).]
How is there edible food in the hells?
It consists of glowing iron balls and molten copper.
If even harmful food were considered nutriment, it would contradict the fourfold classification and the *Prakaraṇapāda* treatise, which states: "What is edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*)?
That edible food depending upon which there is the nourishment of the sense-faculties and the growth, maintenance, and sustenance of the great elements," and so on, in detail, up to consciousness.
There is no contradiction, however, because that statement was made with the intention of referring specifically to nutriment that causes nourishment (*upacaya*).
In the hells, however, food consists of consumption by decay, because it has attained that specific characteristic;
for even that is capable of quelling hunger and thirst.
Moreover, since edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) exists in the individual hells (*pratyekanaraka*) just as it does among humans, it is logical that [food] pertains to all five destinies.

The Blessed One said: "If one were to feed a hundred external seers who are free from passion for sensual pleasures, and another were to feed a single ordinary person (pṛthagjana) situated in the Jambū-ṣaṇḍa, this latter gift would bear much greater fruit than that gift.
Who, then, is this so-called ordinary person situated in the Jambū-ṣaṇḍa?
Some say that those dwelling in Jambūdvīpa are "those who possess bellies.
This is not correct, because of the statement "one" (eka).
What, then, is the distinction here?
It might be that more merit would result from feeding a greater number of ordinary persons than from feeding a smaller number of those free from passion;
others say this refers to a Bodhisattva who is close [to enlightenment].
However, they do not describe it thus, for [the scripture states]: "Indeed, giving to him produces far more merit than giving to ten million Arhats."
Therefore, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that this refers to an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) who has attained the levels conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya).
However, this is not an etymologically meaningful designation, nor is it defined anywhere in the Sūtras or the Śāstras;
it is merely a conceptual construction that one situated in Jambūṣaṇḍa has attained the levels conducive to penetration.
Rather, it is the Bodhisattva himself who is appropriately seated among these groves of Jambūdvīpa;
for he is said at that time to be distinguished from them by virtue of his connection with the detachment from desire characteristic of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana).
Indeed, he is distinguished from them even when compared to those who are infinite in number.
The mention of "one hundred" is due to the preceding context.
And this is indeed so, because by thus excluding [others], he distinguished the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry specifically from those among the outsiders;
otherwise, he would have distinguished him only from those belonging to Jambūdvīpa.
The dependent origination of sentient beings has been explained, as well as their abiding and their death through the exhaustion of the life-span and so forth.
This must now be stated:
in which consciousness being present do death and rebirth occur? To this he says:
The severance [of roots], the reconnection [of roots], detachment, falling away, death, and rebirth are held to occur only in the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
These include the cutting off of the roots of virtue, the reconnecting of the roots of virtue, detachment from the realms and stages, falling away [from attainment], death, and rebirth.
These six factors are held to exist only in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and not elsewhere.
From the mention of "rebirth" (*upapatti*), it should be understood that the linking of existence in the intermediate state (*antarābhava-pratisaṃdhi*) is also of the nature already described.
But at the moment of death and rebirth, there is equanimity with respect to feeling. (42)
Death itself is "passing away" (cyuta), and rebirth is "arising" (udbhava).
These two occur within a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, because that [neutral] feeling is indistinct;
for the other two feelings are indeed distinct.
Furthermore, death and rebirth are not possible in a sharp consciousness;
nor are these two [death and rebirth] possible even in that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it is either one-pointed or without mind.
The terms "death" and "arising" are understood to carry over here.

For one whose mind is in meditative equipoise, there is neither death nor rebirth, because such states belong to a different level (*visabhāgabhūmika*), involve volitional effort (*abhisaṃskārika*), and are beneficial (*anugrāhaka*).
Nor does it belong to one who is without mind, for it is impossible to inflict harm upon one who lacks a mind.

Furthermore, when its physical basis (āśraya) begins to undergo transformation, the mind—which is necessarily bound to that basis—must necessarily manifest and only then pass away; it cannot be otherwise.

Moreover, at the moment of rebirth, a state of being without mind is untenable, because there is no cause for the interruption of the mind, and because rebirth cannot occur without the presence of afflictions (kleśa).
It has been stated that the state of death (maraṇabhava) is of three kinds.
But the Arhat attains parinirvāṇa in one of two neutral states:
either in a state of deportment or in a resultant consciousness.
If there is maturation in the desire realm, it is equanimity;
if there is none, it is only that which pertains to deportment.
For what reason is it only indeterminate and not of any other kind?
For that [state] is conducive to the severance of the mind because of its weakness.
Now, in which part of the body does consciousness cease for one who is dying?
In the case of instantaneous death, the body-faculty together with the mind-faculty disappears all at once.
But if one passes away gradually, then:
