In the gradual dissolution, the withdrawal of the mind occurs in the feet, the navel, and the heart.
Regarding "those who go downward" (*adhoga*) and "those who go among humans" (*nṛga*): they are called *adhoga* because they go downward, meaning those who go to the states of woe (*apāya*);
they are called *nṛga* because they go among humans, meaning those who go to the human realm.
"Going to the gods" (*suragā*) means going to the deities (*devagāmin*).
For them, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is completely arrested respectively at the feet, the navel, and the heart.
Because they are not born again, they are "unborn" (*ajā*), namely the Arhats.
In their case as well, consciousness ceases in the heart;

others say it is in the crown of the head, because the body-faculty (kāyendriya) ceases within them. For, in one who is dying, the body-faculty—like water spat upon a heated stone—undergoes contraction and disappears, starting from the feet and so forth.
Furthermore, the death of living beings generally occurs in this gradual manner for those struck by the sensations of the severing of the vital points (marmans);
the severing of the vital points, however, is caused by the [elements] beginning with earth.
Certain regions of the body, when afflicted, bring about death;
these are indeed called *marmas*.
They [are destroyed] by any one of the elements—water, fire, or wind—having reached an extreme state, through intense pains like the stroke of a sharpened weapon piercing the vital channels.
They seem as if they were being cut, yet they are not actually cut like wood or other such materials; rather, because they no longer move as if they had been cut, they are said to be "cut."
Why not by the earth element?
Because of the absence of the fourth humor;
for wind, bile, and phlegm are the three humors.
And these are dominated respectively by the elements of water, fire, and air, as appropriate.
Others say it is by way of similarity with the destruction of the receptacle world.
Among the gods there is no cutting of the vital organs; however, for a son of the gods subject to the law of passing away, five minor omens appear:
an unpleasant sound issues from his garments and ornaments, the radiance of his body diminishes, and droplets of water remain upon him even after he has bathed.
The bodily functions remain steady, the mind stays fixed upon a single object with an unwavering nature, and the opening and closing of the eyes occur regularly;
yet these may be deceptive signs. However, five other signs never fail to precede death.
His garments become soiled, his garlands wither, sweat is released from his armpits, a foul odor pervades his body, and the son of the gods finds no pleasure in his own seat.
Thus, this world of sentient beings—arising, abiding, and passing away—has been established by the Blessed One within three groups.
The three groups are:
the group fixed in rightness, the group fixed in falsity, and the group that is unfixed.
Furthermore, among those, the ones fixed in the rightness and the falsity [of their destiny] are the noble ones and those who have committed the immediate transgressions. // 44 //
"What is rightness (*samyaktva*)?

That which is the complete abandonment of attachment, the complete abandonment of hatred, the complete abandonment of delusion, and the complete abandonment of all afflictions—this is called rightness," so says the Sūtra.
Who are the noble ones (*ārya*)?
Those in whom the untainted path has arisen are called "Noble Ones" (*ārya*), because they have gone far away from evil states due to their attainment of the acquisition of ultimate dissociation.

For these are "fixed in rightness" (*samyaktva-niyata*) because they are certain to reach the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśakṣaya*). But why are those who have attained the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*)—who are also necessarily destined for final nirvana—not fixed in rightness?
For they might also become fixed in falsity (*mithyātva*).
Furthermore, they are not fixed in rightness by a restriction of time, as are those such as the "seven-times-at-most" (saptakṛtvaḥ-parama) and others.
What is wrongness (mithyātva)? Hells, hungry ghosts, and animals—this is called wrongness.
In that regard, those who commit the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) are fixed in falsehood (*mithyātvaniyata*), because they are certain to go to hell.
It is established that those other than the fixed ones are unfixed (*aniyata*).
For it is in dependence upon conditions (*pratyaya*) that they partake of both [certainty and uncertainty], or partake of neither.
The world of sentient beings has been described; now the receptacle world must be discussed.
Regarding that, they maintain that the configuration of the receptacle world is as follows:
at the bottom is a circle of wind, sixteen hundred thousand [yojanas] in thickness and immeasurable in extent. (45)
They maintain that the arrangement of the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system is as follows:

resting upon space, there arises at the bottom a circle of wind produced by the sovereign power of the karma of all sentient beings; its depth is sixteen hundred thousand yojanas, and its circumference is incalculable, being so firm that even one struck by a thunderbolt cannot break it.
Above that,
the circle of water is eleven thousand and twenty thousand [yojanas] in depth;
the term "circle" continues to apply here as well.
Upon that wind-circle, clouds arise through the karma of sentient beings and rain down in streams as thick as axles;
this becomes the water-circle.
Its extent is eleven hundred thousand yojanas in height and twenty thousand yojanas in depth.
How is it that those waters do not flow sideways?
Through the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings.
For some say that just as food and drink that have been eaten and drunk do not fall into the receptacle for digested food (pakvāśaya) while still undigested, so it is here.
According to other schools, they are maintained by the wind according to the principle of a granary.
Furthermore, those waters, being churned by winds produced by the power of the karma of sentient beings, become gold on the surface through the process of curdling like boiled milk.
That becomes the water-maṇḍala eight hundred thousand [yojanas] in height; thereafter, what remains becomes gold. (46)
Furthermore, what remains?
Three hundred and twenty thousand [yojanas].
That golden earth exists above the waters. Thus has been stated the height of the water and gold spheres.
The circles of water and gold are twelve hundred thousand [yojanas] in extent, and three thousand four hundred and fifty [yojanas] across.
For these two are equal in extent;
however, when calculated as threefold on all sides by way of circumference, it becomes threefold: thirty-six hundred thousand, ten thousand, and three hundred and fifty yojanas.
And as for that golden mandala of the earth situated above the waters, there [are the mountains] Meru, Yugandhara,
Īśādhāra, Khadiraka, and likewise Sudarśana-giri. 48.
Aśvakarṇa, Vinataka, and Nimindhara—
these are the eight great mountains established upon the golden circle;
in their center is Sumeru.
The remaining [mountains] are situated surrounding Sumeru.
Of that [central mass], which is encircled by seven other mountain ramparts, the outermost mountain is Mount Nimindhara. Beyond that—
Beyond that are the four continents;
furthermore, from them...
Outside is the Cakravāḍa mountain range,
by which the four-continent world is encircled.
Of these, however, seven are made of gold, and that [last one] is made of iron. //46//
The seven mountains beginning with Yugandhara are made of gold; Cakravāḍa is made of iron;
and Meru consists of four jewels:
it is made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, respectively, on its four sides.
And by the power of whichever side of Sumeru is composed of a certain substance, the sky in that direction appears to be of that same color.
They describe this side facing Jambudvīpa as being made of beryl;
because of the radiance of that [side], the sky here appears to be made of beryl.
Now, how does their formation occur?
Once again, streams of water fall upon the golden earth.
Those waters, containing various types of seeds, are churned by winds distinguished by many kinds of power, and they transform them into their respective species.
Furthermore, they transform in such a way that they act as conditions through non-conjunction when a specific effect of a different nature arises;
indeed, it is not like the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the Sāṃkhyas.
And what is the transformation of the Sāṃkhyas?
"The transformation of phenomena belonging to a persisting substance consists in the cessation of one phenomenon and the appearance of another phenomenon.
What is the fault here?
For that very substratum (dharmin) does not exist, upon whose persistence the transformation of phenomena could be imagined.
And who says that the substratum (dharmin) is something other than its attributes (dharmas)?
For transformation is merely the alteration of state of that very substance.
Even so, this is incorrect.
"What is unreasonable here?
To say 'this is that very thing, yet this is not thus'—this is a logic never before seen."
Furthermore, once gold and the other substances have thus come into being, they are gathered together and formed into heaps by winds impelled by the power of karma;
these become the mountains and the continents.
Furthermore, those mountains, from Sumeru down to the Cakravāḍa range, are submerged eighty thousand [yojanas] in the water;
there is water eighty thousand yojanas above the golden earth, and they are submerged therein.
Above the water, Mount Meru rises further by eighty thousand [yojanas]. //50//
Thus, the height of Meru is six million yojanas;
there is a reduction by half for each of the eight [surrounding mountains] above the water.
As high as Sumeru is, Yugandhara is half that, forty thousand yojanas.

Half of that is Īśādhara; in this manner, a reduction by half for each subsequent mountain is to be understood, until the Cakravāḍa, which is three hundred and twelve and a half yojanas, being half the height of Nimindhara.
They are equal in both height and thickness;
the meaning is that their thickness or width is exactly as great as their total height above the water.
There are seven cool lakes between these mountains,
and the seven intervals between these mountains ending with Nimindhara are called the "Seven Cool Lakes," which are filled with water endowed with eight qualities.
For that water is cool, sweet, light, soft, clear, odorless, and does not irritate the throat when drunk, nor does it distress the stomach once swallowed.
And among those again, the first consists of eighty thousand [verses]. //51//
The first Sītā [sea] is between Sumeru and Yugandhara;
it is eighty thousand yojanas in width,
and this is the inner ocean.
For there are two oceans: the inner and the outer.
Then, that inner ocean of Śītā is threefold in extent compared to its side.
Its width is said to be eighty thousand *yojanas*.

When measured along the shore of Yugandhara, it is three times as long on its sides, amounting to two hundred and forty thousand *yojanas*. The other Śītā rivers are each half the size of the preceding one;
the distance between Yugandhara and Īṣādhāra is the second Śītā, which is half the size of the first, measuring forty thousand *yojanas*.
Then, by half again, the third [lake] is formed; in this manner, the subsequent cold lakes are each half the size of the preceding one, until the seventh cold lake is seven hundred and fifty leagues.
However, their length has not been fully enumerated because it extends and spreads out over a vast distance.
The remainder is the outer great ocean. // 52 //
What remains?
It is the space between Nimindhara and Cakravāḍa;
for that is the outer great ocean, filled with salt water.
In its extent, it is indeed three hundred twenty-two thousand yojanas;
there, on the four sides of Mount Sumeru, are the four continents.
Therein,
Jambūdvīpa is two thousand [yojanas] on each of its three sides and is shaped like a cart.
Its three sides are each two thousand [yojanas], and its shape is like that of a cart.

In its center, upon a ground made of gold, the Diamond Throne (*vajrāsana*) has been manifested, sitting upon which all Bodhisattvas produce the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*). No other physical basis or location is capable of sustaining it.
Its fourth side, however, is three and a half yojanas;
for this very reason, it has the shape of a cart.
Pūrvavideha is like a half-moon.
To the east of here, on the side of Sumeru, lies the continent of Pūrvavideha;
it is formed in the shape of a half-moon.
As for its measurement,
three of its sides are each two thousand yojanas, just like those of Jambūdvīpa.
One [side] is three hundred and fifty yojanas. // 54 //
The fourth side is three hundred and fifty *yojanas*.

Godānīya is seven thousand five hundred [yojanas] in circumference; on the western side of Sumeru from here lies the continent of Aparagodānīya, measuring seven thousand five hundred *yojanas* in total. It is circular, like the full moon.
The middle [continent] is two thousand five hundred [yojanas], and the middle of the middle is two thousand five hundred. Kuru is eight thousand [yojanas] and is square and level. (55)
Here, to the north of Sumeru, lies the continent of Uttarakuru;
it is eight thousand yojanas in total extent and is square,
like a prepared pedestal.
On all sides it is equal; just as one side is two thousand yojanas, so too are the others, not exceeding that by even the slightest amount.
And whatever the shape of the continent, such is the shape of the faces of the humans there.
Indeed, in the intervals between those continents, intermediate islands have come into existence.
As to what they are and how many there are, he says:
Dehas, Videhas, Kurus, Kauravas, Cāmaras, and Avaracāmaras.
There are eight intermediate islands: Gāṭhā and Uttaramantrin. // 56 //
Among them, Deha and Videha are the satellites of Pūrvavideha;
Kuru and Kaurava are those of Uttarakuru;
and Gāṭha and Uttaramantrin are those of Aparagodānīya.
Cāmara and Avara are the two [regions] of Jambūdvīpa;
all are inhabited by humans,
though others say one is inhabited by rākṣasas.
To the north of here, beyond the nine Kīṭa mountains, lies the Himavat; specifically,

in this very Jambūdvīpa, to the north of it, there are three Black Mountains (Kṛṣṇaparvata), and having crossed those, there are another three, and again three more— beyond these nine Kīṭa mountains stands the Himavat mountain.
Then:
"Beyond that, but before Gandhamādana, there is a lake fifty [yojanas] in width and length. (57)
Beyond that Himavat mountain and before Gandhamādana lies the lake named Anavatapta, from which four rivers flow: the Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, the Śītā, and the Vakṣu.
Its width is fifty yojanas and its length is fifty yojanas;
it is filled with water endowed with the eight qualities.

And it is difficult for humans who lack supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to traverse. Right there, the Jambū tree has grown, whose fruits are sweet and delicious; because of its sovereignty, this [continent] is known as Jambūdvīpa, or it is called Jambūdvīpa by virtue of those fruits.
In what location are the hells situated, and what is their extent? Twenty thousand [yojanas] below, at that same distance, lies Avīci.

Indeed, twenty thousand yojanas beneath this very Jambūdvīpa is the great hell Avīci, which is exactly twenty thousand yojanas in both depth and breadth; thus, its lower surface is forty thousand yojanas from here.
It is called Avīci because suffering is uninterrupted;
in the other hells, suffering is intermittent. For example, in Saṃjīva, when the bodies of beings have been cut, pierced, and crushed, cool winds blow and restore those beings to life once more;
for this very reason, it is called Saṃjīva.
Others say it is called Avīci because there is no "interval" (vīci) of happiness within it.
In other [hells] as well, there is no pleasant feeling that is a result of karmic maturation (vipāka), though pleasant feelings that are outflowing results (naiḥṣyandika) are not excluded.
Above that are the seven hells;
above Avīci, these seven hells are situated one above the other:
Pratāpana, Tāpana, Mahāraurava, Raurava, Saṃghāta, Kālasūtra, and Saṃjīva.
Others say they are on the sides of Avīci; furthermore, all eight of them have sixteen secondary hells (utsada). //58//
For it was said by the Blessed One:
"Thus these eight hells have been described as difficult to escape; they are filled with those of fierce deeds, and each has sixteen secondary hells."
It has four walls and four gates, divided into sections and blackened; it is surrounded by iron ramparts and barred with iron.
"And the ground of heated iron, blazing and endowed with heat,
stands split open for hundreds of many yojanas by its radiance.
What are the sixteen secondary hells?
The Kukūla, the Kuṇapa, the Kṣuramārga and so forth, and the River—
each of these has four secondary hells (utsada) at its gates in the four directions.

There is the *kukūla* (hot embers) hell, knee-deep, wherein when those beings set down their feet, their skin, flesh, and blood are consumed; yet when they lift their feet, the skin, flesh, and blood grow back once more.

There is the *kuṇapa* (corpse) hell, which is a mire of excrement, where creatures called *nyaṅkuṭas* dwell—entirely white with black heads and needle-like mouths—who pierce those beings even to the bone.

There is a great path strewn with razor edges, where, as those beings walk upon it, their skin, flesh, and blood are sliced away as soon as a foot is set down, as described previously. There is the Forest of Sword-leaves (*asipattravana*), where sharp swords fall and hack at the limbs and members of those beings, while black and brindled dogs devour them.
There is the Forest of Iron Silk-cotton Trees (*ayaḥśālmalīvana*), which has sharp thorns sixteen finger-breadths long.
As those beings climb up, the thorns turn downward and pierce their bodies; as they descend, the thorns turn upward.
Furthermore, iron-beaked crows repeatedly pluck out their eyes and devour them.
These three—the Path of Razors and the others—are grouped together as one because they share the common characteristic of being struck by weapons.

The fourth protrusion is the river Vaitaraṇī, filled with boiling caustic water; in it those beings, being driven back from both banks by men with swords, spears, and javelins in their hands, are steamed and cooked as they go upward, and they are steamed and cooked as they go downward or across.
It is, for example, like sesame seeds, rice grains, and so forth, in a large cauldron filled with much water and placed over a fire;
indeed, it has arisen as a moat surrounding the Great Hell.
These four secondary hells (utsada) are said to be sixteen by way of their division according to the directions.
They are called *utsada* because they are places of excessive torment;
for those who have fallen into the hells are tormented further within these. Others say that they are called *utsada* because beings sink down into them after being confined in the hells.
From one question, another arises:
Are those guardians of hell reckoned as sentient beings, or not?
Some say: "No."
How, then, do they move? By the karma of sentient beings, like the seed-wind at the beginning of the cosmic evolution.
As for what was said by the Venerable Dharmasubhūti:
“Those who are prone to anger, performers of cruel deeds, and those who delight in evil, and who rejoice in the suffering of others—they are born as Yama-rākṣasas.
These Yama-rākṣasas mentioned here are those who, having been instructed by Yama, cast sentient beings into the hells; they are not, however, those who act as the actual torturers.
Some say they are reckoned as sentient beings.
Where, then, is the ripening of that karma?
It is in those very same hells. For there is room for the ripening of those who commit the immediate transgressions; what obstacle could there be for them there?
How is it that they are not burned by fire?
Surely it is because the fire has its limits established by their karma,
or because of the cessation of a particular class of beings.
These, first of all, are called the eight great hot hells.
The other eight, beginning with Arbuda, are cold. // 56 //
There are eight other cold hells, namely:
Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma.
These names correspond to the bodily distortions and vocal cries of those beings who are afflicted by intense cold.
They too are situated horizontally beneath this very Jambūdvīpa, below the great hells.
[Question: How can there be space for the Avīci and other hells beneath this much of Jambūdvīpa?
[Answer: For the continents are broad at the bottom, like a heap of grain.
For this very reason, the great ocean slopes gradually downward.
Thus, these sixteen hells are all produced through the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings;
whereas the individual hells are produced by the respective karmas of many sentient beings, or of two, or even of one.
Their divisions are of many kinds, and their location is indefinite, being in rivers, mountains, desert regions, or elsewhere, because they exist below [the earth].
Such, then, is the arrangement of the receptacle-worlds of the hells.
Animals range over land, water, and the air;
it is said that their primary abode is the great ocean, from which they have spread elsewhere.
Yama is the king of the pretas.
His royal capital, which is their primary abode, is located five hundred yojanas beneath Jambūdvīpa; from there they spread out elsewhere.
Some pretas possess great supernatural power and bear a splendor like that of the gods.
The rest is as in the *Pretāvadāna*.
Now, upon what are these two, the moon and the sun, established?
Upon the wind.
The winds in the atmosphere, produced by the sovereign power of the collective karma of all sentient beings, revolve around Mount Sumeru like whirlpools;
likewise, the moon, the sun, and the stars move above it.
How far distant from here are the moon and the sun?
The moon and sun move at a height equal to half of Mount Meru, which is the same as the summit of Mount Yugandhara; what is their size?
Respectively,
they are fifty and one hundred yojanas;
the measure of the lunar disk is fifty yojanas.
The measurement of the solar disk is fifty-one;
that is to say, fifty-one.
Among the celestial palaces of the stars, the smallest measurement is one *krośa*.
Beneath the solar chariot, on its exterior, a fiery crystal sphere has been produced, which provides heat and illumination;
beneath the lunar chariot, there is a watery sphere, cool and radiant.
These exist, as appropriate, for the sake of benefiting or harming the vision, bodies, fruits, flowers, crops, and medicinal herbs of living beings through their respective karmas.
In a single system of four continents, one moon and one sun perform their functions.
But do the suns in the four continents perform their functions simultaneously?
He says: no.
What then?
At those [locations], midnight, sunset, midday, and sunrise occur simultaneously. (60)
When it is midnight in Uttarakuru, then it is sunset in Pūrvavideha, midday in Jambūdvīpa, and sunrise in Godānīya. This same logic should be applied to the other continents as well.
It is by means of the sun’s varying courses here that there is an increase or decrease in the length of nights and days.
Furthermore, in that regard, on the ninth day of the final fortnight of the second month of the rainy season, the night increases.
During the second month of the rains, Bhādrapada, on the ninth day of the second fortnight, the night increases.
But during the fourth month of the winter season, it decreases.
That very [day] decreases again in the fourth month of the winter season; "on the ninth of the final [fortnight]" is understood [from the context].
This refers to the ninth day of the second fortnight of the month of Phālguna.
From the reversal of the day. //61//
When the night increases, then the day decreases;
when the night decreases, then the day increases.
By what measure does it increase?
The increase of night and day occurs by moments (*lava*); that is, the night increases moment by moment, or the day does so.
And those decreases and increases occur respectively.
When the sun moves to the south or north:
when the sun goes to the southern side of Jambūdvīpa, there is an increase in the night; when it goes to the north, there is an increase in the day.
At the beginning of the bright fortnight, the orb of the moon is seen incomplete.
What is the cause of that?
It is the observation of the moon as incomplete due to its proximity to the sun, caused by its own shadow. //62//
For when the lunar mansion moves near the solar mansion, it is said that the solar rays fall upon that mansion;

consequently, a shadow falling on the opposite side makes the disk appear incomplete—such is the explanation in the *Prājñapti*. The former masters maintain that the manner of movement is such that sometimes only half of the mansion is visible.
Now, which beings inhabit these celestial palaces of the sun and other luminaries?
They are the gods belonging to the Realm of the Four Great Kings.
Are these their only abodes?
These belong to those who dwell in celestial palaces (vimāna);
for those who dwell on the earth, however, they consist of the terraces of Mount Sumeru and so forth.
And how many terraces does it have, or how large are they?
It has four terraces, each separated by ten thousand [yojanas];
one is situated at a height of ten thousand yojanas.

In this manner, up to the fourth [ring], half of Mount Sumeru is covered by them; and from that [mountain], they extend outward respectively by sixteen thousand, eight thousand, four thousand, and two thousand [yojanas]. (63)
The first terrace extends sixteen thousand yojanas from Sumeru;
the second, eight; the third, four; and the fourth, two.
On these dwell the Karoṭapāṇis, the Mālādhāras, and the Sadāmadas.
The Mahārājika gods dwell on the first terrace;
on the second terrace dwell the yakṣas named Karoṭapāṇi;
on the third dwell the Mālādhāras, and on the fourth the Sadāmadās and Sadāmattas.
All these belong to the retinue of the Four Great Kings;
however, on the fourth [level], the four Great Kings themselves reside there along with their attendants.
Therefore, that level is called the "Devas belonging to the Retinue of the Great Kings."
Just as it is with the gods of the Four Great Kings on the terraces, so it is likewise on the seven mountain ranges.
On the Yugandhara and other mountains, there are their villages and towns;
for this very reason, this class of gods is the most extensive of all.
The Thirty-three gods dwell on the summit of Meru;
now, how large is the summit of Meru? It measures eighty thousand [yojanas] on each side.
Each side [of the mountain] is eighty thousand [yojanas], just as it is below;
others, however, say that each direction is twenty thousand [yojanas].
It has four sides corresponding to the four directions;
each side is twenty thousand yojanas, and its total circumference is eighty thousand.
And of that...
In the intermediate directions, there are four peaks inhabited by Vajrapāṇis. // 65 //
The intermediate directions from the summit of Sumeru are its corners;
in them, four peaks rise up measuring five hundred yojanas, in which yakṣas named Vajrapāṇis dwell.
And of that summit of Meru...
In the center, with sides of two thousand five hundred [yojanas] and a height of one and a half yojanas,
is the city named Sudarśana, made of gold, with a variegated and soft surface.
In the center of the base of Mount Sumeru is the city named Sudarśana; each of its sides is two thousand five hundred yojanas in length, and it is one and a half yojanas in height.
Its wall is made of gold, and its ground is variegated with one hundred and one kinds of precious minerals.

That surface of the ground is as soft to the touch as cotton wool, sinking and rising when the foot is set down or lifted; it is the royal capital of Śakra, the lord of the gods. Therein stands the Vaijayanta palace, measuring two hundred and fifty yojanas on each side.

In the center of the city is the palace of Śakra, the lord of the gods, named Vaijayanta. By its perfection of arrangements and locations of various jewels, it puts to shame the majesty and splendor of all other dwellings;
it measures two hundred and fifty yojanas on each side.
Such, then, is the delightfulness of the city.
Furthermore, on the outside,
it is adorned with Caitraratha, Pāruṣya, Miśra, and Nandana groves.
For outside that city, on its four sides, there are four parks and so forth, which are the sporting grounds of the gods:
the Caitraratha park, the Pāruṣyaka, the Miśrakāvana, and the Nandana forest.
By these, that city is adorned on the outside.
Between these, at a distance of twenty yojanas in each of the four directions, are excellent grounds (*subhūmi*).

On all four sides of these gardens, there are four excellent grounds separated by twenty yojanas; these are indeed places of recreation for the gods, which spread their splendor as if in mutual competition with one another.
They are located right outside the city on its flanks.
Pārijāta is in the northeast, and Sudharmā is in the southwest.
The *kovidāra* tree named Pārijāta is the locus for the supreme delight of sensual pleasure for the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Its root extends five *yojanas* into the ground, its height is one hundred *yojanas*,
and it stands with its branches, leaves, and foliage spreading out fifty *yojanas*.
Indeed, when it is in full bloom, its fragrance wafts for a hundred yojanas with the wind and fifty yojanas against the wind.
This is reasonable in the case of the windward direction;
but how is it so against the wind?
Some say this was said with reference to the fact that [the fragrance] does not pass beyond the trees;
for indeed, wind does not blow against its own direction.
However, one must acknowledge that the excellence of that fragrance's power is such that even when obstructed by divine, gentle breezes, it continues to produce a succession of further fragrances.
However, because its commencement is progressively weaker and weaker, the continuum is very quickly severed; for this reason, it does not extend over such a great distance.
Furthermore, does this continuum of the fragrance of flowers proceed as something supported by its own primary elements (*svabhūta*), or is it produced as wind that has been perfumed?
There is no fixed rule on this matter.
For the Teacher’s intention applies to both cases.
As for that which was said by the Blessed One:
"The fragrance of flowers does not go against the wind, nor does that of roots, tagara, or sandalwood."

"But the fragrance of the virtuous goes against the wind; the true person pervades all directions"—this was said with reference to the fragrance of human flowers, for that is well-known in the world, yet it does not possess such power. However, the Mahīśāsakas recite: "The fragrance wafts a hundred yojanas with the wind, and fifty yojanas against the wind."
In the southwestern quarter is the divine assembly hall named Sudharmā, wherein the gods sit and deliberate upon what ought and ought not to be done.
Such, then, is the arrangement of the receptacle-world of the Thirty-three [Gods].
Above that, in the celestial palaces (vimāna), dwell the gods;
above the Thirty-three (tridaśa) gods, the gods are established in celestial palaces.
These are the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, as well as those previously mentioned beginning with the Brahmakāyika gods, who occupy sixteen distinct abodes.
Thus, these twenty-two classes of gods are summarized here, for whose [residential] receptacles a foundation is discerned. However, six of them are enjoyers of sensual pleasures;
among them, six classes of gods belonging to the realm of desire enjoy sensual pleasures, but not the remaining ones.
Namely, from the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods;
they, moreover, engage in sexual union through physical coupling, embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing. (66)
For those dwelling on the earth-bound levels, such as the Cāturmahārājakāyika and Trāyastriṃśa gods, sexual union occurs through physical coupling, just as it does among humans. However, for them,
the cessation of passion occurs through the emission of wind, as they lack seminal fluid.
Sexual union occurs through embracing for the Yāma gods, because their feverish passion is dispelled by mere embracing;
through the grasping of hands for the Tuṣita gods; through laughter for the Nirmāṇarati gods; and through a glance for the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods.
For all [of these], however, it occurs through the union of the couple (*dvaṃdvasamāpatti*).
The Vaibhāṣikas, however, state that the measurement of time is explained in the Prajñapti:
"To the extent that the objects are more intense, to that same extent the passion is also more intense."
In the lap of whichever god or goddess a divine boy or a divine girl is born, he becomes their son and she their daughter. To what extent is he born?
As a child resembling five years up to ten years of age.
They are born respectively among these six classes of gods,
and they grow very quickly.
They are complete, clothed, and possessed of beautiful forms. //70//
The gods of the form realm (rūpāvacara) are born with complete bodies, clothed in garments.
All gods speak the noble language (āryabhāṣā).
These [characteristics] are to be understood as applying here within the desire realm (kāmadhātu).

There are three types of rebirths in the realm of desire: the gods of the desire realm together with humans. How so? There are beings for whom sensual pleasures are present, who exercise mastery and control over those present pleasures.
Namely, humans and certain gods;
these consist of four classes of gods.
There are beings who have created desires, who, having created those desires, exercise mastery and control over them.
For example, there are the gods who delight in emanations (*nirmāṇarati*).

There are beings who have desires created by others and exercise mastery and control over those desires created by others; for example, the gods who wield power over the creations of others (*paranirmitavaśavartin*).

These three are called the "births in the realm of desire" because they consist of the enjoyment of things as they arise, the enjoyment of things created by oneself according to one's wish, and the enjoyment of things created by others according to one's wish.
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), however, there are three "births in happiness," which consist of the nine levels of the first three dhyānas. (71)
The nine stages within the three dhyānas constitute the three blissful rebirths (*sukhopapatti*).
For those gods dwell happily for a long duration, abiding in the bliss born of seclusion, the bliss born of meditative concentration, the bliss of joy, and the bliss free from joy;
therefore, because they are free from suffering and possess long-lasting happiness, these are called blissful rebirths, or *sukhopapattis*.
However, regarding rebirth in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), since joy and bliss (*prītisukha*) are absent there, its status as a "rebirth in bliss" (*sukhopapatti*) must be reconsidered.

As for these twenty-two abodes of the gods that have been mentioned, how far is each higher station removed from the one below it? It is not easy to calculate all of this by means of a reckoning in *yojanas*.
Moreover,
from each respective place, the distance upward is equal to the distance downward from that place.
Starting from Jambūdvīpa, whatever higher place there is, the distance from that place up to the lower Jambūdvīpa is equal to the distance from that [lower] place to another higher place.
For example, the fourth terrace, which is the primary abode of the four Great Kings, is forty thousand yojanas from here.
As far as Jambūdvīpa is below that, so far above it is the abode of the Tridaśas. As far as Jambūdvīpa is below that, so far above it is the abode of the Yāmas.
And as far as Jambūdvīpa is below that, so far above it is the abode of the Tuṣitas.
Having thus detailed everything in full sequence, from the Sudarśanas down to Jambūdvīpa below, the abode of the Akaniṣṭhas is that far above.
Beyond that, there is no further abode.
Precisely because they are the most senior (*jyeṣṭha*), they are called Akaniṣṭhas.
Others say [the highest level] is Aghaniṣṭhā;
for "agha" is said to be matter (rūpa) residing in the mind, and this [level] is the limit of that alone.

But do those born in lower stations go to the higher celestial palaces (vimāna) and see them? There is no vision of what is above for them, except through supernatural power (ṛddhi) or by relying on another. //72//
Either by means of supernatural power they might go from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven to the Yāma heaven,
or else they might be led there by another, such as one possessing supernatural power, or by a deity belonging to that very place.
The same applies to the remaining [faculties].
However, one may see a being born in a higher realm who has come [to this world], but not one belonging to a higher element (dhātu) nor a higher stage (bhūmi).
Just as one cannot touch a tangible object [from a lower stage] because it is not within one's range, so too for these.

For this very reason, they do not come with their own bodies; rather, they come by means of a transformation-body belonging to a lower level. According to other schools, one sees them as if they were right here, according to one's wish.
Now, what is the size of these celestial palaces (vimāna) of the Yāma gods and others?
According to some, [the size of the palaces] of the four [classes of gods] extends as far as the summit of Mount Sumeru;
according to others, it doubles at each successive level. However, the first dhyāna [palace] is as large as a world-system of four continents.
The second is as large as a small thousandfold world-system;
the third is as large as a medium two-thousandfold world-system;
the fourth is as large as a great three-thousandfold world-system—so say some.
The first [three] have the dimensions of a thousand [worlds] and so forth,
while others maintain that the fourth is immeasurable.
Now, what is this "small" (cūḍika) thousandfold world system, and what are the two-thousandfold and three-thousandfold [world systems]?
A small chiliocosm (sāhasracūḍika) is considered to consist of a thousand four-continent worlds, moons, suns, Mount Merus, gods of the desire realm, and Brahma-worlds. //73//
A thousand Jambūdvīpas, Pūrvavidehas, Aparagodānīyas, and Uttarakurus; a thousand suns, moons, and Sumerus; a thousand [realms] of the Cāturmahārājakāyika gods up to the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods;
and a thousand Brahmā-worlds—this is called a small chiliocosm (sāhasracūḍika lokadhātu).
A thousand of those is a second-order intermediate world system (*dvisāhasro madhyamo lokadhātuḥ*).

A thousand of those small world systems (*cūḍikā lokadhātavaḥ*) is a second-order intermediate world system. A thousand of those is a third-order great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasro lokadhātuḥ*).
A thousand of those two-thousandfold world systems constitutes a great trichiliocosm; for this entire system undergoes destruction and formation simultaneously. (74)
It dissolves equally and evolves equally;
for "evolution" (vivarta) is indeed "origination" (saṃbhava), as will be explained later.
Now, is it the case that just as there is a difference in the dimensions of the receptacle worlds, there is likewise a difference in the dimensions of the sentient beings dwelling therein?
He said, "There is.
In that regard, first of all,
the inhabitants of Jambudvīpa are four and a half cubits in height.
The humans of Jambūdvīpa are three and a half cubits in height, though some are four cubits; those known as Pūrva, Godā, and Uttara increase by double each time. (75)
The humans of Pūrvavideha, Godānīya, and Uttarakuru have bodies measuring eight, sixteen, and thirty-two cubits respectively.
For the gods of the desire realm, their bodies increase by a quarter-krośa (pāda) up to one and a half krośas.

A *pāda* is a fourth part of a *krośa*. The body of the gods of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*) is that much; those of the Thirty-three (*trāyastriṃśa*) are two *pādas*; those of the Yāma gods are three; those of the Tuṣita gods are four; those of the Nirmāṇarati gods are five; and those of the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods are one and a half *krośas*. Among the gods of the Form Realm (*rūpin*), however, at the beginning it is half a *yojana*.
Among the gods possessing form, in the first station, those of the Brahmakāyika class have bodies measuring only half a yojana; beyond that, they increase. //76//
There is an increase by half a *yojana* at each of the three stages: one *yojana* for the Brahmapurohitas, one and a half for the Mahābrahmans, and two *yojanas* for the Parīttābhas.
Above the Parīttābhas, however, the physical basis increases further.
They double in size successively, except for the Anabhrakas, which are three yojanas less.
The Apramāṇābhas have four yojanas;
the Ābhāsvaras have eight.
In this manner, by doubling the increase, it reaches sixty-four for the Śubhakṛtsnas.
The body of the Anabhrakas is twice that [of the Śuddhāvāsas], less three *yojanas*, amounting to one hundred and twenty-five *yojanas*.
Beyond that, for the Puṇyaprasavas and so forth, up to the Akaniṣṭhas, the body doubles again and again until it reaches sixteen thousand *yojanas* for the Akaniṣṭhas.
Since their physical dimensions differ in this way, is there also a difference in their lifespan?
He said:
"The lifespan among the Kurus is one thousand years."
In two [continents], it is reduced by half and half again.

Having excluded half and half again from two continents, the lifespan of the inhabitants of Godānīya is five hundred years, and that of the inhabitants of Pūrvavideha is two hundred and fifty years; here [in Jambudvīpa], it is indefinite.
In Jambūdvīpa, there is no fixed limit to the lifespan; sometimes it is longer, and sometimes it is shorter.
At the end, however, it is ten years.
"Abda" means a year (saṃvatsara).
At the end, the lifespan decreases until it becomes ten years; at the beginning, it was immeasurable.
From the beginning, the lifespan of humans at the start of the first eon is immeasurable;
it cannot be measured by numbers such as thousands and so forth.
Having spoken regarding humans, that concerning the gods must now be stated.
And since it is possible to speak [of their lifespan] only after establishing what constitutes a day and night, that very [measure] is established for them:
"Fifty human years constitute one day and night for the inhabitants of the desire realm who dwell below."
Fifty human years constitute one day and night for the Cāturmahārājakāyika gods, the lowest among the deities of the desire realm;
by that reckoning, their lifespan is five hundred years. (76)
By that day and night, thirty such nights constitute a month for them, and twelve such months a year; their lifespan is five hundred divine years.
For those in the higher realms, both are doubled successively:
for the gods of the higher realms, both the day-and-night and the lifespan are each doubled in succession.
How so?
One hundred human years constitute a single day and night for the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
With that day and night, their lifespan is one thousand divine years.
In this manner, for the Yāma gods and the others in successive order,
two, four, eight, and sixteen hundred human years constitute one night and day.
By that measure of night and day, their lifespan is two, four, eight, and sixteen thousand divine years respectively.
Since there is no sun or moon above Mount Yugandhara, how is the distinction between day and night established for the gods, or how is the function of illumination performed?

[The distinction is made] by the closing and opening of flowers, like the white water-lily (*kumuda*), and by the singing and silence of birds, as well as by the departure and arrival of torpor (*middha*). As for the function of illumination, it is performed by their own radiance.

The lifespan of those possessed of desire has been stated. Now, for those with form (rūpin), there is no day and night; rather, their lifespan is measured in kalpas equal in number to their own physical stature.

For those material beings whose physical basis is half a *yojana*, their lifespan is half a *kalpa*; for those whose [basis] is one *yojana*, it is one *kalpa*. Thus, for whichever being the physical basis is of such-and-such number of *yojanas*, their lifespan is of that many *kalpas*, up to the Akaniṣṭha gods, whose measure of lifespan is sixteen thousand *kalpas*.
In the formless realm, the lifespan increases by twenty thousand aeons at each successive level.
In the sphere of infinite space, the measure of the lifespan is twenty thousand aeons;
in the sphere of infinite consciousness, it is twenty thousand more than that.
In the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), their lifespan is twenty thousand *kalpas* more than that;
at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), it is twenty thousand *kalpas* more than that.
Thus, their lifespans are respectively twenty, forty, sixty, and eighty thousand *kalpas*.

Which kind of eon (*kalpa*) should be understood here? Is it an intermediate eon (*antarakalpa*), or an eon of dissolution (*saṃvartakalpa*), or an eon of evolution (*vivarttakalpa*), or a great eon (*mahākalpa*)?
A great eon begins from the Parīttābha heaven and extends for half [an eon] below that.
From the class of the Parīttābha gods upward, the lifespan should be understood as being measured in great eons (mahākalpa).
Below that, the lifespan of Mahābrahmā and the others is established by taking half of a great eon and treating it as a full eon.
How is this done?

The period during which the world evolves for twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*), the period during which it remains evolved for twenty intermediate kalpas, and the period during which it dissolves for twenty intermediate kalpas— these sixty intermediate kalpas are said to constitute one and a half kalpas for Mahābrahmā.
Having established this, the measure of their lifespan is stated by treating forty intermediate kalpas as one kalpa, which constitutes half of a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*).
The lifespan in the happy destinies has been explained;
now it must be stated for the miserable destinies.
Regarding that, first:
The days and nights in the six [hells] beginning with Saṃjīva are equal, respectively, to the lifespans of the gods of the desire realm.
It should be understood that the days and nights in the six hells are equal, respectively, to the lifespans stated for the six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm.
In Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, and Tāpana,
their lifespan is like that of the gods of the desire realm.
Now, by means of their own days and nights, their lifespan should be understood to be exactly the same as that of the six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm, respectively. How so?
For that which is the measure of the lifespan of the Cāturmahārājakāyika gods is one day and night in the Saṃjīva great hell.
Thus, by that reckoning, five hundred years there constitute one year.
The lifespan of the Trāyastriṃśa gods is equal to one day and night in the Kālasūtra great hell;
by that day and night, the measure of lifespan there is one thousand years.

In this same manner, it should be applied accordingly to the others as well, up to the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods. With a day and night equal to their lifespan, the lifespan in the Tāpana hell is sixteen thousand years. In the Pratāpana great hell, the lifespan is half an intermediate kalpa (antarakalpa).
In Avīci, it lasts for an intermediate kalpa; however, for animals, there is no fixed limit, though at most it is as follows.
The maximum lifespan of animals is one *kalpa*; for animals, it is an intermediate *kalpa*. This, moreover, refers to the *nāgas* such as Nanda, Upananda, Aśvatara, and others.
For the Blessed One said: "O monks, these eight *nāgas* are great *nāgas*, who endure for a *kalpa* and support the earth," and so forth.
For the pretas, [the lifespan] is five hundred months. // 83 //
That which is one month for humans is one day and night for the hungry ghosts (preta);
by that day and night, their lifespan is five hundred years.
What is the measure of the lifespan in the cold hells?
The lifespan in Arbuda is such that it would be exhausted by removing a single sesame seed every hundred years from a wagon-load;
the lifespans in the subsequent hells increase twentyfold respectively.
The Blessed One described their lifespan by means of a mere analogy: "Monks, suppose there were here a Magadhan sesame-cart of twenty khārīs, filled to the brim with sesame seeds.

If someone were to remove a single sesame seed from it at the end of every hundred years, monks, this Magadhan sesame-cart of twenty khārīs would more quickly reach exhaustion and depletion by such a process."
"But I do not say that there is an end to the lifespan of those born in Arbuda.
Monks, just as twenty Arbudas make one Nirarbuda, and so on in detail, monks, just as twenty Padmas make one Mahāpadma.
[In this way, for these long-lived beings, is there premature death before their lifespan is completed, or is there not?]
Everywhere except in Kuru, there is untimely death; however, among the beings of Uttarakuru, whose lifespan is fixed, they necessarily live out their full life span,
whereas this is not necessarily the case for others.

However, for many individuals, there is no death in the interim [antarābhava], such as for a Bodhisattva residing in Tuṣita who is bound to only one more birth; for a sentient being in their final existence; for those prophesied by a Jina; for one who has become a Jina; for those who follow through faith or through the Dharma; for a Bodhisattva or a Cakravartin king; and for those who are pregnant with them, and so forth.

The dimensions of the abodes and bodies have been stated in terms of *yojanas*, and the lifespan has been stated in terms of years; however, the measurement of those two has not yet been explained, so it must be told. Furthermore, since the arrangement of all these is diverse, their limit must also be stated. To provide a systematic exposition of them, the initial sequence is now begun.
The atom (*paramāṇu*), the syllable (*akṣara*), and the moment (*kṣaṇa*) are the limits of matter (*rūpa*), name (*nāman*), and time (*adhvan*) respectively;
the atom is the limit of matter as it is being diminished.
The limit of time is called a moment (*kṣaṇa*), and the limit of a name is a syllable (*akṣara*), such as "go" (cow). Furthermore, what is the measure of a moment?

It is the duration required for a phenomenon (*dharma*) to acquire its own-being when all conditions are complete; or, in the case of a moving phenomenon, it is the time it takes to travel from one atom (*paramāṇu*) to another.
The Abhidharmikas maintain that sixty-five moments pass in the mere time it takes for a strong man to snap his fingers;
[these are] the atom (paramāṇu) and the minute particle (aṇu). (85)
Iron-dust, water-jet, hare-dust, sheep-dust, cow-dust, aperture-dust, nit, louse-egg, barley-corn, and a finger-joint should be known to increase sevenfold each time. (86)
This sequence, beginning with the atom (*paramāṇu*), should be understood as increasing sevenfold at each step:
seven atoms make one minute particle (*aṇu*);
seven minute particles make one iron-dust particle (*loharajaḥ*).

Seven of those [water-dust particles] make one *abraja*; seven of those make one *śaśarajas* (hare-dust); seven of those make one *eḍakarajas* (ram-dust); seven of those make one *gorajas* (cow-dust); seven of those make one *vātāyanacchidrarajas* (window-opening dust);
and seven of those make one *likṣā*, which means a nit produced from that.
Seven *yūkās* make one *yava*;

seven *yavas* make one finger-joint (*aṅgulīparva*). It is well known that three joints constitute a finger, so this has not been explicitly stated. Twenty-four fingers measured across the side make one *hasta*; four *hastas* [make one *dhanus*].
The meaning is "by the span of a bow.
Five hundred of these [bow-lengths] are considered a *krośa*, as well as a forest retreat (*araṇya*). (87)
Five hundred bows make one *krośa*.
A distance of one *krośa* from a village or similar settlement is considered "wilderness" (*araṇya*).
They say that eight of those [krośas] make a *yojana*.
The measurement of a *yojana* has been stated;
now the [measurement] of a year is being described.
Furthermore, one hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* [make one lava].
One hundred and twenty moments (kṣaṇas) constitute one tatkṣaṇa;
sixty of those, in turn, constitute one lava.
Sixty *tatkṣaṇas* are called a *lava*; each subsequent unit is thirty times the length of the preceding one. (88)
Three *muhūrtas* constitute a day-and-night (*ahorātra*), and thirty *lavas* constitute a *muhūrta*. Thirty *muhūrtas* constitute a day-and-night;
however, sometimes the night is longer, sometimes shorter, and sometimes equal [to the day].
Thirty days and nights constitute a month;
twelve months, together with the omitted nights, constitute a year.
There are four months of winter, four of summer, and four of the rainy season; these twelve months, together with the omitted nights (*ūnarātra*), constitute a year.
For in one year, six omitted nights are subtracted.
How is this done?
"When one and a half months of winter, summer, and the rainy season have passed, and half a month remains, the wise subtract an intercalary day (*ūnarātra*).
The measurement of the year has been stated; now the [measurement] of an eon (*kalpa*) must be explained.
The eon (kalpa) is remembered as being of many kinds. //86//
The intermediate kalpa, the kalpa of dissolution, the kalpa of evolution, and the great kalpa.
In that regard, first,
the eon of dissolution (*saṃvartakalpa*) consists in the destruction of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*),
beginning from the time when beings no longer exist in the hells until the complete exhaustion of the receptacle world.
For there are two types of destruction:
destruction by way of the realms of existence and destruction by way of the elements.
Furthermore, there are two types of destruction.

There occurs a time when beings pass away from the hells but are no longer reborn there; this is the beginning of the aeon of dissolution (*saṃvartakalpa*). This consists of both the dissolution of sentient beings (*sattvasaṃvartanī*) and the dissolution of the receptacle world (*bhājanasaṃvartanī*).
When this world has remained evolved for twenty intermediate kalpas, it should be said that it has emerged [from dissolution].
When it will undergo dissolution for twenty intermediate kalpas, it should be said that it has entered [into dissolution].
When not even a single sentient being remains in the hells, by this much this world has become dissolved.
Namely, by the destruction of the hells. At that time, one who dies with karma certain to be experienced in hell is cast into the hells of other world-systems.
The same should be said for the destruction of the animal realm and the destruction of the hungry ghost realm.
Animals dwelling in the great ocean are the first to be destroyed.

But those who are companions to humans remain together with them at that time when a certain being among humans, by himself and without a teacher, attains through the very nature of things the first dhyāna; having emerged from that state, he utters these words: "O how happy is this joy and bliss born of seclusion!"
"Tranquil indeed is this joy and bliss born of seclusion!
Having heard that sound, other beings also enter into meditative attainment;
and having passed away, they are reborn in the Brahma-world.
When not even a single being remains in Jambudvīpa, to this extent this world is said to have been destroyed, namely by the destruction of Jambudvīpa.
In the same way, the destructions of Pūrvavideha, Godānīya, and Uttarakuru are to be described.
When not even a single being remains among humans, to this extent this world is said to have been destroyed, namely by the destruction of the human realm.
The inhabitants of Uttarakuru, however, having passed away, are reborn among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*),

because they lack detachment (*vairāgya*) there. Likewise, even among the gods of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*), having attained the first dhyāna, they are reborn in the Brahma world (*brahmaloka*).
When not even a single sentient being remains there, to that extent this world has dissolved—namely, by the dissolution of the realm of the Four Great Kings.
In the same manner, the dissolutions up to the realm of the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods should be described.
When not even a single sentient being remains among the gods of the desire realm, to that extent this world has dissolved—namely, by the dissolution of the desire realm.

In the Brahma-world, a certain being, having attained the second dhyāna—which arises through the very nature of things—emerges from it and speaks these words: "O how happy is the joy and bliss born of concentration! O how peaceful is the joy and bliss born of concentration!
Hearing that sound, other beings also enter that state, and upon passing away, they are reborn among the Ābhāsvara gods.

When not even a single sentient being remains in the Brahma-world, to this extent this world has dissolved— namely, by the dissolution of sentient beings. Then, while the receptacle world is empty and the karma of sentient beings that projected it has been exhausted, seven suns appear from the very vicinity of this world and, appearing in succession, burn the earth and Mount Sumeru until nothing remains.
Therefore, from that very [fire], a flame cast by the wind goes forth, burning the empty Brahmā palace;
and that flame should be understood as belonging to that very level (bhūmi),
for calamities of a different nature do not spread.
Because it arises in connection with that, it is therefore called "that.

For the fire belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) connects with the fire belonging to the form realm (rūpāvacara). This should be understood accordingly for the other modes of destruction (saṃvartanī) as well.
This period of time extends from the moment beings cease to be reborn in the hells until the complete destruction of the receptacle world.
The period of evolution (vivartakalpa) lasts from the primordial wind until the manifestation of the hells.
The period from the first wind until the appearance of sentient beings in the hells is called the *vivartakalpa* (the aeon of evolution).

For when the world has thus dissolved, it remains for a long time as nothing but empty space, until once again, through the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings, very gentle winds begin to stir in the sky as the preliminary signs of the receptacle worlds.
At that time, it should be said that the period during which this world has remained dissolved for twenty intermediate kalpas has passed;
and it should be said that the period during which it will evolve for twenty intermediate kalpas has arrived.
Then, those winds increasing give rise to the wind-mandala as previously described.

Then, gradually, according to the sequence and method previously described, everything comes into being: the water-mandala, the great earth made of gold, the continents, Sumeru and the other mountains;
first, however, the Brahma-palace arises, then down to that of the Yama gods, and finally the wind-mandala and the rest.
To this extent, this world becomes evolved, namely, by means of the evolution of the receptacle-world (*bhājana-vivartanī*).
Then, a certain being, having passed away from the Ābhāsvara heaven, is reborn in the empty Brahmā-palace.
Other beings as well, having passed away from there, are reborn among the Brahmapurohitas.

Then they are reborn among the gods of the Brahma-realm, up to those of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations; gradually, they are reborn in Uttarakuru, Godānīya, Pūrvavideha, and Jambudvīpa, as well as among the hungry ghosts, animals, and in the hells.
For this is the natural law: that which was last to dissolve is the first to re-form.
When even a single sentient being has appeared in the hells, then that period of twenty intermediate kalpas during which this world evolves is completed;
and that period of twenty intermediate kalpas during which the evolved world shall remain is commenced.
An intermediate kalpa lasts from the time [beings have] immeasurable lifespans until they have a lifespan of ten years.
During the evolution of the world, nineteen intermediate kalpas pass while human beings have immeasurable lifespans,
as their lives gradually decrease until they reach a lifespan of ten years.
This is the first intermediate aeon (*antarakalpa*) of those [aeons] that have evolved and remain;
after that, there are eighteen other aeons consisting of periods of increase and decrease. (61)
Therefore, there are eighteen subsequent intermediate kalpas consisting of increases and decreases.
How so? From those beings with a lifespan of ten years, as they undergo an increase, their lifespan gradually reaches eighty thousand years.
Furthermore, as they continue to decline, their lifespan becomes ten years;
thus ends the second intermediate kalpa.
In this manner, it continues up to the eighteenth.
There is one period of increase, the twentieth intermediate kalpa, which is an increase; likewise, there is a decrease,
from humans with a lifespan of ten years up to those with a lifespan of eighty thousand years.
Now, to what extent do these increases proceed?

They reach as far as a lifespan of eighty thousand years; they do not increase beyond that. And the duration of the increase and decrease of all other intermediate kalpas is exactly the same as the duration of the decrease of the first and the increase of the last; thus, they are equal in time.
All these come to pass;
thus this world, having evolved, remains for twenty kalpas. //62//
By this method of intermediate kalpas, this world remains evolved for twenty intermediate kalpas;
for as long a time as it remains evolved, for that same length of time it undergoes evolution, and likewise it remains dissolved and undergoes dissolution for an equal duration.
For twenty intermediate kalpas it evolves, for twenty it dissolves, and for twenty it remains dissolved.
Although at that time neither the periods of increase nor decrease occur, the duration is nonetheless calculated as equal.

Among those, in one intermediate kalpa the receptacle worlds are formed; in nineteen intermediate kalpas they are populated; in one intermediate kalpa the receptacle worlds are destroyed; and in nineteen [intermediate kalpas they remain destroyed].
They become empty.
These four sets of twenty intermediate kalpas constitute eighty [intermediate kalpas];
those eighty indeed constitute one great kalpa (mahākalpa).
This is the measure of a great eon (mahākalpa).
What is the intrinsic nature of an eon?
Its intrinsic nature consists of the five aggregates.
As for what is said, "Buddhahood is attained after three incalculable eons (kalpa)," which eons are these? They are precisely those great eons (mahākalpa) that have been described.
That arises from three incalculable eons. // 93 //
Buddhahood is attained in three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
[Question: Since there is no end to what is "incalculable," how can it be said again that there are three?
This should not be understood in that way. What then?
A *muktaka-sūtra* is recited: "An *asaṃkhyeya* consists of sixty place-values.
Which are these sixty?
For one is the first place, being alone and without a second; ten ones constitute the second;
and ten tens constitute a hundred, which is the third.
Ten hundreds are a thousand;
ten thousands are a prabheda; ten prabhedas are a lakṣa.
Ten lakṣas are an atilakṣa; ten atilakṣas are a kauṭi; ten kauṭis are a madhya.
Ten middles are an ayuta; ten ayutas are a mahāyuta; ten mahāyutas are a niyuta.
Ten *niyutas* make a *mahāniyuta*;
ten *mahāniyutas* make a *prayuta*; ten *prayutas* make a *mahāprayuta*.
Ten *mahāprayuta*s are a *kaṅkara*; ten *kaṅkara*s are a *mahākaṅkara*; ten *mahākaṅkara*s are a *visvara*.
Ten *visvara* are a *mahāvisvara*; ten *mahāvisvara* are an *akṣobhya*;
ten *akṣobhya* are a *mahākṣobhya*.
Ten mahākṣobhyas are a vivāha; ten vivāhas are a mahāvivāha; ten mahāvivāhas are an utsaṅga.
Ten utsaṅgas are a mahotsaṅga; ten mahotsaṅgas are a vāhana;
ten vāhanas are a mahāvāhana.
Ten mahāvāhanas are a *tiṭibha*; ten *tiṭibhas* are a *mahātiṭibha*; ten *mahātiṭibhas* are a *hetu*.
Ten *hetu* are a *mahāhetu*; ten *mahāhetu* are a *karabha*;
ten *karabha* are a *mahākarabha*.
Ten *mahākarabhas* are an *indra*;
ten *indras* are a *mahendra*; ten *mahendras* are a *samāpta*.
Ten *samāptas* are a *mahāsamāpta*; ten *mahāsamāptas* are a *gati*;
ten *gatīs* are a *mahāgati*.
Ten *mahāgati*s are one *nimbarajas*; ten *nimbaraja*s are one *mahānimbarajas*;
ten *mahānimbaraja*s are one *mudrā*.
Ten mudrās are a mahāmudrā; ten mahāmudrās are a bala; ten balas are a mahābala.
Ten mahābalas are a saṃjñā; ten saṃjñās are a mahāsaṃjñā;
ten mahāsaṃjñās are a vibhūta.
Ten *vibhūtas* are a *mahāvibhūta*;
ten *mahāvibhūtas* are a *balākṣa*; ten *balākṣas* are a *mahābalākṣa*.
Ten *mahābalākṣas* are an *asaṃkhya*;
eight [of these] constitute a *madhya-vistṛta*.
Thus, the eons that have reached the numerical value situated at the sixtieth place among these are called "incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*).
Then, having turned back, they are counted again;
thus, they are called "three incalculables" (*asaṃkhyeya*),
but it is not that they cannot be calculated at all.
[But indeed, it is only through the great length of time that Bodhisattvas who have made their vows awaken to enlightenment. Will this be so?

For by means of a vast accumulation of merit and wisdom, through the six perfections, and by hundreds of thousands of various difficult practices over three incalculable eons, they awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.]
As for the Bodhisattvas:
[even though there is an opportunity for liberation through other means as well], for what purpose do they undertake such great effort?
They undertake such great effort for the sake of others, thinking: "How might I also be able to rescue others from the great flood of suffering?"
What is their own interest (svārtha) through the interest of others?
That very interest of others is their own interest, because it is what they desire.
[Now this will be believed.]
This is indeed difficult to believe for those who are self-centered and devoid of compassion;

yet it is precisely this that is believed by the compassionate. Just as some are observed here who, having practiced cruelty, take delight in the misfortune of others even when there is no benefit to themselves, so too it is possible to conceive that there are those who, having practiced compassion, find joy in acting for the welfare of others even when there is no benefit to themselves.

Just as those who are ignorant of the characteristics of the conditioned, through the power of habituation, fix their self-attachment upon conditioned formations that are not the self and thereby undergo sufferings for its sake; so too, it is possible that by the power of further habituation, they turn away their self-attachment from those [formations],
increase their concern for others, and thereby undergo sufferings for the sake of others.
For it is indeed another spiritual lineage (*gotrāntara*) that arises in such a manner that one suffers through the suffering of others and rejoices in their happiness, rather than through one's own;
they do not perceive any other self-interest.
And regarding this, it has been said:
The inferior person seeks happiness for their own continuum by whatever means possible;
the middling person seeks only the cessation of suffering, not happiness, because that [happiness] is a locus of suffering;
the superior person seeks the happiness of others at the cost of sufferings belonging to their own continuum.
"And because he brings about the absolute cessation of suffering, he is one who suffers for the sake of that suffering.
Furthermore, do Buddhas arise during the period of increase (*utkarṣa*) or during the period of decrease (*apakarṣa*)?
For their appearance occurs during the period of decrease, down until [the lifespan is] one hundred years.

When the lifespan of living beings has begun to decline from eighty thousand years down to the point where humans have a lifespan of one hundred years, it is during this interval that Buddhas arise. Why not during a period of increase? Because at that time, sentient beings are difficult to stir with a sense of spiritual urgency. And why not when the lifespan is below one hundred years?

For at that time, the five corruptions (*kaṣāya*) become prevalent, namely: the corruption of lifespan, the corruption of the eon, the corruption of afflictions, the corruption of views, and the corruption of sentient beings.
Because, at the lowest point of the decline, lifespan and the other factors are inferior and have become like dregs, they are called "corruptions."
For by two [extremes], there is respectively the ruin of life and the ruin of the requisites for living;
by two others, there is the ruin of the side of wholesome qualities,
due to the pursuit of devotion to sensual pleasures and self-mortification, or alternatively, due to the sides of householders and renunciants.

By one [cause], there is the ruin of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), due to the loss of stature, beauty, health, strength, growth, mindfulness, vigor, and fortitude. Now, at what time do the Pratyekabuddhas arise?
For Pratyekabuddhas, it occurs during both the period of increase and the period of decrease.
For there are two kinds of Pratyekabuddhas: those who move in groups (*vargacārin*) and those who are like the rhinoceros horn (*khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa*).
In this context, those who were formerly disciples and now move in groups are called Pratyekajinas;
others maintain that there are also those who were formerly ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
These are those who, having previously produced the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) elsewhere, fully awaken to the path by themselves in this life.

For they recite this ancient account: "On a mountain, it is said, five hundred ascetics were performing arduous austerities, until a monkey who had lived with a pratyekabuddha arrived and, by demonstrating that [pratyekabuddha's] deportment, they realized the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
And those who are noble ones would not perform arduous austerities.
Furthermore, those who dwell alone are like the rhinoceros horn; among those Pratyekabuddhas, the rhinoceros-like one has been a practitioner for a succession of a hundred eons. (64)
Having practiced the accumulations for enlightenment for a hundred great eons, one becomes like the horn of a rhinoceros;
because they awaken by themselves without instruction, they are called Pratyekabuddhas.
For they discipline themselves alone, and not others.
What, then, is the reason for this?
It is not that they are incapable of teaching the Dharma, because they have attained the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*);
moreover, it is possible for them to teach the Dharma even by recollecting the teachings of previous Buddhas.
Nor are they devoid of compassion,
because they manifest supernatural powers for the sake of favoring sentient beings;
nor is it because sentient beings lack the capacity [to benefit].
For there do exist those who have become free from passion by means of the mundane path.
What then?

Due to their lack of zeal and their inclination [toward lower goals] resulting from the force of prior habituation, they are unable to exert themselves for the sake of others in order to grasp the profound Dharma.
For it is difficult to lead back against the current those beings who flow with the current;
and because he fears distraction and social contact, [the Buddha] avoids the consequence of attracting a multitude. Now, when do wheel-turning monarchs arise?
The arising of a wheel-turning monarch does not occur below eighty thousand [years].
When the lifespan of humans is immeasurable, up to eighty thousand years, there is the appearance of wheel-turning kings (cakravartin), but not below that;
for those whose lifespan is less than that are not fit vessels for such abundance of grain.
They are called "wheel-turners" because it is their nature to rule a kingdom by means of a wheel.
Furthermore, they are of four kinds:
those possessing wheels of gold, silver, copper, and iron;
for them, there exist wheels made of gold, silver, copper, and iron.
Among these, the first is the best, the second is the next best, the third is middling, and the fourth is the lowest; they follow this descending order. //65//
Those whose wheel is made of iron are lords of one, two, three, or four continents;
he whose [wheel] is made of copper is lord of two.
He whose [palace] is made of silver is the lord of three [continents];
he whose is made of gold is the sovereign of the four continents.
This is the explanation according to the Prajñapti.

In the Sūtra, however, because only the primary [wheel] is mentioned, there is only one golden wheel: "When, for a consecrated Kṣatriya king, on that very fifteenth day of the Poṣadha, having bathed his head and observed the Poṣadha fast, while he has ascended to the upper terrace of his palace and is surrounded by a host of ministers, a Wheel-Treasure appears in the eastern direction— having a thousand spokes, with a hub and a rim, complete in all its aspects, not made by a skilled smith, divine, and entirely of gold."
"He becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) king.
And thus these universal monarchs arise;
however, two do not appear simultaneously, just as with the Buddhas.

It is said in the Sūtra: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that two Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas, should arise in the world simultaneously, neither before nor after the other; such a case does not exist. This is the only possibility: that a single Tathāgata [arises].
Just as it is with a Tathāgata, so it is with universal monarchs (cakravartin)."
This must be considered here: is the "world" intended here the single trichiliocosm (trisāhasramahāsāhasra-lokadhātu), or rather all world-systems?
Some maintain that Buddhas do not arise elsewhere.
What is the reason?
Lest there be an obstruction to the Blessed One’s power;
for the Blessed One alone is capable everywhere.
Where one Buddha would not be able to discipline those to be trained, there another would likewise not be able to do so.

And it is said in the Sūtra: "Śāriputra, if someone were to approach you and ask: 'Is there now any ascetic or brahmin who is equal to the ascetic Gautama, that is, in regard to perfect enlightenment?'—being thus questioned, how would you answer?"

"Venerable Sir, if someone were to approach me and ask this, being thus questioned, I would answer him: 'At present, there is no ascetic or brahmin who is equal to the Blessed One with respect to perfect enlightenment. Why is that?

I have heard this directly from the presence of the Blessed One and have received it directly from him: it is impossible, it is out of the question, that two Tathāgatas should arise in the world simultaneously, one before the other; such a thing cannot occur.'"
Thus [it is said].

As for that which was stated by the Blessed One in the *Brahmasūtra*: "As far as the trichiliocosm, this world-system, so far does it abide under my control"—this teaching is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*).
What is the intention here? It is because he surveys [the world] without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
However, with volitional effort, the range of the Buddhas' vision is infinite.
Other schools maintain that there are indeed Buddhas in other world-systems.
What is the reason?

For many are seen engaging together in the accumulations; yet it is not possible for many Buddhas to arise simultaneously in one place, nor is there any obstacle to their arising [elsewhere]. Therefore, they necessarily arise in other world-systems.

The world-systems are infinite; even if the Blessed One were to maintain his life-span for an entire eon, he would not be able to act in other infinite world-systems as he does here, let alone within the span of a human lifetime.
And how does the Buddha act here?
[He knows]: "This person has such a faculty; after such a time, in such a place, having encountered such a person, this fault..."
Because of the avoidance of this factor and the inclusion of this member, it is by means of this application that what has not arisen will arise, or what is incomplete will be brought to completion.

As for this sūtra cited here—"It is impossible, it is out of the question, that two Tathāgatas, neither before nor after, should arise in one world"—this very point must be deliberated upon: was this said with reference to a single world-system, or rather to all [world-systems]?

Furthermore, there would be no arising of even a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) in this world-system, because their simultaneous arising is prohibited, just as it is for Buddhas. If that [prohibition] is accepted, why is this not also accepted: "The arising of Buddhas in the world is a source of merit"?

If there were many [Tathāgatas] in many [worlds], there would be no fault; indeed, there would be the attainment of prosperity and the ultimate good for the majority of beings. Now, why is it that even in a single world two Tathāgatas do not arise simultaneously?
This is because there is no purpose [for them to arise] otherwise, and due to the power of their vows.
For Bodhisattvas make such a vow: "O, may I arise as a Buddha in a world that is blind and without a guide, to be a protector for those who are without a protector!
It is also for the sake of showing reverence and a sense of urgency.

For when there is but one Buddha, people revere him all the more, thinking, "Another such as he is difficult to find," and they hasten even more toward the practice of the teaching, thinking, "Lest we become leaderless once he has departed or entered final nirvana.
Now, how do these wheel-turning kings (cakravartins), conquering the earth with wheels made of gold and other materials, achieve victory?
Respectively, they conquer by being met in procession, by going themselves, by quarreling, or by weapons.
Of him who possesses the golden wheel, the minor kings (koṭarājānaḥ) come forth to meet him of their own accord.
"These territories of Your Majesty are prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and teeming with many people and inhabitants;
may Your Majesty govern them.
We shall be Your Majesty's attendants."
He whose wheel is made of silver goes to them himself, and afterwards they bow down before him. He whose wheel is made of copper goes to them and engages in a quarrel, and afterwards they bow down.
