He whose wheel is made of iron goes to them; they brandish weapons at one another, and afterwards they submit.
But all wheel-turning monarchs are free from violence. //66//
Even when conquering by means of weapons, killing does not occur; and having conquered, they establish sentient beings in the ten paths of wholesome action.
For this very reason, they are certain to be reborn among the gods.

It is stated in the Sūtra: "With the appearance of a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakravartin) in the world, there occurs the appearance of seven jewels in the world; namely, the wheel-jewel, the elephant-jewel, the horse-jewel, the gem-jewel, the woman-jewel, the householder-jewel, and the counselor-jewel.
How is it that elephants and the like, which are reckoned as sentient beings, are produced by the karma of another?

Indeed, no one is produced by means of another's [karma]. Rather, when a particular sentient being has accumulated karma that is conducive to a connection with him, once that [being] has arisen, it is that being's own karmas that produce him.
Is this alone the distinction of the Wheel-turning Kings from other kings?
There is also another distinction:
namely, that they possess the thirty-two marks of a great man, just as the Buddhas do;
however, in that regard—
The excellence of the Sage’s marks consists in their being well-placed, radiant, and complete.
The marks of the Buddhas are more excellently placed, more radiant, and more complete; this is their distinction.
Were the humans of the first eon indeed possessed of kings?
No, he says. What then?
In the beginning, beings were like those living on the shore;
the humans of the first eon were like those belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*).
As it is said in the Sūtra: "They were possessed of form, mind-made, complete with all major and minor limbs, unimpaired, and with all sense faculties intact."
"They were beautiful, abiding in their own radiance, traveling through the sky, feeding on joy, nourished by joy, long-lived, and they remained for a long duration.
Then, from an attachment to taste, [the decline began] gradually. (67)
Out of laziness, having made a store of food, they hired a field-guard with stipulations. While they were in such a state, the essence of the earth appeared, possessing a sweet taste like honey.
One among them, being of a greedy nature, smelled its fragrance, tasted its flavor, and ate it.
In the same way, other beings also did exactly so;
that was the beginning of solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
Through their habituation to that food, coarseness and heaviness entered their bodies, and their [supernatural] powers disappeared.

Then, when darkness had arisen, the sun and moon appeared. As they became greedy for the taste of that essence of the earth, it gradually disappeared and a crust of earth appeared; being greedy for that as well, even that disappeared.
The forest creeper appeared;
they became greedy for that as well, and it too vanished.
Then rice grew without being ploughed or sown, which they consumed.

Now, because that [food] had become coarse, for the sake of discharging its waste, the urinary and excremental passages appeared in sentient beings along with the female and male sexual organs, and their physical forms became differentiated.

As they looked at one another, having fallen prey to the crocodile of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) due to the force of past habituation, sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) arose, whereby they engaged in misconduct.
This was the beginning of the possession by the demon of sensual desire among those who possess lust.
And indeed, they used to bring in that rice in the evening for the sake of their evening meal, and in the morning for the sake of their morning meal.
Then, a certain being who was by nature indolent began to store it up;
and other beings also began to store it up.
When the sense of "mine" arose among them regarding that rice, the rice, once reaped and reaped, did not grow back again.
Thereupon, having divided the fields and developed attachment to their own portions, they began to seize what belonged to others.
This was the first beginning of theft.
To restrain them, they came together and appointed a certain distinguished man to protect the fields in exchange for a sixth share of the produce;

because he was the lord of the fields, the designation "Kṣatriya, Kṣatriya" arose for him. Because he was approved by the great body of people and gladdened the subjects, the designation "Mahāsaṃmata" (Greatly Approved) and "Rāja" (King) arose for him.
This was the beginning of the succession of kings.
Among them, those whose minds turned away from household life received the designation "brāhmaṇas.
Then, because a certain king, out of greed, failed to distribute [wealth] among beings, thievery became widespread among them; he then approached them with weapons.
Then others began to speak false words, saying, "We are not doers of such things.
Consequently, due to the increase in the paths of unwholesome action, there was a decline until the lifespan reached ten years. (68)
Thus, as the paths of action increase in this way, the lifespan of humans gradually diminishes until there arise humans with a ten-year lifespan.
Therefore, two factors are the root source of this entire flood of misfortune: attachment to savory tastes and laziness.
When humans have a ten-year lifespan, the intermediate kalpa reaches its conclusion.
How does it come about? He says: "The eon concludes through weapons, disease, and famine.
The departure of the intermediate eon occurs by means of these three.

By means of weapons, disease, and famine—at the time of the conclusion of the intermediate kalpa—human beings have a lifespan of ten years; they become stained by unrighteous passion, overcome by perverse greed, and enveloped by false teachings. Their malice reaches its peak, and upon seeing one another, a mind of intense hostility and a murderous intent arises within them.
It is just as when, for example, a deer-hunter sees a wild deer in the forest; whatever they seize, whether a piece of wood or a clod of earth, that appears to them as a sharp weapon.
They then deprive one another of life.
Furthermore, at the time of the world's dissolution, when the lifespan of humans is ten years, non-human beings release pestilence because of those very same faults.
For them, incurable diseases and other afflictions arise because of which they die.
Furthermore, when their lifespan is ten years, due to those very same faults, the gods do not release rain, whereby famine arises—namely, the *cañcu*, the *śvetāsthi*, and the *śalākāvṛtti*.
And how is it the *cañcu*?
For two reasons:
that which is now called *samavāya* was at that time called *cañca*; furthermore, a casket (*samudga*) is also called *cañca*.
And those humans, overcome by hunger and weakness, gather together and die; they then deposit seeds in the oceans for the sake of favoring future generations.
Therefore, that famine is called *cañcu*.
How is it "white bones" (*śvetāsthi*)?
It is due to two reasons.
For when those whose bodies are parched and withered pass away, their bones quickly become white; and those struck by hunger collect these white bones, boil them, and drink the broth.
How is there subsistence by means of a tally-stick (*śalākāvṛtti*)?
It is due to two reasons:
for those beings distribute food among their households by means of a tally-stick, thinking, "Today the master of the house shall eat;
tomorrow the mistress of the house," and so forth; and they extract grains from the crevices of the granaries using a stick.
They boil [the seeds] with plenty of water and drink them;
they describe it thus:

"Whoever has protected the abstention from taking life for even a single day, or has respectfully offered a single *harītakī* fruit or a communal alms-offering (*saṃghāya-kapiṇḍapāta*), shall [be spared] during those intermediate kalpas of weapons, disease, and famine."
"They do not arise.
Now, for how long do these [calamities of] weapons, disease, and famine occur for those beings?
For seven days, seven months, and seven years, respectively. (66)
The slaughter by weapons lasts for seven days;
the disease lasts for seven months and days;
and the famine lasts for seven years, months, and days—the word "and" (ca) serves the purpose of conjunction.
And at that time, in those two continents, there appear their counterparts:
malice reaches its peak, as do ugliness, weakness, hunger, and thirst.
As it has been said, "In this same way, it should be understood that the same applies to other modes of destruction (saṃvartanī) as appropriate."
Now, how many are these destructions? There are three destructions: by fire, by water, and by wind.
A *saṃvartanī* is so called because beings are destroyed together in a single meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) within it.
The destruction by fire occurs through seven suns; the destruction by water through rain-water; and the destruction by wind through the agitation of the wind.
And by those [flames], not even a subtle particle of the receptacles remains.
In this regard, however, some Tīrthakaras maintain that atoms are eternal and that they remain at that time.
Why do they hold such a view?
Let it not be that the manifestation of gross things occurs without a seed.
But has it not been stated that the wind produced by the karma of sentient beings, distinguished by its specific power, is the seed?
Or rather, the wind at the summit of the dissolution (saṃvartanī) will be its cause.
"The Mahīśāsakas recite in their Sūtra: 'Seeds are brought from other worlds by the wind.
Even so, they do not maintain that sprouts and the like arise from seeds and the like.
What then?"
From their own constituent parts, and those [parts] likewise from their own;
thus it continues down to the atoms.
What, then, is this capacity of seeds and the like toward sprouts and the like?
There is nothing else [involved] other than the drawing near of those atoms.
But what is the reason they assert this?
It is because arising from a heterogeneous cause is not logical.
Why is it not logical?
Because there would be no restriction;
however, this will not be the case due to the restriction of capacity.
It is like the production of sound or that which is born from ripening (*pākaja*).
For the property of a quality (*guṇadharma*) is indeed variegated, but a substance (*dravya*) is not so;
for it is observed that substances of a similar kind arise only from substances of a similar kind, just as a mat arises from *vīraṇa* grass and a cloth from threads.
This is untenable. What is untenable here? That which is unestablished is cited as a proof. What is unestablished here?
"The mat is different from the vīraṇa grass, and the cloth is different from the threads.
For it is those very same things, arranged in a particular way, that receive this or that designation, just like a row of ants.
How is this to be understood? Because a cloth is not perceived when there is a conjunction with a single thread.
For what obstacle could there be at that time to the perception of a cloth that already exists?
If it were not present in its entirety, there would be only a portion of the cloth here, not the cloth itself;
furthermore, the cloth would be a mere collection [of parts]. And what part of the cloth could there be that is distinct from the threads?

If [the perception of a cloth] were dependent on the conjunction with multiple substrates, then the cloth would either be perceived when in conjunction with only its fringe, or it would never be perceived at all;
this is because the middle and rear parts would not be in contact with the sense organ.
Furthermore, if there were a sequential contact with the parts, there would be no cognition of the parts by means of both sight and touch simultaneously.
Therefore, due to successive contact and the resulting determination of a whole, the cognition of that [whole] occurs only with respect to the parts, like a circle of fire (alātacakravat).
This is because it is impossible for a cloth to possess color and other qualities when its constituent threads have different colors, types, and actions.

Furthermore, if the cloth were to possess a variegated color and so forth, there would be the production of something heterogeneous; moreover, on the non-variegated side, the cloth would either not be seen at all or would be seen as variegated.
It is also highly extraordinary that action (*kriyā*) should likewise be manifold.
Furthermore, if there were a distinction between heat and light, it would be impossible for the forms and touches of fire-light to exist at its beginning, middle, and end.

Even though atoms are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), they are perceived as a whole—just as they initiate effects and as in the case of the eyes and other sense organs—and just as those suffering from ophthalmia perceive scattered hairs.
For them, a single hair, like an atom (*paramāṇu*), is beyond the senses.
Since the designation "atom" is applied only to form and the other [sensory objects], the destruction of the atom is established upon their destruction.
For the atom is a substance (*dravya*), and a substance is something other than form and the rest; thus, when those [form and so forth] are destroyed, its destruction is not established.

It is also illogical for these two to be distinct, since it cannot be determined by anyone that "these are earth, water, and fire" and "these are their qualities such as color (rūpa)," yet they are perceived through sight and touch. Furthermore, when wool, cotton, safflower, saffron, and the like are burned, the cognition of them ceases; therefore, the cognition of them must reside only in the specific variations of color and other qualities.
When a jar is produced through baking, its recognition occurs because of the similarity of its configuration (saṃsthāna), just as one recognizes a row [of people] despite individual changes.
For one who does not perceive the mark, there is an absence of full comprehension;
moreover, what regard can there be for the prattle of fools? Thus, let this non-refutation stand for now.
Now, which destruction has what as its limit?
The three dhyānas, beginning with the second, are their limits respectively. (100)
There are three limits of destruction.
For the destruction by fire, the second dhyāna is the limit; everything below it is consumed by fire.
For the destruction by water, the third dhyāna is the limit; everything below it is dissolved.
The fourth dhyāna is the summit of the destruction by wind; everything below it is dispersed.
For that which is above the destructive agent is called its "summit.
But what is the reason that the first, second, and third dhyānas are destroyed by fire, water, and wind respectively?
Because they share the characteristic of being defects,
in the first dhyāna, applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra) are the defects;
and because they cause the mind to burn, they are like fire.

In the second [dhyāna], joy (*prīti*) is the corruption; and because it makes the basis supple through its connection with pliancy (*prasrabdhi*), it is like water. For this very reason, it is stated in the Sūtra that in that [state] the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) ceases, due to the departure of all bodily rigidity.
In the third dhyāna, inhalation and exhalation (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*) [are the corruptions].
And those winds are indeed [the cause].
Thus, whatever internal corruption exists in a particular meditative attainment (*dhyāna-samāpatti*), there is a corresponding external [corruption] in the rebirth in that meditation.
[Why does the destruction by earth not occur?]
For it is the earth alone that is called the "receptacle"; within it, there is conflict with fire, water, and wind, but not with the earth itself.
Now, why is there no destruction by calamity in the fourth dhyāna?
Because there is no shaking in the fourth;
for the Blessed One has declared that the fourth dhyāna is unshakable because it is free from internal defects.
Therefore, since no external calamity occurs here, there is no destruction (saṃvartanī) here;
others say this is due to the power of the Śuddhāvāsa [deities],
for one cannot enter [from outside] nor depart elsewhere.
[Objection: In that case, the receptacle world of the fourth dhyāna would be eternal.
[Response: It is not eternal, because it arises and perishes together with the sentient beings [who inhabit it]. //101//
The fourth dhyāna is not connected to a single level;
rather,
its various locations are separated like stars.
Even there, this sentient being may be reborn or pass away together with his celestial mansion; thus, it possesses no permanence.
By what sequence, moreover, do these destructions occur?
First, for seven consecutive eons, they are destroyed by fire, being consumed by the heat of the seven suns.
Then,
immediately after the seven destructions by fire, there occurs a destruction by water.
When seven cycles of destruction by water have thus passed, there occurs another cycle of seven by fire;
in this sequence, after seven cycles of destruction by water have elapsed, there occurs a further cycle of seven by fire.
After that, there is the destruction by wind. //102//
Afterwards, there occurs one wind-destruction (*vāyu-saṃvartanī*).
What is the reason?

For just as there is a specific duration for the personal existences (*ātmabhāva*) of those beings due to the excellence of their meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), so too is there a specific duration for the receptacle-worlds (*bhājana-loka*); thus, these constitute fifty-six fire-destructions (*tejaḥ-saṃvartanī*).
There are seven destructions by water and one destruction by wind;
thus the *Prajñaptibhāṣya* is well-explained: "The lifespan of the Śubhakṛtsna gods is sixty-four kalpas. [And as it is said:
"Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause..."
"And their cessation— such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.
Thus ends the third treasury-location (kośasthāna), titled "Exposition of the World" (Lokanirdeśa), in the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya [of the venerable Vasubandhu].
Whatever merit there is herein: The Fourth Treasury Section.
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!
Now, as for this manifold variety of the world of sentient beings and the receptacle world that has been described, by what was it created?
Indeed, it was not created by anyone with deliberate intent;
rather,
it arose from sentient beings.
The variety of the world is born of karma.
[If it is born of karma, why is it that for sentient beings, through their karmas, saffron, sandalwood, and so forth arise as more delightful than their own bodies?

It is because the karmas of those sentient beings who perform mixed deeds are of such a nature that their physical bases arise as if they were wounds, while their enjoyments arise as delightful things serving as remedies for them.]
But for the gods who perform unmixed deeds, both [realms] are delightful.
What, then, is that action? He says:
"It is volition and what is produced by it.
It is stated in the Sūtra: "There are two actions: volitional action and action after having willed."
That which is performed after having intended, and that which is produced by volition—
these two types of action become three:
the actions of body, speech, and mind.
How is the classification of these actions established?
Is it by way of their basis, or rather by way of their intrinsic nature, or by way of their origination?
If it were by way of their basis, it would follow that there is only one type of action, namely bodily action.

Because all [actions] are dependent upon the body, if [action] were defined by its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would follow that there is only vocal action, since speech has the nature of action. If, however,
it were defined by its origination (*samutthāna*), it would follow that there is only mental action.
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that because all [three] arise from the mind,
the three [types of action] correspond respectively to the three causes.
Furthermore, in that regard:
Volition is mental action;
it should be understood that volition is mental karma, while the actions of speech and body arise from it. //1//
That which was described as "action consisting of volition" (*cetayitvā karma*)— generated by volition (*cetanā*)— should be understood as bodily and vocal action.
Furthermore, these two, bodily and vocal action, should each be understood to have the nature of both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) action.
In that regard,
however, bodily intimation is held to be shape.
Bodily intimation is the configuration of the body in such and such a way by the power of the mind.
Others say it is "motion," for they claim that bodily action belongs to that which is moving, not to that which is stationary.
To them it is said: It is not motion, because conditioned phenomena are momentary.
What is this so-called "moment" (kṣaṇa)? It is the acquisition of self-existence that perishes immediately thereafter.
That which possesses this [moment] is "momentary" (kṣaṇika).
It is like a stick.
For every conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta*) does not exist beyond the acquisition of its own self-nature; thus, it perishes at the very place where it was born.
Therefore, its transition to another location is illogical.
Therefore, motion is not bodily action.
This would indeed be so if the momentariness of everything were established;
know that this is already established.
Why?
Because that which is conditioned necessarily undergoes cessation. // 2 //
For the destruction of entities is indeed spontaneous.
What is the reason? For that which is an effect has a cause.
Destruction is non-existence.
And what can be done with that which is non-existent?
If this destruction were accidental, it would not occur even later for an entity that has just arisen, because the entity remains the same.
Now, if it has become otherwise,
it is not logical for that very same thing to undergo alteration.
For it is not logical that the very same thing should be distinct from itself.
Indeed, the destruction of wood and other such things through contact with fire and so forth is observed.
And there is no means of valid cognition more authoritative than what is observed.
Furthermore, the destruction of everything is not causeless. How, then, do you think that you perceive the destruction of wood and other things through contact with fire and so forth?
Furthermore, regarding their non-perception,
this must first be carefully considered:

is it that wood and other things are no longer seen because they have been destroyed by contact with fire, or rather, is it that they have perished of their own accord and others have not arisen in their place, and for that reason they are not seen?
Just as a lamp [is extinguished] through contact with wind, or the sound of a bell [ceases] through contact with the hand;
therefore, this matter is to be established by inference.
What, then, is the inference here?
It has already been stated that non-existence is not an effect.
Furthermore,
destruction would not have any cause; for if it were independent of a cause due to the commonality of being "causeless," it would follow that it is uncaused, just like arising.
Furthermore, since the destruction of momentary cognitions, sounds, and flames is observed to be spontaneous, it does not depend upon a cause.
As for the view that the destruction of a cognition occurs through another cognition, or the destruction of a sound through another sound—
that is incorrect.
Because two cognitions cannot coexist;
for it is not possible for doubt and certainty to coexist, nor for pleasure and pain, or attachment and aversion.
And when a dull cognition and sound arise immediately after a sharp cognition and sound, how could a dull factor of the same kind destroy that which is sharper?

And how is it with the two final [moments]? Even the view that destruction occurs for flames due to the absence of a cause for their persistence, or through the power of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), is also incorrect.
For non-existence cannot be a cause.
Furthermore, it is not possible for merit and demerit—the causes of arising and destruction—to gain or obstruct their activity moment by moment.

Furthermore, it is possible to construct such a conceptualization of causes for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*); therefore, enough with this dispute. Moreover, if the destruction of wood and other substances were caused by contact with fire and so forth, then in the case of qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*), the very cause that brings about the production of increasingly intense degrees of ripening would also be the destroyer.
Thus, the cause itself would be the destroyer.
How so?

When qualities produced by cooking (*pākaja*) arise from the connection of fodder and other materials with fire, or when even more cooked or most cooked states subsequently arise from that very same source or one similar to it, their destruction occurs; thus, the cause itself would be their destroyer, or something no different from the cause.

Furthermore, it is not logical that their existence should arise from that very same cause or from that very same condition, and yet their existence should arise again from that very same cause or from that very same condition.
While they might perhaps imagine a distinction in causes regarding different flames,
what kind of imagination could they possibly conceive when specific results of baking (*pākaja*) arise due to contact with alkali, snow, vinegar, sun, water, and earth?
If that is so, what do the conjunctions with fire do when water being boiled is diminished?

They increase the fire element (*tejodhātu*) by way of their power; through the power of which the mass of water becomes increasingly attenuated until, having reached extreme attenuation, it finally no longer continues its series. This is what the conjunctions with fire do in this case.

Therefore, there is no cause for the destruction of entities; rather, because they are inherently fragile, they perish by themselves. Perishing as soon as they have arisen, their momentary disintegration (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established. And due to this momentary disintegration, there is an absence of motion (*gatyabhāva*). The misconception of motion arises from the uninterrupted production [of moments] in different locations, like a flame in grass. Since motion does not exist, it is established that "bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) is shape (*saṃsthāna*)."

The Sautrāntikas maintain that shape does not exist as a substantial entity. For when a greater amount of color arises in one direction, it is designated as "long" form; and in relation to that same [color], when it is smaller, it is designated as "short."
If it is larger toward the four directions, it is square; if it is equal on all sides, it is circular. Thus it is for everything.

For example, just as a firebrand seen moving rapidly and continuously through successive points in one direction is perceived as "long," and when seen in all directions, it is perceived as a "circle"—
yet shape is certainly not a distinct category of entity—
if it were indeed such [a distinct entity],...

It would have to be grasped by two [faculties], for it is determined that "it is long" both after seeing it with the eye and after touching it with the body faculty; thus, its apprehension by two [senses] would follow.
Yet, there is no apprehension of the sense-sphere of form (rūpāyatana) by two [faculties].

Or, just as there is the perception of length and so forth in the tangible, let it be considered possible in the case of color as well. In that case, it is merely a memory arising from association with the tangible, and not a direct perception— just as, for example, upon seeing the form of fire, there arises a memory of its heat, or upon smelling the fragrance of a flower, a memory of its color.

It is logical that one thing may be remembered by another due to their invariable concomitance; however, no tactile sensation is restricted to any particular shape such that its remembrance would necessarily occur there.

If, on the other hand, the remembrance of a shape were to occur invariably even in the absence of a rule of association, then it should likewise occur for color; or else, like color, the remembrance of shape should also occur without necessity.
But this is not the case; it is illogical for there to be a recollection of the tangible [object] from this [cognition].
Alternatively, because many shapes are seen in a variegated carpet, it would follow that many [shapes] occupy a single location.
And that is untenable, just like [the case of] color.
Therefore, shape does not exist as a substantial entity.
Furthermore, whatever resistant form exists must necessarily be present in the atom.
Neither does that [shape] exist in the atom,
nor is shape— such as length and so forth— found in a single atom.
Therefore, the designation of "long" and so forth applies only when many atoms are arranged in such a manner.
Now, if it is thought that atoms of shape themselves, when arranged in such a manner, come to be designated as "long" and so forth—
this is merely a biased assertion, because those [atoms of shape] are unestablished.
For an accumulation of those things is only logical if their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) are established.
Furthermore, since the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the parts of shape is not established in the same way as that of color and so forth, how could there be an accumulation (*saṃcaya*) of them?

As for the fact that the color of earthen vessels is seen to be non-different while their shapes are different—has it not already been stated that just as the designation "long" and so forth is applied to colors arranged in a certain way, so too is the distinction of a line, a circle, and so forth perceived among ants and the like despite their lack of difference; the same applies to shape.

As for the fact that, when not perceiving color from a distance in the dark, people perceive the length and so forth of posts and other objects— it is because they have perceived the color itself there indistinctly and then construct the conceptualization of "long" and so on,
just like the conceptualization of a "line" or an "army.
And this is indeed the case.

When at some time a mere collection is seen as unmanifest, with its boundaries undetermined, such that one thinks, "What is this?"— now, having rejected both the movement and the shape of the body, what do the venerable Sautrāntikas designate as bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*)?
For they designate shape itself as bodily intimation.
But it is not, however, by way of a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*).
And when they designate that [action], how do they designate bodily action (*kāyakarma*)?
Bodily action is action based upon the body; it is the volition (*cetanā*) that leads the body here and there.
In the same way, vocal and mental actions should also be understood according to their respective applications.
As for what was stated—that "action is volition and having willed"—first there arises the volition of intention (*saṃkalpa-cetanā*), thinking, "I shall do such and such.
Having thus willed, there subsequently arises the volition of performance (*kriyā-cetanā*).
That by which the body is impelled is called "action after having willed" (*cetayitvā karma*).

If that were the case, then because of the absence of informative action (*vijñapti*), non-informative action (*avijñapti*) belonging to the desire realm would also not exist; thus, great faults would follow as consequences.
Furthermore, there will be counter-consequences to these consequences.

If non-informative action (*avijñapti*) were to arise from that very same specific volition designated as bodily action, it would follow the mind, like the non-informative action of one in meditative concentration (*samāhita-avijñapti*). But this will not be the case,
because there is a specific projection of that [non-informative action] by means of a specific volition.

Moreover, that informative intimation (vijñapti), being insentient, depends upon the power of the volition (cetanā) that projects it. However, the Vaibhāṣikas describe shape (saṃsthāna) as a substantial entity (dravya) and maintain that bodily intimation has shape as its essence.
Vocal intimation, however, is vocal sound. //3//
That sound which has speech as its intrinsic nature is itself vocal informative action (*vāgvijñapti*).
Non-informative action (*avijñapti*) has already been discussed;
the Sautrāntikas maintain that it, too, does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*).
Because it is merely the non-performance [of an action] after having undertaken [a vow],

and because even past great elements (*mahābhūta*) are designated based upon [them], and because those [past elements] lack an existing intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and are devoid of the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*).
"It exists," say the Vaibhāṣikas.
How is this known?
By the mention of three kinds of form, by the mention of the untainted (*anāsrava*) form, by the increase [of merit], and by the path of one who does not act, and so forth.
Three kinds of form are mentioned in the Sūtra.
“Form is comprised of form by way of three bases:
there is form that is visible and resistant;
there is form that is invisible and resistant.”
"There is form that is non-demonstrable and non-obstructive.
Furthermore, the Blessed One has spoken of untainted form:
"Which are the untainted dharmas?"
"In that form— whether past, future, or present— in which neither attraction nor aversion arises, and so on up to consciousness, these are called the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.
And apart from non-informative matter (avijñapti), there is no form that is both invisible and non-obstructive, nor is there any such form that is untainted.
Furthermore, increase has been taught:

"For a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family who is endowed with these seven bases of meritorious action consisting of material things, whether walking, sleeping, standing, or waking, [merit] increases constantly and continuously."
"In this way merit arises, indeed merit arises; thus it is with those [actions] not based on material things.
Furthermore, without the existence of non-informative matter (avijñapti), the increase of merit for one whose mind is directed elsewhere would not be logical.
Furthermore, for one who does not act himself but causes others to act, the paths of action would not be established if non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) did not exist;
for it is not logical that the informative matter of the command itself constitutes the fundamental path of action,
since that actual deed has not yet been performed.
"And even when that [unmanifest form] has been produced, because there is no difference in its intrinsic nature.
And it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, dharmas are an external sense-base, not included among the other eleven sense-bases, invisible, and non-obstructive";
however, it was not said that they are "formless" (arūpin).
In that case, what purpose would there be if non-informative form (avijñapti-rūpa), which is included within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), were not perceived?

Furthermore, the eightfold path would not exist without non-informative action (*avijñapti*), because for one who has entered meditative absorption (*samāpanna*), right speech, right action, and right livelihood would be impossible.
As for what was said: "For one who thus knows and thus sees, right view reaches fulfillment through cultivation, as do right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right..."
"His right speech, action, and livelihood have already become completely pure and cleansed.
This was said with reference to the detachment previously achieved through the mundane path.
Furthermore, the restraint of the Prātimokṣa would not exist if non-informative matter (avijñapti) were absent;
for after the formal undertaking [of the vows], there would be nothing by which one could be a monk or a nun even when the mind is directed elsewhere.
Furthermore, in the Sūtra, detachment (*virakti*) is described as a "bridge" because it acts as a barrier against immorality (*dauḥśīlya*).
Since that which does not exist cannot function as a bridge, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) must indeed exist.
On this point, the Sautrāntikas say: "Though this is much and though it is wonderful, it is not so.
What is the reason?"

Regarding what was stated, namely, "because of the mention of three kinds of form," the Yogācāras teach that for those in meditative absorption, a form which is the object of samādhi arises through the power of samādhi;
because it is not an object of the visual faculty, it is non-demonstrable (*anidarśana*).
Because it does not obstruct space, it is non-resistant.
Now, if this is thought:
"In that case, how is it matter (rūpa)?"
This is the same regarding non-informative [action].

As for what was said regarding the mention of "outflow-free form" (*anāsravarūpa*), the practitioners of yoga (*yogācārāḥ*) describe that very form produced by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as being outflow-free within an outflow-free concentration.
Others say it refers to the form of an Arhat and external form,
because they do not serve as a basis for the outflows (*āsrava*).
As for what was stated in the Sūtra: "Which are the contaminated (sāsrava) phenomena? They are precisely the eye, and so forth, up to visible forms," and so on;
in that context, they are called "contaminated" because they are not the antidote to the outflows (āsrava).
In that case, by way of alternation, that very same thing would be both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*).
What would follow?
There would be a confusion of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasaṃkara*).
Just as that [form] is with-outflows (*sāsrava*), so it is never without-outflows (*anāsrava*); what confusion could there be here?

Furthermore, if the sense-bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth were exclusively with-outflows, for what purpose would they have been specified in this sutra as: "those forms which are with-outflows and subject to grasping (*sopādānīya*), being objects of mental stubbornness and hypocrisy," and so on at length?

As for what was also stated, namely, "because of the mention of the increase of merit" and so forth, regarding that as well the former masters point out: "This is indeed the nature of things (*dharmatā*):

just as the gifts of donors are enjoyed, so too—due to the specific qualities and specific benefits of the recipients—the mental continuums (*saṃtati*) of the donors, even when their minds are directed elsewhere, having been permeated by the volition of giving directed toward them, undergo a subtle and specific transformation."
"By means of which they become capable of producing a much greater fruit in the future.
It was with this intention that it was said: "Merit indeed increases; merit indeed arises.
Now, if it is asked: "How can a transformation of another continuum be established for one whose mind is directed elsewhere, due to a specific change in a different continuum?"
This is the same regarding non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).

How, then, will a distinct factor (*dharmāntara*) called non-informative matter be established in one mental continuum (*saṃtāna*) on account of a specific change in another mental continuum? And how will it be in the case of the bases of meritorious action not involving material substrates (*nirupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*)?
[The answer is: Through the repeated practice of volition (*cetanā*) directed toward that object, those [volitions] continue to follow along even in dreams.

But for those who maintain the doctrine of non-informative action (*avijñapti*), how could there be non-informative action in the case of offerings not consisting of material things (*niraupadhika*), where no informative action (*vijñapti*) exists?
Others say that even in the case of material offerings, it arises from the repeated practice of volition directed toward that object.
If so, then what about that which was stated in the Sūtra: "If a monk who is fierce, virtuous, and of excellent character, having consumed alms-food..."?

"In this regard, when one dwells having personally realized and attained the concentration of mind (cetaḥsamādhi) with the body, an immeasurable outflow of merit, an outflow of the wholesome, and a stream of the taste of happiness is to be expected for the donor, the patron who provides the cause for that"— at that time,
what specific volition (cetanā-viśeṣa) does the giver possess?
Therefore, it is logical that it is precisely a specific transformation of the continuum [that constitutes the result].
As for what was also asked—"How will the paths of action (karmapatha) be established for one who causes another to act?"—in that regard they explain as follows:

through the instigation of that [act], because of the specific injury inflicted upon others, a subtle and specific transformation of the continuum (saṃtatipariṇāmaviśeṣa) arises in the agent, by virtue of which the continuum becomes capable of producing even more abundant results in the future. This is also true when one acts oneself.
And this same principle should be understood to apply to one who performs an action at the point of the completion of its fruit;
that specific transformation of the continuum (saṃtatipariṇāmaviśeṣa) is designated as the "path of action" (karmapatha) by metaphorically applying the name of the cause to the effect.
But its being bodily or vocal is due to its being the fruit of those actions, just as the proponents of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) maintain for non-informative matter.
The Venerable [Vasumitra] maintains that one is touched by the path of action of taking life through volition directed toward the three times regarding the appropriated aggregates— [namely],
when the thought "I shall kill," "I am killing," or "it has been killed" occurs.
However, the path of action is not completed by this alone.

Lest there be the consequence that for those who merely conceive the conceit of having killed their mother and so forth—even when she has not been killed—the act would constitute immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*);
whereas for one who actually kills her himself, such a manifestation of volition (*cetanā-samudācāra*) exists—this [explanation] would be the most appropriate intention here.

Now, what is this hostility [toward our view], that you reject *avijñapti* while simultaneously accepting a specific transformation of the continuum (*saṃtati-pariṇāma-viśeṣa*), even though it is likewise imperceptible?
Indeed, there is no animosity here;

rather, it is because satisfaction does not arise from the claim that when an action is completed through a bodily application following from the mind, a distinct entity (*dharmāntara*) arises from those two for the agent.

However, satisfaction does arise from the view that when an action is completed through an application initiated by someone, a transformation of the continuum (*saṃtatipariṇāma*) occurs for that very person, having that [action] as its cause.
And because the fruit arises in the future from the continuum of mind and mental factors,
it has been said in this regard: [What was said?]
"Because of the non-existence of informative [action]," and so forth;
because of the non-existence of that, there is the non-existence of non-informative [action].
As for what was also said— "because the formlessness of the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) has not been stated"—
let that very form which was described here as being non-demonstrable and non-obstructive be what is included within the sphere of phenomena.
As for what was also said— that the noble eightfold path would not exist—
first explain this:
how do right speech, right action, and right livelihood come to be for one who has entered the path?
Does he speak words, perform actions, or seek robes and so forth?
No, it says. What then?

One acquires an unmanifest (avijñapti) of such a nature that is untainted (anāsrava), by the acquisition of which, even when one has emerged from meditative absorption, one no longer engages in false speech and the like, but instead engages in right speech and the like. Therefore, by applying the name of the effect to the cause (nimitte naimittikopacārāt), the term "unmanifest" is applied to it.

If this is so, why is it not accepted here as well: that one who has entered the path, even without non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), acquires such an intention and a basis (*āśraya*) through the acquisition of which, even after emerging [from meditative absorption], he no longer engages in wrong speech and the like, but engages in right speech and the like?
Therefore, by applying a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of the effect to the cause, the eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are established.
However, another says:
"In this context, it would be the mere non-performance of that [action] which is stated to be the factor."
When one attains the certainty of non-action through the power of the Noble Path, that [certainty] would be untainted (*anāsrava*) because it is obtained by relying upon the untainted path.
For not in every case are phenomena (*dharma*) that exist as substantial entities (*dravyasat*) enumerated;
for example, the eight worldly dharmas: gain and loss, fame and infamy, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.
And herein, there is no such distinct entity as "non-attainment" (alābha) of robes and so forth.
The Prātimokṣa restraint would also exist through that volition by which, having performed the formal ritual, one undertakes the commitment to restrain body and speech from prohibited actions.
If it is argued that one would not be restrained when possessing a different state of mind,
we say no.

Because it presents itself to one who remembers it at the time of action through its cultivation; furthermore, there would also be the state of a "bridge," since, by repeatedly recollecting the vow of non-action, one refrains from misconduct out of a sense of shame. And it is for this very purpose that the undertaking of that [vow] occurs.
If, on the other hand, non-manifestation (*avijñapti*) alone were to obstruct misconduct, no one whose mindfulness has been stolen would ever violate the training.
"Enough with this prolixity; non-informative form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) does indeed exist as a distinct substance"—so say the Vaibhāṣikas.

[If it exists, and it has been stated that it is derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), then does non-informative form arise by deriving from those very same primary elements as the informative form, or from others?
It arises by deriving from entirely other primary elements.]
Indeed, it is not logical that the very same causal complex should have both a subtle fruit and a coarse fruit.
[Is it the case that] the informative act (*vijñapti*) exists by depending upon those very same great elements (*mahābhūta*) that exist at that same time?
Generally, all derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is like this; however, some present and future [derived matter] exists by depending upon past great elements.
What, then, is that?
Non-informative action (avijñapti), following the first moment, arises from past primary elements (bhūta) belonging to the desire realm. //4//
After the first moment, the non-informative [matter] belonging to the desire realm arises depending upon past great elements;
these serve as its basis (āśraya),
while the present great elements of the body serve as its support (saṃniśraya).
Because they are the causes for the initial engagement and the subsequent continuation [of action], respectively—
just as, for a wheel revolving on the ground, the thrust of the hand and the region of the ground are the causes—
[now,] from what source do the primary elements (mahābhūta) arise upon which bodily and vocal karma depend?
Bodily and vocal action that is with-outflow (*sāsrava*) arises depending upon its own primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

Bodily and vocal action belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) depends exclusively upon the primary elements of the desire realm; likewise, up to that which belongs to the level of the fourth dhyāna, it depends exclusively upon the primary elements of that same level.
As for the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), it depends upon the primary elements of the place where one is born.

However, regarding untainted (anāsrava) bodily and vocal action: when one born in a particular level produces such action, it should be understood as being based upon the primary elements (bhūta) belonging to that very level.
This is because untainted [elements] do not fall within the realms (dhātu), and because there is an absence of untainted primary elements, yet [the action] arises through their power.
In this context, the two types of action known as informative (vijñapti) and non-informative (avijñapti) are to be understood.
Non-informative [matter] is non-appropriated. //5//
It is outflowing, designated as a sentient being,
and moreover,
it arises from primary elements that are outflowing and appropriated.
Non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) arises based solely on derivative primary elements (*naiḥṣyandika-bhūta*) and based on mind and mental factors;
this is the type belonging to the stage of non-concentrated meditation (*asamāhitabhūmikā*).
That which is born of concentration (*samādhija*) arises from accumulated (*aupacayika*), non-appropriated (*anupātta*), and undifferentiated (*abhinna*) primary elements. //6//

The meditative and the untainted restraints (*dhyāna- and anāsrava-saṃvara*) are informative action (*vijñapti*) born of concentration (*samādhija*). That [informative action] arises depending upon the great elements (*mahābhūta*) produced by concentration, which are accumulative (*aupacayika*) and non-appropriated (*anupātta*). Furthermore, it is undifferentiated; for those very same great elements depending upon which the abstention from taking life arises, those very same ones also serve as the basis for the abstention from everything up to frivolous speech (*saṃbhinna-pralāpa*).
What is the reason?

Because, unlike the mind, there is no differentiation among the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). However, in the case of the Prātimokṣa restraint, the seven types of non-informative action (*avijñapti*) arise based on distinct sets of primary elements.
Informative action (*vijñapti*), however, is of the nature of outflow (*naiḥṣyandika*);
that which pertains to the body is appropriated (*upātta*).
Now, when this informative action arises, does it arise by obstructing the continuity of the previous shape, or not?
What follows from this? If it arises by subverting [the previous state], no;
for since the material form of maturation (vipāka-rūpa) would be interrupted and then resume its continuity, this would result in a position contrary to that of the Vaibhāṣikas.
Alternatively, if it does not contradict [the principle of non-obstruction], how can two shapes be established within a single aggregate of primary elements?
At that time, entirely different [shapes] arise as outflows (*naiḥṣyandika*), based upon which there occurs informative action (*vijñapti*).
If that were so, then whichever limb the informative intimation (*vijñapti*) arises in dependence upon, that very limb ought to become larger,
because it would be pervaded by those primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Furthermore, if it were not pervaded, how could one manifest the intimation with the entire limb?
Because the body is porous, there is space for them.
Indeed, this karma has been described in various ways as being twofold, threefold, and fivefold:
namely, volition (*cetanā*) and that which is performed after having willed (*cetayitvā*).
Having willed, it is further divided into two types:
bodily and vocal action, as well as volition.
Bodily action, moreover, is twofold: that termed informative and that termed non-informative.
Thus, verbal action consists of five types, including volition;
therein, moreover, non-informative action is of two kinds:
wholesome and unwholesome.
There is no neutral (*avyākṛta*) non-informative (*avijñapti*) action.
For what reason?

Because a neutral mind is weak; therefore, it is not capable of projecting a powerful karma that would continue to follow even after that [mind] has ceased. The other [types of karma] are of three kinds.
Other karma is of three kinds: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. What is that "other"?
Informative action and volition.
Furthermore, the impure:
unwholesome matter and action are to be understood as belonging to the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Not elsewhere,
because the unwholesome roots, as well as shamelessness and lack of dread, have been abandoned.
However, the wholesome and neutral [unmanifest] exists everywhere because it is not obstructed;
in that regard,
there is also non-informative [matter] within form.
The word "also" (*api*) implies that [restraint] exists even in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
It does not exist in the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) because of the absence of the primary elements (*bhūta*).
For wherever there is the activity of body and speech, there is the restraint of body and speech.

"In that case, would there not be an outflow-free (anāsrava) non-informative form (avijñapti) for one who has entered meditative equipoise here [in the desire realm], just as there is an outflow-free informative form?
No; because that [outflow-free informative form] does not fall within the realms [of existence].
However, a non-informative form belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara) cannot exist by depending upon primary elements (bhūta) that are of a different category."
Furthermore, because it is turned away from all forms, the formless attainment (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) is not capable of producing form,
since the perception of form has been eliminated.
Morality (*śīla*) is the antidote to immorality (*dauḥśīlya*).
And that immorality belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
Furthermore, the formless realms (*ārūpya*) are distant from the desire realm by way of distance in terms of basis (*āśraya*), aspect (*ākāra*), object (*ālambana*), and antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
Therefore, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that there is no non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) in these [formless realms].
Representation exists in the two stages accompanied by discursive thought. //7//
Informative action (vijñapti), however, exists only in the two stages characterized by discursive thought (savicāra)—
namely, in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the first dhyāna— and not above those. Even within the desire realm, obscured (nivṛta) informative action does not exist.
But obscured informative action does not exist even in the desire realm;
it exists only in the Brahma-world.
For it is heard that the Great Brahmā performed a bodily action arising from deceit.
For he, in the midst of his own assembly, disparaged himself for the purpose of disparaging the Venerable Aśvajit.
Thereafter, since there was no vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*), how could there be the sense-sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*) therein, which is caused by external primary elements?
Others, however, say:
In the second and subsequent dhyānas as well, there is informative action (vijñapti) that is non-obscured and neutral;
it is neither wholesome nor afflicted. What is the reason?
For one born among them does not bring into manifestation a mind of that same kind belonging to a lower stage by which he might produce such an informative act (*vijñapti*);
because it is inferior and because it has already been abandoned, they explain [the matter] as it was previously described.

Furthermore, what is the reason that there is no informative intimation (*vijñapti*) above the Brahma-world, and why is there no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) [intimation] in the desire realm? It is because the motivating cause (*samutthāna*) is absent. For informative intimation is produced by a mind accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*); and such a mind does not exist in the second and higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). Moreover, it is produced by a mind that is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Because that which is to be abandoned by vision functions inwardly;
and that [inward-directed state] does not exist as obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) in the desire realm.
Indeed, should it be understood that the wholesomeness or unwholesomeness of phenomena is to be known solely on the basis of their origination?
He said: No. What then?
By four modes: from the perspective of ultimate reality, from the perspective of intrinsic nature, from the perspective of association, and from the perspective of origination.
In that regard, first,
liberation is the ultimate good;
for nirvana is the complete subsiding of all suffering.
Furthermore, because it is the ultimate security, it is ultimately wholesome like health; it is by its very nature rooted in shame and dread of blame. (8)
The three roots of goodness,

as well as moral shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), are wholesome by their very nature, because they do not depend on association with or origination from anything else, like a medicinal herb that is salutary by itself.

By way of association, those factors associated with those very roots of goodness and moral dread are wholesome by association, because there is no wholesomeness for those not associated with them, like water mixed with medicine.
By way of origination, [wholesome] actions and so forth [are wholesome].

Bodily and vocal actions, as well as the formations dissociated from mind— such as birth and so forth, acquisitions, cessation, and the attainments of non-perception— are wholesome by way of origination (*samutthāna*), because they are produced by those very factors associated with the roots of goodness and so on;
this is like the milk of a nurse produced from [the consumption of] medicinal water.
But it must be explained how the acquisitions (*prāpti*) arisen from a dissimilar mind can be wholesome;
for example, the reconnection of the roots of goodness through doubt, and through the returning to or falling away from a realm.
And just as the wholesome has been explained, the unwholesome is the opposite of that; how so?
Saṃsāra is unwholesome from the perspective of ultimate truth,
because it is supremely insecure by virtue of its nature as the occurrence of all suffering.
The unwholesome roots— lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*)— are unwholesome by their very nature.
The factors associated with it [the root] are [defiled] by way of association (*saṃprayoga*).

Those originated by it—namely, bodily and vocal actions, birth, and acquisitions (*prāpti*)—are [defiled] by way of origination (*samutthāna*). These are to be compared to disease, unwholesome food, and harmful medicine. If that were the case, then nothing would be either outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*), because everything would be included within *saṃsāra*.

This has been stated from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); however, with respect to karmic maturation (*vipāka*), that which is tainted (*sāsrava*) but not defined [as good or bad] is called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).
Furthermore, that which has a desirable maturation is called "wholesome" (*kuśala*).
But if one seeks what is indeterminate in the ultimate sense, then...
It is supremely indeterminate and eternal. // 6 //
Two unconditioned phenomena are, by definition, non-obscured and indeterminate:
space and cessation not through deliberation.
This is investigated: if the wholesomeness or unwholesomeness of bodily and vocal action is due to the power of their origination, why is this not the case for the great elements?
For the agent’s intention is directed toward the action, not toward the great elements.

In the case of non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) of one who is in meditative equipoise (*samāhita*), there is no intention (*abhiprāya*), nor is there a non-equipoised mind that originates it, because such a mind belongs to a different level (*visabhāgabhūmika*). How, then, can this [non-informative action] be wholesome? Otherwise, it would follow that even the divine eye and ear would be wholesome.
Effort must be made on this point.
As for what was said— that the mind to be abandoned by seeing does not give rise to representation—
how then is it that the Blessed One said, "From that wrong view, wrong intention arises, as well as wrong speech and wrong action," and so forth?
This is not contradictory.

Origination is twofold, designated as causal origination and simultaneous origination. Origination is of two kinds: causal origination and simultaneous origination, because [the action] exists at that very moment.
Of these two, the first is the initiator, and the second is the follower.
The causal origination (hetusamutthāna) is the initiator because it projects [the action];
the momentary origination (tatkṣaṇasamutthāna) is the follower because it conforms to the time of the activity.
What, then, is its efficacy regarding that specific activity?
For without that [mind], it would not exist even though it has been projected, just as in the case of one who is dead.
If so, how does the arising of restraint occur for one without mind?
The implication is that it occurs more clearly in the case of one with mind.
And therein,
the consciousness to be abandoned by seeing,
which is to be relinquished through vision, is the instigator of manifestation; it is the mind that initiates the informative act.
This is because it serves as the primary cause (*nidāna*) for the applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) that give rise to those [actions],
but it is not a concomitant (*anuvartaka*),
since those two are absent at the time of the activity of an outward-directed mind.
And the form produced by that [mind] would have to be abandonable by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*). What would follow?
The Abhidharma would be contradicted.
Because there is no contradiction between knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), form (*rūpa*) is not something to be abandoned by vision (*darśanaprahātavya*).
This position is yet to be proven.
In that case, however, the primary elements (*bhūtāni*) would also have to be abandoned by vision.
Because they are produced by a single, identical mind, it will not be as you suggest— that they become neither wholesome nor unwholesome—
or rather, let them be so;
yet this is not possible.
For it is not logical that those [factors] should be abandoned by vision, nor that they should be unabandonable.
What is the reason?
Because an undefiled dharma is not in contradiction with either knowledge (*vidyā*) or ignorance (*avidyā*).
Therefore, since this is recited in the Sūtra with reference to causal origination (*hetu-samutthāna*), there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, both [types] are mental; that which is to be abandoned by cultivation is mental,
and mental consciousness, in turn, is both.
It is both the initiator and the follower;
however, the group of five is only the follower. //11//
The five groups of consciousness are exclusively followers.
This constitutes a fourfold alternative: the mind to be abandoned by seeing is exclusively an initiator;
the five groups of consciousness are exclusively followers.
Both types of mental consciousness are to be abandoned by cultivation; that which is untainted is neither.
Now, does the following consciousness necessarily conform to the initiating consciousness in exactly the same way?
This is not an absolute rule.
For when the initiating [action] is wholesome and so forth, the conforming [action] may be of all three types.
When the initiating action is wholesome, the conforming action may be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.
The same applies to unwholesome and neutral [actions]. For the Sage—
the Blessed Buddha— the conforming [volition] is equal to the impelling [volition].
When the motivating [mind] is wholesome, the conforming [mind] is wholesome; when it is indeterminate, the conforming [mind] is also indeterminate.
Thus, up to the point of being wholesome, the wholesome may be the conforming [mind] even when the motivating [mind] is indeterminate.
However, it never happens that what is wholesome is the instigator while the follower is neutral;
for the teaching of the Buddhas is never indolent.
Other schools maintain that there is no neutral mind in the Buddhas.
For the continuums of the Buddhas consist solely of wholesome states, because they are always in a state of meditative equipoise.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The Nāga is concentrated while walking; the Nāga is concentrated while standing."
"The Naga is concentrated while sleeping, and he is concentrated even while sitting.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that this was said because his mind does not wander due to his lack of desire [for distraction], but it is not the case that Buddhas lack neutral minds born of maturation, those pertaining to postures, or those for emanation.
It has been stated that the mental [mind] is to be abandoned by cultivation, and it is both the initiator and the follower.
All of that—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—should be understood as such; however, that which is born of maturation (vipākaja) is neither. //12//
But a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is neither an initiator (*pravartaka*) nor a follower (*anuvartaka*), because it proceeds without volitional effort (*nirabhisaṃskāra*).
Now, does informative action (*vijñapti*) correspond to the initiator, or does it correspond to the follower? What follows from this?
If it were that which initiates [the action],
then here too, a non-obscured-neutral informative act would result,
because it is initiated by the view of a self-identity and the view of grasping at extremes.
Alternatively, one should not state the qualification that "everything to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) is a motivator (*pravartaka*).
For if it were according to the follower (*anuvartaka*), then the informative action (*vijñapti*) of the Prātimokṣa for one with an unwholesome or neutral mind would not be wholesome.
Informative action is according to the motivator, but not according to what is to be abandoned by seeing.
Because it is interrupted by that which is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

If the virtuous or non-virtuous nature of an informative act (*vijñapti*) does not depend on its concomitant (*anuvartaka*), then one should not say that what was stated in the Sūtra refers to causal origination (*hetu-samutthāna*) and not to momentary origination (*tatkṣaṇa-samutthāna*).
Therefore, it should be stated that there is no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) informative action (*vijñapti*) here; rather,
this was said with reference to a causal origination (*hetusamutthāna*) that is intervened by something else.

The incidental discussion is concluded. That aforementioned non-informative [action] (avijñapti) is to be known as threefold: restraint (saṃvara), non-restraint (asaṃvara), and that which is other than these.
There is restraint (*saṃvara*), non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), and that which is other than these two— neither restraint nor non-restraint.
Restraint is the warding off and the suppression of the proliferation of immoral conduct (*dauḥśīlya*).
Furthermore, in that regard, restraint is called Prātimokṣa, as well as that born of meditative concentration (dhyāna) and that which is untainted (anāsrava). //13//
Restraint is threefold:
the Prātimokṣa restraint is the morality of those here [in the desire realm] belonging to the desire realm;
the meditative (dhyāna) restraint is the morality belonging to the form realm.
The untainted restraint is untainted morality;
furthermore, within that, it is eightfold and is called the Prātimokṣa.

The restraint of a bhikṣu, the restraint of a bhikṣuṇī, the restraint of a śikṣamāṇā, the restraint of a śrāmaṇera, the restraint of a śrāmaṇerī, the restraint of an upāsaka, the restraint of an upāsikā, and the restraint of the upavāsa—
this eightfold restraint is designated as the *prātimokṣa* restraint.
Thus, it is eightfold by name.
In terms of substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*), however, it is fourfold:

the restraint of a monk (*bhikṣu-saṃvara*), the restraint of a novice (*śrāmaṇera-saṃvara*), the restraint of a lay follower (*upāsaka-saṃvara*), and the restraint of the one-day fast (*upavāsa-saṃvara*).
Thus, this fourfold Prātimokṣa restraint exists as a substantial entity.
Because they have distinct characteristics:
the bhikṣuṇī restraint is not different from the bhikṣu restraint; the śikṣamāṇā and śrāmaṇerī restraints are not different from the śrāmaṇera restraint;
and the upāsikā restraint is not different from the upāsaka restraint.
How is this known? From the mark (*liṅga*), because of the transition of names; "mark" is a designation for the sexual organ (*vyañjana*) by which a woman or a man is characterized.
For it is through the mark that the transition of names occurs for monks, nuns, and so forth.
How so?
For when the sexual characteristics (vyañjana) change, a monk is called a nun, and a nun is called a monk;
a novice (śrāmaṇera) is called a female novice (śrāmaṇerī), and a female novice as well as a trainee (śikṣamāṇā) are called a novice.
One is called a lay follower (upāsaka) or a female lay follower (upāsikā), and conversely, a female lay follower is called a lay follower.
However, there is no cause for the abandonment of a previous vow upon the change of gender, nor is there any cause for the acquisition of a previously unobtained vow.
Therefore, the intrinsic nature of these four vows is not distinct from that of the three [other] vows.

When one undertakes the śrāmaṇera restraint from the upāsaka restraint, and subsequently the bhikṣu restraint from that, are these restraints designated as distinct from one another due to the addition of further abstinences— like fifteen, twenty, or a hundred dīnāras— or do they arise separately as entirely distinct wholes?
He said: "Separately;
they arise as unmixed, each with its own distinct characteristic."
In the three types of restraint, there are three abstentions from taking life, up to and including abstention from drinking intoxicants;
the same applies to the remaining [abstentions].
What, then, is the distinction between them?
The distinction arises from the distinction in the cause. How so?
For in whatever measure one undertakes a greater number of training precepts, to that same extent one is [protected] from a greater number of occasions for intoxication and negligence.

When one desists, one turns away from the causes of many more instances of killing and so forth, and instead proceeds toward the causes of non-abstinence; thus, the distinction among the abstinences arises from the distinction among their causes.
If this were not the case, then one who renounces the *bhikṣu* restraint would abandon all three restraints as well, since both [the other two] would be included within it.
And this is not accepted [by us].
Therefore, those vows are indeed distinct, and they are not mutually contradictory. (14)
And these three also exist together;
there is no relinquishing of the preceding restraint upon the undertaking of a subsequent restraint,
lest one become a non-upāsaka simply by relinquishing the bhikṣu restraint.
And how does one become a lay follower (upāsaka), how one who abides in the fast (upavāsastha), and so on, up to a monk (bhikṣu)?

Through the undertaking of abstention from five, eight, ten, or all things to be avoided, there arise the states of a lay follower, one who abides in the fast, a novice (śramaṇoddeśa), and a monk. (Verse 15)
The enumeration should be understood according to their respective order.
By undertaking the restraint from the five things to be avoided, one becomes established in the lay follower's vow (*upāsaka-saṃvara*).
These are: from taking life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from drinking fermented liquors, spirits, and intoxicants.
One who undertakes the restraint from eight things stands in the upavāsa fast:

from taking life, taking what is not given, unchaste conduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants; and from [using] perfumes, garlands, and ointments; from dancing, singing, and instrumental music; from high and large beds; and from eating at improper times.
By undertaking the restraint from ten things, one becomes a śrāmaṇera.
From these very [ten], by adding the acceptance of gold and silver,
and by dividing dancing, singing, instrumental music, perfumes, garlands, and ointments into two categories here, they become ten.
One is called a *bhikṣu* because of undertaking the restraint from all bodily and vocal actions that are to be avoided.
This very Prātimokṣa restraint is called morality (śīla), good conduct (sucarita), action (karma), and restraint (saṃvara);
it is called morality because of the undertaking of abstention from uneven actions.
The etymological derivation is "because of coolness," as stated in the verse: "By undertaking the precepts of happiness, the body is not tormented."
It is called "good conduct" (*sucarita*) because it is praised by the wise;
it is called "action" (*karman*) because its intrinsic nature is that of activity.
But is it not said that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is non-activity?
How does that become an action?
Because those who possess a sense of shame do not commit evil by means of having undertaken it, it is called "non-action.
Nevertheless, since it is performed through both informative intimation (*vijñapti*) and the mind (*citta*), it is an action.
Others say it is so called because it is the cause of action and the fruit of action.
It is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*) because it restrains body and speech.
Thus, for the time being, the Prātimokṣa restraint is designated without distinction.
Furthermore:
In the first [moment], there are both informative and non-informative [actions]; this is the path of action of the Prātimokṣa. (16)
The first moments of informative and non-informative [action] in the undertaking of the vow are called *prātimokṣa*.
The meaning is that by means of it, there is liberation (*prātimokṣaṇa*)—that is, the relinquishing—of evil.
Alternatively, the suffix *vṛddhi* is applied in the sense of the base word itself, as in the cases of *vaikṛta* and *vaiśasa*.

It is called the "prātimokṣa restraint" because it restrains body and speech; it is called a "path of action" (karmapatha) because it is comprised within the fundamental [action]. In the second and subsequent moments, it is only the prātimokṣa restraint, not the prātimokṣa itself.
And the subsequent [action] is not the fundamental path of action.
Now, among these restraints (saṃvara), who is endowed with which?
Eight [types of persons] are endowed with the Prātimokṣa.

The eight classes [of practitioners] are endowed with the *prātimokṣa* restraint: from the bhikṣu and bhikṣuṇī down to the eighth, the one who observes the one-day fast (*upavāsastha*). Is it then the case that outsiders have no morality based on formal undertaking?
They do have it, but it is not the *prātimokṣa* restraint.
What is the reason?
Because it does not lead to the ultimate liberation from evil,
since it is dependent upon cyclic existence (*bhava*).
"One endowed with that which is born of dhyāna":
"born of dhyāna" means produced from dhyāna or in dhyāna.
Whoever is possessed of dhyāna is necessarily possessed of the restraint of dhyāna.
Here, the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) is spoken of by applying the term "dhyāna" [to it],
just as the vicinity of a village is also called a "village," as in the expressions:
"In this village there is a field of rice" or "there is a field of barley."
Noble beings, the noble persons (āryapudgala), are endowed with untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara);
they, moreover, are those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Regarding what was stated, "When the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) is being discussed, two types of restraint (*saṃvara*) are said to follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*)," which are these two?
They are from among these very three.
The last two follow the mind. // 17 //
It consists of the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyānasaṃvara*) and the untainted restraint (*anāsravasaṃvara*),
but not the Prātimokṣa restraint. What is the reason?
Because it continues even for one whose mind is otherwise occupied or who is without mind.
Furthermore, those same two—the meditative and the untainted restraints—receive the designation "restraint of abandonment" (prahāṇasaṃvara).
In what state does this occur? He says:
"In the anāgamya stage, those two arising from the path of immediate succession (ānantaryamārga) are called 'abandonment'."

In the preparatory stage (anāgamya), those two—the meditative restraint (dhyāna-saṃvara) and the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara)—are called "restraints of abandonment" during the nine paths of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga), because through them there is the abandonment of immorality (dauḥśīlya) and the afflictions (kleśa) that give rise to it. For this very reason, a fourfold permutation (catuṣkoṭika) is established: there may be meditative restraint that is not a restraint of abandonment, and so forth.

The first alternative is the contaminated meditative restraint (dhyāna-saṃvara), excluding that which belongs to the path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga) of the threshold concentration (anāgamya).

The second is the uncontaminated [restraint] within the paths of immediate succession of the threshold concentration. The third is the contaminated [restraint] within the paths of immediate succession of the threshold concentration.

The fourth [alternative] is the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) excluding the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) of the threshold stage (anāgamya). In this way, a fourfold logical permutation (catuṣkoṭika) should be understood as applicable: that there may be untainted restraint which is not the restraint of abandonment (prahāṇa-saṃvara), and so forth.
Then what of that which was said by the Blessed One: "Restraint of the body is good; restraint of speech is also good; restraint of the mind is good; restraint in all respects is good"?

As for what was said, “He dwells restrained by the restraint of the faculty of the eye,” what is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these two— the restraint of the mind-faculty and the restraint of the mental faculty?
These two do not have the intrinsic nature of non-informative morality (*avijñapti-śīla*).
What then? The two—clear comprehension and mindfulness—are the restraint of the mental faculty. (18)

The word "twofold" (dvi) is repeated in order to indicate that each [restraint] possesses a twofold nature, so that they might not be understood according to their respective order; for both the restraint of the mind (*manaḥ-saṃvara*) and the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*) have mindfulness (*smṛti*) and clear comprehension (*samprajñāna*) as their intrinsic nature.
This is now considered: which [is which]?
By which kind of informative or non-informative [action] is one possessed, and for how long?
In that regard,
