one who abides in the Prātimokṣa is always possessed of the present [informative action], as long as it has not been relinquished.
One is endowed with non-informative matter (*avijñapti*);
that person who has been described as abiding in the *prātimokṣa* restraint is always possessed of that present non-informative matter for as long as he does not abandon it.
After the first moment, he is possessed of the past [non-informative matter]. (19)
From the moment after the first instant onward, one is also endowed with the past [possession]; "until its abandonment" is to be understood as applicable in all cases.
Just as it was stated for one abiding in the *prātimokṣa* restraint, so it is also for one abiding in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*);
even one abiding in non-restraint is constantly endowed with a present non-informative (*avijñapti*) [action] for as long as he does not abandon that non-restraint.
Even by that which has passed away immediately after the moment.
One who possesses the restraint of meditative absorption (dhyānasaṃvara) always [possesses it] through that which is past and that which is unborn;
for one who has obtained the restraint of meditative absorption is constantly endowed with past and future non-informative (avijñapti) actions until its relinquishment.
For in the first moment, he acquires the restraint of meditative absorption (dhyāna-saṃvara) that was abandoned in a previous life but has now passed away;
however, a noble one (ārya) in the first moment does not acquire it as something past.
A noble person (*āryapudgala*) likewise possesses [the path] through the untainted (*anāsrava*) [path];
however, this is the distinction:
in the first moment, he is not endowed with the past [path], because the path has not previously arisen. Those two, when abiding in the concentrated noble path, are endowed with the present [path].

Those two, being endowed with the meditative and the untainted restraints (dhyāna- and anāsrava-saṃvara) and having entered the concentrated noble path (samāhita-āryamārga), are respectively possessed of the present non-informative action (avijñapti), but not when they have emerged from it.
This is the account, for now, concerning those who abide in restraint and non-restraint.
Now, regarding the neutral person (*madhyastha*):
if a neutral person exists at the beginning, it is by means of the intermediate [vow];
one who abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint is a neutral person.
For him, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) does not necessarily exist.
However, for one who possesses it—comprised of bad conduct, the factors of morality (*śīlāṅga*), and so forth—he is initially endowed with the intermediate [non-informative matter].
For present non-informative matter exists between the past and the future.
Above that, it is associated with two time periods. //21//
From the moment after the first instant, it exists together with both the past and the present;
"until its relinquishment" is understood to apply here as well.
Can one who abides in non-restraint ever be endowed with a wholesome informative act (*vijñapti*), or can one who abides in restraint ever be endowed with an unwholesome one?
If so, when, and for how long? He says:
"One abiding in non-restraint [is endowed] with the auspicious; one abiding in restraint, with the inauspicious."
One is endowed with non-informative matter as long as one possesses the force of faith or the force of affliction. //22//
The force of faith by which a wholesome non-informative action (*kuśalā-avijñapti*) arises in one who stands in non-restraint while performing such acts as bowing to a stūpa,
and the force of affliction by which an unwholesome non-informative action (*akuśalā-avijñapti*) arises in one who stands in restraint while performing such acts as killing, binding, or beating—
these two non-informative actions persist for as long as those forces continue to operate.
In the first moment, he is endowed with the non-informative [action] (avijñapti) as it exists in the present; in other moments, he is also endowed with that which is past.
The section on non-informative action is concluded.
Regarding informative action (*vijñapti*), however, all who perform it are endowed with the intermediate [action].
All those abiding in restraint, non-restraint, or the intermediate state are endowed with that intermediate action as long as they continue to perform it;
after the first moment, they are endowed with the past [informative action] until its abandonment.
From the moment after the first instant until its relinquishment, one is endowed with past informative action;
there is no such thing as being endowed with that which is unborn. //23//

No one is endowed with a future informative act (*vijñapti*). Nor is anyone endowed with past informative acts that are either obscured-unspecified (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*) or unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛta-avyākṛta*).
Indeed, no one is endowed with even past informative acts that are obscured-unspecified or unobscured-unspecified.
For when the Dharma is weak, even its attainment is weak and does not continue as a consequence.
What causes its weakness?
It is caused by the mind.
In that case, let it not be so for the mind (*citta*) that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
This is not the case;
for representation (*vijñapti*) is insentient and dependent on other factors.
The mind is not like this;
for that informative act (*vijñapti*), being produced by a weak [mind], becomes even weaker.
Thus it is said: "one who abides in non-restraint."
What is this so-called non-restraint (asaṃvara)? Non-restraint is misconduct, immorality, action, and the path of that [action]. // 24 //
These are synonyms for non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). In this context, it is called "non-restraint" because it does not restrain body and speech;
it is called "misconduct" (*duścarita*) because it is censured by the virtuous and because it results in undesirable fruits.
It is *dauḥśīlya* (immorality) because it is the opposite of morality (*śīla*).
It is *karma* (action) because it consists of bodily and vocal acts.
It is a *karmapatha* (path of action) because it is comprised within the fundamental [acts].
There is a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika) regarding whether one may be endowed with informative action (vijñapti) but not with non-informative action (avijñapti).
In that regard, first,
one is endowed with informative action alone when, being in a neutral state, one performs an action with weak volition (mṛducetana).

One who performs a wholesome or unwholesome action with weak volition, while abiding in neither restraint nor non-restraint, is endowed with informative action (*vijñapti*) alone and not with non-informative action (*avijñapti*), let alone in the case of an indeterminate action. However, this is not the case regarding the bases of meritorious action consisting of material things (*aupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*) or the paths of action (*karmapatha*).
An Noble Person (*āryapudgala*) who has abandoned or has not yet produced informative action is endowed with non-informative action. (25)

One is endowed with non-informative action alone, and not with informative action, by that noble person who, upon changing to another birth, has neither yet performed an informative action nor lost it.
Thus has been explained the determination regarding the possession of informative and non-informative actions for those situated in restraint, non-restraint, or the intermediate state.
Now, how are these restraints obtained?
That which is born of dhyāna is obtained by means of the dhyāna stage itself;

when a contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind belonging to a dhyāna stage—whether it be the fundamental (*maulīya*) or the preparatory (*sāmantakīya*)—is attained, then the dhyāna restraint (*dhyānasaṃvara*) is also attained, because they are co-existent (*sahabhū*).
The uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) [restraint] is obtained by that same [stage].
In the same way, when the noble, untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative stage (*dhyānabhūmi*) is attained, the untainted restraint (*saṃvara*) is obtained.

In that regard, there are six untainted meditative stages: the four dhyānas, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), and the intermediate concentration (*antara*); these we shall explain later. That which is called Prātimokṣa is [obtained] through the communication of others and so forth. (26)
The Prātimokṣa restraint, however, is obtained through the communication of another;
that is, if another person informs him and he informs the other.
Furthermore, it is obtained either from the Saṃgha or from an individual.

The vows of the bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, and other [vows] from a person—these are the ten kinds of full ordination (*upasaṃpad*), according to the Vinaya-vibhāṣikas. The word "etc. (*ādi*) is used for the purpose of including those.

The admission of the Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas by virtue of their self-awakening; that of the group of five by entering the path of certainty (*niyāma*); that of Yaśas and others by the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikṣukā*); that of Mahākāśyapa through his acceptance of the Teacher; that of Sodāyin by satisfying [the Buddha] with answers to questions; that of Mahāprajāpatī by accepting the eight weighty rules (*gurudharma*); and that of Dharmadinnā by messenger; and [the admission] in border regions by a quorum of five including a holder of the Vinaya.

In the central regions, the going for refuge was performed by groups of ten; thus, for those who were ordained through the sixty-membered *bhadravarga* assemblies, their Prātimokṣa restraint was not necessarily dependent upon formal proclamation (*vijñapti*).
Furthermore, when this Prātimokṣa restraint is being undertaken, for how long a period should it be undertaken?

The undertaking of the Prātimokṣa restraint belonging to the seven classes is for as long as life lasts, while that of the fasting (upavāsa) restraint is for a day and a night; this is the fixed rule. What is the reason?
For there are two limits of time:
the limit of a day and night, and the limit of a lifetime.
From the repetition of days and nights, [longer periods such as] fortnights and so forth arise.
What is this phenomenon called "time"?
It is a designation for the illumination of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
For in the continents, the state of light is called "day."
The state of darkness is night.
It is indeed logical that after life has ended, even if there were a formal undertaking, restraint would not arise;
for the physical basis is of a different nature, and because of that, there is neither application toward it nor recollection of it.

Now, what obstacle is there to the arising of many fasting restraints (*upavāsa-saṃvara*) beyond a single day and night—for instance, for five nights or ten nights—once one has undertaken the vow of fasting?
There is this obstacle: that the Blessed One taught in the Sūtra that the fast lasts only for a day and night.
This point must now be carefully considered.

Was the one-day-and-night fast (upavāsa) taught by the Tathāgata because he saw that the restraint (saṃvara) does not arise beyond a day and night, or rather for the purpose of enjoining those with weak faculties to undertake the restraint even for a single day and night?
From what, then, is this inferred?
Since there is no contradiction with reason even in the arising of restraint (*saṃvara*) after a day and night,
the Vaibhāṣikas do not accept that it is taught for anyone beyond a day and night.
Now, what is the temporal restriction for non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)?
Non-restraint does not exist for a single day and night;

rather, non-restraint arises from the undertaking of evil deeds for as long as one lives, not for a day and night like the *upavāsa* (fasting vow). What is the reason? It is said that it is not undertaken in such a manner. //27//
It is said that no one undertakes non-restraint in this way, as one does with the fast (upavāsa), thinking, "May I be unrestrained for a day and a night," because the action is contemptible;
and likewise, no one undertakes it thinking, "May I be unrestrained for as long as I live."
He would not obtain it even for the duration of his life.

Although one does not undertake it in such a manner, nevertheless, by performing that action with an intention that is utterly corrupted, one acquires non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), but not with an intention that is corrupted only for a limited time.
As for the restraint of the fast (*upavāsasaṃvara*), however, because it is sustained by the power of formal undertaking, it is indeed obtained even when the intention is not ultimate.
This is because one seeks restraint (*saṃvara*).
If, however, someone were to seek non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) as well and were to undertake non-restraint for a limited period of time, they would certainly obtain it;
yet, since this is not observed [in practice], it is not established in that way.
The Sautrāntikas maintain that non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) is not a substantial entity (*dravya*) in the same way that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is;

rather, non-restraint is simply the intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) to perform evil deeds. Because it persists as a continuous sequence (*sānubandha*), one is said to possess it even when one has a wholesome mind (*kuśalacitta*).
Because that has not been rejected.
Now, if the fast is to be undertaken for a day and night, how should it be taken?
It should be taken at dawn from another person while standing in a lower position, repeating what is said by them.
The fast, with all its components complete, is observed by one who is without ornaments until the end of the night. //28//

First, it should be taken at dawn, at the time of sunrise, because the restraint lasts for a full day and night. However, one who has previously made a formal undertaking, thinking "I will observe [the fast] every eighth day," may take it even after having eaten.
Furthermore, it must be received from another and not by oneself alone; this is out of regard for others, so that even when the conditions for transgression exist, one does not overstep the rule.
Standing low, either squatting or kneeling, and having formed the *kapotaka* añjali, one should remain elsewhere;
for restraint does not arise in one who lacks respect.
And one should repeat the words of the giver.
Neither before nor simultaneously;
for in this way, it is received from another. Otherwise, the act of giving and receiving would not be established.
It must be undertaken with all eight limbs complete and not with any missing limb;
and one should be without ornaments,
except for those that are worn daily as a matter of habit.
For a constant ornament does not produce excessive intoxication;
moreover, it must be undertaken until the end of the night, as far as the next sunrise.
Otherwise, for one who undertakes it differently, there would be merely good conduct (*sucarita*), but not the restraint of the fast (*upavāsasaṃvara*).
And by establishing it in this way, the efficacy of the one-day fast (upavāsa) is applied even for those such as sheep-butchers or adulterers who observe it.
It is called "fasting" (upavāsa) because one dwells near (vasati) the Arhats by means of it, through following their training.
Others say it is so called because one dwells near the lifelong restraint (saṃvara) by means of it.

Alternatively, it is called *poṣadha* because it nourishes the roots of merit for those whose roots of merit are small. As it is said: "Because it bestows nourishment (*poṣa*) upon the wholesome mind, this was therefore called *poṣadha* by the Blessed One.
For what purpose, then, are the eight limbs adopted? Because:
The factors of morality, the factor of heedfulness, and the factors of the vow are, in order:
four, one, and three; that is, the factors of morality consist of four, up to the abstention from false speech.
Because it is an abstention from what is naturally reprehensible (*prakṛtisāvadya*),
the single factor of heedfulness (*apramādāṅga*) is the abstention from drinking intoxicants;
for even one who has formally undertaken the moral precepts might become heedless if he drinks intoxicants.
There are three limbs of the vow, up to the abstention from eating at improper times,
because they are conducive to a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
But what would happen if these limbs of heedfulness and limbs of the vow were not undertaken?
By these, there is loss of mindfulness and intoxication. //26//
For one who drinks intoxicants, the very memory of what ought and ought not to be done is destroyed.
In one who indulges in high beds, large couches, dancing, singing, and the like, intoxication arises.
And for the intoxicated person, immorality is not far off.
Furthermore, for one who eats at the proper time, because the usual mealtime has been avoided, mindfulness of the fast and a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) will arise;
in the absence of that [proper timing], both would not exist.
However, some indeed consider the mere abstention from eating at improper times to be the fast itself.
Its remaining eight limbs are formed by treating dance,
song, and instrumental music as one, and perfumes, garlands, and ointments as another two;
however, if this were the case, it would not accord with the reading of the Sūtra.
Having set aside the abstention from eating at improper times, [one says]: "By this eighth limb, I train in accordance with and follow the training of those noble Arhats.
What, then, is that other *upavāsa* (fasting) of which these are the limbs?
The limbs are the constituent parts of the whole.
Just as the parts of a chariot, the fourfold army, and the fivefold musical ensemble are so designated, so too should the eightfold fast (*upavāsa*) be understood.
Abstaining from eating at improper times is both the fast itself and a limb of the fast, just as right view is both the path and a limb of the path.

According to the Vaibhāṣikas, the factor of enlightenment consisting of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is both enlightenment and a limb of enlightenment, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is both meditation (*dhyāna*) and a limb of meditation.
It is not, however, that those very same factors such as right view and so forth can function as limbs for themselves.
If the preceding moments of right view and so forth were to serve as limbs for the subsequent ones, then the Noble Path arising in its first moment would not be eightfold.
Furthermore, is this observance (upavāsa) intended only for a lay follower (upavāsaka), or for others as well?
The fast exists for others as well, but not for one who has not gone for refuge.

Even for one who does not normally observe the fast, if they go for refuge to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha for that day and night and then undertake the fast, the restraint of the fast arises for them;
it does not arise otherwise, except in the case of ignorance.
It is said in the Sūtra: "Mahānāman, when a householder, a man clothed in white, endowed with the male faculty,
goes for refuge to the Buddha, goes for refuge to the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and speaks the words, 'Please accept me as a lay follower'—
by this much one becomes a lay follower."
In that case, does one become an upavāsaka merely by taking refuge?
"It exists," say the outsiders;
"not without the vow," say the Kaśmīris.
[What then of that which was said in the Sūtra?]
There is no contradiction here,
because the restraint arises from that very same undertaking of the status of a lay follower (upāsaka).
The restraint of a lay follower (*upāsaka-saṃvara*) arises for him simply from the undertaking of the status of a lay follower.

This occurs when he undertakes [the vow], saying: "Hold me to be a lay follower; from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, may I be free from taking life. The phrase "free from taking life" (*prāṇāpeta*) means "free from killing living beings" (*prāṇātipātāpeta*), due to the elision of the middle term.
Even for the sake of explaining the minor vows, the statement of the training rules is like that for a monk. //30//

Just as a monk, even though he has already obtained the vows (*saṃvara*), is made to take up the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) again for the sake of instruction—being told, "Your restraint consists of this and that"—and just as a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) does likewise, so too it is with the lay follower (*upavāsaka*). For there is no such thing as a lay follower without the vow. If all are thus restrained, how is it that there are those who practice in one part and so forth?

If all lay followers (upāsakas) abide in the lay follower's vow (upāsaka-saṃvara), why did the Blessed One describe them as "one who practices a single part," "one who practices a limited portion," "one who practices the majority," and "one who practices in full"? It is said that they are so designated because of their observance [of the precepts]; for whoever observes whichever training rule (śikṣāpada) is called "one who practices that."
But all [of them] abide equally in the restraint (*saṃvara*). This proceeds contrary to the sūtra (*utsūtra*). What here is contrary to the sūtra?

The acquisition of the restraint (*saṃvara*) occurs simply by the formal acceptance of being a lay follower (*upāsaka*), because [the Buddha] said, "from the abstention from taking life," and so forth.
For there is no such reading of the Sūtra; rather, the reading is as stated in the Mahānāma-sūtra.
Furthermore, the instruction on the characteristics of a lay follower is given in that very [sūtra] and nowhere else.

But where there is this reading, "For as long as life lasts, [I am] one who has gone for refuge, one who has attained serene confidence, having abandoned [life]," there those who have seen the Truths demonstrate that following the True Dharma even at the cost of their lives is consequent upon their verified confidence (avetyaprasāda),
saying: "Even for the sake of our lives, we are incapable of abandoning this Dharma."
However, this is not an instruction on the characteristics of restraint (*saṃvara*);
moreover, the phrase "devoid of life" (*prāṇāpeta*) is nowhere recited [in that context].
And who would recite such a thing whose meaning is not clear?

However, regarding those who have broken the training by violating only a portion of it, the very question [of their status] is not appropriate; how much less so the case of the *āveṇika-dharmas* (unshared qualities)? For who, knowing the lay follower’s vow (*upāsaka-saṃvara*), would not know this: that whoever does not violate a particular precept becomes one who fulfills that [precept]?

However, this question— "To what extent, Venerable Sir, does a lay follower (*upāsaka*) become one who practices a single part, up to becoming one who practices the complete set?"— is appropriate for those who are ignorant of the measure of the lay follower's restraint (*saṃvara*) and are capable of undertaking only that much training.
If, on the other hand, one could be a lay follower without the restraint or with an incomplete one, then monks (*bhikṣu*) and novices (*śrāmaṇera*) would also be so.
How, then, is there a fixed determination of the constituent parts for these, such as the lay follower's vows (upāsaka-saṃvara) and so forth?
It is by virtue of the Teacher’s designation.
Let it be accepted that even the specific determination of being a lay follower and so on is by virtue of the Teacher’s designation.
For even without the vow (*saṃvara*), one is designated as a lay follower (*upāsaka*), but not so for a monk (*bhikṣu*) or a novice (*śrāmaṇera*); however, the Kashmiris do not accept this.
Furthermore, the mildness and so forth of all vows correspond to the mind. (31)
The mild, medium, or intense nature [of the vow] depends on the strength of the mind that undertakes it.
If this were the case, even an Arhat could possess a mild Prātimokṣa restraint, while an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) could possess an intense one.
Furthermore, would one become a lay follower (upāsaka) merely by taking up the restraint, without having gone for refuge?
It would not be so, except for ignorance.

When one goes for refuge to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, what is it that he takes as his refuge? He takes as his refuge the dharmas that constitute the Buddha and the Saṅgha: the dharmas of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) and both [the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training].
And he who goes for refuge to the three refuges, including Nirvana. // 32 //

He who goes for refuge to the Buddha goes for refuge to those dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) that constitute a Buddha— those by virtue of which that personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is called "Buddha," or by the acquisition of which one becomes a Buddha through the capacity for universal awakening.
What, then, are they?
The knowledge of destruction and so forth, along with their retinues, [are common].
Since there is no difference in the form body (rūpakāya) before or after [attainment],
does this refer to all Buddhas or to one?
One takes refuge in all Buddhas by way of their characteristics, because the path has no different characteristics.

He who goes for refuge to the Saṅgha goes for refuge to those dharmas—both those of the learners (śaikṣa) and those beyond learning (aśaikṣa)—which constitute the Saṅgha; through the attainment of which the eight types of persons become the Saṅgha.
Because there is no distinction.
Does this refer to all Saṃghas or to one?
From the perspective of their characteristics, it refers to all Saṃghas, because the Path does not differ in its characteristics.

As for that which was stated in the Sūtra, "Whosoever there shall be a community named 'Saṃgha' in the future time, go to him also for refuge," that is for the purpose of highlighting the nature of restraint (saṃvara) that will exist in the future.
When one goes for refuge to the Dharma, one goes for refuge to Nirvāṇa, which is analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha).
Because it has the single characteristic of pacifying the afflictions and suffering within the continuums of both oneself and others.

If the Buddha is nothing other than the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), how can there be an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) from shedding the blood of a Tathāgata with a malicious mind?
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that because the physical basis (*āśraya*) is destroyed, those [dharmas] are also destroyed.
However, the Treatise (*śāstra*) does not state that the Buddha is solely the dharmas of one beyond training.
What then?
[They are] "those that produce a Buddha.
Therefore, since the Buddhahood of the basis is not denied, this objection is indeed invalid.
Otherwise, one abiding in a mundane state of mind would be neither a Buddha nor the Saṅgha; furthermore, the monk would be the mere possession of the precepts that constitute a monk.

Just as one who honors monks actually honors the precepts that constitute a monk, so too, one who goes for refuge to the Buddha goes for refuge to those dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) which constitute a Buddha.
Others say that he who goes for refuge to the Buddha [takes refuge] in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharmas).
What is the intrinsic nature of the acts of going for refuge?
Their intrinsic nature is vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).
Furthermore, what is the meaning of "refuge" (*śaraṇa*)?
The meaning of "refuge" (śaraṇa) is the sense of protection (trāṇa), because by relying upon it, one attains the ultimate liberation from all suffering. For it was said by the Blessed One:
“Driven by fear, many people go for refuge to mountains and forests, to groves, trees, and shrines.”
But this refuge is not the best; this refuge is not the supreme.
Having come to this refuge, one is not liberated from all suffering.
But he who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha,
when he perceives the Four Noble Truths with wisdom—
Suffering, the origin of suffering, the transcendence of suffering,
and the noble eightfold path leading to the security of Nirvana.
"For this indeed is the best refuge, this is the supreme refuge;
having come to this refuge, one is liberated from all suffering.
For this very reason, the acts of going for refuge serve as the gateway for the undertaking of all vows.
What, then, is the reason that in other vows abstaining from unchaste conduct is established as a training rule, whereas for a lay follower it is from sexual misconduct?
Because sexual misconduct is extremely censurable in the world, because it is easy [to avoid], and because of the attainment of non-action;
for sexual misconduct is utterly condemned in the world.
Because violating another's wife leads to rebirth in the miserable realms (*apāya*),

whereas unchastity (*abrahmacarya*) does not; and because for those living as householders, abstaining from sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*) is easy to do, while abstaining from unchastity is difficult, they might not venture to perform what is difficult.

The noble ones obtain the restraint of non-action regarding sexual misconduct, because they do not engage in it even in future births; however, this does not apply to unchaste conduct. Therefore, for a lay follower (*upāsaka*), the training rule (*śikṣāpada*) is established as abstention from that [sexual misconduct] alone, so that a trainee (*śaikṣa*) who has changed to another birth might not remain unrestrained regarding the components of the lay follower's vow.
For the restraint of non-action is indeed the commitment to refrain from performing [unwholesome deeds].
When those who are lay followers (*upāsaka*) take wives, have they obtained restraint (*saṃvara*) with respect to them as well, or not?
It has been obtained; let it not be that there is the acquisition of a partial restraint (*prādeśika-saṃvara*).
How, then, is there no disturbance of the restraint?
Because the acquisition of the restraint occurs according to the undertaking, and not with respect to the continuum. // 33 //
For just as there is their formal undertaking, so too is the acquisition of restraint.
And how is their undertaking?
It is: "I abstain from sexual misconduct."

However, it is not the case that one thinks, "I must not practice celibacy (*brahmacarya*) within this [specific] continuum"; rather, because they obtain restraint (*saṃvara*) precisely from the limb of sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*) as its basis—and not from non-celibacy—there is no violation of the restraint regarding a woman who has become one's wife.

Now, why is it that only the abstention from false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) is a training precept (*śikṣāpada*) of the lay follower’s restraint (*upāsakasaṃvara*), and not the abstention from slander and so forth?
And for these very three reasons:
"Because lying is extremely censurable, because it is easy to do, and because by its non-performance one acquires [the opposite],
and because through the occurrence of lying there is a transgression of all the precepts."
For when one is questioned regarding a transgression of the training in any instance, this thought arises: "I did not do such a thing.
Thus, there is the possibility of false speech; therefore, abstention from false speech is prescribed so that even one who has committed a transgression might not conceal it within themselves.
What, then, is the reason that a precept of prohibitive offense (*pratikṣepaṇasāvadya*) was not established?
For what reason is it only from intoxicants that there is an offense of prohibition, and not from anything else?
It is for the sake of guarding against other [transgressions]. (34)
For one who drinks liquor, other limbs [of conduct] would also become unprotected.
How, then, is the drinking of liquor understood to be a fault by prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇasāvadya*),
given that it lacks the characteristics of a natural fault (*prakṛtisāvadya*)?

For an offense by nature (*prakṛtisāvadya*) is committed only with a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*). However, it is possible to drink intoxicants with the very intention of using them as a remedy, provided they do not cause intoxication. That mind which drinks knowing [the substance] to be intoxicating is indeed defiled.
That is not defiled when one drinks having recognized the non-intoxicating measure.
"Alcohol is a natural transgression (*prakṛtisāvadya*)," say the holders of the Vinaya. "Venerable sir, how should one attend to the sick?"
The Blessed One said, "Upāli, setting aside what is naturally reprehensible (*prakṛti-sāvadya*)," and he did not permit the drinking of intoxicants even for the Śākyas when they were ill.

Furthermore, it was said: "O monks, those who designate me as their teacher must not drink intoxicants, even [as much as] a drop on the tip of a blade of kusa grass. From this, it is known that [the drinking of intoxicants] is naturally reprehensible.
And because the Noble Ones do not transgress it even when they have passed into other births—
just as they do not commit the killing of living beings and so forth— and because it is described as a bodily misconduct and leads to rebirth in the miserable destinies.

"No," say the Abhidharmikas. Although it was prescribed as a general rule that alcohol is a conventional offense (*prajñapti-sāvadya*) for those who are ill, there is a further exception regarding alcohol in order to avoid the undesirable consequence [of excessive consumption], because the amount sufficient to cause intoxication is not fixed. For this very reason, drinking even as much as a drop on the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass is prohibited. The Noble Ones (*āryas*) do not indulge in it because they possess a sense of shame (*hrī*), and because [alcohol] causes the loss of mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Even a small amount [of alcohol] is not to be drunk because it lacks moderation, like poison;
it is called "misconduct" because it is a basis for negligence (*pramādasthāna*).
For this very reason, the term "basis for negligence" is used here [for intoxicants] and not for the others, because those [other three] are inherently reprehensible (*prakṛtisāvadya*).

The statement that one goes to an evil rebirth through excessive indulgence means that, due to such addiction, there is a continuous flow of unwholesome states, which either projects or brings about the activity of karma leading to the miserable realms. What is the meaning of "the basis for negligence consisting of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants"?
*Surā* is a non-distilled liquor;
*maireya* is a distilled liquid liquor.
Since these two may sometimes exist in a state where they have not yet reached or have already passed the stage of being intoxicants, the term "intoxicant" (*madya*) is included [in the definition].
Since even betel nuts, *kōdrava* grain, and the like cause intoxication, the specific mention of *surā* (liquor) and *maireya* (fermented liquor) is made.
The term "basis of negligence" (*pramādasthāna*) is used to make known the reason why even that which is a transgression by convention (*prajñaptisāvadya*) must be abandoned with care;
for it is the locus of all forms of negligence.
Regarding these three—the Prātimokṣa, dhyāna, and untainted (anāsrava) restraints—is it the case that when one is obtained, the remaining two are also obtained from that same source?
No, he says. What then?

The Prātimokṣa restraint, which pertains to the desire realm, is acquired with respect to all [objects], both [types of action], and those that are present; [that is, it is acquired] only with respect to the present aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu). "Pertaining to the desire realm" refers to the Prātimokṣa restraint. "With respect to all" means with respect to the fundamental, preparatory, and subsequent actions.

"From both" means from those designated as sentient beings and non-sentient beings, and from those that are naturally reprehensible or reprehensible by prohibition; it is obtained only from present aggregates, bases, and elements, because [the vows] function based upon sentient beings, and not from past or future ones,
since those are reckoned as non-sentient.
The meditative and the untainted restraints arise from the fundamental [paths] at all times. (35)

The meditative (*dhyāna*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) restraints are acquired only from the fundamental paths of action (*karmapatha*), not from the preliminary (*prayoga*) or subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*) stages, much less from offenses of conventional designation (*prajñaptisāvadya*). Furthermore, they are acquired from all times—that is, from the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) of the past and the future as well.
For this very reason, a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) is established:

There are those aggregates, elements, and sense-bases from which only the Prātimokṣa restraint is obtained, and not the dhyāna or the untainted (anāsrava) restraints; such is the detailed explanation.
The first category consists of present preparatory and consecutive stages, as well as from prohibited offenses (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya).
The second category consists of past and future fundamental paths of action (maula-karmapatha).
The third [alternative] refers to the fundamental paths of action in the present; the fourth refers to the preliminary and subsequent stages of those in the past and future.
However, since there are no paths of action existing in the present at the time of undertaking restraint (*saṃvara*), one should say "from present bases.
It is logical that restraint applies only to future [actions], not to those that are past or present.

Now, are restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) acquired only with respect to all sentient beings, all factors (*aṅga*), and by all causes (*kāraṇa*), or is there a distinction? To begin with, restraint is definitely acquired with respect to all sentient beings, but regarding the factors and causes, it is variable (*vibhāṣā*).
Restraint is obtained from all sentient beings, but regarding certain factors, there is a distinction:
some [restraint] is obtained from all [factors],
namely the restraint of a bhikṣu.
Someone [possesses] four;
others than that [possess fewer].
For the paths of action are the members of the restraint.
By causes as well, [the wholesome is established] either by all [causes] in some way, or by one [cause] in some way.
First, by what sense is it "by all"?
It is if non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are accepted as the causes.
By which one?
If the weak, medium, and superior minds are intended as the causes.
Setting aside the final alternative, it is said: there is one who abides in restraint and is restrained toward all sentient beings, yet not by all factors and not by all causes;
this refers to one who undertakes the lay follower’s (*upāsaka*) or novice monk’s (*śrāmaṇera*) restraint with a weak, middling, or intense state of mind.
There is also one who is restrained toward all sentient beings and by all factors, but not by all causes.
There is one who undertakes the bhikṣu restraint with a weak, middling,
or intense mind toward all sentient beings, in its entirety and by all means; and there is one who undertakes the three restraints with the three types of minds.

There is [the case] where one undertakes the vows of a lay follower, the fasting vows, or those of a novice monk toward all sentient beings by means of all causes, but not with all members [of the restraint], according to weak, medium, or superior degrees.
However, there is no one who would not be such toward all sentient beings;
for one obtains the restraint by abiding in a virtuous intention that extends to all sentient beings, and not otherwise, because a sinful intention would not have ceased.
One does not obtain the *prātimokṣa* restraint by making five restrictions,
because of the restrictions regarding sentient beings, limbs [of the body], place, time, and occasion.
"I refrain from this particular sentient being" is the restriction regarding sentient beings.
"From this limb" is the restriction of the limb;
"in this place" is the restriction of the place;
"for as long as a month or the like" is the restriction of time.
"Except in battle"—this is a restriction regarding the occasion.
However, for one who takes [the vow] in that manner, it would be merely good conduct (*sucarita*).
How is there the acquisition of restraint (*saṃvara*) from those [beings] who are incapable [of being avoided]?
This is because one undertakes the vow with the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) not to harm the lives of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, if restraint were obtained only from those [beings] who are capable [of being harmed], it would be subject to increase and decrease,
due to the mutual transition between those who are capable and those who are incapable.
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that this being the case, the acquisition and abandonment of restraint would occur even without the causes of acquisition and abandonment [of the objects].
But it will not be so;

for just as there is no increase or decrease of restraint when previously non-existent grass and such things grow or wither, likewise there would be no such [increase or decrease] even when there is a transition between what is possible and what is impossible.

[The opponent argues: "Because sentient beings exist both before and after [the Buddha's passing], whereas grass and such do not, what indeed is the distinction here? Or rather, would there not be a lack of restraint (*saṃvara*) when grass and such are absent? Or perhaps it would be impossible [to maintain restraint] in that same way. And since those who have entered final nirvāṇa no longer exist at all, how could there not be a diminution of restraint? Thus, this rebuttal is not logical."
Therefore, the previous resolution alone is correct.

If that is so, since later Buddhas do not obtain the Prātimokṣa restraint from those Buddhas who have previously entered Parinirvāṇa, how does it not follow that there is a deficiency in their ethical discipline?
[The answer is: because they obtain it with respect to all sentient beings.
For if those [beings] were to exist in the future, they would have obtained [the non-restraint] from them as well;
since it has been stated from what [source] restraint is obtained, non-restraint, however, is obtained from all [beings], from all limbs, and not by [specific] causes. // 36 //
Non-restraint, however, is acquired with respect to all sentient beings and through all paths of action;
for there is no one who possesses non-restraint through a deficient non-restraint.
Yet it is not acquired through all causes simultaneously, because a weak mind and so forth cannot exist at once.

One who acquires non-restraint with a weak mind, even when depriving a living being of life with an intense mind, remains endowed with that same weak non-restraint, but is endowed with an intense informative act (*vijñapti*) of taking life. The same should be applied to the medium and intense [degrees of mind].

In this regard, these are the persons of non-restraint (*āsaṃvarika*), namely: sheep-butchers, poultry-slaughterers, pig-butchers, bird-catchers, fishermen, deer-hunters, thieves, executioners, prison guards, elephant-trappers, dog-cookers (outcastes), and trappers. Kings, administrators of punishment, and judges are also effectively persons of non-restraint. They are called "persons of non-restraint" because they exist in a state of non-restraint, or because non-restraint exists in them by virtue of their abiding therein.
Those who kill sheep are called *aurabhrikas* (sheep-slaughterers);
other [categories] should be applied in the same way.
It is indeed logical that the acquisition of restraint (*saṃvara*) occurs with respect to all sentient beings.
Because it is undertaken with the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) for the welfare of all sentient beings.

But how is it logical that those such as butchers—who, though their intentions toward their own parents, children, wives, and so forth are not corrupted, would not wish to kill them even for the sake of their own lives—possess non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) toward *all* sentient beings?
For they might indeed kill their mother or others if she were to turn into a sheep.
For those who know that "they are indeed those very same persons" would not kill them;

moreover, since there is no possibility for those who have become noble (*ārya*) to become animals again, how could non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) exist toward them? Furthermore, if one were to be unrestrained toward the present [being] with respect to a future existence, then they would never kill even sheep and the like who have become their sons; thus, there would be no non-restraint toward them.
For how indeed could there not be non-restraint (asaṃvara) toward those very people whom one intends to kill?
This is the same in the case of one's mother and others.
For how indeed could there be non-restraint toward them for one who does not intend to kill?
And how could there be non-restraint for one who, though a butcher by birth, takes nothing, is content with his own wife, and is mute,
if it were not because of the corruption of his intention?

And even a mute person is capable of conveying through the body a meaning that is to be conveyed by speech. Therefore, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that one who undertakes two or three precepts is in no way deficient or partial in their non-restraint.

The Sautrāntikas maintain that according to one's undertaking, there can be both incomplete and partial non-restraint (asaṃvara) as well as restraint (saṃvara), except in the case of the eightfold [Prātimokṣa vows].
This is because even a limited amount of ethical discipline (śīla) acts as an obstacle to immorality (dauḥśīlya).
Thus has been explained from whom the acquisition of non-restraint occurs.
But how is it acquired? It has not been stated;
therefore, this is said:
non-restraint is acquired through action or through formal undertaking.
Non-restraint is acquired through two causes:
by those born into such families through the performance of the preliminary action of killing, and by those born into other families through the formal undertaking of that occupation,
thinking, "We too shall live by this livelihood."
The acquisition of the remaining non-informative [karma], however, results from the field, the undertaking, and the performance with respect.

Or the field may be of such a nature that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) arises merely by the gift of a grove and so forth, as in the case of the material bases of meritorious action (*aupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*).

Alternatively, one undertakes a formal commitment (*samādāna*), such as: "I shall not eat without having paid homage to the Buddha," or "I shall regularly observe the fast-day meal, the monthly meal, or the half-monthly meal," and so on.
With such earnestness and in that form, one strives toward a wholesome or unwholesome action, from which non-informative action (avijñapti) arises for him.
This has been explained regarding how restraint, non-restraint, and that which is other than these are acquired;
now, their relinquishment must be discussed.
In that regard, first,
the abandonment of the restraint of the Prātimokṣa occurs through the renunciation of the training, through death,
through the emergence of both sexual organs, through the cutting off of the roots [of merit], and through the passing of the night. (38)
"Dama" (self-restraint) is so called because by means of it one becomes subdued; it refers here to restraint (*saṃvara*), since it involves the subduing of the sense faculties.
The Prātimokṣa restraint is relinquished through four causes, with the exception of the *upavāsa* (fast-day observance).

The abandonment of the training precepts occurs through the intention to renounce them in the presence of a person capable of understanding, through the relinquishing of the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), through the simultaneous manifestation of both sexual organs, and through the total severance of the roots of virtue.
However, for the fast-day restraint (*upavāsasaṃvara*), it occurs through these four causes as well as the passing of the night;
thus, taken together, there are five causes for its abandonment.
Furthermore, for what reason does abandonment [of the vows] occur through these causes?

It is because of the arising of an informative act (*vijñapti*) contrary to the undertaking, the abandonment of the basis (*āśraya*), the disturbance of the basis, the severance of the cause (*nidāna*), and the projection being limited only to that duration. Some say it is also through a "falling offense" (*patanīya*);
others, however, state that the abandonment of the vows of a monk or a novice occurs through any one of the four falling offenses.
Others say it is due to the disappearance of the True Dharma;
others say it is because of the vanishing of the True Dharma,
since when the True Dharma has disappeared, all training rules, boundaries, and ritual procedures are brought to an end.
The Kashmiris maintain that for one who has committed an offense, both [the transgression and its purification] are like wealth and debt. (36)
The Vaibhāṣikas of Kaśmīr, however, maintain this position:
there is no abandonment of the bhikṣu vow for one who has committed a fundamental transgression.
What is the reason?
For it is not logical that the abandonment of the entire vow should result from the disturbance of a single part;
nor indeed is there a severance of morality for one who has fallen into another transgression.
What then?
He possesses both virtue and immorality,
just as someone might possess both wealth and debt.
However, once that offense has been confessed, he becomes virtuous and no longer immoral, just as one who has cleared a debt becomes wealthy and no longer a debtor.

As for that which was said by the Blessed One: "He becomes a non-monk, a non-Śākyaputrīya; he is fallen from the state of a monk. For whom does the state of a śramaṇa become destroyed, fallen, and defeated?"—this was said with reference to the state of being a monk in the ultimate sense (paramārtha).
This is an act of rashness.
What here is rash? That the definitive meaning (nītārtha) taught by the Blessed One is again interpreted otherwise.
And conditions are provided for immorality and for many afflictions. How is this of definitive meaning? For this is an instruction concerning discipline.
“There are four kinds of monks:
the monk by designation (*saṃjñā-bhikṣu*), the monk by self-claim (*pratijñā-bhikṣu*), the monk because he begs (*bhikṣate*), and the monk because he has shattered the afflictions (*bhinna-kleśa*).
But in this context, a monk is one who has been fully ordained through a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karma*)."

Nor was he previously a bhikṣu in the ultimate sense such that he would later become a non-bhikṣu. As for what was said regarding "the disturbance of one part," the rebuttal has already been given in this very treatise by means of a simile: "Just as a palm tree with its crown severed is incapable of sprouting, incapable of reaching growth, increase, or expansion."
What, then, is the meaning of the simile?
It is that just as when even a single part that constitutes the root is severed, the remainder of the enclosure can no longer stand;

so too, when one commits a fundamental offense (*maulāpatti*) that violates the essential boundaries of the state of a monk, one severs the root of the restraint due to the presence of intense lack of shame (*anapatrāpya*), and thus the abandonment of the entire restraint is logical.

For him, even the consumption of a single mouthful of food belonging to the Saṅgha, or the use of even a space as small as the heel of one foot belonging to the Saṅgha, is not permitted; he has been excluded from all communal enjoyment with the monks by the Teacher, and it was said concerning him:
"Destroy the kāraṇḍavaka weed; pull out the rotten grass!"
"Now, drive away the one who is a mere babbler, who is not a monk but claims to be a monk"— what kind of monkhood can he possibly possess?
Let it be whatever it may be.
But the state of being a monk does exist;
for thus the Blessed One said: "Cunda, there are four types of ascetics, there is no fifth."
“The victor of the path, the teacher of the path, he who lives by the path, and he who defiles the path”—this has indeed been said.

However, because only the mere outward form remains, such a person is called a *śramaṇa* [only nominally], like burnt wood, a dried-up lake, a parrot’s beak, a rotten seed, a circle of firebrands, or a dead being.
For if one were no longer a monk (*bhikṣu*) due to immoral conduct (*dauḥśīlya*), there would be no such thing as one who has been granted the training (*śikṣādattaka*).
We do not say that everyone becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense simply by the occurrence of a transgression.
However, whoever is a *pārājika* is necessarily no longer a monk.

But some, due to a particularity of their mental continuum (*saṃtāna*), do not become *pārājika* because they do not conceal [the offense] even for a single moment of thought; this has been established by the Lord of Dharma.

If, then, one who has committed a *pārājika* offense is no longer a monk, why is he not ordained again? It is because his mental continuum (*saṃtati*) has been ruined by an intense lack of moral dread (*anapatrāpya*), rendering him incapable of restraint; it is certainly not with regard to his status as a monk [that he cannot be ordained]. For even one who has renounced the training (*nikṣiptaśikṣa*) is not ordained again.
And what is this basis for such a calamity? If even one who has become such as that is still a monk, then homage be to such monkhood!
However, when the True Dharma disappears, because there is no longer the performance of Vinaya rituals, there is no acquisition of a new restraint (*saṃvara*);
yet, there is no loss of that which has already been acquired.
Now, how is there the relinquishing of the meditative and the untainted restraints?
The wholesome [state] attained through meditation is relinquished by means of changing levels and by falling away.
All wholesome states attained through meditation are abandoned for two reasons.

Some [wholesome states] are abandoned through rebirth, or by moving upward or downward between levels, or through falling away, or by abandoning the homogeneous class of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-nikāyasabhāga*).

Just as wholesome states belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāpta*) are abandoned by moving between levels or by falling away, so too are those belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāpta*); however, noble states (*ārya*) are abandoned by the attainment of a fruit, by the intensification of faculties, or by falling away. (40)
However, the untainted wholesome [state] is relinquished by three causes:
the previous path is relinquished through the attainment of a fruit;
and the path of dull faculties is relinquished through the sharpening of the faculties.
The higher path is abandoned through falling away,
as is the fruit or that which is superior to the fruit;
in this way, for now, the restraints are relinquished.
Non-restraint [is lost] through the attainment of restraint, death, or the emergence of both sexual organs; thus,
non-restraint is severed by three causes,
beginning with the attainment of restraint.
If one undertakes restraint or attains the restraint of meditative concentration—
due to the attainment of concentration through the power of causes and conditions—
thereby non-restraint is abandoned.
Because the opposing force is stronger;
because death causes the abandonment of the physical basis;
and because the production of both sexual organs causes the transformation of the physical basis.
Even when one abandons the collection of weapons, if there is no intention of non-action,
there is no severance of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) without a formal vow (*saṃvara*);
it is like the failure to cure an advanced disease even after avoiding its causes, in the absence of medicine.
If one who is unrestrained (āsaṃvarika) undertakes the fast (upavāsa), does he return from that restraint (saṃvara) back to non-restraint (asaṃvara), or rather to neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint?
Some say it is non-restraint,
because the intention to abandon [the restraint] is not final.
Others maintain that it is like a glowing iron ball which does not return to its black state unless [the conditions for] application are present,
because the acquisition of that [non-informative action] is dependent upon informative action (*vijñapti*).
Now, how is non-informative action (*avijñapti*) that is free from both restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) abandoned?
The intermediate [course of action] occurs through the cutting off of the roots of existence by means of the actions of taking up the vital force. //41//
For that non-informative [action] is projected by the force of either faith or affliction; it is cut off when that force is severed, like the motion of a potter’s wheel or an arrow.
It is also cut off through the relinquishing of what was undertaken.
If one abandons the undertaking by thinking, "Enough with this undertaking," it is also severed through the interruption of the action, as in the case of one who fails to perform what was undertaken;
it is also severed through the cessation of the object.
Of what object?
Of material things such as shrines, groves, monasteries, lodgings, machines, and nets;
it is also severed by the cutting off of the life-span and of the roots of merit.
When one begins to sever the roots of merit, the intermediate non-informative [matter] is abandoned through these six causes.
"Wholesome form pertaining to the desire realm is abandoned through the cutting of the roots and through birth in a higher stage.
Wholesome form belonging to the desire realm that has a non-material nature is relinquished by two causes.

Non-material defilement is abandoned either through the total severance of the roots of merit or through rebirth in the form or formless realms; however, it is abandoned through the arising of its antidote. //42//
However, all that is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) which does not have form as its intrinsic nature (*arūpasvabhāva*) is abandoned solely through the arising of its antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
Whatever type of secondary affliction (*upakleśa*) there may be, it is relinquished along with its retinue by whichever path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*) corresponds to it, and not otherwise.
Now, for which sentient beings does non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) exist, and for which does restraint (*saṃvara*) exist?
Non-restraint exists among humans, excluding those who are sexually impotent, eunuchs, hermaphrodites, and those born in Kuru;
non-restraint occurs only within the human realm and nowhere else.

In that case as well, one must exclude the *ṣaṇḍha*, the *paṇḍaka*, those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), and the inhabitants of Uttarakuru. Restraint (*saṃvara*) is likewise [restricted] to humans, excluding those already mentioned; and it also exists for the gods—thus, restraint pertains to these two realms of existence.
How is it understood that there is no restraint (*saṃvara*) for eunuchs and others?
From both the Sūtras and the Vinaya.

It is said in the Sūtra: "Insofar as, Mahānāman, a householder clad in white, a man endowed with male organs, goes for refuge to the Buddha... [and] speaks these words: 'Make me a lay follower (*upāsaka*')..."
"Maintain [the precepts]; by this much one becomes a lay follower.
In the Vinaya as well, it is stated that such a person should be expelled.
But what is the reason that these [lay followers] lack restraint (*saṃvara*)?

Because the afflictions based on both [roots] are excessive, one is incapable of analytical reflection (*pratisaṃkhyāna*), and because there is an absence of intense shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*vyapatrāpya*).
Why, then, is there no non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)? Because even regarding evil, one's intention (*āśaya*) is unstable.
And wherever there is restraint (*saṃvara*), there is also non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), because they exist as opposites.

Among the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, there is an absence of both restraint and non-restraint due to the lack of formal undertaking (*samādāna*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), as well as the absence of the intention to perform evil deeds.

Among those in the miserable states (*āpāyika*) as well, there is no intense sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*vyapatrāpya*); it is through connection with these, or their destruction, that restraint and non-restraint would otherwise exist.
Furthermore, the very basis (āśraya) of those beings—such as eunuchs, impotent persons, hermaphrodites, the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, and those in the miserable destinies—is like a saline field;
it is such that neither restraint (saṃvara) nor non-restraint (asaṃvara) can grow within that basis, just as neither grain nor even weeds grow in a saline field.

[If this is so, then what about the statement in the Sūtra: "O monks, on the eighth day of the fortnight, a nāga born from an egg emerges from his abode and observes the fast (upavāsa) endowed with the eight limbs"?]
For them, that is merely good conduct and not restraint;
therefore, restraint belongs only to gods and humans.
Furthermore, among humans there are three [types]. //43//

All three types of vows, beginning with the Prātimokṣa, exist among human beings. Among the gods born in the desire and form realms, there is the vow born of meditative concentration (dhyāna-saṃvara); however, for gods reborn in the desire and form realms, there is none above that.
Furthermore, the untainted [attainment] belongs also to those in the formless realm, excluding those in the intermediate dhyāna and the non-percipient beings. (44)

The untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara), however, exists even for those born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the form realm (rūpadhātu), excluding those born in the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntarika) and the non-percipient beings (asaṃjñisattva).
It also exists for those born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), but for them it exists through possession (samanvāgama) and not through manifest presence (saṃmukhībhāva).
Hereafter, within the context of the exposition of karma, the explanation of the karmas indicated in the Sūtra will now begin.
There are three types of karma:
wholesome karma, unwholesome karma, and indeterminate karma. Among these:
Secure, insecure, and other than those are actions that are wholesome, unwholesome, and other;
this is the definition of the wholesome and so forth.
Wholesome action is secure because it brings about a desirable maturation and leads to the attainment of nirvana, thereby providing protection from suffering.
At that time and ultimately, that which is insecure and unwholesome is so by virtue of being the opposite of security, having an undesirable maturation.
Action other than those two is neither secure nor insecure; it should be understood as that which is other than the wholesome and the unwholesome.
This means it is "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
Furthermore, there are the meritorious, the non-meritorious, and the imperturbable; and the triad beginning with that to be experienced as pleasure. // 45 //
There are three types of karma: meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable.
Again, there are three:
karma to be experienced as pleasure, karma to be experienced as pain, and karma to be experienced as neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
In that regard, first, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), wholesome (*śubha*) karma is merit (*puṇya*); that which arises in the higher realms is immovable (*āneñja*).
The term "wholesome" continues to apply here.
Wholesome karma pertaining to the realms of form and formlessness is immovable (*āniñja*).
But has it not been stated by the Blessed One that the first three meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are movable?
"Whatever is here thought out and deliberated upon, this the Noble Ones call 'movement' (*iñjita*) in this context," and so forth.
This was said with reference to the fact that those [attainments] possess defects within meditative concentration;
however, they are also called "imperturbable" (*āniñja*) in the *Āniñja-sūtra*, starting from the discussion of the practice leading to the imperturbable.
But what is the reason that what is "shaken" elsewhere is called "unshakable"?
Because, in those stages, it does not shake with respect to the ripening of karma. (46)
For that which belongs to the sense-sphere wavers with respect to its maturation.
How does it waver?
Because of its lack of fixed determination.
For even that which belongs to one destiny may ripen in another destiny;
and that which belongs to one class of gods may ripen in another class of gods.

Indeed, the very same karma that would ripen among the gods—producing such things as stature, strength, complexion, happiness, and enjoyments—may, at times, through the power of other conditions, ripen among humans, animals, or hungry ghosts.
It ripens.
However, karma belonging to the realms of form and formlessness can never possibly ripen on a level other than its own; therefore, because its ripening is fixed, it is called "unshakable" (*āneñja*).

However, it is well known in the world that non-meritorious action is unwholesome (*akuśala*). And regarding a matter that is already established by worldly convention, what is the need for further effort?
Thus, the exposition of meritorious and other types of actions has been completed.
The [karma] to be experienced as pleasant and so forth must be explained;
that very [explanation] is now being made:
wholesome [karma] up to the third dhyāna is to be experienced as pleasant.
Wholesome karma to be experienced as pleasure extends up to the third dhyāna;
for this is the ground of pleasant feeling, namely, the desire realm and the three dhyānas. Beyond that, however, [it is not].
However, "to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant" refers to what is wholesome (*śubha*).
Beyond the third dhyāna, wholesome karma is to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, because of the absence of pleasant and painful sensations.
In this world, that which is unwholesome is to be experienced as suffering. //47//
Unwholesome karma is to be experienced as suffering.
The inclusion of the word "here" is for the purpose of making known that this exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, sensation alone is not their fruit.
What then?
It is together with its equipment.

Some say that even below [the fourth dhyāna] there is intermediate [karma]; others, however, say: "This karma described as to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant exists even below the fourth dhyāna. For what reason?
It is due to the maturation of the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
For otherwise, there would be no maturation for the karma of the intermediate dhyāna, nor would there be any maturation for any karma within the intermediate dhyāna,
because of the absence of pleasure and pain therein.
Some maintain that the ripening of the karma of the intermediate dhyāna is the faculty of pleasure within that very dhyāna;
others hold that its ripening is not feeling at all. This [latter] view is contrary to the treatise.
For it is stated in the Śāstra: "Could it be that from karma, only mental feeling ripens as its maturation?
It could be so, in the case of wholesome karma that is without vitarka.
Since it is maintained that the maturation of these three occurs neither before nor after one another. (48)
Furthermore, because it is stated in the Sūtra: "Could there be a ripening of three types of karma that occurs neither before nor after?

Yes: for karma to be experienced as pleasure, the ripening would be matter (*rūpa*); for karma to be experienced as suffering, the ripening would be mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*); for karma to be experienced as neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, the ripening would be factors dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta*). For this reason as well, there exists karma to be experienced as neither-suffering-nor-pleasure in the lower realms.
For nowhere other than in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) is there a simultaneous conjunction of the maturation (vipāka) of the three types of karma.
Now, is that [karma] wholesome or unwholesome?
It is wholesome, but it is weak.
If that is the case, then there is a contradiction with the statements: "Wholesome [karma] up to the third dhyāna is to be experienced as pleasure," and "The wholesome has a desirable maturation.
This teaching should be understood as being based on the majority of cases.
But how is it that karma, which does not have the nature of feeling (*vedanā*), is said to be "to be experienced as pleasure" (*sukhavedanīya*) and so forth?
It is "to be experienced as pleasure" because it is conducive to pleasant feeling, or because pleasure is what is to be experienced by it. And what is it that is to be experienced?
That which is the maturation (vipāka) indeed exists; or rather, it is that which is to be experienced as pleasure— that by which pleasure is felt—
just like a bathing powder.
In the same way, that which is to be experienced as suffering and that which is to be experienced as neither-suffering-nor-pleasure are to be understood.
Furthermore,
[karma is distinguished] by way of its intrinsic nature, its association, its object, and its maturation.
And by way of manifestation—thus, there are five ways of being experienced. //46//
The state of being experienced by way of intrinsic nature belongs to feelings,
because they are experienced precisely by their own intrinsic nature.
The state of being experienced by way of association belongs to contact.

Regarding the phrase "contact to be experienced as pleasant," this refers to the objects being experienced by way of their being the focal point (*ālambana*). As it has been said: "Having seen forms with the eye, one experiences the form, but does not experience passion for the form," and so forth.
For, by means of feeling, one experiences that [karma] while taking it as an object;
this refers to the ripening-experiencability of karma, as in the detailed explanation:
"karma to be experienced in the present life," and so forth.
There is experience through manifestation (*saṃmukhībhāvavedanīyatā*).
As it has been said: "At the time when one experiences a pleasant feeling, at that time two other feelings have ceased for him.
For at the time when a pleasant feeling is present, there is no other feeling existing which he could experience.
When one brings that [result] into manifestation, one is said to "experience" it.
Therefore, because the ripening (vipāka) is to be experienced, karma is also described as "to be experienced as pleasure" (*sukha-vedanīya*), and so forth.
Furthermore, this threefold karma— namely, that which is to be experienced as pleasure and so forth— is to be understood as both determinate and indeterminate;
the indeterminate is that which is not necessarily to be experienced.
Furthermore, the determinate [karma] is of three kinds,
because it is to be experienced in the present life and so forth.

Karma that is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*), and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*)—these three types of karma are determinate (*niyata*). Together with indeterminate karma (*aniyatavedanīya*), there are thus four types of karma. Some maintain that there are five types of karma. (50)
Others, however, maintain that there are five kinds of karma, having divided karma with indefinite fruition into two types: that which is definite in its maturation and that which is indefinite.
In this regard, karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) ripens in the very same birth in which it was performed;
karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) ripens in the second birth; and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) ripens from that point onward.

Others maintain that even in another lifetime there is the ripening (*vipāka*) of karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*); its designation as such is established by virtue of its initial commencement.
[They argue] lest there be a case where such intended karma should have a very slight ripening.
The Vaibhāṣikas do not accept this.
For there is indeed karma whose fruit is proximate and not remote, and the opposite; it is like external seeds.
For example, the *suvarcalā* plant ripens in three fortnights and yields fruit after three fortnights, whereas barley, wheat, and the like take six months.
Others say that this constitutes a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*).
The Dārṣṭāntikas, however, formulate four alternatives:
there is karma that is fixed as to its state but not fixed as to its maturation;
namely, karma to be experienced in the present life and so forth, which is indeterminate with respect to its maturation.
There is karma that is fixed with respect to its ripening (*vipāka*) but not fixed with respect to its timing;
this refers to karma that is not fixed as to when it will be experienced, yet is fixed in its ripening.
There is karma fixed in both respects; this refers to karma that is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*) and so forth, and is also fixed in its ripening.
There is that which is not fixed in either way: namely, karma that is non-fixed as to its experience and non-fixed as to its ripening.
For those [beings], that karma is of eight kinds: karma to be experienced in the present life, whether fixed or non-fixed; and likewise up to karma that is non-fixed as to its experience.
However, they describe it thus: that which is to be experienced in the present life and so forth is necessarily fixed, while the fourth is unfixed.
It may be that one projects four types of karma in a single moment;
it may be that one employs another in three [unwholesome actions] while engaging oneself in sexual misconduct, such that they all reach completion simultaneously.
Furthermore, regarding these four types of karma:

The projection of a *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class of beings) occurs by means of three [types of karma]. For a *nikāya-sabhāga* is not projected by karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya*).
In which realm (*dhātu*) and in which destiny (*gati*) is how many kinds of karma projected?
In all cases, there is the projection of four [karmas];
in all three realms and in all destinies, there is the projection of the four karmas—both wholesome and unwholesome—as applicable. This is the general rule, and the following is its exception.
Wholesome [karma] has three types of results in hell. // 51 //
In the hells, there is the projection of three types of wholesome karma, but not that which is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*),

because of the absence of desirable maturation (*iṣṭavipāka*) there. Furthermore, a stable fool who is detached from a certain realm does not perform karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) in that realm.

From whichever stage a worldling becomes free from passion and remains firm, being of a nature not subject to falling away, he does not perform karma to be experienced upon rebirth in that very stage;
he performs the other three types. It continues: "The Noble One who is firm does not even perform karma to be experienced in another [life]."

However, since an noble person (āryapudgala) who is free from passion and is not subject to falling away does not perform karma to be experienced upon rebirth (upapadyavedanīya) or in subsequent lives (aparaparyāyavedanīya) in that [attained] state, he is not capable of returning again to a lower plane; he may, however, perform indeterminate (aniyata) karma or karma to be experienced in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya) while born there. Even one who is unstable [in the Peak of Existence], when born in the Desire Realm or at the Peak of Existence, does not [perform such karma]. // 52 //

However, even a noble person (āryapudgala) of the nature of falling away who is free from passion for the desire realm or the peak of existence is incapable of performing karma to be experienced upon rebirth or in subsequent lives within those two realms.
What is the reason?
Because such a person has fallen away from the fruit [of their meditative attainment].
Furthermore, we shall explain later that there is no passing away for one who has fallen away from the fruit.
Is there also the projection of karma in the intermediate state?
He says: there is.
The intermediate state projects twenty-two types [of karma] within the desire realm.
For the intermediate state belonging to the desire realm projects twenty-two types of karma.
How so?
For there are five stages of the embryo:
the stages of the kalala, arbuda, peśī, ghana, and praśākhā;
and five stages after birth.
There are the stages of infancy, childhood, youth, middle age, and old age.
Among these, the intermediate state projects karma to be experienced as a *kalala* (embryonic stage), whether it be of indefinite or definite timing;
and likewise up to karma to be experienced in old age and karma to be experienced in the intermediate state itself.

That [karma] has its fruit in the present life, and that same karma belonging to the intermediate state which was described as the elevenfold determinate [karma] should be understood as "to be experienced in the present life. What is the reason?
For that collection is indeed one alone. // 53 //
For this single homogeneous group (nikāyasabhāga) is projected by a single karma, comprising both the intermediate state (antarābhava) and the ten stages that follow it;
for this very reason, no separate karma to be experienced in the intermediate state is mentioned,
since it is projected by the same karma that projects [the experience] to be undergone upon rebirth (upapadyavedanīya).
Furthermore, what kind of action is to be understood as determinate?

That which is performed with intense affliction or faith, and that which is performed continuously; that which is done toward a field of qualities, and that which consists in the killing of one's parents. (54)

Indeed, that karma which is performed with intense affliction, that which is performed with intense faith, and that which is performed continuously or toward a field of qualities— this should be understood as determinate. In this context, the "field of qualities" refers to the Three Jewels, or to a certain distinguished person who has attained a specific fruit or meditative attainment.
For in those cases, even in the absence of intense defilements or pure faith, and even without continuity, wholesome and unwholesome karma becomes fixed;

this applies especially to one's parents— the mother and the father— and regarding them, whatever karma constitutes an act of killing, whether in such a manner or otherwise, that karma becomes fixed, and no other.
Now, what kind of action is to be understood as "to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*)?
An action that has its fruit in the present life arises from a distinction of field or intention;
or, an action is to be experienced in the present life due to a distinction of field.
