Their seasonal transformations are irregular; through covetousness they have dry fruits, through malice they have bitter fruits, and through wrong view they have few fruits or no fruits at all—this is their dominant fruit (adhipati-phala).
Is it by that very same karma that one becomes short-lived here, or by another?
Some say it is by that very same [karma];
they maintain that this is the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) while that was the outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*).

Regarding this, some say that it is by means of the preliminary application here [in this life] and the fundamental act there [in the next]; others say that it is stated to be "by way of taking life" because the inclusion of the accompanying factors is intended.

Furthermore, although this so-called "outflow fruit" (*niḥṣyanda-phala*) has been mentioned, it does not transcend these two: the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
It is described as such, however, because of a specific similarity.
What, then, is the reason that these paths of action (*karmapatha*) produce these three kinds of fruits?

For one who commits the taking of life, suffering is produced for the victim being killed, he is slain, and his vital energy (*ojas*) is destroyed; therefore, from this suffering, killing, and destruction of vital energy, there is a threefold result. // 85 //
By causing suffering to another, one becomes miserable in hell as the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*);
by killing, one becomes short-lived as the flow-on fruit (*niḥṣyandaphala*);
and by destroying vitality, external medicinal herbs become weak in potency as the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
The same should be applied to the others as well.

In this way, the threefold fruit of the wholesome paths of action should also be understood. By practicing, cultivating, and frequently performing the abstention from taking life, one is reborn among the gods.
If such a person returns to this state, coming into the common lot of human beings, they become long-lived; thus, everything should be applied by way of the opposite of the unwholesome [results].
Regarding that which was stated by the Blessed One—"false speech, false action, and false livelihood"—what is this "false livelihood" that is distinct from those two?
It is not something else;
rather, bodily and vocal action born of greed is itself false livelihood.
But the two ends of bodily and vocal action arise from hatred and delusion;
and this [category] has been set apart from those two.
Because it is difficult to purify;
for the nature of greed is captivating,
and the mind cannot be well-guarded against the karma arising from it.
Therefore, because livelihood is difficult to purify, it is specified separately therein in order to generate a sense of urgency.
And it is said in this regard:
"For householders, a view that is constantly diverse is difficult to purify."
"And livelihood indeed depends upon others for a monk whose view is dependent on others."
Furthermore, it is considered that wrong livelihood consists only of bodily and vocal action arising from greed for the requisites of life, and nothing else.
For dancing, singing, and so forth, when performed for the sake of one's own pleasure, are not considered part of the means of livelihood; such is the view.
Not according to the Sūtra. //86//
For in the *Śīlaskandhikā*, the Blessed One has classified even such things as watching elephant fights under wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
What is the reason?
Because they involve the enjoyment of improper objects.
This has been explained.
Regarding those five fruits previously mentioned, which action is abandoned by how many fruits?
In the path of abandonment that is still with outflows (*sāsrava*), action is accompanied by all five fruits.
The path for the sake of abandonment, or that by which afflictions (*kleśa*) are abandoned, is the "path of abandonment," namely the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Whatever contaminated (*sāsrava*) action exists within that [path], it possesses five fruits.
For its fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) is the maturation established within its own level.
The outflow fruit (*niḥṣyandaphala*) consists of subsequent similar dharmas born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*) is dissociation itself,
which is that very abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) consists of those factors drawn forth by it, such as the path of conviction (*adhimuktimārga*) and its co-arising factors,
as well as that which is cultivated in the future and the abandonment [of defilements].
The sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*) consists of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) other than its own nature, excluding those previously arisen.
Karma that exists within the four pure, untainted paths of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*) is fruitful by way of four fruits, excluding the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
Furthermore, this applies to any other tainted wholesome or unwholesome karma. (87)

Furthermore, whatever other wholesome (*kuśala*) contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma there is besides the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*), and whatever unwholesome (*akuśala*) karma there is—that too has four fruits, excluding the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*). However, the remaining uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma and that which is neutral (*avyākṛta*) have three fruits;
that is, uncontaminated karma other than the path of abandonment and neutral karma have three fruits, excluding the fruits of ripening (*vipākaphala*) and dissociation.
For a wholesome [mind], the wholesome and so forth are four, two, and likewise three. (88)
He will explain "in sequence" later.
For wholesome karma, wholesome dharmas are four fruits, excluding the ripened fruit (vipākaphala).
Unwholesome [dharmas] are two: the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) and the sovereign fruit (adhipatiphala).
The three neutral [dharmas] are [the results] excluding the outflow-result (niḥṣyanda-phala) and the disjunction-result (visaṃyoga-phala).
For an unwholesome [dharma], wholesome and so forth are two, three, and four respectively; the meaning is "in due order."
For unwholesome karma, wholesome factors are two results: the result of human effort and the dominant result;
unwholesome factors are three results, excluding the result of maturation and the result of dissociation;
and neutral factors are four results, excluding the result of dissociation.

For the two views—the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi)—which are neutral, are the outflow fruits (niḥṣyandaphala) of the unwholesome universal [defilements] and those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
For a neutral [cause], there are two, three, and three [results] respectively; these are the wholesome and so forth. (86)
For neutral (avyākṛta) karma, wholesome factors (kuśala-dharma) are two fruits: the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala) and the sovereign fruit (adhipati-phala).
Unwholesome factors (akuśala) are three fruits, excluding the fruit of maturation (vipāka-phala) and the fruit of dissociation (visaṃyoga-phala).
For unwholesome factors to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and so forth are the outflow fruit (niḥṣyanda-phala) of the two neutral views.
The indeterminate dharmas are these same three.
All [dharmas] are four [conditions] for a past [dharma];
"all" means those belonging to the three time periods.
For past karma, dharmas belonging to the three time periods constitute four fruits,
excluding the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*).
For middle [present] karma as well, future [dharmas] are likewise [four fruits].
For present karma as well, future dharmas are these same four fruits;
intermediate [dharmas] are two, and present dharmas are two for present karma: the fruit of human effort and the sovereign fruit.
For that which has not yet arisen, there are three fruits belonging to the future.
For a future [action], there are three future fruits—
excluding the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) and the fruit of disjunction (*visaṃyogaphala*).
For dharmas of its own level, there are four.

For karma belonging to its own level, dharmas of its own level constitute four fruits, excluding the fruit of disconnection (visaṃyogaphala). Dharmas of other levels constitute either three or two fruits;
if those dharmas of other levels are untainted (anāsrava), they constitute three fruits.
Excluding the fruits of maturation and disjunction—
because they do not fall within the realms—
if they are with outflows, there are two fruits: the fruit of human effort and the sovereign fruit.

For the karma of one in training (śaikṣa), the dharmas of one in training and so forth are three fruits, excluding the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala) and the fruit of dissociation (visaṃyogaphala).
The same applies to the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Those that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner [dharmas] are also [the results], excluding the fruition result (vipākaphala) and the outflow result (niḥṣyandaphala).
However, this is the case for the karma of a non-learner (aśaikṣa). // 61 //
The dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa) and so forth are one fruit, three fruits, and two fruits [respectively] for the karma of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
For the karma of one beyond training, the dharmas of those in training are one fruit—the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala).
The dharmas of those beyond training are three fruits, excluding the ripening fruit (vipākaphala) and the fruit of disconnection (visaṃyogaphala).
Neither-learner-nor-non-learner dharmas have two fruits: the fruit of human effort and the sovereign fruit.
For others than those two, learner and so forth have two, two, and five fruits respectively. (62)

For a karma other than those of the learner (śaikṣa) and the non-learner (aśaikṣa)—that is, for karma that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner—the learner dharmas are two fruits: the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala) and the dominant fruit (adhipati-phala). The non-learner dharmas are likewise. The neither-learner-nor-non-learner dharmas are five fruits.
Three, four, and one [are the fruits] of that which is to be abandoned by seeing; these are its subsequent [fruits].
For karma to be abandoned by seeing, dharmas to be abandoned by seeing constitute three fruits, excluding the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*).
Dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) constitute four fruits, excluding the fruit of dissociation.
Those [results] not to be abandoned are one: the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Of karma to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), there are two, four, and three [results respectively]. (63)

For karma to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), dharmas to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*) are two fruits: the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation are four fruits, excluding the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*).
Dharmas not to be abandoned (*apraheya*) are three fruits, excluding the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and the outflow fruit (*niḥṣyandaphala*).
For that which is not to be abandoned, there are respectively one, two, and four [fruits].

For an action that is not to be abandoned, dharmas to be abandoned by seeing constitute one fruit, the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*). Those to be abandoned by cultivation constitute two fruits, the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the sovereign fruit. Those not to be abandoned constitute four fruits, excluding the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Furthermore, the repetition of the term "in due order" is for the purpose of making it known that [the sequence] applies to the middle as well, just as it does to the beginning and the end;
for this is the nature of an elliptical expression (*peyāla*).
In the context of explaining karma, this point also ought to be inquired about.
In the treatises, action is described as being improperly performed, properly performed, neither properly nor improperly performed, and neither [of those].
What are the characteristics of each?
Some say that what is performed improperly is afflicted, as is that which deviates from the prescribed rule. // 94 //
Some say that afflicted action is that which is performed improperly because it arises from improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*).
Others say it is also that which deviates from the prescribed rule—
namely, that by which one ought to go, stand, eat, move about, and so forth.

And it performs that [action] in an improper manner; because it is performed in an improper way, it is "performed through non-application" (ayogavihita). Others maintain that wholesome karma is "performed through application" (yogavihita) and is not deviant from the rule.
Other than these two, there is that which is neither;
it is neither prescribed by yoga nor not prescribed by yoga.
Does a single karma project only a single birth, or does it project more than one?
Likewise, does a single karma project a single birth, or many?
For this is the established tenet:
a single [karma] projects a single birth.
A single karma projects only a single birth, not many births; this is what is meant by the term "homogeneous class" (nikāyasabhāga).
For when that [class] is obtained, one is said to be "born."

As for what was said by the Elder Aniruddha: "By the ripening of that single alms-offering, I was reborn seven times among the gods of the Trayastriṃśa heaven, and finally I have been born here in this foremost Śākya family"—
for it was because he had attained such prosperity and remembered his former births that he performed yet further meritorious deeds.

Then he demonstrated his emergence from it, just as a man who, having started with one dīnāra and accumulated a thousand by means of it, says: "By means of this single dīnāra, I have attained this sovereignty.
But others say:
Taking that alms-food as the basis, a great stream of volitions for giving arose within him; by some [volition], a certain fruit was grasped.
Even by many [moments], only one [projective force] is projected, so that the projection of the homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga) does not occur in fragments.
However, it is maintained that while the defiled group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*) is produced by a single karma, many karmas are required for its completion;
just as a painter, having sketched a form with a single brush-stroke, completes it with many more.

For instance, though human status is equal, one person possesses all sense faculties, limbs, and minor members, shining with the excellence of complexion, form, stature, and strength, while another among them is deficient in some respect.
Furthermore, it is not karma alone that projects birth;
what then?
Other things as well that possess maturation [project it].
In every respect, however, the two mindless attainments do not project [a rebirth], nor do their acquisitions. //65//
The homogeneous group (nikāyasabhāga) is not projected by the two mindless attainments (acittasamāpatti), even though they possess fruition (savipāka),
because they do not coexist with karma;
nor is it projected by acquisitions (prāpti), because karma has multiple fruits.
The Blessed One has spoken of three obstructions:
the obstruction of karma, the obstruction of afflictions, and the obstruction of maturation.
What is their intrinsic nature?
The deeds of immediate retribution, intense afflictions, and the miserable destinies; as well as the beings of Kuru and the non-conceptual beings—these are considered the threefold obscuration. (66)
The five actions of immediate retribution constitute the obstruction of karma;
namely: killing one’s mother, killing one’s father, killing an Arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and drawing blood from the body of a Tathāgata with a malicious mind.
The state of intense affliction is the obscuration of afflictions.
For affliction is of two kinds:
that which is intense, meaning habitual, and that which is sharp, meaning excessive.
In this context, that which is intense constitutes an obstruction, as in the case of eunuchs and others.
For even a defilement with an excessive force can be overcome if it is occasional; however, a continuous defilement cannot be overcome even if it is weak.
For when affliction is constant, one finds no time to exert effort for its destruction;
depending upon a weak [affliction], a middling one arises, and depending upon a middling one, an intense one arises.

Therefore, the obscuration consists of the three types of miserable destinies; and the obscuration of maturation consists of certain regions of the happy destinies, namely the inhabitants of Uttarakuru and the non-percipient beings.

To what do these constitute obstacles? They are obstacles for the Noble Path and the roots of goodness preparatory to the Noble Path. Indeed, other karmas—such as those fixed for the miserable realms, those fixed for birth from an egg or moisture, those fixed for being female, and those fixed for an eighth existence—should also have been mentioned.

However, only those [five] which are easily discerned and clearly understood through five criteria—by way of their basis, their fruit, their destiny, their mode of rebirth, and the person—are mentioned here, and no others.
Among these, the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is the most inferior;
after that is the obscuration of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*).
For the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that because of these two, one becomes incurable even in a second birth, due to their successive induction of further [obscurations].
What is the meaning of "immediate" (*ānantarya*)?
They are called immediate because they cannot be interrupted by another karma that has its fruit in a subsequent birth with respect to their own maturation;
that is to say, they cannot be set aside.

Alternatively, for the person who has committed that [act], there is no interval (*antara*) between passing away from here and going to rebirth in hell; thus, it is "immediate" (*ānantarya*). The state of being such is "immediacy. It is by connection with that dharma that one becomes immediate.
Like the state of a recluse (*śrāmaṇya*).
Now, among these obscurations, which one is to be understood as occurring in which realm of existence? First of all, the immediate offenses (*ānantarya*) occur exclusively in the three continents.
Not in Uttarakuru, nor in other destinies; how much less in another realm? Even there, it occurs only for men and women.
But it is not accepted for eunuchs and the like.
What is the reason?
That very reason which was indicated for the absence of non-restraint [is the same here].
Moreover,
due to the smallness of their assistance and their lack of shame, [respect] is respectively [lacking] toward one's mother and father, and toward them [the aforementioned persons].
It is said that for these beings, their parents provide little assistance, because they are the masters of an impaired physical existence and because their affection is slight;
thus, even toward their parents, no intense sense of shame (*apatrāpya*) arises in them such that by violating it they would be touched by an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*).
For this very reason, it is not accepted that animals or hungry ghosts (preta) can [commit such an offense].
The Venerable [Vasumitra] maintains that it would apply to those with sharp intellects, like a noble thoroughbred horse (ājāneya).
Furthermore, for a human who kills non-human parents, there would be no immediate retribution (ānantarya).
The obstruction of karma has been explained.
In the remaining five destinies. //67//
What, then, are the remaining two? They are the obscuration of afflictions and the obscuration of maturation.
Among these, the obscuration of maturation exists among human beings.
The Kauravas are beings who lack perception among the gods.
What is the intrinsic nature of the immediate offenses (*ānantarya*)?
Four are bodily actions and one is vocal action; three are the taking of life, one is false speech, and one is the preparation for the taking of life.
For the Tathāgatas are by nature incapable of being harmed.
The schism of the Saṅgha is called an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) because the fruit is metaphorically attributed to the cause;
or else, it is so called because [the Saṅgha] is split by means of it.
Schism in the Saṃgha (saṃghabheda), however, is by nature a lack of concord (asāmagrī); it is a dissociated (viprayukta) factor, non-defiled and neutral (akliṣṭāvyākṛta).
This lack of concord is a formation dissociated from mind (cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra), specifically an unobstructed-neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) phenomenon; that is what constitutes schism in the Saṃgha.
How could that be an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*)? Furthermore, the schismatic is not at all possessed of it;
rather, the Saṅgha is possessed of it. //68//
For the division belongs to that which is divided, not to the divider.
Now, with what is the divider endowed?
That fault, namely false speech, is what the divider is endowed with.
The schismatic is possessed of the fault of causing a schism in the Saṃgha;
that, moreover, is false speech;
and that, in turn, consists of the vocal intimation and non-intimation co-nascent with the schism in the Saṃgha.

And that schismatic, being possessed of that fault, is cooked in Avīci; he is cooked in the great hell of Avīci for an intermediate kalpa or a full kalpa. But by others, one is not necessarily cooked in Avīci.
Now, if one has committed many acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), they ripen immediately;
however, what happens to him because of them?
"From the excess [of deeds], there is an excess of suffering. (96)

For he, through numerous immediate [karmas], obtains in that Avīci hell a physical basis that is denser and more sensitive, as well as causes that are more numerous and more intense, by which he experiences sensations two, three, four, or five times greater. Who, then, is it that splits the Saṃgha?
One who is a monk, characterized by views and established in his conduct, causes a schism; it is a monk who causes the schism, not a householder, nor nuns and the like.
Furthermore, he is one whose temperament is dominated by views, not one whose temperament is dominated by craving.
One who abides in right conduct does not break that conduct, because his words would otherwise be untrustworthy.
Where does he break it? From wherever the Blessed One is present.
It cannot be split elsewhere, for it can only be split in the very presence of the Teacher;
this is because the Tathāgatas are difficult to overcome and their words are authoritative.
Whom does he split? Only the foolish worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), not the noble ones (*ārya*), because the latter have directly realized the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Others say that even they have not attained receptivity (*kṣānti*).
To what extent is the Saṃgha split?
It is split when there is receptivity toward another teacher and another path.
When they accept a teacher other than the Tathāgata and a path other than the path taught by him, to that extent the Saṃgha is said to be split.
For how long does it remain split?
Only for that very night.
He does not dwell [there]. // 100 //
For as soon as the schism in the Saṃgha has occurred, the Saṃgha is necessarily reunited;
this which is called a schism in the Saṃgha is also considered a schism of the Wheel (cakrabheda).

For at that time, the Wheel of Dharma of the Blessed One is indeed split, because the proceeding of the Path is brought to a halt; for this very reason, it is called both a "splitting of the wheel" (cakrabheda) and a "schism in the Saṃgha" (saṃghabheda).
Furthermore, where does the schism of the wheel (cakrabheda) occur? It occurs in Jambūdvīpa, not in the other continents.
By how many monks?
By means of "nine" and so forth; having begun with nine and so forth,
there is no fixed rule beyond that.
Eight monks constitute a Saṃgha;
the ninth is the schismatic.
For the Saṃgha must necessarily be divided into two factions.
In this way, there is a schism.
However, another kind of schism in the Saṃgha arises from a schism in formal acts (*karmabheda*);
that is, if they perform formal acts separately within a single boundary (*sīmā*).
And this differentiation of karma exists only in those three continents where the teaching is present.
By how many monks? By eight or more. //101//
The schism of the Wheel, however, does not occur during six times.
Which ones?
At the beginning, at the end, before the *arbuda* stage, before the pair [of disciples], when the Sage has passed away, and while he is still present.
Furthermore, when the boundary has not been formally established, a schism of the wheel does not occur. //102//
In the beginning, when the Wheel of Dharma has recently been set in motion;
and at the end, at the time of the Blessed One’s final nirvana—
in these two states, the Saṅgha becomes of one flavor.

Even during the intermediate period, it does not split until before the *arbuda* stage, as long as neither a moral corruption (*śīlārbuda*) nor a doctrinal corruption (*dṛṣṭyarbuda*) has arisen within the Teaching.
Furthermore, it does not split before the pair [of disciples], as long as the foremost pair of disciples (*śrāvakāgrayuga*) has not appeared;
for [the Sangha] must undergo a probationary period for the method of schism, and because it can be reunited by that means.

When the Sage, the Teacher, has passed away and entered parinirvāṇa, because there is no adversary; when the boundary has not been fixed—that is, as long as the boundary has not been established—for in a single boundary, a schism in the Saṅgha occurs due to the presence of two factions; during these times, there is no schism in the Wheel.
Furthermore, a schism of the Wheel does not occur for all those who have committed the [five] bound [offenses],
because it is dependent upon karma.
Why is it that the immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) exists in cases such as matricide and so forth, but not elsewhere?
Because of the rejection and destruction of the field of those who have been beneficial and of those possessing virtuous qualities:
first, regarding the killing of mother and father, it is due to the rejection of those who have been beneficial.
In what way, then, are they beneficial?
Because the personal existence (ātmabhāva) originates from those two,
what is their negation?
It is their relinquishment.
Because the Arhat is a field of merit, killing him constitutes an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*).
Furthermore, if the sexual characteristics (*vyañjana*) of the mother or the father were to change, the transgression would still exist in that one case even when the characteristics have shifted;
for this very reason it is said: "It may happen that one deprives a man of life who is neither his father nor an Arhat."
And one would be touched by the fault of an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-avadya*).
It might be that the mother's sexual organs (*vyañjana*) have been transformed.
[It is said: "It may be that one deprives a woman of life who is neither one's mother nor an Arhat, yet one would still be touched by the fault of an immediate transgression."
It might be that the father's sexual characteristics have been transformed. Thus, the *kalala* of one woman was discharged and swallowed by another through her womb.
Which of these two is his mother, such that killing her would constitute an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*)?
Because it originates from the mother's blood. //103//

The woman from whose blood this being was born is his mother; however, the second [woman] is to be regarded as such in all practical matters, for she is the one who nurtures, nourishes, and raises him. If, having directed an action against the biological mother, one kills another woman, there would be no immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
Even if one kills by means of a stratagem directed at someone other than the mother, there would still be no [resulting offense].
Here, one should cite as examples the killing of a mother who was hidden beneath a bed, and the killing of a father by a washerman’s son through a stratagem directed at a mosquito.
When one kills both a mother and another woman with a single blow, two non-informative (avijñapti) actions arise.
Informative action (*vijñapti*), however, is indeed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*),
because that karma is more powerful.
Furthermore, the Venerable Ghoṣaka maintains that informative action is also twofold, because it is an accumulation of atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Even when one kills an Arhat while perceiving him as not being an Arhat, it constitutes an immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), because the basis [of the act] is determined by the thought "I am killing [him].
If someone were to harm his father who is an Arhat, he would still incur only a single immediate retribution, because the basis is one and the same.
How then is this avadāna to be interpreted: "Go and say to Śikhaṇḍin: 'Two immediate retributions have been committed by you'?"
Regarding the statement, "Because his father was deprived of life and because he [was killed] as an Arhat," it should be said that this was due to two causes,
or rather, he was censured from two perspectives.
Is it necessarily an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) for a Tathāgata to have blood drawn by one with a wicked mind?
It would be so for one who intends to kill;
not for one who merely desires to strike the Buddha.
If he had produced the intention to strike, it would not [be an offense].
If he strikes one who is not an Arhat, but that person becomes an Arhat after the blow, then from the blow onwards he is an Arhat;
[the offense] does not apply to what follows the blow.
The term "immediate transgression" (ānantarya) continues to apply here.
For he has not performed the preliminary application (prayoga) toward that [transgression].
Would one, having performed the application for an immediate transgression and not having turned away from it, fail to attain detachment (vairāgya) or its fruit?
For one who has engaged in an immediate transgression (ānantarya), the attainment of detachment or its fruit is impossible. //104//

However, having performed the preliminary application for the path of action of another [type], when the Noble Path arises, the path of action does not arise again, because the basis (the body) is absolutely opposed to it.
Among these immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), which is the most blameworthy?
False speech regarding a schism in the Saṃgha is considered the most blameworthy of all.

That false speech intended for the purpose of causing a schism in the Saṅgha—which, for one who knows what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, reveals the contrary—is the most blameworthy among all forms of misconduct.
Why?
Because it strikes at the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata and because it creates an obstacle for the world regarding the path to heaven and liberation.
For when the Saṅgha is split, the world’s entry into the fixed course [of liberation], the attainment of the fruits, the fading of passion, and the destruction of the outflows are obstructed;

even the practices of meditation, study, recitation, and reflection do not proceed; and the world, including its gods, nāgas, and humans, remains agitated and dejected until it is reunited again. Furthermore, because the maturation [of that act] takes place in the Avīci hell for an eon.

Among the remaining immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), the fifth, third, and first are progressively more grave; the lightest of all is the killing of one's father. [If that is so, then why did the Blessed One state that among the three types of punishment, mental punishment is the most blameworthy, and further stated that wrong view is the supreme among blameworthy things? Having restricted the discussion to the immediate transgressions, it was stated that causing a schism in the Saṃgha is the most blameworthy.]
Restricting the three types of action, the punishment of mind (*manodaṇḍa*) is foremost; restricting views, false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is foremost.

Alternatively, with respect to the extent of their maturation (*vipākavistara*), the killing of many people, and the severance of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla-samuccheda*), they are foremost respectively.
Furthermore, among the well-conducted actions (*sucarita*), which one has the greatest fruit?
In the world, volition regarding the peak of existence is the most fruitful among wholesome [actions]. (105)
Furthermore, among wholesome karmas, the volition of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) is the most productive of great fruit for all [wholesome actions].
Its maturation (*vipāka*) is extremely peaceful for eighty thousand eons;
this was said with reference to the fruit of maturation.

However, with reference to the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*), the volition associated with the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) has the greatest fruit among all [volitions], because its fruit is the total exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*).
For this very reason, it is said to be "in the world.
Is one necessarily reborn in the hells only through the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*)?
One is necessarily reborn [in hell] even by actions similar to those of the immediate [offenses], though others say it is not necessarily immediately after.
He asks: "Which are those? and says:
Defiling one's mother who is an Arhatī, killing a Bodhisattva established in certainty, killing a Śaikṣa, and stealing from the means of subsistence of the Saṅgha. (106)
There are five actions similar to the immediate [offenses], the fifth being the destruction of a stūpa.
These five are, respectively, similar to the five immediate offenses:

if one defiles one’s mother who is an Arhat by committing unchaste acts; if one kills a Bodhisattva who has entered the state of certainty; if one kills a Śaikṣa; if one steals from the Saṅgha what is intended for its comfort; and the destruction of a stūpa.
It performs [this function].
Furthermore, other karma that possesses ripening (savipāka) also excessively obstructs [the path] at three times.
At which three?
Karma acts as a supreme obstacle to the attainment of patience, the state of a non-returner, and arhatship.
For one who is progressing from the Summits toward Receptivity, karmas leading to the miserable realms stand as obstacles,
because he is transcending the ground where their maturation occurs;
just as creditors confront a man who is abandoning his country.

For one attaining the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), the [karmas] belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) stand as obstacles, with the exception of those to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*). Likewise, for one attaining arhatship (*arhattva*), the [karmas] belonging to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyāvacara*) stand as obstacles in the same way.
Regarding what was stated as "the killing of a bodhisattva," from what point,
and starting from what basis, is one to be called a bodhisattva?
Because he performs the deeds that produce the marks;
from the moment he begins to perform the deeds whose maturation is the marks, he indeed becomes one who has entered the state of certainty.
How so?
For from that time onward, he always possesses a happy rebirth, is born into a noble family, has unimpaired faculties, is male, remembers his past lives, and does not turn back [from the path]. (108)
"His destination is praiseworthy" means he has a "good destination" (*sugati*) because of rebirth among gods or humans.
And within that good destination, he is born into a great *śāla* family of *kṣatriyas*, *brāhmaṇas*, or householders, and not into any other [low] lineage.
"His faculties are impaired" means he is one whose faculties (*akṣa*) are deficient.
"Not deficient" means not lacking any sense faculty (*avikalendriya*).
He is indeed a male, not a woman, much less a eunuch or the like.
And he becomes one who remembers his past lives (*jātismara*).
That which ceases in every birth is "nivṛt" (ceased); that which is not ceased is "anivṛt" (unceased),
meaning that which does not cease.
Because they are not wearied by any forms of suffering or by the various forms of misconduct of all sentient beings for the sake of benefiting them;

they are what the world calls "slaves who have not been purchased. For those great-souled Bodhisattvas, although they have attained the highest excellence of every kind of prosperity, remain subject to others through their causeless compassion toward all sentient beings.

Establishing themselves as being like the sons of outcasts through their lack of pride, they become those who endure all forms of humiliation from sentient beings and those who bear all hardships and constraints.
Furthermore, regarding that which was called "karma ripening into the marks": it is performed by a male in Jambūdvīpa, in the presence [of a Buddha], with a mind directed toward the Buddha.
For when only a hundred eons remain, one projects that [wisdom] consisting of reflection. // 106 //
Only in Jambudvīpa does a bodhisattva project the karma that ripens into the primary marks;
not elsewhere,
because the inhabitants of Jambudvīpa possess sharp intelligence.

It is performed by a male and not by a female; it occurs only while the Teacher is present; it is performed with volition directed solely toward the Buddha as its object; that karma consists of reflection (*cintā-maya*) and not of hearing (*śruta-maya*) or cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*);
and it projects [its result] when only one hundred eons remain, not during many more births.
However, by means of his intense vigor, the Blessed One Śākyamuni turned back nine eons and projected [the result] in ninety-one eons.

For this very reason it was said: "O village headman, from ninety-one eons ago until now, I do not recall nor do I know of even a single family that has been harmed or injured on account of giving alms-food to one who observes the vows."

From that time forth, because he possesses the innate recollection of his former births (*jātismara*), the Bodhisattva—having already emerged from the first incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*)—averts these four faults and acquires two virtues;
so say the former masters (*pūrvācāryāḥ*).
And as for those marks (*lakṣaṇa*):
Each [major mark] arises from a hundred merits.
What is the measure of that merit?
Some say it is the amount of the fruit of enjoyment belonging to all sentient beings, excluding those bodhisattvas who are close to enlightenment.
Others say that the trichiliocosm is brought into existence by the sovereign power of the karma of all sentient beings;
still others say that only the Buddhas know its measure.
Now, when the Blessed One was a bodhisattva, how many Buddhas did he attend upon?

In the first incalculable eon (*kalpāsaṃkhyeya*), there were seventy-five thousand Buddhas; in the second, seventy-six thousand; and in the third, seventy-seven thousand. Now, at the end of which incalculable eon was which Buddha? [They are listed] in reverse order, respectively.
Those born at the end of the three incalculable eons were Vipaśyin, Dīpaṃkara, and Ratnaśikhin;
during the time of the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin, the first incalculable eon was completed.
The second was under the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara;
the third was under the Tathāgata Vipaśyin;
and [the fourth was] under all of them.
Śākyamuni was formerly [thus]. // 110 //

There was formerly a perfectly enlightened Buddha named Śākyamuni, under whom the Blessed One, while still a bodhisattva, made his first vow: "May I become a Buddha of exactly this kind. Just as we have appeared in this Kali Yuga, so too did he; and like ours, his teaching lasted for a thousand years at its conclusion.
Now, in what state does a bodhisattva fulfill which perfection?
For one who gives everything to everyone out of compassion, there is the fulfillment of generosity.

When one gives everything to everyone—down to the eyes and down to the marrow—out of compassion and without desiring any special worldly prosperity, by this much the perfection of generosity becomes fulfilled.
Because he remains free from anger even when his limbs are being severed, he possesses both patience and ethical discipline, despite being subject to passion.

When even one who is not yet free from passion does not feel the slightest anger while his limbs are being severed, then his perfections of patience and ethical discipline become fulfilled. Regarding the perfection of vigor:

while the Blessed One was still a bodhisattva, he saw the Tathāgata Tiṣya entering the fire-element concentration within a jeweled cave; standing on one foot for seven days, he praised him with a single verse.
Neither in heaven nor on earth, neither in this world nor in the abode of Vaiśravaṇa,
neither in the divine realm of the gods nor in the cardinal or intermediate directions.
"Let him wander over the entire, flourishing earth with its mountains and forests;
for where else, O Great Śramaṇa, could there be another bull among men equal to you?
At that time, it is said, the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā) was fulfilled and nine eons were turned back.

Immediately following wisdom and meditative concentration, and immediately prior to enlightenment, there is the fulfillment of the perfections of meditation and wisdom; they are called "perfections" (pāramitā) because, in the diamond-like samādhi, one has reached the further shore of their own excellence.
It is stated in the Sūtra: “There are three bases of meritorious action:
the basis of meritorious action consisting in giving, that consisting in ethical discipline, and that consisting in cultivation.
How are these three the bases of meritorious action?
Merit, action, and its basis—these three are like the paths of action. (112)
These three are both merit (*puṇya*), action (*kriyā*), and basis (*vastu*) as appropriate; thus they are called "bases of meritorious action" (*puṇyakriyāvastu*).
For example, they are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*) because they are both actions and paths, or simply paths of action.
Among these, in the case of the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving (*dānamaya*), bodily and vocal action are of three kinds.
The volition that originates it is both merit and action;
the factors co-arising with it are merit alone;
however, that which consists of ethical discipline is only bodily and vocal action, and thus it is threefold.

Loving-kindness consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*) is both merit (*puṇya*) and the basis for meritorious action (*puṇyakriyāvastu*), because the volition associated with it performs its formative activity (*abhisaṃskaraṇa*) by way of loving-kindness. The volition and the ethical discipline (*śīla*) co-arising with that [loving-kindness] are both merit and action. Other factors co-arising with them are merit alone. Alternatively, "meritorious action" refers to the cause of merit, which is the application of merit (*puṇyaprayoga*); these three are its bases.
"Because one undertakes the application of merit for the sake of accomplishing these.
Others maintain that meritorious action is, in the ultimate sense, wholesome volition, and these are its bases.
What is this so-called "giving"?
That which is given is giving; however, in this context—
That by which something is given is "giving" (dāna).
One gives even by means of passion and other such afflictions.
And that is not what is intended here;
therefore, for the sake of specification, he says:
"out of a desire to honor and favor."
That by which one gives, out of a desire to honor or benefit others— what, then, is that?
It is bodily and vocal action, together with its motivation.
What, then, is that origination?
It is the group [of factors] by which that [mind] is originated.
And it is said in this regard:
“When a person gives away their own property with a virtuous mind, at that very moment the wholesome aggregates (skandhas) are designated as ‘giving. Thus it is said;
and that [giving] has the fruit of great enjoyment. // 113 //
And this basis of meritorious action consisting of giving has great wealth as its fruit; furthermore,
this suffix *-maya* should be understood in the sense of "consisting of," just as in the expressions "a house made of grass" or "a vessel made of leaves."
Now, this gift is indeed given for the benefit of oneself,
for the benefit of both, or for the benefit of neither. In that regard,
when a noble one who is not yet free from passion, or an ordinary person who is free from passion, gives a gift at a shrine (caitya), that is for their own benefit alone.
Because there is no benefit to others by that [gift].
When a noble one who is free from passion gives a gift to other beings— excluding that which is to be experienced in the present life— that gift is for the sake of others,
because they are benefited by it.
It is not for one's own sake,
because one has completely transcended the level where such [giving] would ripen.
When an ordinary person who is not free from passion, or one who is free from passion, gives to other beings, that gift is for the benefit of both.
When a noble one who is free from passion gives to a shrine— excluding that which is to be experienced in the present life— that gift is for the benefit of neither [the recipient nor the giver],
for it is given solely out of reverence and gratitude.
Generally, giving has been said to have great wealth as its fruit.
Furthermore, its distinction arises from the excellence of the giver, the object, and the field. (114)
In that regard, first,
the donor is distinguished: a donor endowed with qualities such as faith, ethical discipline, and learning becomes distinguished by means of faith and so forth.
The bestowal of the fruit by that [gift] is distinguished by the excellence of the donor of that gift;
and such a donor gives with reverence and so forth.

Because one gives with respect, with one's own hand, at the proper time, and without harming others, there results: respectfulness, delight in the sublime, obtaining gains at the proper time, and the state of being unassailable. // 115 //
Therefore, by giving such a gift as this, four specific benefits accrue to the donor in due order:
he becomes a recipient of honor,
and he gains a taste for sublime enjoyments.
And he obtains enjoyments at the proper time, not at an improper time;
and he obtains enjoyments that cannot be confiscated,
for his enjoyments are neither seized by others nor destroyed by fire and the like.
It has been explained how the giver is distinguished, and how, through that distinction, there is a distinction in the gift.
Now, how is the object distinguished?
The object is distinguished by its excellence of color and other qualities.
The term "distinguished" (viśiṣṭa) carries over [from the previous context].
If that which is given is endowed with even one of the qualities of color, fragrance, taste, or touch,
in this way the object is distinguished.
What results from giving such an object?
In due order,
one becomes handsome or famous.
From that, there arises loveliness and the quality of having limbs with a delicate touch pleasant for the seasons. // 116 //
By giving that which is endowed with excellent color, one becomes handsome; by giving that which is endowed with fragrance, one becomes renowned,
because one's fame, like a fragrance, is established in all directions.
By giving that which is endowed with flavor,
one becomes beloved, being as sweet-tasting as flavor itself.

By giving that which is endowed with pleasant touch, one comes to have delicate limbs, and one's limbs become pleasant to the touch according to the season, just like those of the Woman-Jewel (strīratna).
Now, how is the field distinguished?
The field is distinguished by way of its destiny, suffering, beneficence, and qualities.
First, it is distinguished by the distinction of destiny.
For it was said by the Blessed One: "Having given a gift to one who has gone to the animal realm, a hundredfold maturation is to be expected;
having given a gift to a human being who is immoral, a thousandfold [maturation is to be expected].
It is distinguished by the particularity of suffering.
For it has been said regarding the material bases of meritorious action (*aupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*):

after describing the gift to the sick, the gift to those who attend to the sick, and the gifts during the cold season and so forth, it was stated: "It is not possible for a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family endowed with these seven material bases of meritorious action [to calculate the measure of their merit]."
"In order to grasp the measure of merits.
[This occurs] due to the distinction of being a benefactor, as in the case of one's mother and father, or other benefactors, as illustrated in the *Ṛṣyamṛga-jātaka* and other such stories;
and due to the distinction of qualities, as in the statement: "Having given to one who possesses moral discipline (*śīlavat*), the ripening result is a hundred-thousandfold," and so forth.
Of all gifts, however, the foremost is that given by one who is liberated to one who is liberated.
As it was said by the Blessed One: "That which a person free from passion gives to another free from passion—this is the most excellent gift among material gifts."

Furthermore, whatever gift a bodhisattva gives to another bodhisattva for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings—that is the foremost kind of giving, even among those who are not yet liberated giving to one who is not yet liberated.
Setting that aside, there are eight other types of giving spoken of by the Blessed One; of these, [the former is supreme].
The eighth [chapter]. //117//
The word "foremost" (agram) continues [from the previous context].
Which are the eight?
Giving upon approaching; giving out of fear; "he gave to me, so I give"; "he will give to me, so I give"; "giving was previously given by my ancestors."

Thinking, "I give for my grandfathers," one gives a gift for the sake of heaven, a gift for the sake of fame, a gift for the sake of adorning the mind, a gift for the sake of purifying the mind, and a gift for the sake of the equipment of yoga in order to attain the supreme goal. In that regard, "giving upon arrival" refers to giving to those who are nearby or have approached, according to the ancient teachers.
The gift out of fear is that which one gives, seeing [the recipient] facing destruction, thinking, "It is better that I give this.
The remainder is not analyzed because it is easy to understand.

It is stated in detail in the Sūtra that giving a gift to one who has entered the path toward the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala-pratipannaka*) yields immeasurable maturation; even more immeasurable than that is the gift given to a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
Furthermore, [immeasurable merit is gained from giving] to one's mother, father, the sick, those who practice the Dharma, and those in their final birth.
And the gift given even to those who are not noble ones yields immeasurable merit for a bodhisattva. //118//
From these five individuals, even though they are still ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), the sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*) results in immeasurable fruit.
Among them, the one in his final birth is the Bodhisattva who is in his last existence (*caramabhavika*).
To which of the four types of distinguished fields should the righteous one be assigned?
To the category of benefactors.

For he is a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), a giver of the eye of wisdom to beings blinded by ignorance, an illuminator of the even and the uneven, and, in brief, a bringer about of the untainted Dharma-body (*anāsrava-dharmakāya*).
The performer of the Buddha's work.
One who wishes to know the gravity or lightness of karmas should, in brief, understand six causes;
namely:
the subsequent action, the field, the basis, the preliminary application, the volition, and the intention.
Due to the mildness or intensity of these [faculties], there is mildness or intensity of karma. //116//
"Repetition" (pṛṣṭha) refers to the subsequent re-enactment of what has already been done.
"Field" (kṣetra) refers to that toward which benefits or harms are performed.
"Basis" (adhiṣṭhāna) is the course of action (karmapatha).
Application is the bodily and vocal action for that purpose;
volition is that by which one brings the course of action to completion;
intention is the very disposition [to act], thinking, "I shall do such and such," and "I shall not do such and such."

For some, that action becomes heavy solely by virtue of being undertaken for the sake of another; because it remains fixed by the necessity of its maturation (*vipāka-naiyamyena*). For others, it becomes heavy solely by virtue of the field (*kṣetra*).
In that very field, moreover, it becomes a heavy [karma] by virtue of the basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and not otherwise.
For example, it is so through the taking of life of one's mother or father, but not in the same way through taking what is not given and so forth.
The same should be applied to other cases as well.
However, for one whose [mental states] are all intense, their karma should be understood as exceedingly intense and heavy;
for one whose [mental states] are weak, it should be understood as exceedingly weak.
Action is said to be both performed (*kṛta*) and accumulated (*upacita*).
How does action become accumulated?
By means of five factors.
Karma is said to be "accumulated" (upacita) by way of intentionality and completion, by way of being free from regret and its opposite, by way of its retinue, and by way of its maturation. //120//
How is it through intention? It is that which is done intentionally, not without prior awareness, nor done impulsively.
How is it through meditative attainment?
Someone goes to the states of woe through one misdeed, someone through as many as three;
someone through one path of action, someone through as many as ten.
In that regard, for whichever number of factors one goes by, as long as that [process] is not completed, that karma is "done" but not "accumulated"; once it is completed, however, it is accumulated.
How is it [determined] by way of being free from the opposite of remorse?
That action becomes one that is without regret and without an antidote.
How is it [determined] by way of its retinue?
It is unwholesome and accompanied by an unwholesome retinue. How so in terms of its maturation?
It is certain in the giving of its maturation.
In the same way, this should also be applied to wholesome [karma].
Otherwise, the action is merely performed and not accumulated.
[It has been stated that giving at a shrine by one who still possesses passion is for one's own sake.]
In that case, since there is no enjoyer, how can there be merit?

For merit is of two kinds: that which follows from relinquishment, which arises from the act of giving itself, and that which follows from enjoyment, which arises from the enjoyment of the gift by the recipient.
In the case of a shrine (caitya), the merit is that which follows from relinquishment.
There is no merit resulting from enjoyment.
How, then, can there be merit in that case when nothing is being accepted? Furthermore, what is the reason that merit must exist when there is a recipient, but not when there is none?
This is without cause, because there is an absence of benefit to anyone whatsoever.
For if merit were to arise solely from benefiting others, then it would not exist in the cultivation of the immeasurables such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), nor in the cultivation of right view.
Therefore, it must be admitted that merit exists even in the case of a shrine (*caitya*),
even though no one receives it, just as in the case of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth.

Just as in the practices of loving-kindness and the like, merit arises from one's own mind even without a recipient or a benefit conferred upon others, so too, even when a virtuous person has passed away, merit produced by devotion toward them arises from one's own mind.
Merit arises;
however, it might follow that the act of giving and honoring would then be useless. This is not so, because the devotion that motivates those actions is more excellent.

For just as when one intends to kill an enemy, a much greater demerit arises for one who, with the perception of that person as an enemy, performs the physical or verbal action instigated by that intention even after the enemy has died;
it does not arise through the mere intention alone.
Likewise, when the Teacher has passed away, for one who performs acts of giving and honoring arising from devotion toward him, a much greater merit is produced than by mere devotion alone.
If the seed of the act of giving in one's own field yields a desirable fruit, then in that [same] field it would yield an undesirable fruit;
yet even in a bad field, there is the attainment of a desirable fruit, because of the non-inversion of the fruit and the seed. //121//
Even in a bad field, it is observed that the fruit does not deviate from its seed: from a grape seed, only a sweet grape fruit arises; from a neem seed, only a bitter neem tree.
Likewise, even in a bad field, the seed of giving that proceeds from an intention to benefit others results only in a desirable fruit, or else it becomes fruitless.
The section on the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving, along with its related discussion, is concluded.
That which consists of morality (śīlamaya) should be explained;
it is said that immorality (dauḥśīlya) is unwholesome form (rūpa), and morality is the abstention from that.
For unwholesome form is called misconduct;
therefore, abstention from it is ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Furthermore, that abstention—
It is twofold:
the informative act (*vijñapti*) by which one abstains, and that non-informative act (*avijñapti*) which is the very state of abstaining.
Furthermore, morality (*śīla*) is not merely the abstention from immoral conduct (*dauḥśīlya*).
What then?

It is the twofold abstention even from that which, while not inherently immoral, has been prohibited by the Buddha; that is, the abstention from eating at improper times and so forth, which was prohibited by the Blessed One, the Buddha. This is ethical discipline (*śīla*).
However, for one who has undertaken the training rules, immorality arises from the transgression of them.
Ethical conduct has been explained in brief.
But when it is purified, it possesses four qualities. //122//
That ethical discipline possesses four qualities;
by the opposite [of these], it is impure. Now, as to how it possesses four qualities, he says:
It is unimpaired by immorality and its causes, and it relies upon their opposites and tranquility.
First, it is unimpaired by immorality— that is, by the aforementioned immorality—
and it is also unimpaired by its causes.

It is free from the afflictions and secondary afflictions such as greed; it relies on the antidote to immorality because it is based upon the foundations of mindfulness; it is well-supported, not relying on any particular excellence of rebirth.
Because it is dedicated toward nirvāṇa.
Others say it is by five reasons:
it is purified by the fundamental paths of action, purified by the preliminary stages, unimpaired by discursive thoughts, sustained by mindfulness, and dedicated toward nirvāṇa.
Others say that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is fourfold:
discipline out of fear (*bhaya-śīla*), which is observed out of fear for one's livelihood, ill repute, punishment, or an unfortunate rebirth;
and discipline of aspiration (*āśāsti-śīla*), which is produced by craving for existence, enjoyments, and honor.
Ethical discipline in conformity with the factors of enlightenment is that which belongs to those possessing right view for the sake of liberation;
it is pure ethical discipline, being untainted because of its stainlessness.
The section on ethical discipline is concluded.

But what is this "cultivation" (bhāvanā) that consists of wholesome states associated with meditative concentration (samāhita)? What is meant by "associated with concentration"? It refers to that which has concentration as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and that which is co-existent (sahabhū) with it.
For what purpose is this called "cultivation" (bhāvanā)? Because it perfumes the mind (cittavāsanāt). // 123 //
For that concentrated wholesome state perfumes the mind exceedingly,
because it causes the continuum to become permeated with its qualities,
just as sesame seeds are perfumed by flowers.
It has already been stated that giving leads to great wealth; now,
as for ethical discipline and cultivation,
ethical discipline leads primarily to heaven, while cultivation leads to dissociation from the defilements.
Generosity also leads to heaven, but ethical discipline is primary;
ethical discipline also leads to dissociation from defilements, but cultivation is primary.
The Sūtra states: "Four types of persons generate Brahma-merit.
What is this Brahma-merit?
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that it is what was stated in order to make known the measure of the karma that has the marks [of a Great Man] as its maturation.
The former teachers, however, explain that the four [types of gifts] possess the merit of a Brahma-world because one rejoices in the heavens for an eon (kalpa).
The merit by which one rejoices in the heavens for an eon is this "Brahma-merit," because the lifespan of the Brahmapurohita deities is one eon. In another school, they recite this verse:
“He generates Brahma-merit and rejoices in the heavens for an eon.”
The gift of material things has been explained;
the gift of the Dharma must now be discussed.
This is what is said:
The gift of Dharma is the teaching of the sūtras and so forth as they truly are, without affliction.
Teaching the sūtras and so forth as they truly are and without affliction is the gift of Dharma.
Therefore, those who teach the Dharma erroneously inflict a great loss of merit upon themselves.
Or with defiled minds, desiring gain, honor, and fame.

It has been stated that the wholesome is threefold according to the distinction of the bases of meritorious action; furthermore, the wholesome is of three types: conducive to merit, conducive to nirvana, and conducive to penetration. (125)
That which has a desirable maturation is conducive to merit (*puṇyabhāgīya*). That which, once arisen, makes one destined for final nirvāṇa is conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).

When someone, upon hearing a discourse that illuminates the defects of cyclic existence, selflessness, and the qualities of nirvāṇa, experiences horripilation and the shedding of tears, it should be understood that they possess the roots of goodness conducive to liberation; just as the presence of seeds in a granary hole is inferred from the sprouting of shoots during the rainy season.

The four stages conducive to penetration, beginning with "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), we shall explain later. Regarding that which is called in the world "writing, sealing, calculation, poetry, and arithmetic," what is their intrinsic nature?
Action set in motion by yoga, together with its motivator, is threefold; writing, sealing, calculation, poetry, and arithmetic follow this sequence respectively. (126)
"Initiated by yoga" means initiated by a specific skillful means (*upāya*).
"Threefold action" refers to the actions of body, speech, and mind.
Among these, writing and seals are first of all bodily action initiated by yoga, together with its origination.
Calculation and poetry are vocal action;
these have the nature of the five aggregates.
Enumeration is mental action.
That which is the mental synthesis of phenomena (dharmas).
Now, some synonyms for phenomena are stated:
faulty, obscured, inferior, and afflicted phenomena.
Defiled phenomena have synonyms such as "faulty," "obscured," and "inferior. Pure and stainless phenomena are "excellent."

"Exquisite" (*praṇīta*) is a synonym for wholesome and untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena. It follows as a matter of course that those other than the inferior and the exquisite are "intermediate. Conditioned wholesome phenomena are to be cultivated.
The term "to be cultivated" is a synonym for wholesome conditioned phenomena;
it follows as a matter of course that the remaining ones are not to be cultivated.
Why, then, is the unconditioned not to be cultivated?
Because it is not to be practiced repeatedly and because it is without fruit;
for service is undertaken for the sake of a fruit,
whereas all other phenomena are surpassed by it.
But liberation is unsurpassed. // 127 //
Indeed, there is nothing more distinguished than nirvāṇa;
and it is distinguished above all else because it is wholesome and eternal.
This concludes the fourth chapter of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, titled "Exposition of Karma. Now begins the fifth chapter.
"Oṃ, homage to the Buddha.
It has been said that "the variety of the world is born of karma.

Furthermore, those karmas undergo accumulation by the power of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*); without the latent dispositions, they are not capable of bringing about the production of existence (*bhava*).
Therefore, it should be understood that the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are the root of existence;
for when a defilement (*kleśa*) is active, it performs ten functions.

It strengthens the root, establishes the continuum, brings about the field, produces the outflow, brings forth karmic existence, grasps its own equipment, causes delusion regarding the object, bends the stream of consciousness, causes one to deviate from the side of the wholesome, and pervades for the sake of bondage by means of not transcending the realms.
And how many are these latent dispositions?
In brief, there are six. Which ones?
There are six: attachment, as well as aversion, pride, ignorance, views, and doubt;
the inclusion of "as well as" (tathā) is for the purpose of making known that the others also adhere to their respective objects by the power of attachment.
And this we shall explain later; they, moreover, are as follows: //1//
Due to the division of attachment into six, seven are taught;
these same six underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are stated as seven in the Sūtra by making a twofold division of attachment:

the underlying tendency of attachment to sense-pleasures (kāmarāga-anuśaya), the underlying tendency of aversion (pratigha-anuśaya), the underlying tendency of attachment to existence (bhavarāga-anuśaya), the underlying tendency of pride (māna-anuśaya), the underlying tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya), the underlying tendency of views (dṛṣṭi-anuśaya), and the underlying tendency of doubt (vicikitsā-anuśaya).

How is this to be understood: is the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of sensual desire itself the "latent tendency of sensual desire" (*kāmarāgānuśaya*), or is it the latent tendency *of* sensual desire that is the "latent tendency of sensual desire"? What follows from this?
If the latent tendency were identical to sensual desire itself, there would be a contradiction with the Sūtra.
"In this case, a certain person does not frequently dwell with a mind obsessed by sensual desire.
He understands, as it truly is, the further transcendence of the obsession that has arisen regarding sensual desire.
That obsession with sensual desire is thoroughly and correctly struck down by him with force, and is abandoned along with its underlying tendencies."

If the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) were distinct from sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), it would follow that the latent tendency is dissociated [from consciousness], which contradicts the Abhidharma statement: "The latent tendency of sensual desire is associated with three faculties.
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that sensual desire itself is the latent tendency;
thus, up to and including doubt, the defilement itself is the latent tendency.
[But was it not already stated that such a view contradicts the Sūtra?]
There is no contradiction;
the meaning is "with latent tendencies" (*sānuśaya*) and "with continuations" (*sānubandha*).
Alternatively, the word "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) in the Sūtra is used figuratively for "possession" (*prāpti*).
Just as fire is suffering;

however, in the Abhidharma, the term *anuśaya* refers specifically to the afflictions (*kleśa*) according to their defining characteristics. Therefore, the *anuśayas* are exclusively associated [with the mind].
How is this understood?
Because the latent dispositions (anuśaya) cause affliction of the mind, act as obstructions, and are contrary to wholesome states.

Because the mind becomes afflicted by the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), new wholesome states do not arise, and one falls away from those already arisen; therefore, they are not dissociated (*viprayukta*).
(Now, suppose it were the case that this were so even for dissociated factors.)
Wholesomeness would never be perceived,
because those [unwholesome states] are always present;
yet it is indeed perceived.
Therefore, as for the statement:
“And because the wholesome is observed, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) here are non-associated,” this is not a proof;
for one who maintains that the latent disposition is a non-associated factor does not accept all of this as being produced by a latent disposition.
He maintains that it is indeed produced by the afflictions.
But this is correct according to the Sautrāntikas.
And how is it for the Sautrāntikas?
The latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of sensual desire is the "sensual-desire-latent-tendency" (*kāmarāgānuśaya*).
Furthermore, the latent disposition (*anuśaya*) is neither associated (*saṃprayukta*) nor dissociated (*viprayukta*), because it is not a separate substantial entity.
For a defilement that is dormant is called a latent disposition,
whereas one that is awakened is called an outburst (*paryavasthāna*).
And what is its dormancy? It is the persistence of the state of being a seed when it is not manifest. What is its awakening?
Manifestation.
What is this so-called "state of being a seed"?
It is the capacity of the personal existence (ātmabhāva) to produce afflictions, which has arisen from afflictions.
Just as the power to produce memory arises from the knowledge of experience, and just as the power to produce a rice seedling arises from a rice fruit;

for one who postulates a separate, dissociated entity called *anuśaya* (latent tendency) as the meaning of the "seed" of the afflictions (*kleśa*), it follows that he must also postulate a separate entity as the "seed" of memory.
As for the fact that in the *Ṣaṭṣaṭka-sūtra* the affliction itself is stated to be the *anuśaya*: "In him, there exists a latent tendency of attachment toward a pleasant feeling."
Because of the statement "it exists," it is not the latent tendency (anuśaya) at that very moment.
When, then, does it exist?
When it is dormant (prasupta).
Or rather, this should be regarded as a metaphorical designation applied to the cause.
Let this incidental discussion rest;
let the treatise proceed.
Regarding this classification of attachment made in the Sūtra— namely, attachment to sense-pleasures (*kāmarāga*) and attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*)—
what is this attachment to existence?
Attachment to existence arises from two realms.
Attachment arising from the realms of form and formlessness is designated as "attachment to existence" (*bhavarāga*).
For what reason is it so designated?
It is so designated because it is inwardly directed and to prevent the misconception that it is liberation. //2//
For their attachment is generally to meditative attainments (*samāpatti-rāga*);
and since that is directed inwardly, it is therefore "attachment to existence" (*bhava-rāga*).
It is said that this was stated for the purpose of turning back certain people's notion that there is liberation within those two realms.
Existence (*bhava*), however, is simply the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).

And those beings, while relishing the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) together with its basis, relish the personal existence itself because they are free from passion for the sense-desires (*kāma*).
Therefore, that passion is called "passion for existence" (*bhavarāga*).
Furthermore, these six underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are made ten in the Abhidharma. How so?
The views (dṛṣṭi) are five: the view of a self-identity (satkāya-dṛṣṭi), false views (mithyā-dṛṣṭi), and the view of grasping at extremes (antagrāha-dṛṣṭi).
Furthermore, there are ten [factors] consisting of the adherence to views and the adherence to rules and observances. //3//
When the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are divided by treating views as fivefold, they become ten.

Five have the nature of views: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Five do not have the nature of views: attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Furthermore, these ten underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are made into ninety-eight in the Abhidharma:
thirty-six belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara), thirty-one belonging to the form realm (rūpāvacara), and thirty-one belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara).
How is this done?
In brief, these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the three realms are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Among them, first, there are thirty-two belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by insight.
To the question "Which are they?", he says: "These ten, seven, seven, and eight, excluding three and two views respectively."
They are abandoned in due order within the realm of desire by means of the vision of suffering and the other [truths]. //4//
Regarding these ten underlying tendencies that have been mentioned, all ten exist in the desire realm as being abandonable by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaheya*).
From among these very same [ten], seven are abandonable by the vision of origin (*samudayadarśanaheya*).

Seven are abandonable by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśanaheya*), excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the misapprehension of rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Eight are to be abandoned by the vision of the path,
excluding the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of grasping at extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi).
Thus, these thirty-two latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) are to be abandoned through vision.
Because they are abandoned by the mere vision of the truths,
there are four [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation;
namely, attachment, aversion, pride, and ignorance.
Because, after one has seen the truths, [the defilements] are abandoned through the cultivation of the path.

Thus, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is of one type, to be abandoned by seeing suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaheya*). The same applies to the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). The false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is of four types, to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origin, cessation, and the path (*duḥkha-samudaya-nirodha-mārga-darśanaheya*).
In the same way, adherence to views and doubt [are abandoned through the vision of suffering].
Adherence to rules and observances is of two types: that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the path.
Attachment, aversion, pride, and ignorance are of five types: those to be abandoned by the vision of the four truths and those to be abandoned by cultivation.
Of these, what kind are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, and so on, up to what kind are to be abandoned by cultivation?
Those whose objects are to be abandoned by the vision of a particular truth are themselves to be abandoned by the vision of that truth; the remainder are to be abandoned by cultivation.

These same twelve views, along with four doubts, five attachments, five aversions, five conceits, and five ignorances— these constitute the thirty-six proclivities belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*).
Furthermore, those same [proclivities], excluding the aversions,
exist in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
Having abandoned the fivefold hostility, those same thirty-one underlying tendencies (anuśaya) belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara) remain;
as it is in the realm of form, so it is in the formless realm (ārūpya).
There are thirty-one underlying tendencies;
thus, they are considered to be ninety-eight. (5)

Thus, these six underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are considered by the Abhidharmikas to be ninety-eight through the distinctions of their aspects (ākāra), types (prakāra), and realms (dhātu). Regarding those underlying tendencies said to be abandoned by vision (darśana-prahātavya), are they necessarily abandoned by vision alone?
He says: "No. What then?
Those [defilements] born of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) that are to be abandoned by patience (*kṣānti*) are to be abandoned by insight (*dṛgheya*) alone;

those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) born of the stage of the peak of existence which are to be abandoned by the patience of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānakṣānti*) are to be abandoned by insight alone, not by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).
As for those born of the remaining [stages]:
The phrase "to be abandoned by vision and cultivation" continues [from the previous context].

In the remaining stages, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are to be abandoned by the receptivities (*kṣānti*) of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) are, for the noble ones (*ārya*), to be abandoned by vision; for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), they are to be abandoned by cultivation, as appropriate.
But those which are to be destroyed by non-acceptance are destroyed by cultivation alone. //6//
Those latent dispositions (anuśaya) in all stages that are to be destroyed by knowledge are always to be abandoned through cultivation for both [types of practitioners].

Others maintain that for outsiders (*bāhyaka*), those views to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) are not actually abandoned. For instance, in the *Mahākarmavibhāga-sūtra*, it is stated that there is the active manifestation of views— directed toward the desire realm— even among those who have attained freedom from passion (*vītarāga*), such as those who speculate about the past (*pūrvāntakalpaka*), the eternalists (*śāśvatavādin*), the partial-eternalists (*ekatya-śāśvatika*), and those who advocate for causeless origination (*ahetusamutpattika*).
Furthermore, the desire realm is not the object of the afflictions belonging to the form realm, because [those in the form realm] are free from passion for it.
Therefore, those [afflictions] that have not been abandoned are exclusively associated with the desire realm.
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that they fall away at the very same moment as the arising of the [wrong] view, just like Devadatta.
The five views have been specified by name, but not by way of their intrinsic nature (svabhāva). What, then, is their intrinsic nature?
