The views of self and what belongs to self, of permanence and annihilation, of non-existence, and of regarding the inferior as superior; the view of causelessness and the view regarding what is not the path—these are the five views. (7)

The view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) or the view of what belongs to a self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*) is the view of a real body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*). It is "real" (*sat*) because it perishes (*sīdati*); "body" (*kāya*) means an accumulation, a collection, or an aggregate (*skandha*).
This body is real, thus it is called "satkāya," referring to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandhāḥ*).
It is explained in this way precisely to cause one to abandon the notion of permanence and the notion of a composite whole;
for it is preceded by this [notion] that the grasping at a self occurs with respect to them.
The view regarding the existing body is the "view of a self-existent body" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
While every view that has an outflowing object (*sāsrava-ālambana*) pertains to the existing body,
it is specifically the view of "self" and "mine" that is designated as the "view of a self-existent body."
It is so that it may be understood that this [view] does not refer to a self or to what belongs to a self.

As it has been said: "Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins regard anything as a self, they all regard these very five aggregates of clinging as such. The view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is either the view of permanence (*dhruvadṛṣṭi*) or the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) regarding that very thing which is conceived of as a self.
Because it involves grasping at the extremes of eternalism and nihilism, the view that "it does not exist" when the truths such as suffering do exist is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Indeed, every view that functions with a perverted nature is wrong view; however, only one [such view] has been mentioned here.
Because it possesses an exaggeration [of deficiency], like [the perception of] a foul-smelling wound;
for this is a deprecating [view], whereas others are superimposing. Viewing what is inferior as supreme is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
What is inferior?
Everything that is with outflows (sāsrava),
because it has been abandoned by the noble ones (ārya).
The grasping at that as foremost is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Although it should have been stated as "the adherence to views and so forth" (*dṛṣṭyādiparāmarśa*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) has been omitted.
The view of a cause in what is not a cause, and the view of a path in what is not a path, is the adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
For example, Maheśvara is not the cause of the worlds, yet one regards him as such; or Prajāpati or some other being.
Furthermore, entering fire or water and so forth are not causes for rebirth in heaven, yet one regards them as such.
Mere rules and observances, as well as the knowledge of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and so forth, are not the path to liberation; yet one views them as the path.
In this case too, it is said that the word "and so forth" has been omitted; these are to be understood as the five views.
If the view of a cause in what is not a cause is the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*),
why is this not to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśanaprahātavya*)?
For whoever perceives Īśvara, Prajāpati, or another as the cause, does so by being dogmatically attached to that [being] as eternal, unitary, and a self that is the agent.

Therefore, because of the misconception of a permanent self regarding Īśvara and other such entities, one engages [in worldly activity]; thus, this attachment to a [primary] cause is to be abandoned only by the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana). //8//
For it is precisely through the vision of suffering that those two graspings—of permanence and of self—are abandoned in regard to them;
therefore, the attachment to a cause produced by those two is also abandoned for that very reason.

Furthermore, one who perceives the attainment of heaven through such acts as entering water or fire, or purity through moral precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), must also be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*). For this is the scriptural reading: "Those who hold such views and speak thus: 'Insofar as this person or individual lives having undertaken the cow-vow, the deer-vow, or the dog-vow...'"

By that [view], he is purified, liberated, transcends pleasure and pain, and attains the transcendence of pleasure and pain. He perceives what is not a cause as a cause. "The adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering," and so forth in detail.
But for what reason is this to be abandoned by the vision of suffering?
Because they are mistaken regarding suffering; because all [afflictions] that have contaminated objects as their focus are mistaken regarding suffering.
Or else, what other kind of adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is there that is to be abandoned by the vision of the path?
What of that which has as its object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*)?
For even that is indeed a misconception regarding suffering (*duḥkha*).

Furthermore, how could one who possesses false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) or doubt (*vicikitsā*) directed toward the path—either seeing "there is no path to liberation" or doubting it—ever rely on that [false view or doubt] for purification? Or, if having clung to another path to liberation, one says, "This is not the path to liberation," [how can they be purified]?
He also believes in purification through that other [view] alone, and not through that false view;
thus, for him as well, it is not established that this [false view] has as its object what is to be abandoned by the vision of the path.

Furthermore, why is he who believes in purification through a false view that has as its object what is to be abandoned by the vision of origin or cessation not himself to be abandoned by the vision of those [truths]?
Therefore, this matter must be examined:
regarding what was stated as "the inversion of a permanent self" and so forth,
are there only these two inversions?
There are four perversions:
[taking] the impermanent as permanent,
and [taking] suffering as happiness.
"Pure in the impure," and "self in the non-self"— what is the intrinsic nature of this fourfold set of inversions?
From three views, the four perversions arise: from the view of extremes, the eternalist view is the perversion of permanence;
from the esteeming of views, there are the perversions of pleasure and purity.
The view of self within the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the perversion of self. Others say it is the entire [view of a real body]. How is the view of "mine" a perversion?
"And how is there no perversion?
From the *Viparyāsa-sūtra*:

'Seeing oneself as the master therein, one sees [what belongs to] the self'; thus, this view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) itself has two aspects. Now, if from the notion 'I' there were a distinct view 'mine', [it would follow that...]"
The term "by me" (*mayā*) might also mean "for me" (*mahyam*).
Why are the other afflictions (*kleśa*) not considered inversions (*viparyāsa*)?
Because inversions are established by way of three causes. What are these three?
Because of judging erroneously, because of superimposition;
that is, because it judges its object with one-sided perversion and because it superimposes [a false nature].
The view of annihilation and false view are not superimpositional, because they function by way of negation (*abhāvamukha*).
Adherence to rites and rituals is not exclusively inverted, because it takes as its object purification through those [rites] alone.
Other afflictions are not investigative; therefore, they are not perversions.

As for what is stated in the Sūtra: "To perceive the impermanent as permanent is a perversion of perception (saṃjñā-viparyāsa), a perversion of mind (citta-viparyāsa), and a perversion of view (dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa)," it is the view itself that is the perversion here; perception and mind, however, become perversions by virtue of its influence. //6//
It is solely by virtue of the perversion of view that the perception and thought associated with it are called "perversions.
Why are feeling and the other [mental factors] not also so called?
Because of what is well-known in the world.
For in the world, it is well known that one has "perverted perception" (*viparyasta-saṃjñā*) and "perverted mind" (*viparyasta-citta*), but not "perverted feeling" (*viparyasta-vedanā*).

All these perversions are abandoned by the stream-enterer (*srotaāpanna*), because views (*dṛṣṭi*) along with their associated mental factors (*saṃprayoga*) are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-praheya*).
There are twelve inversions (*viparyāsa*).
Regarding the impermanent as permanent, there are three inversions of perception (*saṃjñā*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), and mind (*citta*);
and so on, up to regarding the non-self as self.
In that regard, eight [of these misconceptions] are to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) and four are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Furthermore, according to other schools (*nikāyāntarīya*), there are misconceptions of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) and mind (*citta-viparyāsa*) regarding suffering as pleasant and regarding the impure as pure.
Otherwise, how could sensual desire (*kāma-rāga*) arise in a noble one (*ārya*) who has not yet transcended passion, if he were devoid of the perception of pleasure and purity?
The Vaibhāṣikas do not accept this.

For if the two perversions [of permanence and self] are attributed to a noble one because of the occurrence of the perception and thought of pleasure and purity, why are the two perversions [of existence and delight] not likewise attributed [to him] because of the occurrence of the perception and thought of a sentient being?
For indeed, sexual desire toward a woman or toward oneself is not possible without the perception of a sentient being (*sattva-saṃjñā*).
It is also stated in the Sūtra: "When the learned noble disciple understands, as it truly is, that 'this is the noble truth of suffering'...
at that time, whatever perversion of perception, perversion of mind, and perversion of view he had regarding the impermanent as permanent is abandoned," and so forth in detail.

Therefore, the two types of perversion—perception and thought—arise only from [wrong] views and not from others, because those others are merely temporary delusions, like the illusions of a whirling firebrand, a painted figure, or a yakṣa.
As for what was then said by the Elder Ānanda concerning the noble Vāgīśa: "Your mind is consumed by the perversion of perceptions;
therefore, abandon the sign that is associated with passion and is beautiful."
Therefore, others maintain that all eight distortions of perception and mind are unabandoned by one in training (śaikṣa).
These too are abandoned through the thorough knowledge of the noble truths (āryasatya) as they truly are;
since they are not abandoned without that [knowledge], there is no contradiction with the Sūtra because of this explanation of the means.
Now, is this division [of latent tendencies] unique to the view-latent-tendency (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*) and not of others?
It also exists for pride (*māna*).
To explain how, he says: "seven."
The [seven] types of pride are: pride, excessive pride, pride beyond pride, the pride of "I am," conceit, inferiority pride, and false pride.
In general, pride is said to be the inflation of the mind.
It becomes sevenfold through its different modes of operation:

pride (*māna*) is the loftiness of one who thinks, "I am superior to the inferior," or "I am equal to the equal. Excessive pride (*abhimāna*) is the conceit of one who thinks, "I am superior to the equal."

"Excessive pride" (*atimāna*) is the thought, "I am superior to one who is superior. "The pride of 'I am'" (*asmimāna*) belongs to one who conceives of the five aggregates of clinging as self or as belonging to a self.
"Overweening pride" (*abhimāna*) is the conceit, "I have attained a distinguished realization," when such a realization has not been attained.
The conceit of inferiority (*ūnamāna*) is the thought, "I am only slightly inferior" compared to one who is vastly superior.
The false conceit (*mithyāmāna*) is the thought, "I possess qualities" when one actually possesses no qualities.
If so, then why are nine types of conceit (*māna*) taught in the treatise:
"The conceit that 'I am superior'";
"the conceit that 'I am equal'";... [and so forth]?
The various forms of conceit are: "I am inferior";
"There is one superior to me, there is one equal to me, there is one inferior to me";
and "There is no one superior to me, there is no one equal to me, there is no one inferior to me."
From these very three types of pride, these nine kinds [of pride] arise.
From which three? From pride, over-pride, and under-pride.
In that regard, the first triad consists of the three types of conceit based on views:
overweening conceit (*atimāna*), conceit (*māna*), and inferiority conceit (*ūnamāna*).
The second triad consists of inferiority conceit (*ūnamāna*), conceit (*māna*), and overweening conceit (*atimāna*).
The third triad consists of pride, excessive pride, and inferiority pride.
It is indeed reasonable that "inferiority-complex" (*ūnamāna*) is a state of pride, because one considers oneself only slightly inferior to someone who is vastly superior.
But what is the basis for pride in the thought, "I have no inferior"?
It exists when, even though one is inferior, one holds oneself in high regard within a group of beings intended as superior.

Moreover, there is indeed a rule established in the *Jñānaprasthāna*. However, by adopting the exposition in the *Prakaraṇapāda*, even this pride that "I am superior" may be pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), or pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), depending on whether one compares oneself to those who are inferior, equal, or superior.
Now, as to whether these seven conceits are to be abandoned, he says: "They are exhausted by vision and cultivation.
Their exhaustion occurs through both vision (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

This is what is meant: all [defilements] are to be abandoned through vision and cultivation. If that which is to be abandoned by cultivation has not yet been abandoned, does it necessarily manifest for the Noble Ones? Not necessarily; for example, the obsession with killing and so forth, though to be abandoned by cultivation, may not manifest.

Whatever obsession of the afflictions (*kleśaparyavasthāna*) by which one would intentionally commit the killing of a living being, up to and including false speech—that is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), because it has as its object phenomena that are themselves to be abandoned by cultivation.
Thus [it is said]. (10)
The desire for non-existence (*vibhavecchā*) and craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) are also to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).
What kind of phenomenon is this so-called "non-existence" (*vibhava*)?

Impermanence belongs to the three realms; therein, longing is craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*). By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), a portion of craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*) is included.
"O, would that I were Airāvaṇa, the king of elephants!"—such [thoughts] as these are mentioned;
furthermore, it has been stated that there are various types of pride (*māna*) that are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and among them is the pride of "I am" (*asmimāna*).
Yet, such varieties of pride and the like do not occur in a noble one (*ārya*).
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of everything up to the craving for existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*).
What is the reason that these [afflictions] do not manifest even though they have not been abandoned?
Because they are nourished by views—
specifically, being nourished by the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the conceit "I am" (asmimāna)—
they have their backs broken; therefore, they do not venture to rise up again.
The obsession with killing and so forth is nourished by wrong view; craving for non-existence is nourished by the view of annihilationism;
and a portion of craving for existence is nourished by the view of eternalism.
Nor is there unwholesome remorse. //11//
Furthermore, unwholesome remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is also to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*);
yet it cannot arise in a noble one (*ārya*), because it is originated from doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Now, among these ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many are universal (*sarvatraga*) and how many are non-universal (*asarvatraga*)?

The universal [defilements] are the views to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its cause, as well as doubt together with those [views], and the ignorance that is not associated with them. (12)

The views and doubts to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin, along with the ignorance associated with them and the independent (āveṇika) ignorance to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin—
these eleven underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are universal within their own realm (sabhāga-dhātu).
This is because the seven views and two doubts, as well as the two types of ignorance, take the entirety of their own realm as their object.
Does he take these as objects simultaneously or successively?
If successively, there would be the same consequence for other [objects] as well.
If simultaneously, who could believe in purification through the entire realm of desire, or [believe in] a non-cause as a cause?
It is not said that "all" means they take all as their object simultaneously;

rather, it means that even though there are five types, they take all of them simultaneously. Even so, wherever there is the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), there is craving for self (*ātmatṛṣṇā*); wherever there are the views of excellence and purity (*agra-śuddhi-dṛṣṭī*), there is longing for them, and from that, pride (*māna*) arises. Consequently, it follows that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and pride (*māna*) would also be universal (*sarvatraga*).

This being the case, since these two have as their objects that which is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and that which is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), how should they be abandoned?
They should be abandoned by cultivation, because their objects are mixed.
Alternatively, let them rather be abandoned by seeing, because they function through the reinforcement of the power of [wrong] views (*dṛṣṭi*).

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that these two are afflictions of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-kleśa*) and not universal afflictions (*sāmānya-kleśa*); therefore, they are not omnipresent (*asarvatraga*). These eleven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that have been described as omnipresent within their own respective realms (*sabhāga-dhātu*)—
Of these, nine have the upper realms as their object, excluding two views.

Excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the other nine latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are universal (*sarvatraga*) with respect to a different realm. Sometimes they take one different realm as their object, and sometimes two.

Because of the statement: "Those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that have the form realm as their object; those associated with the desire realm that have the formless realm as their object; and those associated with the desire realm that have both the form and formless realms as their objects.

When one abiding in the desire realm generates the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of permanence (*nityadṛṣṭi*) regarding Brahmā, how is it that the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) do not have a different realm as their object?
Because it does not grasp [the aggregates] as "self" or "belonging to self," and because the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) arises from that, what kind of view is this?
The Abhidharmikas say: "This is not a view; rather, it is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*)."

How indeed can it be established that while one view has that same object as its basis, this other view does not? For the established doctrine (siddhānta) must be proven by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Furthermore, are the latent dispositions (anuśaya) themselves exclusively universal (sarvatraga)?
He says: "No."
Those factors which coexist with these [universal defilements], excluding acquisition (prāpti), are also universal. //13//

Those other factors that coexist with the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) are also universal; however, their acquisitions (*prāpti*) are not so, because they have multiple fruits. For this very reason, there is a fourfold logical alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) concerning whether something may be a universal proclivity without being a cause by way of being a universal cause.
The first category consists of all pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are future;
the second consists of those [dispositions] that are past or present and co-existent with them;
the third and fourth categories should be applied accordingly.

Among these ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many have contaminated objects (*sāsravālambana*) and how many have uncontaminated objects (*anāsravālambana*)? Wrong view, doubt, and the ignorance associated with them, as well as independent ignorance—these six, when abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, have the uncontaminated as their domain. (14)

There are three proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation: false view, doubt, and ignorance; those associated with these two, as well as the independent (*āveṇika*) [ignorance], and likewise these same three to be abandoned by the vision of the path—these six have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.
It is established that the remaining [afflictions] have the contaminated as their object. Furthermore, among those,
the path that is the cessation of one's own level belongs to six levels or nine levels.
The path is indeed the object of those whose domain it is, for they are mutually causal. //15//

For those [afflictions] such as wrong view that take cessation as their object, the object is exclusively the cessation of their own level: for those belonging to the desire realm, it is the cessation of the desire realm alone; up to those belonging to the level of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), it is the cessation of the peak of existence alone.

For those that take the path as their object, in the case of those belonging to the desire realm, the entire path consisting of the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) pertaining to six levels is the object.
This includes even that which is the antidote to the form and formless realms. For those belonging to the form and formless realms across eight levels, the object consists of nine levels.
The entire path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) is the object [of the knowledge of suffering], because the paths are mutual causes for one another.
Although both the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge are mutual causes, subsequent knowledge is not the antidote to the desire realm;
therefore, those factors belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge that have the path as their object do not take the factors of the desire realm as their objects.

In that case, dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), because it is the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to the realms of form and formlessness, will be the object of those paths belonging to those levels that take [the truths] as their objects. [Response: It is not so; for that [dharma-knowledge] is not an antidote in its entirety, because the dharma-knowledges of suffering and origin are not antidotes to those [realms].

Nor is it an antidote to all [defilements] of the realms of form and formlessness that are to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), and so forth; thus, due to such absences, it does not become an object.

Now, why are attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), and the two types of adherence—adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—not accepted as having the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object?

It is because attachment is not [so accepted], since it is something to be abandoned; for attachment is indeed to be abandoned. If it were to have the untainted as its object, it would not be something to be abandoned, just like the desire for wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharmacchanda*).
Aversion is not [so accepted] because the untainted is not harmful.
For hostility arises toward an object that causes harm, but this is not the case for cessation and the path.
There is neither pride nor the two types of grasping [at views], because they are peaceful, pure, and supreme by nature. //16//

Because cessation and the path are peaceful, arrogance toward them cannot arise; because they are pure in their true nature, the grasping at them as pure is not the "clinging to rules and observances" (śīlavrataparāmarśa);
and these two are supreme.
And the grasping at what is inferior as supreme is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Therefore, it is logical that these have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.
Among these ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many adhere by way of being an object (*ālambana*), and how many [adhere] solely by way of association (*saṃprayoga*)?
The universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) adhere to their entire [level];
the non-universal ones adhere to their own category within their own level by way of the object (ālambana). //17//

Those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal (*sarvatraga*) adhere (*anuśerate*) to their own entire level (*bhūmi*), comprising all five categories, by way of being its object (*ālambana*). However, those that are not universal adhere only to their own category within their own level, and not to another;
for example, those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*) adhere only to the category to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
In this way, up to those [afflictions] to be abandoned by cultivation, they are abandoned only by cultivation and not by anything else.
Having stated this general rule (*utsarga*), he makes an exception (*apavāda*): "Those whose objects are untainted (*anāsrava*) or belong to a higher realm [are not abandoned by cultivation]."
Latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have the untainted (anāsrava) as their object do not adhere by way of being an object,
nor do those that have a higher stage as their object.
What is the reason?
Because the entity that serves as its object is not appropriated due to being an adverse factor;
for when an entity has been appropriated by the view of self and craving, other latent dispositions (anuśaya) are also able to follow along within it.
Just as dust cannot settle on a wet cloth, so too the outflows do not persist in this way in the untainted state, nor do they persist in this way in the higher realms;
therefore, those [afflictions] do not increase with respect to them by taking them as objects.

He who, while remaining here [in this world], aspires for that [higher] stage possesses a skillful desire for the Dharma. Furthermore, Nirvana and the Path are the adversaries of the afflictions that take them as their objects; likewise, a higher stage is the adversary of those belonging to lower stages.
Therefore, those [afflictions] do not find a foothold within them.
Like the soles of feet upon a heated stone.
In this context, the meaning of "anuśaya" is "conformity.
Others, however, maintain that those [defilements] do not conform to them,
just as a person with a wind disorder does not have a latent tendency for dry things.
Therefore, it has been stated that [the proclivities] adhere by way of their object;
however, whichever [proclivity] is associated with whatever [mental state], it adheres to that [state] by way of association. (18)

The term "underlies" (anuśeta) continues [from the previous context]. Whatever latent disposition (anuśaya) is associated with a particular factor, it underlies that factor by way of association (saṃprayoga).
The word "tu" (but/however) is used for the purpose of qualification, meaning "as long as it has not been abandoned."

There may be latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have untainted objects (*anāsravālambana*) but are not universal to a different realm (*avisabhāgadhātusarvatraga*); those latent dispositions would adhere through association (*saṃprayoga*), but not through their object (*ālambana*). There would also be no latent dispositions that are universal to a different level (*visabhāgabhūmisarvatraga*).

Among these ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*) and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? All those belonging to the higher realms— the [tendencies] of the form and formless spheres— are entirely indeterminate.
What is the reason?
Afflicted phenomena would have suffering as their maturation;
however, that is not present in those two [the *anāsrava* paths], because they lack the cause for harming others.
In the realm of desire, the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, and the delusion associated with both of these are indeterminate;
that is, in the desire realm, the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, and the ignorance associated with them are indeterminate.
What is the reason?
Because it is not in contradiction with generosity and the other perfections.
Thinking, "I shall become happy after passing away," one gives gifts and guards moral discipline.
Even the view of annihilationism (ucchedadṛṣṭi) is conducive to liberation;
for this very reason it was said by the Blessed One: "This is the foremost among the views of outsiders, namely: 'May I not be, and may nothing be mine; may I not come to be, and may nothing be mine.
Furthermore, because these two views involve delusion regarding one's own substance and because they do not engage in causing harm to others.
The same logical consequence applies to the thirst for heaven and the conceit "I am. The innate view of a self-existent entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
it exists even among beasts and birds.
The former masters maintain, however, that the conceptualized [notion of impurity] is unwholesome; the remaining ones are both non-impure and wholesome. //16//
The remaining latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are unwholesome (*akuśala*).
How many are roots of the unwholesome (*akuśalamūla*), and how many are not?
In the desire realm, the roots of the unwholesome are attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), and delusion (*mūḍhi*).

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all attachment (*rāga*), all aversion (*pratigha*), and all delusion (*moha*)—except for those associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—are, respectively, [the afflictions of the desire realm].
There are three unwholesome roots: greed is an unwholesome root, hatred is an unwholesome root, and delusion is an unwholesome root.
That which is unwholesome and is also the root of the unwholesome is intended to be an unwholesome root.
It is established that the remaining latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are not unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*).
How many are neutral roots (*avyākṛtamūla*), and how many are not? There are three neutral roots.
Which three?
They are craving, ignorance, and that which is intellect. //20//

This demonstrates its neutral (avyākṛta) nature. The Kashmiris maintain that whatever craving, ignorance, or wisdom is neutral—even if it is ultimately born of maturation (vipākaja)—all of this constitutes a neutral root. Because doubt functions in two ways and the [other] two function upwardly, they cannot be roots;
for doubt, being twofold in its operation, cannot properly be a root.
Because it is mobile;
because pride functions upwardly by way of its characteristic of elevation, it is not a root.
For in the world, roots are seen to be stable and functioning downwardly. Thus, the outsiders maintain that there are only four [roots].
The outsiders (bāhyaka) assert four roots of the indeterminate (avyākṛta-mūla):
craving (tṛṣṇā), views (dṛṣṭi), pride (māna), and delusion (moha).
By mentioning "they," he shows that these are indeed indeterminate.
Indeterminate craving, views, pride, and ignorance—what is the reason they are asserted as these indeterminate roots? Because of the three types of meditators, due to ignorance. (21)
Because there are three types of meditators—
those who meditate on craving, views, and pride—
and these arise through the power of ignorance.
Regarding those fourteen indeterminate points mentioned in the Sūtra, are they called "indeterminate" because they are [ontologically] indeterminate?
No, he says. What then?
It has been stated that a question to be set aside is "unexpounded" (*avyākṛta*).
For there are four kinds of questions:

those to be answered categorically (*ekāṃśavyākaraṇīya*), those to be answered analytically (*vibhajyavyākaraṇīya*), those to be answered by counter-question (*paripṛcchyavyākaraṇīya*), and those to be set aside (*sthāpanīya*).
In this regard, it should be understood according to the following sequence:
[the Buddha’s teaching] consists of categorical explanation, analytical explanation, and explanation by way of questioning;
and there is also that which is to be set aside, as in the cases of death, rebirth, [whether the self is] superior, or whether [the self is] other than [the body], and so forth. (22)

Should one answer categorically that all sentient beings will die? One should answer categorically: "They will die. Should one answer that all will be born? One should answer by way of analysis: "Those with afflictions will be born; those free from afflictions will not.
Should one answer whether a human being is superior or inferior? One should answer by asking a counter-question.
"Regarding whom do you ask?
If he should say, "The gods," one should answer, "They are inferior."
If one should say "the states of woe," it should be answered that he is distinguished.
Whether the sentient being is other than the aggregates or not other than them is to be set aside.

Because a substantial entity (*sattvadravya*) does not exist—just like the dark or fair complexion of the son of a barren woman—how can this be an explanation? It is an explanation because it is explained in this way: "This is undeclared (*avyākṛta*)."
Another says:
"This too is a categorical answer—that not all will be born.
But if one were to ask, 'Will those who will die be born? this would be a question to be answered by analysis."
Among human beings, both inferiority and superiority exist relatively; therefore, both should be explained categorically [as relative].
For example, consciousness is both an effect and a cause, so for one who asks about it definitively, an analytical explanation is appropriate rather than a categorical one.
As for the question of whether a sentient being is other than the aggregates, this remains simply undeclared.
Nor is it logical that non-explanation itself constitutes an explanation.
However, when a question that is to be set aside is explained by way of being set aside, how could it not be considered explained?
The Abhidharmikas say:
"The Tathāgata is the Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One; his Dharma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha of disciples has practiced it correctly.

Form is impermanent, up to consciousness; from the designation of suffering up to the designation of the path—these must be answered categorically (ekāṃśena), because they are connected with the goal."
Analytical exposition (vibhajya-vyākaraṇa) means that if someone should say, "Speak of the dharmas," he should be asked, "The dharmas are many—past, future, and present—which ones shall I speak of?
If he should say, "The past ones," he should be told, "The past ones are also many: form, up to consciousness."
If he should say "form," he should be told that form is also of three kinds: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
If he says "wholesome," [he should be asked:]
That too is of seven kinds, from abstention from taking life up to abstention from frivolous speech.
If one says "abstention from taking life," that too is of three kinds: born of non-greed, born of non-hatred, and born of non-delusion.

If one says, "It is born of non-greed," then it must be explained by making such a distinction as follows: "Even that which is born of non-greed is of two kinds, due to the division into informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*).
And this very [method] is the "explanation after questioning" (*paripṛcchya-vyākaraṇa*) for one who is evasive.
To them it should be said, "The dharmas are many," but they should not be analyzed further until they remain silent or explain for themselves.
When those two do not ask anything at all but merely request [instruction], and nothing is explained to them but only questions are posed, how then can there be a question from these two? How...
Or [it is] an explanation by way of questioning. For when someone says, "Tell me the path," has he not asked about the path?
And since the explanation follows precisely from that questioning, how is it not an explanation by way of questioning?

But that which is to be set aside (*sthāpanīya*) is, for example, [the question] whether the world is finite or infinite, and so forth. However, the characteristics of the explanations of questions (*praśnavyākaraṇa*) should be understood from the Sūtras themselves.
The venerable Mahāsāṃghikas recite this Sūtra:
"O monks, there are these four ways of explaining questions."
Which four?
Monks, there is a question to be answered categorically;
there is [a question to be answered with a counter-question], up to [a question] to be set aside.
And what, monks, is the question to be answered categorically?
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent"—this, monks, is the question to be answered categorically.
And what, monks, is the question to be answered by way of analysis?
"Having performed an intentional action (*saṃcetanīyaṃ karma*), what does one experience?"—this is a question to be answered by way of analysis (*vibhajyavyākaraṇīya*).
And what, monks, is a question to be answered by way of inquiry (*paripṛcchyavyākaraṇīya*)?

When asked, "Is a person's self identical to their perceptions (*saṃjñā*), or is perception one thing and the self another?", one should inquire in return: "But which self, venerable sir, do you maintain?"

If he should say, "Venerable sir, I indeed perceive the self as gross," he should be told: "In that case, the perception is one thing and the self is another. For this is a question that must be answered by means of a counter-question.
And what, monks, is a question that should be set aside? It is as follows: "Is the world eternal? Is it non-eternal?
Is it both eternal and non-eternal?
Is it neither eternal nor non-eternal?"
It is finite; it is infinite;
it is both finite and infinite;
it is neither finite nor infinite.
"Whether the Tathāgata exists after death, or does not exist after death, up to: whether the soul is one thing and the body another—this, monks, is a question that should be set aside."

Whichever latent disposition (*anuśaya*) of whichever person (*pudgala*) lies dormant with respect to whichever object (*ālambana*), that person is associated (*saṃprayukta*) with it by means of that [disposition].
However, this must be explained: with what [object] is one associated by means of a past [disposition], and so on, up to the present? In brief, these afflictions (*kleśa*) are of two kinds.
The afflictions of specific characteristics are attachment, aversion, and pride;
the afflictions of general characteristics are views, doubt, and ignorance.
Regarding these, first:
One is bound by attachment, aversion, and pride—whether past or present—to that object in which they have arisen and have not yet been abandoned. (23)
One is bound by those past and present afflictions of attachment, aversion, and pride that have arisen with respect to a particular object and have not yet been abandoned;

for, because these are afflictions characterized by their own specific marks (*svalakṣaṇakleśa*), they do not necessarily arise in relation to every object. However, one is bound by all future mental afflictions in relation to every object.

The phrase "wherein they have not been abandoned" carries over here. By means of these very same future lust, aversion, and pride belonging to the mental level (*manobhūmika*), one is bound to all objects throughout the three time periods,
because the objects of mental states pertain to the three times.
Regarding those belonging to one's own time period,
one is bound by other future attachments and aversions to a future object itself.
But what are these "others"?
Those which belong to the five groups of sensory consciousness— namely, attachment and aversion—
are only those that possess the nature of arising.
And by those very [factors]...

The unarisen [factors], which possess the nature of non-arising— even those belonging to the five bodies of sensory consciousness— are associated with all objects and throughout the three time periods.
But with all the remaining [factors], he is endowed everywhere. //24//
What, then, are the remaining ones?
They are the views, doubt, and ignorance belonging to the three time periods.
One is bound to all objects by means of all of these as well.
Because they are common afflictions (*sāmānyakleśa*).
The governing context "as long as they have not been abandoned" continues to apply.
Furthermore, regarding this which is called "the past and the future": does it exist or not?
If it exists, then because conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) exist at all times, they would result in being eternal (śāśvata).
On the other hand, if it does not exist, [how can there be action and its fruit?]
How, then, is one joined with or disjoined from that, or by that?
The Vaibhāṣikas do not assert the permanence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), because they possess the characteristics of the conditioned;
yet, this [other point] is clearly asserted.
What is the reason for the existence [of dharmas] at all times?
Because it has been stated.
For it was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, if past form did not exist, the learned noble disciple would not be indifferent toward past form.
But because past form does exist, therefore the learned noble disciple is indifferent toward past form.
If future form did not exist, the learned noble disciple would not delight in future form."
Therefore, since future form exists, and so forth;
because of duality,
it was said that "consciousness arises dependent upon a pair."
What is the dyad?
It is the eye and visible forms, up to the mind and mental objects. If the past and future did not exist, then consciousness having them as its object would not arise in dependence upon that dyad.
Thus, first of all, the past and the future exist according to scripture; they exist also according to reasoning,
because consciousness arises only when there is an existent object, not when there is no object.
Furthermore, if the past and future did not exist, consciousness would have a non-existent object;
consequently, consciousness itself would not exist due to the absence of an object,
because [consciousness] is the fruit [of its object].
Furthermore, if the past did not exist, how could there be a fruit of wholesome or unwholesome karma in the future?
For at the time of the arising of the fruit, the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) does not exist in the present.
Therefore, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the past and the future certainly exist.
And indeed, this must necessarily be accepted by one who is a Sarvāstivādin;
for it is from the doctrine that "that exists" (tad-asti-vāda) that they are recognized as Sarvāstivādins.

Those who assert that "everything exists"—namely, the past, the future, and the present—are the Sarvāstivādins. However, those who speak by making a distinction, saying that "whatever is present and whatever past karma has not yet yielded its fruit exist, whereas that which has already yielded its fruit, as well as the future, do not exist," are the Vibhajyavādins. [He asks: "How many types of these Sarvāstivādins are there? He says:
They are of four kinds. //25//
These are designated as the "change of state," the "change of characteristic," and the "change of condition. The Venerable Dharmatrāta is the proponent of the change of state (*bhāvānyathika*).
He, it is said, stated: "When a dharma proceeds through the time-periods (adhvan), there is a change in its state (bhāva-anyathātva), but not a change in its substance (dravya-anyathātva)."
Just as when a golden vessel is broken and fashioned into something else, there is a change in its shape but no change in its color;

and just as milk, when transforming into curd, relinquishes its taste, potency, and maturation but not its color— in the same way, a dharma, when coming from the future time-path into the present time-path, abandons its future state but not its substantial existence.
Thus, as it passes from the present into the past time, it abandons its state of being present, but not its substantial existence.
This is the view of the Venerable Ghoṣaka, who maintains that change consists in the alteration of characteristics (lakṣaṇānyathika). He is reported to have said:
A dharma, as it proceeds through the time-periods, when past is endowed with the characteristic of the past, yet is not devoid of the characteristics of the future and the present.

When future, it is endowed with the characteristic of the future, yet is not devoid of the characteristics of the past and the present. Likewise, the present is also not devoid of the characteristics of the past and the future.
For example, it is like a man who is attached to one woman but not detached from the others.
This is the view of the Venerable Vasumitra, who maintains that change occurs through a difference in state (*avasthānyathika*).
He reportedly said:

Dharma, as it proceeds through the time-periods (*adhvan*), is designated as one thing or another upon reaching each successive state; this is due to a difference in state (*avasthāntara*), not due to a difference in substance (*dravyāntara*).

It is just as when a single counting-stick (*vartikā*) is placed in the ones-column, it is called "one"; in the hundreds-column, it is "a hundred"; and in the thousands-column, it is "a thousand. Otherwise, there is the Vātsīputrīya, the venerable Buddhadeva. He, it is said, asserts:
Dharma, as it proceeds through the time-periods, is called one thing or another in relation to what precedes and follows it;
just as a single woman is called both "mother" and "daughter.
These are the four Sarvāstivāda schools.
However, among these, the first should be classified under the Sāṃkhya position because he maintains the doctrine of transformation (pariṇāmavāda).
In the second case, a confusion of the time-periods (adhvan) would result, because everything would be connected with every moment.

However, in the case of a person, passion toward one woman is actively manifest (*samudācarati*), while toward another there is merely possession (*samanvāgama*); what similarity is there here [between these two cases]?
In the case of the fourth [position] as well, three time-periods would result within a single time-period:
in the past time-period, the preceding and succeeding moments would be past and future, while the middle moment would be present;
the same applies to the future time-period as well.
Therefore, among all these, the third— the one which maintains that change consists in a difference of state— is the best.
It is said that its time-periods (adhvans) are established by way of their functional activity (kāritra). //26//
When that dharma does not perform its activity, it is future;
when it performs it, it is present;
and when, having performed it, it has ceased, it is past.
All of this has been understood;
however, this must be stated:
if the past and the future also exist as substantial entities (dravyataḥ).
Why is that called "past" or "future"?
Has it not been stated that the time periods are established by way of their activity (*kāritra*)?
If this is so, what is the activity of the present eye that is "of the same class" (*tatsabhāga*)?
[Regarding] the giving and receiving of a fruit:

if that were so, then even for past factors such as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and others, there would follow the consequence of them possessing activity (*kāritra*), or else they would possess only half-activity; thus, there would be a confusion of definitions.
And this must be said:
what obstacle is there to a dharma that exists by its very nature performing its activity eternally?
If it is argued that the reason why it sometimes performs its activity and sometimes does not is the incompleteness of the conditions (*pratyaya*),
we say no.
It exists eternally because you accept its existence;
and as for that activity which is said to be past, future, and present, how is that so? Does activity itself possess another activity?
Now, if that [dharma] is neither past, nor future, nor present, yet it exists,
then because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it follows that it exists eternally. Therefore, one should not say that when a dharma does not perform its activity (*kāritra*), it is then "future."
This fault would indeed arise if the activity were something other than the dharma;
however,
it is certainly not other than it.
Therefore, this fault does not arise;
however, in that case, there is still the same lack of connection with the time periods (adhvan).

If activity (*kāritra*) is indeed the very nature of a phenomenon (*dharma*), why is that same phenomenon, existing with that very same essence, sometimes called "past" and sometimes called "future"? Thus, the establishment of the time-periods (*adhvan*) would not be possible.
[What here is not established? For a phenomenon that has not yet arisen is the future.]
That which has been born and has not yet perished is the present;
that which has perished is the past—
this alone is what must be stated here.
If the past and the future exist substantially just as the present exists, then for that which exists in such a manner:
By what means is there "unbornness" or "perishedness"?
Since a dharma exists by that very same intrinsic nature (svabhāva), how can it be established as either "unborn" or "perished"?
What was previously non-existent for this [dharma], due to the absence of which it is said to be "unborn"?
Furthermore, there is nothing subsequent whose absence would cause something to be called "destroyed. Therefore, the three time periods cannot be established in any way here,
if one does not accept that [something] comes into being after not having existed, and that after having existed, it no longer exists.
As for what was said— "Because of its connection with the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*), there is no consequence of eternalism"—
this is merely empty words, because arising and destruction are impossible [for such a thing].
To say that "there exists a phenomenon called 'eternal,' yet it is not eternal" is a truly unprecedented manner of speaking.
Moreover, it has been said:
"The intrinsic nature (svabhāva) exists at all times, yet the entity (bhāva) is not admitted to be eternal;
nor is the entity other than its intrinsic nature—this is clearly the work of a Lord (īśvara). As for what was stated regarding "because it has already been explained," [that too is refuted].
We also say that the past and the future exist;
for the past is that which has previously occurred,
and the future is that which will come to be when the cause is present.
And having established it thus, it is said that "it exists," but not again as a substantial entity (dravyataḥ).
And who indeed says that it exists in the same manner as the present?
How else could it exist? [If you say] "by way of its past and future self," then this further point arises for you:
How can that which is past and future be said to exist if it is eternal?

Therefore, in order to make known the state of having previously existed for a cause and the state of being about to exist for a result, and for the purpose of refuting the view that denies cause and effect, the Blessed One said: "The past exists; the future exists.
This is because the word "exists" (*asti*) is an indeclinable particle (*nipāta*).

Just as people say, "There is the prior non-existence of the lamp" and "There is its posterior non-existence," and just as they say, "That lamp has ceased, but it was not extinguished by me," so too is it said that the past and the future exist;
for otherwise, the very existence of the past and the future would not be established.

[If that is so, then what about that which was said by the Blessed One concerning the wandering mendicants of Laguḍaśikhī: “That action which has passed away, ceased, stopped, departed, and transformed—that exists”?
Did they not accept that each such action had previously occurred?
In that regard, however, it was said with reference to the capacity to yield a fruit, which was deposited therein within that continuum.]
Otherwise, the past, existing by its own nature, would not be established.
And this is exactly as stated by the Blessed One in the *Paramārtha-śūnyatā-sūtra*: "The eye, when arising, does not come from anywhere; when ceasing, it does not go to any accumulation.
Thus, monks, the eye comes into being after having not been, and having been, it passes away."
Furthermore, if the future eye were [already] existent, it would not have been said that "it comes into being after having not existed.
If you argue that this means "it comes into being after having not existed" within the present time-period (*adhvan*), we say no; for the time-period is not a separate entity from the thing itself.
Now, if it comes into being after not having existed within itself, it is established that this future eye does not exist.
As for what was also said—that "consciousness arises in dependence upon a dyad"—this must first be carefully considered here:

when mental consciousness arises in dependence upon the mind (*manas*) and mental objects (*dharma*), are the mental objects a productive condition (*janaka-pratyaya*) for it just as the mind is, or are they merely the objective support (*ālambana-mātra*)?
If, first of all, mental objects were a productive condition, how could that which is future—perhaps to occur after a thousand eons, or perhaps not at all—produce consciousness now?
Furthermore, since nirvāṇa is the cessation of all activity, it cannot logically be a producer [of cognition].
Now, if phenomena are merely objects of cognition,
we maintain that even the past and the future can serve as objects of cognition.
If it does not exist, how can it be an object? To this we now reply:
when that object exists in such a manner, how could it have been an object in the past or be one in the future?
For no one, when recollecting past form or feeling, perceives it as "it exists";
rather,
they perceive it as "it was."
Just as a present form that has been experienced is remembered as past,
so too is a future [form] grasped by the intellect as it will become present;
and if that [future form] exists in exactly that way, it would follow that it is present.
Now, if it does not exist, it is established that even a non-existent thing can be an object of cognition.
[If it is argued: "That very same thing is what is scattered [into atoms]."
No, because that which is dispersed is not perceived.
Furthermore, if each and every form were merely divided into atoms,
it would follow that atoms are eternal.

In this case, it would follow that there is merely the aggregation and disintegration of atoms; nothing at all would be produced, nor would anything cease. Thus, the doctrine of the Ājīvikas would be adopted, and the Sūtra would be cast aside, including its detailed statement: "When the eye arises, it does not come from anywhere," and so forth.
How can there be a dispersal of [factors] such as sensation, which are not composed of atoms?
Moreover, they are remembered exactly as they were experienced when they arose;
and if they existed in that very same way [at the time of recollection], it would follow that they are eternal.
If, on the other hand, they do not exist,
then it is established that even a non-existent thing can be an object of cognition.
If even a non-existent thing could be an object of cognition, then even a thirteenth sense-base (āyatana) would be an object of cognition.

Now, if there is no thirteenth base (*āyatana*), what is the object (*ālambana*) of this consciousness? Its very name is the object. If that is so, then it would follow that one perceives that the name itself does not exist.
And what is the object of apprehension for one who takes the prior non-existence of sound as his object? It is sound itself.
If that is so, then for one who seeks the absence of sound, sound itself would have to be produced.
If it is argued that [the object] exists in a future state,
how can there be the cognition "it does not exist" when it actually exists?
If it is argued that [the cognition refers to the fact that] the present [state] does not exist, we say no.
Because of its oneness;
for as far as there is a distinction in it, the establishment of its non-existence after having not existed [is also established].
Therefore, both existence and non-existence are the objective support (*ālambana*) of consciousness.

As for that which was said by the Bodhisattva: "It is impossible that I should know or see that which does not exist in the world"—the intention there is this: others, being conceited, perceive even what is non-existent as existent; I, however, perceive only what is existent as existent.
For otherwise, if all cognitions always possessed an existent object, from where would this deliberation arise, or what would be the distinction?
And this is indeed so, as the Blessed One has stated elsewhere: "This monk is my disciple; as long as he is instructed by me in the morning, he will strive for excellence by evening."
"Having been instructed in the evening, he will strive for distinction during the [following] kalpa;
he will know the existent as existent and the non-existent as non-existent, the surpassable as surpassable and the unsurpassable as unsurpassable.
Therefore, this too is not a valid reason.
"Because consciousness has an object," as it is said;
and as for what was stated regarding "the fruit," the Sautrāntikas certainly do not describe the arising of a fruit from a past action.
What then?
[The result arises] from a specific transformation of the continuum preceded by that [action]; we shall explain this in the refutation of the doctrine of a self (*ātman*).
But for one who holds that the past and future exist as substantial entities (*dravyataḥ*), the fruit exists eternally; what, then, would be the efficacy of the action (*karman*) in that case?
[If you say] there is capacity for production,
then it is established that production occurs as something coming into being after not having been. But if everything indeed exists, what now has capacity for what?
And thus the doctrine of Vārṣagaṇya is illuminated: "What exists, exists indeed;
what does not exist, does not exist at all.
There is no arising of the non-existent."
"There is no destruction of that which exists. If that is so, then there must be a capacity for bringing something into the present. What, then, is this so-called "bringing into the present"?
If it were an attraction to another location,
then permanence would necessarily follow;
and how could that [attraction] occur for things that are formless?
And that which is this drawing forth (*ākarṣaṇa*) has come into being after not having been.
If it is a qualification of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then its coming into being after not having been is established.
Therefore, such a Sarvāstivāda is not tenable within the Teaching.
When one asserts that the past and the future exist as substantial entities (*dravyataḥ*),
it is correct provided that one asserts them in the same manner as it was stated in the Sūtra: "everything exists."
And how is it stated in the Sūtra that "everything exists"?
"O Brāhmaṇa, 'everything exists' refers to as much as the twelve bases (āyatana),
or else the three time periods (adhvan)."
However, how that [past and future] exists has already been explained. Now, if the past and future are non-existent, how does one become associated with them, or how is one associated in them?

One becomes associated with an object because of the existence of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) born from it and having it as their cause, and because of the existence of the latent dispositions of the afflictions that take that object as their focus.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the past and the future truly exist. Where it can be logically established, it should be understood by means of one's own reasoning; indeed, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is profound. (27)
It is not necessarily established by logical reasoning.
There is a way of explaining it: that which arises ceases;
form arises, form ceases.
There is another way [of explaining it]: one thing arises and another ceases;
the future arises and the present ceases;
even a temporal period (adhvan) arises.
Because that which is arising is comprised within the time-periods (adhvan),
it also arises from the time-period;
for the future time-period consists of multiple moments.
That which arose as a secondary topic has been concluded.
Now this is to be investigated: Is one who has abandoned a given object dissociated from that object?
Or, conversely, is that object abandoned for one who is dissociated from it?
In a case where one is dissociated from a thing, that thing has been abandoned for him; however,
there may be cases where a thing is abandoned but one is not dissociated from it— for example,
when the objects to be abandoned by the vision of suffering have been abandoned, one remains bound to them by means of the remaining universal [defilements].
And when a category has been previously abandoned, [it is not abandoned] by the remaining defilements that have that as their object. //28//
When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen, the category [of afflictions] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering is abandoned.
When that is abandoned, one remains bound by those universal [afflictions] to be abandoned by the vision of origin which have that [abandoned category] as their object.

Regarding the category to be abandoned by cultivation as well, even when that particular type among the nine types which was previously abandoned has been abandoned, it should be understood that one is still bound by the remaining afflictions that have that [category] as their object.
If one were to explain this phrase by phrase— namely, "In which object do how many latent dispositions (anuśaya) adhere?"— it would result in a vast amount that must be said.
Therefore, they provide a summary exposition (piṇḍavibhāṣā), thinking, "How may we resolve these great masses of questions with the least possible effort?"
In brief, these sixteen factors consist of those belonging to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness—fivefold in each—and the untainted (anāsrava).
The minds are likewise exactly sixteen.
Having understood which factor is the object (ālambana) of which mind, one should then infer how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) adhere to that particular object.
In that regard, first,

those [factors] of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, by the vision of its cause, and by cultivation have as their objects the three [categories] belonging to themselves, one [category] belonging to the form realm, and the pure consciousness. (26)
One's own and those three [realms] are "one's own three" (*svakatraya*).
One and that which belongs to the form realm are "one and the form-realm-attained" (*ekarūpāpta*).
This is the type of compound analysis (*vigraha*).

First, the dharmas of the desire realm (kāmāvacara) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya), are the objects of five types of consciousness:
of the three belonging to their own realm, of one belonging to the higher realm—which is exclusively that which is to be abandoned by cultivation—and of the untainted (anāsrava).
Those born in the form realm (rūpadhātu) are the objects of the three of their own [realm], the three of the lower [realm], the one of the higher [realm], and the pure (amala).
Those same three types of dharmas belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) are the objects of eight minds:
of the three [minds] of their own realm, those very same three;
and of the three [minds] of the lower realm, those very same three.

Of one [object] belonging to the higher realm—namely, that which is to be abandoned by cultivation—and also of the untainted (anāsrava). Those born in the formless realm have as their objects the three categories pertaining to the three realms and the untainted. //30//
Those same three types of factors belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) are the objects of ten minds:
those of the three types belonging to the three realms,
and the untainted (*anāsrava*) mind.
The phenomena (dharmas) of the three realms that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation, have been explained.

All those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path have their own kind as their objective sphere (*gocara*). For those [phenomena] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, their own mind—which is likewise to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path—is their basis;
it should be understood that these [other] phenomena are the objects (*ālambana*) of that [mind].
How is this so? For the phenomena of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśanaheya*) are the objects of six consciousnesses:
the five previously mentioned and that very same [sixth] which is additionally to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
Those to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaheya*) are likewise [ten]:
the five previously mentioned, plus that very same category which is to be abandoned by the vision of the path.
The same applies to those belonging to the realms of form (*rūpāvacara*) and formlessness (*ārūpyāvacara*).

The [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path are the objects of that very same additional mind to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path; thus, they become the objects of nine and eleven minds respectively.
The fivefold factors belonging to the three realms have been explained.
The untainted (anāsrava) factors are the domain of the last three [paths] and of the untainted [minds]. (31)
Untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are the objects of ten types of consciousness:
the three types belonging to each of the three realms—those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, by the vision of the path, and by cultivation—and the untainted [consciousness] itself.
Furthermore, this same point is summarized by one and a half verses:

"Those [factors] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its cause, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, exist within the three realms; they are stainless; they consist of five, eight, and ten consciousnesses respectively; and they are the objects of ten consciousnesses."
“Those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path all have as their object their own category and those above it.
Having thus understood the establishment of the sixteen types of dharmas as objects for these sixteen minds, how should the activity of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) be applied?
We shall show just the general direction.
When the question arises as to how many latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) adhere to a consciousness that has the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as its object, it must be investigated as follows:

The faculty of pleasure is of seven kinds—namely, that belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) which is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*), that belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) of five types, and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Thus, in brief, this becomes the object of twelve kinds of consciousness.

This twelvefold consciousness has the faculty of pleasure as its object: namely, the four types of consciousness belonging to the desire realm—excluding that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation; the five types belonging to the form realm; the two types belonging to the formless realm—those to be abandoned by the vision of the path and by cultivation; and the untainted (anāsrava) consciousness.

In that regard, it should be understood that, as far as possible, the four classes of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) and those of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), as well as two classes of the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) having conditioned phenomena as their object, and the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*), all adhere there.
How many latent dispositions adhere in the consciousness that takes as its object the consciousness which itself takes the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as its object?
Furthermore, with respect to that twelvefold consciousness which has the pleasure faculty as its object, of what consciousness is it the object?

It is the object of that same twelvefold [consciousness] and, moreover, of two types of formless-sphere consciousness—that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the origin.
Thus, this fourteen-fold consciousness has the pleasure faculty as its object; therein, the two belonging to the formless sphere are those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin.

It should be understood that after having increased [the objects], the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the desire realm, the four classes belonging to the formless realm, and those belonging to the form realm that have conditioned phenomena as their objects,
persist. By this method, other cases should also be inferred.
Those latent dispositions (anuśaya) by which a mind is "possessed of latent dispositions" are those that lie latent within that mind.

Those latent dispositions which lie latent [in it] are those that are associated with that mind and have not been abandoned, as well as those that take that mind as their object and have not been abandoned.

Those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) which do not underlie [the mind]— namely, those which are associated with that mind and have been abandoned, as well as those which have that mind as their object— [do not underlie it].
Having established this, it follows that:
That which is accompanied by latent dispositions (sānuśaya) is of two kinds: the defiled and the non-defiled, [the former] because of the presence of the latent dispositions.

A defiled mind is "with latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*) both through the latent dispositions that are currently active (*anuśayāna*), which have not been abandoned and for which it is associated and takes as its object, and also through those associated [dispositions] that are already abandoned but are no longer active; this is because it is accompanied by them. A non-defiled mind, however, is "with latent dispositions" only through those [dispositions] that are active and for which it has not been abandoned as its object.
Now, how do these ten latent dispositions function?

From the very beginning, due to the association with ignorance, one is deluded regarding the truths; as long as suffering does not appeal to him, so too the path [does not appeal]. From that delusion, doubt arises.
Having heard both sides, the deluded person gives rise to doubt, thinking, "Is this suffering, or is this not suffering? and so forth;
from that, wrong view arises.
From doubt, wrong view arises;
for one who is in doubt, there occurs a false hearing and reflection, from which a false certainty arises,
such as "suffering does not exist," and so forth.
From that [view of self-existence], the view of a self-identity [arises]. //32//

It is said that from false view (mithyādṛṣṭi), the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) arises, because one rejects the aggregates as suffering and instead adheres to them as a self. From that, the grasping at extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) arises; from the view of a self-identity, the view of grasping at extremes proceeds.

Because of grasping at the extremes of the self’s eternalism or annihilationism; from that arises the adherence to [wrong] views, and from the grasping at extremes arises the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Because one returns to purity by means of whichever extreme one grasps,
"the reflective awareness of vision" follows from that.

From the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) arises, because one grasps that by which one believes purification is attained as being supreme. From that...
Attachment and pride exist toward one's own view, because of the clinging to it and because of the sense of superiority arising through it;
hatred exists toward others.
Hatred arises toward the views of others, which are contrary to that which one has determined through one’s own view.

Others, however, maintain that hatred occurs even toward one’s own view when it is abandoned after having been grasped elsewhere; for the passion and other afflictions to be abandoned by seeing have as their object the very views belonging to one’s own continuum.
Such is the sequence. (33)
This is the sequence of the manifestation of these ten afflictions.
When they arise, however, they arise due to three causes:
from an unabandoned latent disposition (*anuśaya*), and from an object that has presented itself.

From improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) arises affliction (*kleśa*); that is to say, when the latent tendency of attachment (*rāgānuśaya*) is neither abandoned nor fully understood, and objects conducive to the outburst of sensual desire (*kāmarāgaparyavasthānīya*) come into range, and there is improper mental attention toward them— in this way, sensual desire arises.
These, respectively, are the powers of cause, object, and application.
In this same way, it should be understood that any other affliction which possesses its complete causes arises. //34//
It is said that sometimes [defilements] arise solely through the power of the object, not through the power of the cause,
as in the case of an Arhat subject to regression.

These very latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) were taught by the Blessed One in the Sūtra as the three outflows (*āsrava*): the outflow of sensuality (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).

There are also four floods (*ogha*): the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*), and the flood of ignorance. These same [dispositions] are also the four yokes (*yoga*).

There are four types of clinging (*upādāna*): clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmopādāna*), clinging to views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*), clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*), and clinging to the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*).

Among these, first, the afflictions (*kleśa*) associated with sensual pleasures, together with their outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), constitute the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*), excluding [the latter two types of clinging].

Excluding delusion (*moha*), which is ignorance (*avidyā*), the other afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), together with the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), should be understood as the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*), consisting of forty-one entities: thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)— excluding the fivefold ignorance— and ten outbursts.
In the realms of form and formlessness, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) alone constitute the outflow of existence (bhavāsrava). //35//
The phrase "without delusion" (vinā mohena) carries over [from the previous context].
The outflow of existence (bhavāsrava) consists of the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) belonging to the realms of form and formlessness, excluding ignorance (avidyā), totaling fifty-two entities.
This is because there are twenty-six underlying tendencies belonging to the realm of form, excluding the five types of ignorance.
There are twenty-six [defilements] belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*).
But is it not the case that even there two types of outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) exist, namely torpor (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*)?
And it is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*: "What is the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*)?"

"Excluding ignorance, those other fetters (saṃyojana), bonds (bandhana), latent dispositions (anuśaya), secondary afflictions (upakleśa), and outbursts (paryavasthāna) associated with the realms of form and formlessness"—
why is that [ignorance] not included here?
The Kashmiris say it is because of a lack of independence.
But what is the reason that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the realms of form and formlessness are grouped together and called the single "summit of existence" (*bhavāgra*)?
For they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), inwardly directed, and belong to the stages of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmika*).

Therefore, these two are unified because they share three common characteristics: both are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), they function inwardly (*antarmukha-pravṛtta*), and they belong to the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmika*).

For the very same reason that "attachment to existence" (*bhavarāga*) was previously mentioned, "outflow of existence" (*bhavāsrava*) is likewise established; thus, it is now proven that the "outflow of ignorance" (*avidyāsrava*) refers to the ignorance belonging to the three realms (*traidhātuka-avidyā*).
These are fifteen entities.
For what reason is this [ignorance] established separately? Because ignorance is the root of them all, it is classified as a separate outflow (*āsrava*). (36)
Just as these outflows (āsravas) have been explained, so too should the floods (oghās) and yokes (yogās) be understood. However, the views (dṛṣṭis) are treated separately because of their sharpness.
The flood of desire and the yoke of desire are simply the outflow of desire itself.
In this way, the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*) is itself the flood of existence (*bhavaugha*) and the yoke of existence (*bhavayoga*), with the exception of the views (*dṛṣṭi*).
It is said that because they are sharp, the views are established separately from the floods and yokes;
