however, when unaccompanied [by other defilements], they are not conducive to the outflows (*āsrava*). (37)

The etymological definition of the outflows (*āsrava*) as "that which causes one to settle" will be explained later. It is said that views alone are not conducive to settling because of their sharpness;
therefore, they are not established separately among the outflows.
"Having been mixed and established"—thus, the flood of desire (*kāmaugha*) consists of twenty-nine entities:
fifteen consisting of attachment, hostility, and pride; four consisting of doubt; and ten consisting of the secondary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*).
The flood of existence (*bhavaugha*) consists of twenty-eight entities.
Attachment and pride consist of twenty [factors]; doubt consists of eight;
the flood of views consists of thirty-six entities;
and the flood of ignorance consists of fifteen entities.
The yokes (yoga) are to be understood as being like the floods (ogha).
That very ignorance, when distinguished by way of views, is the two kinds of clinging (upādāna), as previously stated.
The clinging to sensual desire (*kāmopādāna*) is the yoke of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*) together with ignorance (*avidyā*), consisting of thirty-four entities:
twenty instances of attachment, aversion, pride, and ignorance; four instances of doubt; and ten secondary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*).
The clinging to the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*) is the yoke of existence (*bhavayoga*) together with ignorance, consisting of thirty-eight entities.
There are thirty [factors] consisting of passion, pride, and ignorance, and eight [factors] consisting of doubt.
From the yoke of views (*dṛṣṭiyoga*), having extracted the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*), the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*) consists of thirty entities (*dravya*);
the clinging to rules and observances consists of six entities. Why was it extracted from among the views?
Because it is the adversary of the path and because it deceives both sides—

laypeople are deceived by this through practices such as fasting under the notion that it is the path to heaven, and renunciants are deceived by the renunciation of desired objects under the notion that it leads to the attainment of purity.
For what reason was ignorance stated as being mixed with grasping rather than separately?
They are called "graspings" because they involve the grasping for existence; however, ignorance is not a grasper [in that sense], and thus it is mixed [with the others]. (38)
Because it is characterized by non-clarity and is dull, ignorance (*avidyā*) is not a grasper; therefore, it is said to be mixed [with other afflictions].
However, in the Sūtra the Blessed One said: "What is the bond of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*)?
In detail, up to: whatever sensual passion (*kāmarāga*), sensual longing (*kāmacchanda*), sensual affection (*kāmasneha*), and sensual love (*kāmaprema*) he has toward sensual pleasures..."

Desire for sensual pleasures, infatuation with sensual pleasures, greed for sensual pleasures, grasping at sensual pleasures, delighting in sensual pleasures, being bound by sensual pleasures, and fixation on sensual pleasures— when these persist by completely taking possession of one's mind, this is called the yoke of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*).
In this way, it extends up to the "yoke of views.

Furthermore, since desire and attachment (*cchanda-rāga*) are described as "clinging" (*upādāna*) in other sūtras, it is understood that clinging to sensual pleasures and so forth is likewise desire and attachment toward sensual pleasures and so forth.
This has been stated: that the very latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are designated in the sūtras as the outflows (*āsava*), floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), and clingings (*upādāna*).
Now, what is the meaning of "proclivity" (*anuśaya*), and what is the meaning of [the terms] up to "clinging" (*upādāna*)?

Because they are subtle (*aṇu*), because they are pervasive (*anugata*), because they adhere in two ways (*dvidhāpy anuśerate*), and because they bind (*anubadhnanti*), they are therefore known as proclivities (*anuśaya*). (36)
In this context, they are called *aṇavaḥ* (atoms/subtle) because they are difficult to discern due to their subtle activity;
they are "concomitant" (*anugatāḥ*) because of their continuous association;
and they "proliferate" (*anuśerate*) in two ways: by way of the object (*ālambana*) and by way of association (*saṃprayoga*).
They bind [the mind] even without conscious application, because they manifest again and again despite one's efforts to restrain them.
For these reasons, they are called *anuśaya*s (latent tendencies). They cause one to dwell [in saṃsāra], they flow [toward rebirth], they carry away [one's virtue], and they adhere [to the mind].
And thus, the etymological definitions of these [terms], such as "outflow" (āsrava) and so forth, are established. //40//
They are called *āsravas* because they cause one to settle in *saṃsāra* and flow [into it], from the Peak of Existence down to the Avīci hell, through the six wounds of the sense bases.
They are called *oghas* because they carry away. They are called *yogas* because they bind.

They are called "appropriations" (upādāna) because they grasp; however, it would be more accurate [to define them] as "outflows" (āsrava), since by means of these the continuum flows toward sense objects.
"For example, Venerable Ones, a boat is led against the current by great exertions;
yet, through the relaxation of those very same exertions, it moves with the current with little difficulty— so it is according to the teaching of the Sūtra."
They are called floods (*ogha*) because they possess excessive momentum; thus, one is carried away by them, as one conforms to their flow.
They are called yokes (*yoga*) because they join one to various forms of suffering, even when they do not manifest excessively.
They are called "appropriations" (upādāna) because they consist in the repeated attachment to or the grasping of desire and so forth.

Furthermore, they are taught as fivefold according to the distinctions of fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth. Those same latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are further explained by dividing them into five types: fetters, bonds (*bandhana*), latent dispositions, secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
Among these, there are nine fetters: the fetters of attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, views, adherence to views, doubt, envy, and avarice.
Therein, the fetter of attachment is craving belonging to the three realms.
In this manner, other [fetters] should be applied according to their possibility.
The fetter of views consists of three views;
the fetter of grasping consists of two views.

Therefore it is said: "Could it be that one is bound by the fetter of attachment (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) to those phenomena associated with views, but not by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), and yet the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭy-anuśaya*) does not fail to underlie them? He replied: "It could be so. When the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, regarding those phenomena associated with the view of grasping at precepts and observances (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*) which are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path—one is bound to them by the fetter of attachment, but is not bound by the fetter of views that takes them as its object."
Because the universal fetter has been abandoned, and because there is no non-universal fetter of views that takes those [factors] as its object or is associated with them;
yet the latent tendency of views still adheres to them,
for those very two [types of views] are the grasping-views by virtue of their association.

What, then, is the reason that among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), three views are stated separately as the "fetter of views" (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), while two other views are stated separately as the "fetter of grasping" (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*)?
Because of the commonality of being a substance and the act of grasping, these views constitute a distinct fetter. (41)

There are eighteen substances that constitute the three views (*dṛṣṭi*), and likewise eighteen that constitute the two views of grasping (*parāmarśadṛṣṭi*). It is said that because they are identical in terms of their substantial nature (*dravyasāmānya*), these are established as separate fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Furthermore, these two have the nature of *parāmarśa* (adherence), whereas the others do not; thus, on account of this commonality of being *parāmarśa*, these two are established separately from the rest due to the distinction between the object of grasping (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).
Now, why are envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) stated as two separate fetters (*saṃyojana*), and no other *paryavasthāna* (envelopment)?
Because both are exclusively unwholesome (*ekāntākuśala*) and because both are independent (*svatantra*).
Among these, envy and avarice are said to be two distinct fetters. //42//

For there is no other type of envelopment (*paryavasthāna*) in which both these qualities—being exclusively unwholesome (*ekāntākuśalatva*) and being independent (*svatantratva*)—are found. This would apply to one for whom there are eight envelopments; however, for one who has ten, both anger (*krodha*) and hypocrisy (*mrakṣa*) are likewise of both types.
Therefore, others maintain that this is not a valid resolution.

Furthermore, elsewhere the Blessed One has stated that the fetters are fivefold, pertaining to the lower realm (*avarabhāgīya*): namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), and ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
Why are these called "pertaining to the lower realm"?
Because they belong to the lower portion;
for the lower portion is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and these [factors] are conducive to it.
Because:
By two [hindrances], there is no transcendence of the desire realm;
by three, however, there is a return.
Through sensual desire and ill will, one does not transcend the desire realm.
Even though one has transcended the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the others, one is turned back again due to their similarity to gatekeepers and attendants.

By three [fetters], one does not transcend the inferiority of sentient beings, namely the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*); by two, one does not transcend the inferiority of the realm, namely the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
For this very reason, others maintain that these are called "belonging to the lower portion" (*avarabhāgīya*).

When, for a stream-enterer, six afflictions have been abandoned through the complete abandonment of the three fetters, for what reason does [the Buddha] set aside the other views and mention only these three: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)?
All of this ought to be explained.
But why was it said that the triad [of faculties] is grasped by means of the "mouth" and the "root"? //43//

It is said that the afflictions are of three types: those of one type, two types, and four types; their essential nature is thus grasped by these three [categories]. Furthermore, the view of grasping at extremes is set in motion by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Adherence to views is set in motion by adherence to rules and observances, while false view is set in motion by doubt; therefore, the root has been grasped. Others, however, say:

The desire to go elsewhere, confusion regarding the path, and doubt about the path—these are the obstacles to proceeding toward liberation; therefore, the teaching of the Three Jewels [is given]. (44)
There are three obstacles to traveling to another country:
the lack of desire to go, confusion regarding the path due to resorting to a wrong path, and doubt concerning the path.
In the same way, these very same three are obstacles to proceeding toward liberation.
In that regard, for one who has fallen into fear of liberation due to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), there arises an unwillingness to approach it.
Due to the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), there is a deviation from the path by resorting to other paths.
Due to doubt (*vicikitsā*), there is uncertainty regarding the path.
Illuminating the abandonment of these obstacles to the attainment of liberation, the Blessed One taught the abandonment of the three afflictions alone.
Just as the Blessed One has spoken of the fivefold lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), so too has he spoken of the fivefold higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*).
To the question "How so?", he says:
"There are two types of passion, those born of the form realm and the formless realm."

Excitement, pride, and delusion—these are the five fetters pertaining to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*). Namely: attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*), attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*), excitement (*auddhatya*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because one cannot transcend the higher realms without abandoning these,
the discussion on the fetters (*saṃyojana*) is concluded.
What are the bonds (*bandhana*)?
There are three fetters:
all lust is a fetter, all hatred is a fetter, and all delusion is a fetter.
Why has the Blessed One declared that these three alone are fetters?
From malice, there is the threefold bondage. //45//
Due to the three types of sensation, there are three fetters:
for passion underlies pleasant sensation through both its object and its association;
hatred underlies painful sensation.
Delusion [predominates] in the state that is neither painful nor pleasant, whereas passion and hatred do not;
or rather, the restriction is based on their having their own internal continuum as their object.
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have already been explained; the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) must now be discussed.
Among them, those which are afflictions (*kleśa*) are also secondary afflictions.
Because they defile the mind:

those other afflicted mental factors included within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) are also secondary afflictions (upakleśa) in relation to the primary afflictions (kleśa), yet they are not designated by the term "affliction. //46//

Furthermore, those other afflicted mental factors (*caitasika*) subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) that arise from the afflictions (*kleśa*) are indeed secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). These are the ones enumerated in the *Kṣudravastuka*;
however, here we shall explain only those included within the categories of the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), the afflictions (*kleśa*), and the stains (*mala*).
What, then, are the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*)? He says:
even an affliction (*kleśa*) is an envelopment, because it is stated in the Sūtra, "Suffering has the envelopment of sensual desire as its condition.
However, in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*...
Lack of shame, lack of dread, envy, avarice, restlessness, regret, torpor-languor—these are the eight types of envelopments (paryavasthāna). 47.
Furthermore, according to the Vaibhāṣika system, there are ten secondary afflictions (paryavasthāna): these eight, plus anger (krodha) and concealment (mrakṣa).
Among them, lack of shame (āhrīkya) and lack of dread (anapatrāpya) have already been explained.
Envy (*īrṣyā*) is resentment of the mind toward the prosperity of others. Avarice (*mātsarya*) is a grasping of the mind that opposes the giving of Dharma, material goods, or skills.
Restlessness (*auddhatya*) is the lack of tranquility of the mind.
Remorse and lethargy have already been explained.
Torpor (*middha*) is a contraction of the mind that renders one incapable of sustaining the body;
it is exclusively a defiled entanglement (*paryavasthāna*).
And remorse. Anger (*krodha*) is a state of malice toward sentient and non-sentient beings, excluding ill-will (*vyāpāda*) and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*).
Concealment of one's faults (*mrakṣa*) is the hiding of what is blameworthy.
And as for these ten secondary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), [the following applies]:
Shamelessness, restlessness, and avarice arise from attachment;
these three secondary afflictions are the outflows of attachment. Some say that in the case of hypocrisy, dispute is the outflow of craving.
Others say it is the outflow of ignorance;
others say it is of both;
and [others] say it is respectively for those who have known and those who have not known.
From ignorance [arise] sloth, torpor, and lack of shame. //48//
These three are the outflows of ignorance (*avidyā-niṣyanda*):

remorse arises from doubt; anger and envy arise as a consequence of and originate from hostility (*pratigha*). Thus, these ten secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are the outflows of the primary afflictions (*kleśa*).
And there are six other stains of the afflictions, namely:
deceit, guile, and likewise pride. //46//
[The remaining secondary afflictions are] malice, resentment, and harmfulness.
Among these, *māyā* is the deception of others;
*śāṭhya* is crookedness of mind, by which one does not reveal things as they truly are, or acts in a way that is evasive or unclear.
Arrogance (*mada*) is as previously described.
Resentment (*pradāśa*) is the stubborn adherence to blameworthy things, by which one does not accept reasoned instruction. Enmity (*upanāha*) is the frequent cultivation of objects of malice.
"Affliction" (*viheṭhanā*) is violence (*vihiṃsā*), by which one afflicts others through blows, harshness, and so forth.
Furthermore, among these six stains of the afflictions (*kleśamala*), two arise from attachment (*rāga*).
Deceit and intoxication arise from anger; enmity and harmfulness [arise] from resentment. //50//
"From attachment to views comes spite; deceit arises from views.
Because of the statement in the verse, "What is crooked? It is an evil view," it is logical that deceit is the outflow of views.
[Which among these are to be abandoned?

Regarding those ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) that have been mentioned, therein shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), torpor (*styāna*), drowsiness (*middha*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*) are twofold. //51//]
These five factors are of two kinds—namely, those to be abandoned by vision and those to be abandoned by cultivation—because they are associated with both types of afflictions.
That which is associated with what is to be abandoned by a particular vision is itself to be abandoned by that vision;
the others are to be abandoned by cultivation.
Other secondary afflictions (upakleśa) comprised within the envelopments (paryavasthāna) are to be abandoned only by cultivation (bhāvanāheya).
Envy, avarice, regret, anger, and concealment are independent;
these five secondary afflictions are independent because they are associated with ignorance alone.
Just as these five secondary afflictions, beginning with envy, are to be abandoned through cultivation and are independent, so too are the stains;
likewise are the six stains of the afflictions.
Furthermore, these aforementioned secondary afflictions (upakleśa) are unwholesome (akuśala) in the realm of desire;
that is, they are unwholesome within the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Therein, three— namely, lethargy, restlessness, and torpor— are of two kinds: unwholesome and indeterminate.
Beyond that, they are indeterminate. //52//

Above the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), as far as they occur. Furthermore, how many of these are to be understood as belonging to which realms?
Deceit (*māyā*) and guile (*śāṭhya*) exist in the desire realm and the first dhyāna;
these two are present in the desire realm and in the first dhyāna.
How can there be illusions in the Brahma-world?
Because of Brahma’s deception; for there, that Mahābrahmā proceeded to deceive the venerable Aśvajit by displaying a false appearance of himself.
Although deceit (*śāṭhya*) was already mentioned, it is stated again here because it arises in this context.
Torpor, restlessness, and pride (*styānauddhatyamada*) exist in the three realms; these three belong to all three realms (*traidhātuka*).
Others are born in the desire realm. // 53 //
Excluding five from the sixteen, the remaining eleven secondary afflictions belong exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
The primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) have been explained.
Now, among these, how many belong to the level of the mental consciousness (*manobhūmika*), and how many belong to the level of the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñānabhūmika*)?
In brief,
those to be abandoned by seeing that are established as being equal [to their counterparts] belong to the level of mental consciousness;
all [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing belong to the level of the mind, together with pride and torpor, even though these two are also [partly] to be abandoned by cultivation.

For those secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that belong entirely to the mental level (*manobhūmika*), as well as any independent secondary afflictions whatsoever— though they are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*)— are to be understood as belonging exclusively to the mental level.
The others have the six consciousnesses as their supports. // 54 //
Other afflictions and secondary afflictions should be understood as belonging to the level of the six consciousnesses.

Which, then, are these others? They are attachment, aversion, and ignorance that are to be abandoned by cultivation, along with the secondary afflictions associated with them—namely, shamelessness, lack of dread, lethargy, and restlessness.
Regarding those [factors] mentioned among the universal defilements (*kleśamahābhūmika*),
as for these five faculties beginning with pleasure (*sukha*), with which faculty is which primary or secondary defilement associated?
For passion (*rāga*) is indeed associated with the two [faculties of] pleasure.
Attachment is associated with pleasure and mental joy;
hatred is the opposite,
meaning it is associated with the two types of suffering.
[They arise] with suffering and mental distress,
because attachment and aversion function in the forms of joy and dejection, and because they belong to the level of the six consciousnesses;
delusion [arises] with all [of them].
Because ignorance is associated with all afflictions, it is associated with all five faculties. False view, however, is associated with mental suffering and pleasure. (55)
Mental suffering is *daurmanasya* (dejection), and mental pleasure is *saumanasya* (contentment).
False view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is associated with these two respectively for those who perform meritorious deeds and those who perform evil deeds.
Doubt (*kāṅkṣā*) is associated with dejection.
For one who desires certainty becomes dejected when faced with doubt; others [become dejected] through mental pleasure (*saumanasya*),
while other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are associated exclusively with mental pleasure.
What others are there? The four views and pride,
because they function with the aspect of exhilaration.
With what are these underlying tendencies (anuśaya) associated?
He replied:
"They are born of desire. Having thus explained their specific association, he spoke generally:
All of these latent dispositions (anuśaya) are associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya),
for it is said that at the time when the continuity [of existence] is severed, equanimity necessarily remains present among the afflictions (kleśa).
He explains how those belonging to the lower stages [attain] it:
"Those belonging to the higher stages [attain it] by means of their own respective [paths], according to their stage. (56)
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the higher stages are associated with their respective sense-faculties;
in whichever stage there are however many faculties,

therein those belonging to the four groups of consciousness are associated with those belonging to the four groups of consciousness, and those belonging to the mental stage (*manobhūmika*) are associated only with those belonging to the mental stage, according to what is possible.
The association of the primary afflictions with the faculties has been explained.
Furthermore, regarding the secondary afflictions: remorse, envy, anger, and harmfulness are associated with mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*).
Enmity (*upanāha*) and spite (*pradāśa*) are included among the associated [mental factors],
because they function in the form of dejection and because they belong to the mental level (*manobhūmika*).
But stinginess is the opposite. //57//
The meaning is "by means of mental joy" (*saumanasya*),
because, being associated with greed (*lobha*), it functions in the form of exhilaration.
Deceit (*māyā*), guile (*śāṭhya*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), and torpor (*middha*) [function] in both ways.
They are associated with both mental pleasure and mental pain;
for sometimes one who is joyful deceives another, and sometimes one who is dejected does so.

In this way, it continues up to sleep. Intoxication [arises] from the two types of pleasure: in the third dhyāna, from pleasure; below that, from mental joy (*saumanasya*); and above that, from equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Because all latent dispositions (anuśaya) are associated with equanimity (upekṣā), which is universal.
For there is no negation of that [emptiness] anywhere, as there is of ignorance; the other four [noble truths] are each associated with five [factors]. 58.

Lack of shame (āhrīkya), lack of dread (anapatrāpya), lethargy (styāna), and restlessness (auddhatya)—these four envelopments (paryavasthāna) are associated with all five faculties, because they belong both to the category of the great unwholesome ground (akuśalamahābhūmika) and the category of the great afflictive ground (kleśamahābhūmika).

As for those which are stated in the Sūtra as the five hindrances (nivaraṇa): "sensual desire (kāmacchanda), ill-will (vyāpāda), lethargy-and-drowsiness (styānamiddha), restlessness-and-regret (auddhatyakaukṛtya), and doubt (vicikitsā)."
In that regard, are the sloth, restlessness, and doubt belonging to all three realms included? Or are they associated only with the desire realm?
Because it is stated in the Sūtra that they are exclusively unwholesome: "This entire, complete mass of the unwholesome consists of the five hindrances."
The hindrances exist only in the desire realm and not in other realms.
But what is the reason that torpor and drowsiness are declared to be one hindrance, while restlessness and remorse are declared to be another?
The unity of the two [factors] arises from their having a single adversary, a single nutriment, and a single function;
this is the "unity of the two."

The adverse side (*vipakṣa*), the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*), and that which is not nutriment (*anāhāra*) have one and the same meaning. In the Sūtra, both the nutriment and the non-nutriment of sloth and torpor (*styānamiddha*) are mentioned.
What is the nutriment of the hindrance of sloth and torpor?
There are five factors:
languor, restlessness, yawning, irregularity in eating, and mental depression. Now, the non-nutrient for the hindrance of sloth and torpor is the perception of light.
The function of these two is also one;
for both of them incite the mind toward lethargy.
Furthermore, it is said that excitement and remorse have one and the same nutriment and one and the same non-nutriment.
And what is the nourishment for the hindrance of restlessness and remorse?
It consists of four factors:

discursive thought concerning relatives, discursive thought concerning one's country, discursive thought concerning the gods, and being one who recollects former instances of laughter, play, delight, and amusement.
And what is the nourishment for the hindrance of restlessness and regret?
It is tranquility (*śamatha*).
Furthermore, the function of these two is also one and the same.
For both of these cause the mind to remain unpeaceful;
therefore, because they perform the function of providing nourishment for the same single adversary, the two are said to be one.
[If all afflictions are hindrances, why are only five mentioned?]
The state of being fivefold [is established] because of the destruction of the aggregates and the removal of doubt. //56//
Through sensual desire and ill will, there is the destruction of the aggregate of ethical discipline;

through sloth and torpor, the aggregate of wisdom is destroyed; and through restlessness and remorse, the aggregate of concentration is destroyed. Since one becomes skeptical regarding the truths when concentration and wisdom are absent, five [hindrances] are thus taught.
"In this interpretation, however, it would follow that the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, which is opposed to the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), should be mentioned first.
Therefore, others say: 'The destruction of the aggregates of concentration and wisdom occurs by these two [hindrances] respectively;
for one engaged in concentration, there are indeed the two [hindrances of] sloth-torpor and restlessness-remorse.'"
For one engaged in the discernment of phenomena, [the obstacle arises] from restlessness and remorse.
Others, however, describe it differently.
How do they describe it?

They say that for one who has gone on his rounds, the grasping of signs regarding objects of a pleasant or unpleasant nature leads, when he has returned to his dwelling, to sensual desire and ill-will preceded by those signs; these two create an obstacle at the very beginning of entering into meditative concentration.

Then, for one who has entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*), through the practice of serenity (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) without deliberate application, lethargy-and-drowsiness (*styāna-middha*), restlessness-and-regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) respectively create obstacles to serenity and insight.
Furthermore, even for one who has emerged from absorption, at the time of investigating the Dharma, doubt creates an obstacle.
Therefore, the five hindrances have been taught.
This is now considered:

when the objects of those universal [defilements] belonging to a different realm, as well as those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path which have contaminated objects, are fully understood, they are not yet abandoned at that time.
When they are abandoned, their object is not fully understood; thus, how can there be the abandonment of these [afflictions]?
The destruction of afflictions does not necessarily result from the full understanding of their objects.
What then?
By four modes.
Which four?
First, regarding those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing:
Through the full comprehension of the object, through the destruction of that which has it as its object,
and through the abandonment of the object—

therein, "through the full comprehension of the object" refers to those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin, which have their own level as their object and which have the untainted as their object.
Due to the destruction of those objects, the universal [defilements] belonging to a different realm are abandoned;
for the universal [defilements] belonging to their own realm have those as their objects,
and when those [objects] are abandoned, they too become abandoned.
[They are abandoned] through the abandonment of their objects: namely, those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path that have contaminated objects.
For those [defilements] which have the uncontaminated as their object serve as the objects for these [others];
therefore, when those [objects] are abandoned, they too become abandoned.
Furthermore, the destruction of those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation occurs through the arising of their antidote. //60//
For whichever type of affliction the path that serves as its antidote arises, that affliction is abandoned.
But which [affliction] has which as its antidote?
We shall explain this in detail later: that the mild-mild [path] is the antidote for the intense-intense [affliction], and so forth.

And as to how many kinds there are of the counteragent (pratipakṣa), he says: the counteragent is fourfold, known as abandonment (prahāṇa), support (ādhāra), remoteness (dūratva), and non-defilement (adūṣaṇa).
The counteragent of abandonment (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*) is the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*).
The supporting counteragent (*ādhārapratipakṣa*) is the noble path subsequent to that, by which the abandonment attained is maintained.
The counteragent of distancing (*dūrībhāvapratipakṣa*) is the path subsequent to the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), because it distances the possession (*prāpti*) that has been severed.
Others say that the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) is also [the counteragent].
For it too distances that possession (*prāpti*).
The counteragent of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā-pratipakṣa*) is that path by which one reviles that realm by seeing it as faulty.
However, this sequence would be correct:
the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) has as its object the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudaya*) and functions as the counteragent of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇāpratipakṣa*);
all paths of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) function as the counteragent of abandonment (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*).
The path of liberation is the counteragent of support;
the path of distinction is the counteragent of distancing.
From where, then, is the affliction being abandoned to be abandoned?
It is held that an affliction is to be abandoned by means of its object. //61//
For a defilement cannot be separated from its associated mental factors, but it can be separated from its object;
because, once separated, it does not arise again by taking that as its object.
At least in the case of future defilements, they can be separated from their objects.
But how is that which is past [to be abandoned]?

Now, if it is argued that it is to be abandoned through the thorough knowledge of its object (*ālambana-parijñāna*), this is not its definitive meaning; for even this is not absolute. Therefore, this must be explained.

To what extent should it be said that a defilement (*kleśa*) has been abandoned? A defilement belonging to one’s own continuum is abandoned through the severance of its acquisition (*prāpti*). However, a defilement belonging to another’s continuum, as well as all matter (*rūpa*) and all non-defiled phenomena (*dharma*), are abandoned through the abandonment of the defilements belonging to one’s own continuum that take them as objects.
It is called "becoming distant. How many kinds of becoming distant are there? It is said that distance is of four kinds.

Remoteness is of four kinds: due to difference in nature, due to being an opposing factor, due to spatial separation, and due to time—just as, for example, there is remoteness between the elements, moral conduct, different locations, and the two time periods [past and future]. (62)
Remoteness by way of characteristic is, for example, the remoteness of the primary elements from one another despite being co-nascent, due to their differing characteristics.
Remoteness by way of opposition is, for example, that of ethical discipline from immorality.
Remoteness due to spatial separation (*deśaviccheda*) is, for example, like that of distant places, such as the eastern and western oceans, because of their spatial separation.
Remoteness due to time (*kāladūratā*) is, for example, as when the past and the future are said to be remote. Why are they remote? [Because of the interval between them.]
From the present—
[that which has just passed away or is currently arising]— how can that be distant?
It is distant by virtue of being a different time-period (*adhvan*), not because it occurred long ago or will occur long hence.
In that case, even the present would become distant.
If it is because of its lack of activity (*akāritra*) that it is distant,
then how is the proximity of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) established?
Because it would follow that it is attained everywhere;
[otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of its attainment even in the past and the future,
and what of space?
In that case, then, the past and the future are distant from each other because they are separated by the present;
the present is near to both because it is proximate to them;
and the unconditioned is also [near] because it is not separated [by anything].
Even so, because the past and the future are proximate to the present, both would be considered near.
However, this would be more logical:
the future is distant from the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a phenomenon because it has not yet been attained.
And the past [defilements] have already fallen away.
[Question: Is there a further distinction in the abandonment of defilements resulting from proceeding through specific stages of the path?
[Answer: This is not so.
For all afflictions are destroyed simultaneously; whichever is the path of abandonment for a particular affliction, by that very path its destruction occurs.

The attainment of dissociation from those [defilements] occurs again and again; as for at how many times, it is said: at six times—namely, at the arising of the counteragent, the attainment of the fruit, and the increase of the faculties. //63//
The counteragent intended here is the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
The fruits are the four fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
The increase of the faculties is the transformation of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*).
At these times, there is the attainment of dissociation from the afflictions;
furthermore, this should be understood according to the circumstances:
for some, it occurs at six times, and for others, up to two.
That very dissociation receives the designation "thorough knowledge" (parijñā) in various states.
For there are two kinds of thorough knowledge: thorough knowledge as cognition and thorough knowledge as abandonment.
Among these, thorough knowledge as cognition is untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
But thorough knowledge as abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) is indeed abandonment itself,
because the cause is metaphorically designated by the name of the fruit.
[Is it then that there is only one single thorough knowledge for all abandonments?]
He said: "No.
What then?
"The thorough knowledges are nine."
In that regard, first,
the destruction of the first two types of desire and so forth constitutes one [perfection].

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the abandonment of the first two types—those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*) and the origin (*samudaya*)—is one thorough knowledge (*parijñā*). There are two [thorough knowledges] for the destruction of the [remaining] two;
that is, in the desire realm alone, the abandonment of the type to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha*) is one thorough knowledge.
There is one [complete knowledge] for that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the path.
Just as there are three complete knowledges for the abandonment of those things to be abandoned by vision belonging to the desire realm, so too are there exactly three above that. //64//

The abandonment of those factors belonging to the realms of form and formlessness that are to be abandoned by seeing likewise constitutes three thorough knowledges (*parijñā*). The abandonment of those factors to be abandoned by seeing suffering and its origin is the first; the abandonment of those to be abandoned by seeing cessation is the second; and the abandonment of those to be abandoned by seeing the path is the third. Thus, the abandonment of all factors of the three realms to be abandoned by seeing constitutes six thorough knowledges. The others are the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), the abandonment of form, and the destruction of all outflows (*āsrava*).
There are three thorough knowledges (*parijñā*): the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*) is one thorough knowledge;
the abandonment of the outflow of form (*rūpāsrava*) is one thorough knowledge, namely the thorough knowledge of the destruction of attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāgakṣayaparijñā*).

For those pertaining to the formless realm, the abandonment of all outflows (*āsrava*) constitutes a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), namely, the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojana-paryādāna-parijñā*).

Why is the abandonment of the [defilements] of the form and formless realms to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) a distinct thorough knowledge, whereas that of those to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*) is not?
Because the counteragents (*pratipakṣa*) for those to be abandoned by cultivation are not uniform.
Thus, these are the nine thorough cognitions.
Of these, the first six are the fruit of patience (kṣānti), which have the nature of abandoning what is to be abandoned by seeing (darśana-heya).
They are the remnants of knowledge. //65//

The thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) such as the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*) are the fruits of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). How, then, can the thorough knowledges be the fruit of the receptive patiences (*kṣānti*)?
Because the receptive patiences have knowledge (*jñāna*) as their retinue.
It is like the royal attendants' service toward the king;
and because its sole fruit is gnosis.

The fruit of the *anāgamya* stage consists of all [nine] knowledges (*parijñā*). Alternatively, according to the Vaibhāṣika school, the fruit of the fundamental dhyānas consists of five knowledges, which have the nature of abandoning the afflictions belonging to the realms of form and formlessness.

Because the abandonment of the afflictions belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) is the fruit of the *anāgamya* [attainment], according to the opinion of the Venerable Ghoṣaka there are eight. For he maintains that even for one who is already free from passion (*vītarāga*), the abandonment of those afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*) is the fruit of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
due to the acquisition of the untainted possession of dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*).
The full comprehension consisting in the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-prahāṇa-parijñā*) is indeed the fruit of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
The intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) is to be regarded as being like the [fundamental] dhyānas.
However, regarding the formless attainments (*ārūpyas*), [the situation is different].
One [result] belongs to the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*);

one is the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of passion for the form realm (*rūparāgakṣayaparijñā*) as the fruit of the preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-sāmantaka*); and [one each] belongs to the three fundamental (*maula*) formless attainments. //66//
And for the three fundamental formless [attainments], there is only one fruit: the thorough knowledge consisting in the total exhaustion of all fetters.
For the noble path, all nine thorough knowledges are the fruit.
Two are the fruits of the mundane path: the two thorough knowledges of the destruction of the lower fetters and of attachment to the realm of form;
and also that of subsequent knowledge.
For subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) as well, two thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) are the result, namely the last two.

For dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), however, there are three results; these are indeed the last three, because it serves as the antidote to that which is to be abandoned through cultivation in the three realms.
Six for that side, and five. //67//
Six thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) are the fruit of the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), namely those which are the forbearances (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) of dharma-knowledge.
Five are the fruit of the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), namely those which are the forbearances and knowledges of subsequent knowledge.
For by the mention of the "category" (*pakṣa*), both the forbearances and the knowledges are included.
Why is each individual abandonment not established as a thorough knowledge (*parijñā*)?
Because, first of all, abandonment is established as the fruit of the receptivities (*kṣānti*),
due to the attainment of untainted disjunction (*anāsrava-viyoga-prāpti*) and the impairment of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Thorough knowledge is the eradication of two causes; that abandonment in which these three conditions are present is called thorough knowledge.
Since an ordinary person lacks the untainted attainment of dissociation and the impairment of the peak of existence, their abandonment does not receive the designation of "thorough knowledge."
Regarding the abandonment that constitutes the fruit of patience for the Noble One as well:

therein, up until the patience for the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñānakṣānti*), there exists an untainted acquisition of dissociation (*anāsravā visaṃyogaprāpti*), yet the summit of existence (*bhavāgra*) has not been impaired.

At the stage of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna*), both [the acquisition of dissociation and the impairment of the summit of existence] exist, yet there is no eradication of the two causes.
Because the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin has not yet been abandoned,
all three [factors] exist in other dharma-knowledges and subsequent knowledges; therefore, in those respective states, abandonment receives the designation of "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).
But abandonment is the fruit of knowledge;
therefore, due to these three reasons and the fourth as well, it receives the designation of "thorough knowledge."
Because of the transcendence of the realms. // 68 //
When one transcends an element (*dhātu*),
others say that the fifth cause is the dissociation from both [the object and the defilement] due to detachment from the entire element;
this refers to a case where, even if a certain category has been abandoned, one becomes dissociated from the defilement that takes it as its object by means of another [path].
But we do not say that the other [type of abandonment] is due to the eradication of both causes and the transcendence of the realm (*dhātu*).
[Regarding the question: "Who is endowed with how many thorough knowledges (*parijñā*)?"—one who abides in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is endowed with either one or up to five.
First of all, an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is not at all possessed [of this].
Even a noble one (ārya) abiding on the path of seeing is not at all possessed of it up until the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (samudaya-dharmajñānakṣānti).
At the moment of the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (samudaye dharmajñāna), one is possessed of one [moment].
In the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaye 'nvayajñāne*), one possesses two;

in the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodhe dharmajñāne*), three; in the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāne*), four; and in the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārgadharmajñāne*), five.
Furthermore, one abiding in the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) possesses six, or one, or two. (69)

Furthermore, a noble person (āryapudgala) abiding on the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) is endowed with six thorough knowledges (parijñā) during the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna), as long as they have not attained detachment from the desire realm (kāmavairāgya) or have not fallen away from it. Once detachment from the desire realm has been attained—whether previously or subsequently—they are endowed with one thorough knowledge, namely, the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters (avarabhāgīya-prahāṇa-parijñā). Upon attaining arhatship, they are endowed with only one thorough knowledge: the thorough knowledge of the total exhaustion of all fetters (sarvasaṃyojana-paryādāna-parijñā).
Even when fallen away due to an outburst belonging to the form realm, one possesses one thorough knowledge: the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters.

Having attained detachment from the form realm, one possesses two: the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters and the thorough knowledge of the destruction of passion for the form realm.
Even when fallen away due to an outburst belonging to the formless realm, one likewise possesses those same two.
What, then, is the reason that for the non-returner (anāgāmin) only one single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) is established, and not more?
Because their consolidation occurs through detachment from a realm and the attainment of a fruit.

The consolidation of thorough knowledges—that is, their establishment as a single unit—occurs by way of two causes: through detachment from a realm (*dhātuvairāgya*) and through the attainment of a fruit (*phalaprāpti*).
In these two states, both of these [conditions] occur;
therefore, summing up all abandonments, a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) is spoken of. Now, which person abandons or acquires how many thorough knowledges?
Someone abandons one, two, five, or six [faculties], but no one acquires five [that they did not previously possess]. //70//
One abandons one [parijñā] when falling away from arhatship or from detachment from the desire realm.
One abandons two parijñās when a non-returner who is detached from the form realm falls away from detachment from the desire realm.
One abandons five [parijñās] when one who was previously detached from the desire realm [attains] the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna).
For upon attaining the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), one abandons the five previous thorough knowledges;
likewise, one who follows the gradual path (*ānupūrvika*) abandons six thorough knowledges through the detachment from desire (*kāmavairāgya*).
It is exactly the same regarding their attainment.
Someone attains one thorough knowledge; someone attains one that was previously unattained;
and someone attains two, namely, one who falls away from the state of detachment from the formless realm alone.
One person—the one who falls away from the fruit of a non-returner—possesses six;
however, no one possesses five.
The discussion concerning thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) is concluded.
Thus ends the fifth treasury-location (kośasthāna) of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, titled "The Exposition of the Latent Dispositions" (anuśayanirdeśa).
Whatever merit is herein from Śrī Lāmāvāka, [may it be for the sake of all beings]. The sixth treasury-location.
Homage to the Buddha.
It has been explained how abandonment receives the designation of "thorough knowledge.
Furthermore, that abandonment of the afflictions is declared to result from the vision and cultivation of the truths.
It has been explained in detail that the afflictions (*kleśa*) are to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Now, it must be stated whether these two—the path of seeing and the path of cultivation—are untainted (*anāsrava*) or tainted (*sāsrava*).
Therefore, this is said:
The path of cultivation is twofold, whereas that called the path of seeing is exclusively untainted. //1//
The path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) is twofold: mundane (laukika) and supramundane (lokottara).

The path of seeing (darśanamārga), however, is exclusively supramundane; for it serves as the antidote to the three realms and because it abandons the nine categories of afflictions to be abandoned by seeing all at once.
For a worldly person does not possess this power.
It was stated, "from the vision of the truths.
What are these truths? And how many are there?
The truths have been stated to be four.

Where were they stated? In the exposition of contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena: the Truth of the Path was stated by its own name as "the uncontaminated is the Truth of the Path"; the Truth of Cessation as "cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyānirodha*), which is disjunction (*visaṃyoga*"); and the Truths of Suffering and Origination in the passage "suffering, origination, and the world."
Is this indeed their sequence?
No, he says; what then?
Suffering, its origin, cessation, and the path— this is their sequence.
The word "thus" (*tathā*) is for the purpose of demonstrating that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is exactly as it was previously stated.
Furthermore, this—namely, the sequence of these [elements]—is according to their realization (*yathābhisamaya*). //2//
For that truth whose realization occurs first is taught first;
otherwise, there would have been a teaching of the cause first and the result later.
For some, the teaching follows the sequence of their arising.
Just as with the applications of mindfulness, the meditative absorptions, and so forth;
for some, the teaching is arranged according to their systematic exposition, as is the case with the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
For there is no fixed rule that one must first generate the will (*chanda*) for the abandonment of those [defilements] already arisen.
"Subsequently, for the sake of the non-arising of those [dharmas] that have not yet arisen.
However, the teaching of the truths is in accordance with their realization (*abhisamaya*).
But what is the reason that the realization of these truths occurs in this very order?
For that to which one is attached, by which one is afflicted, and from which one seeks liberation—that very thing, namely the Truth of Suffering, is first examined during the stage of investigation.
Subsequently, one examines the Truth of Origination as "what is its cause?", the Truth of Cessation as "what is its cessation?", and the Truth of the Path as "what is its path?".
This is like seeing an illness and then seeking out its cause, its remedy for destruction, and the medicine.
This very same illustration of the truths is also shown in a sutra.
In which sutra? In this one: "A physician who removes arrows is endowed with four factors."

Just as there is an investigation of the truths during the stage of analytical examination, so too is there a clear realization of the truths during the stage of clear realization, due to the momentum of the former, like a horse running unimpeded over ground already seen.
What is the meaning of *abhisamaya*?
It means "perfect awakening" (*abhisambodha*), because the root *i* has the sense of "awakening.
Why is it only untainted (*anāsrava*) and not tainted (*sāsrava*)?
For that is right awakening directed toward nirvāṇa;
"right" means in accordance with reality.
In this context, the appropriated aggregates, which constitute the fruit, are the truth of suffering.
Those which have become causes are the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*), because [suffering] originates from them.
For this very reason, there is a distinction between these two by name due to their relationship as effect and cause, but not substantially.
But as for cessation and the path, they are said in the Sūtra to be "Noble Truths" even in terms of substantial entity. What is the meaning of this?
"These are the truths of the noble ones; therefore they are called 'Noble Truths,'" as it is stated in the Sūtra itself.
Are these false for others?
These are truths for everyone, because they are non-erroneous.
However, these are seen by the noble ones (ārya) as they truly are, and not by others.
Therefore, these are called the truths of the noble ones, but not those of the non-noble ones, because of their contrary vision.
"What the noble ones declare to be happiness, others know as suffering."
"What others call happiness, the noble ones know as suffering"— this is the verse.
Others say that there are two truths of the noble ones and two noble truths, meaning they are both noble and the truths of the noble ones.
If only a portion of feeling has the nature of suffering, how is it said that all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering?
[The answer is: They are suffering because they are connected with the three types of suffering, without exception, as appropriate.
Those that are agreeable, disagreeable, and others besides these, which are all with outflows (sāsrava). //3//

For there are three types of suffering: the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*).
By means of these, all contaminated (*sāsrava*) formations are, as appropriate, entirely suffering.
Among them, those that are pleasant are [suffering] through the suffering of change.
Unpleasant things [are suffering] through the suffering of suffering;
those other than these are [suffering] through the suffering of conditioned formations.
But which are the pleasant? Which are the unpleasant? And which are neither?
There are three feelings, respectively; by virtue of them, the formations that are to be experienced as pleasant and so forth also receive the designations of "agreeable" and so on.
For pleasant feeling is suffering through its transformation (*vipariṇāma*);
as it is said in the Sūtra: "Pleasant feeling is pleasant in its arising, pleasant in its remaining, and suffering in its transformation."
The suffering of that which is painful is its very nature of suffering, as stated in the Sūtra: "Painful feeling is suffering in its arising and suffering in its duration.
The suffering of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is its suffering by way of its conditioned nature (*saṃskāra*).
Because it is conditioned by conditions, [it is said]: "That which is impermanent is suffering.
Just as with feeling (*vedanā*), the formations (*saṃskāra*) that are to be experienced are also so called.
Suffering itself is the state of suffering; this is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*).
In this way, others maintain that even conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are themselves suffering.

Because pleasant and unpleasant things are not common to all [beings], their respective sufferings—suffering due to change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) and suffering as pain (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*)—have been explained.
However, all conditioned phenomena are suffering by virtue of the suffering inherent in conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Only the noble ones see them;
and it is said in this regard:
"Just as a single eyelash placed upon the palm of the hand is not perceived by ordinary people,"
For that very same thing, when it enters the eye, produces both distress and pain.
"The fool, who is like the palm of the hand, does not perceive the eyelash of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations;
but the wise man, who is like the eye, is deeply distressed by that very same thing."

For the perception of suffering does not arise in fools even regarding the aggregates of the Avīci hell in the same way that it arises in the noble ones even regarding those at the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
If that were so, then it would follow that the Path (mārga) is also the suffering of conditioned formations (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā),
because it is conditioned (saṃskṛta).
For suffering is defined by the characteristic of being disagreeable; therefore, the Path is not suffering.
Indeed, its arising is not disagreeable to the Noble Ones, because it brings about the destruction of all suffering.
Even when they perceive Nirvana as peace, they perceive the cessation of that very thing which was seen as suffering, and not the cessation of the Path.
Even though there is some pleasure here as well, why is it called only the Noble Truth of Suffering?
Some say it is because of the scarcity of that pleasure, just as a heap of black gram (*māṣa*) is designated as such even when mung beans (*mudga*) and other grains are present.
For what wise person would determine that an abscess is "pleasure" on account of a tiny bit of pleasure from sprinkling water?
It is indeed said:

"Because it is a cause of suffering, because it is produced together with no small amount of sufferings, and because one desires it only when suffering exists, they determine that what is called 'pleasure' is actually suffering. However, the Noble Ones perceive the entirety of existence as suffering, together with pleasure itself.
Because conditioned phenomena have the single flavor of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*),
it is established that only suffering is a noble truth (*āryasatya*), not pleasure.
How, then, do they perceive a feeling that has the nature of pleasure as suffering?
Because they are disagreeable due to their impermanence,
one views even the perceptions of form and so forth as suffering;
yet these are not suffering in the same way that the feeling of pain is suffering.
But for one who thinks that [the form aggregate is suffering] because it is a cause of suffering,
that would be its aspect as origin (*samudaya-ākāra*), not its aspect as suffering (*duḥkha-ākāra*).
Furthermore, how could the perception of suffering (*duḥkha-saṃjñā*) arise for the Noble Ones when they are reborn in the realms of form (*rūpa*) or formlessness (*arūpya*)?

For indeed, the aggregates do not again become a cause for their painful feeling; otherwise, for what purpose would the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) have been taught in the Sūtra?
If, then, they perceive them as suffering because of their impermanence, [what is the point of teaching *saṃskāra-duḥkhatā* separately?]
What is the specific distinction between the aspects of impermanence and suffering?
One perceives something as impermanent because it possesses the nature of arising and passing away; one perceives it as suffering because it is disagreeable.
However, that which is seen as impermanent becomes disagreeable; thus, the aspect of impermanence draws forth the aspect of suffering.
Some teachers maintain that there is no pleasant feeling at all, but rather that every feeling is indeed suffering.
How is this understood?
From scripture and from reasoning.
First, how is it known from scripture?
For it was said by the Blessed One: "Whatever is felt, that herein is suffering."
"Pleasant feeling is to be viewed as suffering;
[to perceive] pleasure in what is suffering is a perversion of perception.
Such is the position, first of all, according to the Sūtra.
How so by way of reasoning?
Because the causes of pleasure are not fixed.
For whatever things—such as food, drink, cold, or heat—are desired as causes of pleasure, those very same things, when consumed in excess or at the wrong time, result instead in causes of suffering.

Furthermore, it is not logical that suffering should arise at another time through the increase or even the maintenance of the causes of pleasure; therefore, from the very beginning, those are causes of suffering, not of pleasure.
It is only at the end that this suffering, having reached an increase, becomes manifest.
The same should be said regarding the transformation of postures (*īryāpatha*).
And because the notion of pleasure arises from the remedy of suffering and from the transformation of suffering:
for nothing is experienced as "pleasure" so long as one is not afflicted by some other form of suffering arising from hunger, thirst, cold, heat, fatigue, or the passion of desire.

Therefore, for the ignorant, the notion of pleasure occurs only toward the remedy, not toward actual pleasure. Furthermore, fools produce the notion of pleasure regarding the transformation of suffering, just as when they shift a burden from one shoulder to the other.
Therefore, some say that pleasure does not exist at all;
however, the Abhidharmikas maintain that it certainly exists,
and this alone is the correct principle.
How so? First of all, this denier of pleasure should be asked:
"What indeed is this that is called 'suffering'?"
If it is of the nature of affliction,
it must be explained how so;
if it is injurious, [how so?]
It is established that pleasure is that which is beneficial;
if it were not intended [to be so], it would be established that pleasure is that which is intended.
For that very same thing which is desired becomes undesired for the Noble Ones at the time of their detachment;
therefore, if you argue that the state of being desired is not established,
we say no, because it is undesired in another way.
For whatever feeling is intended by its own characteristic never becomes unintended by that very same [characteristic].

Thus, the Noble Ones revile it through another aspect; they see it as a basis for negligence, as something to be accomplished through great effort, as subject to transformation, and as impermanent—by which means it becomes unintended, but certainly not by way of the aspect of its own characteristic.

Furthermore, if this [feeling] were undesirable in its own nature, no one would ever have attachment toward it; for it is precisely for the sake of detachment that people perceive it as faulty even through other aspects.
Therefore, pleasant feeling certainly exists by way of its own characteristic.
As for that which was said by the Blessed One—"Whatever is felt, all that is here [included] in suffering"—that has been explained as *nītārtha* (of explicit meaning) by the Blessed One himself:

"It was with reference (*saṃdhāya*) to the impermanence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), Ānanda, and to the changeability of conditioned phenomena, that I said: 'Whatever is felt, all that is here [included] in suffering.
Therefore, it is established that this was not said with reference to the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*).
And if everything that is felt were suffering by its very nature, for what purpose would the noble Ānanda have asked the Blessed One as follows:
"Three kinds of feeling have been spoken of by the Blessed One: pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
yet this has also been said by the Blessed One: 'Whatever is felt, that is here [included] within suffering'?"
With what intention did the Blessed One say: "Whatever is felt, that here is suffering"?
For he would have asked thus: "With what intention did the Blessed One say there are three feelings?
And the Blessed One would have answered in this way:
When [the Buddha] said, "It was with this in mind that I spoke of the three feelings," he did not say it in that [absolute] sense;
therefore, the three feelings do indeed exist by way of their own-nature (svabhāva).
This demonstrates that the statement, "Whatever is felt, all that is here [regarded] as suffering," was spoken by me with a specific underlying intention (*abhiprāya*).
As for what was also said— "Pleasurable feeling should be viewed as suffering"—
both [aspects] exist within it.
It is pleasant by nature because it is agreeable, and it is painful by way of its characteristics because it possesses the quality of change and impermanence.
When it is viewed as pleasure, it leads to bondage for those possessed of passion, due to their relishing it;
when it is viewed as suffering, it leads to liberation.
Regarding the phrase "due to detachment from that":
the Buddhas command that this [body] be viewed in such a way that, when seen, it conduces to liberation.
How is it understood that, by its very nature, it is suffering?
As it is said:
"Having understood the impermanence of conditioned phenomena and their subject to change,
the Fully Awakened One, who possesses true knowledge, declared that feelings are suffering."
Furthermore, as for what was said— that "the perception of pleasure in what is suffering is a perversion of perception"—
this teaching is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*).
For the world’s perception of pleasure pertains to sensation, to the qualities of sensual desire, and to rebirth.

In this regard, there is a misconception for one who views a pleasant feeling—which is actually painful by way of its transformation—as being exclusively pleasant. There is also a misconception for one who views the objects of sensual desire—which involve little pleasure and much suffering—as being exclusively pleasant.
The same applies to rebirth.
Therefore, the non-existence of pleasant feelings is not established on this basis.
If, however, everything that is felt were suffering by its very nature, what purpose would there be in the statement, "There are three feelings"?
If you say it is for the sake of conforming to worldly convention, we say no;
because the teaching that all that is felt is suffering was spoken with a specific underlying intention (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*), and because it was stated as it truly is.
Having stated in detail, "That which is the faculty of pleasure and that which is the faculty of mental joy— this is to be seen as the feeling of pleasure," and so forth, [it continues]:
"By whomsoever these five faculties are thus seen as they really are with right wisdom, his three fetters become abandoned," and so on.
And how, moreover, could the world determine that painful feeling is threefold?
If it is argued that the perception of pleasure and so forth occurs respectively toward weak, intense, and middling [degrees of pain],
we say no.
Since pleasure is also of three kinds, there would have to be a perception of "intense" pleasure even toward mild forms of suffering and so forth.

Furthermore, when one experiences pleasure born from a particular odor, taste, or tangible object, what mild form of suffering could exist at that time for which this perception of pleasure occurs? Moreover, when that mild suffering has not yet arisen or has already ceased, the perception of pleasure should be even more pronounced.
Because all suffering has been eliminated.
The same should be said regarding the manifestation of sensual pleasure.
And how could it be logical that a clearly manifest and intense experience is perceived when the feeling is mild, yet is unmanifest when it is moderate?

Furthermore, because "pleasure" is mentioned in relation to the three [lower] dhyānas, there would have to be mild suffering; and because "neither-pain-nor-pleasure" is mentioned above those, there would have to be moderate suffering. Thus, it is not logical to establish the sensations of pleasure and so forth based on mild and other degrees of suffering.
And it was said by the Blessed One: "Mahānāman, if form were exclusively suffering, and not pleasure, nor accompanied by pleasure," and so forth.
Therefore, there is indeed some pleasure.
Thus, for now, the non-existence of pleasant feeling is not established on the basis of the Sūtra.
As for what was further stated, "because the causes of pleasure are not fixed," [that too is incorrect].
This is said because of a lack of thorough understanding of the cause:
for an object becomes a cause of pleasure or a cause of pain depending upon a particular basis,
not as an object alone.
Having attained a certain state of the body, that which becomes a cause of pleasure does not ever fail to be so upon attaining that same state again; thus, the cause of pleasure is indeed fixed.

For example, the very same fire, depending on the specific nature of the substance to be cooked, becomes the cause of a delicious cooking, or the very same [fire] becomes the cause of an unpleasant cooking. However, having attained a certain state of the substance to be cooked, that which is the cause of a delicious cooking does not fail to be the cause upon attaining that same state again—this is the illustration.
Furthermore, how could the cause of pleasure not be established within the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*)?
As for the statement that "the notion of pleasure is merely the counteracting of suffering," a remedy has already been provided for that:

when one experiences pleasure born from specific qualities such as fragrance and so forth, then toward what would there be a notion of pleasure in the form of a remedy? Moreover, when that suffering has not yet arisen or has already perished, the notion of pleasure should be even more pronounced.
Regarding the question, "In the bliss born of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), what is the remedy for what? and so forth:
even during the shifting of the burden, a bliss arising from a different state indeed arises, as long as that particular bodily state has not disappeared.
For otherwise, there would later be an even greater perception of pleasure.
This should be understood in the same way regarding the variations in postures for one who is fatigued.
If it is asked: "Whence comes the perception of suffering at the end, if there was no beginning [of suffering] from the start?"
Due to specific transformations of the body, just as wine and other substances end in sweetness turning to acidity,
it is therefore established that pleasant sensation (sukhā vedanā) indeed exists;
or else, because of its association with the three types of suffering (triduḥkhatā), all that is contaminated (sāsrava) is suffering.
As for that which is called the truth of origination, this is a departure from the sūtra; for in the sūtra, craving alone is mentioned.
It was mentioned in the sūtra because of its predominance.
But there are other [factors] as well that constitute origination.
How is this to be understood?
From the statement of others as well.
For it was said by the Blessed One:
"Karma, craving, and ignorance are the cause of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) in the future.
And again it was said: "'The five kinds of seeds' is a designation for consciousness accompanied by grasping (*sopādāna-vijñāna*)."
“The earth element is a designation for the four stations of consciousness.
Therefore, the teaching in the Sūtras is intentional (ābhiprāyika), whereas in the Abhidharma it is based on the defining characteristics (lākṣaṇika).
Furthermore, when speaking of the cause of production, only craving (tṛṣṇā) was stated as the truth of origination (samudayasatya).
By explaining the cause for the production of rebirth along with its underlying causes, the verse mentions karma, craving, and ignorance;

for it is stated in the Sūtra: "Karma is the cause for rebirth, and craving is the cause for its actualization," or according to the sequence of the *Sahetu-sapratyaya-sanidāna* Sūtra. Furthermore, consciousness and the other factors are also mentioned by way of establishing their status as the seed and the field.
What, then, is birth (*upapatti*) and what is manifestation (*abhinirvṛtti*)?

Birth is the production of a personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) through various modes such as realm, destiny, and womb. Manifestation, on the other hand, is the linking of rebirth without such distinctions.
For these two, respectively, karma and craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*) are the causes.

For example: a seed is the cause for the production of a sprout according to the distinction of its species, such as rice or barley; water, however, is the cause for the mere growth of all sprouts without such distinction—this is the illustration.
What is the reasoning here for [saying] that craving is the cause of production?
Because there is no birth for one who is free from craving;
yet both [types of people] die.
There are those with craving and those free from craving.
Only those with craving are seen to be born, not those free from craving;
for without craving, there is no birth.
We recognize craving as the cause for the production of existence,
because of the bending of the continuum;
and we observe that wherever there is craving, there the mental continuum repeatedly bends toward that object.
Therefore, we conclude that it is the same regarding future existence as well;
and no other thing seizes the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) as thirst does,
like a limb smeared with a paste of dried lentil soup.
And there is no other cause so closely associated [with suffering] as self-attachment; this is the reasoning.
The Blessed One has taught four truths, as well as two truths: conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) and ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

What are the characteristics of these two? That which, when broken, no longer produces the cognition of that thing, and which [no longer produces the cognition of that thing] when other factors are excluded by the intellect—that is [conventional truth].
That which is like a jar or water is conventionally real; that which is otherwise is ultimately real. //4//
That which, when broken down into its constituent parts, no longer evokes the cognition of that thing, is conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*).
For example, a jar;
for when it is broken into shards, the cognition of a "jar" no longer occurs.
Furthermore, that which, when other dharmas are excluded by the intellect, no longer produces the cognition of it, should also be understood as conventionally existent (*saṃvṛtisat*).
For example: water.
For in that case, when dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are excluded by the intellect, the cognition of water does not arise.

However, since those very things are designated by those names conventionally, when people say "the jar exists" and "the water exists" by the force of convention, they speak the truth and not a falsehood; this is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*). Ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is otherwise than that:
it is that in which the cognition of the thing persists even when it is broken.
That which remains even when other properties are mentally excluded is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*),
such as form (*rūpa*).

For in that case, when the object is broken down into its atoms and even other properties such as taste are mentally excluded, the cognition of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form still persists.
Feeling and the other aggregates should be viewed in the same way.
This is called ultimate truth because it exists in the ultimate sense;
that which is apprehended by supramundane knowledge, or by the mundane knowledge subsequently obtained, is thus the ultimate truth.
"Just as it is by another [means], so is conventional truth"—thus say the former teachers.
The truths have been explained.
Furthermore, how their vision occurs must be explained;
therefore, it is stated beginning from the initial setting forth:
Established in virtuous conduct and possessing [the wisdom of] hearing and reflection, one applies oneself to cultivation.
For one who desires to see the truths from the very beginning observes moral discipline;
thereafter, one acquires the scriptural learning that is conducive to the vision of the truths, or hears its meaning.

Having heard [the teaching], one reflects; having reflected without error, one applies oneself to cultivation in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Relying upon that wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*), the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*) arises; relying upon the wisdom consisting of reflection, the wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*) arises.
Furthermore, what is the characteristic of these types of wisdom?
The cognitions consisting of hearing and the others have as their objects names, both [names and things], and things. (5)
