It is said that wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*) has names as its object, while wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*) has both names and meanings as its object;
sometimes it draws out the meaning by means of the phrasing, and sometimes it draws out the phrasing by means of the meaning.
The cultivation consisting of meditation has the meaning alone as its object;
for it proceeds toward the meaning independently of the literal expression.
It is just as one who has not learned to swim does not let go of the float at all while swimming in the water.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that this is an illustration: one who is somewhat trained might sometimes let go [of the bank] and sometimes hold on, whereas one who is well-trained crosses by means of swimming independently.
However, others argue that according to this conception, wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*) would not be established.

For that which has names as its object would result in being "consisting of hearing" (*śrutamayī*), and that which has meanings as its object would result in being "consisting of cultivation" (*bhāvanāmayī*).
However, this definition of them is faultless:
the certainty born from the authority of the words of a reliable person is "consisting of hearing."

That which arises from the contemplation of reasoning is "consisting of reflection" (*cintāmayī*); that which arises from meditative concentration is "consisting of cultivation" (*bhāvanāmayī*); for the suffix *-maya* is prescribed in the sense of cause (*hetu*).
For example: "Life-breaths consist of food; cows consist of grass."
Furthermore, for one thus engaged in cultivation, how is that cultivation accomplished? It is said:
"For one possessing the two kinds of withdrawal.
For if one is withdrawn from both body and mind, [cultivation is accomplished].
Because it removes association with unwholesome thoughts,
for whom, then, is that twofold seclusion easy to accomplish?
For one who has few desires and is contented.
It does not exist for one who is discontented or has great desires.
But what is this discontent,
and what is having great desires?
Non-contentment is the desire for more than what has been obtained; great desire is the longing for what has not yet been obtained. //6//

The Abhidharmikas maintain that dissatisfaction (*asantuṣṭi*) is the desire for more when fine robes and other requisites have already been obtained, whereas great ambition (*mahecchatā*) is the desire for them when they have not yet been obtained. But one must explain this: since that desire for more also occurs only regarding what has not yet been obtained and not regarding what has been obtained, what is the distinction between these two?
It is, however, logical as follows:
non-contentment (*asantuṣṭi*) is the distress felt regarding what has been obtained that is not excellent or not abundant;
while great desire (*mahecchatā*) is the longing for what has not been obtained that is excellent and abundant.
The opposites of those two are their antidotes;

by way of the reversal of discontent and great desire, their respective counteragents should be understood as contentment and fewness of wishes. Furthermore, these two pertain to the three realms and are also stainless.
The phrase "their opposites" carries over [from the previous context].
They belong to the three realms and are also unconditioned (apratisaṃyukta),
because they are both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava).
And discontent and great desire belong only to the realm of desire.
What, then, is the intrinsic nature of these two—fewness of desires and contentment? He says:
non-greed;
for these two have non-greed as their intrinsic nature.
And the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) are also [characterized by] non-attachment (alobha);
they are called the four noble lineages because the noble ones (ārya) are produced from them.
These also have non-greed as their intrinsic nature; however, among them, three consist of contentment. (7)
They have contentment as their intrinsic nature:
namely, contentment with robes, alms-food, and lodgings.
How is the fourth noble lineage—the delight in abandonment and cultivation—of the nature of non-attachment?
Because of turning away from attachment to existence and sensual desire.
Now, what has been shown by the Blessed One through the four noble lineages?
By the last one, action; by the [first] three, livelihood.

For the Blessed One, the Lord of Dharma, has prescribed two things—livelihood and activity—for those disciples who have renounced their own former modes of livelihood and occupations and have set out for the sake of liberation:
livelihood by means of three noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) and activity by means of the fourth.
"By practicing this activity with this livelihood," he said, "you will before long attain liberation."
But why has such a mode of conduct and this kind of action been prescribed?
It is as an antidote to the arising of craving.
Four arisings of craving are taught in the Sūtra.

“Craving arises, persists, and becomes fixed when it arises for the sake of robes; it arises, persists, and becomes fixed when it arises for the sake of alms-food, for the sake of lodgings, and for the sake of existence and non-existence,” and so forth. As an antidote to these, the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) have been taught.
The desire for things characterized by "mine" and "I" is for the sake of their temporary and ultimate pacification. //8//
That same meaning is stated again by way of elimination:
the objects of the notion of "mine" (*mamakāra*) are robes and so forth; the object of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) is the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
In that regard, desire is craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
In that regard, there are three noble lineages for the immediate pacification of the desire for things regarded as "mine," and the fourth is for the ultimate pacification of both types of desire.
Thus it has been explained how the cultivation of reality as it is is accomplished.
But for one who has thus become a fit vessel, how does the entry into that cultivation occur?
Therein, the entry is by means of the meditation on the foul and by mindfulness of breathing;
"mindfulness" (smṛta) is simply mindfulness itself (smṛti).
For whom, then, is it by means of the foul (aśubhā), and for whom by means of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti)?
[It is] respectively for those who have excessive passion and for those who have excessive discursive thought (vitarka).
Those in whom passion (*rāga*) and discursive thought (*vitarka*) are predominant are called "those with predominant passion and discursive thought.

For one whose conduct is excessively dominated by passion due to its proximity, the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) is prescribed; for one whose conduct is dominated by discursive thought, mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) is prescribed.
Some say that because these [meditations] have non-variegated objects, they lead to the cutting off of discursive thought (*vitarka*);
however, the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) brings about discursive thought because its object is a specific form.
Others say it is because [the latter] is not directed outwardly.
For the meditation on the foul is outward-directed, like visual consciousness, because it involves the close contemplation of its object.
Furthermore, in that regard, there are four kinds of attachment: attachment to color, attachment to shape, attachment to touch, and attachment to service.

As an antidote to the first, they describe the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) with objects such as a livid corpse; for the second, with objects such as a corpse being devoured or scattered; for the third, with objects such as a bloated corpse, one festering with pus, or bones; and for the fourth, with the object of a motionless dead body.
However, for all those possessed of passion, the skeleton (śaṅkalā) is praised as being non-different [from the deity]. //6//

For within this skeleton, none of these four kinds of objects of passion exist. Because the contemplation of the foul consists of resolute conviction and partial attention, it does not result in the abandonment of the afflictions, but only in their suppression.
Furthermore, this practitioner of yoga who cultivates the meditation on the foul is said to be of three types:
the beginner, the one who has mastered the practice, and the one who has transcended mental attention (*atikrāntamanaskāra*).
Among these:
The beginner practitioner, desiring to cultivate the meditation on the foul by expanding and contracting the visualization from the bones to the ocean,
first fixes the mind upon a limb or part of his own body— such as the big toe, the forehead, or wherever he finds delight.
There, by means of the sequence of resolving upon the putrefaction and dissolution of the flesh, he purifies the bones and beholds the entire skeleton.

In that same manner, he further resolves upon a second one, and so on, until for the sake of increasing his resolve, he resolves upon the earth as far as the ocean's edge, filled with skeletons, proceeding through the stages of the monastery, the grove, and the field.
Then, contracting it again, he resolves upon his own single skeleton alone for the sake of concentrating the mind.
In this much time, it is said, the meditation on the foul becomes fully perfected;
this is the beginner practitioner of yoga.
One is considered to have achieved victory by discarding the bones of the feet up to the skull. //10//
Furthermore, for the sake of a specific contraction of the mind, he sets aside the bones of the feet within that skeleton and attends to the remainder;
in this manner, having achieved mastery through the process of elimination, he eventually sets aside half of the skull and attends to the other half.
One who has transcended mental attention does so by fixing the mind between the eyebrows.
Having abandoned even half of the skull, he fixes the mind between the two eyebrows.
This, indeed, is the practitioner of yoga who has transcended mental attention regarding the meditation on the foul.
There is a fourfold alternative regarding the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*): it may be limited by way of the limitation of its object, but not limited by way of the limitation of mastery.
This is because for those who have mastered or have not yet mastered mental attention, the object extends from one's own body to the limits of the ocean.
Now, what is the intrinsic nature of this meditation on the foul (aśubhā), how many stages does it comprise, what is its object, and where does it arise?
In due order:
[it is] non-attachment, belongs to ten stages, has the visible objects of the desire realm as its object, and arises among humans. (11)

It has non-attachment (*alobha*) as its intrinsic nature, belongs to ten stages—namely, the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) along with their preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), the intermediate meditation (*dhyānāntara*), and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—and has visible objects belonging to the desire realm as its objective support (*ālambana*). What, then, is the configuration of these visible objects?
For this very reason, it is established that its object is the referent (*artha*).
It arises only among human beings.
Not in any other destiny (gati), much less in any other realm (dhātu); even there, not in Uttarakuru.
It is established by its very name as having an impure aspect.
That which belongs to a particular time-period has that time-period as its object;
however, that which is subject to non-arising has all three time-periods as its object.
Because it consists of attention through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manaskāra*), it is with outflows (*sāsrava*);
and it is both acquired through detachment (*vairāgya-lābhikī*) and acquired through application (*prāyogikī*),
depending on whether it has been previously practiced or not.
The definition of the meditation on the foul, along with its classifications, has been stated.
Mindfulness of breathing is wisdom; it belongs to the five stages, has wind as its object, and is based in the desire realm. Inhalation is the breath, which is the wind that enters.
Exhalation is *apāna*, which is the out-breath, the wind that issues forth;
mindfulness of these two is *ānāpānasmṛti*.
That very [wisdom] has wisdom as its intrinsic nature;
however, it is called "mindfulness" because it functions by being sustained by the power of mindfulness, just like the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
In the five stages—the three preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—it is associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*).
It is said that because pleasure and pain are conducive to discursive thought (*vitarka*), it is not associated with them, as it is their antidote.

Furthermore, because pleasure and mental joy (*saumanasya*) are obstacles to focused attention (*avadhāna*), and because this [equanimity] is to be accomplished through focused attention, it is not associated with them either.

However, for those who maintain that there is equanimity even for one who has entered the fundamental dhyānas, [the practice] belongs to eight stages, because above those, inhalation and exhalation do not exist as a stage.

This [meditation] has wind as its object; it is based in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) among gods and humans; it is both acquired through application (prāyogikī) and acquired through detachment (vairāgyalābhikī);
and it consists of mental attention to reality (tattvamanaskāra).
This [is] only of internal phenomena (*dharma*),
not of external ones, because there is no instruction regarding them.
And because he himself has not fully awakened to the subtle dharmas.
And this [mindfulness] is sixfold, by means of counting and so forth. //12//
And this [practice] becomes complete when endowed with six causes:
counting (*gaṇanā*), following (*anugama*), fixing (*sthāpanā*), observing (*upalakṣaṇā*), transforming (*vivarta*), and purifying (*pariśuddhi*).

Among these, "counting" means that, having directed the mind toward the inhalations and exhalations, one counts from one to two up to ten by means of mere mindfulness, while remaining without mental fabrication and maintaining equanimity toward both body and mind.
Out of fear of mental contraction or distraction, one should count neither too few nor too many;
however, in that practice there are three faults:
undercounting, if one takes two as one; [and so forth].
If one counts "one, two" when there are more [breaths], that is over-counting. If one takes an inhalation for an exhalation, or vice versa, that is confusion.
Other than these cases, it is correct counting.
If there is an internal distraction, one must count again from the beginning until meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is attained.
"Following" (*anugama*) means that, without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), one follows the course of the inhalations and exhalations, [observing]:
"How far do these enter or exit? Do they pervade the entire body or move only in a single part?"
As they enter, one follows them through the sequence of entry into the throat, heart, navel, hips, thighs, and shanks, down as far as the feet.
As they exit, others say one follows them for a distance of a span or a fathom, or even as far as the wind-circle and the Vairambha winds.
However, this is not tenable because it is a mental attention directed toward [mere] phenomena (*tattva*).
"Fixing" (sthāpanā) means that one sees [the breath] as it remains from the tip of the nose down to the big toe, like a thread through a jewel.
One considers: "Are these beneficial or harmful? Are they cold or hot?"
"Observation" (*upalakṣaṇā*) means that these are not merely winds alone;

rather, it observes the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), namely: these four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) produced from the great elements, and the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) supported by them.

"Transformation" (*vivarta*) means turning away from the increase that has wind as its object and applying oneself to the subsequent roots of merit (*kuśalamūla*), up to the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*).
Others maintain that purification is the entry into the path of seeing and so forth; that the turning back consists of everything from the foundations of mindfulness up to the diamond-like samādhi;
and that purity is the knowledge of destruction and so forth.
"Counting, following, fixing, observing characteristics, transforming, and purification—this sixfold mindfulness of breathing is considered [the practice]. This is the summary verse.
Furthermore, it should be understood that inhalation and exhalation belong to the same level as the body;
for whatever level the body belongs to, these two belong to that same level.
Because they are a part of the body:
inhalation and exhalation proceed in dependence upon specific states of body and mind,
since they are absent in those who have entered the formless realm, those in the embryonic stage (kalala), and those who are without mind or have attained the fourth dhyāna.
For if the body is porous and the mind belonging to the stage of inhalation and exhalation has become manifest, then they proceed in this way:
they enter for one who is being born or emerging from the fourth dhyāna; they exit for one who is dying or entering the fourth dhyāna.
And these two, inhalation and exhalation, are classified as belonging to sentient beings;
they are not classified as non-sentient.
They are non-appropriated because they are dissociated from the sense faculties;
they are outflowing, not produced by accumulation or by maturation.
Because it increases and decreases with the growth and decay of the body, and because severed parts are rejoined;
for these characteristics do not belong to matter that is the result of karmic maturation (*vipāka*).
And those two are not perceived by a mind that is inferior.
The observation of those two [realms] occurs by means of a mind belonging to their own level or a higher level,
but not by a lower one— neither that pertaining to deportment nor that pertaining to emanation.
Thus have the two gateways of entry been explained.

Having attained meditative concentration through those two and having perfected calm abiding (*śamatha*), one should cultivate the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) for the sake of accomplishing insight (*vipaśyanā*).
And how, moreover, should one practice?
By examining the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena through their two characteristics. (14)
One examines the body by means of its specific and general characteristics;
and likewise feeling, mind, and phenomena.
The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of these is their very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The general characteristic, however, is the impermanence of conditioned phenomena, the suffering of those with outflows, and the emptiness and selflessness of all dharmas.
Furthermore, what is the intrinsic nature of the body?
It is the state of being the primary elements and their derivatives.
Dharmas are other than these three.
It is said that for one who is concentrated and perceives the body as consisting of atoms and as being momentary, the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) becomes perfected.
Now, what is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the applications of mindfulness?
The threefold application of mindfulness consists of the application of mindfulness by way of intrinsic nature, association, and object.
Among these, the application of mindfulness to intrinsic nature is wisdom;
what kind of wisdom is it?

The foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are threefold: consisting of hearing, consisting of reflection, and consisting of cultivation; that is, they consist of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. Others [are so called] because of association and object.
Other factors that co-arise with it are the application of mindfulness through association;
those which have that [body] as their object are the application of mindfulness through the object.
How can it be said that the application of mindfulness as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*) is wisdom (*prajñā*),
given the statement: "The application of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body within the realm of desire"?
What, then, is contemplation? It is wisdom;
for by means of it, one who possesses it is made a contemplator.
And because it has been said, "He dwells contemplating the body in the internal body," one who possesses such contemplation—
that is, vision— is a "contemplator" (*anupaśyin*).
One who contemplates the body is a "body-contemplator" (*kāyānupaśyin*).
Why did the Blessed One state that wisdom (*prajñā*) is the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)?
The Vaibhāṣikas say it is because of the predominance of mindfulness;
the meaning is that it functions through the sustaining power of mindfulness.
It is like the wedge that supports the splitting of wood.

However, it is logical that wisdom (prajñā) is the "application of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna), because mindfulness (smṛti) is established by means of this [wisdom] through the verbal expression of what has been seen.
For it has been said by the Venerable Aniruddha: "As he dwells contemplating the body in the body, mindfulness with the body as its object remains and becomes well-established," and so forth.
It has also been said by the Blessed One: "As he dwells contemplating the body in the body, his mindfulness is established and undeluded.
However, where it is asked: "Monks, how is there the arising and the passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness?"

In the passage, "From the arising of nutriment comes the arising of the body; from the cessation of nutriment comes the passing away of the body," it is the object itself that is called the application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), because mindfulness is established upon it.
Their names correspond to their respective objects; because they take as their objects one's own continuum, another's continuum, or both, each of them is of three kinds.
The sequence is according to their arising; but why do they arise in this order?
Because the coarse [aggregate] is perceived first;

or, according to the Vaibhāṣikas, because the body is the basis for sensual desire, that [desire] arises from a longing for feeling, that [longing] arises from the mind being unsubdued, and that [lack of subduing] arises from the non-abandonment of those afflictions.
The tetrad, however, is established by way of being the antidote to the perversions. //15//

The four foundations of mindfulness are taught as the antidotes, respectively, to the four perversions of purity, pleasure, permanence, and self; they are neither more nor fewer than that. Furthermore, three have unmixed objects, while the fourth is of both kinds:
if one contemplates only phenomena (*dharma*), it has an unmixed object.
Then, when one perceives two, three, or all four of the body and so forth together, that is the "mixed object" (saṃbhinnālambana).

Having thus practiced the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) with the body and so forth as their objects, he abides in the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) with all things as its object;
there he discerns them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. //16//
Abiding in the application of mindfulness to phenomena with a combined object, he views all those [objects], beginning with the body, by synthesizing them and observing them through four aspects:
as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self.
From that arises the stage of "heat" (*ūṣmagata*);

from that very application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), when practiced in this manner, there sequentially arises the root of merit called "heat. It is called "heat" because it is like heat.
Because it is the precursor to the fire of the Noble Path that burns the fuel of the afflictions,
it has the four truths as its objective range;
that state of "Heat" (ūṣmagata), due to its prolonged nature, takes the four truths as its object.
It has sixteen aspects:
one views suffering through four aspects—as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self;
and one views the origin through four aspects—as cause, as origin, as production, and as condition.

Cessation is [contemplated] through four aspects: as cessation, as peace, as excellence, and as emergence. The Path is [contemplated] through four aspects: as the path, as the method, as practice, and as the means of deliverance.
We shall explain the specific distinctions of these later.
From the heats arise the summits; from the heats that have increased through the sequence of weak, medium, and intense, the summits arise. They, too, are of that same nature. //17//

Just as the "heat" (*ūṣman*) stages have the four truths as their object and sixteen aspects, these [stages] are given a different name because they are more excellent. They are called "summits" (*mūrdhan*) because they are the peak of the fluctuating roots of merit;
for from these, there is either a falling back or a transcending.
The cultivation of both by means of the dharma;
furthermore, the cultivation of both these, namely the levels of "Heat" and "Summits," is by means of the application of mindfulness to phenomena.
What is this "cultivation"?
The initial arrangement of the aspects within the truths;
furthermore, their increase occurs through others as well,
for their increase takes place by means of all four foundations of mindfulness.
For one who is increasing [the roots of merit], there is the manifestation of those previously acquired [roots], because there is no lack of esteem for them.
Furthermore, from those [levels of insight] that have increased through the sequence of weak, medium, and intense, patience arises;
because of the endurance of the truths at the highest level, there is no falling back.
That [patience] is also of three kinds: weak, medium, and intense;
it is likewise twofold.
Just as the "summits" were described, so too are the weak and medium stages of patience, because they are produced in that same manner.
But in the case of its increase, this is the distinction:
the increase of all forbearance is through the Dharma. //18//
It is by means of the application of mindfulness to phenomena alone, and not by any other;
however, it continues that "the highest degree of receptivity has as its object the suffering pertaining to the desire realm."
Due to its connection with the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*), this [level] has as its object only the suffering belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
For this very reason, there is no statement regarding a restriction for the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and subsequent stages concerning their having the suffering of all three realms as their object;

rather, it is said that through the gradual reduction of each truth as an object—beginning with the antidotes to the form and formless realms—until finally only the suffering of the desire realm remains.

She attends to it for two moments; all of this is the medium degree of patience (*madhyā kṣānti*). When it lasts for only a single moment, that is the superior degree (*adhimātrā*). And it is momentary (*kṣaṇika*); it is not protracted.

The supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*) are exactly like the highest degree of receptivity (*adhimātra-kṣānti*); for they too have the suffering of the desire realm as their object and are momentary. Moreover, these are the mundane dharmas that are supreme.
They are called the "supreme mundane dharmas" because they are the most excellent among all mundane things;
for, even without a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), the Path is drawn forth by their specific efficacy (*puruṣakāra*).
These [stages], beginning with "heat" (ūṣmagata), are said to have the nature of wisdom because their intrinsic nature is the foundations of mindfulness;
however, all of them consist of the five aggregates when taken together with their attendants.
Except for the acquisitions (prāpti). // 16 //

The acquisitions (*prāpti*) are not included within the levels of heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, lest there be the manifestation of the levels of heat and so forth for a noble one (*ārya*) simply because of the manifestation of those [acquisitions].

In that regard, when the stage of "heat" (*ūṣmagata*) takes the three truths as its object, the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is present, and the four [applications of mindfulness] are cultivated in the future.
When it takes the truth of cessation as its object, that same [application of mindfulness to phenomena] is cultivated in both ways [present and future].
In all cases, the aspects (*ākāra*) are of the same kind.
In the cultivation for increase, one of the four [foundations] has the four future ones as its objects;
in that same case when cessation is the object, the last [foundation] has the four future ones as its objects and all aspects,
because the lineages have already been acquired.

In the stage of the Summits (*mūrdhan*), although the four truths are the objects of focus, when increasing the focus on cessation, the last [moment] consists of all four aspects (*ākāra*) among the four future ones.
When increasing the focus on the other three truths, it consists of any one of the four [moments] with all four aspects among the four future ones.
In the case of the Patiences (*kṣānti*), the last [moment] occurs in all instances.
In the future, all four aspects [are cultivated] in the four [stages]; in the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*), only the last four aspects are cultivated in the future,
because of the absence of others and because of their similarity to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Thus, the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are fourfold; these are the four roots of virtue conducive to penetration, namely: heat (*uṣmagata*), summits (*mūrdhan*), patiences (*kṣānti*), and supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*).
Among these, two are weak because they are subject to regression due to their instability; the patiences are middling, and the supreme mundane dharmas are superior.
[What is the meaning of "aids to penetration"?]
*Vidh* means division (*vibhāga*).

*Nirvedha* is certain penetration (*niścito vedhaḥ*). It is the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), because by it there is the abandonment of doubt and the discernment of the Truths, [realizing] "this is suffering" up to "this is the path.
Its part (*bhāga*) is one portion of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
They are called "aids to penetration" because they are beneficial as that which brings [the path] forth.
And all four of these aids to penetration consist of cultivation;
they do not consist of hearing or reflection.
Its stages are the threshold (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara),
and the four dhyānas, because it is comprised within them; it does not exist in the higher realms,
because it is an attendant of the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
Their absence [is established] because they have the desire realm as their object,
and because that [object] must first be fully known and then abandoned;
for them, there is a maturation consisting of the five aggregates in the form realm.
These [karmas] merely complete [the life-span] and do not project it;
because they are hostile toward existence, two [of them] may also [project] in the lower realms. //20//
The word "or" (*vā*) signifies an alternative view.
However, according to Bhadanta Ghoṣaka, the first two aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) belong to seven stages; they also exist in the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
However, all four of these have the desire realm as their basis; three arise only among human beings.
In the three continents, however,
they manifest for those who have previously generated them; the fourth [dhyāna] manifests even among the gods.
Both women and men obtain the three [worldly supreme dharmas] based on both supports (the male and female faculties).

A woman obtains the supreme dharmas based on two supports; however, it is only a woman who obtains the supreme dharmas based on two supports. A man, however, obtains them based on the male support alone.
Because of the attainment of the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha) of femininity.
How is there the relinquishing of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)?
A noble one (*ārya*) relinquishes them through the relinquishing of the level (*bhūmi*);

when a noble one relinquishes that level on which those [aids] were obtained by him, he relinquishes them as well, and not otherwise. Furthermore, the relinquishing of the level occurs through the transition to another level.
But the ignoble one [is afflicted] by death. //21//

An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), however, abandons [the roots of goodness] solely by abandoning the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), whether or not there is a transition between stages (*bhūmi*).
The first two [roots] are also abandoned through falling away (*parihāṇi*) and through death, but only as an ordinary person.
However, for the noble one (ārya), there is no falling away from those two;
likewise, even for an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), there is no falling away from the stages of patience (kṣānti) and the supreme mundane dharmas (agradharma).
The vision of the truths occurs right there through the fundamental [attainments].
One who produces the aids to penetration belonging to the stages of the fundamental dhyānas necessarily perceives the truths in that very same birth,
because of the intensity of their spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).

Regarding the acquisition of what was not previously attained: when there is a re-acquisition of those [roots] that had been lost, then only those that were not previously possessed are obtained, not those already abandoned before.
This is because, like the *prātimokṣa* restraint, they must be accomplished through effort applied to what has not been habituated.
When there is another person who acts as a boundary-defining instructor, one produces it again; when there is none, one produces it from the very beginning.
Furthermore, what is the intrinsic nature of these two types of loss—the loss through relinquishment and the loss through falling away?
These two losses are non-possession. (22)
Both of these are, by their very nature, non-possession (*asamanvāgama*).
However, falling away (*parihāṇi*) is caused by defects, whereas loss (*vihāni*) is not necessarily so;
moreover, that [loss] is brought about by a distinction in qualities.
Even one who has fallen away from the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata) is necessarily of a nature destined for final nirvāṇa.
What, then, is the distinction between this and the "Aids to Liberation" (mokṣabhāgīya)?
It is that, in the absence of obstacles, it is closer to the vision of the Truths. One who attains the "Summits" (mūrdhan) does not cut off the roots [of merit].
Even one who has fallen away from the stage of the Summits does not sever the roots of merit;
however, he may go to the miserable realms and even commit the deeds of immediate retribution.
One who has attained Receptivity does not go to the miserable realms.
Even when one has fallen away from *kṣānti*, one does not go again to the miserable destinies (*apāya*), because of the distancing of the karma and afflictions belonging to those levels.

Indeed, by the very attainment of *kṣānti*, one acquires the quality of non-arising (*anutpatti-dharmatā*) for certain destinies, modes of birth, rebirths, physical bases, and existences beginning with the eighth, as well as for certain afflictions.

These include: the miserable destinies; the egg-born and moisture-born modes of birth; rebirth among the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), in Uttarakuru, or as a Mahābrahmā; physical bases that are eunuchs, impotent, or possess both sexual organs; existences beginning with the eighth; and the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*).
And that [result] occurs, as appropriate, in both the weak and the intense [stages of the path]:
in the weak stage, it pertains to the states of miserable rebirth.
In the highest degree, it belongs to the others.
The aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) belong to three lineages (gotra), due to the distinction between the lineages of the śrāvakas and so forth.
Among these, one who has turned away from the lineage of the disciples (śiṣyagotra) may become a Buddha after having cultivated two [of the four aids].
It is possible that one who has produced the stages of "heat" (ūṣmagata) and "summits" (mūrdhan) might turn away from the lineage of the śrāvakas and subsequently become a Buddha;
however, once "patience" (kṣānti) has been attained, such a possibility no longer exists.
What is the reason?
It is said that because the miserable realms have been turned away from,
and because Bodhisattvas plunge even into the miserable realms due to their dependence on performing the welfare of others,
it is impossible for that very lineage to be irreversible.
The other [teacher] also holds that there are three. //23//
The phrase "it may be" (syāt) continues [from the previous context].

The meaning is that even all three levels of the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) can be diverted from the lineage of the Śrāvakas so that one who is other than a Buddha becomes a Pratyekabuddha;
however, those belonging to the Pratyekabuddha lineage cannot be diverted.
For both the Teacher and the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha], everything up to enlightenment occurs in a single sitting during the final dhyāna.
"Teacher" refers to the Buddha; "rhinoceros-like" refers to the pratyekabuddha.

For these two, relying on the fourth dhyāna alone in a single session, because of its immovability and sharp concentration, starting from the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) up until enlightenment arises. We shall establish later that enlightenment consists of the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising.
Others maintain that [the turning back] begins from the stage of the foul (aśubhā) up until enlightenment.
However, for those who hold that there are Pratyekabuddhas other than the rhinoceros-like (khaḍga), there is no prohibition against the turning back of those belonging to that lineage (gotra).
Furthermore, can one who has applied effort in the very first birth produce the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)?
This is not so; for one must necessarily [produce] the aids to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) prior to those.
It must be generated;
for even with the very least [of practice], liberation is swiftly attained within three existences. //24//
In one birth, one may produce the roots of merit conducive to liberation;
in the second, the factors conducive to penetration;
and in the third, the noble path.
It is like the sequence of sowing the seed, the growth of the crop, and the production of the fruit;
for through this very nature of things (*dharmatā*), there occurs, in due order, the entry, the maturation, and the liberation of this continuum.
Furthermore, they describe that as the "factors conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
It consists of hearing and reflection, not of cultivation.
How many types of karma are there?
There are three types of action, but mental action is primary;
however, because it is embraced by that resolve, bodily and verbal actions also become conducive to liberation.
Someone, by giving even a single alms-meal and by undertaking even a single precept, projects the factors conducive to liberation through the empowerment of the aspiration for liberation; however,
this projection occurs only among humans.
Only among humans in the three continents, and not elsewhere; because,
as the case may be, there is an absence of wisdom and world-weariness.
The factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) have been explained as a digression; now,
however, the sequence of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) has begun to be taught,
and therein, everything up to the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*) has been stated.
The remainder must be stated;
therefore, this is said: "From the mundane supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), there arises the untainted receptivity to the dharma (*dharmakṣānti*). (25)
Immediately after the supreme mundane dharmas, the untainted receptivity to the knowledge of dharmas arises.
Upon what object?
On the suffering of the desire realm.
The suffering belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is its object;
thus, this is called "receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
It is distinguished by its outflow (*niḥṣyanda*) for the sake of indicating that it is untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*).
Receptivity is for the sake of the knowledge of phenomena,
like a tree that bears flowers and fruit.
And that very state is called the "entry into the determination" (*niyāmāvakrānti*),
because of entering the determination of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
In the Sūtra, correctness is said to be Nirvāṇa.
In this context, *niyama* (determination) is *niyāma*, which is the state of absolute certainty;
its "approach" (*abhigamana*) is the "entry" (*avakramaṇa*).
And when that has arisen, one is called a noble person (āryapudgala).
Ordinary personhood (*pṛthagjanatva*) is turned back by [the path] when it is yet to come;
this alone is accepted as its activity while it is future, and nothing else,
just like the arising of a lamp.

Others say it is by means of the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*). No; there is no fault, because although they are of that same nature, they are opposed to it—just like killing an enemy while mounted upon his shoulders.
Others say it is by both,
because of the similarity between the path of uninterrupted transition and the path of liberation.
Then, right here, there is the dharma-knowledge;
thereafter, immediately following the receptivity to dharma-knowledge regarding suffering, there arises dharma-knowledge regarding that very suffering of the desire realm.
That is called "dharma-knowledge regarding suffering."
It should be understood that the section concerning the untainted (*anāsrava*) applies everywhere.

And just as the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñānakṣānti) and the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) arise regarding suffering in the desire realm, so too do the subsequent receptivity (anvayakṣānti) and knowledge (anvayajñāna) arise regarding the remaining [realms of] suffering.

Immediately after the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering, there arises the subsequent-knowledge-receptivity (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) which has as its object the suffering of the form and formless realms collectively;
this is called the subsequent-knowledge-receptivity regarding suffering.
Following that, the subsequent-knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) arises.
That is called the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering.

From the initial knowledge of the reality of phenomena (dharmatattva) comes the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna). Following that, subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) is the knowledge that takes suffering and the other [truths] as its object,
because it follows in that very same manner.
And just as these four patiences and knowledges arise with respect to the truth of suffering, so too do they arise with respect to the [other] three truths. //26//

Immediately after the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñāna*), the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge regarding the origin [of suffering] in the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) arises; following that, there is the dharma-knowledge of the origin. In this same manner, through the sequence of immediate succession, there arises the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding the remaining origin, and then the subsequent knowledge of the origin.

The receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding the cessation of suffering in the desire realm, the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation; the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding the remaining cessations, and the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation; the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path that is the antidote to the suffering of the desire realm, the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path;
the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding the remaining paths, and the subsequent knowledge regarding the path.
Thus, this realization of the truths consists of sixteen moments of consciousness;
by this sequence, this realization of the truths becomes characterized by sixteen states of mind.
As for those belonging to other schools who describe a single simultaneous realization (*ekābhisamaya*) of the truths, this must be understood as their underlying intention (*abhiprāya*);
for they speak of a realization of the truths without making distinctions.
It is threefold:
known as the vision, the object, and the result.
The clear realization through vision (*darśanābhisamaya*) consists of the [realization] of the truths by means of untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*).
There is realization through the object (*ālambanābhisamaya*) by means of the [mental factors] associated with it, such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth;
there is also realization through the task (*kāryābhisamaya*) by means of even those dissociated [factors], such as morality (*śīla*) and birth (*jāti*).
For when suffering (*duḥkha*) is being seen, its realization is threefold, while for origination (*samudaya*) and the others, there is only realization through the task.
Because of [the sequence of] abandoning, realizing, and cultivating;
if one were to say that the clear realization of the truths through vision is a sequential clear realization, one would be speaking incorrectly, because of the difference in their aspects (*ākāra*).
Furthermore, if one were to say that all [truths] are seen through the aspect of selflessness (*anātman*), then there would be no seeing of the truths as suffering and so forth;
and in that case, there would be a contradiction with the Sūtra.

"If it is argued that [this] refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)— namely, 'here, for a noble disciple who attends to suffering as suffering, or to the origin as the origin, up to attending to the path as the path, the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsravamanasikāra*)'— " no, it is not so.
Because cultivation proceeds according to what has been seen;
furthermore, if one were to speak of a single realization (*ekābhisamaya*) on the grounds that through the vision of one [truth] one attains mastery over the remaining ones, there would be no fault.
However, it remains to be investigated whether or not there is an emergence from meditative absorption in the interim.
Furthermore, if he should say: "One fully understands suffering, abandons its origin, realizes cessation, and cultivates the path;

therefore, there is a single clear realization (ekābhisamaya)," even so there would be no fault, because it is stated that upon the vision of one [truth], there is a clear realization of the tasks regarding the remaining ones.

However, with respect to the realization through vision (*darśanābhisamaya*), it appears that the sequential realization of the truths is taught in the Sūtras. There are three Sūtras in detail, along with similes, which state: "O Householder, there is no single realization of the truths; rather, there is a prior realization," and so forth.

If it is argued that there is a single realization based on the Sūtra stating, "He who is free from doubt and free from uncertainty regarding suffering is likewise so regarding the Buddha," we say: No.
Because it is stated with the intention of referring to the necessary abandonment of what has not yet arisen.
This aforementioned realization consisting of sixteen moments of consciousness belongs to the same stage as the supreme mundane dharmas. //27//
These sixteen moments of consciousness belong to the same stage as the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*agradharma*).
Furthermore, it was stated previously that these belong to six stages.
Why, then, must there necessarily be both Patiences (*kṣānti*) and Cognitions (*jñāna*)?
Because the patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) are, respectively, the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*);
the paths of uninterrupted transition are the patiences, because they cannot be interrupted with respect to the severance of the possession of afflictions (*kleśa-prāpti*).
The paths of liberation, however, are the knowledges,
because they arise simultaneously with the acquisition of dissociation for those who have been liberated from the acquisition of afflictions;
therefore, both must necessarily exist.
It is like the expulsion of a thief and the closing of the door by two [actions].
If, however, the acquisition of dissociation were to arise together with the second path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) itself, what would happen?
The knowledge that has abandoned doubt would not have arisen with respect to that very object.

If it is argued that this contradicts the treatise which states that because the afflictions are abandoned by means of the patiences (kṣānti), the nine classes of fetters are to be destroyed by knowledge (jñāna), we say no;
for the patiences are the retinue of knowledge.
It is like the designation "done by the king" applied to something done by the king's retinue.
But are all sixteen moments of mind the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) because they involve the vision of the truths?
No, he says. What then?
The path of seeing consists of fifteen moments therein, because it is the vision of what was previously unseen. //28//

Beginning from the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti) up to the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārge'nvayajñānakṣānti), these fifteen moments constitute the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
What is the reason?
Because of the seeing of truths not previously seen.
In the sixteenth moment, however, there is no previously unseen substance;
thus, it is indeed the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) due to the repeated practice of what has already been seen.
But does he not, by that [sixteenth moment], see what was previously unseen—the receptivity to subsequent knowledge (*mārge 'nvayajñānakṣānti*) regarding the path?
One should not have concern for truth even for a moment;
for truth does not become unseen by being unseen for a single moment,
just as a field does not remain unharvested because a single stalk has not been cut.

Because it is a fruit, because it consists in the cultivation of the eight knowledges and sixteen aspects, because it abandons the previous path, and because it is continuous, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). If it is argued that it is called the "path of seeing" (*darśanamārga*) precisely because it maintains the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*), we say no.
Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the definition].
Why are the seven knowledges considered the path of seeing?
Because the process of seeing is not yet complete.
For it is not the case that the vision of the truths is fully completed; therefore, because they occur in the interval between them, those [moments] are also the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Having explained how the path of seeing and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) arise, we shall now describe the classification of persons (*pudgala*) who have produced the noble path.

Regarding these fifteen moments that have been described as being of the nature of the path of seeing, it should be understood that those with dull and sharp faculties are, respectively, the followers by faith (śraddhānusārin) and the followers by dharma (dharmānusārin).
One who abides in those [moments] with dull faculties is called a follower by faith.
"One of sharp faculties who follows the Dharma" means:
"following by faith" is *śraddhānusāra*;
one who possesses that [following] is a *śraddhānusārī*.
Alternatively, it means one whose nature is to follow by means of faith;
this is because, previously, one followed the meaning through reliance on the conviction of others.
In the same way, there is the "follower of the Dharma."

Because they previously pursued the meaning by means of the dharmas such as the sūtras on their own; furthermore, those two are not to be abandoned by cultivation, and they have not yet entered the first fruit. //26//
The first of the fruits is the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), because it is the first among the attainment of all fruits.

If those two—the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*)—have not previously abandoned the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) through the worldly path, and are thus "bound by all fetters" (*sakalabandhana*), they are called candidates for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphalapratipannaka*).
This continues until they have destroyed five types [of defilements].

If, previously, by means of the mundane path, up to five categories of the defilements of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation have been abandoned, they are likewise called "candidates for the first fruit. Regarding the second [fruit], it is prior to the destruction of the [remaining] nine; it is for the sake of the second, thus it is "in the second."
If, beyond that [first fruit], six, seven, or eight categories have been previously abandoned by those two, they are called candidates for the second fruit.
And what is the second?
The fruit of once-returning;
those who are detached from the desire realm, or above it, are candidates for the third [fruit]. //30//

If, moreover, through the abandonment of even the ninth category [of afflictions], they become free from passion for the desire realm, or for the higher realms up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*), those two are called "candidates for the third fruit.
And what is the third?
It is the fruit of the non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).
But in the sixteenth [moment], those two who were candidates (pratipannaka) for their respective fruits become established in those fruits.
When the sixteenth mind has arisen, they are no longer called followers by faith (śraddhānusārin) or followers by dharma (dharmānusārin), nor are they called candidates.
What then?
They are established in the fruit.
Whichever candidate for a particular fruit has previously been practicing for it, at that time he becomes established in that fruit.
One may attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning;
however, it is not possible to attain arhatship from the very beginning,
because the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation have not yet been eliminated by the path of seeing.

And because detachment from the peak of existence (bhavāgra) was previously impossible, at that time, those of dull and sharp faculties [respectively] become those liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) and those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta). //31//
At that time, one who possesses dull faculties and was previously a follower by faith (śraddhānusārin) is called "one resolved through faith" (śraddhādhimukta);

one who possesses sharp faculties and was previously a follower of the Dharma (dharmānusārin) is called "one who has attained vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta). This is because they are characterized respectively by resolution and vision, due to the predominance of faith and wisdom.

What, then, is the reason that one who has abandoned even five categories [of afflictions] is called only a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) at the sixteenth moment of mind, and not one practicing for the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmiphala-pratipannaka*)?
Because,
in the case of a fruit, there is no attainment of a path superior to that fruit.
One who abides in the fruit, if not exerting effort for further distinction, is not a candidate for the next stage. //32//
For when a fruit is being attained, it is a fixed rule that the path distinguished by that fruit is not yet attained;
therefore, as long as one abiding in a fruit does not apply themselves toward excellence for the sake of attaining another fruit, they are not called a "candidate" (pratipannaka).
This should be understood in the same way regarding other fruits as well.
However, one who is free from passion for the third dhyāna and enters the path of certainty (niyāma) by relying on a lower stage necessarily brings face-to-face a path distinguished by its fruit.
For otherwise, having been reborn above that stage, he would not be endowed with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).
Such, then, is the classification of persons regarding the entry into the path of certainty for those who are largely free from passion for the desire realm.
However, the gradual [attainment] must be explained;
therefore, this is first established:
just as these nine types of afflictions have been taught in the desire realm, so too [are they in the higher realms].
For there are nine grades of defilements on each level, up to the peak of existence;
and as for the defilements, [they are as follows].
Likewise, the qualities—

the qualities known as the paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) which serve as their antidotes— are also of exactly nine types on each stage (*bhūmi*).
How so?
Furthermore, [these] weak, medium, and intense [levels of faculties] are distinguished by the further divisions of weak and so forth. //33//
There are three basic types: weak, medium, and intense.
Since each of these is further divided into three categories—weak, medium, and intense—nine types are established.
They are as follows: the weak-weak type, the weak-medium, the weak-intense; the medium-weak, the medium-medium, the medium-intense; and the intense-weak, the intense-medium, and the intense-intense.

In that regard, the abandonment of the most intense-of-the-intense afflictions occurs by means of the weakest-of-the-weak path; and so on, up to the abandonment of the weakest-of-the-weak afflictions by means of the most intense-of-the-intense path. This is because a superior path is impossible from the very beginning, and once a superior path has arisen, it is impossible for the most intense afflictions to remain. For coarse impurity is shaken off from a cloth first, and the subtle impurity afterwards.
Coarse darkness is destroyed by subtle light, and subtle darkness by intense light; such is the application of this analogy.
For white dharmas are powerful, whereas black ones are weak;
for even a momentary, mild Noble Path uproots the afflictions that have been intensified through the succession of beginningless saṃsāra.

Just as long-accumulated defects are extracted by means of *trivṛt* medicine, or just as great darkness is destroyed by a momentary, small lamp, so it is with the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*). One who abides in the fruit and has not yet exhausted all those [afflictions] to be abandoned through cultivation is one who will be reborn seven times at most (*saptakṛtparama*). For that person established in the fruit for whom even a single grade of what is to be abandoned through cultivation remains uneliminated, he is a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
"One who acts for seven births" is called *saptakṛt*; "the most [frequent]" refers to the absolute maximum, for there is no one who acts as a *saptakṛt* in every respect.

The reading of the sutra is *saptakṛtvaḥ-paramaḥ*. The meaning is that his births are at most seven times (*saptakṛtvaḥ paramam janma*). The word *parama* is used here in the sense of excellence or maximum limit (*prakarṣe*).
For the path is indeed the stream to nirvāṇa, because one goes to it by means of it;
thus, having entered (āpanna), come to, and attained that, he is a "stream-enterer" (srotaāpanna). How has he entered?
If it were by the attainment of the initial path, then even one who has reached the eighth stage would be [an *aṣṭamaka*];

if it were by the attainment of the initial fruit, then even one who is largely free from passion (*bhūyovītarāga*) or one who is entirely free from passion regarding the desire realm (*kāmavītarāga*) would be [an *aṣṭamaka*].
This refers to one who is destined to attain all the fruits, because of their attainment of the first fruit.
But what is the reason that this person alone—and not the eighth [stage]—is so designated?

It is because they have attained both the path of the candidate and the path of the fruit, because they have attained both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, and because of their complete realization of the stream at the moment of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
From that state, he takes rebirth seven more times among humans as seven intermediate existences (*antarābhava*).
Likewise among the gods; thus, he takes rebirth twenty-eight times in total.
However, because of the commonality of the number seven, it is said "seven times."
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that it is called "supreme" because it possesses skill in seven points, like the *saptaparṇa* (seven-leaf) tree.
If that is so, then what about the statement in the Sūtra: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should bring about an eighth existence"?
"This possibility does not exist"?
The intention here is that it refers to a single *gati* (destiny).

Or, if one were to interpret it according to the literal wording, even the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) would not exist. Even so, for one who "flows upwards" and has the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) as the limit, an eighth birth within a single *gati* would not be possible.
There is no fault, because this was spoken with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) in mind.
What is the scriptural authority (*sūtra*) or reasoning (*yukti*) for this?
And here, what is the authority for [the claim] that it is seven times each among gods and humans, rather than seven times among both combined?
For it is recited thus:
"Seven times among gods and humans.
However, the Kāśyapīyas recite this even for each [of the seven] individually.
Regarding the statement, "seven times among the gods, seven times among humans," one should not be dogmatic about this. Furthermore,
one who becomes a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) among humans attains parinirvāṇa having returned to those very same [human] realms.
He who is among the gods goes to those very ones.
What, then, is the reason that he does not produce an eighth existence?
Because by that much time, the continuum necessarily reaches maturation;
for the Path is of such a nature.
It is like one bitten by a seven-step venomous snake, or like a quartan fever;
it is because seven fetters remain:
namely, the two belonging to the lower realm and the five belonging to the upper realm.
Even while manifesting the Noble Path, one does not attain parinirvāṇa,
because of the sustaining power of karma to be experienced in future existence.
In the absence of the appearance of a Buddha, one attains arhatship while remaining a householder.
Furthermore, he does not dwell in a house;
rather, he obtains the marks of a monk acquired through the very nature of things (*dharmatā*).
Others say it is by means of the marks belonging to another stage of life (*anyāśramika*).
Why is one of a nature not subject to falling into the states of misery?

Because of the non-accumulation of karma leading to those states, because of the impairment of the maturation of karma already accumulated, because the continuum is perfumed by powerful wholesome states, and because of the purity of application and intention.
However, if the karma were fixed for the miserable states, one would not even produce patient acceptance (*kṣānti*).
And it is said in this regard: "Having committed even a small sin, the fool goes downward;
having committed even a great [deed], the wise man abandons misfortune;
for even a small mass sinks beneath the water."
"Even a great thing, when made into a vessel, floats.
What is the end of suffering?
It is that beyond which there is no further suffering.
The meaning is that it brings about suffering that is without reconnection.
Alternatively, "end" refers to nirvana.
How does it bring about nirvana?
Because it removes the obstacles to attaining that [state]. Just as people say, "Make space; tear down the pavilion."
Furthermore, there may be others who are "seven-times-at-most" (saptakṛtvaḥ-parama), but because they are not restricted [to that specific number], they are not so designated.
Thus, first of all, one established in the fruit who has not yet exhausted the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation is "seven-times-at-most.
However, one who is liberated from three or four categories [of defilements] and has two or three births remaining is a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner. //34//

That same stream-enterer becomes a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner for three reasons: by way of the abandonment of afflictions, because he has abandoned three or four categories [of them];
and by way of the faculties, because he has attained the untainted faculties that are their antidotes.
This is because, from birth, there remain two or three births remaining;

however, in the verse, only two are mentioned because, for a stream-enterer (*srotaāpanna*), once [the defilements] have subsequently been abandoned, it is established that the untainted faculty which is their antidote has not yet been liberated [from its object].
As for birth, it might sometimes be fewer.
Because of the potential for future excellence,
this [attainment] is included here. Why is it not [included] because of the abandonment of the five types [of afflictions]?

Because when that [sixth category] is abandoned, the sixth must necessarily be abandoned; for a single category of that [defilement] is not capable of obstructing the fruit, just as in the case of the "one-interval" (ekavīcika) practitioner, since there is no transcending of the realm.
That same "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner is of two types.

One who goes from family to family among the gods (*devakulaṃkula*) is one who, having passed through two or three families among the gods—whether in that very [realm] or in another divine assembly—attains final nirvana (*parinirvāti*). One who goes from family to family among humans (*manuṣyakulaṃkula*) is one who attains final nirvana among humans—either in that very [continent] or in another continent.
Such a person is again one who abides in the fruit (*phalastha*).
One who has destroyed up to the fifth category [of afflictions] is a candidate for the second fruit.
It should be understood that when one established in a fruit has abandoned from one up to the fifth category, he is a candidate for the second fruit.
However, when the sixth category is exhausted, he is a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin). //35//
He attains the second fruit;
having gone to the gods, he returns to the world of humans only once, and thus is a "once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmin),
because there is no further birth beyond that.
And it is said that this is because of the attenuation of passion, hatred, and delusion;
because only their mild forms remain.
Furthermore, he is one who abides in the fruit.
One who has exhausted seven or eight portions of the defilements is a "single-birth" (ekajanman) or a "one-interval" (ekavīcika) practitioner,
and is also one who has entered the third stage,
by virtue of three causes.
That very once-returner should be understood as being "separated by one interval" (ekavīcika) because of having abandoned seven or eight categories [of afflictions],
due to the attainment of the untainted faculties that are their antidotes, and because only one birth remains.
How can a single type [of karma] be able to obstruct its fruit?
Because of the transcendence of the realms (*dhātu*).
For it was stated previously that "karmas stand as obstacles during the three stages."

Just as it is with karma, so too should the afflictions (kleśas) be understood. Because he has transcended the stages of the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala) and the fruit of outflow (niḥṣyandaphala), and because "interval" (vīci) means a separation— since for him Nirvana is separated by only one birth, or since the fruit of the Non-returner (anāgāmiphala) is separated from him by only one type of affliction— he is called an "Ekavīcika" (One-intervaller).

And he should be understood as one who has entered upon the third fruit. Having abandoned seven or eight categories [of afflictions], yet while the previously abandoned categories remain, he does not become a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) or a "one-interval" (ekavīcika) until the path distinguished by that fruit has been manifested. He becomes a non-returner (anāgāmī) through the destruction of the ninth [category]. //36//

Furthermore, that same person, established in the fruit, is taught as a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) because of the abandonment of nine categories [of defilements] and because of not returning to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
It is said, "by the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*)," because of the consolidation of the abandonments.
Necessarily, two or three [fetters] have been previously abandoned;
he is one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, upon rebirth, with effort, or without effort,
as well as one who goes upstream.
"Antarāparinirvṛtiḥ" means that his parinirvāṇa occurs in the interval;
in the same way, it should be applied to one who has been reborn [as having parinirvāṇa] "with exertion" (sasaṃskāra) or "without exertion" (asaṃskāra).

That very non-returner (anāgāmin), moreover, is of five types: the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyī), who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate existence (antarābhava).
The one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyī) is one who, having just been reborn, attains parinirvāṇa before long due to being diligent and possessing a swift path,
by means of nirvāṇa with a remainder of substrate (sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa). Others say that he also [attains it] by means of nirvāṇa without a remainder of substrate (nirupadhiśeṣa).
It is not [the case] because of mastery over the relinquishing of life-span.
It is said that one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī), having been reborn, possesses an application that is not yet relaxed;
he attains parinirvāṇa with exertion because his path is both diligent and swift.
However, one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī) does so because of the absence of a path that flows through application without exertion.
Others say it is because of nirvāṇa through a path that has both conditioned and unconditioned things as its object;
but that is not correct.
Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the argument].
However, in the Sūtra, the one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī) is mentioned first;
and it is logical that it should be so.

This is because the two paths—the one that carries [the practitioner] outward and the one that carries them inward—are respectively accomplished through non-application and application, and are thus attained with and without effort.
As for the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyī*), their path is more powerful and more intense, while their underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are weaker.
Regarding the "one who flows upward" (*ūrdhvasrotas*), their movement is directed upward; they do not attain parinirvāṇa in the very place where they were reborn.
"Stream" and "going" have the same meaning.
He who is mixed in dhyāna goes to Akaniṣṭha. (37)

The one who flows upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*) is twofold: by way of cause and by way of fruit. By way of cause, it is due to the state of having either mixed or unmixed meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). By way of fruit, it is due to having either the Akaniṣṭha heaven or the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as the limit. Among these, he by whom meditation has been mixed goes to the Akaniṣṭha heaven and attains final nirvana (*parinirvāti*).

He is of three kinds: the leaper (*pluta*), the half-leaper (*ardhapluta*), and the one who dies everywhere (*sarvacyuta*); furthermore, this is the "one for whom the Akaniṣṭha heaven is the limit" (*akaniṣṭhaparama*), who belongs to the category of those with upward-streaming (*ūrdhvasrotas*), distinguished as the leaper and so forth.

Among these, the one called a "leaper" (*pluta*) is as follows: having practiced the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) here [in this world], he falls away from the [higher] three absorptions; having relished the first absorption, he is reborn among the Brahma-kāyika gods. By virtue of his previous practice, he again practices the fourth absorption and, passing away from there, is reborn among the Akaniṣṭha gods. He is indeed called a "leaper" because he does not sink into the intermediate realms.
The one called "Half-Leaper" (ardhapluta) is he who, having been reborn among the Śuddhāvāsa deities, bypasses even a single intermediate station from the middle and enters the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
A noble one is not reborn among the Mahābrahmās because that is a station of [wrong] views and because there can be only one leader.
The one called "All-Descender" (sarvacyuta) is he who, having wandered through all the intermediate stations, enters the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Furthermore, a non-returner never produces a second birth in that very same place of rebirth,
because he is one who proceeds toward distinction.
In this way, his state of non-returning (anāgāmitva) becomes complete,
because he never returns again to the lower realms where he was previously born.
Thus, when dhyāna has been practiced in a mixed manner, it should be understood that he goes to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Then there is another who reaches the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Having unadulterated meditative absorptions (*avyavakīrṇadhyāna*), he is one who flows upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*) and has the peak of existence as his limit.

For, relishing other attainments (*samāpatti*), he is reborn in all the intermediate stages; without entering the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), he proceeds through the formless realms (*ārūpya*) in succession, reaches the peak of existence, and attains final nirvana (*parinirvāti*).
For this one is indeed a practitioner of śamatha,
whereas the former was a practitioner of vipaśyanā.
However, we observe that even for those who "stream upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*), intermediate parinirvāṇa is possible;

yet their status as having Akaniṣṭha or the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as their limit is due to the absence of any further destination beyond them, just as the status of a stream-enterer (*srotaāpanna*) is limited to seven births at most.
These, then, are the five non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who go to the realm of form (*rūpopaga*).
The other who goes to the formless realm is of four types.
This other non-returner who goes to the formless realm is one who is detached from passion for the realm of form and, having passed away from here, is reborn in the formless realms.
He, moreover, is of four kinds due to the distinction between those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth and so forth.
These are the six types of non-returners (anāgāmin); beyond them, there is another who attains nirvāṇa here [in this very life]. //38//
Another attains final nirvana in this very life;
he is the seventh, one who attains final nirvana in the present life (dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin).
Furthermore, by dividing each of the three [types] into three, nine who have reached the realm of form (rūpopaga) are taught.
By further dividing each of the three non-returners (anāgāmin) into three, there are nine non-returners who have reached the realm of form.
Which are these three?

[This refers to] those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), and those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
How is there a threefold division?
First, regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, it is due to their attaining parinirvāṇa quickly, not-so-quickly, or after a long time, as illustrated by three similes.
The one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth is so called because they attain parinirvāṇa after being reborn, whether with exertion or without exertion.
For all three of these types attain parinirvāṇa after having been reborn, and thus are "those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth.
As for those who "stream upwards," they are distinguished by the divisions of the "leaper" (pluta) and so forth.
Alternatively, there is a threefold division based on whether all three [types] attain parinirvāṇa quickly, not quickly, or after a long time;
furthermore, their specific distinctions arise from differences in karma, afflictions, and faculties. //36//
Furthermore, among these three types and nine types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*), there is a distinction based on the differences in their karma, afflictions (*kleśa*), and faculties (*indriya*).

First, regarding the three types, the distinction arises because they have accumulated karma to be experienced respectively in the intermediate state (*abhinirvṛtti-vedanīya*), upon rebirth (*upapadya-vedanīya*), or in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*); because their afflictions manifest as weak, medium, or intense respectively; and because their faculties are superior, medium, or inferior respectively.
Among those nine types as well, each has its own distinction according to the same principle, as appropriate.
In the first two triads, [the distinction] is as before, due to the differences in afflictions and faculties;
in the final triad, it is due to the difference in karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).
Thus, these non-returners (*anāgāmin*) become ninefold by virtue of the nine types of afflictions and faculties.
How then are the seven destinations of the noble persons (satpuruṣagati) taught in the Sūtra?
The seven good destinies are considered [as such] by not differentiating the one who flows upwards (ūrdhvasrotas).
One whose nature is to flow upwards is "one who flows upwards" (ūrdhvasrotas).
Because they are taught without distinction, seven destinations of the noble persons (*satpuruṣagati*) are mentioned in the Sūtra.
Why, then, are only these considered the destinations of the noble persons, and not other destinations of those in training (*śaikṣagati*)?
For it is because of these destinations that those who possess them have their activity only in wholesome action and no activity in unwholesome action.
And for those who have gone to these destinies, there is no returning again;
however, this as it has been described does not exist elsewhere.
Therefore—
They [the meditations] are so called because of their practice with regard to what exists and what does not exist, and because of the absence of returning once gone. //40//
"The seven destinations of the noble persons (satpuruṣagati) are none other than these.
But if that is so, why does the Sūtra itself state: "Who is the noble person? It is the learner (śaikṣa) endowed with right view," and so forth?
