Others also possess a figurative status as "true persons" (satpuruṣa) because they have attained the restraint of never again committing the five kinds of evil and have generally abandoned unwholesome states; however,
it is those who possess this status in a non-figurative sense who are the subject of discussion here.
Furthermore, does this distinction also apply to a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who has undergone a change of birth?
For it is said:
"A noble one (*ārya*) who has changed birth does not go to another realm within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)."
A noble one who has undergone a change of birth in the desire realm does not go to another realm,
because having attained the fruit of non-returning, they attain parinirvāṇa in that very birth.
However, one who has undergone a change of birth in the form realm sometimes enters the formless realms.
As for one who is an "upward-streamer" (ūrdhvasrotas) with the peak of existence (bhavāgra) as his limit:
what then of that which was said by Śakra, "Those gods who are renowned as the Akaniṣṭhas—
when I finally fall away, my rebirth shall be there"?
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that this is because [the Abhidharma] is not mastered [by those born there].
You yourself have not refuted this, as it is something to be welcomed. Furthermore, one who is born in a higher realm does not possess the shifting of faculties or falling away. //41//
Furthermore, a noble one who has undergone a change of birth in the desire realm or has been reborn in a higher realm neither transforms their faculties nor falls away from them in any way.

Furthermore, what is the reason that for a noble one (*ārya*) who has undergone a change of birth, the transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), entry into the form or formless realms, and falling away (*parihāṇi*) are not admitted?
Because they do not exist.
Why do they not exist?
Because the faculties have become more fully matured through dwelling in other births, and because of the attainment of a particular basis.
Now, why does a learner (śaikṣa) who is free from passion not become one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state?

The Vaibhāṣikas say: because the path has not been mastered and thus is not present, and because the latent dispositions (anuśaya) are not extremely weak; for the realm of desire (kāmadhātu) is difficult to transcend.
Indeed, much still remains to be done by him.

The abandonment of unwholesome and neutral afflictions, the attainment of two or three fruits of the religious life, and the transcendence of the three realms—these he is unable to accomplish while remaining in the intermediate state. This is why it was said: "When dhyāna is mixed, he goes to Akaniṣṭha."
Now, which dhyāna is mixed first? The fourth is mixed first,
for it is a concentration that is fully functional (*sarvakarmaṇya*) because it is the foremost among the easy paths of practice (*sukhapratipad*).
Furthermore, it is mixed in this way: an Arhat or a Non-returner enters the fourth dhyāna, which is untainted (*anāsrava*) and characterized by a continuous flow;
emerging from that, he enters that same dhyāna while it is tainted (*sāsrava*) and characterized by a continuous flow, and then again the untainted.

When, through the reduction of the flow, he enters two moments of the untainted, then two of the tainted, and again two of the untainted—this is said to be the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for the mixing.
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that perfection [of the practice] occurs through the mixing of moments:
when one brings a contaminated moment immediately after an uncontaminated moment of destruction,
or an uncontaminated moment immediately after a contaminated one, then, by this mixing of a contaminated moment with two uncontaminated ones, the intermingling (*vyavakiraṇa*) becomes perfected.
For two moments are similar to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), while the third is similar to the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
Having thus mixed the fourth dhyāna, by its power the others are also mixed.
It is first mixed in the desire realm within the three continents; afterwards, it is mixed in the form realm by one who has fallen away [from it].
However, the intermingling of moments is impossible except for a Buddha;
therefore, we see that it is accomplished through the attainment of the three streams at will.
For what purpose, then, is dhyāna mixed? It is for the sake of rebirth and for the sake of dwelling [in peace], as well as out of fear of the afflictions. //42//
They intermingle the meditative absorptions for three reasons:
non-returners with sharp faculties do so for the sake of rebirth in the Pure Abodes and for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life;
those with dull faculties do so out of fear of the afflictions and for the sake of non-retrogression by distancing themselves from concentration associated with relishing.
The Arhats with sharp faculties [cultivate it] for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life,
while those with dull faculties do so for the sake of non-retrogression due to their fear of the afflictions.
Now, why are there exactly five rebirths among the Pure Abodes?
Because that fourth dhyāna which was described as being cultivated in a mixed manner is of five kinds, there are exactly five rebirths among the Pure Abodes.
For that mixed cultivation is of five types, distinguished as weak, medium, strong, stronger, and strongest.
In the first [type], three moments of consciousness are brought into manifestation:
the untainted, the tainted, and the untainted.
In the second [week] there are six;
in the third, nine;
in the fourth, twelve.
In the fifth [dhyāna], there are fifteen;
their fruits, respectively, are the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Rebirth occurs in those [Abodes] by virtue of whatever therein is with-outflows (*sāsrava*).
Others say there are five because of the predominance of the faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
Furthermore, the Non-returner who has attained cessation is considered a "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*). (43)
One who possesses the attainment of cessation is called "one who has attained cessation" (*nirodhalābhī*).
For any non-returner (*anāgāmī*) who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is termed a "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣī*),
because they have personally realized with the body a state that resembles nirvāṇa.
But how does one realize it with the body?
Because, due to the absence of mind, it arises based on the body.
However, it must be understood in this way.
For upon emerging from that state, he attains a tranquility of the body accompanied by consciousness such as he has never attained before;
because of this, the thought occurs to him: "Truly peaceful is the attainment of cessation! Truly like nirvāṇa is the attainment of cessation!
In this way, its peacefulness is realized by him directly with the body.
For direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) consists in making [the truth] manifest through the attainment of knowledge and the realization of that knowledge.
Regarding the statement "the eighteen learners" in this Sūtra, for what reason is the body-witness (kāyasākṣin) not mentioned?
Because there is no [specific] reason.
What, then, is that reason?
The three untainted trainings and their fruit constitute [the category of] the learner;
for it is by virtue of these specific qualities that learners are established.
Furthermore, the attainment of cessation is neither a learner nor the fruit of a learner.
Therefore, it is not stated that there is a distinction among those in training (śaikṣa) due to their connection with that [attainment].
This, then, is the classification of non-returners according to their coarse distinctions;
however, when distinguished subtly, they are divided into thousands.
There are three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, due to the distinction between weak, medium, and sharp faculties.

There are four [types] by way of the distinction of stages (*bhūmi*). There are six by way of the distinction of lineages (*gotra*), such as those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) and so forth.
There are sixteen by way of the distinction of different locations. There are thirty-six by way of the distinction of stages and detachment from passion (*vairāgya*):
[this refers to] one who is bound by all fetters in the form realm up to one who is free from passion for eight categories of the fourth dhyāna.
Due to the distinctions of place, lineage (*gotra*), detachment (*vairāgya*), and faculty (*indriya*), there are nine hundred and twenty-five [types].
How so? In a single place, there are six lineages.

In each lineage (*gotra*), there are nine types of persons (*pudgala*), ranging from those bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) to those who have abandoned the eight categories [of afflictions] in their own stage. Six times nine makes fifty-four; sixteen times fifty-four makes eight hundred and sixty-four.

When multiplied by three due to the distinction of faculties (*indriya*), the total is thus established. Furthermore, one who has abandoned the nine categories of afflictions in a lower dhyāna is described as being "bound by all fetters" (*sakalabandhana*) with respect to the higher [dhyāna].
For the purpose of calculation:

just as with those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, so it is up to those who "stream upwards"; thus, when taken together, there are twelve thousand nine hundred non-returners (anāgāmin) in total.
Up to the destruction of the eighth part of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one is a candidate for Arhatship;
this refers to the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Indeed, from the detachment from the first category of the first dhyāna up until the abandonment of the eight categories of the Peak of Existence, he is a candidate for Arhatship.

In the ninth path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga), for the sake of abandoning even the ninth category of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), he is indeed one who has entered the state of striving for arhatship;
and that [path] is like a diamond (vajropama). //44//
And that path of immediate succession is called the "diamond-like concentration" (*vajropama-samādhi*) because it shatters all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); yet,
having already shattered them, it does not shatter them again.
However, [the diamond-like concentration] is capable of breaking all [obstructions],
because it is the most supreme among all paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Regarding the diamond-like concentrations, they describe many varieties.

There are eight [moments] comprised within the stage of non-returning (*anāgāmin*) that are associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*), having as their objects the suffering and origin belonging to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
There are eight associated with the aspects of the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-dharma-jñāna*).
There are four associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*), having as their object the cessation of the first dhyāna.
In this way, there are four [applications of mindfulness] having the cessation of the peak of existence as their object;
and four associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), because they take the entire category of subsequent knowledge as their object.
These constitute fifty-two diamond-like concentrations (*vajropamasamādhi*), distinguished by differences in their knowledge, aspects, and objects.
Just as they are comprised within the *anāgamya* stage, so too are they comprised within the stages up to the fourth dhyāna;
those comprised within the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, and nothingness are, respectively, twenty-eight, twenty-four, and twenty in number.
This is because among them there is an absence of *dharmajñāna* and of *anvayajñāna* that takes the cessation of a lower level as its object.
However, it does have the counteragent of a lower stage as its object,
because they serve as mutual causes for one another.

For those, however, who maintain that even the subsequent knowledge of the path has each individual stage’s counteragent as its object, they add twenty-eight more, so that the diamond-like concentrations included in the *anāgamya* stage become eighty.
In this way, up to those included in the fourth dhyāna,
there are forty, thirty-two, and twenty-four [types] respectively in the spheres of infinite space and so forth.
Furthermore, they become even more numerous through the distinctions of lineage (*gotra*) and faculties (*indriya*).

As for that ninth category at the peak of existence which was mentioned— the abandonment of which occurs through the diamond-like concentration— the knowledge of destruction arises for that ninth category simultaneously with the attainment of its destruction.
Immediately following the diamond-like samādhi (vajropama-samādhi) is the final path of liberation (vimukti-mārga).
For this very reason, that knowledge of destruction (kṣaya-jñāna) is first [of all knowledges], because it arises simultaneously with the attainment of the destruction of all outflows (āsrava).
At that time, he is an Arhat beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Furthermore, when the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) has arisen, that one who was practicing for arhatship becomes a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) and an Arhat who has attained the fruit of arhatship.
He is a non-learner because there is nothing further to be learned regarding another fruit.

For this very reason, he is established as an "Arhat" because he has accomplished the ultimate goal and because he is worthy of worship by all those still possessed of passion; it is thus established that the other seven previously mentioned persons are learners (*śaikṣas*).
Why are they called "those in training" (*śaikṣa*)?

Because they have the habit of constantly training for the sake of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) in the three trainings: higher ethics (*adhiśīla*), higher mind (*adhicitta*), and higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
Furthermore, these consist of the intrinsic natures of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Does an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) also become a learner (śaikṣa)? No;
because they do not understand the truths as they truly are (yathābhūtam), and because they subsequently fail to train.
For this very reason, it is stated twice in the Sūtra: "O Śivaka, one trains in the training, one trains in the training; therefore, one is called a learner."
"One who trains and does not fail to train is a learner (śaikṣa)"—this is a restrictive definition intended to be understood in this way.
How can a noble one (ārya) abiding in his natural state be of a training disposition?
By way of intention (āśaya).
And because of the concomitance with attainment, like a traveler who has already set out on the road, there is the threefold training.
Now, what are the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*)? They are the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas of one in training.
What are those belonging to one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
They are the untainted (*anāsrava*) factors of one beyond training.
Why is *nirvāṇa* not considered "belonging to one in training" (*śaikṣa*)?
Because even non-learners (aśaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) possess that [quality],
why is it not considered "of the non-learner"?
Because even learners (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings possess that [quality].
All these together constitute the eight noble persons (*āryapudgala*):

the four who are practicing the path (*pratipannaka*) and the four who are established in the fruit (*phale sthita*). They are as follows: one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotaāpatti-phala*), and the stream-enterer (*srotaāpanna*).
Thus, up to the one who has entered the path for the realization of the fruit of arhatship and the arhat,
these are eight by name;
however, in terms of substantial entity, they are five.
The first candidate for the fruit and the four who abide in the fruits [are distinct];
as for the remaining candidates, they are not separate from those abiding in the three fruits. This is stated with reference to the sequential attainment [of the fruits].

However, those who have further abandoned desire for the realm of desire may, while on the path of seeing, be candidates for the fruits of once-returner and non-returner, yet they are not yet stream-enterers or once-returners.
For it has been stated that the path of cultivation is twofold: mundane and supramundane.
By which [path] does this trainee attain detachment from what?
Detachment from the peak of existence is attained through the supramundane path,
not through the mundane. What is the reason?
Beyond that, because there are no worldly [paths] higher than that, or because [a path] belonging to its own level is not an antidote;
why is it not an antidote?
Because it is permeated by the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of those afflictions.

For a defilement that underlies a particular object does not lead to the abandonment of that object; and a defilement does not underlie that which is its antidote. From another perspective, there are two kinds. //45//
From all stages other than the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), detachment occurs both through the mundane (*laukika*) and the supramundane (*lokottara*).
Furthermore, in that regard,
when a noble one attains detachment through the mundane path, the acquisitions of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*) are twofold.
For one who attains noble detachment by means of the mundane path, two kinds of acquisitions of dissociation arise: mundane and supramundane.
Some say that [this occurs] also by means of the supramundane path;
others say that it is likewise even by means of the supramundane path.
What is the reason? Because when [the body] is abandoned, there is no longer possession of the afflictions. //46//

For if a worldly acquisition of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*) were not to arise for one attaining detachment by means of the noble path (*āryamārga*), then it would follow that a person who, having become detached from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) by means of the noble path, transforms their faculties (*indriya-saṃcara*) by relying on meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), would— due to abandoning the entire previous path and acquiring only the path of the fruit— not be possessed of dissociation from the afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to the higher stages.

And once that [disconnection] has been relinquished, one would again become possessed of those afflictions; however, "there is non-possession [of them], like one who is liberated from the lower stages of the Peak of Existence and is born in a higher stage. Even in the absence of that worldly attainment of disjunction (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*), there would be no possession of those [afflictions].

For example, in the case of one who is half-liberated from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), even though the worldly attainment of dissociation from those [defilements] does not exist and the supramundane attainment has been relinquished through the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), there is no further possession of those defilements.

And just as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) born above the level of the first dhyāna does not again possess the defilements of the desire realm because of the relinquishment of the attainment of dissociation from them— this [example] is not a proof [for the point at hand].
Furthermore, by means of which stage does detachment from what occur? Detachment from all [stages] occurs through the untainted *anāgamya* [attainment]. //47//
Up to the peak of existence.

Now, regarding one who attains detachment from a lower stage by relying on a preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*): do all its paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) arise from the preparatory stage, just as its path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) does?
No, he says. What then?
In the conquest of the three realms, the final path of liberation arises either from a dhyāna or its preparatory stage (sāmantaka).
For there are nine planes of rebirth:
the entire realm of desire and the eight [levels] of the dhyānas and formless attainments.

In that regard, the conquest of the three levels extends up to the detachment from the second dhyāna. Within that process, the final path of liberation arises either from the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) or from the fundamental dhyāna itself; it does not arise from a preparatory stage of a higher level.

Beyond the conquest of the three stages, [the path of liberation] arises from the fundamental (maula) absorption itself and not from the preparatory stage (sāmantaka), because of the commonality of the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).

For in the first three dhyānas, due to the difference between the faculties of the preparatory and the fundamental stages, some are unable to enter the fundamental dhyāna; this is because the transformation of the faculties (indriyasaṃcāra) is difficult to accomplish.
Therefore, upon the attainment of detachment from the three stages, there is another path of liberation even from the preparatory stage of dhyāna.
It has been stated [in verse 47] that "detachment from all [levels] occurs through the untainted [path] and the preparatory stage (anāgamya)," but this was not stated by others.
Therefore, it is said:
"By the eight noble [paths], there is victory over one's own and higher levels. (48)

By means of the eight untainted [attainments]—the dhyānas, the intermediate dhyāna, and the formless [attainments]—there is detachment from one's own level and from higher levels, but not from lower levels, because one has already become free from passion for them.

In that regard, it is established that the supramundane paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) proceed with the aspects of the truths (*satyākāra*), because they have the truths as their object. However, the mundane paths of liberation and uninterrupted transition proceed,
respectively, with the aspects of "calm" (*śānta*) and so forth, and "gross" (*audāra*) and so forth.

The paths of liberation have the aspects of being peaceful and so forth, while the uninterrupted paths have the aspects of being gross and so forth; furthermore, these respectively have the higher and lower [realms] as their objects. //46//
The paths of liberation (vimuktimārga) take the higher stage as their aspect in terms of being peaceful, excellent, and a state of departure, as far as possible.
The uninterrupted paths (ānantaryamārga) take the lower stage as their aspect in terms of being gross, painful, and like a thick wall;
they are gross because it is not peaceful and because it requires greater effort.
Because it is not sublime, because it is characterized by suffering, and because it is disagreeable due to its great abundance of *dauṣṭhulya*;

and because it is like a thick wall, since one cannot escape that level by means of it alone, just as one cannot escape through a wall— these [aspects] are the opposites of those [faults], and thus constitute the aspects of being peaceful (*śānta*), sublime (*praṇīta*), and an escape (*niḥsaraṇa*).
The incidental discussion is concluded. What must now be stated is the subject at hand:
what arises immediately after the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna)?
If he is of immovable nature, the knowledge of non-arising follows the knowledge of destruction;
if the Arhat is of immovable nature, immediately after the knowledge of destruction, the knowledge of non-arising arises for him.
If not, there is either the knowledge of destruction or the vision of one beyond training.

If one is not of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*), then from the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) there arises either further knowledge of destruction itself or the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣī samyagdṛṣṭi*);
however, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) does not arise, because of the possibility of falling away.
But then, does that [knowledge of non-arising] never arise for one of immovable nature?
That [attainment] belongs to every Arhat. // 50 //

Even for one of immovable nature (akopyadharman), following the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), sometimes only the knowledge of non-arising arises, and sometimes the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣī samyagdṛṣṭi).
Regarding these four fruits that have been mentioned, whose fruits are they?
They are the fruits of asceticism (śrāmaṇyaphala).
What is this so-called *śrāmaṇya*?
*Śrāmaṇya* is the stainless path;
the untainted (*anāsrava*) path is *śrāmaṇya*.
For that reason, one becomes a *śramaṇa* because of the pacification of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
As it is said in the Sūtra: "By him, various kinds of evil and unwholesome states have been stilled, in detail up to those leading to old age and death; therefore, he is called a *śramaṇa*."
Because their pacification is not ultimate, an ordinary person is not a śramaṇa in the ultimate sense;
furthermore, the fruit of that śrāmaṇya is both conditioned and unconditioned.
For the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) are indeed taught in the Sūtra as being both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
and furthermore,
they are said to be eighty-nine in number.
What, then, are those?
They are the paths to liberation together with the destructions. // 51 //

For the abandonment of those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*), there are eight paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) and eight paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*). For the abandonment of those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), in each of the nine stages, there are an equal number of paths of uninterrupted transition and paths of liberation for the abandonment of the nine grades of afflictions. Among these, the paths of uninterrupted transition constitute the state of a recluse (*śrāmaṇya*), while the paths of liberation are the conditioned fruits of recluseship (*saṃskṛta-śrāmaṇyaphala*).
Because they are the outflow-results (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the results of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*),
the unconditioned abandonments (*asaṃskṛta-prahāṇa*) of those afflictions are the fruits of *śrāmaṇya*. Thus, there are eighty-nine [fruits].
If that is the case, then it follows that an addition must be made for the Buddha.
It need not be made;
for although there are many fruits, [the category remains sufficient].
The establishment of the four fruits, however, occurs due to the presence of five causes.
For it is said that in whichever state of the path of abandonment these five causes are present, therein the Blessed One has established a fruit.
What are these five?
In the case of the fruit, there is the abandonment of the previous [path], the attainment of another path, and the accumulation of destruction. //52//
Then there is the attainment of the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) and the cultivation of the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra-bhāvanā*).
There is the abandonment of the previous path and the acquisition of a new path, due to the abandonment and acquisition of the paths of the candidate (*pratipannaka*) and the fruit (*phala*).
And there is the consolidation of all abandonments (*prahāṇa-saṃkalana*), because of the acquisition of a single possession (*ekaprāpti*).
The simultaneous acquisition of eight knowledges refers to the fourfold dharma-knowledges and subsequent knowledges;
the cultivation of the sixteen aspects refers to the aspects of impermanence and so forth.
Indeed, these five causes exist for each and every fruit.

If the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) constitutes the state of a recluse (*śrāmaṇya*), how can the two fruits obtained by means of the worldly path (*laukika-mārga*) be appropriately termed "fruits of recluseship"? [The answer is: But that which is obtained through the worldly path is a fruit because it is a mixture; however, the attainment of the untainted is the fruit because of its maintenance. (53)
For in that case, the abandonment that constitutes the fruit of the once-returner or the fruit of the non-returner is not solely the fruit of the mundane path;
rather,
the abandonment that is the fruit of the path of seeing is also mixed therein.
This is because one attains the single acquisition of dissociation (visaṃyoga-prāpti) which subsumes all those fruits.
For this very reason, it is said in the Sūtra: "What is the fruit of a once-returner?
It is the abandonment of the three fetters and the attenuation of greed, hatred, and delusion."
"What is the fruit of non-returning?
It is the abandonment of the five lower fetters.
And that abandonment is maintained by means of the untainted attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*).
Because one is protected from death by the power of that [attainment],
for this reason as well, it is fitting that this constitutes a fruit of asceticism (śrāmaṇyaphala).
That which is called "asceticism" (śrāmaṇya),
"brahminhood" (brāhmaṇya), and the "Wheel of Brahmā" (brahmacakra) is precisely that;
it is "brahminhood" because it carries away the afflictions (kleśa), and it is the "Wheel of Brahmā" because it is turned by Brahmā.
The Blessed One is Brahmā because of his union with unsurpassed Brahmanhood;
for the Sūtra states: "This Blessed One is indeed Brahmā; he is called 'the Peaceful' and also 'the Cooled'.
This is his wheel, thus it is "Brahmic," because it was set in motion by him.
The wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra), however, is the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
It is called a "wheel" because of its turning; due to its similarity to that [physical wheel], the path of seeing is the wheel of Dharma.
In what way is there this similarity?
[The Buddha is like a wheel] because of his swift movement and so forth, and because of [the qualities of] the spokes and so forth. // 54 //

Because of its swift movement, its progressive abandonment, its conquest of the unconquered and its mastery over what has been conquered, and because of its rising and falling— thus, through such qualities as swift movement and so forth, and by virtue of its similarity to spokes and other parts, the Noble Eightfold Path is called a "wheel," according to the Venerable Ghoṣaka.
For right view, right intention, right effort, and right mindfulness occupy the position of the spokes.

Right speech, right action, and right livelihood correspond to the hub; right concentration corresponds to the rim. Thus, the path of seeing is the Wheel of Dharma. Why is this so? Because when it arose for the noble Kauṇḍinya, there was the statement: "The Wheel of Dharma has been set in motion. How is it that this wheel has three revolutions and twelve aspects?
"This is the noble truth of suffering; this must indeed be fully understood; this has indeed been fully understood"—these are the three turnings.
And in each turning, "the eye arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and awakening arose"—these are the twelve aspects.
In this way, [the aspects] occur for each truth individually;
however, because of the commonality of three sets of twelve,
it is described as having "three turnings and twelve aspects," just like the teaching on the two types of skill regarding the seven bases.
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that by these three turnings, the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) are shown respectively.
If this is so, then it is not the path of seeing alone that has three turnings and twelve aspects; how, then, can it be established as the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*)?
Therefore, it is more appropriate that the discourse on the Dharma (*dharma-paryāya*) itself is the Wheel of Dharma, possessing three turnings and twelve aspects.
And how, moreover, is it "three turnings"?
Because of the threefold turning of the truths. How is it "twelve aspects"?

Because of the threefold treatment of the four truths— as suffering, origin, cessation, and path; and as that which is to be fully known, that which is to be abandoned, that which is to be realized, and that which is to be cultivated.
"It is fully understood, abandoned, realized, and cultivated"—
its "setting in motion" means its proceeding into the mental continuum of another through the communication of its meaning.
Alternatively, the entire Noble Path is the Wheel of Dharma, because it proceeds through the continua of those to be trained.

Because that [path] has begun to proceed by producing the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) within the continuum of another, it is said to be "set in motion" (*pravartita*). Now, in which realm are how many fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) obtained?
Regarding the attainment of three: the attainment of three fruits of asceticism occurs only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and not elsewhere.
Regarding the last [fruit] among the three, the final fruit of asceticism is arhatship; its attainment occurs in all three realms.

Since the first two fruits are attained by those already free from passion, it is logical that they are not attained in the higher realms. However, for the last one, since it is attainable by one who has not yet become free from passion, its attainment in the higher realms is appropriate.
But why is there no attainment of the third?
Because there is no path of seeing above;
for indeed, the path of seeing does not exist above the desire realm.
Furthermore, there is no attainment of the fruit of non-returning for one free from passion without that [path]; this is the reason.
But what is the reason that the path of seeing does not exist there?
First, it is because of the absence of hearing [the Dharma] in the formless realms, and because they do not take the lower realms as their object.

But in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), because there is no sense of spiritual urgency (asaṃvega) and because of the scriptural authority stating that "the culmination occurs here [in the desire realm] and the finality occurs there [in the form realm]," there are three types [of persons]. // 55 //

For ordinary beings in the realm of form (rūpāvacara) are attached to the bliss of meditative attainment (samāpatti-sukha), and because of the absence of painful feeling (duḥkhavedanā), they do not experience spiritual urgency (saṃvega). And without such urgency, it is impossible to attain the Noble Path (āryamārga).
This, first of all, is the reasoning.

There is also this scriptural authority: "For five types of persons—ranging from the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state to the one who flows upwards—there is the undertaking here and the completion there.
For "undertaking" (vidhā) refers to the commencement of the path, as it is the means to nirvāṇa.
This has been stated: "If one is immovable, after the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna), there is the cognition of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
In that regard, is there also a distinction among Arhats?
It is said that there is.
Six types of arhats are recognized;

it is stated in the Sūtra that there are six arhats: those subject to regression (*parihāṇadharman*), those intent on volition (*cetanādharman*), those intent on guarding (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), those stable and unshakable (*sthitākampya*), those capable of penetration (*prativedhanābhavya*), and those of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*). Among these, five are born from those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimuktaja*); excluding the one of immovable nature, the other five were previously of the type resolved through faith.
Their liberation is occasional;
and for these five, it should be understood that their liberation of mind is occasional and pleasant,
because it must be constantly guarded.
For this very reason, these are called "liberated by occasion" (*samayavimukta*).
They are "liberated by occasion" because they are both dependent on an occasion (*samaya*) and liberated (*vimukta*), with the middle term elided, like the word "ghee-jar" (*ghṛtaghaṭa*).
For their manifestation of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) depends on an occasion, as it requires specific conditions such as provisions, health, and a particular location.
The unshakable [Arhat] possesses an unshakable nature. // 56 //
But for one of immovable nature, liberation is immovable,
because it cannot be shaken due to the absence of falling away;
therefore, he is "liberated at all times."
For this very reason, he is called "one liberated at any time" (asamayavimukti);
for his liberation is independent of time,
since he brings the meditative absorption (samādhi) into manifestation according to his own wish.

Alternatively, the distinction between one liberated at times and one liberated at all times (samaya- and asamaya-vimukta) pertains to those of "shakable" and "unshakable" nature (*kopya* and *akopya-dharman*), based on the possibility or impossibility of falling away.
Furthermore, he is a follower of one who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta-anvaya*);
that is, it should be understood that one of unshakable nature was previously a follower of one who has attained through vision.
Furthermore, do these six types of arhats belong to that lineage from the very beginning, or do they become so later?
Some belong to that lineage from the beginning; others have attained it through refinement (uttāpanā). (57)

Some are of the lineage characterized by volition from the very beginning; others, however, having been of the lineage characterized by falling away, reach the state of being characterized by volition through the refinement of their faculties.
In this same manner, it should be understood that they proceed up to reaching the state of being characterized by immovability.
Among these, one of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) is one who is liable to fall away, but not one of the nature of volition and so forth;
one of the nature of volition (*cetanādharman*) is one who is liable to will [liberation];
one of the nature of guarding (*anurakṣaṇādharman*) is one who is liable to guard [his attainment].

The "steadfast and unshakable" (sthitākampya) is one who, even while guarding against causes of falling away, is capable of remaining as they are without falling away or increasing [their attainment], provided there is no strenuous effort.

The "capable of penetration" (prativedhanābhavya) is one who is capable of penetrating the unshakable state. The "one of unshakable nature" (akopyadharman) is one who is not at all capable of falling away.
The first two were already, while in the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*), devoid of both constant application and respectful application;
the third was one who applied himself constantly;
the fourth was one who applied himself respectfully.
The fifth is one who practices in both ways but has dull faculties;
the sixth is one who practices in both ways and has sharp faculties.
Furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that one of a nature to fall away actually falls away, nor does one who is capable of penetration necessarily penetrate.
However, this is stated with reference to the possibility [of falling away].
By adopting this view, it is logical that there are six types of Arhats even within the three realms (*dhātutraya*).

But for those who maintain that one necessarily falls away [from the fruit] until one penetrates [the next], there are six types in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while in the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātvoḥ*), there are only the "unshakable in stability" (*sthitākampya*) and the "immovable by nature" (*akopyadharman*).
Because for those two, there is no falling away from [the fruit] nor the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).
Furthermore, which of these falls away from what— from the fruit or from the lineage (*gotra*)?

Regarding the four [types of practitioners], there is falling away from the fruit; regarding the five, beginning with those of the nature of falling away (*cetana-dharman*), there is falling away from their lineage (*gotra*).
For one of the nature of falling away does not fall away again from his own lineage.
For the five types beginning with those subject to falling away (parihāṇadharman), there is falling away from the fruit;
however, even for them,
there is no falling away from what was previously attained.
Whichever is one's original lineage (*gotra*), from that one does not fall away,
because it has been made firm by both the path of training (*śaikṣa*) and the path beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
However, a trainee (*śaikṣa*) does not fall away from their own lineage because it has been made firm by both the mundane and supramundane paths.
However, one may fall away from that which was subsequently attained through refinement (*uttāpanā*).
Furthermore, one does not fall away from whichever fruit was first attained;
one falls away only from the remaining [fruits].

Therefore, there is no falling away from the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*). And having established this, there are three types for one of a nature subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*):
attaining final nirvana while remaining in that state, or the transformation of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*).
Or, having fallen away from the state of a learner (*śaikṣatva*),
there are four types for one of the nature of volition (*cetanādharman*):
these same three [types] and the returning to the lineage of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*).
In this way, for the other three types, it should be understood that there are five, six, and seven varieties respectively, through an increase of one variety at each stage.
Furthermore, whichever lineage was one's original, once that person has fallen away and become a *śaikṣa*, they remain in that very lineage and not in another.
Otherwise, because of the acquisition of a superior lineage, there would only be progress for them, not falling away.
Furthermore, what is the reason that there is no falling away from the first [fruits]?
It is because those things to be abandoned by seeing lack a real objective basis;
for these [defilements] proceed by taking the self as their foundation.
Because they are rooted in the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and that self does not exist,
it follows that [these views] would have non-existent objects.
But they do not have non-existent objects.
Because [the former] has reality as its object, whereas [the latter] have what is unreal as their object.
Which affliction, however, is not like this? There is indeed this distinction.

For the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) superimposes a false selfhood upon the entity consisting of form and so forth, by way of its being an agent, an experiencer, or one who exercises mastery. Since the views of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and the others follow from that basis, they are said to be "without a real object" (*avastuka*).

However, those [afflictions] to be abandoned by cultivation—namely attachment, aversion, pride, and ignorance—operate toward the entity of form and so forth merely through the modes of clinging, hostility, arrogance, and lack of clarity; thus, they are said to be "with a real object" (*savastuka*).
And there exists that mere [object] consisting of the beautiful and so forth, wherein those [afflictions] operate; yet there is not even a trace of a self (*ātman*) or the like.

For instance, for those [afflictions] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there is a specific object characterized as pleasant or unpleasant; however, for those to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), there is no such object characterized as a self and so forth.
Therefore, they are also said to be "without a real basis" (*avastuka*).

Furthermore, for a noble one (*ārya*), an affliction (*kleśa*) arises from the loss of mindfulness when not reflecting (*anupanidhyāyataḥ*), but not when reflecting—just as the perception of a snake in a rope [arises for one who does not examine it].

Moreover, it is not logical that views such as the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) could arise for one who is not reflecting, because they possess the nature of investigation (*santīrakatva*). Therefore, there is no falling away (*parihāṇi*) from the abandonment of those afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*).
The Sautrāntikas maintain that there is no falling away even from the state of an Arhat;
this indeed is the correct principle.
How is this understood?
This is established both through scripture and through reasoning. How is it established through scripture?
It is said: "O monks, that which has been abandoned by noble wisdom is truly abandoned."
Furthermore, the realization of the two fruits at the beginning and the end is achieved through noble wisdom alone.

It is said, "I declare that heedfulness must be practiced by one in training (śaikṣa)," but not for an Arhat. In this sutra, "Ānanda, I declare that even for an Arhat, gain and honor are obstacles," it is stated that falling away occurs only from the pleasant dwelling in the present life (dṛṣṭadharma-sukha-vihāra).
And it has also been said: "As for that unshakable liberation of mind which has been realized by him with his own body, I do not say that there is any way in which he can fall away from it.
If you argue that this refers to [falling away] from the temporary [liberation], then:
We also say this;
however, it must be investigated whether that is arhatship or rather the meditative absorptions (dhyānas).
For fundamental meditative absorption (dhyāna-samādhi) is called "temporary liberation" (sāmayikī vimukti) because it manifests at a specific time;
and it is called "delightful" (kāntā) because it is to be sought again and again for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life (dṛṣṭadharma-sukhavihāra).
Others say it is so called because it is to be relished (āsvādanīya).
However, the liberation of arhatship is not appropriately termed "occasional" because it is eternally present, nor is it termed "delightful" because it does not need to be sought again.

Furthermore, if falling away from arhatship were possible, for what reason would the Blessed One have spoken only of falling away from the "abidings in happiness in the present life" that pertain to the higher mind?

From this it is understood that the liberation of every Arhat is unshakable (*akopyā*). Let it be granted that there is a dwelling in happiness in the present life; however, some who have dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*) fall away from it due to the fault of distraction caused by gain and honor, because of the loss of their mastery (*vaśitva*).
Others who have sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*) do not fall away.
In this regard, he who falls away is one of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*);
he who does not fall away is one of the nature of non-falling away (*aparihāṇadharman*).
In the same way, those of the nature of volition (*cetanādharman*) and the others should also be applied accordingly.

What is the distinction between those of the nature of non-retrogression (*aparihāṇadharman*), those who are steadfast (*sthitākampya*), and those of the immovable nature (*akopyadharman*)? One of the nature of non-retrogression has not attained refinement through heating (*anuttāpanāgata*); one of the immovable nature, however, has attained refinement through heating (*uttāpanāgata*).
For those two [the immovable and the steadfast], whichever specific attainment they produce, they do not fall away from it.

However, the steadfast one (sthitākampya) merely does not fall away from the particular quality in which he abides, but he does not produce another; or if he does produce another, he wavers from that—this distinction is thus characterized.

The Venerable Gautika, while still a trainee (*śaikṣa*), repeatedly fell away from his temporary liberation (*sāmayikī vimukti*) due to excessive relishing of it and because of his dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*).
Becoming despondent, he took up a weapon; yet, being indifferent to both body and life, he attained arhatship at the very moment of death and entered final nirvana (*parinirvṛta*).
Therefore, even he did not fall away from arhatship.
And it is said in the *Daśottara-sūtra*: “One dharma is to be produced: the temporary, pleasant liberation of mind (*cetovimukti*).
One dharma is to be realized: the unshakable liberation of mind.”
Furthermore, if arhatship were the occasional and pleasant liberation of mind (*sāmayikī kāntā cetovimukti*), why would arhatship have been mentioned twice in that very same set of ten?
Moreover, it is nowhere stated that arhatship is something to be produced;
what then [is it]?
"One must realize [the fruit] and generate the state of arhatship comprised of dull faculties.
What is indicated by this?
If it is first possible to generate it, then that other [state] is also possible.
Now, as for the claim that it "deserves to be produced," it deserves even more so something else;
therefore, occasional liberation (sāmayikī vimukti) is not arhatship.
How, then, is an Arhat called "liberated by occasion" (samayavimukta)?
It is one for whom the manifestation of meditative absorption depends upon specific occasions due to having dull faculties;
conversely, one is "liberated without regard to occasion" (asamayavimukta).
It is also stated in the Abhidharma: "The arising of the latent tendency of sensual desire occurs through three conditions:

the latent tendency of sensual desire is neither abandoned nor fully understood; phenomena conducive to the outburst of sensual desire come into range; and there is improper mental attention toward them.
[If it is argued that the arising [of the afflictions] is thus complete:]
Or how could there be the arising of anything whose causes are incomplete?
Thus, first of all, it is established by scripture.
How is this so from the perspective of reasoning?

If, first of all, such an antidote has arisen in the Arhat by which the afflictions have attained the state of being absolutely non-arising, how then could he fall away? On the other hand, if it has not arisen, [how can he be an Arhat]?
How can one be one whose outflows are exhausted?

If the nature of the seeds of those outflows has not been utterly uprooted, how could one whose outflows are not yet exhausted be an Arhat? Such is the logical argument. In that case, the *Aṅgārakarṣūpama-sūtra* must be interpreted [otherwise].

Regarding that which was said: "In the case of that learned noble disciple who thus conducts himself and thus dwells, at some time or other, due to a lapse of mindfulness, evil and unwholesome thoughts arise";
for it is there that he is indicated to be an Arhat indeed.
Because of the statement: "For a long time his mind has been inclined toward seclusion, even unto its leaning toward nirvāṇa.
For this is declared elsewhere to be the power of an Arhat: "He has become cooled and has vomited out [the defilements] with respect to all states conducive to the outflows. This is indeed so.

However, as long as the course of conduct has not been thoroughly penetrated, there remains the possibility of the arising of afflictions even for a trainee (śaikṣa) who practices in such a way; thus, because this statement refers specifically to the stage of a trainee, there is no fault.
For it is indeed admitted that there is falling away from the two fruits obtained by means of the mundane path.
The Vaibhāṣikas, however, maintain that there is falling away even from the state of arhatship.
Furthermore, do only these arhats possess the six lineages, or do others also possess the six lineages?
Learners (śaikṣas) and noble ones who are not yet arhats also possess the six lineages.
Trainees (śaikṣa) and ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) likewise possess these six lineages (gotra), for the lineages of Arhats are preceded by those very same [lineages]. However—
There is no shifting in the case of direct perception. //58//
The transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) occurs elsewhere than on the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*);
it does not occur on the path of seeing because of the impossibility of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Some transform their faculties while in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Someone [falls away] while in the stage of being resolved through faith;

as it is said in the Sūtra: "Regarding those four higher mental abidings in the present life which have been attained by him, I declare that he may fall away from any one of them; however, regarding that unshakable liberation of mind which has been realized by him alone through the body, I do not declare that he can fall away from it by any means whatsoever."
How can there be falling away from the pleasant dwellings in this very life for one of immovable nature?
Falling away should be known as threefold: by way of what has been attained, what has not yet been attained, and enjoyment.
Falling away from what has been attained occurs if one falls away from a quality already acquired.
There is falling away from what has not yet been attained if one does not attain a quality that is to be attained;
there is falling away from enjoyment if one does not bring a quality already attained into manifestation.
Furthermore, regarding these types of falling away:
The last [attainment] belongs to the Teacher and the Immovable One; the middle one also belongs to the latter, while for others it is of three kinds. //56//
For a Buddha, there is only decline in enjoyment and no other;
for one of immovable nature, there is both that [decline in enjoyment] and decline through non-attainment, because of not having attained the qualities of a superior person.
For other Arhats, there is also falling away from what has been attained;
therefore, because of the mention of "falling away from enjoyment," there is no contradiction with the Sūtra regarding one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*).
The untainted liberation of everyone is unshakable;
however, the formal establishment of one as "of unshakable nature" is as previously explained. Therefore, this objection is invalid, according to the proponent of non-retrogression.
Now, if one falls away from the fruit of arhatship, is such a person reborn?
This is not the case; for:
One does not die having fallen from the fruit;
for no one indeed passes away while deprived of the fruit.
This is because of the statement in the Sūtra: "O monks, although there may be a lapse of mindfulness in a noble disciple, it nevertheless very quickly reaches its end and destruction immediately."
For otherwise, the holy life would be unreliable;
and because one falls away from a fruit, that which is not to be done by one established in that fruit— namely, performing an improper act— one does not do.
Even when he has fallen away, he does not perform an action contrary to that fruit,
just as a hero may stumble but does not fall.
Now, for those who are transitioning between the faculties (*indriya*), how many paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are there?
There are nine paths of liberation and nine paths of immediate succession regarding the immovable (*akopya*).

When the immovable lineage (*gotra*) is being penetrated, for one capable of penetration through cultivation (*prativedha-bhāvanā-bhavya*), there arise nine paths of immediate succession and nine paths of liberation.
Just as for one attaining arhatship.
What is the reason?
Because of excessive cultivation. //60//
His lineage of dull faculties has been practiced for so long that it cannot be turned back by a small effort,
because it has been made firm by both the paths of training and beyond training.

Regarding the attainment of one who has seen [the truths], when the state of "one who has attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) is being realized, there is exactly one path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) and one path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
However, the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) is in every case only one. Furthermore, all of these paths of uninterrupted transition and paths of liberation—
They are untainted (*anāsrava*);
for the Noble Ones do not effect the transformation of their faculties by means of a tainted (*sāsrava*) path.
Where, then, are the faculties increased?
It is an increase among humans;
the transformation of the faculties occurs only among human beings and nowhere else,
because falling away is impossible [in other realms].
Furthermore, relying on which stages does one transform the faculties?
One who is beyond training (aśaikṣa) transforms them by relying on nine stages:
the threshold stage (anāgamya), the four meditative absorptions (dhyāna), and the three formless attainments (ārūpya).
But for one in training (śaikṣa), there are six [abandonments], excluding those of the formless realm.
What is the reason?
For this reason: //61//
Having abandoned the fruit along with its specific distinctions, one attains the fruit while increasing [the faculties].

For, as the faculties progress, having abandoned the path of the fruit and the path of a fruit characterized by [inferior] faculties, one who belongs to the lineage of sharp faculties attains only the path of the fruit.
And this is the reason: there is no fruit of a Non-returner (anāgāmiphala) included within the formless realm (ārūpyabhūmi).
All these Arhats are of nine types due to the distinction of their faculties. How so?
Two are Buddhas, seven are Śrāvakas; these nine possess ninefold faculties. //62//
Which are the seven types of śrāvakas?

They are the five beginning with those subject to retrogression (parihāṇadharman), and the two types of those of immovable nature (akopyadharman): those who have attained it through refinement (uttāpanāgata) and those who belong to that lineage from the very beginning (āditaḥ tadgotra). These are indeed the divisions of the immovable type.
There are two types of Buddhas: the Pratyekabuddha and the [Samyak-]sambuddha.
Thus, through the distinction of the nine grades of faculties—beginning with the "weak-weak"—there are nine types of persons (pudgala).
However, all noble persons (āryapudgala) together constitute seven types.

The follower by faith, the follower by Dharma, one liberated through faith, one who has attained vision, the body-witness, the one liberated by wisdom, and the one liberated in both ways; these, moreover,
are distinguished by their application, faculties, meditative attainments, liberation, or both.

There are seven types of persons; by way of application, there are those who follow through faith and those who follow through the Dharma, because they previously applied themselves to the meanings by means of reliance on others and reliance on the Dharma respectively.
In terms of faculties, there are those liberated through faith and those who have attained vision,
due to the distinction between dull and sharp faculties, and the predominance of either conviction through faith or wisdom.
In terms of meditative attainments, there is the bodily witness, because of the direct realization of the attainment of cessation.

By way of liberation, there is the one liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*); by way of liberation through meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), there is the one liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*). By name, these are the seven types of persons (*pudgala*).
However, these are six;
in terms of substantial entity, these are six because there are two for each of the three paths. //63//
For on the path of seeing, there are two types of persons: the follower by faith and the follower by dharma;
these same two become the one liberated by faith and the one who has attained vision on the path of cultivation.

Furthermore, on the path of one beyond training (aśaikṣamārga), there are two types: those liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) and those liberated irrespective of occasion (asamayavimukta). Among these, from the perspective of their faculties (indriya), there are three.
Regarding those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin): there are five from the perspective of lineage (gotra) and fifteen from the perspective of the path (mārga),
namely those abiding in the eight patiences (kṣānti) and the seven knowledges (jñāna).
From the perspective of detachment, there are seventy-three:
those who are bound by all fetters,
and nine who have attained detachment from the desire realm.
In this way, up to the detachment from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
there are nine [types] by way of basis (*āśraya*):
those born in the three continents and the six classes of gods.

When condensed according to faculties (*indriya*), lineage (*gotra*), path (*mārga*), detachment (*vairāgya*), and basis (*āśraya*), they amount to one hundred forty-seven thousand eight hundred and twenty-five.

In this way, other types of persons (*pudgala*) may also be enumerated as far as they exist. Who is called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), and who is "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñāvimukta*)?
One who has attained cessation (*nirodha*) is liberated in both ways; the other is liberated by wisdom.
One who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is "liberated in both ways" (ubhayatobhāgavimukta),
because they are liberated from both the afflictions (kleśa) and the hindrances to liberation (vimokṣāvaraṇa) through the powers of wisdom (prajñā) and concentration (samādhi).
The other is "liberated by wisdom" (prajñāvimukta).
Because they are liberated solely from the obscuration of afflictions by the power of wisdom.
Regarding what was said by the Blessed One: "He who, having abandoned the five afflictions here, is of unshakable nature—that is a complete trainee (śaikṣa).
To what extent is a trainee complete?
A trainee is declared complete by way of meditative attainments (samāpatti), faculties (indriya), and fruits (phala). //64//
The perfection of a trainee (śaikṣa) is threefold:
by way of fruit, by way of faculties, and by way of meditative attainments (samāpatti).
There is perfection by way of fruit alone for the non-returner (anāgāmin) who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) and is not a bodily witness (akāyasākṣin).
From the perspective of the faculties alone, there is the one who has attained vision but is not yet free from passion;
from the perspective of both fruit and faculties, there is the non-returner who has attained vision but is not a body-witness;
and from the perspective of both fruit and meditative attainment, there is the one liberated by faith who is a body-witness.
For one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) and is a body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*), there is fulfillment through both the fruit and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*);
for there is no fulfillment of the attainment and the faculties (*indriya*) through attainment alone without the fruit.
The fulfillment of the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is by means of two [factors].
[The distinction is made] by way of the faculties (*indriya*) and by way of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).

However, since one who is incomplete in terms of the fruit (*phala*) does not possess the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣatva*) at all, his completeness or incompleteness is not further established by way of the fruit.
[This applies] specifically by way of the faculties to the one liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*), that is, the one liberated through wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*).
For one who is liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) and liberated in both ways (ubhayabhāgavimukta), it is solely by means of meditative attainment (samāpatti).
For one who is unconditionally liberated (asamayavimukta) and liberated in both ways, it is by means of both faculties (indriya) and meditative attainment.

[Many of these different types of paths have been taught: the mundane and supramundane paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning; the paths of preparation, uninterruptedness, liberation, and excellence.
In brief, how many kinds of path are there?
The path, in brief, is as follows:
It is fourfold, consisting of the distinguished liberation, the uninterrupted path, and the preparatory application. //65//

The path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) is that from which the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) arises immediately thereafter; the path of uninterrupted transition is that by which one abandons the obscurations;
and the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) is that which first arises for one who is liberated from the obscurations to be abandoned by that [path of uninterrupted transition].
The path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*) is that path which is other than these [three].
Why is it called a "path"?
Because this is the way to *nirvāṇa*, for by means of it one goes there.
Or alternatively, it is so called because one seeks *nirvāṇa* by means of it.
How do the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*) possess the nature of a "path"?

Because they are of the same kind [as the path of seeing] but are more intense, because they lead to ever higher stages, or because they bring about entry into *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).
Furthermore, the path itself is called "the practice" (*pratipad*) because it leads to the realization of *nirvāṇa*. There are four practices:
there is a practice that is painful and characterized by slow direct knowledge.
There is that which is painful with swift direct knowledge;
likewise, that which is pleasant is also twofold.
In this regard:
The path within the dhyānas is the pleasant practice;
in the four dhyānas, the path is a pleasant practice because it proceeds without effort due to the possession of the factors [of dhyāna] and the equilibrium of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
On other stages, it is difficult.

In the other stages—the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the formless realms (*ārūpya*)—the path is difficult because it is not supported by the [meditative] factors (*aṅga*), due to the deficiency of either calm abiding (*śamatha*) or insight (*vipaśyanā*), and because it must be cultivated with effort. For in the preparatory stage and the intermediate dhyāna, calm abiding is deficient;
in the formless realms, insight is deficient.
Furthermore, that path is of two kinds.
For one of dull intellect, direct knowledge is slow; for the other, however, it is swift. //66//

For one of dull faculties, whether the practice is pleasant or painful, it is slow direct knowledge; for one of sharp faculties, it is quick direct knowledge. "Slow direct knowledge" means that direct knowledge is slow in this practice;
likewise for "quick direct knowledge."
Or, it is called "slow superknowledge" because it belongs to a person who is slow.
Furthermore, this path receives the designation of "factors conducive to enlightenment";
these are the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣyadharma).
The four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts, and the four bases of psychic power.
The five faculties, the five powers, and the seven factors of enlightenment.
Regarding "the noble eightfold path":

therein, awakening (bodhi) consists of the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna); that is, the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising.
Through the distinction of individuals, three types of awakening arise:
the awakening of a śrāvaka, the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, and unsurpassed perfect complete awakening,
due to the abandonment of ignorance without remainder.
And because, through those two, there is the realization that one's own purpose has been accomplished as it truly is and need not be done again;
and because they are favorable to that [realization].
Furthermore, there are thirty-seven factors belonging to that side.
Because they are in conformity with enlightenment, thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment arise; by name there are thirty-seven, but in substance there are ten.
All factors conducive to enlightenment consist of ten substances.
Which ten?
Faith, vigor, mindfulness, wisdom, concentration, joy, and equanimity.
These ten entities consist of pliancy, morality, and resolve.
How so?
For wisdom is indeed the application of mindfulness. //68//
Vigor is called the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), and the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are concentrations.

For the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right abandonments, and the bases of psychic power have as their intrinsic nature wisdom (*prajñā*), vigor (*vīrya*), and concentration (*samādhi*). Therefore, first of all, the faculties (*indriya*) and the powers (*bala*)—by way of designating them by name—are the substances of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. As for the foundations of mindfulness:
The factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) are indeed wisdom itself.
The right efforts (*samyakprahāṇas*), the factor of enlightenment of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), and right exertion (*samyagvyāyāma*) are indeed energy itself.
The bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipādas*), the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) are indeed concentration itself.
The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) are simply mindfulness itself.
What remains?
The factors of enlightenment of joy, tranquility, and equanimity; right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*); and the factors of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
These are the five substances; thus, these factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣya) consist of ten substances.
According to the Vaibhāṣikas, there are eleven, because bodily and vocal actions are distinct, and thus ethical discipline (śīla) and knowledge (jñāna) constitute two separate substances.

Regarding what was stated—that "the foundations of mindfulness and so forth have wisdom, energy, and concentration as their intrinsic natures"—it should be understood here: this is a mention of the predominant factors; however, all of them are indeed acquired through application (prāyogika). //66//
This was stated by way of mentioning the primary factor;
however, all the qualities resulting from application (*prāyogika*)—namely, the foundations of mindfulness, the right exertions, and the bases of psychic power—are included.
Why, then, is vigor specifically called "right exertion" (*samyakpradhāna*)?
By means of that, body, speech, and mind are correctly applied.
Why is concentration called a "basis of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*)?
Because it is the foundation for the attainment of all excellent qualities.

As for those who say, "Concentration itself is the supernormal power (ṛddhi), while the bases (pāda) are zeal and the rest," for them the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣya) would amount to thirteen in substance due to the addition of zeal and mind; furthermore, this contradicts the Sūtra.

"And I shall show you, monks, the supernormal power (ṛddhi) and the bases of supernormal power (ṛddhipāda); as for what supernormal power is: here, monks, a monk experiences various kinds of supernormal domains;
having been one, he becomes many," and so forth in detail.
Why are the faculties themselves called powers?
Because of the distinction between weak and intense, and because they are respectively suppressible and non-suppressible.
What determines the sequence of the faculties?
For one who possesses faith initiates vigor for the sake of the fruit;
for one who has initiated vigor, mindfulness is established;
for one whose mindfulness is established, the mind becomes concentrated through non-distraction.
"One whose mind is concentrated understands things as they truly are.
In what state are which of those factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣya) manifested?
They are manifested during the stages of the beginner and the levels conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya).
In cultivation and in vision, there are seven groups respectively. //70//
In the stage of a beginner, there are the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) for the purpose of observing the body and so forth.
With the attainment of distinction, because of the intensification of vigor (*vīrya*), there are the right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*) during the stages of "heat" (*ūṣmagata*).
Because they lead to the entry into roots of virtue that do not regress, there are the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) during the stages of "summits" (*mūrdhan*).
The faculties (*indriya*) exist in the stages of patience (*kṣānti*) because one has attained mastery through the absence of further regression;

the powers (*bala*) exist in the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*) because they cannot be crushed by the afflictions, or alternatively, because they cannot be crushed by any other mundane dharmas;
and the limbs of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) exist on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) because of the proximity to awakening.
Because it is characterized by movement, the factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are present in the path of seeing (darśanamārga), due to its rapid progression.
However, for the sake of establishing their numerical order, seven were taught first and eight afterwards.

Regarding this, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the factor-of-enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is both enlightenment (*bodhi*) and a limb of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and that right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is both the path (*mārga*) and a limb of the path (*mārgāṅga*).

Others, however, describe the sequence of the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣya*) without breaking the order: first of all, the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are bound to the mind for the sake of restraining cognitions that wander by being scattered among various objects, as it is said in the Sūtra: "solely for the purpose of dispelling recollections and intentions based on craving."
By means of that power, through the intensification of vigor, one correctly applies the mind toward the accomplishment of the fourfold task; thus, these are the right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*).
From that, through the purification of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), come the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Based upon meditative concentration, faith and the other faculties (*indriya*) become dominant over supramundane phenomena.
And those very same [factors] are the powers (*bala*) when the activity of their opposites has been conquered;

they are the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) because of the initial vision of the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*); and they are the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) on both paths.

For it has been said: "Indeed, when the Noble Eightfold Path reaches the fulfillment of cultivation, the four foundations of mindfulness reach the fulfillment of cultivation, up to the seven factors of enlightenment.

Furthermore, it has been said: "O monks, 'proclaiming speech as it truly is' is a designation for the Four Noble Truths; O monk, 'proceeding by the path as it has come' is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path."
"This is a designation for the path.
Therefore, the noble eightfold path must be accepted by both [parties].
The sequence is established;
however, this must be stated:
how many factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are with outflows (sāsrava), and how many are without outflows (anāsrava)?

The factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and the factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are untainted (anāsrava), because they are established as such on the paths of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) and seeing (darśanamārga). For are there not also mundane (laukika) right view and so forth?
But they do not receive the designation "noble path";
the others are of two kinds, while the other factors conducive to enlightenment are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
On which stage are how many factors of enlightenment present?
All thirty-seven are present in the first dhyāna; all thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are found in the first dhyāna.
In the preparatory stage (anāgamya), they are devoid of joy (prīti). //71//
Why is there an absence of joy (*prīti*) in the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*)?

Because the threshold concentrations must be driven by effort (*balavāhanīyatva*) and because they involve apprehension regarding the lower stage. In the second [dhyāna], with the exception of right intention (*saṃkalpa*);
in the second dhyāna, there are exactly thirty-six factors, excluding right intention.
In that regard, because of the absence of applied thought (*vitarka*),
in the second [dhyāna] they are devoid of those two;
in the third and fourth dhyānas, they are devoid of both joy (*prīti*) and applied thought, numbering thirty-five.

In the intermediate dhyāna as well, there are likewise thirty-five [factors], being devoid of those same two; and in the three formless realms, they are devoid of the factors of morality and those two. (72)
The term "excluded" (varjitā) continues [to apply here].
In the formless realms (ārūpya), thirty-two [factors] are excluded: namely, right speech, right action, right livelihood, joy (prīti), and right intention (saṃkalpa).
In the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and at the peak of existence (bhavāgra), the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and the factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are excluded.
There are twenty-two factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣya) because those two [realms] lack the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga).
In what state should it be understood that one who abides in the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) attains verified clarity (avetyaprasāda)?
It is at the vision of the three truths that there is verified clarity regarding the Dharma and verified clarity regarding the Saṅgha. (73)
There is also the attainment [of faith] regarding the Buddha and his Saṅgha upon the realization of what is not the Path.
Upon realizing the truths of suffering, its origin, and its cessation, one attains verified clarity regarding the Dharma and the ethical conduct dear to the Noble Ones.
Upon realizing the truth of the Path, one attains verified clarity regarding the Buddha and his Śrāvaka-Saṅgha.

For that which is faith in those two is faith in the qualities that constitute a Buddha—those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—and in the qualities that constitute the Saṅgha—those both in training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond training.
By the word "also" (*api*), one also acquires serene confidence in morality (*śīla*) and the Dharma through realization (*avetyaprasāda*).
What is intended here by the term "Dharma"? The Dharma consists of the three truths and [the paths] of the Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddhas. (74)
And because the path [is realized] from this [attainment], there is the acquisition of verified clarity regarding the Dharma upon realizing all four truths.
These are called the four verified clarities by name, according to the distinction of their respective bases of faith.
In terms of substantial entities (*dravya*), however, there are two: faith (*śraddhā*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*).
