All Buddhas are equal by virtue of their equipment, their Dharma-body, and their service for the sake of the world; they are not equal in terms of lifespan, birth, or physical stature. //34//
All Buddhas possess equality through three causes:

through the complete attainment of the accumulations of all merit and knowledge; through the perfection of the *dharmakāya*; and through their conduct for the benefit of the world. However, there exists a distinction based on lifespan, caste, lineage, and physical stature.

It is according to the time, due to the difference in the length of life—whether long or very short—the distinction between the Kṣatriya and Brāhmaṇa castes, the distinction between lineages such as Kāśyapa and Gautama, and the difference in physical stature, whether small or large.

And by reflecting upon these very three kinds of perfection—a wise person is able to generate intense love and reverence toward the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones: namely, the perfection of cause, the perfection of fruit, and the perfection of benefit.
Among these, the perfection of cause is fourfold.
The practice consists of the prior cultivation of the accumulations of merit and knowledge, long-term cultivation, uninterrupted cultivation, and respectful cultivation.
The perfection of the fruit is fourfold:
the perfection of knowledge, the perfection of abandonment, the perfection of power, and the perfection of the form-body.

The perfection of the fourfold assistance consists either in the perfection of the ultimate liberation from the suffering of the three miserable realms and of saṃsāra, or in the perfection of establishing [beings] in the three vehicles and in happy rebirths.
Furthermore, the perfection of knowledge is fourfold.
There is knowledge that is untaught, knowledge that is universal, knowledge that is omniform, and knowledge that is effortless.
There are four kinds of perfection of abandonment:

the abandonment of all afflictions, absolute abandonment, abandonment together with their latent predispositions (*savāsanā*), and the abandonment of all hindrances to meditative concentrations and attainments. There are four kinds of perfection of power.

The perfection of mastery over the emanation, transformation, and sustaining of external objects; the perfection of mastery over the sustaining and relinquishing of life-span; the perfection of mastery over passing through obstructions, traveling swiftly to distant places through space, and entering into what is small and large; and the perfection of various innate and marvelous qualities—these constitute the fourfold perfection of the form body (*rūpakāya*).
The perfection of the primary marks, the perfection of the secondary characteristics, the perfection of strength, and the perfection of a body with bones as solid as adamant—
this is the summary of the majesty of the Buddhas; however,
its actual manifestations arise in infinite varieties.
Furthermore, only the Buddhas themselves are capable of knowing and explaining that in its entirety, even if they were to sustain their life for many incalculable eons.
Thus, the Tathāgatas are indeed great repositories of jewels consisting of infinite, marvelous qualities, knowledge, power, and benefit.
Nevertheless, fools—stricken by the poverty of their own virtues and lacking resolute faith—even upon hearing of such an abundance of qualities, pay no heed to the Buddha nor to his Dharma.
The wise, moreover, take refuge in that Blessed One and in his Dharma even with their very marrow.

For those who are single-mindedly devoted even by means of mere faith, having overcome heaps of evil whose ripening is not yet fixed, and having surpassed both divine and human prosperity, they become destined for Nirvana.
For this very reason, the Tathāgatas are called the unsurpassed field of merit.
Because its fruit is unfailing, desirable, preeminent, swift, and final.
For it was said by the Blessed One:
"Those who perform even minor services for the Victor, the Guide..."
"Having gone to the wondrous heaven, they shall attain the state of immortality.
These, then, are called the eighteen unique qualities of the Buddhas.
Other qualities are shared with disciples, while other virtues of the Buddhas are shared with Śrāvakas;
some are even shared with ordinary worldlings.

What, then, are these? They are, as appropriate, the qualities such as the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), and the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). //35//

These include the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and so forth. Among these, "absence of conflict" (*araṇā*) refers to a certain person who, having understood that the suffering of sentient beings arises from their afflictions (*kleśa*), and desiring to prevent others from generating afflictions directed toward himself— since he is a distinguished object of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*)— produces such a knowledge by which [he prevents] others [from doing so].
In every respect, it does not produce conflict;
no one’s passion, hatred, or pride arises with that as its object. Because this practice does not cause anyone to conflict, it is called "the absence of conflict" (araṇā).
Furthermore,
this [attainment] is conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) and non-contention (araṇā);
such is its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
In the final dhyāna— that is,
belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna— because it is the foremost among the easy paths of practice; [this applies] to one of immovable nature (akopyadharman).
Not of any other Arhat;
for another [Arhat] might at times be unable to avoid the battle with the afflictions even within his own continuum.
It is born of humans.
They arise only among humans in the three continents;
they have as their object the unarisen afflictions belonging to the desire realm that possess a real basis. //36//

The future afflictions belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) that have a real objective basis (*savastuka*) are its object, because it functions in such a way that "no other affliction shall arise. However, afflictions without a real objective basis (*avastuka*) cannot be avoided, because the universal (*sarvatraga*) [afflictions] take the entirety of their own level as their object.
Just as it was described for the knowledge of others' minds (*cetaḥparyāya-jñāna*),

so too is the knowledge resulting from resolution (*praṇidhi-jñāna*); for that too is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), belonging to one of unshakable nature (*akopyadharman*) in the final dhyāna, based on the human body,
and it has everything as its object.
However, the specific distinction is that the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) has all phenomena as its object.
Yet, the formless realms (*ārūpya*) are not known directly by the knowledge resulting from aspiration;
what then?
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that this is due to the distinction in the specific outflow of conduct, and they provide the illustration of a farmer here.
Knowledge preceded by a vow is "vow-knowledge" (praṇidhijñāna); for one enters the fourth dhyāna of the ultimate limit after having made such a vow.
Thinking, "May I know this," he knows it as it truly is,
to the full extent that it is the object of his concentration.
Thus.
And [the attainment] of the higher knowledges regarding phenomena, their meaning, etymological definitions, and eloquence. //37//
For there are four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*):

the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
These—namely, the analytical knowledges of phenomena, meaning, expression, and eloquence—are likewise [to be understood] in the same manner as the absence of conflict (*araṇā*).
In what way are they similar? They are similar in being the support for humans of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*).
However, their distinctions regarding object (*ālambana*), stage (*bhūmi*), and intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) are stated separately:
the three are, respectively, knowledge of names, meanings, and speech, which is irreversible.

The analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of phenomena, meaning, language, and eloquence are, respectively, the irreversible knowledge regarding the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes, and their referents; the fourth [analytical knowledge] consists in mastery over appropriate and fluent expression and the path. //38//
The term "irreversible knowledge" carries over [from the previous context].

Irreversible knowledge regarding the state of being one who speaks appropriately and fluently, as well as the manifestation [of speech] through mastery of meditative concentration, is the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-saṃvid*).
Furthermore, this has both speech and the path as its objects.

Speech and the path are its objects. The analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) has the nine knowledges as its intrinsic nature, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*). It belongs to all stages.
And this [analytical knowledge] belongs to all stages, from the desire realm up to the peak of existence, because it takes as its object either speech or the path.
The analytical knowledge of meaning consists of ten or six knowledges;
the analytical knowledge of eloquence consists of all [ten] knowledges, as its purpose is the cutting off of all phenomena.

If *nirvāṇa* is the object, there are six knowledges: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). That [knowledge] exists everywhere.
Furthermore, this analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid) belongs to all stages;
however, the others belong to the conventional (sāṃvṛta). //36//

Others, however, maintain that the two analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) regarding phenomena (*dharma*) and etymological explanation (*nirukti*) have conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) as their intrinsic nature, because their nature consists in taking the sets of names (*nāmakāya*) and so forth, as well as speech, as their objects.

Knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) exists in the desire realm and the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), thus belonging to five stages; it is comprised within the desire realm and the four meditative absorptions, because above those [stages] there is an absence of the sets of names.
Regarding speech, it pertains to the first dhyāna and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"Speech" and "etymological definition" (*nirukti*) have the same meaning.
The analytical knowledge of etymology (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) belongs to the levels of the desire realm and the first dhyāna, because there is an absence of applied thought (*vitarka*) above that.

In the *Prajñapti*, however, there is this explanation of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*): "The irreversible knowledge regarding words and phonemes, regarding their meaning, regarding their designations as singular, dual, plural, feminine, masculine, and so forth, and regarding non-attachment to them, is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*). For this very reason, their sequence is established.
Etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) is etymology (*nirukti*).
"Form is so called because it is transformed," and so forth.
Others say that *pratibhāna* (eloquence) is the successive manifestation [of knowledge].

It is said that the preliminary practice for these analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) consists respectively of mathematics, the Buddha’s word, grammar, and logic; for one who has not achieved skill in these cannot produce them.

However, they describe the word of the Buddha alone as the application for all [the analytical knowledges]. And for whomsoever there is one, he necessarily possesses all four analytical knowledges; one does not possess them when they are incomplete.
For one does not become a possessor of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) by means of those [perfections] when they are incomplete.
Furthermore, these six qualities taught here, beginning with *araṇā*, are those that reach the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika*). //40//
The attainment of these occurs through the power of the *prāntakoṭika* (ultimate-limit) meditative absorption.
That [absorption] is of six kinds;
furthermore, that ultimate-limit fourth dhyāna consists of six aspects.

The knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), the three analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and that same [knowledge] when it is "reaching the ultimate limit" (*prāntakoṭika*).
Through the power of that [ultimate limit], one attains the analytical knowledge of etymology (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), though it itself belongs to the level of the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, what is this so-called "limit-of-the-peak" (prāntakoṭika)?
It is the final dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna,
which has been made compliant with all stages.
And how does that [concentration], having reached its peak of development, become adapted to all stages?
From a mind belonging to the desire realm, one enters the first dhyāna.

Then, in this same manner, one proceeds to the second [dhyāna] and so on by stages up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Then, in reverse order, one descends back down to a mind belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*). From there, once again in forward order, one ascends up to the fourth dhyāna; thus, one has brought all the stages into conformity.
How does it reach the pinnacle of increase?
Having cultivated it thus, one enters from the weak [level] into the medium, and from the medium into the intense;
for the culmination of increase is the limit of increase. This is called "reaching the ultimate limit" (*prāntakoṭika*) because its end-point (*anta-koṭi*) has gone forth (*pragata*).
Furthermore, "limit" (*koṭi*) here means either increase or a mode, as in the case of the "fourfold limit" (*catuṣkoṭika*).
Moreover, these six qualities arise from application for one other than a Buddha. (41)
For anyone other than a Buddha, [supernormal powers] are acquired through application (*prāyogika*) and not obtained through detachment (*vairāgyalābhika*).
For a Buddha, however, there is nothing acquired through application;
because he is the sovereign of all phenomena (*sarvadharmeśvara*), the manifestation of the perfection of all qualities is dependent upon his mere wish.

These, first of all, are the qualities common to the śrāvakas; the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth are shared even with ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). What is this so-called "supernormal power"? It consists of:
psychic power, the divine ear, knowledge of the minds of others, recollection of former births, and knowledge of death and rebirth, as well as the knowledge of the destruction [of the outflows].
The direct realization of knowledge regarding the sixfold supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) is the higher knowledge (*abhijñā*).

The higher knowledges consist of the direct realization of knowledge of the divine ear, of others' minds, of the recollection of former abodes, of death and rebirth, and of the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*).
These are the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Of these, five are shared with ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*);
however, all of them [are possessed by] these [noble ones].
The cognition of the path to liberation. //42//
They have the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) belonging to the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*),
like the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*);
the four [knowledges] are conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Excluding the supernormal knowledges of the knowledge of the modes of others' minds and the destruction of the outflows, there are five knowledges regarding the mind.

The supernormal knowledge of the modes of others' minds consists of five: the knowledges of phenomena (dharma), subsequent (anvaya), path (mārga), conventional (saṃvṛti), and others' minds (paracitta).
The supernormal knowledge of destruction (kṣayābhijñā) is to be understood in the same way as the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayajñānabala) has been explained;
it consists of six or ten knowledges.
This [knowledge] should be understood to exist on all stages in the same way;
however, the remaining five exist only within the four dhyānas. //43//
The five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā) belong to the level of the fourth dhyāna. Why do they not exist on the levels of the formless realm (ārūpyabhūmi)?
First of all, three of them do not exist there.
Because it has form as its object,

the supernormal knowledge of the minds of others (*cetaḥparyāyābhijñā*) does not exist [in that regard], since it is accomplished by means of the gateway of form. Furthermore, the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsasmṛti*) does not exist [there], because it is accomplished through the successive stages of existence and death.
Furthermore, it is because it takes as its object [the other's] station, lineage, and so forth.

For one who desires to know another's mind first grasps the signs of his own body and mind, thinking, "In such a body of mine, what kind of mind arises? By thus attending to others as well, the knowledge of their minds becomes fully accomplished.
When supernormal knowledge has been fully accomplished, one knows independently of form.
Desiring to recollect former abodes, one grasps the sign of the mental consciousness that has just ceased, and then attends to the successive stages of existence in reverse order,
back as far as the mind at the beginning of the current aeon.
Then, even by recollecting a single moment of the intermediate state (antarābhava), it becomes perfected;
in this way, one also recollects that of others.
Once it is fully perfected, there is recollection even by skipping over [intervals].
Recollection is only of that which has been previously experienced.
How, then, can there be recollection of the Śuddhāvāsa deities?
Because they have been experienced through hearing.
For one who has passed away from the formless realm and is reborn here, [the production of supernatural powers] occurs by means of presiding over another's continuum;
for others, it occurs by means of presiding over their own continuum.
However, for the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and so forth, the preliminary application consists of mental attention to lightness, sound, and light.
Furthermore, these five superknowledges have as their domain one's own level and the levels below;
whichever level the superknowledge of supernormal power (*ṛddhyabhijñā*) belongs to, one travels to that level by means of it.
Or he creates [an emanation] of a lower level, but not of a higher one.
Likewise, through the supernormal knowledge of the divine ear, one hears sounds belonging only to one's own level or to a lower level, but not to a higher level.
Through the supernormal knowledge of the penetration of others' minds, one does not know a mind belonging to a higher level.
One does not recollect by means of the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*),
nor does one see by means of the supernormal knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutopapādābhijñā*).

For this very reason, a mind belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyabhūmika*) is not grasped by the supernormal knowledges of the modes of others' minds (*cetaḥparyāya*) or of past lives, because it belongs to a higher level (*ūrdhvabhūmikatva*).
How are these obtained?
Those not previously cultivated are obtained through application; those already cultivated are obtained through detachment.
The superknowledges (*abhijñā*) practiced in previous lives are obtained through detachment (*vairāgya*), whereas the specific ones are obtained through application (*prayoga*).
However, the production of all of them occurs through application.

As for the third [superknowledge], it consists of three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); the superknowledge of the mental states of others (*cetaḥparyāyābhijñā*) consists of the three foundations of mindfulness: feeling, mind, and phenomena.
Because it has the mind and mental factors as its object;
the first [type of knowledge] arises from the ear up to the eye.
The term "higher knowledge" (abhijñā) carries over [from the previous context].
This means that the higher knowledges of supernatural power, the divine ear, and the divine eye are the first application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna),
because they have form (rūpa) as their object.
The supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) has the four external sense-bases (*bāhyāyatana*) as its object, with the exception of sound.
The two higher knowledges (*abhijñā*) of the divine ear and divine eye have the sense-bases of sound and form as their respective objects.
How then is it that, through the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutopapādajñāna*), one knows: "These worthy beings are possessed of bodily misconduct," and so forth?
One does not know that [object] by means of that [knowledge];
rather, another knowledge, which is the retinue of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), arises for the noble ones (*ārya*) by which they know in this way.
Since there is no specific restriction, it is established that the remaining [superknowledges] have the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
The supernormal powers of the ear and the eye are neutral; the others are wholesome.
The supernormal powers of the divine eye and the divine ear are neutral;
these, moreover, are wisdom associated with visual and auditory consciousness.
How, then, are those two established as belonging to the level of the four dhyānas?
Because they are designated as being of that level by virtue of their basis (*āśraya*).
For the eye and the ear, which serve as their basis, belong to the level of the four dhyānas.
Or, by virtue of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), the other four are wholesome. As for what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*: "What is supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*)?"
"Wholesome wisdom.
This is a statement made either from the perspective of what is predominant or what is most frequent among these supernormal knowledges (abhijñās). And of these supernormal knowledges...
The three knowledges—

the realization through direct experience of the knowledge of former abodes, of death and rebirth, and of the destruction of the outflows— are called the "knowledges of one beyond training" (aśaikṣī vidyā).
Why are only these, and no others?
Because ignorance is brought to cessation at the beginning of the prior limit and so forth. //45//
For these [three knowledges] dispel delusion regarding the past, the future, and the middle [present], respectively.

In the ultimate sense, among these, only the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows belonging to one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is the "knowledge of one beyond training" (*aśaikṣī vidyā*).
The two [paths] so named are called "of the learner" because they arise from the continuum of a learner;
the other two are called "of the non-learner" because they arise from the continuum of a non-learner.
However, they are neither of the learner nor of the non-learner.
Why, then, are these two supernormal powers not called "belonging to one in training" (śaikṣya)?
Because the two knowledges (vidyā) are not said to belong to one in training;
for it is accepted that the two knowledges are not stated to belong to one in training because his continuum is still associated with ignorance (sāvidyasaṃtati). //46//
For it is not logical to establish the presence of knowledge within a continuum that is still possessed of ignorance,
because ignorance would once again overcome them;
and this is the case with these supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).
The first, the third, and the sixth are the miracles (*prātihārya*).

The supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of psychic power (*ṛddhi*), knowledge of others' minds (*cetaḥparyāya*), and the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) are the three miracles, which correspond respectively to the miracle of psychic power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*), the miracle of instruction (*ādeśanāprātihārya*), and the miracle of admonition (*anuśāsanaprātihārya*).
They are called "miracles" because they captivate the minds of those to be trained from the very beginning; for the prefixes *prāti-* and *ati-* signify "beginning" and "intensity," respectively.
Alternatively, they are called "prātihāryas" because they win over the minds of those who are hostile or indifferent;
furthermore,
these constitute the teaching.
The miracle of instruction is supreme because it is infallible and because it connects [beings] with beneficial and desired fruits. //47//

For both miraculous power (*ṛddhi*) and the instruction of others (*ādeśana*) can also be performed by means of spells (*vidyā*); for there exists a spell called *Gāndhārī* by which one travels through the sky, and a spell called *Īkṣaṇikā* by which one knows the minds of others.
However, it is not possible to provide instruction according to reality in any other way, because [the Buddha's teaching] is infallible.

The primary function of these two is merely to attract others; however, through the miracle of instruction (*anuśāsanapratihārya*), there occurs a connection with what is beneficial and the desired fruit by means of teaching the methods [for attaining it]. This very [miracle] is called the supreme supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). What is this supernormal power?
According to the system of the Vaibhāṣikas:
Supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) is meditative concentration (*samādhi*); it should be understood as such because one succeeds by means of it. What is it that succeeds through that?
Going and emanation;
thus, there is a threefold movement therein.
Therein, movement (gati) is of three kinds: that which carries the body, that which consists of resolve, and that which is swift as thought.

Among these, the movement "swift as thought" belongs only to the Teacher; it is called "swift as thought" because its speed is like that of the mind, and it belongs to the Buddha alone, not to anyone else.
Because one reaches even a very distant land at the very moment of generating the thought [of going],
for this reason the Blessed One said, "The sphere of the Buddhas is inconceivable.
As for the other two modes of movement, they are established for the Buddha even without being explicitly stated.
For others, even the vehicle is that which consists of resolute conviction. //48//
The movement of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is both that which carries the body and that which is like a bird; it is "body-carrying" because the body is transported step by step,
and it is "resolute" because they travel swiftly by resolving upon what is distant as being near.
Furthermore, emanation is of two kinds:
that belonging to the desire realm and that belonging to the form realm.
Regarding these, first:

The external emanation belonging to the desire realm consists of four sense bases; this emanation of the desire realm has the nature of the sense bases of visible form, taste, odor, and tangible objects.
Furthermore, it is of two kinds.
It is connected with one's own body or the bodies of others.
However, that which pertains to the realm of form consists of two [bases]:
the form and tangible-object bases, as these constitute the two types of emanation belonging to the form realm.
In that case, because of the absence of odor and taste, that [transformation] is likewise twofold.
Thus, these four types of transformation exist in the desire realm, and likewise eight types in the form realm; such, in brief, is transformation.
How is it that one born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) does not possess fragrance and taste when manifesting an emanation belonging to the desire realm?
It is not a possession [in the sense of being internal], just as one possesses clothing or ornaments.
Others say that he manifests two bases (āyatana).
Is it then the case that a transformation is created by means of supernormal power alone?
No, it is said. What then?
Together with the fruits of the superknowledges and the minds of emanation, these [minds] are fourteen. //46//

Furthermore, those fourteen transformation-minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) are, in order, the fruits of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*): two up to five are the fruit of the first absorption; these two transformation-minds belong to the levels of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first absorption.
The fruit of the second dhyāna consists of three [types of emanation-mind], belonging to the levels of the desire realm, the first dhyāna, and the second dhyāna.
In the same way, four and five [types] belonging to the levels of the third and fourth dhyānas should be applied respectively.
It should be understood that the emanation-mind which is the fruit of a dhyāna belongs to its own level or to a lower level.
The transformation-mind belonging to a higher stage has as its fruit a [transformation] belonging to a lower dhyāna.
The transformation belonging to the desire realm, which is the fruit of the second dhyāna and above, is superior in terms of its range compared to that belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna.
The acquisition of those emanation-minds is like that of the meditative absorptions; their acquisition is indeed like that of the meditative absorptions.
But does emergence [from the absorption] occur directly from the emanation-mind itself?

This is not so, because [the transformation mind] arises: the transformation mind arises immediately after a pure dhyāna that is itself pure, or from a transformation mind, and not from anything else.
From that too, they [arise]. //50//
From a mind of emanation (*nirmāṇacitta*), both a pure meditative absorption (*śuddhakadhyāna*) and a mind of emanation arise, but nothing else.
For one who abides in the fruit of meditative concentration, there is no emergence from that [fruit] without first re-entering meditative concentration.
And this applies to every emanation.
Emanation is produced by a mind of its own level; an emanation of another level is not produced by an emanation-mind of a different level.
However, speech [is produced] by a mind of a lower level as well.
The word "and" (ca) implies "and by that which belongs to its own level.

For an emanation belonging to the level of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the first dhyāna speaks by means of a mind belonging solely to its own level; however, one belonging to a higher level speaks by means of a mind belonging to the level of the first dhyāna.
Because, above that level, there is an absence of that which originates informative action.
Regarding the speech of many emanations:
for the Teacher, the Buddha, the emanation speaks together with the emanator;
for anyone other than the Buddha, the emanation speaks together with the emanator.
And when many emanations have been produced, they speak simultaneously;
while one speaks, all the emanations speak,
and when one becomes silent, all become silent— thus says the verse.

The emanations created by a Buddha speak either before or after [the creator], or whenever he desires. [Objection: When there is the mind of speaking, then there is no mind of emanation; and because there is no mind of emanation, there is no emanation. How, then, do they make it speak? [Response: By means of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), another [mind] is set in motion. //51//
Having empowered a transformation-body with the desire for it to remain, they set speech in motion by means of another mind.
Does this empowerment continue only as long as one is alive, or even after death?
Empowerment exists even for one who is dead.
Because that skeleton of bones remained through the empowerment of the noble Mahākāśyapa;
however,
that does not belong to one who is unstable.
However, for an unstable state, there is no sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*),
because the noble Kāśyapa did not sustain his flesh and other [limbs]; others, however, say he did.
Others, however, say that there is no empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for one who is dead;
rather, the persistence of the skeletal frame is due to the power of deities.
Does one create a single emanation with a single mind?
At first, one [is attained] by means of many; but when it has been conquered, it is the reverse. //52//
At first, one creates a single emanation by means of many emanation-minds;
however, once supernormal power has been mastered, one creates many by means of a single mind, as many as one wishes to create.
Now, is every emanation-mind neutral (avyākṛta)?
That which is born of cultivation is indeterminate;
whatever is the fruit of cultivation is necessarily indeterminate.
However, that which is born of rebirth is of three kinds.
However, the mind of emanation acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhika*) can be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral, as in the case of gods, *nāgas*, *piśācas*, and others.

The emanation of one's own or another's body produced by that mind consists of nine bases (*navāyatana*), because it lacks the base of sound and because it is not dissociated from the sense faculties;
yet, the sense faculty itself is not emanated.
Is this [supernormal power] only of two kinds—consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī*) and acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhikā*)?
Furthermore, this supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) is fivefold when including that produced by mantras, medicinal herbs, and karma. (53)
In brief, they describe five kinds of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*):
that which is the fruit of cultivation, that acquired at birth, that produced by mantras, that produced by medicinal herbs, and that produced by ritual action.
As in the case of Māndhātṛ and those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Regarding what has been called the divine ear and the divine eye:
are these truly divine, or are they merely like the divine?
Just as, for example, the divine ear and eye belong to the Bodhisattvas, the Wheel-turning Kings, and the Householder Treasures;
because of that, they...
The two translucent forms (rūpaprasāda) belong to the stage of meditative absorption (dhyānabhūmika).

For one who has entered meditative absorption, through the application of attention toward sound and light, the two translucent forms—the eye and the ear—are produced by taking as their basis the primary elements belonging to the stage of meditative absorption; because they belong to the stage of meditative absorption, they serve as the causes for seeing forms and hearing sounds in the vicinity of the eye and the ear.
Their eye and ear faculties are indeed divine; moreover, they are homogeneous and unimpaired, and their range is eternally directed toward objects that are distant, subtle, and so forth. //54//

The divine eye and ear are not "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*), because they are always accompanied by consciousness; nor are they "defective," because there is no absence of vision (as in being one-eyed) or distortion. Like beings in the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*), distant and subtle forms and sounds are also the objects of those two.
And it is said in this regard:
"Because the fleshly eye does not see forms that are distant, obscured, or subtle, nor those [obstructed] in every way,
the divine eye is therefore desired."
Furthermore, to what distance does one see with the divine eye?
It depends on the kind of eye one possesses.
Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas, however, without any deliberate effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), see respectively a thousand, two thousand, and three thousand world-systems.
However, through volitional effort (*abhisaṃskāra*), the Arhats—the Pratyekabuddhas and the Teachers—possess vision of two, three, or incalculable thousands of worlds respectively.
Even a great Śrāvaka, by means of the utmost volitional effort, perceives a two-thousandfold world system with his divine eye;
one who is like the rhinoceros horn perceives a three-thousandfold world system.
The Blessed Buddha, however, sees incalculable world-systems for as far as he wishes. Is it only supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) that is acquired at birth, or is there something else as well?
There is indeed something else acquired at birth.
There is also a fourfold set beginning with the divine ear that is acquired through birth;
however, nothing acquired at birth receives the designation of "superknowledge" (abhijñā).
As for the divine eye that is acquired through birth, it—
That which is visible to him does not exist internally. // 55 //
For the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is seen only by the eye of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñācakṣus*), not by that acquired at birth; however,
the knowledge of others' minds (*cetojñāna*) therein is of three kinds.
The term "obtained by birth" (upapattyāpta) continues to apply here.
However, the knowledge of others' minds obtained by birth should be understood as being of three kinds: wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral;
as well as that which is produced through reasoning and spells.
Furthermore, that knowledge of others' minds which belongs to diviners based on reasoning, as well as that produced by spells (*vidyā*), should also be understood as being of three kinds;
it is not exclusively wholesome like the fruit of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāphala*).
However, [it differs] from the two—knowledge of others' minds and recollection of past lives—which are acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhika*).
The denizens of hell know [this] at first,
as long as they have not yet been overwhelmed by the sensation of suffering;
those dwelling in other realms of existence know it constantly.
For humans, it is not acquired through birth. //56//

Among humans, these aforementioned qualities such as supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and so forth do not exist as innate (*upapatti-pratilambhika*). As for those who naturally remember their past lives (*jātismara*), that is produced by a specific type of karma (*karma-viśeṣaja*).
For the recollection of former abodes is threefold: that which is the fruit of cultivation, that which is obtained through birth, and that which is born of karma.
In the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, the seventh treasury-location, titled "Exposition of Knowledge" (Jñānanirdeśa).
Whatever merit is herein belongs to the Elder Śrīlāta. Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!
Under the heading of "Knowledge," the description of qualities consisting of knowledge has been completed.

However, since the description of those qualities of a different nature remains to be done, the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are commenced from the very beginning, as they are the basis for all qualities.
The meditative absorptions are of two kinds.
In brief, meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are of two kinds, distinguished as those of rebirth and those of meditative attainment; these, moreover, are fourfold.
From the first dhyāna up to the fourth;
furthermore, the rebirths within those dhyānas need not be explained here,
as they have already been treated in the section of the *Abhidharmakośa* that explains the world (*lokadhātu*).
Their proofs have been stated.
How have they been stated?
"Individually."
"In that context, dhyāna consists of three stages, whereas the fourth consists of eight stages.
Now, the dhyāna of meditative attainment (samāpatti-dhyāna) must be explained;
therefore, it is said:
Attainment (*samāpatti*) is pure one-pointedness; specifically, it is the one-pointedness of a wholesome mind, which is meditative absorption (*dhyāna*),
because its intrinsic nature is concentration (*samādhi*).
But the five aggregates, together with their attendants, [constitute the person]. // 1 //
But together with its retinue, it should be understood as having the nature of the five aggregates.
What is this so-called one-pointedness?
It is the state of having a single object.

If that were the case, it would follow that concentration (*samādhi*) is merely minds having a single object, and not a distinct mental factor (*caitasika dharma*). However, concentration is not merely the minds themselves.
That factor by which those [mental states] proceed with one-pointedness is concentration (*samādhi*);
it is indeed this very one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
If it is argued that because of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), every state of mind is already one-pointed, since there is no second [moment] from which it could be distracted; [we reply:]...
If it were associated [with concentration], concentration would be redundant.
Furthermore, why is it not accepted that the state of having a single object for thoughts arises from the very same cause as concentration?
Moreover, since concentration is a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*), it would follow that all thoughts possess one-pointedness.
It is not because concentration (*samādhi*) is weak;
rather, it is the very states of mind that are one-pointed which constitute concentration.

For others hold that this is so because the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*), which has the purification of the mind as its primary aim, is described in the Sūtra as the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
What is the meaning of "dhyāna"? It means that by means of this, they meditate; that is to say, they understand.
Because one who possesses a concentrated mind perceives reality as it truly is;
for this root (dhātu) has the sense of "thinking," and it is an established tenet that thinking is wisdom (prajñā).
If that were so, it would follow that all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) and dhyānas [would be called "dhyāna"]. No;
for that name is applied only to that which possesses excellence (*prakarṣa*), just as the term "sun" (*bhāskara*) is used.
And what is it that possesses excellence?

That concentration which is endowed with the [necessary] factors is indeed called a "dwelling in happiness in the present life" because it proceeds by the yoking together of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), and it is called an "easy path. Therefore,
one meditates most effectively by means of it.
How can that which is afflicted be considered meditative absorption?
Because it is a false contemplation.
[If so,] there would be an over-extension of the definition.
No, for that designation is applied only to what resembles it, just as one speaks of "rotten seeds";
moreover, the Blessed One has also spoken of unwholesome meditations (*akuśala-dhyāna*).
Furthermore, what kind of wholesome one-pointedness constitutes the first dhyāna, and what kind up to the fourth?
First of all, the first [dhyāna] possesses investigation (vicāra), joy (prīti), and bliss (sukha).
The first dhyāna is wholesome one-pointedness of mind associated with investigation, joy, and bliss;
by the mention of "investigation," "applied thought" (vitarka) is also implied due to their constant association, like smoke and fire.
For there is no vicāra accompanied by joy and bliss that exists without vitarka;
furthermore, the remaining three dhyānas are each devoid of the factors of their respective predecessors.
The term "pure one-pointedness" carries over [from the previous definition].

The second [dhyāna] is devoid of investigation (vicāra) and possesses joy (prīti) and bliss (sukha); the third is devoid of investigation and joy; and the fourth is devoid of investigation, joy, and bliss—just as with the dhyānas.
Likewise for the formless realms (ārūpyas); in what manner?
For these also are twofold, by way of rebirth and meditative attainment (samāpatti), and there are four [realms]; and the rebirths of these have also been explained.

However, the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), by way of their non-differentiation, have the nature of wholesome one-pointedness; thus, together with their attendants, they consist of four aggregates (*catuḥskandha*), because of the absence of any concomitant form (*anuparivarti-rūpa*).
They are born from seclusion from the lower stages. //2//
For the sphere of infinite space arises from seclusion from the fourth dhyāna;
the sphere of infinite consciousness arises from seclusion from that;
and the sphere of nothingness arises from seclusion from that.
That which is born of seclusion is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; thus there are four formless attainments.
What is this so-called "seclusion"?
It is that path by which one becomes secluded from what is below.
Because they have reached detachment,
these very formless attainments (ārūpyas), together with the three preparatory stages (sāmantakas), are designated as "those in which the perception of form has been overcome."

The preparatory stage (sāmantaka) of the sphere of infinite space does not receive the designation "the state where perception of matter has been mastered" because it takes the fourth dhyāna as its object;
for in that stage, the perception of matter has not been mastered, meaning it has not departed.

Regarding what was stated, that "there are four aggregates," it must first be established that there is no form (*rūpa*) in the formless realms (*ārūpya*). For if there were form, how could they be called "formless"?
They would be so called only because of having a slight amount of form, like the word *āpiṅgala* ("slightly reddish").
What kind of subtle form (*īṣadrūpa*) is intended there?
If it is merely the restraint of body and speech, how can those two restraints exist in the absence of that [subtle form]?
Furthermore, it is not logical for a derivative material phenomenon (*bhautika*) to exist when its primary material cause (*bhūta*) is absent.
If it is argued that it is like the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*), [we reply] no, because the tainted primary elements (*sāsrava-bhūta*) still exist;
furthermore, its negation has already been stated even in the case of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
Now, if the body exists and the sense faculties are also material,
how can they be considered to have "slight form"?
If it is argued that this is because of their small size, [then...]
The same consequence would apply even to aquatic organisms whose forms are invisible.

If you argue that this is because [the latter] are transparent, then the same consequence would apply to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and to those belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*).
If there were nothing more transparent than that, then the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) alone would be the formless realm (ārūpya),
because its specific state of rebirth is like that of meditative attainment (samāpatti).

Furthermore, since the sense faculties of a lower level do not perceive even the form belonging to the rebirth-state of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), what distinction is there [between that form and the formless]?
If it is argued that the designation for both [the formless attainments and the formless realm] is literal, whereas that of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is not,
what is the reasoning for this?

If it is argued that the existence of form (*rūpa*) in the formless realms (*ārūpya*) is established because of the statement that vitality and heat are conjoined, because of the statement that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are mutually dependent like two bundles of reeds, because of the statement "name-and-form have consciousness as their condition," and because of the prohibition of the coming and going of consciousness apart from form up to the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
No;

for this must first be carefully considered: as for what was stated regarding the conjunction of vitality and heat, was this said with reference to vitality belonging to the desire realm, or rather to all [vitality]?

Regarding that which was stated concerning the mutual dependence of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), was this said with reference only to those belonging to the realms of desire and form, or rather to all of them?

And regarding that which was stated that name-and-form has consciousness as its condition (*vijñānapratyaya*), was it here stated that all consciousness is the condition for name-and-form, or that all name-and-form has consciousness as its condition?
Furthermore, regarding the denial elsewhere of the coming [of consciousness] from form and so forth—
Is the negation of that [object] here intended by all of those [reasons] together, or even by just one?
If it is argued that no deliberation is required because the statement is made without qualification,
there would be an over-extension of the principle (atiprasaṅga).
For even external heat would not exist without life-force (*āyus*);
and because it is stated without distinction, even external matter (*rūpa*) would be dependent upon consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Furthermore, just as there are the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), and because of the mention of the fourfold food (*āhāra*), it would follow that even in the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpārūpyadhātu*), edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) would exist.

If it is argued that there is no such contingency [of matter] because of the statement, "having transcended the gods who subsist on edible food (kavaḍīkārāhāra)," and because of the mention of the food of joy (prītyāhāra),
then there would likewise be no contingency of matter in the formless realms (ārūpya), since it is said,
"the formless realms are the escape from forms."
"These peaceful liberations, which transcend forms and are formless," and because of the statement: "There are beings who are formless, through the complete transcending of perceptions of form.
For if form were present, they would necessarily perceive their own form.
If it is argued that this was said with reference to coarse form belonging to the lower stages,
then the same would apply to edible food (*kavaḍīkāra*).
Furthermore, since the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) also constitute an escape from the lower stages, it would follow that they too are formless (*ārūpya*).
And why are the transcendences of feeling and so forth not mentioned?
Because [the formless attainments] transcend the feelings and so forth of the lower stages,
whereas they have transcended the entire category of form, but not the category of feeling and so forth.
Therefore, it is said that there is an escape from material forms (*rūpa*).
However, the statement that existence (*bhava*) does not escape from existence is because existence cannot escape from itself, and because it is neither the entirety nor the ultimate escape.

Furthermore, regarding the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the Blessed One said: "Whatever exists therein, whether belonging to the category of form (*rūpagata*) or up to the category of consciousness (*vijñānagata*)."
Regarding the formless realms (ārūpya), however, it is said: "Whatever is there, whether belonging to feeling (vedanā) up to belonging to consciousness (vijñāna).
If there were any kind of matter (rūpa) existing in them, why would he not have said "or belonging to matter"?
Therefore...
There is no existence of form in the formless realm.
How, then, does form arise again for those who have passed away from there, after form has been severed for many eons?
Form arises, however, from the mind. (3)
The arising of form occurs solely from the mind, which has acquired its activity through being permeated by the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) of that [form].
How can the mind function without depending on form?
Why should it not so function?
Because it is not observed to be so here;
for even without solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), one would not be able to subsist in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
What is the reason?
Because they are not observed in this way here;
and it has already been stated previously how they proceed.

This point has been settled, and now this must be addressed: Is it because space and so forth are themselves the objects of focus for these [attainments] such as the Sphere of Infinite Space that they are designated in this manner?
No, indeed not.
How then?
First, there are three.
Those termed "infinite space," "infinite consciousness," and "nothingness" are applied to them respectively,
as one applies oneself by attending to them in this way: "space is infinite," "consciousness is infinite," and "there is nothing at all."
Therefore, these are their designations;
however, because of its dullness, it is neither with perception nor without perception. (4)
However, because perception (*saṃjñā*) is so subtle there, it is called the "sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
For that perception is not sharp, yet it is not the case that there is no perception at all.

Even though they apply themselves there with the thought: "Perception is a disease, perception is a boil, perception is a thorn; non-perception is delusion; this is peaceful, this is sublime—namely, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," [it is still so called].
But why is that very [state] grasped by them in such a way? This must necessarily be explained:
it is because of its subtlety that it is called "perception" (*saṃjñā*); this is precisely what has been stated.
Thus, the fundamental substance of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-dravya*) is of eight kinds.
Thus, these are the eight fundamental substances of attainment, namely: the four meditative absorptions (dhyānas) and the four formless attainments (ārūpyas).
Furthermore, they are of three kinds.
The seven [stages] other than the Peak of Existence are of three kinds:
associated with relishing, pure, and untainted.
They are associated with relishing, pure, and untainted; the eighth is of two kinds. //5//
The Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is associated with both relishing (āsvādana) and the pure (śuddhaka);
it is not untainted (anāsrava).
Furthermore, therein:
That which is associated with relishing is accompanied by craving,
for craving is indeed relishing;
it is mundane wholesomeness.
The pure mundane wholesome substance of meditative attainment is called "pure" (śuddhaka) because it is associated with pure factors such as non-greed.
But what is tasted by that [attainment] which is not associated with tasting?
That which is to be tasted is that pure substance of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-dravya*); it is tasted immediately after it has passed away.
When one tastes it, one has emerged from that [attainment]; by means of that [tasting], one has entered into that [attainment].
It is supramundane and free from outflows. //6//
That substance of meditative attainment which is supramundane is untainted (*anāsrava*).
And among these substances of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), only the dhyānas possess factors (*aṅga*); the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) do not.
Among those, there are five in the first [dhyāna].
In the first dhyāna, there are five factors: applied thought (vitarka), sustained thought (vicāra), joy (prīti), bliss (sukha), and concentration (samādhi).
These five factors—namely, vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgratā)—constitute the limbs; indeed, concentration is both a limb and the dhyāna itself.

"The remaining factors" means that just as there is an army with four components, so too is dhyāna fivefold. Joy and the others, along with serenity (*prasāda*), constitute the four factors in the second [dhyāna]. (7)
In the second dhyāna there are four factors:
internal serenity, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.
In the third, however, there are five: equanimity, mindfulness, discernment, bliss, and stability.
In the third dhyāna, however, there are five factors:
equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, bliss, and samādhi;
for "stability" (sthiti) is a synonym for samādhi.
"What is right concentration?
It is the stability of the mind," according to the statement in the Sūtra.
At the end [of the path], there are four: equanimity, mindfulness, and concentration, which are neither painful nor pleasant. (8)
The fourth dhyāna is the last.
It has four factors:
neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation, purity of equanimity, purity of mindfulness, and concentration.
These constitute the eighteen factors of meditative absorption (dhyānāṅga),
because the first and third [dhyānas] possess five factors each,
while the second and fourth possess four factors each.
Thus they are so by name; substantially, there are ten and one,
for substantially these become eleven.
There are five factors belonging to the first dhyāna;
in the second, internal clarity increases;
in the third, equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and bliss [increase].
"In the fourth [dhyāna], there is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
For this very reason it is said: "Those factors which are in the first dhyāna are also in the second"—this constitutes a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika).
The first alternative consists of applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra).
The second [limb] is internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*);
the third is joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*);
the fourth category consists of those factors (*dharmāḥ*) excluded from what has been mentioned.
In this way, all the factors of meditative absorption (dhyānāṅga) are to be applied to one another.
Why is it that in the third dhyāna, pleasure (sukha) is said to be a distinct entity (dravyāntara)?
Because that feeling is pleasure; however, in the first two dhyānas, there is the pleasure of pliancy.
It is said that in the first and second dhyānas, there is the pleasure of pliancy.

Why is it that here there is the pleasure of pliancy (*prasrabdhi-sukha*), while there [in the higher stages] there is the pleasure of feeling (*vedanā-sukha*)? Because the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is not applicable to the two meditative attainments (*dhyāna-samāpatti*). For it is not logical that such [pleasure] in those two states should be physical (*kāyika*).
Because for one who has attained [meditative absorption], the groups of consciousness do not exist;
nor is it mental, because of the mention of "joy" (prīti),
for joy is indeed mental well-being (saumanasya).

Furthermore, there is no simultaneity of pleasure (*sukha*) and mental joy (*saumanasya*), nor is it logical for the two to function alternately within a single dhyāna, because of the statement that [the first dhyāna] possesses five factors (*pañcāṅga*). Others, however, say:
"There is no mental faculty of pleasure at all in any of the three dhyānas."
[The Vaibhāṣika replies: "Only bodily pleasure (*kāyika-sukha*) is established as a [distinct] factor.

[The opponent objects: "If that is so, then what about that which is stated in the Sūtra: 'What is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)? It is that which arises in one touched by a contact to be experienced as pleasant—whether it be bodily or mental, agreeable, felt, and belonging to the category of sensation; this is called the faculty of pleasure'?"
This reading is interpolated;
for in all other schools (nikāya), the reading is simply "bodily" (*kāyika*), and because it is stated in its own words: "and he experiences pleasure with the body."
If it is argued that [it is] "with the mental body" (*manaskāyena*),
what benefit is there in saying this?
For even though pliancy (*prasrabdhi*) is more abundant in the fourth dhyāna, pleasure (*sukha*) is not mentioned there.
If it is argued that pliancy (prasrabdhi) conducive to pleasant feeling is what constitutes pleasure,
then why is pliancy not called "pleasure" in the third dhyāna?
If it is argued that this is because it is impaired by equanimity (upekṣā), [the response follows].

No; for its increase occurs through equanimity (*upekṣā*) alone, since it is distinct from the two preceding [factors]. In the Sūtra which states, "At whatever time the noble disciple, having realized with his own body the joy born of seclusion, dwells having attained it," pliancy (*prasrabdhi*) and bliss (*sukha*) are mentioned separately; therefore, it is not pliancy itself [that is meant by "bliss"].
[It is] pleasure.
[If it is asked: "How can there be body-consciousness for one who has attained meditative absorption?
[The answer is: because of the pervasion of the body by a wind produced by a specific concentration, which is designated as pliancy (*prasrabdhi*) and is to be experienced as pleasure.
If it is argued that there is a loss of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) due to external distraction,
we say no;
for the physical pleasure (*kāyasukha*) born of concentration and produced within the body is conducive to concentration.
If it is argued that [the practitioner] would have emerged from meditative absorption at the time of body-consciousness, we say no;
for this very reason.
If it is further argued that body-consciousness of the form realm cannot arise by means of a body-faculty belonging to the desire realm, we say no.
Because of the arising of the consciousness of pliancy.
(If it is argued that even the tangible object and body-consciousness could be untainted, lest some members [of the path] be tainted while others are untainted:)
Because of the mention of the factor of enlightenment that is physical pliancy (*kāyikaprasrabdhi-bodhyaṅga*).
If it is argued that [the factors] are desirable because they are conducive to the limbs of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), then the same would apply to their being untainted (*anāsrava*).
[The Sūtra asks: “Which are the tainted phenomena (*sāsravā dharmāḥ*)? Namely, all...”

If it is argued that this contradicts the Sūtra which states, "from the eye up to the tangible," we say no; for that statement was made with the intention of referring to other tangibles and body-consciousness.
Furthermore, if it is argued that within the untainted (anāsrava), one part could not be tainted (sāsrava) while another part is untainted, [we reply: no.

If it is asked, "What is the fault if they are not simultaneous? [the answer is: "Because pleasure (*sukha*) and joy (*prīti*) cannot coexist, the [first dhyāna] would not have five factors. [To this we reply:

No, because the teaching is given with respect to their possible occurrence, as in the case of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). [If it is argued that this point remains] to be proven:
This is established because of the contradiction between the grossness and subtlety of the mind, and because no fault has been stated [in this regard].
Therefore, the establishment of the second and subsequent dhyānas occurs through the removal of two, three, or four of those very five factors that exist in the first dhyāna.
For this very reason, it is said that there are five factors in the first dhyāna,
because the higher dhyānas are established by the removal of those [factors].
But it has not been stated that perception (*saṃjñā*) and the others are factors (*aṅga*).
For what reason, then, was the status of being a factor stated for only these five? (If it is argued: "Because they are beneficial," [then we reply:])
No;
because mindfulness and wisdom are more beneficial than applied thought and sustained thought.
This is the doctrine of some.
However, the former teachers did not define it in exactly the same way as it has been set forth here;
therefore, this matter requires further investigation.

What is this dharma called internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*)? Internal clarity is the tranquil flow of the mental continuum due to its freedom from the agitation of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
For the continuum, when agitated by applied and sustained thought, proceeds without clarity, like a river with waves.
In that case, it is not a separate substance; how then can there be eleven factors in terms of substance?
Therefore, faith is clarity (*prasāda*).
For upon attaining the second dhyāna, a conviction arises regarding the departure from the levels of meditative concentration;
this is what is called "inner serenity" (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).

Others, however, maintain that neither the applied thought (*vitarka*), the sustained thought (*vicāra*), nor the concentration (*samādhi*), nor even inner serenity, are distinct substantial entities.
How can it be established that [this] is a mental factor (*caitasika*) if it is not a distinct substance?
For even a particular state (*avasthāviśeṣa*) of the mind is indeed called a mental factor;
however, this is not the established tenet (*siddhānta*) of the treatise.
[As it was said, "For joy (prīti) is mental ease (saumanasya)," how is this understood?
What else could it be?
As other schools maintain, joy (*prīti*) is indeed a distinct mental factor (*caitasika*), whereas mental ease (*saumanasya*) is the pleasure (*sukha*) in all three meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
It is certainly not physical pleasure (*sukha*).
Mental ease (saumanasya) is appropriate in the [first three] dhyānas;
however, joy (prīti) is mental ease, according to two scriptural sources. //6//

For it was said by the Blessed One in the *Aviparītaka-sūtra*, after describing the third dhyāna: "Here, the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*) that has arisen in him ceases without remainder.

And regarding the fourth dhyāna, it is said: "The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) ceases. Furthermore, it is said: "With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of mental pleasure and mental pain (*daurmanasya*)," etc.; for this reason as well, the faculty of mental pleasure does not exist in the third dhyāna.

Therefore, joy (*prīti*) alone is mental ease (*saumanasya*), not pleasure (*sukha*). Furthermore, do the factors (*aṅga*) exist in the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) exactly as they have been prescribed? No, indeed. What is it that does not exist in those defiled states? In the defiled states, there is no joy, pleasure, clarity (*prasāda*), discernment (*saṃpradhī*), or mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Furthermore, in the first dhyāna, there is no joy and bliss born of seclusion, because it is not yet secluded from the afflictions; rather, there is purity of equanimity and mindfulness.
In the second dhyāna, internal clarity (adhyātmasaṃprasāda) is absent because of the turbidity of the afflictions;
in the third, mindfulness and clear comprehension (smṛtisaṃprajanya) are absent.
Because one is distracted by afflicted pleasure;
in the fourth [dhyāna], there is no purity of equanimity and mindfulness because of the defilement of the afflictions.
Thus, first, some say this; others [say it consists of] pliancy and equanimity. (10)
Others, however, maintain: "In the first and second [dhyānas], when they are afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), there is no pliancy (*prasrabdhi*);
in the third and fourth, there is no equanimity (*upekṣā*), because these two belong to the great ground of the wholesome (*kuśalamahābhūmika*)."
And the Blessed One has stated that the first three meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are subject to movement because they possess defects; however,
the fourth is immovable because it is free from the eight defects.
What, then, are those imperfections? They are applied thought and sustained thought, the two breaths, and the fourfold group beginning with pleasure. //11//

Applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), mental joy (*saumanasya*), mental grief (*daurmanasya*), and inhalation and exhalation (*śvāsapraśvāsa*):
among these eight, not even a single one of these defects exists in the fourth [dhyāna]; therefore, it is called "imperturbable" (*āneñjya*).

Others say that the fourth dhyāna is imperturbable because it cannot be shaken by applied thought, sustained thought, joy, or pleasure, as illustrated in the Sūtra by the simile of a lamp in a windless place.
In the first two dhyānas, mental joy (*saumanasya*) is mentioned because of the term "rapture" (*prīti*);
in the third, there is pleasure (*sukha*); and in the fourth, equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Now, are the feelings (*vedanā*) that exist in the meditative attainments (*dhyāna-samāpatti*) the very same as those in the rebirths (*dhyāna-upapatti*)?
"No," he said. "What then?
Mental joy, pleasure, and equanimity; equanimity and mental joy; pleasure and equanimity; and equanimity alone are known to exist in the rebirths of the dhyānas. (12)
In the rebirth of the first dhyāna, there are three types of feeling:
pleasure belonging to the three groups of consciousness, mental joy belonging to the level of the mind,
and equanimity belonging to the four groups of consciousness.
In rebirth in the second dhyāna, there are two feelings: mental joy (*saumanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*), both belonging to the level of the mind (*manobhūmika*).
There is no [bodily] pleasure (*sukha*) because of the absence of the other groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*).
In rebirth in the third dhyāna, there are two feelings...
Pleasure and equanimity belong to the mental level;
however, upon rebirth in the fourth dhyāna, there is only equanimity.

[If the three groups of consciousness and applied and sustained thought do not exist in the second and subsequent dhyānas, how do they see, up to and including how they touch, and how do they originate informative action?]
It is certainly not the case that those born in [those realms] lack visual consciousness and the others;
however, they do not possess those belonging to their own level.
What then?

The visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses, as well as that which originates informative action (*vijñapti*), belonging to the first level—the first dhyāna—are brought into manifestation in the second and higher dhyānas; these belong to the first dhyāna stage.
Thus, they manifest the eye, ear, body, and consciousness, as well as the originator of informative action, within the second and subsequent dhyānas.
By means of that [mind], they see just as they do with a mind of transformation (nirmāṇacitta), up until the point that they produce informative action (vijñapti);
and that [mind] is non-defiled and neutral (akliṣṭāvyākṛta). //13//
That consciousness belonging to the level of the first dhyāna which they bring into manifestation should be understood as being unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*);
it is not afflicted because they are free from passion, nor is it wholesome because it is inferior.
The discussion on the function of dhyāna is concluded.
Now, how is the attainment of the pure (*śuddhaka*) and other meditations (*dhyāna*) and formless attainments (*ārūpya*)?
One who does not possess them acquires the pure [state] through detachment (*vairāgya*) or through rebirth (*upapatti*).
That is to say, one who is not in possession of it acquires the pure meditation or the formless attainment.
Either through detachment from a lower level,
or through rebirth in a lower level—
with the exception of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
For there is no acquisition of it through rebirth. Why say "one who does not possess it"? Because one is endowed with it.

One acquires the pure *nirvedhabhāgīya* through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), or the *hānabhāgīya* through falling away (*parihāṇi*). One may acquire a dhyāna through detachment (*vairāgya*) and abandon it through detachment.
Thus, it may be both through falling away and through rebirth.
The first dhyāna can be of the type conducive to decline;
for that is obtained through detachment from the realm of desire.
It is abandoned through detachment from the Brahma-world;
it is acquired through falling away from detachment from the Brahma-world;
it is abandoned through the loss of detachment from the realm of desire.
One who is being reborn in the Brahma-world above acquires it;
one who is being reborn again in the desire realm from there abandons it.
However, the untainted [attainment] is acquired through detachment.
The phrase "one who does not possess it obtains" carries over [from the previous context].

However, one who already possesses it obtains the state of a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) even through the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), and the state of a learner or non-learner (*śaikṣa-aśaikṣa*) even through the transformation of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*).
But is it not the case that one also obtains the untainted (*anāsrava*) state for the first time through the entry into the path of certainty (*niyāmāvakrānti*)?
It is not necessarily [attained] through the serial order, because it is not obtained [in that way];
rather, it has been explained how it is necessarily attained.
"The defiled [attainment is lost] through falling away or rebirth" (14).
The phrase "one who does not possess it obtains it" continues to apply here.
[One obtains it] through falling away, if one falls away from that state of detachment;
or through rebirth, if one is born from a higher plane into a lower one.
Immediately after which substance of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-dravya*) how many arise?
Immediately after the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna, six arise:
the pure (*śuddhaka*) and the untainted of its own level, as well as those belonging to the levels of the second and third dhyānas.

Immediately after the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), there are seven [minds] belonging to its own level— both pure (śuddhaka) and untainted (anāsrava)— and those belonging to the levels of the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana) and the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana).
As for the peak of existence (bhavāgra), it is only pure, because the untainted does not exist there.
Immediately after the second dhyāna, there are eight:
the pure (*śuddhaka*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) states belonging to its own level, as well as those belonging to the levels of the third, fourth, and first dhyānas.
Immediately after the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), there are nine.

There are two belonging to its own level, four belonging to the levels of the Sphere of Infinite Space and the Fourth Dhyāna, and three belonging to the levels of the Sphere of Nothingness and the Peak of Existence.
In this manner, ten substances are to be applied immediately after any other dhyāna or formless attainment.
This, however, is the summary.

From the third level upward and downward, immediately after an untainted (*anāsrava*) state, a wholesome (*śubha*) state arises. By the term "wholesome," both the pure (*śuddha*) and the untainted are included because they are both virtuous (*kuśala*). Immediately after an untainted meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), both pure and untainted states belonging to its own level arise;
furthermore, from the third level upward and downward, [states of those levels] also arise.
For those who achieve the leaping meditative attainments (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*) are not able to leap beyond the third [dhyāna];
furthermore, they enter the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) immediately after subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and not immediately after dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*),
because the latter has its basis and its object in the lower realms.

Just as it was stated immediately after [the discussion on] the untainted (*anāsrava*), so too should it be understood that from the pure (*śuddha*) [state], there also arises the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) of its own level (*svabhūmika*). //15//
Immediately after the pure [attainment], an additional defiled state belonging to its own level arises;
the remainder is exactly as in the case of the uncontaminated [attainment].
For indeed, there is no arising of a defiled state immediately after the uncontaminated.
From a defiled attainment-substance, its own pure and defiled states arise immediately after;
likewise, the pure state of a lower level arises.

For one oppressed by afflictions (kleśa) highly values even a pure attainment of a lower level. If, having discerned it as afflicted, one descends to a lower level, that descent is from a wholesome state, not from an afflicted one.
Now, if it is not delimited, how does one transmigrate?
Because of a prior determination. For previously he has such a desire: "Better the pure [state] below than the afflicted [state] above.
And the continuum of sentient beings follows that prior intention.
Just as one who has fallen asleep after making a vow awakens at the intended time,
the untainted [state] does not arise in any way immediately after a defiled state.
This was stated with reference to the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*):
immediately after a pure or afflicted [state], only an afflicted state belonging to its own level arises, not one belonging to another level;
however, at the time of death (*cyuti*), an afflicted state of any level may arise from a pure state.

At the time of death, however, immediately after the pure state acquired at birth, a defiled state belonging to any level arises; but from a defiled state, a higher [pure] state does not arise. //16//
However, immediately after a defiled dhyāna or formless attainment—at the time of death—a defiled state belonging to its own level or a lower level arises; one belonging to a higher level does not.
Furthermore, the undefiled substance of meditative attainment does not arise from every kind of pure [attainment].
What then?
The pure [attainment] is of four types, beginning with that which partakes of decline (hānabhāgīya).
The pure [attainment] is of four kinds: conducive to decline, conducive to distinction, conducive to stability, and conducive to penetration.
However, that of the peak of existence is of three kinds, excluding the one conducive to distinction.
What is its characteristic?
For it is, respectively, conducive to the arising of afflictions, to its own level, to higher levels, and to the outflow-free state. //17//

That which is conducive to the arising of afflictions is *hānabhāgīya* (partaking of decline); that which is conducive to its own level is *sthitibhāgīya* (partaking of stability); that which is conducive to a higher level is *viśeṣabhāgīya* (partaking of distinction); and that which is conducive to the untainted (*anāsrava*) is *nirvedhabhāgīya* (partaking of penetration).
From that [the latter], the untainted arises.
Now, among these four, how many arise immediately after which?
Two, three, three, and one arise immediately after the [states] beginning with the part conducive to decline (*hānabhāgīya*).
The "part conducive to decline" is that which partakes in decline;
immediately after it, two arise.
Regarding the [states] conducive to decline and conducive to stability:
immediately after those conducive to stability, three arise, excluding those conducive to penetration.
Immediately after those conducive to distinction, three arise, excluding those conducive to decline. Immediately after those conducive to penetration, only that one [state] arises.
How does the leaping meditative attainment (vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti) arise?
Having gone to and returned from the eight stages in two ways—either in immediate succession or by skipping one—[it arises]. //18//
The leaping meditative attainment (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*) proceeds to the third level of a different class.
"Having gone" means having attained [the levels] in direct order;
"having come" means having attained them in reverse order.
