"Of two kinds" refers to the levels (bhūmi) being both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava).
"Eight" refers to the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti).
"Contiguous" means following one another in succession.
"Leaping over one by one" means skipping each one individually.
Having mastered the eight contaminated (*sāsrava*) stages through meditative attainments in both forward and reverse order, as well as the seven uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) stages,
he subsequently enters from the first contaminated dhyāna into the third contaminated dhyāna.
From that, one enters the sphere of infinite space; from that, the sphere of nothingness.
Having thus mastered them again in reverse order, one also enters the untainted states by skipping one, proceeding both in direct and reverse order.
This is the preliminary practice for the leaping meditative attainment (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*).
But when one enters from the first impure dhyāna into the third pure dhyāna, from that into the impure sphere of infinite space, and from that into the pure sphere of nothingness—
and likewise again in reverse order— then,
by proceeding to a third substance of a different class, it becomes fully accomplished.
Because it is too remote, the fourth [dhyāna] is not attained there;
moreover, only an Arhat who is liberated at all times (asamayavimukta) produces it in the three continents,
due to being free from afflictions and possessing mastery over meditative concentration.
Although one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) possesses mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*) due to having sharp faculties, he is not free from defilements (*niṣkleśa*).
Although one liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) is free from defilements, he does not possess mastery over meditative concentration.
Based on what support (*āśraya*) are how many dhyānas and formless attainments (*ārūpya*) manifested?
The meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and formless attainments (ārūpya) have as their basis only their own level and the levels below;
the peak of existence (bhavāgra) is manifested both at the peak of existence itself and below, down to the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
The remaining [attainments] belong to their own level and those below it. What is the reason? One who has been reborn in a higher realm does not bring a lower attainment into manifestation;
therefore, for him...
The lower lip is useless. //16//
For no purpose is served by an attainment-substance (samāpatti-dravya) that is inferior to it,
because of its lowliness.
Having stated the general rule (utsarga), he now states the exception (apavāda).
The destruction of the outflows occurs at the peak of existence through the manifestation of the noble state of nothingness.
For one born at the peak of existence, the destruction of the outflows occurs due to the manifestation of the untainted sphere of nothingness.
How does that manifestation occur for one born there?
Because of the absence of [objects] for oneself and because of the cultivation of that [object]. Now, what is the object of these meditations (dhyāna) and formless attainments (ārūpya)?
Those associated with craving have their own existence as their object;
those associated with relishing take the existence belonging to their own level as their object.
By the term "existence" (bhava), contaminated things (sāsrava-vastu) are grasped.

They do not take lower [levels] as objects because they are free from passion (vītarāga); nor do they take higher [levels] as objects because the stages (bhūmi) are delimited by craving (tṛṣṇā); nor do they take uncontaminated (anāsrava) things as objects because that would entail [them being] wholesome (kuśala).
Meditative absorption has a real object and is virtuous. //20//
Wholesome meditative absorption is both pure (*śubha*) and untainted (*anāsrava*).
It has everything as its object—whatever exists, whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
However, the fundamental wholesome formless absorptions do not have the tainted lower realms as their sphere of activity.

For the fundamental wholesome formless attainments (*ārūpya*), a contaminated (*sāsrava*) entity belonging to a lower level is not an object, because they take as their objects only those belonging to their own or higher levels.
However, an uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) entity is an object;
specifically, it consists of all categories of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), but not the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), nor the cessation (*nirodha*) of a lower level.
However, for the preparatory (sāmantaka) and uninterrupted (ānantarya) paths, the lower stage is the object of focus.
Furthermore, among these three types of meditative absorptions and formless attainments, the afflictions are abandoned by means of the untainted (*anāsrava*),
not by the pure (*śuddhaka*).
How much less so by a defiled [mind]?
Because he is free from passion, it does not arise from a lower level;
because that very [defiled mind] is not its antidote, it does not arise on its own level.
Because it is more distinguished, there is no [attainment] above;
and also not by means of the preparatory stages (sāmantaka). //21//
Furthermore, the afflictions are abandoned by means of the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) of the dhyānas and the formless attainments (ārūpya), even by those that are pure (śuddhaka),
because these serve as the antidotes (pratipakṣa) to the lower levels.
Furthermore, how many preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) are there? There are eight preparatory stages, one for each [dhyāna], by means of which one enters them.
Are those [dhyānas] also of three kinds, and is feeling in them exactly the same?
No, it is said:

they are pure and characterized by neither-pain-nor-pleasure. They are "pure" (śuddhaka), associated with the faculty of equanimity, because they must be produced through effort, because the agitation of the lower stages has not yet departed, and because they constitute the path to detachment; thus, they are not associated with relish (āsvādana).

The first noble [attainment] and the first preparatory stage (sāmantaka), namely the "not-yet-arrived" (anāgamya), are both pure (śuddhaka) and untainted (anāsrava). Although the connection of rebirth (pratisaṃdhibandha) by means of a preparatory mind is defiled (kliṣṭa),
defilement is excluded for one who is in a state of meditative concentration (samāhita).
Some say it is threefold;
others, however, maintain that the *anāgamya*— which is associated with tasting (*āsvādana*)— is also called a "preparatory stage" (*sāmantaka*) as well as the "intermediate dhyāna" (*dhyānāntara*).
Is this [term] "dhyāna" synonymous or does it have different meanings?
For the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) is the path of detachment, while the intermediate dhyāna (*antara-dhyāna*) is without vitarka. (22)
Indeed, the first dhyāna itself, when dissociated from *vitarka*, is the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), because it is a specific variety of dhyāna.
For this very reason, it is not established as such in the second and subsequent dhyānas, due to the absence of such a distinction.
Furthermore, that intermediate dhyāna—
It is threefold: associated with tasting, pure, and untainted.
It is neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
since there is neither pleasure nor pain therein, it is "neither-painful-nor-pleasant," meaning it is associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
It is not associated with joy (*prīti*), because it proceeds with effortful application (*sābhisaṃskāra-vāhitva*).
For this very reason, it is a difficult path of practice.
What, then, is the specific distinction of the fruit of that intermediate dhyāna?
For it—
And that is the fruit of the Great Brahma.
For by cultivating that intermediate dhyāna, one becomes a Great Brahma.
Furthermore, having summarized all meditative absorptions, three types of samādhi are taught in the Sūtra.
There is concentration with applied thought and sustained thought;

concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only; and concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought. Among these, it is indicated that the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) is concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only.
Because only applied thought (*vitarka*) is negated,
the lower meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is therefore accompanied by both applied thought and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
Therefore, the concentration below that intermediate dhyāna is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra;
this includes the first dhyāna and the anāgamya stage.
Beyond that, it is without both. //23//

Because there is no duality here, it is "non-dual" (*advaya*). However, according to others, from the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) onwards, concentration is without applied thought (*avitarka*) and without sustained thought (*avicāra*), extending from the preparatory stage of the second dhyāna up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Furthermore, three concentrations have been taught: the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), the wishless (*apraṇihita*), and the signless (*ānimitta*).
Among these:
The signless concentration (*ānimitta-samādhi*), associated with the aspects of tranquility and the aspects of the truth of cessation, possesses four aspects.
For nirvāṇa is "signless" (*animitta*) because it is free from the ten signs.
The concentration that has that as its object is the signless (*animitta*).
There are ten signs: the five sense objects, woman, man, and the three characteristics of the conditioned;
[the signless is] through emptiness and selflessness.
The concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), associated with the two aspects of selflessness and emptiness, possesses two aspects.
The wishless (*apraṇihita*) [concentration] consists of the remaining aspects of the [noble] truths. (24)

Conjoined with the remaining aspects of the truths, concentration is "wishless" (apraṇihita) and possesses ten aspects. Because of the agitation caused by impermanence, suffering, and their causes, and because the path must necessarily be abandoned due to its resemblance to a raft, the concentration that takes those as its aspects is wishless; this is because it is oriented toward transcending them. However, there is no agitation regarding emptiness and selflessness, because they are common to both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
These three concentrations are of two kinds: pure and stainless (*amalā*), and pure (*śuddhaka*) and untainted (*anāsrava*),
because they are both mundane and supramundane.
The mundane [attainments] exist in eleven stages; the supramundane [attainments] exist wherever there is the path.
These, however, are stainless; these three untainted concentrations are called the three gates of liberation:
emptiness as a gate of liberation, the wishless, and the signless as a gate of liberation.
Because it is the gateway to liberation.
Furthermore, three other samādhis are mentioned, known as "emptiness of emptiness" and so forth. //25//
The emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), the wishlessness of wishlessness (*apraṇihitā-praṇihita*), and the signlessness of signlessness (*ānimittānimitta*).
They are so named because they take emptiness and the others as their objects; furthermore, of these...
Two take the state beyond training (aśaikṣa) as their object, both by way of emptiness and impermanence. Two other concentrations take the concentration beyond training as their object:
the "emptiness-of-emptiness" takes the emptiness-concentration beyond training as its object by way of the aspect of emptiness.

The wishless-without-wish (apraṇihitāpraṇihita) also [takes as its object] the wishless of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) by way of the aspect of impermanence; it does not take it as suffering, nor as cause and so forth, because that which is without outflows (anāsrava) does not possess those characteristics, nor does it take it by way of the aspects of the path, because it is to be rejected [by them]. However, the signless-without-sign (ānimittānimitta) [takes as its object] the cessation [of the wishless] through the aspect of peace, by means of non-analytical cessation (asaṃkhyayā). //26//

The signless-signless concentration, however, takes as its object the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) of the signless [concentration] of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), by way of the aspect of "peaceful.
This is because there is no analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) for that which is untainted (*anāsrava*).

They are not [contemplated] through the aspects of cessation (*nirodha*), excellence (*praṇīta*), or renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*), because they are common to both impermanence and cessation, because they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and because they are not a dissociation [from outflows].
Furthermore, these other concentrations are exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*) because they are hostile to the Noble Path; for the untainted (*anāsrava*) states are not like this.
Where do they arise?
Only among humans, that is, among men, and not among the gods.
In whom do they arise?
In the immovable [Arhat],
and not in any other Arhat.
How many stages do they belong to?
Excluding the seven preparatory stages,
they exist in the other eleven stages, having set aside the seven preparatory stages.
In the desire realm, the preparatory stage, the intermediate dhyāna, the [four] dhyānas, and the formless realms.
Furthermore, four cultivations of concentration (*samādhibhāvanā*) are taught:
"There is a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to dwelling in happiness in the present life," and so forth.
In that regard:
The cultivation of concentration is indeed the first pure dhyāna for the sake of happiness. //27//
The cultivation of concentration for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life consists of the first wholesome [dhyāna], whether it be pure (*śuddhaka*) or untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because it begins with that, the others should also be understood [in the same way].

It is not necessarily for the sake of dwelling in happiness in future lives, because such [happiness] is absent for those who have fallen away, those reborn in higher realms, and those who have attained final nirvana.
The supernormal power of the divine eye is desired for vision; the cultivation of meditative absorption is for the sake of knowledge and vision;
and those born of application are for the sake of the differentiation of wisdom.
All qualities born of application, whether belonging to the three realms or being untainted, constitute the cultivation of concentration for the sake of the differentiation of wisdom.
That which is like a diamond, occurring in the final dhyāna, is the cultivation for the destruction of the outflows. (28)
The diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) which occurs in the fourth dhyāna is the cultivation of concentration for the sake of the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*).
Indeed, this teaching of the Dharma by the Blessed One is said to be directed toward himself;
therefore, he spoke [of it] specifically in the context of the fourth [dhyāna].
The exposition of the meditative concentrations (samādhi) has been completed.
Now is the time for the exposition of the qualities (guṇa) that rely upon those concentrations; thus, they are explained.
There are four immeasurables (apramāṇa).
Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
they are called "immeasurable" because immeasurable sentient beings are their objective referents.
For what reason are there exactly four?
Because they are the antidotes to ill-will and so forth.
For those who abound in ill-will, harmfulness, discontent, and sensual desire-ill-will, there are four [immeasurables] respectively for the sake of abandoning them.
What is the distinction between the foul (aśubha) and equanimity (upekṣā) as antidotes to sensual desire (kāmarāga)?
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the foul is the antidote for desire for physical beauty (varṇarāga), while equanimity is the antidote for desire for sexual intercourse (maithunarāga).
However, it is more logical [to view them] in this way:
The meditation on the foul is for the lust of sexual intercourse, and equanimity is for attachment to one's mother, father, children, and kinsmen.
In that regard,
loving-kindness is non-hatred; loving-kindness has non-hatred as its intrinsic nature.
There is also compassion; compassion is likewise thus. Joy is mental gladness. //26//
Sympathetic joy has the nature of mental gladness;
equanimity is non-attachment,
for equanimity has non-attachment as its essence.
How is it the antidote to ill-will?
Because it draws out that [ill-will] through greed;
however, it is more appropriate for this [non-harming] to have the nature of both.

Regarding these [immeasurables] such as loving-kindness and the rest, their mental aspect (*ākāra*) is as follows: one enters into the meditative attainment of loving-kindness by attending to sentient beings with the thoughts, "O, may they be happy! regarding those who are suffering, and "O, may sentient beings be happy! regarding those who are already happy.

Thinking, "Alas, beings are suffering," one enters compassion (*karuṇā*); thinking, "May beings rejoice," one enters sympathetic joy (*muditā*). Thinking simply "beings," one enters equanimity (*upekṣā*) because of impartiality.
Since those [beings] do not actually possess happiness, how is it that the mental resolve for their happiness does not become a distortion?
This is because of the intention that "may they be so," or because of the non-erroneous nature of one's disposition (*āśaya*), or because of the perception of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
Alternatively, what fault is there in such erroneousness?
If it is argued that they are unwholesome, we say no; for they are roots of the wholesome and are the antidotes to malice and so forth.
Their aspects have already been explained.
But beings of desire are its sphere of activity. //30//
Beings belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) are their object,
because these [immeasurables] serve as the antidotes to ill-will (*vyāpāda*) and so forth that take those beings as their objects.
As for what was said regarding "resolving upon one direction," that indicates the contents of the vessel by means of the vessel itself.
To how many stages do these belong?
Joy belongs to two dhyānas; joy belongs to the first and second dhyānas.
Because of the presence of mental joy (*saumanasya*),
the other three immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) exist in six stages, while the other three exist in all six stages.
In the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), and the [four] dhyānas;
some, however, say they are in five;
others, moreover, excluding the preparatory stage, maintain that these exist in five.

Others say there are ten, by including the desire realm and the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), because this encompasses both the concentrated and non-concentrated, as well as the fundamental and the preliminary applications.
Regarding what was stated, "because they are the opposites of ill-will (*vyāpāda*) and so forth," does the grasping of the afflictions (*kleśa*) also occur through the immeasurables?

It is not their abandonment; for [the immeasurables] belong to the level of the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*), consist of attention based on resolute conviction (*adhimuktimanaskāra*), and have sentient beings as their object. However, because ill-will and the like are suppressed through their preliminary practice (*prayoga*), they are said to be their antidotes.
And because of the distancing of what has been abandoned:
for there exist in the desire realm and on the stage of the *anāgamya* preparatory concentration states such as loving-kindness that resemble the fundamental immeasurables;
having suppressed those [defilements] with these, one abandons them through the paths of abandonment.
Then, in the state of one free from passion, because of the attainment of the fundamental immeasurables,
he becomes invincible even when encountering powerful conditions.
Furthermore, how does a beginner apply himself to loving-kindness (*maitrī*)?

Just as he considers himself happy, or hears of others—the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and noble Śrāvakas—being happy, he resolves upon that happiness for all beings, thinking: "O, may all beings be thus happy!"

If he is unable to do so because the afflictions have arisen with a dominant activity, he divides the category of friends into three parts and directs his resolve toward that happiness for the highest degree of friend,
then for the middling, and then for the mild.
If he attains equal loving-kindness toward them, he then proceeds to the category of neutral persons.
Then, having divided the side of the enemy into three parts, one resolves upon happiness for them in a mild degree;
then in a moderate degree, and then in an intense degree.
If, then, the resolution upon happiness for the side of friends does not regress even as it was [applied] to the intense degree, [one proceeds further].
Then, by degrees, through the mental resolve for the happiness of a village and a kingdom, one pervades one direction and finally the entire world with loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
One who perceives only virtues quickly generates loving-kindness;

for it is possible for one who perceives virtues to exist even toward someone whose roots of merit have been severed, and for one who perceives faults to exist toward a Pratyekabuddha, because of the visible manifestation of the fruits of prior merit and demerit.

In this way, one applies oneself to compassion and sympathetic joy, resolving: "May these beings, though submerged in a flood of manifold calamities, be thus liberated from suffering; may they thus rejoice.
But equanimity, however, one begins from the side of neutrality.
And these immeasurables are produced only among humans;
they are generated among human beings.
Not otherwise.
How much more so, then, for one who is endowed with even a single immeasurable—such a person is necessarily endowed with all of them; however, one is certainly endowed with three. (31)
One born in the third or fourth dhyāna is not endowed with sympathetic joy (*muditā*);
however, one who has attained the [first] three immeasurables is always endowed with them.
Regarding the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*): "Possessing form, one sees forms"—this is the first liberation.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally: this is the second [liberation].
Having personally realized the beautiful liberation with the body and having attained it, one dwells therein: this is the third.
Then there are the four formless [attainments].
And the cessation of perception and feeling is the eighth;
among these,
the first two are the foul (aśubhā).
The first two liberations have impurity as their intrinsic nature, because they consist of aspects such as the livid corpse and so forth; therefore,
the method for these two should be understood as being like that of impurity meditation.
And these two exist in two meditations—
the first and second meditations— and not on any other level.
As counteragents to the passion for color-form belonging to the levels of the desire realm and the first dhyāna, respectively;
the third, the pure liberation, is in the last [dhyāna], namely the fourth dhyāna.
And that [contemplation] is non-greed; it has the nature of non-greed and not the nature of the foul,
because its aspect is pure.
These, together with their attendants, have the five aggregates as their intrinsic nature;
however, the formless liberations are the pure formless states in meditative equipoise. //32//

Only those that are wholesome (*kuśala*) and concentrated (*samāhita*) receive the designation "formless liberation" (*ārūpyavimokṣa*); they are neither afflicted (*akliṣṭa*) nor unconcentrated (*asamāhita*), such as [the states] in the existence at death (*maraṇabhava*).
Others maintain that there are also unconcentrated [states] at other times.
Furthermore, the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) also receive the designation "liberation."
The paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) are not [liberations] because they take a lower realm as their object;
for the meaning of "liberation" (*vimokṣa*) is the sense of turning away (*vaimukhya*).

As for cessation, it is an attainment (*samāpatti*); specifically, the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*), which is the eighth liberation, is the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

And that has been previously explained as being due to turning away from perception and feeling, or from all conditioned phenomena; others say it is called "liberation" because it is the liberation from the hindrances to meditative attainment.
They enter that [attainment] immediately after the extremely subtle [state].
For the Peak of Existence has the subtlest perception; having made that even subtler, they enter cessation.
But for those who have attained meditative absorption, emergence from it occurs through a mind that is either pure of its own level or noble of a lower level. //33//

Emergence from that [attainment] occurs either by means of a pure mind belonging to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) or by means of an untainted (*anāsrava*) mind belonging to the stage of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Thus, its mind of attainment is tainted (*sāsrava*), whereas its mind of emergence is both tainted and untainted.
Among these liberations,

the first ones have as their objects visible forms belonging to the desire realm; their objective support is the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) of the desire realm, being either unpleasant or pleasant as the case may be.
But those which are formless have as their objects the subsequent knowledge category, the higher realms, and the suffering and so forth of their own level. //34//

The objects of the formless liberations (*ārūpyavimokṣa*) are the suffering belonging to their own level and higher levels, as well as its cause and its cessation; they also include the entire path that belongs to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), as well as non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*). It should be stated that space (*ākāśa*) is the object of one [liberation].
Why is there no liberation in the third dhyāna?
Because of the absence of attachment to the color-form belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, and because it is agitated by the essence of pleasure.
Why does one produce the beautiful liberation?
In order to gladden the mental continuum that has become sluggish through the meditation on the foul, or for the sake of inquiry— namely,

to ascertain whether the two liberations regarding the foul have been accomplished— it is said: "Furthermore, those two are considered accomplished if, even when one attends to the object as beautiful, no affliction arises."
For practitioners of yoga produce the liberations and so forth for two reasons: to distance themselves from the afflictions and to attain mastery over meditative attainments.
And the noble ones [produce them] for the sake of manifesting qualities such as the absence of strife (araṇā), as they desire.
Furthermore, that [power] is by which acts such as the transformation of objects, miraculous empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and the relinquishing of the life-span (*āyus*) are performed.
Why is it said that the realization occurs only in the third and eighth [liberations], and not in the others?
Because they are predominant and because they abide at the limits of the realms (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*). There are eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are limited, beautiful or ugly; having mastered those forms, one knows them and sees them, and being thus percipient, this is the first base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
It is the same for extensive [forms].
Likewise for one who is internally percipient of the formless;
thus there are these four.
Furthermore, when one who is internally percipient of the formless sees blue, yellow, red, and white, there are eight.
Of these, two are like the first liberation;
just as it is with the first liberation, so it is with the first and second bases of mastery.
Two are like the second;
just as the second liberation is, so are the third and fourth spheres of mastery.
The others, moreover, are like the beautiful liberation.
Just as with the pure liberation (*śubho vimokṣaḥ*), so it is with the other four;
however, this is the distinction: by those [liberations], there is merely turning away (*vaimukhya*);
but by these [mastery-liberations], there is the overcoming of the object through resolving it as one wishes and through the non-arising of afflictions.
There are ten totalities;
there are ten spheres of totality because they pervade everything without interval:
the totalities of earth, water, fire, air, blue, yellow, red, and white.
And in the two totalities of the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness,
non-greed constitutes eight of them.
The first eight have non-attachment as their intrinsic nature;
they exist only in the final dhyāna, that is, the fourth dhyāna. Furthermore, their objective sphere is as follows:
Desires; for these, the object of focus is the visible-form base belonging to the desire realm. Some say it is the tangible-base of wind.
The two pure formless attainments and the last two totalities have the nature of the pure formless realms; their objects are their own four aggregates. (36)
The four aggregates belonging to their own level are the objects of these two.
The spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) are the means of entry into the liberations (vimokṣa); the totalities (kṛtsnāyatana) are the means of entry into the spheres of mastery,
because each subsequent stage is more distinguished than the preceding one.

All these [attainments], beginning with the liberations (*vimokṣa*), belong to the mental continuums of both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*), with the exception of the liberation of cessation (*nirodhavimokṣa*).
As for cessation,
the liberation of cessation has already been explained in its entirety.
However, the remainder is obtained through the application of detachment (*vairāgya*).
The [attainments] other than cessation, such as the liberations (*vimokṣa*) and so forth, are both acquired through detachment and acquired through application (*prāyogika*),
depending on whether they have been previously practiced or not.
That which has the three realms as its basis is designated as "formless"; the remainder is born of humans. //37//

The formless liberations (ārūpyavimokṣa) and the formless totalities (ārūpyakṛtsna) have their bases in all three realms; the remainder have their basis exclusively in human beings, because they are produced through the power of instruction.
How is the production of the specific formless attainments and dhyānas within the realms of form and formlessness [brought about]?
The production of the dhyāna and formless attainments occurs through three causes: the powers of cause, karma, and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Among these:

The production of the formless realm (*ārūpya*) from the two realms occurs through the power of causes and karma. The production of the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) in both the form and formless realms occurs through the power of causes—namely, through recent or habitual practice—and through the power of karma, because the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) belonging to a higher plane has become present. For it is not possible for one who is not free from passion for a lower level to be reborn in a higher one.
But for the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), [the attainment] occurs through those two as well as by way of their intrinsic nature (dharmatā). //38//

In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the production of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) occurs through these two— the powers of cause and karma— and also by way of natural law (*dharmatā*) at the time of cosmic dissolution (*saṃvartanī*).
For at that time, all beings belonging to the lower stages produce that meditative absorption because wholesome factors (*kuśaladharma*) have become manifest in their activity.
Furthermore, for how long will this True Dharma remain,
wherein such categories of phenomena as these are made known?
The True Dharma of the Teacher is twofold, consisting of scripture (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*).

In this regard, the *āgama* consists of the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, and the *adhigama* consists of the factors conducive to enlightenment; thus, the True Dharma (*saddharma*) is twofold. Its upholders are those who teach it and those who practice it. (36)
For those who uphold the scripture are its speakers,
and those who have realized it are its practitioners;
therefore, it should be understood that as long as these individuals remain, so long does the True Dharma endure.
They say that their duration is one thousand years;
this refers to realization (adhigama).
However, others maintain that the duration of scripture (āgama) is for a much longer time.
"This Abhidharma which has been taught here in this treatise—is it only this Abhidharma of the treatise that has been expounded?

This Abhidharma has for the most part been related by me as established according to the system of the Kaśmīra Vaibhāṣikas. Whatever has been poorly grasped herein is my own fault; regarding the principles of the True Dharma, the Sages are the authority. (40)
For the most part, this Abhidharma has been explained by us according to the system established by the Vaibhāṣikas of Kaśmīra. Whatever we have here misapprehended is our own fault;
however, regarding the system of the True Dharma, the Buddhas alone are the authority, as are the sons of the Buddha.

When the Teacher, the eye of the world, had closed his eyes, and when the witnesses for the most part had passed away, this teaching was thrown into confusion by unbridled sophists who had not perceived the truth. (41)

Now that the Self-Existent One has attained supreme peace, and the upholders of the burden of the Self-Existent One’s teaching have likewise passed away, the world is left without a protector; today, unrestrained doctrines that destroy virtue are practiced here at will. (42)
Thus, knowing that the Sage’s teaching has its life-breath at the throat and that it is the time of power for the defilements, those seeking liberation must not be heedless. (43)

Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What four? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. When, monks, a noble disciple understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these four nutriments, he is then called a noble disciple who has understood the Dhamma, who has reached the Dhamma, who has attained the Dhamma, who has crossed over doubt, who has transcended uncertainty, who has gained intrepidity, and who has become independent of others in the Teacher’s dispensation.”
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, titled "Exposition of the Meditative Attainments. Homage to the Buddha!
Is it then that there is no liberation elsewhere than this?
No, there is not. What is the reason?
Because they are settled in a false view of self;
for they do not determine that the designation "self" applies merely to the continuum of the aggregates.
What then?
They falsely imagine the self to be a distinct substance, and all afflictions arise from this grasping at a self.
But how is it understood that this designation "self" applies only to the continuum of the aggregates (*skandha-saṃtāna*) and not to any other referent?
Because there is an absence of both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
For those phenomena (*dharma*) that exist, their perception occurs through direct perception provided there is no obstruction.
For example: [the cognition] of the six objects and of the mind;
and inference, for example, [the cognition] of the five sense-faculties.
In this regard, the following inference is established:
when a cause is present, the absence of another cause is seen to result in the absence of the effect, and its presence results in the presence of the effect, as in the case of a sprout.

Likewise, even when the object has reached the range of perception and attention—the cause—is present, the absence of the apprehension of the object is observed in those who are blind or deaf, while its presence is observed in those who are not blind or deaf.
Therefore, even in that case, the absence and presence of another cause are ascertained;
and since that other cause is the sense faculty, this is an inference.
Since such [a cause] does not exist for the self, there is no self.
As for the fact that the Vātsīputrīyas maintain that the person (*pudgala*) exists,
this must first be examined:
do they maintain it as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*) or as a mere designation (*prajñaptitaḥ*)?
Furthermore, what does "substantially" mean, or what does "conceptually" mean?
If it is a distinct entity like form and so forth, it is substantial;
if it is a collection like milk and so forth, it is conceptual.
And what follows from this?
If, first of all, it exists as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*),
then because it possesses a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it must be declared to be other than the aggregates (*skandha*), just like one aggregate is other than another.
Furthermore, its cause must be stated;
or else, it would be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of falling into the views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), as well as the fault of being purposeless.
Now, if it is from the perspective of designation (*prajñapti*),
we also say this:
for it exists neither substantially (*dravyataḥ*) nor even as a designation.
What then?
The person (pudgala) is designated in dependence upon the internal, appropriated, and present aggregates (skandhas).
We do not understand this blind statement, whose meaning has not been clarified.
What is the meaning of "based upon" (*upādāya*)?
If it means "having taken the aggregates as an object," then it follows that the designation of a person (*pudgala-prajñapti*) applies only to those [aggregates],
just as the designation of "milk" applies only to those [elements] such as form (*rūpa*), having taken them as its object.
Now, if this meaning is "in dependence upon the aggregates," then because the aggregates are the cause for the designation of a person (*pudgala*),
that same fault remains.
It is not designated in that manner.
How, then? Just as fire is designated in dependence upon fuel.
And how is fire designated in dependence upon fuel? It is so designated.
For fire is not designated without fuel, nor can fire be asserted as something other than fuel, nor as non-other.
If it were other, the fuel would be without heat;
if it were non-other, that which is burned would itself be the burner.
Thus, a person (pudgala) is not designated apart from the aggregates (skandhas),
nor can it be asserted as other than the aggregates, because that would entail the consequence of eternalism;
nor is it non-other than them, because that would entail the consequence of annihilationism.
My dear friend, first tell me: what is fuel and what is fire?
Then we shall understand how fire is designated in dependence upon fuel.
What is there to say about this? That which is to be burned is the fuel; that which burns is the fire.
This alone must be addressed here: what is the fuel to be burned, and what is the burner?
In the world, indeed, wood and the like that are not yet ignited are called fuel and the "to-be-burned," while the ignited fire is the burner.
And because that which is luminous, hot, and intense, it is by means of that [fire] that it is ignited and burned,
due to the production of a transformation in the continuum.
Both of these consist of eight substances, and fire arises in dependence upon that fuel.
Just as curd depends upon milk and vinegar depends upon honey,
therefore it is said that [fire] exists by taking fuel as its basis; and yet fire is other than that fuel because they exist at different times.
And if the person (pudgala) were thus produced in dependence upon the aggregates (skandhas), it would follow that he is both different from them and impermanent.
Furthermore, in the case of wood or the like being set ablaze, if that which is the heat is accepted as fire and the three co-nascent primary elements (bhūtas) are accepted as the fuel,
then their distinctness is established even there due to the difference in their characteristics (lakṣaṇa).
However, the meaning of "depending on" must be explained:
how is it that fire is designated depending on that fuel? For fuel is neither the cause of that [fire], nor is it the cause of its designation.
For fire alone is the cause for the designation of that [heat];
if the meaning of "appropriating" (*upādāya*) is the sense of a support, or the sense of coexistence,
then it follows that the aggregates would likewise be the support and coexistent with the person, whereby their distinctness is clearly asserted.
And in the absence of that [fuel], it follows that the person (pudgala) would be non-existent,
just as there is no fire in the absence of fuel.
As for what was said— that if fire were other than fuel, the fuel would be without heat— [that argument is refuted].
What is this so-called "heat"?
If it is heat itself, then fuel is indeed not hot, because its intrinsic nature consists of other elements. Or, if it is that which possesses heat—
Furthermore, other things are established as hot because they possess heat through their connection with fire, which is itself of a hot nature;
thus, there is no fault in their being distinct. Alternatively, if it is maintained that all of that—such as burning wood—is both fuel and fire, [then...]
Furthermore, the meaning based on that [appropriation] must be stated;
and since the aggregates themselves would be the person, their non-difference [from the aggregates] becomes unavoidable.
Therefore, this [position] is not established.
"Just as fire is designated in dependence upon fuel, so too is the person (pudgala) designated in dependence upon the aggregates (skandhas).

If this [person] were not to be described as other than the aggregates, then it would follow that one could not say: "The objects of knowledge are fivefold: past, future, present, unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and the inexpressible (avaktavya).
For that [inexpressible] could certainly not be described as either the fifth among the past and so forth, nor as not the fifth.
And when a person (*pudgala*) is designated, is it designated by not perceiving the aggregates (*skandha*), or rather by perceiving the person?
If it is by means of the aggregates, then the designation of the person would apply to those very aggregates themselves,
because the person is not perceived [as something distinct].
Now, regarding the person (*pudgala*): how is its designation (*prajñapti*) based upon the aggregates (*skandha*)? For it would follow that the person itself is the basis of that designation.
If it is thought that because the person is perceived when the aggregates exist, its designation is therefore said to be based upon the aggregates—
Thus, since form is likewise perceived when the eye, mental attention, and light are present, it must be said that [the designation "person"] is a conceptual construction based upon those [factors].
Furthermore, the distinctness of the person from form is as clear as the case of form itself;
this, first of all, must be stated.
By which of the six consciousnesses is a person to be cognized?
It is said: by all six. How so?

If one discerns a person (pudgala) in dependence upon forms cognizable by the eye, that person should be said to be cognizable by the eye; yet it should not be said whether he is the forms or not. Likewise, up to: if one discerns a person in dependence upon mental objects (dharmas) cognizable by the mind, that person should be said to be cognizable by the mind; yet it should not be said whether he is the mental objects or not.
In that case, it follows that [the substance] is identical to milk and so forth.

If one discerns milk or water based on visible forms (*rūpa*) cognizable by the eye, then it should be said that "milk or water is cognizable by the eye," but it should not be said whether they are "visible forms" or "not visible forms.
Likewise, it should be said that they are "cognizable by the nose, tongue, or body," but it should not be said whether they are "tangible objects" (*spraṣṭavya*) or "not tangible objects."
Lest there be the undesirable consequence of milk and water being [each] fourfold,

it is therefore established that just as milk or water is designated based on the collection of visible forms and so forth, so too is the person (pudgala) designated based on the aggregates (skandhas).
As for what is said— that one discerns a person (pudgala) in dependence upon forms cognizable by the eye—
what is the meaning of this statement?
Does it mean that forms are the cause for the perception of the person, or rather that while perceiving forms, one perceives the person?
If visible forms are the cause for the perception of a person (pudgala), yet that person is not to be described as something other than them,
then likewise, visible form itself should not be described as something other than light, the eye, and attention,
because these are the causes for its perception.
Now, if one apprehends a person while apprehending visible forms, does one apprehend it by that very same apprehension or by another?
If by that very same [apprehension],...
The person (pudgala) would either have a nature non-different from form, or the designation "person" would apply to form itself.
Furthermore, how could it be determined that "this is form" and "this is the person"?
If it cannot be determined in this way, how can it be asserted that both form exists and the person exists?
For its existence would have to be asserted by virtue of its apprehension;
this should be stated in the same way for all phenomena up to the dharmas.
Alternatively, if it were [apprehended] by another [cognition], then because of being apprehended at a different time, it would follow that it is other than form.
Just as yellow is [inexpressible] in relation to blue, and one moment in relation to another moment,
so it should be stated for all phenomena up to that point.
Now, if— as in the case of form and the person— the identity or difference between their respective perceptions is also inexpressible, [then...]
In that case, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) would also be inexpressible; thus, there is a contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhāntabheda*).

Furthermore, if this [person] exists but cannot be said to be either "the forms" or "not the forms," then why did the Blessed One say, "Form is not-self, up to and including consciousness is not-self"?
By which visual consciousness this person (*pudgala*) is perceived: does that [consciousness] arise in dependence upon visible forms, or rather upon the person, or upon both?
If it arises in dependence upon visible forms,
It will not be able to cognize a person (pudgala), just like [the cognition of] sound and so forth.
For whatever object (viṣaya) consciousness arises in dependence upon, that alone is its objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Now, does it arise in dependence upon the person, or upon both?
This contradicts the Sūtra;
for it is determined in the Sūtra that the arising of consciousness occurs in dependence upon a duality:
"In this way, O Bhikṣu, the eye is the cause and visible forms are the condition for the arising of visual consciousness."
For what reason?
O monk, whatever visual consciousness there may be, all of it arises in dependence upon the eye and visible forms.
Consequently, it follows that the person (pudgala) would likewise be impermanent.
Because of the statement in the Sūtra: “Those causes and those conditions for the arising of consciousness are also impermanent.
Now, if the person (pudgala) is not its object, then it cannot be cognized by that [consciousness].
Furthermore, if it is asserted that the person (pudgala) is cognizable by the six consciousnesses,
then, because it is cognizable by auditory consciousness, it follows that it is other than visible form, just like sound;
and because it is cognizable by visual consciousness, it follows that it is other than sound, just like visible form.
The same should be applied to other cases as well.
Furthermore, this scriptural passage would be contradicted:
"O Brahmin, these five faculties have different ranges and different objects; each experiences its own respective range and object."
"One faculty does not experience the range and object of another; for example, the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, and the body-faculty.
It is the mind that experiences the range and object of these five faculties, and the mind is their point of reliance."
Or rather, the person (pudgala) is not an object;
if it is not an object, then it is not cognizable.
[If this were so,] it would follow that the mental faculty (manaindriya) also lacks deviation [from its object].
It is stated in the *Ṣaṭprāṇakopama-sūtra* that "these six faculties have different ranges and different objects; each seeks its own respective range and object.
In that context, it was not said by taking the faculty itself as the faculty, because it is impossible for the five [faculties] to seek seeing and so forth, nor for their respective consciousnesses.
Therefore, it is said here that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) drawn forth by the predominance of that [eye] constitutes the faculty.
And as for that mental consciousness which is drawn forth solely by the predominance of the mind (*manas*), it does not at all desire the objects of the others; thus, this fault does not exist.
And it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, I shall teach you the Dharma-discourse concerning everything that is to be directly known and fully understood," having so spoken.

The eye is to be directly known; forms, eye-consciousness, and eye-contact are to be directly known; and whatever internal feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by that eye-contact, up to and including what is conditioned by mind-contact:
this is called the discourse on the Dharma concerning all that is to be directly known and fully understood.
Therefore, it is determined that only this much is to be directly known (*abhijñeya*) and fully understood (*parijñeya*), and not the person (*pudgala*).
Consequently, even that [person] is not an object of cognition (*vijñeya*), because wisdom (*prajñā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) share the same objective domain.

And those who maintain the existence of a person (*pudgala*), seeing with the eye that "we see a person," have fallen into a basis for wrong view by thinking, "we see a self through what is not-self."
And in the Sūtra, this has been definitively established by the Blessed One:
"The designation 'person' (pudgala) applies only to the aggregates (skandhas). This refers to the *Mānuṣyaka-sūtra*:
"Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact (sparśa); born simultaneously with contact..."
Feeling, perception, and volition—these four formless aggregates, together with the eye faculty and form, are what is called "humanity.
Herein, this is the designation: "sentient being," "person," "human," "mortal," "nourisher," "man," "individual," "living soul," and "creature.
Herein, this is the claim: "I see forms with the eye."

In this regard, even this conventional usage— that "this venerable one has such a name, belongs to such a birth, belongs to such a clan, has such food, experiences such pleasure and pain, has such a long life, remains for such a long time, and has such a limit to his lifespan"—
is, O monks, merely a designation, merely a proposition, and merely a conventional expression.
"All these phenomena are impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated.
The Blessed One has stated that a sutra of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is to be relied upon;
therefore, it is not to be further scrutinized.
And thus it has been said: "O Brahmin, 'everything exists' refers only to the twelve bases (āyatanas).
If this person (pudgala) is not a base, then it is established that he does not exist. If, on the other hand, he is a base, then he cannot be something inexpressible (avaktavya).

And for those who see it thus: "To the extent, O monk, that there is the eye, and to the extent that there are forms—in detail, to that extent, O monk, the Tathāgata designates everything and all designation."

And it is said in the Bimbisāra-sūtra: "O monks, the ignorant, unlearned worldling, following after mere designations, thinks 'self' and 'belonging to self,' yet herein there is neither self nor anything belonging to self; rather, it is this suffering that, when arising, arises," and so forth in detail.
The Arhatī Śailā also addressed Māra, saying: "O Māra, do you imagine that there is a 'being'? For that is merely a view held by you.
This is a heap of conditioned formations; no being is found here at all."
"For just as the designation 'chariot' is used based on a collection of parts, so too, by way of conventional truth, a 'sentient being' is spoken of in dependence upon the aggregates.
Thus it is said; and in the *Kṣudraka Āgama* as well, with reference to the Brahmin Bādarī, it was stated:
Listen, O Bādari, to the Dharma that releases all knots:
how the mind becomes defiled, and how the mind is purified.
For the self itself does not exist for the self; it is imagined through perversion.
Here there is no sentient being or self; there are only these phenomena together with their causes.
Having thoroughly reflected upon all these twelve factors of existence— the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements— a person (pudgala) is not to be found.
"Behold the internal as empty; behold the external as empty.
Even that person who cultivates emptiness is not to be found.
Thus it has been said: "There are five disadvantages in the apprehension of a self."
There arises the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a living soul;
one becomes indistinguishable from the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika);
and one has entered upon a wrong path.
"His mind does not enter into emptiness, does not become serene toward it, does not abide in it, and is not liberated;
his noble qualities (āryadharma) do not become purified"—
they do not, however, take this textual passage as authoritative in that way.
What is the reason? [They say:
"This is not recited in our school (nikāya).
But do they take their own school alone as authority, or rather the word of the Buddha?
If the school alone is the authority, then the Buddha is not their teacher,
nor are they followers of the Son of the Śākyas.
On the other hand, if the word of the Buddha is the authority, [then the school is not the authority].
Why is this treatise not an authoritative source?
For it is said that this is not the word of the Buddha.
What is the reason?
"It is not recited in our school"—
this is an improper position. What is the impropriety here?

For regarding a text that is transmitted in all other schools and does not contradict the Sūtras or the nature of reality (dharmatā), the claim that it is not the word of the Buddha simply because we do not recite it is mere recklessness.
Furthermore, do they even lack this Sūtra: "All phenomena (dharmas) are without self"? It might be thought:
"The person (pudgala) is certainly not called a phenomenon (dharma), nor is it something other than a phenomenon."
If that is the case, then it is not established as being cognizable by the mental consciousness (*manovijñeya*), because of the restriction that "the arising of consciousness depends upon a dyad.
And in this very context, how can it be conceptualized thus: "The inversion of perception, the inversion of mind, and the inversion of view consist in [conceiving] a self in what is not-self"?
The misconception is that there is a self in what is not-self, but not in a self. Furthermore, what is it that is not-self?
It is the aggregates, the sense bases, and the elements. As for what was previously stated—that it should not be said whether [the self] is the forms or not—that has now been refuted.
And it is said in another sutra: "O monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins regard anything as a self, they all regard these very five aggregates of clinging as such."
Therefore, all grasping at a self is indeed directed toward what is not-self.

Thus it has been said: "Whoever, in various ways, have recollected, did recollect, do recollect, or will recollect their former abodes—all of them [recollected] these very five aggregates of clinging.
If this is so, why was it said: "I possessed form in past time"?
Thus, he demonstrates that those who recollect [the self] in these various ways [are mistaken].
For if one were to perceive a person (*pudgala*) as possessing form (*rūpavant*), it would entail the fallacy of the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
However, in this case, the very absence of such a reading would be our refuge.
Therefore, the person (*pudgala*) exists as a mere designation (*prajñaptisat*), like a heap or a stream.
If this is so, then it follows that the Buddha would not be omniscient;
for there is no mind (*citta*) or mental factor (*caitta*) whatsoever that could know everything.
Because of momentariness,
the person (pudgala) would have to be the one who knows.
If that were the case, then since you accept that the person does not perish when the mind perishes, you have effectively accepted its permanence.
Nor do we declare the Buddha to be omniscient because of the simultaneous manifestation of knowledge regarding everything;
rather,
it is by virtue of his capacity.
For that continuum which is called "Buddha" possesses this capacity: that by mere attention, non-erroneous knowledge arises regarding whatever is desired.
And it has been said in this regard:
"Because of its capacity through the continuum, just as fire is considered to be all-consuming."
Likewise, one should be understood as "all-knowing" not because of knowing everything simultaneously, but because of the scriptural statement regarding the past and so forth.
How is this understood?
From the mention of the past and so on.

"Those who were the perfectly awakened ones of the past, those Buddhas who are yet to come, and he who is the perfectly awakened one at present— the destroyer of the sorrow of many"— thus you maintain that it is only the aggregates (*skandha*) belonging to the three times that exist, and not a person (*pudgala*).
If the person (*pudgala*) is nothing other than the aggregates (*skandhas*), why did he say this:
“O monks, I shall teach you the burden, the taking up of the burden, the laying down of the burden, and the bearer of the burden”?
Why would this not have been said?
For it is not logical that the burden itself should be the bearer of the burden.
What is the reason?
Because it is not observed to be so.
Even that which is "inexpressible" is not tenable.
For what reason?
Because it is not observed to be so.
Furthermore, it would follow that the taking up of the burden (*bhārādāna*) itself would not be included within the aggregates (*skandha*).
For this very reason, the Blessed One specified the bearer of the burden (*bhārahāra*), saying:
"That venerable one who has such a name, who lasts for such a long time, and whose lifespan extends to such a limit"—this was said so that he might be understood as being that very person.
Let it not be understood otherwise—that [the self] is either eternal or inexpressible.

It is the aggregates themselves that lead to the affliction of the aggregates, the former ones leading to the affliction of the subsequent ones; thus, having designated them as "the burden" and "the bearer of the burden," they were spoken of in this way, for the meaning of "burden" is "affliction."
The person (pudgala) certainly exists, because it has been said: "To say 'there is no spontaneously born being' is a false view."
And who says this: "There is no spontaneously born being"?
We say that a being exists in the manner as it was analyzed by the Blessed One.
Therefore, for one who denies the continuum of aggregates called a "spontaneously born being" in the next world, this is a false view: "There is no spontaneously born being."
Because the aggregates are of spontaneous birth (*upapāduka*),
if this were a false view that denies the person (*pudgala-apavādikā*), how could it be abandoned?
Indeed, it is not logical for this [view] to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satya-darśana*) or through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

If it is argued that the person (*pudgala*) is not the aggregates because it is not included among the truths, and because of the statement, "A single person, arising in the world, arises," [we reply: No;

for even in the case of a collection, there is a metaphorical application of the singular, as in the cases of "a single sesame seed," "a single grain of rice," or the singular expression used for "a single heap."
Or rather, the person (pudgala) must be said to be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), because it is admitted that it possesses arising.
Yet it does not arise in the same manner as the aggregates (*skandha*), which appear as something previously non-existent.
How then?
Because of the appropriation of another set of aggregates (*skandha*); just as one says "a sacrificer is born" or "a grammarian is born" because of the appropriation of knowledge (*vidyā*),
or "a monk is born" or "a wandering ascetic is born" because of the appropriation of a mark (*liṅga*).
[The opponent argues: "An old man is born, a sick man is born," because there is the acquisition of different states.
[The author replies: No, because this has been refuted. For it was refuted by the Blessed One himself in the *Paramārthaśūnyatā-sūtra*:
"Thus, monks, there is karma and there is its maturation, but an agent is not found."
"He who casts off these aggregates and links with other aggregates, except for the conventional designation of dharmas"—thus it is said.
And in the *Phālguna Sūtra* it is stated: "I say, Phālguna, that there is one who appropriates.
Therefore, there is no appropriator of the aggregates, nor is there any caster-off.
Furthermore, whom could one call a ritualist (yājñika) such that he would provide an illustration concerning a sick person? If [the opponent refers to] a person (pudgala),
then that [person] is unestablished (asiddha).
Now, regarding the mind and mental factors:
their arising at every moment is strictly that of something previously non-existent.
Now, as for the body:
its case is likewise.
Furthermore, by virtue of the distinction between the knowledge of the body and its marks, it follows that there is a difference between the aggregates and the person.
The aged body and the diseased body are indeed other bodies;
for the Sāṃkhya theory of transformation (pariṇāmavāda) has been refuted. Therefore, these are not valid examples.
And if the arising of the aggregates is held to be unprecedented while that of the person is not, then it is clearly demonstrated that the person is both distinct from them and eternal.
By asserting that "the five aggregates are one person," how is their difference not stated?
For instance, although there are four primary elements (*bhūta*) and yet matter (*rūpa*) is one, matter is not something other than the primary elements.
This fault is contingent upon a particular position. In which position?
In the position that there are only the primary elements (*bhūtamātrika*).
Nevertheless, just as form is nothing more than the elements, so too the person (pudgala) is accepted as being nothing more than the aggregates (skandha).
If the person is merely the aggregates, why did the Blessed One not provide a definitive answer to the question of whether the soul is the same as the body or different from it?
[It was because he took into account] the intention of the questioner.
For he questioned with reference to a single substantial entity, the living soul (*jīva-dravya*), which is a person possessing internal activity;
and since that [soul] does not exist in anything whatsoever, how can its difference or non-difference be explained?
It would be like the roughness or softness of a hair on a tortoise.
And this treatise was indeed composed by the predecessors themselves.
For the Elder Nāgasena was approached by King Milinda and addressed thus: "I would like to question the Venerable One; however, śramaṇas are generally very talkative."
"If you would answer exactly what I ask," he said.
Being told, "Ask," he asked:
"Is the soul the same as the body, or is the soul one thing and the body another?"
The Elder said, "This has been left undeclared.
He replied,
"But did not the Venerable One previously cause me to undertake the vow that nothing else was to be declared?"
"What is this? You have said one thing, yet you say, 'This is undeclared.
The Elder replied:
'I too would ask the Great King a question; however, kings are often talkative.'"
"If you would answer exactly what I ask," he said.
Being told, "Ask," he questioned him:
"Regarding that mango tree in your inner apartments, are its fruits sour or are they sweet?"

He said, "There is no mango tree at all in my inner apartments. [The king replied,] "Did I not previously make the Great King give his word that nothing else was to be explained? Why is this something else being said now—that there is not even a mango?"
He said: "How can I explain the sourness or sweetness of the fruits of a tree that does not exist?
In the same way, Great King, since that very *jīva* does not exist, how could I explain its being either different from or non-different from the body?
Why, then, did the Blessed One also not say that it simply does not exist?
This is out of consideration for the questioner's disposition;
for he might, by understanding the non-existence of even that continuum of aggregates which is designated as a "living being," fall into wrong view due to his ignorance of dependent origination.
And he was incapable of understanding that teaching.

This is further ascertained by what the Blessed One said: "Ānanda, if, when asked a question by the wandering mendicant Vatsagotra, I were to answer 'the self exists,' would that not be unsuitable, given that all phenomena are without self?"

“Ānanda, if I were to answer the question asked by the wanderer Vatsagotra with ‘there is no self,’ would not the wanderer Vatsagotra, who was already confused beforehand, fall into even greater confusion, thinking: ‘I had a self, but now it no longer exists’?
Ānanda, by saying ‘there is a self,’ one falls into the view of eternalism.”
"It is not that there is no self, Ānanda, for that would lead to annihilationism," and so forth.
And it is said here:
"Considering both the bite of the fangs of [wrong] views and the loss of [the fruits of] karmic actions..."
The Victors teach the Dharma like a tigress carrying away her cub.
"For one who has accepted the existence of a self would be pierced by the fangs of [wrong] views;
failing to reach conventional reality, he would cause the destruction of the ship of virtue.
Thus it was said, and further:
Because it does not exist, the Blessed One did not state that the living being is identical to or different from the aggregates;
nor did he say that it does not exist, lest even the conventional designation be rendered non-existent.

For in whichever continuum of aggregates there is the existence of the fruits of good and evil, that [continuum] would not be designated as a "living being," because it is taught that no living being exists.
He did not even say that the "living being" (jīva) exists as a mere designation among the aggregates;
for at that time, such people were incapable of realizing emptiness.
For instance, when asked by Vātsya whether the self exists or does not exist, [the Buddha] did not answer;
out of consideration for the questioner's disposition, why would he not have said "it exists" if it were indeed so?
The non-explanation regarding whether the world is eternal and so forth is also due to consideration of the questioner’s intention.
For if "the world" were intended to mean the self, then since that [self] does not exist, a fourfold explanation would be improper.
Alternatively, if "the world" refers to the entirety of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), for that too it would be improper.
If the world were eternal, no one would attain parinirvāṇa;
if it were non-eternal, there would be annihilation for all;
if it were both, some would necessarily attain parinirvāṇa while others would not.
If it were neither way, one would attain neither final nirvāṇa nor non-final nirvāṇa.
Therefore, because final nirvāṇa depends upon the path, it is not categorically declared in any of the four ways, just as in the case of the Nirgrantha’s disciple and the sparrow.
For this very reason, there is no categorical explanation regarding the fourfold set beginning with "Is the world finite?

Indeed, this tetrad has the same meaning. To illustrate, after the wanderer Uktika had asked this tetrad, he asked again: "Does the entire world escape by means of this path, or only a portion of the world?"
The Elder Ānanda said: "Uktika, you are now asking the very same question that you first asked the Blessed One, though by means of this different formulation.
The tetralemma regarding whether the Tathāgata exists after death was not explained because it depended on the intention of the questioner;
for he had asked the question by identifying the liberated self with the Tathāgata.
But the proponent of the *pudgala* (person) must be questioned: "For what reason does the Blessed One declare that a living *pudgala* exists, yet does not declare it after death?
[Otherwise] the fault of eternalism would follow.
If that is so, then why does he declare: 'Maitreya, you shall become in a future time a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha'?"
Furthermore, why does the Blessed One prophesy the rebirth of a deceased disciple who has passed away, saying, "So-and-so has been reborn in such-and-such a place"?
For even in this way, there would be the consequence of eternalism (*śāśvatatva*).

Moreover, if the Blessed One, having previously seen a person, does not see them again because they have attained final nirvana, and thus does not prophesy their state due to a lack of knowledge, then the Teacher’s omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) is undermined. Alternatively, one must admit that such a person does not exist at all.
If it is seen that even though this is not being stated, it is established that "this exists and is eternal," then if even this is not to be said— namely, whether he sees it or not—
then in that case, let this also be made gradually inexpressible: whether the Blessed One is omniscient or not.
The person (pudgala) certainly exists, because it is stated as a locus for views that "in truth, according to its established nature, there is no self for me."
"Existence" (asti) is also described as a ground for views;
therefore, this [scriptural passage] is not a proof.
However, the Abhidharmikas maintain that both of these extremes are subsumed under the views of eternalism and nihilism;
and this is indeed logical, because it is stated in the Vātsya-sūtra: "Ānanda, to say 'the self exists' leads to eternalism; Ānanda, to say 'the self does not exist' leads to nihilism."
If, then, the person (pudgala) does not exist, who is it that transmigrates?
For it is not logical that transmigration itself transmigrates.
And yet, the Blessed One has said: "Of beings hindered by ignorance, who run on and transmigrate."
Now, how does a person transmigrate? By means of abandoning one set of aggregates and taking up another.
This position has already been answered.

Just as a momentary fire is said to "move" by means of its continuity (*saṃtati*), so too the collection of aggregates (*skandhasamudāya*) called a "sentient being," which is fueled by craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇopādāna*), is said to "wander" in saṃsāra.
If this is merely the aggregates, why did the Blessed One say, "At that time, on that occasion, I myself was the teacher named Sunetra"?
Why should he not have said so?
Because the aggregates are distinct [from it],
what then is the person? It is that very same thing.
In that case, [the self] would be eternal.
Therefore, by saying "I am indeed that," he demonstrates the continuity of a single stream,
just as one says, "That same fire has come burning."
If the self were to exist, the Tathāgatas alone would perceive it most clearly;
and for those who perceive it, the grasping at a self would become even firmer.

Furthermore, because of the statement in the Sūtra, "When there is a self, there is what belongs to a self," their grasping at what belongs to a self would also operate excessively toward the aggregates.
This would be their view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
And when there is the view of "mine," there arises attachment to what belongs to the self.
Thus, for those whose bonds are gripped by an increasingly firm attachment to self and "mine," liberation becomes even more remote.

Now, if it is thought that "affection does not indeed operate toward a self," then what kind of logic is this, that affection arises through the conviction of a self in what is not-self, yet does not arise toward the self itself?
Therefore, this is a tumor of views that has arisen within this teaching: namely, the grasping at a person (pudgala) by some, and the grasping at the non-existence of everything by others.
Furthermore, for those non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthakāra*) who consider the self (*ātman*) to be a distinct substance, this fault of the impossibility of liberation remains unshakable.
[If, then, there is no self whatsoever, how is it that there occurs the recollection or recognition of an object experienced long ago within momentary states of consciousness?
It is from a particular state of consciousness (*cittaviśeṣa*) that follows upon the continuity of the perception (*saṃjñā*) of the object of memory.]

From what kind of specific state of mind does it arise, such that memory occurs immediately thereafter? It arises from a specific state of mind that possesses an application [of attention] (*ābhoga*) similar to the object, as well as perceptions (*saṃjñā*) and so forth related to it, and whose power has not been impaired by factors such as a particular physical basis (*āśraya*), grief, or distraction.

For even a specific state of mind of that sort is incapable of producing that memory if it does not belong to that same continuum; likewise, even if it belongs to that continuum, a different kind of state of mind is incapable of producing that memory.

However, the memory occurs in both ways because it is precisely that [consciousness] which possesses the capacity, since no other consciousness is seen to have such capacity. [Objection: How then can one consciousness remember what was seen by another?
For if this were so, the consciousness of Yajñadatta would remember what was seen by the consciousness of Devadatta.
No, because there is no connection.
For there is no connection between those two—since they lack the relationship of cause and effect—as there is between two [moments] belonging to a single continuum.
Nor do we say that one consciousness remembers what was seen by another.
Rather, from the mind of seeing, another mind of recollection arises through the transformation of the continuum, as has been stated; what fault is there in this being so?
And it is precisely from recollection that recognition occurs.
If there is no self, who is it that remembers?
What is the meaning of "remembers"?
It means that one grasps the object by means of memory.
What is that apprehension other than recollection?
[If you say it is recollection,] then it produces recollection; but that which produces it has already been explained: it is a particular state of mind that is the cause of recollection.
[As for the statement that "Caitra remembers":
it is because one observes that memory arising from the continuum designated as Caitra that one says, "Caitra remembers.
If there is no self, to whom does this memory belong?]
For what purpose is this genitive case? It has the sense of ownership;
as in, "Who is the owner of what?"
Just as Caitra [owns] a cow.
In what sense is he her owner?
For it is dependent upon him that she is employed for carrying loads, milking, and so forth.
But where, moreover, is the Smṛti to be applied, such that an owner of this [Smṛti] is sought?
[Regarding an object that ought to be remembered:
For what purpose should it be employed?
[For the purpose of remembering.]
"Oh, how well-spoken are the words of those nurtured in happiness!
Indeed, that very [happiness] must be employed for that purpose.
And how is it to be employed?"
Is it by way of producing [the action] or by way of sending [it forth]?
Since there is no connection between memory and motion, it must be by way of producing.
In that case, the cause alone would become the master, and the fruit alone would become the property.
Because the cause exercises sovereignty over its fruit, and by means of that fruit, the cause is said to "possess" it;
for this [sovereignty] belongs only to that specific cause from which memory arises.
Furthermore, when this continuum of the collection of formations (saṃskāra) designated as "Caitra" is apprehended as a single unit, it is called the "owner" of what is termed "the cow."

Furthermore, he is called "master" by taking into account his causal role in the production of changes in that [animal] when it is in another location; however, there is certainly no single entity named Caitra, nor is there a cow [as a separate substance].
Therefore, even in that case, the state of being a master does not exist apart from the state of being a cause.
In this way, regarding such questions as "Who cognizes? and "Whose is the cognition?", it must be said:
its causes are the sense faculty, the object, and attention, according to their respective application; this is the distinction.
Furthermore, there is one who says: because an action depends upon an agent, for every action indeed depends upon an agent.
Just as in the expression "Devadatta goes," the action of going depends upon the goer, Devadatta;
so too is consciousness an action.
Therefore, there must be one who cognizes.
