He should be asked: "Who is this Devadatta?
If it is the self (*ātman*), then that very thing is what remains to be proven.
Now, as for the person who engages in worldly activity (*vyavahārapuruṣa*), he too is not some single entity; for those very conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) are designated by such names.
In this regard, just as one says "Devadatta goes," so too does one say "he cognizes."

And how does Devadatta go? For conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary; yet, because their continuum (*saṃtāna*) is uninterrupted, they are conceived by the foolish through the grasping of a single sentient being as "Devadatta. When these [phenomena] act as the cause for the arising of their own continuum in another location, it is said that "Devadatta goes."
And that arising in another location is what is called "motion," just as in the case of the designations "it goes" and "going" applied to a series of flames or sounds.
Furthermore, it is those very [moments] which, while serving as the cause for consciousness, are said to be "Devadatta cognizes."
Even the Noble Ones speak of them in that way by means of conventional designations for the sake of worldly discourse.
As for what was stated in the Sūtra—that "consciousness cognizes"—what does consciousness do there?
It does nothing at all.
Just as it is said that an effect conforms to its cause because it acquires its own nature through similarity— even though it performs no action—
so too consciousness is said to "cognize" an object.
Since it acquires its own nature through similarity, even though it does nothing at all—
what, then, is its similarity?
It is the possession of that [object's] form.

For this very reason, it is said that consciousness cognizes the object even though it has arisen from the sense faculty, and not the sense faculty itself. Alternatively, here too, because the continuum of consciousness serves as the cause for the act of cognizing, the statement "consciousness cognizes" is faultless, since the term denoting an agent is used for the cause— just as one says, "the bell rings."
Moreover, just as one says "the lamp goes," so too does one say "consciousness cognizes.
And how does the lamp go?
The term "lamp" is used metaphorically for a continuum of flames.
Just as it is said that a person goes to various places when they arise in those different locations,
so too consciousness is metaphorically designated as a "stream" (*saṃtāna*) of moments of mind;
when it arises with respect to various objects, it is said to "cognize" each respective object.
Or, just as in the case of "form comes to be, arises, and persists," where the agent of becoming is not distinct from the act of becoming itself, so it would be for consciousness as well.

If consciousness arises from consciousness and not from a self, why does it not always arise as exactly the same? And why is there no fixed order of succession, as in the case of a sprout, a stalk, and a leaf?
This is because "alteration of duration" (*sthityanyathātva*) is a characteristic of the conditioned;
for this is the inherent nature of all conditioned things: that there must necessarily be alteration within their continuity.

Otherwise, for those who are absorbed in meditative concentration at will, since the arising of a similar body and mind would be indistinguishable from the first moment, there could be no self-emergence even later on.
For the sequence of mental states is indeed fixed,
because whatever is to arise arises only from that specific [preceding state].
For even things that have an identical form may be capable of producing [a certain result] due to a distinction in their lineage (*gotra*).

For example, if immediately after a woman's mind there arises a mind of revulsion toward her body, or a mind directed toward her husband, son, and so forth— [this occurs despite the similarity of the preceding state].

Furthermore, later on, through the transformation of the continuum (*saṃtati-pariṇāma*), a female mind arises; that [mind] becomes capable of producing a thought of revulsion toward her own body, or of producing thoughts directed toward her husband,
children, and so forth, because it belongs to that lineage (*gotra*).
Otherwise, it would not be capable [of arising].
Furthermore, if through a sequence of conditions various types of mind have arisen from a female mind, then whichever is more frequent, more acute, or more proximate will arise,
because the cultivation of that [particular state] is more powerful.
Except for a specific external condition affecting the body at that time,
why does that very same powerful cultivation not always bear fruit?
Because alteration (anyathātva) is a characteristic of the conditioned, and because that alteration is conducive to the arising of the fruit of another cultivation;
for this is merely a brief indication regarding all types of mind.
However, mastery over the knowledge of the uninterrupted causal sequence belongs only to the Buddhas.
For thus they say:
"The causes for every single aspect even of one eye of a peacock’s feather cannot be known by those who are not omniscient; for that knowledge is the power of the Omniscient One."

This is even more so for the various types of formless minds. However, this objection clearly applies to that particular non-Buddhist who believes that the arising of the mind originates from a self: "Why does [the mind] not always arise in exactly the same way, rather than following a fixed sequence like a sprout, a stalk, and a leaf? If it is argued that this is because [the mind] depends on a specific conjunction with the *manas*, we say no;
for the conjunction with anything else is unestablished.

Furthermore, since the two things that conjoin are limited in extent, and because conjunction is defined as "the attainment [of what was previously] unattained," it follows that the self must be limited in extent.
Consequently, from the movement of the mind, there would follow either the movement of the self or its destruction.
If it is argued that this is a conjunction in a specific location (*pradeśasaṃyoga*), we say no.
Because it is impossible for that [manas] to occupy that very same location.

Or, even if there were such a conjunction, how could there be a specific distinction in the conjunction when the manas is eternal and undifferentiated? [If it is argued: "It depends upon a specific cognition."
That very point is further questioned: "How is there a particularity of cognition?
If it is argued that it arises from the contact between the self and the mind depending on a particularity of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), [then...]
Let it be that [memory and so forth] arise from the mind itself, depending upon specific conditioned factors (*saṃskāra-viśeṣa*).
For no capacity whatsoever is perceived in a self, just as there is none in the "phuḥ svāhā" incantations of a quack doctor when the efficacy of a medicine is being accomplished.
[If it is argued: "Even if a self exists, those two [memory and so forth] are possible [only through it]."
It is a mere matter of words.
If you say that it is the basis,
then what is the basis for what?

For it is not logical that he be supported by them as a painting or a jujube fruit is supported by a wall or a bowl; nor is it logical that he be their support as a wall or a bowl is the support for those things, because of the fault of being subject to resistance (*pratighātitva*). How, then, is he a basis? It is not at all a basis in that manner.
How, then, is it?
If you say that it is like earth being the [substratum] of odors and so forth,
we are thoroughly satisfied!
For this very point is our proof that there is no self.
Just as earth is not something other than its odor and so forth—
who indeed could distinguish an earth that is separate from its odor and the rest?
The designation "the odors and so forth of the earth" is used for the purpose of specification.
For it is only those [faculties] designated as "smell" and so forth that are perceived as such, and not others,
just as a wooden statue is designated as a "body.
Furthermore, even though there is a dependence on specific conditioning factors (*saṃskāra*), why is there no simultaneous arising of all cognitions?
For that which is strongest acts as an obstruction to others;
why does that very same strongest factor not always produce its fruit? Let the principle that applies here be the same for cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

But the self is postulated without purpose. [If it is argued: "The self must necessarily be admitted, because memory and so forth belong to the category of qualities (*guṇapadārtha*), and because a quality must necessarily reside in a substance (*dravya*), and because it is impossible for them to have anything else as their substratum"—[we reply: no, because that [premise] is unproven.

For it is not established that these [factors] have the category of quality (*guṇa*) as their nature; rather, for us, everything that exists is substance (*dravya*), because of the statement: "The fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) are six substances."
Nor is it established that these [qualities] reside in a substance;
for the meaning of "residence" has already been examined.
Therefore, that [assertion] is merely something arbitrary.
If the self does not exist, for what purpose is there the undertaking of action?
It is for the purpose of thinking, "May I be happy; may I not be miserable.
What, then, is this so-called "I" that is the object of this ego-conception (*ahaṃkāra*)?
What is the object of this ego-conception (*ahaṃkāra*)? Its object is the aggregates (*skandha*).
How is this known?
Because of attachment to them.
Furthermore, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with cognitions such as "fair-skinned" and so forth— namely,
"I am fair," "I am dark," "I am fat," "I am thin," and "I am old"— this ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is observed to be coreferential with cognitions such as "fair-skinned.
And these modes are not admitted to belong to the Self (*ātman*).
For this reason as well, it is understood that "this" refers to the aggregates.

[The metaphorical designation of "self" is applied to the body, which is merely a benefactor to the self, just as one says: "This very person is I," or "This very person is my servant. While the metaphorical designation of "self" occurs even toward a benefactor, the *ahaṃkāra* (the sense of "I") does not. [If the body were the objective support for the *ahaṃkāra*, why would it not also take another's body as its objective support?]
Because there is no connection [to anything else].
For this ego-sense arises only with respect to that with which it has a connection— whether that be the body or the mind— and not elsewhere,
due to such habitual practice throughout beginningless saṃsāra.
And what is the relationship?
It is the relationship of cause and effect.
"If there is no self, to whom does this 'I-conceit' (ahaṃkāra) belong?
This leads back once again to the question: 'For what purpose is this genitive case? up to the point where it is said, 'It belongs to that very thing which is its cause.'"
And what is its cause?
It is the faulty mind that has one's own continuum as its object and has been permeated by prior ego-grasping.
If there is no self, who is it that is happy or miserable? Upon what basis has pleasure or pain arisen?
It is just as one says, "the tree is in bloom" or "the forest has borne fruit."
What, then, is the basis for these two?
It is the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
This has been explained according to how it was established.
If there is no self, who is the agent of these actions, and who becomes the experiencer of their fruits?
What is the meaning of the phrases "agent" or "experiencer"?
One who acts is an agent (*kartṛ*).
"One who eats is an eater (*bhoktṛ*);
this is a synonym (*paryāya*) being stated, not a distinct meaning.
Grammarians declare that 'one who is independent is the agent' (*svatantraḥ kartā*) is the definition of an agent."
Furthermore, is independence observed in the world for anyone with respect to some particular action, such as Devadatta’s bathing, eating, or walking? But whom do you mean by this "Devadatta"?
If it is the self, that itself is what is to be proven;
if it is the five aggregates, that itself is the agent.
And this action is threefold: bodily, vocal, and mental action.
In that regard, concerning bodily action first, the activity of the body is dependent upon the mind;
the activity of the mind with respect to the body is likewise dependent upon its own causes, and those [causes] are also thus—there is no independence whatsoever for anything.
For all phenomena proceed as dependent upon conditions.
Furthermore, since it is admitted that even the self, being independent, is not a cause, its autonomy is not established.
Therefore, no agent characterized in such a manner is perceived.
Rather, that which is the primary cause of something is called its "agent."
Furthermore, the self is never observed to be a cause in any instance;
therefore, even in this way, it is not logical for it to be an agent.

For desire is born from memory, discursive thought is born from desire, effort arises from discursive thought, wind arises from effort, and from that comes action; what does the self do in this process?
Furthermore, what is this enjoyment of the fruit that you postulate for this self as its enjoyer when it performs [actions]?
If you say it is "apprehension," the self lacks the capacity for apprehension, because that has been refuted in the case of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
If there is no self, why does the accumulation of demerit and merit not occur without a basis for a sentient being?

Because feeling and so forth lack a substratum; and that substratum is the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), not a self, as has already been explained. [How can the fruit arise in the future from an action that has perished if there is no self?]
Even if a self exists, how can there be the production of a fruit in the future from a karma that has perished?
[The answer is: It arises from merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) which are dependent upon that [self].
This mode of expression—"What depends on what?"—has already been answered.
Therefore, let it arise from dharma and adharma themselves, without depending on anything else.
We do not, however, say that the production of a fruit in the future arises from a perished action.
How then?
From a specific transformation of its continuum, like a seed and its fruit.
Just as it is said that a fruit arises from a seed,
yet it does not arise from a seed that has already perished, nor does it arise immediately [after the seed].
What then?
It is from a specific transformation of its continuum—produced through the sequence of sprout, stalk, leaf, and so forth, ending with the flower—that [the fruit arises].
Furthermore, why is that which is produced from the flower called the "fruit" of that seed?
For that capacity has been deposited in the flower through a continuous succession;
for if it had not been preceded by that [action], it would not have been capable of producing such a fruit.
In this way, it is said that the fruit arises from the action.
Nor does it arise from that karma once it has perished, nor does it arise immediately after it;
how then?
It arises from a specific transformation within the continuum of that [karma].
What, then, is the continuum (*saṃtati*), what is transformation (*pariṇāma*), and what is the specific distinction (*viśeṣa*)?
That which is the successive arising of moments of consciousness preceded by karma is the continuum; the arising of that [continuum] in various different ways is transformation.
Furthermore, that [moment] which is immediately capable of producing a fruit is called a "specific transformation" because it is a particular kind of transformation distinct from others.
For example, the death-consciousness accompanied by grasping [determines] rebirth;
and although various karmas may have preceded it, the capacity produced by that karma which is weighty, proximate, or habitual is manifested, and not that of any other.
As it has been said:
"Whatever karma is weighty, whatever is proximate, whatever is habitual, and whatever was performed previously— in the cycle of existence, each preceding one among these ripens first."
In that regard, the capacity to yield a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*), which was deposited by the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), ceases once it has given its ripened fruit.

However, the capacity to yield a concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), which was deposited by the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), ceases in the case of afflicted states upon the arising of their antidote;

in the case of non-afflicted states, it ceases through the absolute cessation of the mental continuum when one attains final nirvana (*parinirvāti*). Now, why does another ripened fruit not arise from a [prior] ripened fruit—just as a subsequent fruit arises from a seed-fruit?
In any case, everything is not identical by way of a mere analogy;
for even there, another fruit does not arise from the fruit itself.
What then?
[It arises] from a specific transformation produced by a specific degree of decomposition.
For that particular mode of the primary elements (*bhūta*) which brings about the sprout therein is its seed, and nothing else.
However, the preceding continuum is also designated as the "seed" either by way of a future designation or because of its similarity [to the actual seed].

In the same way here as well, if from that maturation (*vipāka*) there arises—due to specific conditions such as hearing the true or false Dharma—a wholesome-with-outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala*) or unwholesome mental transformation, then from that [transformation] another maturation arises, and not otherwise; thus this is the same [as the previous case].
Alternatively, this should be understood in the following way:

Just as from a citron flower dyed with lac juice, a red filament is produced in the fruit arising from a specific transformation of the continuum, yet no further [filament] arises from that one, so too, from a ripening born of karma, no further ripening arises.
This has been shown in its coarse form as it is accessible to our intellect.
However, that various continuities (*saṃtati*), perfumed by actions distinguished by manifold powers, reach such a state and produce such a fruit—this is the domain of the Buddhas alone.
As it has indeed been said:
"Karma, its cultivation, the attainment of its activity from that [cultivation], and the resulting fruit—
no one other than a Buddha knows these in every way with certainty.
This [teaching] is purified by a well-established path of causes.
Having perceived the true nature of the Buddhas' teaching,
those who are no longer blind cast aside the views of the heterodox teachers— who are themselves blind and characterized by various wrong views— and proceed on their way.

For this very selflessness— which leads exclusively to the city of Nirvana, which is radiant with the rays of the sun-like words of the Tathagata, and which has been traversed by thousands of Noble Ones—
One with dull vision does not see it, even when it is wide open.

Thus, this has been taught as merely a mere indication for those of keen intelligence, like the site of a wound for poison spreading by its own power. Thus ends the *Pudgalakośa*, the commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa*.
This is the work of the venerable teacher Vasubandhu.
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has explained their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.

This is the religious gift of the venerable Śrīlāmāvāka, a scholar from the Northern Region and a bearer of the burden of the entire teaching of the Tathāgata according to the most excellent Mahāyāna; whatever merit is herein, [may it be for the welfare of all beings], and so forth.
May there be auspiciousness!
